title: Effect on the Audience: Evaluation Beyond Description
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Why can audience response, like a sudden silence, count as evidence in an evaluation?
cards.answer: Because it is an observable, real collective reaction that confirms whether a specific theatrical choice actually achieved its intended effect.

cards.front: Why did the top-light and slow circling of the ensemble around the kneeling protagonist succeed, according to the worked example?
cards.answer: It communicated the character's willing surrender to forces beyond their control, making them both centre of the world and its prisoner.

cards.front: Name the three fears Juliet voices in her Act 4 Scene 3 soliloquy before drinking the potion.
cards.answer: The mixture might not work at all / It might be a poison meant to kill her / She might wake before Romeo arrives
items: The mixture might not work at all
It might be a poison meant to kill her
She might wake before Romeo arrives

cards.front: Name the five figures the lesson says share blame for the tragedy.
cards.answer: The feuding families / Capulet's tyranny / Friar Lawrence's failed plan / Fate (the plague) / The lovers' haste

cards.front: Why is Juliet's conversation with Paris in Act 4, Scene 1 dramatically ironic?
cards.answer: Paris believes Juliet is speaking as his loving bride, but her equivocating words secretly refer to her devotion to Romeo.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present Juliet drinking the potion as her bravest moment?
cards.answer: She imagines horrific visions of suffocation and Tybalt's corpse yet drinks the potion anyway despite her terror.

cards.front: Name the four landmark laws that transformed women's legal position between 1967 and 1975.
cards.answer: Abortion Act (1967) / Equal Pay Act (1970, in force 1975) / Sex Discrimination Act (1975) / Employment Protection Act (1975)

cards.front: Why did pay gaps persist even after the Equal Pay Act came into force?
cards.answer: Many workplaces were sex-segregated, with men and women doing different jobs on different pay scales, so the Act was hard to enforce.

cards.front: Why did the contraceptive pill matter for women's working lives from 1961?
cards.answer: It gave women reliable control over family planning, enabling more women to stay in or return to work and plan around choices rather than pregnancies.

cards.front: Why was Margaret Thatcher's election as Prime Minister in 1979 seen as debatable for women's progress?
cards.answer: Because it provoked debate over whether one woman reaching the top signified real structural change, given only 19 women MPs existed.

cards.front: Name the three buses on the motherboard that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Data bus / Address bus / Control bus

cards.front: Why is a GPU much faster than a CPU at rendering graphics?
cards.answer: A GPU has thousands of simpler cores working in parallel, letting it do the same pixel calculation on many pieces of data at once.

cards.front: Why does a wider data bus improve system performance?
cards.answer: A wider bus has more parallel wires, so more bits can be transferred between components in one go.

cards.front: What does the control bus carry between the CPU and other components?
cards.answer: Control signals from the CU, such as read or write signals telling RAM whether to accept or send data.

cards.front: Why is T_ON always longer than T_OFF in a standard 555 astable circuit?
cards.answer: The capacitor charges through R1 and R2 in series but discharges through only R2, making charging slower than discharging.

cards.front: How do you find the amplitude of a waveform from an oscilloscope trace?
cards.answer: Count the vertical divisions from the bottom of the waveform to the top of the HIGH level and multiply by V/div.

cards.front: The lesson gives four common exam errors in 555 astable questions. Name them.
cards.answer: Mishandling k and μ multipliers / Multiplying R1 by 2 instead of R2 / Giving amplitude in ms or period in volts / Confusing peak-to-peak and amplitude
items: Multiplying R1 by 2 instead of R2
Giving amplitude in ms or period in volts

cards.front: Why does a 555 astable need a diode to achieve a 1:1 mark-space ratio?
cards.answer: Without a diode R1 always adds extra charging time, so T_ON exceeds T_OFF unless R1 is zero, which would damage the IC.

cards.front: Name the three example activities the lesson gives for the pulse-raising phase.
cards.answer: Jogging around the pitch / Light cycling / Steady swimming

cards.front: Name the three example mobility exercises given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Arm circles / Hip rotations / Ankle rolls

cards.front: How does mobility work reduce the risk of joint injury during a warm up?
cards.answer: Mobility work increases synovial fluid production, which lubricates joint surfaces and reduces friction that could otherwise cause cartilage wear.

cards.front: Why is controlling arousal levels an important psychological benefit of a warm up?
cards.answer: A nervous performer can use techniques like controlled breathing or imagery during the warm up to regulate their activation level to an optimum state.

cards.front: Name the four social functions the lesson says monasteries performed.
cards.answer: Hospitality for travellers / Education for some boys / Medical care for the poor and elderly / Relief for beggars at their gates
items: Medical care for the poor and elderly
Relief for beggars at their gates

cards.front: Name the five types of matters the lesson says Church courts had jurisdiction over.
cards.answer: Conduct of the clergy / Probate of wills / Marriage disputes / Cases of immorality (fornication, heresy) / Debt cases where an oath was sworn
items: Debt cases where an oath was sworn

cards.front: Why could Henry VIII use popular anticlericalism to attack Church jurisdiction without most people expecting a Protestant Reformation?
cards.answer: Anticlericalism was resentment of the institution, not rejection of faith, so critics still attended mass and sought sacraments.

cards.front: Why did the 'mortmain' problem frustrate gentry families?
cards.answer: Land given to the Church was held in perpetuity, so it could never be recovered by the original family through inheritance or purchase.

cards.front: Name the three properties scientists consider when choosing a radioactive isotope for a particular use.
cards.answer: Type of radiation emitted / Half-life / Toxicity

cards.front: Name the six safety precautions workers use when handling radioactive sources.
cards.answer: Minimise exposure time / Maximise distance from source / Use shielding / Wear protective equipment / Monitor exposure with dosimeters / Use tongs

cards.front: How does a smoke alarm use alpha radiation to detect smoke?
cards.answer: Alpha particles ionise air creating a current; smoke particles absorb the alpha radiation, reducing the current and triggering the alarm.

cards.front: Why is a beta emitter with a longer half-life preferred for industrial thickness gauges?
cards.answer: So the source does not need frequent replacement.

title: Conservation of Energy, Stores and Transfers
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Why does doubling an object's speed quadruple its kinetic energy?
cards.answer: Because kinetic energy depends on speed squared (Ek = ½mv²), so doubling speed multiplies energy by four.

cards.front: Why is no work done if you push hard against a wall that doesn't move?
cards.answer: Work done equals force × distance moved (W = Fs), and since the wall moves zero distance, no energy is transferred.

cards.front: Name the five key drivers of change in family structure identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Secularisation / Feminism and changing status of women / Economic factors / Technology / Immigration and cultural change
items: Feminism and changing status of women

cards.front: Name the Rapoports' five types of family diversity (besides organisational and cohort, already covered).
cards.answer: Organisational / Cultural / Social class / Life cycle / Cohort

cards.front: How did the availability of reliable contraception since the 1960s change family structure?
cards.answer: It separated sex from reproduction, making cohabitation more common and contributing to declining birth rates and smaller families.

cards.front: Why has the age of first marriage risen since the 1970s?
cards.answer: High housing costs and lack of affordable independent housing lead young adults to delay family formation and marriage.

cards.front: Name the six characters Sherriff uses to form his cross-section of the officer class in Journey's End.
cards.answer: Stanhope, the heroic wreck / Osborne, the steady mentor / Raleigh, the innocent newcomer / Trotter, the cheerful pragmatist / Hibbert, the man at breaking point / The Colonel, detached authority
items: Hibbert, the man at breaking point

cards.front: Why does Sherriff choose to kill Osborne, the most universally loved character, during the raid?
cards.answer: To show that war does not spare the good, making Osborne's death the play's emotional turning point.

cards.front: Why does Stanhope threaten to shoot Hibbert instead of showing him sympathy, even though Stanhope feels the same fear?
cards.answer: Because the difference between them is not bravery but that Stanhope's sense of duty is stronger than Hibbert's.

cards.front: How does Raleigh's reaction to Osborne's death reveal the limits of his understanding of front-line life?
cards.answer: His refusal to eat at dinner shows genuine moral feeling but reveals he cannot understand the coping mechanisms soldiers need.

cards.front: Name the three conditions used in the Haber process to make ammonia.
cards.answer: Temperature 450°C / Pressure 200 atmospheres / Iron catalyst

cards.front: Why is 200 atmospheres pressure used in the Haber process?
cards.answer: There are fewer gas moles on the product side, so higher pressure shifts equilibrium forward, increasing ammonia yield.

cards.front: Why does the iron catalyst not change the yield of ammonia in the Haber process?
cards.answer: It speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged.

cards.front: Why is 450°C used in the Haber process instead of a lower temperature?
cards.answer: A lower temperature would give more ammonia but make the reaction rate too slow, so 450°C is a compromise.

title: Derivations and the Short Final Section
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: In the grammar-analysis option, which verb tenses and form are the verbs limited to?
cards.answer: present indicative active / imperfect indicative active / perfect indicative active / present active infinitive

cards.front: Why must you know a Latin word's exact core meaning to answer a derivation question well?
cards.answer: A vague guess at the Latin meaning makes it much harder to justify why the English word means what it does.

cards.front: Name the three main types of audience segmentation used by media organisations.
cards.answer: Demographic segmentation / Psychographic segmentation / Geographic segmentation

cards.front: Name the six NRS social grades in order from highest to lowest.
cards.answer: A / B / C1 / C2 / D / E

cards.front: Why do media organisations invest heavily in audience research and categorisation?
cards.answer: Because advertisers want to know audience details like age, income, values and habits, not just total viewer numbers, to justify ad space and production budgets.

cards.front: Why might a low BARB share for a programme on a Friday night not mean the content was poor?
cards.answer: It might indicate poor scheduling rather than poor content.

cards.front: Name the six stages of Silas's character arc, in order.
cards.answer: Trust / Betrayal / Isolation / Gold-hoarding / Loss / Love (Eppie) and community reintegration

cards.front: Why does Dunsey's theft of Silas's gold end up producing positive events in the novel?
cards.answer: Without the theft Silas would never have been forced out of his isolation, so Eppie's arrival could not become transformative.

cards.front: How does Eliot use Dolly Winthrop's faith to contrast with Lantern Yard's religion?
cards.answer: Dolly cannot explain doctrine but trusts things will work out if people do their best, making her faith flexible and kind unlike Lantern Yard's rigid, manipulable religion.

cards.front: Name the three main skills tested in the Germany 1919–1939 exam.
cards.answer: Knowledge and understanding (recall and understanding) / Historical analysis (explanation and analysis) / Source and interpretations work (source/interpretation analysis)

cards.front: Name the four things interpretations of Germany 1919–1939 often differ on.
cards.answer: Hitler's personal role / How ordinary Germans related to the regime / Whether economic recovery was genuine or illusory / The degree of terror versus consent
items: How ordinary Germans related to the regime
Whether economic recovery was genuine or illusory
The degree of terror versus consent

cards.front: Why can a source still be very useful even if it is biased?
cards.answer: Because the bias itself can tell us something important about the attitudes or aims of the time.

cards.front: Why do most students lose marks in the exam despite having enough knowledge?
cards.answer: They apply the wrong skill to the wrong question type instead of matching their answer to what's asked.

cards.front: Name the four key techniques Shelley uses in 'England in 1819'.
cards.answer: Subversive use of sonnet form / Accumulation of grievances / Violent imagery / Dramatic volta

cards.front: Name the three key techniques khan uses in 'pot'.
cards.answer: Everyday object as vehicle for ideas / Anaphora and short single-line stanzas / Free verse with no fixed stanza pattern
items: Everyday object as vehicle for ideas
Free verse with no fixed stanza pattern

cards.front: How does pathetic fallacy work in Eliot's 'In a London Drawingroom'?
cards.answer: The grey sky mirrors the emotional and spiritual greyness of Victorian conformity.

cards.front: Why does khan repeat 'or / did they say' when listing how the pot arrived in Britain?
cards.answer: The repetition makes each explanation for the pot's arrival sound like an excuse, exposing the dishonesty behind its looting.

title: Engineering Developments — Bicycles, Theme-Park Rides & Smart Phones
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Besides frame material, name the three other structural improvements to bicycles given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pneumatic tyres (comfort and grip) / Geared drivetrain (choose ratio for hills/flat) / Hydraulic disc brakes on mountain bikes
items: Hydraulic disc brakes on mountain bikes

cards.front: Name the three key developments the lesson gives for how mechanical design in theme-park rides improved.
cards.answer: Three-sided wheel-and-rail system preventing derailment / Shift from wooden to steel structural frames / Electronic launch and braking systems replacing mechanical control
items: Shift from wooden to steel structural frames
Electronic launch and braking systems replacing mechanical control

cards.front: Why did structural steel replace wood as the frame material for roller coasters?
cards.answer: Steel allowed taller, more complex track layouts that could withstand repeated loading cycles without fatigue failure.

cards.front: How did digital signal processing improve on analogue radio in mobile phones?
cards.answer: It replaced analogue radio and allowed more calls to share the same radio spectrum.

title: Practitioner Application: Brecht in Russell's Stage Directions
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the five staging conventions of Brecht's epic theatre described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Narrator commenting from outside the action / songs that interrupt to reflect on action / placards announcing events beforehand / visible stage lighting rig / performers stepping outside roles to address audience
items: Narrator commenting from outside the action
songs that interrupt to reflect on action
performers stepping outside roles to address audience

cards.front: Why does the Narrator's spatial position in a thrust or in-the-round staging reinforce his Greek-chorus function?
cards.answer: It lets him move between audience and acting area so the audience never knows whose side he is on, keeping him both storyteller and judge.

cards.front: Why is 'Tell Me It's Not True' described as an act of denial that becomes a lament?
cards.answer: Sung over her sons' bodies, it is so clearly futile that the audience cannot receive it as a prayer, only as grief.

cards.front: How might a lighting designer use a colour wash to signal a song's Brechtian interruption in Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: A whole-stage colour wash removes local realism and places every performer in the same theatrical light, showing the scene has paused for comment.

cards.front: What three symptom groups does the ICD use to classify schizophrenia's clinical characteristics?
cards.answer: Positive symptoms / Negative symptoms / Disorganised speech and behaviour

cards.front: How does an overactive dopamine system lead to positive symptoms in schizophrenia?
cards.answer: Neurons fire more or receptors become oversensitive, so excess dopamine overstimulates brain pathways for perception and thought.

cards.front: Why did Daniel, Weinberger, Jones et al (1991) give participants amphetamine during the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test?
cards.answer: To increase dopamine release and test whether raising dopamine improved prefrontal blood flow and task performance.

cards.front: Why is it hard to know if social class causes schizophrenia or schizophrenia causes low social class?
cards.answer: Most evidence linking schizophrenia and social class is correlational, so it cannot show which came first.

title: The Atlantic Slave Trade and Plantation Slavery
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three goods did British ships carry back from the Americas on the final leg of the Atlantic trade triangle, according to the lesson's Key Fact?
cards.answer: Sugar / Rum / Tobacco / Rice

cards.front: The lesson gives four differences between indentured servitude and chattel slavery. What made indentured servitude different from chattel slavery?
cards.answer: Time-limited, not lifelong / Voluntary, not forced for life / Ended in freedom / Not inherited by children

cards.front: Why did Chesapeake planters shift from indentured servants to enslaved Africans by the early eighteenth century?
cards.answer: Rising British wages after 1660 cut the supply of indentured servants, and after Bacon's Rebellion elites feared arming poor whites, so they turned to permanent, inheritable enslaved labour.

cards.front: How did the task system on Carolina rice plantations differ in practice from the gang system, despite both being slavery?
cards.answer: Task system workers had a fixed daily quota and could use remaining time for themselves, but this reflected rice farming's rhythm, not any lessening of bondage.

title: London at war 1939: target, port and government capital
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three types of gas mask were issued, matched to age group?
cards.answer: Black rubber mask with metal filter for adults / Brightly coloured 'Mickey Mouse' mask for small children / Helmet-and-pump gas helmet for babies
items: Black rubber mask with metal filter for adults
Brightly coloured 'Mickey Mouse' mask for small children

cards.front: What were the three waves of evacuation from London mentioned in the lesson?
cards.answer: First wave from September 1939 / Second wave after Black Saturday, September 1940 / Third wave in 1944 with the V1 attacks
items: Second wave after Black Saturday, September 1940
Third wave in 1944 with the V1 attacks

cards.front: Why did the Home Office initially ban Londoners from sheltering in Tube stations?
cards.answer: It feared a 'deep shelter mentality' — that civilians who went underground would refuse to come up and work would stop.

cards.front: Why did Anderson shelters work less well in the East End during Black Saturday?
cards.answer: Flat-roofed terraced backyards there were less practical for burying a shelter than the suburban semi-detached gardens the shelters were designed for.

cards.front: Name the four main ways Christians interpret the Bible.
cards.answer: Literal / Conservative / Symbolic / Biblical myth

cards.front: In the parable of the sheep and goats, what four actions decide the final judgement?
cards.answer: Fed the hungry / Welcomed strangers / Clothed the poor / Visited prisoners

cards.front: Why do Quakers and the Salvation Army not use sacraments?
cards.answer: They believe God's grace needs no outward sign.

cards.front: How is Confirmation understood in relation to baptism?
cards.answer: It is a personal completion of baptism, where the candidate affirms their faith and receives a strengthening of the Holy Spirit.

cards.front: Name the three types of field the lesson gives that allow objects to interact at a distance without contact.
cards.answer: Gravitational fields / Magnetic fields / Electrostatic fields

cards.front: Name the two everyday examples the lesson gives of static electricity effects.
cards.answer: Sparks from a door handle after walking on carpet / Lightning from charge building in clouds
items: Sparks from a door handle after walking on carpet
Lightning from charge building in clouds

cards.front: Why is it always electrons that transfer between objects, and never protons?
cards.answer: Protons are locked inside the nucleus by the strong nuclear force, but outer electrons are held weakly and can be dislodged by friction.

cards.front: How does rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth make the rod negatively charged?
cards.answer: Friction transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod, so the rod gains electrons and becomes negatively charged.

title: Akhand Path, Langar and Nam Japna
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: The lesson names three pillars of Sikh teaching. What are they?
cards.answer: Honest work (kirat karni) / Sharing with others (vand chakna) / Meditating on God's name (nam japna)

cards.front: The lesson gives four dietary restrictions from different faiths that explain why langar is vegetarian. What are they?
cards.answer: Muslims require halal meat / Jews require kosher food / Hindus may not eat beef / Many Buddhists are vegetarian

cards.front: Why does the akhand path reading never have any gaps, even during the night?
cards.answer: Because when one reader finishes their section, the next begins immediately, keeping the reading continuous and unbroken.

cards.front: Why is the akhand path timed to end just before a wedding ceremony begins?
cards.answer: So the final words are read right before the key event, placing it under the eternal Guru's guidance at that moment.

title: Library Modules: random, math, time and turtle
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four library modules the PLS says you must know.
cards.answer: random / math / time / turtle

cards.front: What are the four common mistakes listed for using these library modules?
cards.answer: Forgetting to import the module / Using the wrong range in random.randint / Using a turtle subprogram not in the PLS / Leaving out turtle.done()
items: Using the wrong range in random.randint
Using a turtle subprogram not in the PLS

cards.front: Why does math.floor(-3.5) return -4 instead of -3?
cards.answer: Because math.floor always rounds down towards negative infinity, not towards zero.

cards.front: Why does the filled square program only need one begin_fill() and one end_fill(), even though its loop repeats four times?
cards.answer: Because the fill colour applies to everything drawn between begin_fill() and end_fill(), covering all four sides the loop draws.

title: Anschluss and the Reasons for Appeasement
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six pressures behind Chamberlain's decision to appease Hitler in 1938.
cards.answer: Military weakness / Imperial overstretch / Public pacifism / Lack of strong allies / Dominion opinion against war / Belief Hitler's grievances could be negotiated
items: Belief Hitler's grievances could be negotiated

cards.front: Name the three stages of Anschluss given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Berchtesgaden meeting, 12 February 1938 / Cancelled Austrian plebiscite, 9 March / Wehrmacht entry into Austria, 12 March

cards.front: Why was Britain's military weakness in 1938 a reason for appeasing Hitler?
cards.answer: Rearmament had only begun in 1936-37, so key systems like radar and fighter aircraft were not yet ready, risking defeat in war.

cards.front: Why did the Dominions' attitude push Britain towards appeasement in 1938?
cards.answer: Canada, Australia and South Africa told London they would not fight a European war that looked unjustified to them.

cards.front: Name the four main causes of uneven development given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Colonialism / Trade patterns / Natural resources / Aid

cards.front: Name the five main types of aid described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Bilateral aid / Multilateral aid / Emergency aid / Long-term development aid / NGO aid

cards.front: Why did colonial-era infrastructure fail to help colonies develop after independence?
cards.answer: Roads, railways and ports were built mainly to move raw materials to coastal export points, not to connect colonies internally.

cards.front: Why can tariffs on processed imports like roasted coffee harm LIDCs?
cards.answer: Wealthy countries put tariffs on processed goods but not raw materials, discouraging LIDCs from adding value at home.

title: Revelation, Visions and Miracles as Proof of God
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three ways Catholics believe God has progressively revealed himself throughout history.
cards.answer: Through the natural world / Through the prophets and scriptures of the Old Testament / Most completely through Jesus Christ
items: Through the prophets and scriptures of the Old Testament

cards.front: Why do Humanists say the content of visions cannot prove God exists?
cards.answer: Because a vision is a subjective, unverifiable experience whose content just reflects the visionary's own cultural expectations.

cards.front: How do Catholics respond to Hume's argument that we should always doubt miracle reports?
cards.answer: They say Hume's argument assumes the outcome before examining evidence, and verified Lourdes cases have withstood medical scrutiny.

cards.front: List the three types of radiation from most to least ionising.
cards.answer: Alpha particles / Beta particles / Gamma rays

cards.front: What three observations did Rutherford make in the gold foil experiment?
cards.answer: Most alpha particles passed straight through / Some particles were deflected / A few bounced straight back
items: Most alpha particles passed straight through

cards.front: Why does higher ionising power mean lower penetrating power for radiation?
cards.answer: Radiation with higher ionising power transfers its energy quickly, so it cannot travel far before losing all its energy.

cards.front: Why must you subtract the background count rate when measuring a radioactive source's activity?
cards.answer: This gives a corrected count rate that represents radiation from the source alone, not the environment around it.

cards.front: Name the three main left-wing critics of the New Deal mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Huey Long / Father Charles Coughlin / Francis Townsend

cards.front: Which two major New Deal programmes did the Supreme Court strike down in 1935-1936?
cards.answer: NRA (Schechter Poultry case) / AAA (United States v Butler)

cards.front: Why did the Social Security Act fail to help most Black Americans?
cards.answer: It excluded domestic servants and agricultural labourers, the two occupations employing most Black Americans, especially in the South.

cards.front: Why did Roosevelt propose the court-packing plan in 1937?
cards.answer: The Supreme Court had struck down major New Deal programmes, so he proposed adding a new justice for each sitting justice over 70 to protect his reforms.

cards.front: Name the five types of stress covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Tension / Compression / Torsion / Shear / Bending

cards.front: Why do hollow tubes resist bending and torsion better than solid rods of the same cross-sectional area?
cards.answer: Material near the centre contributes little to resisting these forces, so placing it at the outer surface where stress is highest is more efficient.

cards.front: Why are ribs added inside an injection-moulded plastic casing instead of just making the walls thicker?
cards.answer: Ribs resist bending without increasing outer wall thickness, which would cause sink marks and extend cooling time.

cards.front: Why do gussets at frame joints in timber structures prevent racking?
cards.answer: Triangular corner reinforcements resist the shear forces that would otherwise push a rectangular frame into a parallelogram.

cards.front: Name the three advantages of computer networks given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Files shared without physical media / Single internet connection shared across devices / Centralised storage makes backups easier / Users can communicate in real time
items: Single internet connection shared across devices
Users can communicate in real time

cards.front: Name the three disadvantages of computer networks given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cost of hardware setup and maintenance / Risk of spreading malware / Need for security measures
items: Cost of hardware setup and maintenance

cards.front: Why do LANs typically offer higher speeds and lower latency than WANs?
cards.answer: Because devices on a LAN are physically close together with dedicated infrastructure, unlike WANs which depend on third-party links.

cards.front: Why is fibre optic cable used for backbone connections between buildings?
cards.answer: It carries data as pulses of light, achieving very high speeds over long distances with minimal signal degradation.

title: Physical Indicators of Health & Interpreting Data
subject: health-social-care-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five physical indicators of health that students must know.
cards.answer: Blood pressure / Peak flow / Body mass index (BMI) / Waist-to-hip ratio / Pulse rate (resting and recovery)

cards.front: Name the four contributing factors considered when interpreting physical health indicators.
cards.answer: Age / Sex / Lifestyle / Environment

cards.front: Why is a peak flow reading 50% or below an asthma patient's usual reading significant?
cards.answer: It signals a severe asthma attack requiring immediate treatment.

cards.front: Why does regular blood pressure monitoring matter even if someone feels fine?
cards.answer: Many people have hypertension without experiencing any symptoms, so regular checks are needed to detect it.

cards.front: What four forms of racism does the play show?
cards.answer: Formal colour bar (employment discrimination) / Informal exclusion (housing, social spaces) / Casual everyday hostility (verbal abuse, suspicion) / Internalised effects (self-doubt, fear, proving worth)

cards.front: According to the lesson, in what four ways does Odimba present unity across difference?
cards.answer: Without erasing difference / As earned rather than given / As historically grounded / As fragile

cards.front: How do characters resist casual, everyday hostility in the play?
cards.answer: Through dignity and pride — refusing to be diminished, using cultural expression, self-naming (Princess), and asserting their presence.

cards.front: How does Princess resist the internalised effects of racism?
cards.answer: Through imagination — her imaginative world resists the psychological damage of being told she is less than, making dreaming itself an act of defiance.

cards.front: Name the four events that make up the Paschal Mystery.
cards.answer: Suffering of Jesus / Death of Jesus / Resurrection of Jesus / Ascension of Jesus

cards.front: Name the five 'last things' covered by Catholic eschatology.
cards.answer: Resurrection / Judgement / Heaven / Hell / Purgatory

cards.front: Why does Luke 24 show that Jesus' resurrection was a bodily event, not just a spiritual symbol?
cards.answer: Because it describes the risen Jesus walking, talking and eating with his disciples, not merely appearing as a spirit.

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching hold that hell is a real possibility?
cards.answer: Because God respects human freedom, even allowing individuals who freely and completely reject him to remain separated from him.

title: Metamorphic Rocks: Heat, Pressure and Texture
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the two types of metamorphism described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Contact metamorphism / Regional metamorphism

cards.front: Name the four metamorphic rocks covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Slate / Schist / Marble / Metaquartzite

cards.front: Why is contact metamorphism driven mainly by heat rather than pressure?
cards.answer: Because within the metamorphic aureole pressure is not significantly elevated, so heat from the intrusion is the main agent of change.

cards.front: How can you tell metaquartzite apart from sandstone by how each rock breaks?
cards.answer: In metaquartzite fresh breaks pass through the quartz grains because recrystallisation destroyed grain boundaries, whereas in sandstone breaks go around grains.

cards.front: Name Kohlberg's three levels of moral development, in order.
cards.answer: Pre-conventional / Conventional / Post-conventional

cards.front: Why does a pre-operational child say a tall thin glass has 'more water' than a short wide one with the same amount?
cards.answer: They lack conservation, so they judge quantity by appearance rather than understanding it stays the same despite the shape change.

cards.front: How did Kohlberg study people's level of moral development?
cards.answer: He presented moral dilemmas, like the Heinz dilemma, and studied the reasons people gave for their answers, not just the answers.

cards.front: Name the six typical pop ballad features the lesson lists to listen for.
cards.answer: Slow tempo / Expressive vocal with vibrato and melisma / Piano or guitar-led opening that builds in texture / Slow harmonic rhythm / Verse-chorus form with a contrasting middle eight / Key change before the final chorus
items: Expressive vocal with vibrato and melisma
Piano or guitar-led opening that builds in texture
Verse-chorus form with a contrasting middle eight
Key change before the final chorus

cards.front: Which three artists' versions of 'Make You Feel My Love' does the lesson compare?
cards.answer: Bob Dylan / Billy Joel / Adele

cards.front: Why do pop ballads typically use a slow harmonic rhythm?
cards.answer: Chords change infrequently, creating a stable harmonic backdrop so the melody and vocal ornamentation can be heard clearly.

cards.front: What is the purpose of the middle eight in a pop ballad's structure?
cards.answer: It breaks the repeating verse-chorus pattern, offering contrast through new harmony, a rise in register, or a changed accompaniment texture.

cards.front: Why must you avoid bridging the central gap on a breadboard when placing an IC?
cards.answer: Bridging the central gap can short-circuit the IC's power pins, since the gap separates the two independent halves of connected rows.

cards.front: How does the middle section of a breadboard connect components electrically?
cards.answer: Holes are joined in short horizontal rows of five, so pushing two leads into the same row of five connects them electrically.

title: Break-Even and the Importance of Cash
subject: cambridge-nationals-enterprise-and-marketing

cards.front: Name the four causes the lesson gives for a start-up running out of cash.
cards.answer: Customers paying late / Paying suppliers upfront / High stock levels / Seasonal demand

cards.front: Name the three assumptions the break-even formula makes.
cards.answer: Selling price stays constant for every unit / Variable cost per unit does not change / Every unit produced is sold
items: Selling price stays constant for every unit
Variable cost per unit does not change

cards.front: Why does a rise in variable cost per unit increase the break-even quantity?
cards.answer: Each unit contributes less towards covering fixed costs, so more units must be sold to break even.

cards.front: Why does the total revenue line on a break-even graph start at zero?
cards.answer: Because if no units have been sold yet, there is no revenue at all.

title: Chapters 7–10: The Last Night and Jekyll’s Statement
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why does the window scene in Chapter 7 mirror the door scene from the novel's opening?
cards.answer: Both show Utterson and Enfield witnessing something disturbing at Jekyll's house then silently agreeing not to discuss it, reinforcing Victorian repression.

cards.front: Why did the axe breaking down the laboratory door matter symbolically in Chapter 8?
cards.answer: It symbolises the violent exposure of Jekyll's secret, smashing apart the barriers between his public and private selves.

cards.front: Why did Jekyll originally design his experiment, according to his Chapter 10 confession?
cards.answer: To separate his respectable public self from his hidden, pleasure-seeking private self.

cards.front: How did Jekyll's control over his transformations change over time in Chapter 10?
cards.answer: Hyde grew stronger and more violent while Jekyll grew weaker, until transformations began happening involuntarily without the potion.

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for choosing the right scale of production.
cards.answer: How many products are needed / How much can be spent on tooling / How much customisation the customer wants
items: How much can be spent on tooling
How much customisation the customer wants

cards.front: Name the three mass-production processes the lesson gives for shaping metals.
cards.answer: Casting and forging / Pressing and stamping / Robotic welding

cards.front: Why is unit cost high in one-off production?
cards.answer: It uses general-purpose tools and hand skills, so labour and set-up time aren't shared across other products.

cards.front: How does quality control usually work on a mass-production line?
cards.answer: It is often automated, with sensors checking dimensions and finish as products move along the line.

cards.front: Name the three daytime symptoms that must occur alongside poor sleep for insomnia to be diagnosed.
cards.answer: Tiredness / Irritability / Poor concentration or low mood

cards.front: How does low orexin lead to the symptoms of narcolepsy?
cards.answer: Low orexin makes the brain's sleep-wake switch unstable, letting REM features like cataplexy and hallucinations intrude into wakefulness.

cards.front: Why does insomnia often become a vicious cycle?
cards.answer: Worrying about not sleeping raises anxiety and arousal at bedtime, making sleep even less likely and causing the next poor night.

cards.front: What is the key difference between insomnia and narcolepsy?
cards.answer: Insomnia is a lack of sleep from the brain staying too alert, while narcolepsy is uncontrolled sleep from an unstable wake-sleep switch.

title: Newspapers: The Sun — Industry and Audience
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four roles involved in the pre-press stage of producing The Sun.
cards.answer: Journalists (newsgathering) / Editor (sets agenda, signs off content) / Sales team (sells advertising space) / Page designer (lays out stories/adverts)

cards.front: Name the four sources of revenue the lesson gives for how The Sun is funded.
cards.answer: Advertising / Advertorials / Digital subscriptions / Diversification into gambling brands

cards.front: Why is The Sun written using bold text, strong visuals and short chunks of copy?
cards.answer: To make it accessible and quick to skim for readers with weaker literacy or those reading on a commute.

cards.front: Why do rival publishers dispute whose online newspaper audience is really the biggest?
cards.answer: Because reach figures alone don't show engagement, so rivals like MailOnline instead compare total reading minutes to claim a bigger audience.

cards.front: The lesson gives five arguments against capital punishment now held by the Catholic Church — name them.
cards.answer: Dignity of person can't be forfeited / Execution is irreversible, risks killing innocents / Modern incarceration protects society safely / Execution prevents repentance and reform / Deterrent effect not statistically supported
items: Dignity of person can't be forfeited
Execution is irreversible, risks killing innocents

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church say forgiving an offender doesn't remove the need for punishment?
cards.answer: Forgiveness works on the personal, spiritual level, healing the victim, while justice works on the social, legal level for the common good.

cards.front: Why did the Church's teaching on capital punishment shift from acceptable to inadmissible by 2018?
cards.answer: Modern understanding of human dignity (imago Dei) made execution incompatible with the Gospel, since dignity cannot be forfeited.

cards.front: Name three group members whose reactions show cracks appearing when Phil orders Adam's killing.
cards.answer: Richard questions the plan / Lou is uneasy / Brian seems to recognise this is different
items: Brian seems to recognise this is different

cards.front: How does Cathy's willingness to kill Adam differ from reluctant obedience to Phil's order?
cards.answer: Cathy shows enthusiasm and pleasure in violence, volunteering for the worst tasks rather than being forced into it.

cards.front: Why does Kelly show the group treating Adam as a problem rather than a person in Act 3?
cards.answer: It shows their dehumanisation of him — they ask only what to do with him, never how he feels.

cards.front: Name the four unresolved tensions the lesson gives about the play's ending.
cards.answer: Don John captured but not punished / Hero returned to the same system / Claudio shows no real transformation / The honour code remains intact
items: Don John captured but not punished
Hero returned to the same system

cards.front: Why do many critics find Claudio's penance inadequate?
cards.answer: He never apologises to Hero directly, doesn't seek the truth himself, and agrees to marry a stranger sight unseen.

cards.front: How does Beatrice explain her reason for accepting Benedick's marriage proposal?
cards.answer: She claims she accepts him partly to save his life, since she was told he was in a consumption.

cards.front: Name the four types of reason the lesson gives for why performers use PEDs.
cards.answer: Desire for competitive advantage / Financial reward and career pressure / Cultural and peer pressure / win-at-all-costs culture / To recover from injury and train harder
items: Cultural and peer pressure / win-at-all-costs culture
To recover from injury and train harder

cards.front: Name the three counter-points the lesson gives against the 'level playing field' argument for PED use.
cards.answer: Not all athletes dope, so refusers are disadvantaged / Wealthier athletes/nations can dope more effectively / Normalising doping raises health risks for everyone
items: Not all athletes dope, so refusers are disadvantaged
Wealthier athletes/nations can dope more effectively
Normalising doping raises health risks for everyone

cards.front: Why can an athlete be banned even if they didn't know they'd taken a prohibited substance?
cards.answer: Athletes have strict liability, so a positive test result leads to a ban regardless of the performer's knowledge or intent.

cards.front: Why can anabolic steroid use permanently reduce adult height in adolescent users?
cards.answer: It causes premature closure of growth plates in adolescents, stopping bones from growing further before full height is reached.

cards.front: Name the five main climatic regions described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Tropical (equatorial) / Hot desert / Temperate / Polar / Mediterranean

cards.front: Name the four conditions tropical storms need to develop.
cards.answer: Sea temperature at least 27°C / around 70m of warm water / low wind shear / location 5-30° from the equator

cards.front: How does the Ferrel cell create the UK's typical weather?
cards.answer: It carries air polewards near the surface, forming prevailing south-westerly winds that bring wet, mild weather.

cards.front: How does condensation make a tropical storm stronger as it forms?
cards.answer: Warm moist air rises rapidly and its water vapour condenses, releasing energy that drives the storm harder.

cards.front: How does motivation affect what we notice in a scene?
cards.answer: A strong need or desire makes us more likely to perceive things related to that need, prioritising need-relevant stimuli.

cards.front: How does emotion create a perceptual set?
cards.answer: Emotion directs attention toward mood-congruent information, so an anxious person may perceive ambiguous stimuli as threatening.

cards.front: What was the method used in Gilchrist and Nesberg's study?
cards.answer: Food/water-deprived participants viewed images at fixed brightness, then adjusted darkened images to reproduce the brightness they thought they'd seen.

title: Changes of State and Internal Energy
subject: science-ocr

cards.front: Name the five changes of state described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Melting (solid to liquid) / Freezing (liquid to solid) / Evaporation/boiling (liquid to gas) / Condensation (gas to liquid) / Sublimation (solid directly to gas)

cards.front: Why does evaporation cause cooling of a liquid?
cards.answer: The fastest-moving particles escape from the surface, reducing the average kinetic energy of the particles left behind.

cards.front: Why is the specific latent heat of vaporisation always greater than the specific latent heat of fusion for the same substance?
cards.answer: Because particles must completely overcome the intermolecular forces between them to become a gas.

cards.front: Name the three British historical figures Agard says he was taught about in school.
cards.answer: Dick Whittington / Lord Nelson / Florence Nightingale

cards.front: What are the three stages 'London' moves through across its four stanzas?
cards.answer: Observation (stanza 1) / Analysis (stanzas 2-3) / Devastating conclusion (stanza 4)

cards.front: Why does Blake use synaesthesia in 'the hapless Soldier's sigh / Runs in blood down Palace walls'?
cards.answer: It turns a sigh into blood on the walls, creating a horrifying image that directly blames the monarchy for soldiers' deaths.

cards.front: How does the 'youthful Harlot's curse' line show poverty's effect on future generations in 'London'?
cards.answer: The prostitute's suffering destroys even a newborn's innocence, showing poverty corrupts everything, even the next generation.

cards.front: Name the three locations where Nigeria's government has set up Free Trade Zones.
cards.answer: Lekki / Calabar / Lagos

cards.front: Give the three reasons the lesson gives for why TNCs are attracted to Nigeria.
cards.answer: Oil reserves / A vast consumer market / English as the language of business
items: English as the language of business

cards.front: Why does turning raw materials into manufactured goods add more value for Nigeria?
cards.answer: Raw cocoa beans sold unprocessed earn one price, but chocolate bars made from them in Nigeria earn far more.

cards.front: Why did the Nigerian government set up Free Trade Zones?
cards.answer: To attract factories by offering low taxes and reliable electricity.

title: UK Weather Hazards: The Storm Desmond Floods
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that combined to make Storm Desmond so extreme.
cards.answer: Saturated ground from a wet November / Steep relief forcing air upwards (orographic rainfall) / An atmospheric river of tropical moisture / Climate change adding extra water vapour
items: Saturated ground from a wet November
Steep relief forcing air upwards (orographic rainfall)
An atmospheric river of tropical moisture
Climate change adding extra water vapour

cards.front: Name the five types of UK weather hazard the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Wind storms / Heavy rain and flooding / Snow and ice / Heatwaves / Drought

cards.front: Why did Cumbria flood again so soon after the 2009 floods, even though defences had been raised?
cards.answer: Desmond's rainfall was so far above the 2009 totals that the newly raised flood defences were overwhelmed.

cards.front: How did climate change make Storm Desmond's rainfall worse?
cards.answer: Warmer Atlantic waters held more water vapour, making a downpour like Desmond about 40% more likely.

title: Plant Transport: Xylem, Phloem and Transpiration
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that affect the rate of transpiration.
cards.answer: Light intensity / Temperature / Humidity / Air movement (wind)

cards.front: Name the three leaf adaptations the lesson gives that reduce unnecessary water loss.
cards.answer: Waxy cuticle on upper surface / Stomata mostly on lower surface / Guard cells close stomata when dark or water is scarce
items: Guard cells close stomata when dark/dry

cards.front: How does the cohesion-tension mechanism pull water up through the xylem?
cards.answer: Water evaporating from leaves creates tension, and cohesion between water molecules keeps a continuous column that gets sucked upward.

cards.front: Why does higher temperature increase the rate of transpiration?
cards.answer: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy, increasing evaporation and diffusion of water vapour from the leaf.

title: Aryan ideas, racial policy and the Final Solution
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five stages the lesson gives for the radicalisation of Nazi racial policy.
cards.answer: Boycotts and dismissals (1933) / Legal exclusion under Nuremberg Laws (1935) / Organised violence at Kristallnacht (1938) / Mass shootings by Einsatzgruppen (1941) / Industrial murder coordinated at Wannsee (1942)

cards.front: Name four groups other than Jews that the lesson says were targeted by the Nazi regime.
cards.answer: Sinti and Roma / Disabled Germans / Gay men / Soviet prisoners of war / Polish elites

cards.front: Why did around half of Germany's Jews fail to emigrate by September 1939?
cards.answer: They lacked the visas, money or contacts needed to leave the country.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say concentration camps and death camps should not be treated as the same thing?
cards.answer: Concentration camps held prisoners who died from labour, disease and execution, while death camps were built solely for industrial murder, mainly of Jews.

title: Wool, Banks and the Royal Purse
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What three pillars did Edward I's royal finance rest on?
cards.answer: The wool customs (maltolt) / Loans from Italian banking houses / Parliamentary grants of taxation

cards.front: Which four regions fed the flocks that produced England's wool in the thirteenth century?
cards.answer: The Cotswolds / Lincolnshire / The Welsh borders / The Yorkshire moors

cards.front: Why did the Riccardi banking house collapse in 1294?
cards.answer: French officers seized their Paris assets while Edward froze their English accounts, so they lost income from both ends and went bankrupt.

cards.front: How did the 1279-80 re-coinage make it harder to clip coins?
cards.answer: New pennies were struck on a heavier flan with a larger inscription that made any clipping obvious.

cards.front: Name the three main employers or sectors that recruited Caribbean and South Asian migrants after 1945, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: NHS (nurses) / London Transport (from 1956) / British textile towns (Bradford, Leicester, Coventry)

cards.front: Why did tens of thousands of Kenyan Asians lose their right to enter Britain freely under the 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Act?
cards.answer: The Act only allowed free entry to those with a parent or grandparent born in Britain, which most Kenyan Asians lacked despite holding British passports.

cards.front: Why did the Learie Constantine case in 1943 fail to change the law on racial discrimination?
cards.answer: Although Constantine won damages, his case attracted attention but did not change the law, which offered no general protection until 1965.

cards.front: Why does Princess go missing before the boycott resolves in Act 3?
cards.answer: She endures racist abuse at school and cuts her hair short as an act of self-transformation expressing distress and refusal.

cards.front: How does Margot's role in sheltering Princess show cross-racial solidarity?
cards.answer: Margot shelters Princess despite never backing the boycott, making the solidarity personal rather than political.

cards.front: What three strange events at Thornfield are blamed on Grace Poole, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: The mirthless laugh from the third floor / A fire in Rochester's bedroom / A violent attack on Mason
items: The mirthless laugh from the third floor

cards.front: Why does Jane leave Thornfield after discovering the truth about Bertha?
cards.answer: She refuses to compromise her moral integrity, not because she stops loving Rochester.

cards.front: Why does Jane find Thornfield both freeing and confining?
cards.answer: She has escaped Lowood's cruelty but remains a dependent, paid, housed and controlled by her employer.

title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Why is the live wire dangerous even when the switch is off?
cards.answer: It is still at 230 V relative to earth, so touching it creates a potential difference that drives current through your body.

cards.front: Why does increasing the transmission voltage reduce the current in the National Grid cables?
cards.answer: Since P = IV, if power stays the same, increasing the voltage means the current must decrease.

title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that affect the resistance of a wire.
cards.answer: Length of wire / Cross-sectional area / Material / Temperature

cards.front: In a series circuit, what happens to current across the components (as stated in the lesson)?
cards.answer: Current is the same everywhere

cards.front: Why is total resistance in a parallel circuit less than the smallest individual resistance?
cards.answer: Because current can flow through multiple branches at once, giving it more paths and reducing overall resistance.

cards.front: Why don't filament bulbs follow Ohm's law?
cards.answer: They are non-ohmic, meaning their resistance changes with temperature instead of staying constant.

title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things the amount of internal energy in a substance depends on.
cards.answer: Temperature / Mass / What material it's made from

cards.front: Name the four changes of state described in the particle model explanation.
cards.answer: Melting (solid to liquid) / Boiling (liquid to gas) / Condensing (gas to liquid) / Freezing (liquid to solid)

cards.front: Why does a metal spoon heat up quickly in hot soup compared to the water around it?
cards.answer: Metals generally have lower specific heat capacities than water, so they need less energy to heat up.

cards.front: How does the particle model explain why gases take up much more space than liquids or solids?
cards.answer: During boiling, energy completely overcomes the forces between particles, letting them move freely and spread far apart.

cards.front: How did Malotki's 1983 research challenge Whorf's claim about the Hopi language?
cards.answer: Malotki found Hopi actually has tense and extensive time vocabulary, undermining Whorf's claim that Hopi speakers conceptualise time differently.

cards.front: How does learning new words later in childhood challenge Piaget's view that language depends on thought?
cards.answer: Learning a new word can introduce a new concept, suggesting language can shape thought rather than only expressing existing thoughts.

cards.front: Why is high carbon steel hard but not tough?
cards.answer: High carbon steel holds a chisel edge well but is brittle, so it can shatter suddenly if struck sideways instead of bending.

cards.front: Why does stainless steel have low machinability?
cards.answer: Stainless steel work-hardens during cutting, which dulls tools rapidly and forces slower cutting speeds, increasing cycle time and tool costs.

cards.front: What are the three regular past participle endings for -er, -ir and -re verbs in the perfect tense?
cards.answer: -er verbs end in -é / -ir verbs end in -i / -re verbs end in -u

cards.front: Name the five time phrases given for signalling the past tense in French.
cards.answer: l'année dernière (last year) / l'été dernier (last summer) / la semaine dernière (last week) / hier (yesterday) / il y a deux ans (two years ago)
items: il y a deux ans (two years ago)

cards.front: Why do verbs of movement and reflexive verbs use être instead of avoir in the perfect tense?
cards.answer: They belong to a specific group of verbs, mainly verbs of movement, that take être as their auxiliary rather than avoir.

cards.front: How does the past participle change when the subject of an être verb is feminine plural?
cards.answer: Add -es to the past participle to agree with the feminine plural subject, e.g. elles sont allées.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says resource exploitation changes the environment where it happens.
cards.answer: Overfishing collapses food chains / Intensive farming erodes soil and depletes aquifers / Mining and drilling pollute air and water / Deforestation removes habitat and releases stored carbon
items: Intensive farming erodes soil and depletes aquifers
Mining and drilling pollute air and water
Deforestation removes habitat and releases stored carbon

cards.front: What are the four PEEL steps for describing a choropleth resource map?
cards.answer: Pattern - where is the highest band / Exception - which country breaks the pattern / Explain - what factor causes that / Link - how it connects to another map
items: Pattern - where is the highest band
Exception - which country breaks the pattern
Link - how it connects to another map

cards.front: Why does the UK's north-west receive far more rain than the south-east?
cards.answer: South-westerly winds carry moist Atlantic air, which rises over uplands, cools and releases relief rainfall, leaving little moisture by the south-east.

cards.front: Why did Russia's gas exports give it political influence over Europe?
cards.answer: Populous, resource-poor European countries depended on Russia's gas exports, giving Russia geopolitical leverage over European energy security until 2022.

title: Jesus as God Incarnate, Salvation and the Resurrection
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What three gifts did the Magi bring to Jesus in Matthew's birth account?
cards.answer: Gold / Frankincense / Myrrh

cards.front: Name the four events the lesson says together form the Christian 'Gospel' (good news).
cards.answer: The Incarnation / The crucifixion / The Resurrection / The Ascension

cards.front: Why is the virgin birth significant for Christians?
cards.answer: It shows Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, not a human father, confirming he was uniquely both divine and human from birth.

cards.front: Why did Paul argue that the Resurrection is essential to Christian faith?
cards.answer: Because without the Resurrection, Paul said, Christian faith would be pointless, so it is the foundation of belief.

title: Redemption, the Church and the Mystery of Salvation
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three models the lesson gives for what Christ's death on the Cross accomplished.
cards.answer: Anselm's satisfaction theory / Aquinas's perfect sacrifice / Liberation model

cards.front: Name the four marks of the Church affirmed in the Nicene Creed.
cards.answer: One / Holy / Catholic / Apostolic

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church affirm the reality of hell despite teaching that God's love is unconditional?
cards.answer: Hell is the logical consequence of a person freely and finally refusing the love and mercy God offers, not something God sends.

cards.front: Why is the Church described as 'apostolic'?
cards.answer: It stands in direct succession from the apostles, as bishops succeed the apostles and the Pope succeeds Peter.

cards.front: Name the three sections of a river's course from source to mouth.
cards.answer: Upper course / Middle course / Lower course

cards.front: According to the Bradshaw model, name the four variables that fall as you move downstream.
cards.answer: Gradient / Sediment size / Channel roughness

cards.front: Why do interlocking spurs form in the upper course of a river?
cards.answer: The young river lacks power to cut through ridges of higher land, so it weaves around them.

cards.front: How do levees and floodplains build up in the lower course of a river?
cards.answer: Floodwater spreads over flat ground, slows down and drops sediment, coarsest near the channel, building levees and deepening floodplain soil.

cards.front: Name the six adaptation strategies Australia used after the Millennium Drought.
cards.answer: Water-saving rules in cities / New water sources (desalination plants) / Smarter farming methods / Murray-Darling Basin Plan (2012) / Better ENSO forecasting / Greywater reuse

cards.front: Give three effects the Millennium Drought had on Australia's environment.
cards.answer: Murray-Darling stopped reaching the sea / Wetlands shrank, killing river red gums / Bushfires intensified / Dust storms swept across cities
items: Wetlands shrank, killing river red gums

cards.front: How does El Nino cause drought in Australia and Indonesia?
cards.answer: Trade winds weaken, so the warm water pool shifts eastward, taking the rain that normally falls on the western Pacific with it.

cards.front: Why did Australian farming losses become less severe by the 2015-16 El Nino compared with 2002?
cards.answer: Cities used desalination plants and stricter water rules built after the Millennium Drought, reducing the impact of the later drought.

title: Cell Structure, Microscopy and Specialised Cells
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four adaptations of the sperm cell described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Streamlined head with acrosome containing enzymes / Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy / Long flagellum for propulsion / Nucleus carrying haploid genetic information
items: Streamlined head with acrosome containing enzymes
Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy

cards.front: Name the five organelles found in an animal cell, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Nucleus / Cytoplasm / Cell membrane / Mitochondria / Ribosomes

cards.front: Why do muscle cells contain more mitochondria than other cells?
cards.answer: Muscle cells have high energy demands, so they need more mitochondria to carry out aerobic respiration.

cards.front: Why does the plant cell wall stop the cell bursting when water enters by osmosis?
cards.answer: The cellulose cell wall provides structural strength that resists the pressure created as water enters the cell.

cards.front: Name the five psychological factors the lesson identifies that affect injury risk.
cards.answer: Motivation / Arousal / Anxiety and stress / Confidence / Aggression

cards.front: How does anxiety and stress increase injury risk in an athlete?
cards.answer: Elevated cortisol impairs immune function and slows healing, while anxiety causes muscle tension that restricts movement and alters gait.

cards.front: How can overconfidence increase injury risk for an athlete?
cards.answer: A highly confident athlete may attempt skills beyond their current ability, exposing them to injury through poor technique or mistimed actions.

cards.front: How can a previous knee injury lead to a new injury elsewhere in the body?
cards.answer: It may cause a footballer to alter their running technique, placing excess stress on the opposite hip and creating a new overuse injury site.

cards.front: Name the four things Gothic fiction thrives on, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Isolated settings / Supernatural terror / Psychological dread / The idea the past cannot be escaped
items: The idea the past cannot be escaped

cards.front: Name the four familiar Gothic elements Hill uses in The Woman in Black.
cards.answer: Fog / Marshland / A decaying house / A vengeful spirit

cards.front: Why did Hill choose to write in the traditional ghost story form?
cards.answer: She admired James's restraint and psychological complexity and wanted to prove the classic ghost story could still terrify a modern reader.

cards.front: Why does Kipps choose to write down his story rather than tell it aloud?
cards.answer: Writing lets him control the narrative and impose order on an experience that shattered his understanding of the world.

title: The Great American Desert and Manifest Destiny
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three push factors driving Americans west in the 1840s given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Overcrowded cities / The 1837 Panic / Soil exhaustion in the East

cards.front: Name the three older ideas that Manifest Destiny bundled together.
cards.answer: Religious belief God favoured the US / Racial belief in Anglo-Saxonism / Political confidence in republican institutions
items: Religious belief God favoured the US

cards.front: Why did easterners begin to see the Plains as a gateway rather than a barrier in the 1840s?
cards.answer: Missionary reports of fertile Oregon valleys, California's climate and harbours, and gold strikes after 1848 made the risky journey worthwhile.

cards.front: How did Manifest Destiny affect attitudes towards Native nations on the Plains?
cards.answer: It treated the land as empty, legitimising the removal and confinement of the hundreds of thousands of Native people already living there.

cards.front: Name the six qualities (the 6Cs) that enable practitioners to deliver person-centred values.
cards.answer: Care / Compassion / Competence / Communication / Courage / Commitment

cards.front: Name the three person-centred values that together form the 'empowerment cluster'.
cards.answer: Independence / Choice / Encouraging decision making

cards.front: How do independence, choice and encouraging decision making combine to produce empowerment?
cards.answer: Independence lets service users do things themselves, choice gives them options, and encouraging decision making builds confidence to use those options.

cards.front: Why does a community nurse close the door before discussing medication even when the patient lives alone?
cards.answer: Because the habit of maintaining privacy protects the service user's dignity, regardless of whether anyone else could actually overhear.

title: Political change, 1960-2000: from Kennedy to Clinton
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four goals of Kennedy's New Frontier programme.
cards.answer: Tackle poverty / Extend civil rights / Invest in education / Create Medicare

cards.front: Name the four effects Watergate had on American political life.
cards.answer: Public trust in government collapsed / War Powers Act passed (1973) / Campaign finance reform legislation passed / The suffix '-gate' entered the language

cards.front: Why did Kennedy struggle to pass his New Frontier programme through Congress?
cards.answer: He faced a conservative Congress that blocked much of his ambitious domestic agenda.

cards.front: Why did the federal deficit increase substantially under Reagan despite economic growth?
cards.answer: Because Reagan's tax cuts outpaced the reductions in government spending.

title: Exploring the Moon: Origin, Far Side and Apollo
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three key evidence strands supporting the Giant Impact Hypothesis.
cards.answer: Moon's composition matches Earth's mantle / Moon has a disproportionately small iron core / Apollo rock samples share Earth's oxygen isotope ratios
items: Moon has a disproportionately small iron core
Apollo rock samples share Earth's oxygen isotope ratios

cards.front: Name the three missions that revealed the Moon's far side, in order.
cards.answer: Luna 3 (1959) / Apollo 8 (1968) / Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (2009)

cards.front: Why does the Moon have a relatively small iron core compared to its size?
cards.answer: Theia's iron core merged with Earth's core during the impact, so the ejected debris that formed the Moon came only from the mantles.

cards.front: Why is the Moon's far-side crust thicker than the near-side crust?
cards.answer: Earth's heat likely warmed the near side more, delaying its crust solidifying, while the far side cooled and solidified faster into a thicker crust.

cards.front: Name the four layers of the Earth's structure, from outer to inner.
cards.answer: Crust / Mantle / Outer core / Inner core

cards.front: Name the five factors the lesson gives that affect hazard risk.
cards.answer: Population density / Wealth / Frequency of the hazard / Type of hazard / Climate change

cards.front: Why do richer countries usually have a lower death toll from natural hazards?
cards.answer: They can afford early-warning systems, stronger buildings and well-funded emergency services.

cards.front: Why do intraplate earthquakes happen even though most hazards occur at plate boundaries?
cards.answer: They are caused by ancient faults reactivating or a magma plume punching through the plate from below.

title: The Third Crusade: Causes, Acre and Arsuf
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson gives as motives for why English crusaders went on the Third Crusade.
cards.answer: Moved by loss of Jerusalem, wanted indulgence / Hoped for booty and lands / Wanted to escape debts or law-suits / Summoned by feudal duty to their lord
items: Moved by loss of Jerusalem, wanted indulgence
Wanted to escape debts or law-suits
Summoned by feudal duty to their lord

cards.front: Why was the capture of Acre in 1191 such an important victory for the crusaders?
cards.answer: Acre was the gateway to the Holy Land, so its fall reopened the supply line to Europe and gave crusaders a base to march on Jerusalem.

cards.front: Why did Richard's discipline during the march to Jaffa help him win at Arsuf?
cards.answer: He kept the army in three tight blocks with baggage shielded, so knights held ranks under harassment until able to counter-charge and break Saladin's force.

title: Titrations, Chemical Cells and Fuel Cells
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three disadvantages the lesson gives for hydrogen fuel cells.
cards.answer: Hydrogen hard/expensive to store and transport / Most hydrogen made from fossil fuels / Fuel cell technology is expensive
items: Hydrogen hard/expensive to store and transport
Most hydrogen made from fossil fuels

cards.front: Why does a chemical cell made of zinc and copper produce a higher voltage than one made of iron and copper?
cards.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, and a bigger reactivity difference between the two metals gives a higher voltage.

cards.front: Why does electric current flow through the external circuit in a chemical cell?
cards.answer: The more reactive metal is oxidised and loses electrons, which flow through the circuit to the less reactive metal where they are gained (reduction).

title: The Origin of Evil and the Problem of Suffering
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: According to Catholic teaching, what three things does Original Sin damage in human nature?
cards.answer: A tendency towards self-centredness / A weakening of the will / A darkening of the intellect

cards.front: Why do Catholic thinkers treat moral evil and natural evil differently when explaining the problem of evil?
cards.answer: Moral evil can be traced to human freedom being misused, but natural evil is harder to explain without reference to God's purposes.

cards.front: How does the Irenaean 'soul-making' view explain why evil and suffering exist?
cards.answer: It sees humanity as created immature, so evil and suffering are conditions for moral and spiritual growth, not just consequences of sin.

cards.front: Name the three forces the lesson gives for rising global water demand.
cards.answer: Growing world population / Richer middle class eating more meat and dairy / Spread of intensive farming
items: Richer middle class eating more meat and dairy

cards.front: Name the five strategies the lesson gives for a sustainable water future.
cards.answer: Efficient drip irrigation / Recycling treated wastewater for industry / Rainwater harvesting in homes / Repairing leaky pipes / Pricing water so heavy users pay more
items: Pricing water so heavy users pay more

cards.front: Why can groundwater over-abstraction cause saltwater to ruin coastal aquifers?
cards.answer: Pumping too much fresh groundwater lowers water tables, letting seawater seep into coastal aquifers and contaminate drinking supplies.

cards.front: Why do big dams like the Three Gorges Dam harm downstream farmland?
cards.answer: Sediment that used to flow downstream and fertilise farms instead collects behind the dam wall.

title: Glorious Revolution and the Hanoverian succession
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the five constitutional landmarks the lesson lists between 1689 and 1714.
cards.answer: Bill of Rights (1689) / Toleration Act (1689) / Act of Settlement (1701) / Act of Union with Scotland (1707) / George I crowned (1714)

cards.front: Name the three effects the Glorious Revolution had within the British Isles outside England, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Williamite War in Ireland followed by Penal Laws / Jacobite rising at Killiecrankie in Scotland collapsed / Scotland pushed towards the Act of Union 1707
items: Williamite War in Ireland followed by Penal Laws
Jacobite rising at Killiecrankie in Scotland collapsed
Scotland pushed towards the Act of Union 1707

cards.front: Why did George I become king in 1714 despite having over 50 closer Catholic blood relatives?
cards.answer: The Act of Settlement barred Catholics from the throne, so religion rather than bloodline now decided who could rule.

cards.front: How did the Bill of Rights shift power away from the Crown towards Parliament?
cards.answer: It stopped the monarch suspending laws, levying taxes or keeping a peacetime army without parliamentary consent, and guaranteed free elections and speech.

cards.front: Name the six categories of security measure covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Identifying staff / Monitoring of keys / Receiving and monitoring visitors / Reporting concerns to line managers / External doors restricting access / Window locks and restraints

cards.front: Name the two emergency procedures the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Fire drill / Evacuation

cards.front: Why is a fire drill carried out regularly in a care setting?
cards.answer: It is a practised rehearsal so all staff know the assembly point and their responsibilities in an evacuation.

cards.front: Why must faulty equipment have a reporting system in a care setting?
cards.answer: So faulty equipment is taken out of service immediately rather than left for another staff member to unknowingly use.

cards.front: What three interlocking plots does Act 1 establish, all driven by money?
cards.answer: Antonio's bond with Shylock / Bassanio's quest to win Portia via the caskets / tension between Christians and Jews in Venice
items: Bassanio's quest to win Portia via the caskets
tension between Christians and Jews in Venice

cards.front: Why does Shylock propose a pound of flesh instead of charging interest on the loan?
cards.answer: It seems like a joke on the surface but hides genuine menace, since Antonio has publicly abused and humiliated Shylock.

cards.front: Why does Portia have no control over who she marries?
cards.answer: She is bound by her dead father's will, which forces suitors to choose correctly between three caskets to win her hand.

title: Girlhood: Representation and the Paris Banlieue
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five key sequences the lesson identifies for micro/representation analysis in Girlhood.
cards.answer: Opening American-football tracking shot / Train-station fight / Hotel-room karaoke 'Diamonds' set piece / Boxing fight in the second act / Closing crossing-the-road sequence
items: Boxing fight in the second act

cards.front: How does Sciamma's use of the Cinemascope frame represent the four friends as a collective rather than individuals?
cards.answer: The wide frame holds all four friends simultaneously so none are cropped or marginalised, presenting Black femininity as a collective, social experience.

cards.front: Why does the opening football-game tracking shot avoid introducing Marieme with an individualising hero shot?
cards.answer: It follows a collective of young Black women already occupying public space, so Marieme emerges from the group rather than being singled out.

title: Votes for Women: Suffragists, Suffragettes, and 1918
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four militant suffragette tactics listed for the period after 1905/1912.
cards.answer: Heckling cabinet ministers / Chaining themselves to railings / Smashing shop windows on Oxford Street / Burning letters in postboxes / Arson attacks on empty country houses / Slashing paintings like the Rokeby Venus
items: Smashing shop windows on Oxford Street
Arson attacks on empty country houses
Slashing paintings like the Rokeby Venus

cards.front: Why did the government introduce force-feeding of imprisoned suffragettes from 1909?
cards.answer: Imprisoned suffragettes went on hunger strike, so the government force-fed them with a tube to stop them dying in custody.

cards.front: Why did excluding women from voting become harder to justify by 1917-18?
cards.answer: Around 1.7 million women were doing vital war work in munitions, transport and agriculture, undermining claims they were 'unfit' for political responsibility.

cards.front: Why did Parliament have to legislate on the franchise during the First World War?
cards.answer: The existing male franchise required residence, so soldiers serving abroad would lose their vote on returning, forcing Parliament to redraw the franchise.

cards.front: Why does Claudio's honour demand public revenge rather than private investigation of Hero?
cards.answer: Because the honour system prioritises public male judgement of female chastity over fairness or truth.

cards.front: Why does love based on appearance fail while love based on connection survives in Much Ado?
cards.answer: Conventional love has no foundation in genuine knowledge, so a single deception destroys it, unlike tested, earned love.

title: Britain in the early 1950s: austerity and rationing
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six goods that still required ration books by 1951, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Meat / Butter / Cooking fats / Sugar / Tea / Cheese
