cards.front: What were the three weekly adult ration allowances given in the lesson for the early 1950s?
cards.answer: 13 ounces of meat / 1½ ounces of cheese / 6 ounces of butter

cards.front: Why was sterling convertibility suspended within weeks of being restored in 1947?
cards.answer: Restoring convertibility triggered a run on the pound, showing how fragile Britain's finances were, so it was quickly suspended.

cards.front: Why did young couples often wait five or more years for council housing in the early 1950s?
cards.answer: Despite government building programmes, demand for housing consistently outpaced the supply of new homes being built.

cards.front: Name the four parts of the essay structure this lesson recommends for a Jane Eyre answer.
cards.answer: Introduction (1-2 sentences) / Extract analysis (2-3 paragraphs) / Whole novel (2-3 paragraphs) / Brief conclusion

cards.front: Why does the lesson say you must memorise quotations for the Jane Eyre exam?
cards.answer: The paper is closed book, so you cannot take a copy of the novel in and must reference it from memory.

cards.front: Why should context be embedded inside analysis rather than given its own separate paragraph?
cards.answer: Context should be linked directly to the writer's purpose within the analysis, not bolted on separately.

cards.front: What is the most common mistake students make when structuring their Jane Eyre essay, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Spending too long analysing the extract and neglecting the whole-novel section, instead of aiming for an even split.

cards.front: Name the four staging choices Odimba uses (besides lighting) to shape meaning in Princess & The Hustler.
cards.answer: Flexible set / Sound design / Costume and period detail / Physical storytelling

cards.front: What four structural techniques does the lesson say give the play its distinctive quality?
cards.answer: Cyclical framing / Dual timelines / Episodic scenes / Small cast

cards.front: Why does Odimba use a small cast of only seven characters?
cards.answer: The boycott arrives as news carried into the flat, keeping the play's scope intimate.

cards.front: How does Odimba use episodic scenes with gaps between them?
cards.answer: Short scenes with gaps of weeks or months allow time jumps and tonal shifts without losing momentum.

cards.front: Name the six religious traditions/concepts the lesson gives as key foundations for social justice.
cards.answer: Amos 5:24 (Hebrew prophetic tradition) / Galatians 3:28 (Christian equality) / Tzedek and tikkun olam (Judaism) / Adl (Islamic justice) / Sewa (Sikh service) / Ahimsa (Hindu non-harm)

cards.front: Why did Archbishop Desmond Tutu argue that apartheid was theologically wrong, not just politically wrong?
cards.answer: He drew on the Christian teaching of imago Dei and ubuntu philosophy to show apartheid denied the God-given dignity all people share.

cards.front: How did Martin Luther King Jr justify resisting unjust laws in his 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'?
cards.answer: He argued Christians had a moral duty to resist unjust laws, drawing on the natural-law tradition rooted in Augustine and Aquinas.

title: Cromwell, Government Reform and the Fall, 1534–40
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four new revenue departments Cromwell created to manage royal finance.
cards.answer: Court of Augmentations / Court of First Fruits and Tenths / Court of Wards / Court of General Surveyors
items: Court of First Fruits and Tenths

cards.front: Name the six pieces of Reformation Parliament legislation the lesson lists between 1532 and 1540.
cards.answer: Act in Restraint of Appeals 1533 / Act of Supremacy 1534 / Act of Succession 1534 / two Acts of Dissolution / Statute of Uses 1536 / Act of Six Articles 1539

cards.front: Why was Cromwell able to be condemned without a trial in 1540?
cards.answer: He was condemned by Act of Attainder, the same legal weapon he had previously used against the Nun of Kent and Anne Boleyn.

cards.front: How did the failed Cleves marriage help bring about Cromwell's fall?
cards.answer: It looked like a personal humiliation for Henry, making him willing to listen to the conservative faction's case against Cromwell.

title: The Five-Year Plans and Soviet Industry
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: The lesson gives four reasons why Stalin pushed rapid industrialisation. Name them.
cards.answer: Defence against industrial powers / Autarky (self-sufficiency) / Ideology (need an industrial working class) / Succession (defining himself against Bukharin)

cards.front: How did factory managers respond to quota pressure under the planning system, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Hoarding raw materials / Padding workforce numbers / Ignoring quality / Faking returns

cards.front: Why can't Five-Year Plan output figures be treated as accurate measurements of growth?
cards.answer: Output was measured in inconsistent units, padded by managers to fulfil quotas, and over-fulfilment was reported as a political survival tactic during the Terror.

cards.front: Why were around 10,000 foreign engineers hired during the First Five-Year Plan?
cards.answer: To install machinery, train Soviet workers and run the new plants until Soviet engineers could take over.

title: Designing Sociological Research and Interpreting Data
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: What are the eight steps in the research design sequence, in order?
cards.answer: Aim / Hypothesis / Operationalisation / Method choice / Sampling / Pilot study / Data collection / Analysis and conclusions

cards.front: The lesson gives four steps for interpreting sociological data correctly. What are they?
cards.answer: Read the axis labels first / Cite specific figures not vague claims / Describe the pattern before explaining it / Consider what data might be missing
items: Cite specific figures not vague claims
Describe the pattern before explaining it
Consider what data might be missing

cards.front: Why must a sampling strategy match the research method chosen?
cards.answer: A random or stratified sample suits a large survey aiming for representativeness, while a snowball sample suits interviews with hard-to-reach groups where depth matters more.

cards.front: Why can different operationalisations of 'social class' produce different research findings?
cards.answer: Because concepts like class can be defined differently (e.g. free school meal eligibility, parental occupation, self-reported class), each measuring something slightly different.

cards.front: Name the three linked moves Mao used between 1962 and 1966 to prepare his comeback against the party.
cards.answer: Socialist Education Movement to attack rural cadres / Lin Biao's PLA cult of Mao / Campaign in education and culture against 'bourgeois' thinking
items: Socialist Education Movement to attack rural cadres
Lin Biao's PLA cult of Mao
Campaign in education and culture against 'bourgeois' thinking

cards.front: What four things did Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping do to run the recovery after the Great Leap Forward?
cards.answer: Scaled back the communes / Allowed peasants small private plots / Restored material incentives in factories / Rebuilt the bureaucracy

cards.front: Why did Mao see Liu and Deng's recovery policies as a betrayal of the revolution?
cards.answer: They looked like the Soviet Union under Khrushchev, with the revolution quietly buried under managers, technicians and bonuses.

cards.front: Why did Mao attack examinations in his reform of education?
cards.answer: He argued they restored privilege, filtering out peasants' sons in favour of pupils taught bourgeois entrance tests by middle-class teachers.

cards.front: What four primary research techniques does the lesson describe for designers?
cards.answer: Market research & interviews / Ergonomics & anthropometric data / Focus groups / Product analysis

cards.front: What secondary research sources does the lesson name?
cards.answer: Published books / Academic journals / Manufacturer datasheets / Government statistics / Online databases

cards.front: Why are interviews often more useful than written surveys for design research?
cards.answer: The designer can ask follow-up questions and observe body language, giving richer data than a survey alone.

cards.front: Why do designers usually combine secondary research with primary research?
cards.answer: Secondary research is quick and cheap for background knowledge, then primary research fills gaps it doesn't cover.

cards.front: Name the eight main energy stores the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Chemical / Nuclear / Kinetic / Gravitational potential / Elastic potential / Thermal / Electrostatic / Electromagnetic

cards.front: What three wires does a home appliance's three-core cable contain?
cards.answer: Live / Neutral / Earth

cards.front: Why does double-glazing reduce heat loss through a window?
cards.answer: It traps a layer of air or gas between two panes, and air is a poor thermal conductor, so less heat transfers across.

cards.front: How does a generator in a power station produce electricity?
cards.answer: A turbine, driven by the fuel source, spins a magnet near a coil of wire, which generates electricity.

cards.front: Name the three constraints placed on Portia as a woman that the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Cannot choose her own husband (casket test) / Cannot enter a courtroom without disguise / Transfers all her property to Bassanio on marriage
items: Cannot choose her own husband (casket test)
Cannot enter a courtroom without disguise
Transfers all her property to Bassanio on marriage

cards.front: Name the four critical readings of Shylock given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Traditional (comic villain defeated) / Sympathetic (moral centre of the play) / Postcolonial (the scapegoated Other) / Marxist (exposes capitalism's hypocrisy)

cards.front: Why does Antonio's self-description as a "tainted wether" suggest he passively accepts death?
cards.answer: The wether metaphor is self-pitying and sacrificial, suggesting Antonio sees his own life as expendable.

cards.front: How does Jessica's line "never merry when I hear sweet music" show the cost of her elopement?
cards.answer: It indicates persistent sadness and displacement despite gaining a husband and wealth through assimilation.

cards.front: What five reasons does the lesson give for why a business needs finance?
cards.answer: Establishing a new business / Funding expansion / Running the business / Recruitment / Marketing

cards.front: What four factors does the lesson say suitability of a finance source depends on?
cards.answer: How much is needed / How quickly it's needed / How long it's needed for / How established the business is

cards.front: Why is retained profit a low-risk source of finance for a business?
cards.answer: It costs nothing in interest, doesn't need repaying, and doesn't cause loss of control to outsiders.

cards.front: Why is a bank loan better than an overdraft for a large one-off purchase like a delivery van?
cards.answer: A loan gives a fixed sum repaid over an agreed period, while an overdraft is only meant to cover short-term cash-flow problems.

title: How Rights Have Developed Over Time
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the four rights the lesson lists as protected by the Human Rights Act 1998.
cards.answer: Right to life / Right to a fair trial / Freedom from torture / Freedom of expression

cards.front: Name the four tactics the suffragette movement used in its campaign for women's votes.
cards.answer: Protests / Hunger strikes / Property damage / Arson

cards.front: Why did early trade unions operate illegally before 1871?
cards.answer: Because the Combination Acts of 1799 and 1800 banned workers from organising collectively.

cards.front: Why was taking a human rights case to Strasbourg before 1998 a problem for UK citizens?
cards.answer: Because it was costly and time-consuming to take a case all the way to the European Court of Human Rights.

cards.front: The lesson names four volcanic hazards that can kill people. What are they?
cards.answer: Pyroclastic flows / Lava flows / Lahars / Ash clouds

cards.front: Name the six social and economic factors the lesson says increase a community's vulnerability.
cards.answer: High population density / Low income / Poor building quality / Limited emergency services / Lack of education/drills / Weak government/infrastructure

cards.front: Why did the 2010 Haiti earthquake kill far more people than the much more powerful 2011 Tōhoku earthquake?
cards.answer: Japan had stronger buildings and a tsunami warning system, while Haiti had weak buildings and limited emergency services, so vulnerability was lower in Japan.

cards.front: How does Japan's Earthquake Early Warning system reduce risk during an earthquake?
cards.answer: It uses fast primary waves from the rupture to send a warning before slower damaging surface waves arrive, letting trains brake and surgeons pause.

cards.front: The lesson tracks Elizabeth's growth through five specific moments in the novel. What are they?
cards.answer: Amused defiance at the assembly / Trust in Wickham / Shock at Darcy's letter / Humility at Pemberley / Mature love in the second proposal
items: Mature love in the second proposal

cards.front: Name the four character contrasts the lesson says Austen uses to build her characters.
cards.answer: Wickham's charm vs Darcy's awkwardness / Elizabeth's wit vs Jane's gentleness / Mrs Bennet's anxiety vs Mr Bennet's detachment / Collins's obsequiousness vs Elizabeth's independence
items: Mrs Bennet's anxiety vs Mr Bennet's detachment

cards.front: Why does Jane's goodness almost cost her Bingley?
cards.answer: Her inability to think ill of anyone makes her too reserved, so her true feelings for Bingley stay invisible to him.

cards.front: How does Lady Catherine's interrogation of Elizabeth at Rosings reveal her worldview?
cards.answer: It shows she believes her rank entitles her to dictate others' marriages and behaviour, enforcing social rules as rigidly as law.

cards.front: Name the four brutal conditions Hari faces as a lascar, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Long hours / Dangerous cargo / Racial abuse from white sailors / Pay far below British crew

cards.front: Why does Gupta use Hari's exploitation to show injustice was deliberate, not just neglect?
cards.answer: His brutal pay, conditions and abuse show exploitation was active and built into the system, not accidental.

cards.front: How does Gupta structure the play to move from individual suffering to collective resistance?
cards.answer: She converges the ayahs' abandonment, Hari's exploitation and the memory of 1857 to reveal systemic injustice needing collective political action.

cards.front: Name the three conditions collision theory says must be met for a reaction to occur.
cards.answer: Particles must collide with each other / Collide with sufficient energy (at least activation energy) / Collide with the correct orientation
items: Particles must collide with each other
Collide with sufficient energy (at least activation energy)

cards.front: Name the four main factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction.
cards.answer: Temperature / Concentration / Pressure / Surface area

cards.front: Why can a fine powder of a combustible material in air cause a dust explosion?
cards.answer: The surface area is so enormous that the reaction rate becomes dangerously fast.

cards.front: Why can 1/t be used as a measure of reaction rate?
cards.answer: A shorter time (t) to complete a set amount of reaction means a faster rate, so 1/t is proportional to rate.

cards.front: Why does a Punnett square only show probabilities rather than guaranteeing the outcome for individual offspring?
cards.answer: Inheritance involves random fertilisation, so the ratios are a long-run statistical expectation, not a fixed prediction.

cards.front: Why do genes on the Y chromosome affect sex development in a human embryo?
cards.answer: Genes on the Y chromosome trigger the development of testes during embryo development.

cards.front: Why was Mendel's explanation for inheritance patterns significant, given he didn't know about DNA or chromosomes?
cards.answer: His explanation correctly predicted inheritance patterns we now explain in molecular terms, even without knowledge of DNA or chromosomes.

cards.front: Name the four non-hormonal contraceptive methods described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Barrier methods (condoms/diaphragms) / Spermicidal agents / Surgical sterilisation / Abstinence or natural family planning

cards.front: How do copper IUDs prevent pregnancy?
cards.answer: Copper IUDs are non-hormonal devices in the uterus that prevent implantation.

cards.front: How does IVF help a couple conceive?
cards.answer: The mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate multiple eggs, which are collected, fertilised outside the body, and transferred to the uterus.

cards.front: Name the three areas of social treatment the lesson says this scene deepens.
cards.answer: Race / Gender / Class

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson describes Jo and the Boy doing together that show their innocence.
cards.answer: Play together / Tease each other / Share physical closeness

cards.front: How does the Boy's departure differ from Helen's earlier abandonment of Jo?
cards.answer: The Boy leaves with genuine regret, whereas Helen leaves Jo with barely a backward glance.

cards.front: Why is Act 1 Scene 2 structurally crucial to the rest of the play?
cards.answer: It creates the pregnancy that drives the second half, giving Geof a reason to stay and Helen a reason to return.

title: Early Bolshevik Decrees and the Constituent Assembly
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four headline decrees issued by the Bolsheviks between October and December 1917.
cards.answer: Decree on Peace / Decree on Land / Decree on Workers' Control / Decree on Nationalities

cards.front: Name the three steps the lesson gives towards banning rival parties after October 1917, before the 1921 factions ban.
cards.answer: Kadets outlawed as 'enemies of the people' (Nov 1917) / Left SRs quit Sovnarkom and were shut out of soviets (March 1918) / Right SRs and Mensheviks banned from soviets (summer 1918)
items: Kadets outlawed as 'enemies of the people' (Nov 1917)
Left SRs quit Sovnarkom and were shut out of soviets (March 1918)
Right SRs and Mensheviks banned from soviets (summer 1918)

cards.front: Why did Lenin close down the Constituent Assembly on 6 January 1918?
cards.answer: The Assembly, dominated by the SRs, refused to endorse Sovnarkom's decrees, so the Red Guard locked the doors and Sverdlov declared it dissolved.

cards.front: Why were the Romanovs executed without trial in July 1918?
cards.answer: White and Czech Legion forces were approaching, and as long as the Romanovs lived they remained a rallying point for monarchist resistance.

title: The Structure and Function of the Brain
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four lobes that the cerebral cortex is divided into.
cards.answer: Frontal lobe / Temporal lobe / Parietal lobe / Occipital lobe

cards.front: Why does cerebellum damage cause jerky, poorly timed movement instead of stopping movement completely?
cards.answer: The cerebellum refines and times movement by comparing intended and actual movement, rather than switching movement on or off.

cards.front: Why is understanding a spoken sentence not the job of just one lobe?
cards.answer: It draws on the temporal lobe to recognise words and the frontal lobe to work out meaning and form a response, working as a network.

title: Catholic Social Teaching, Mission and Funeral Rite
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What are the six core principles of Catholic Social Teaching named in the lesson?
cards.answer: Dignity of the human person / The common good / Solidarity / Subsidiarity / Preferential option for the poor / Care for creation

cards.front: What are the three areas of work CAFOD carries out?
cards.answer: Emergency relief / Long-term development / Justice and advocacy

cards.front: Why does the Sheep and Goats parable make serving the poor a matter of justice rather than optional charity?
cards.answer: Jesus says whatever is done for the poor is done for him, making service of the vulnerable a criterion of the Last Judgment.

cards.front: How does the Catholic funeral rite differ from most Protestant funeral rites regarding the Eucharist?
cards.answer: The Catholic rite includes a full Requiem Mass centred on the Eucharist, while most Protestant funerals focus on Scripture, hymns and preaching instead.

cards.front: Name the three narrative techniques the lesson says together turn memory into the film's dominant device in Slumdog Millionaire.
cards.answer: Frame narrative (quiz show as present frame) / Dual timeline editing (alternating past and present) / Ellipsis (omitting years between key scenes)
items: Frame narrative (quiz show as present frame)
Dual timeline editing (alternating past and present)

cards.front: How does the opening interrogation sequence use colour to create a tonal shock in Slumdog Millionaire?
cards.answer: It cuts from the warm, saturated orange and gold quiz-show stage to cool, single-source police-station grey, jolting the spectator into the frame.

cards.front: Why does the quiz-show format naturally create suspense in Slumdog Millionaire?
cards.answer: The spectator already understands the game's rules, since each round is a multiple-choice question, making them wait for each answer with Jamal.

cards.front: How does camera stability in Slumdog Millionaire create different meanings for the slum and studio spaces?
cards.answer: Handheld camerawork makes slum scenes feel kinetic and precarious, while locked-off camerawork makes the studio feel exposed and stable.

cards.front: Name the original Seven Commandments of Animalism (in order).
cards.answer: Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy / Whatever goes on four legs or has wings is a friend / No animal shall wear clothes / No animal shall sleep in a bed / No animal shall drink alcohol / No animal shall kill any other animal / All animals are equal
items: Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy
Whatever goes on four legs or has wings is a friend
No animal shall sleep in a bed
No animal shall kill any other animal

cards.front: Name the three rhetorical techniques Old Major uses in his speech.
cards.answer: Tricolon for emotional impact / Rhetorical questions to seem inevitable / A unifying song for collective identity
items: A unifying song for collective identity

cards.front: Why does Orwell make the milk and apples disappear so early in the novella?
cards.answer: To show that corruption begins immediately after revolution rather than developing gradually over time.

cards.front: Why does Orwell suggest the Rebellion happens almost accidentally rather than through planned ideology?
cards.answer: Because Jones forgets to feed the animals, showing revolutions arise from desperation rather than ideology.

cards.front: Why does Wells never explain the science behind the Heat-Ray?
cards.answer: Because the weapon is simply beyond human understanding, showing Martian technology's overwhelming superiority.

cards.front: How does the narrator's clinical detachment create dramatic irony in the novel?
cards.answer: It makes the reader feel the horror of events that the narrator himself suppresses while describing them scientifically.

title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three common methods the lesson gives for measuring the rate of a reaction.
cards.answer: Collecting gas in a gas syringe or over water / Measuring the loss of mass on a balance / Timing how long it takes for a solution to become opaque
items: Collecting gas in a gas syringe or over water
Measuring the loss of mass on a balance
Timing how long it takes for a solution to become opaque

cards.front: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
cards.answer: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

cards.front: Why does changing the temperature or concentration alter the steepness of a rate graph but not the final volume of gas produced?
cards.answer: These changes only affect how fast particles collide, not the amount of reactant present, so the same total gas forms if the amount of reactant is unchanged.

title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps: Crisis and Triumph
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four style devices in Livy's Style Toolkit for Passages E to H.
cards.answer: Oxymoron / Hyperbaton / Asyndeton / Antithesis

cards.front: Why did soldiers behind the leading infantry fall through the snow at the cliff in Passage G?
cards.answer: Old hard-packed snow lay under a softer new layer, and once many men and animals had trampled it, the surface broke into slippery slush.

cards.front: How does the ablative absolute 'arboribus circa immanibus deiectis detruncatisque' work grammatically?
cards.answer: It describes a completed background action — the huge trees having already been felled and stripped of branches before the main action.

cards.front: Why did the cavalry report to Hannibal that the cliff path was impassable in Passage G?
cards.answer: A landslide had torn away part of the path, leaving a drop of almost 1,000 feet with nothing to grab onto.

cards.front: Name the five parts a full genetic diagram must include.
cards.answer: Parental phenotypes and genotypes / Gametes produced by each parent / A 2x2 Punnett square / Offspring genotypes with phenotypes stated / Probabilities or ratios

cards.front: Why is there a 50:50 chance of a baby being male or female?
cards.answer: Fathers can pass either an X or a Y chromosome in their sperm, giving an equal chance of XX or XY.

cards.front: Why do actual offspring ratios from a genetic cross sometimes differ from the expected ratio?
cards.answer: The ratios are only probabilities based on chance, so actual results may vary, especially with small samples.

title: African Drumming: Polyrhythm, Master Drummers and Oral Tradition
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the three tones a djembe player can produce on the drum.
cards.answer: Bass / Tone / Slap

cards.front: Give the three sizes of dunun drum by name.
cards.answer: Kenkeni / Sangban / Dundunba

cards.front: Why is African drumming described as belonging to an oral tradition?
cards.answer: It is passed down by ear and imitation, with no written notation, so children learn by watching experienced players.

cards.front: How does texture typically build in a piece like Rhythms of the Malinke?
cards.answer: It opens with a single dunun or bell pattern, then further dunun and djembe parts enter one by one adding ostinato layers.

cards.front: Name the four customer needs the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Price / Quality / Choice / Convenience

cards.front: Name the four sources of secondary research given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Internet / Published market reports / Government statistics / Industry trade bodies

cards.front: Why can getting price and quality wrong threaten a business's survival?
cards.answer: The wrong price loses customers to cheaper rivals or cuts profit, while poor quality drives customers away and spreads negative reviews.

cards.front: Why does market research reduce risk when launching a new product?
cards.answer: It gives evidence of what customers want before money is spent on production, narrowing uncertainty even though it can't eliminate risk entirely.

title: Gender, Stereotypes and the Mulvey Male Gaze
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three example stereotypes the lesson gives to show how stereotypes work as cognitive shortcuts.
cards.answer: A gruff older male detective / A vain teenage girl obsessed with looks / A nerdy male computer scientist
items: A vain teenage girl obsessed with looks

cards.front: Name the three examples of counter-types given in the lesson.
cards.answer: A male nurse / A female action hero / An older woman shown as professionally authoritative
items: An older woman shown as professionally authoritative

cards.front: Why do most contemporary media scholars favour social constructionism over essentialism?
cards.answer: Because it can explain why gender representations change over time and vary across cultures.

cards.front: How do stereotypes become naturalised so audiences see them as reality rather than construction?
cards.answer: Through repetition across hundreds of media products, genres, platforms and time periods until audiences stop noticing the construction.

title: The Nervous System and Reflex Arc
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the five parts of the brain named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cerebrum / Cerebellum / Medulla oblongata / Hypothalamus / Pituitary gland

cards.front: Name the four variables the lesson says could affect ruler drop reaction time results.
cards.answer: Caffeine / Fatigue / Distractions / Practice

cards.front: Why do synapses only allow impulses to travel in one direction?
cards.answer: Because neurotransmitters are released from the pre-synaptic side only, and receptors are only present on the post-synaptic side.

cards.front: Why is the ruler drop test a measure of voluntary reaction rather than a true reflex?
cards.answer: Because the information passes through the brain (visual cortex to motor cortex) rather than being processed only in the spinal cord.

cards.front: Name the three irreversible losses Golding uses to track the loss of innocence.
cards.answer: Percival forgets his name and address / The unnamed littlun dies in the first fire / Simon is murdered by the group
items: Percival forgets his name and address
The unnamed littlun dies in the first fire
Simon is murdered by the group

cards.front: What five-step pattern does the lesson give for analysing the printed extract?
cards.answer: Point / Quotation / Analysis of language / Effect on reader / Link to Golding's purpose

cards.front: Why do most of the boys choose to follow Jack rather than Ralph?
cards.answer: Following a strong leader is simpler than thinking for themselves; authoritarianism offers protection, belonging and excitement, while democracy demands effort and self-discipline.

cards.front: How does Roger's story arc support Golding's claim that evil is innate?
cards.answer: Roger moves from throwing stones to deliberately missing to committing murder, showing civilisation's taboo alone restrained his cruelty, and once removed, violence became inevitable.

cards.front: Name the three combined factors the lesson gives for why UK landscapes vary.
cards.answer: Geology (hard upland rocks vs softer lowland rocks) / Climate (wetter, cooler in north and west) / Human activity (farming, settlement and tourism)
items: Geology (hard upland rocks vs softer lowland rocks)
Climate (wetter, cooler in north and west)

cards.front: Name the three management strategies used in the Lake District National Park to handle tourist pressure.
cards.answer: Footpath repair / Visitor management / Planning controls

cards.front: How did glaciers shape the Lake District's landscape?
cards.answer: Glaciers carved deep U-shaped valleys, ribbon lakes such as Windermere, and sharp ridges.

cards.front: Why do cereals and root crops thrive in the Norfolk Broads?
cards.answer: Drier continental air brings only about 600mm of rain a year onto deep, fertile soils.

title: The Revolt of the Earls & William’s Legacy
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five effects the 1075 revolt had on the rebel earls and their earldoms.
cards.answer: Roger's lands forfeited and imprisoned for life / Ralph's estates confiscated / Earldom of Hereford abolished / Earldom of Norfolk abolished / William never let earls hold such power again
items: Roger's lands forfeited and imprisoned for life
William never let earls hold such power again

cards.front: What four traits does the lesson use to describe William the Conqueror's character?
cards.answer: Ruthless / Politically shrewd / Militarily brilliant / Deeply religious

cards.front: Why did the 1075 revolt collapse so quickly?
cards.answer: The rebels could not join forces: Roger was blocked at the River Severn, Ralph fled, and a Danish fleet arrived too late.

cards.front: How did William Rufus defeat Odo's 1088 revolt?
cards.answer: He secured the loyalty of the English people and key Norman barons by promising good government and lower taxes.

cards.front: Name the four actions the lesson gives that show Scrooge reversing his cruelty from Stave 1.
cards.answer: Sends the prize turkey anonymously / Donates to charity collectors he rejected / Attends Fred's Christmas party / Raises Bob Cratchit's salary
items: Donates to charity collectors he rejected

cards.front: Why does Dickens make the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come silent throughout Stave 4?
cards.answer: Its silence forces Scrooge to interpret the terrifying visions alone, making the reader share his growing horror.

cards.front: How does Dickens use the contrast between the unnamed dead man and Tiny Tim's death to make his message about greed?
cards.answer: The man dies alone and mocked while Tiny Tim dies mourned by loving family, showing greed leads to an empty death and love creates lasting bonds.

title: England before 1066 and the Norman impact on migration
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three claimants to the English throne after Edward the Confessor died in 1066.
cards.answer: Harold Godwinson / Harald Hardrada of Norway / William, Duke of Normandy

cards.front: What four things did Norman migrants bring with them to England after 1066?
cards.answer: their language (Norman French) / their legal customs / their building techniques / their ecclesiastical networks

cards.front: Why did William I launch the Harrying of the North in 1069-70?
cards.answer: Danish forces had allied with English rebels in 1069 to challenge William's authority, so he responded with deliberate destruction.

cards.front: Why is the Domesday Book's category of 'Frenchmen' significant evidence of Norman impact?
cards.answer: It recorded Frenchmen as a distinct legal category on hundreds of manors, showing rapid replacement of the English landowning class with a French elite.

title: Bush, Thatcher and Building the Coalition
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three Arab contributions to the coalition described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Egypt sent two divisions / Syria sent one division / Saudi Arabia provided forces and bases
items: Saudi Arabia provided forces and bases

cards.front: Name the four financial contributions to the $61 billion Gulf War cost given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Saudi Arabia paid about $16 billion / Kuwait-in-exile paid about $16 billion / Germany paid about $6 billion / Japan paid about $13 billion

cards.front: Why was it crucial for the coalition to include visible Arab support?
cards.answer: Without Arab cover the operation would look like a colonial war by Christian powers on a Muslim country, letting Saddam's pan-Arab framing gain support.

cards.front: Why did Gorbachev's refusal to veto the UN resolutions matter for the coalition?
cards.answer: It showed Soviet acquiescence despite Iraq being a former client, denying Saddam the cover of superpower rivalry.

cards.front: Name the five design strategies given in the specification.
cards.answer: Collaboration / User-centred design / Systems approach / Iterative design / Avoiding design fixation

cards.front: Name the four techniques the lesson gives for avoiding design fixation.
cards.answer: Brainstorming / Mind mapping / SCAMPER / Looking at the problem from different perspectives
items: Looking at the problem from different perspectives

cards.front: How does user-centred design reduce the risk of a product failing in practice?
cards.answer: By gathering data through interviews, observation and usability testing, then designing specifically around those findings.

cards.front: Why do designers use physical models as well as drawings?
cards.answer: Physical models help test form, proportion and ergonomics in ways that drawings cannot.

title: Religious Life and Catholic Forms of Expression
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three monastic orders described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Benedictines / Cistercians / Trappists

cards.front: Name the three mendicant orders described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Franciscans / Dominicans / Carmelites

cards.front: Why are the evangelical counsels seen as freeing rather than just a sacrifice?
cards.answer: They liberate the religious from anxiety about possessions, divided loyalties and self-will, making them wholly available for God and others.

cards.front: Why does Michelangelo's Creation of Adam show God reaching to touch Adam's finger?
cards.answer: It visually shows that human life is a gift from God and that humans are made in the divine image.

cards.front: Name the three boys stranded on the island in Ballantyne's The Coral Island.
cards.answer: Ralph / Jack / Peterkin

cards.front: How does Simon's encounter with the Lord of the Flies in Chapter 8 show Golding's view on evil?
cards.answer: The beast tells Simon it cannot be hunted and killed, revealing that evil lives inside every boy, not as an external monster.

cards.front: Why did Golding set Lord of the Flies during an unspecified nuclear war?
cards.answer: To show adults have already destroyed the world through the same violence the boys will replicate on the island.

title: Sacraments, Mission and Evangelisation in Britain
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four steps in the Sacrament of Reconciliation.
cards.answer: Confession of sins to a priest / Contrition (genuine sorrow) / Penance (prayer or service) / Absolution given in Christ's name
items: Confession of sins to a priest

cards.front: Name the four Catholic groups the lesson gives as promoting mission in Britain.
cards.answer: CAFOD / Catholic Education Service / Missio / St Vincent de Paul Society

cards.front: Why do Catholics celebrate Mass for the dead?
cards.answer: Because of the Catholic belief in purgatory and the communion of saints.

cards.front: How does the Anointing of the Sick help a person who is seriously ill or dying?
cards.answer: It strengthens the person spiritually, may restore physical health if God wills it, and prepares them for eternal life.

cards.front: The lesson gives four things a business's legal structure affects — what are they?
cards.answer: How much control owners keep / How profits are shared / Where the business can raise money / What happens if things go wrong
items: Where the business can raise money
What happens if things go wrong

cards.front: Why would a lone builder just starting out usually choose to be a sole trader?
cards.answer: It's cheap and simple with no reporting, and the work is low-risk enough to accept unlimited liability.

cards.front: Why is the key difference between an Ltd and a Plc about how they raise money?
cards.answer: An Ltd can only sell shares to people it invites, while a Plc can sell shares to anyone through the stock exchange.

cards.front: Name the three people who carry out the attack on Adam.
cards.answer: Josh / Logan / Paul

cards.front: What four things make up the long aftermath of the attack that Blackman insists on showing, instead of skipping to recovery?
cards.answer: Hospitalisation / Depression / Withdrawal / Suicidal ideation

cards.front: How does Blackman make Josh's violence psychologically coherent rather than simple hatred?
cards.answer: His violence comes from shame, not hatred, as he attacks the version of himself he cannot accept.

cards.front: Why is Adam's depression after the attack presented as a rational response rather than weakness?
cards.answer: It is a reaction to being severely beaten by someone he trusted while those who might have protected him could not help.

cards.front: What three safety precautions does the lesson give for investigating Hooke's Law?
cards.answer: Do not overload the spring / Use a clamp stand secured to the bench / Place a cushion or tray below the masses
items: Use a clamp stand secured to the bench
Place a cushion or tray below the masses

cards.front: What three types of material does the lesson describe different density-measuring methods for?
cards.answer: Regular solid / Irregular solid / Liquid

cards.front: Why does deforming an object (stretching, bending or compressing) require at least two forces?
cards.answer: A single force would simply accelerate the object rather than change its shape, so two opposing forces are needed.

cards.front: Why does ice float on liquid water even though it is a solid?
cards.answer: Ice has a more open crystal lattice structure than liquid water, making it less dense despite being solid.

cards.front: Name the three pieces of evidence for evolution given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Fossils / Antibiotic-resistant bacteria / Comparative anatomy

cards.front: Name the seven levels of Linnaeus's classification system, from broadest to narrowest.
cards.answer: Kingdom / Phylum / Class / Order / Family / Genus / Species

cards.front: How do antibiotic-resistant bacteria show natural selection happening?
cards.answer: Resistant bacteria survive antibiotic exposure and reproduce, so resistance becomes more common, showing selection in action.

cards.front: Why does comparative anatomy support the idea that species share common ancestors?
cards.answer: Similar bone structures found in different species suggest those species evolved from the same ancestor.

title: The Home Front in the Second World War
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three women's auxiliary services mentioned that women could be conscripted into.
cards.answer: ATS / WRNS / WAAF

cards.front: Why did the government introduce blackout regulations during the war?
cards.answer: To cover all windows after dark so enemy bombers could not identify towns from the air.

cards.front: Why have historians like Angus Calder questioned the 'Blitz spirit' narrative?
cards.answer: Because censorship suppressed panic and looting, and class inequalities like wealthier families leaving cities were glossed over.

cards.front: Why did women's wartime factory work challenge pre-war assumptions?
cards.answer: Because factory managers who doubted women's ability to operate machinery found them capable and productive.

title: The Gunpowder Plot and the start of the Bloody Code
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three items early modern town watchmen carried on patrol.
cards.answer: A lantern / A staff / A rattle

cards.front: Name the four corporal punishments the lesson gives for theft, vagabondage and minor disorder.
cards.answer: Flogging / Branding / Ear-cropping / The pillory and stocks

cards.front: Why did the state rely on public, harsh punishment in the early modern period instead of a police force?
cards.answer: With no professional police, authorities used terrifying public spectacle as deterrence to make onlookers too scared to commit crime.

cards.front: Why did Parliament create so many new capital offences under the Bloody Code?
cards.answer: Fear of crime, lack of an effective police force, and landowners in Parliament wanting to protect property drove its expansion.

title: Creating the Dictatorship: Reichstag Fire to Führer
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three tactics Hitler used to secure a two-thirds majority for the Enabling Act.
cards.answer: Banned the 81 Communist deputies / Used the SA to intimidate opponents / Promised the Centre Party Catholic rights
items: Used the SA to intimidate opponents
Promised the Centre Party Catholic rights

cards.front: Name the three major consequences of the Night of the Long Knives given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Removed the SA as a rival power / Won over the army / Showed Hitler would use murder to keep power
items: Removed the SA as a rival power
Showed Hitler would use murder to keep power

cards.front: Why was Hitler alarmed by Ernst Röhm's ambitions for the SA in 1934?
cards.answer: Röhm wanted the SA to absorb the army and push a socialist 'second revolution', threatening army support and industrialist backing Hitler needed.

cards.front: Why did other political parties fail to resist Hitler's takeover in 1933?
cards.answer: The SA and Gestapo arrested opponents and sent them to camps like Dachau, while many Germans accepted lost democracy for promised stability and recovery.

cards.front: Name the five principal methods for joining polymer components given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Solvent/chemical adhesives / Epoxy adhesives / Plastic welding / Mechanical fixings / Designed-in snap-fit features

cards.front: Name the three plastic welding methods described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Hot gas welding / Ultrasonic welding / Hot plate welding

cards.front: Why can nuts and bolts with washers reduce the risk of cracking a brittle polymer like acrylic?
cards.answer: The washers distribute the clamping force over a larger area instead of concentrating stress at one point.

cards.front: Why does eliminating a painting or plating stage for self-finishing polymers benefit production economically?
cards.answer: It removes the need for capital equipment, material, energy, time and VOC emissions associated with a secondary finishing process.

cards.front: The lesson says the Roman forum was 'at once' four things. Name them.
cards.answer: A marketplace / A law court / A political meeting place / A religious precinct

cards.front: According to the Key Fact, which four things stood around the Pompeii forum?
cards.answer: Temple of Jupiter / The basilica / The comitium / Offices of magistrates

cards.front: Why was the macellum built as a separate building from the rest of the forum?
cards.answer: To separate the messier business of food retail from the more formal civic activities at the forum's centre.

cards.front: What does the fruit sellers' electoral inscription reveal about civic life in Pompeii?
cards.answer: It shows tradespeople actively took part in local elections and highlights how competitive those elections were.

title: The Six Day War and Its Aftermath, June 1967
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three fronts on which Israel fought during the Six Day War of June 1967.
cards.answer: Southern front against Egypt in Sinai / Eastern front against Jordan in West Bank / Northern front against Syria on Golan Heights
items: Southern front against Egypt in Sinai
Eastern front against Jordan in West Bank
Northern front against Syria on Golan Heights

cards.front: How did the pre-emptive air strike of 5 June 1967 make Israel's rapid ground victories possible?
cards.answer: Destroying about 300 Egyptian aircraft on the ground gave Israel air supremacy on every front from the first morning, enabling the ground campaign.

cards.front: Why did the Khartoum Resolution of September 1967 close off the diplomatic route opened by Resolution 242?
cards.answer: The Arab League's 'three nos' ruled out peace, recognition and negotiation with Israel, blocking immediate progress on land for peace.

cards.front: Name the five major themes that essays on Frankenstein connect to.
cards.answer: Dangerous knowledge and ambition / Creation and responsibility / Monstrosity and prejudice / Isolation and companionship / Nature versus nurture

cards.front: What are the three assessment strands your response to the 19th-century novel question is judged on?
cards.answer: AO1: critical response with well-chosen references / AO2: analysis of the writer's methods / AO3: understanding of context
items: AO1: critical response with well-chosen references
AO2: analysis of the writer's methods

cards.front: Why does the passive phrasing 'it breathed hard' distance Victor from responsibility for the Creature?
cards.answer: The passive construction removes Victor as the active subject of the sentence, distancing him from responsibility for the being he created.

cards.front: How does Shelley's own biography connect to Victor's rejection of the Creature in the creation scene?
cards.answer: Shelley's own mother died in childbirth, making her deeply aware that creation carries moral obligations, which Victor evades.

cards.front: Name the five stages the argument moves through across the stanzas of 'Decomposition'.
cards.answer: Description of the photograph / Dehumanising stone and fossil imagery / The indifferent crowd / The speaker's original pride in his composition / His present-day reconsideration
items: The speaker's original pride in his composition

cards.front: Name the three anthology poems the lesson pairs with Ghose's 'Decomposition'.
cards.answer: War Photographer by Carol Ann Duffy / Disabled by Wilfred Owen / Remains by Simon Armitage
items: War Photographer by Carol Ann Duffy

cards.front: Why does Ghose's plain, documentary style make the final confession in 'Decomposition' land more powerfully?
cards.answer: It breaks sharply from the detached, matter-of-fact tone used throughout the rest of the poem.

cards.front: How does the structure of 'Decomposition' mirror the way memory works?
cards.answer: The speaker isn't just describing an old photograph but re-examining it, so his understanding changes stanza by stanza.

cards.front: Name the three functions Russell's songs serve in Blood Brothers.
cards.answer: Windows into characters' inner lives / Vehicles for Russell's political argument / Structural bridges that compress time

cards.front: Name the three parallel scenes Russell uses to make the class divide visible on stage.
cards.answer: Policeman aggressive with Johnstones, polite with Lyons / Mickey gets a factory job, Eddie goes to university / Mickey made redundant, Eddie becomes a councillor
items: Policeman aggressive with Johnstones, polite with Lyons
Mickey gets a factory job, Eddie goes to university
Mickey made redundant, Eddie becomes a councillor

cards.front: How does the cyclical structure reinforce the play's theme of fate?
cards.answer: It makes the tragic outcome feel inevitable, just as the class system makes Mickey's downfall feel inevitable.

cards.front: How does the cross-cutting between storylines in the final act affect the audience?
cards.answer: It creates a sense of accelerating catastrophe as multiple storylines converge, making the audience feel powerless to stop the inevitable ending.

cards.front: The lesson pairs four sets of contrasting characters in Romeo and Juliet. Name the four contrasts.
cards.answer: Romeo's idealism vs Mercutio's cynicism / Juliet's decisiveness vs Nurse's earthiness / Tybalt's honour-rage vs Benvolio's peacemaking / Mercutio's fluid energy vs Tybalt's rigid control
items: Mercutio's fluid energy vs Tybalt's rigid control

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Mercutio's death is the clearest demonstration that the feud destroys bystanders?
cards.answer: Because Mercutio belongs to neither the Montagues nor the Capulets, yet still dies because of their feud.

cards.front: How should a performer change Romeo's voice between Act One and Act Three?
cards.answer: From a languid, self-absorbed, meandering pace early on to sudden volume, clipped pace and physical stillness by Act Three.

cards.front: Why does Lord Capulet's staging change so much in Act Three, Scene Five?
cards.answer: Because he shifts from a magnanimous host in Act One to a threatening, physically imposing father when Juliet refuses to marry Paris.

title: Earth Hazards: Earthquakes, Eruptions, Landslides and Tsunamis
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four triggers of landslides given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Earthquake shaking / Volcanic activity loading slopes with ash and lava / Heavy rainfall saturating soils / Undercutting by rivers or coastal erosion
items: Volcanic activity loading slopes with ash and lava
Undercutting by rivers or coastal erosion

cards.front: Name the three causes of subsidence given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Withdrawal of groundwater or hydrocarbons / Dissolving limestone (sinkholes) / Mining

cards.front: Why does a magnitude 7 earthquake release far more energy than a magnitude 6 earthquake?
cards.answer: The moment magnitude scale is logarithmic, so each whole number increase means roughly 32 times more energy released.

cards.front: Why does low-viscosity basaltic magma produce effusive eruptions instead of explosive ones?
cards.answer: Its low viscosity lets gases escape gradually, so pressure doesn't build up and lava flows out rather than exploding.

title: Selecting Papers & Boards for a Purpose
subject: design-technology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three types of forces packaging must withstand during manufacture, transit and retail display.
cards.answer: Compressive forces (stacking) / Tensile forces (pulling walls apart when lifted) / Shear forces (at glued joints when dropped)

cards.front: Name the three standard stock forms paper and board are supplied in by merchants.
cards.answer: Sheets / Reams / Rolls

cards.front: Why is solid white board (SWB) the default choice for luxury packaging and cosmetics?
cards.answer: It achieves the highest whiteness and brightness values, making colours appear vivid and conveying premium quality.

cards.front: Why might a designer choose clay-coated board with a water-based barrier instead of foil-lined board?
cards.answer: It gives moisture protection but is recyclable, avoiding foil-lined board's end-of-life recycling problem, though it is a less effective barrier.

title: Brahman and the Three Features of the Divine
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three similar-sounding words the lesson distinguishes and what each means.
cards.answer: Brahman - ultimate reality, ground of all being / brahman (lower case) - sacred power in Vedic ritual / Brahmin - the priestly caste of Hindu society
items: Brahman - ultimate reality, ground of all being
brahman (lower case) - sacred power in Vedic ritual
Brahmin - the priestly caste of Hindu society

cards.front: Why do Hindus honour a murti (sacred image) in a mandir?
cards.answer: Because the murti represents divine reality, so worshippers are reaching towards Brahman, not worshipping a piece of stone.

cards.front: How does the ocean-and-waves analogy explain the relationship between the universe and Brahman?
cards.answer: The universe emanates from Brahman like waves from the ocean - the waves are real, but ultimately made of ocean.

cards.front: What four groups did Hitler tailor his promises to during the Depression, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: The unemployed — jobs and economic recovery / Middle classes and farmers — protection of property and anti-communism / Nationalists — national greatness and revenge for Versailles / Those who saw coalitions as weak — strong leadership
items: The unemployed — jobs and economic recovery
Middle classes and farmers — protection of property and anti-communism
Nationalists — national greatness and revenge for Versailles
Those who saw coalitions as weak — strong leadership

cards.front: What four social consequences of the Depression does the lesson describe in Germany?
cards.answer: Hunger / Poverty / Family breakdown / A pervasive sense of hopelessness

cards.front: How did the Wall Street Crash trigger economic collapse in Germany?
cards.answer: American banks recalled the short-term loans underpinning Germany's recovery, so factories lost credit, banks failed, and unemployment rocketed.

cards.front: How did the political violence of 1932 damage support for the Weimar Republic?
cards.answer: Hundreds of political killings showed Weimar couldn't protect citizens, discrediting democracy and pushing voters towards parties promising decisive action.

cards.front: List the four groups seated in the Colosseum, from front to back.
cards.answer: Senators / Equestrian class / Ordinary male citizens / Women and the poor

cards.front: Name the three major types of gladiator described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Murmillo / Retiarius / Thraex

cards.front: Why did the seating arrangement inside the Colosseum matter beyond just seating people?
cards.answer: The tiers corresponded to social rank, making the amphitheatre a visual map of Roman society.

cards.front: Why might an editor choose to spare a defeated gladiator instead of having him killed?
cards.answer: Killing a well-trained gladiator unnecessarily was costly, whereas keeping him alive meant he could fight again.

cards.front: Name the six future tense endings used for all French verbs, in order (je/tu/il/nous/vous/ils).
cards.answer: -ai / -as / -a / -ons / -ez / -ont

cards.front: Give the four environmental problems named in the lesson's vocabulary list (besides pollution and global warming).
cards.answer: l'effet de serre / la déforestation / les déchets / les espèces menacées

cards.front: How do you form the future tense of a regular -re verb like prendre?
cards.answer: Drop the final -e from the infinitive, then add the future endings, e.g. je prendrai.

cards.front: How does the future tense differ between regular and irregular verbs in French?
cards.answer: Regular verbs use the infinitive as the stem, while irregular verbs use a special stem that must be learned by heart.

cards.front: Name the three barriers used in modern landfill engineering to stop leachate reaching groundwater, from bottom to top.
cards.answer: Geomembrane plastic liner / Compacted clay layer / Drainage pipes collecting leachate to treatment
items: Drainage pipes collecting leachate to treatment

cards.front: Name the three remediation options the lesson gives for cleaning up contaminated groundwater.
cards.answer: Pump-and-treat systems / Permeable reactive barriers / Bioremediation using microorganisms

cards.front: Why does chalk make a good aquifer despite having tiny pores?
cards.answer: Chalk has high porosity but most water moves through its extensive network of fractures and joints instead of the pores.

cards.front: Why must a good aquifer rock be both porous and permeable?
cards.answer: Porosity lets it store water while permeability lets water flow through it fast enough to supply a well.

title: The Gulling Scenes & Don John's Plot
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: What three factors does the lesson give as reasons behind Don John's villainy?
cards.answer: he is illegitimate / he is socially marginalised / he was recently defeated in war by his own brother
items: he was recently defeated in war by his own brother

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare give Beatrice's gulling scene a different tone from Benedick's?
cards.answer: Hero speaks in verse to signal emotional sincerity, so Beatrice's surrender feels dignified rather than comic like Benedick's.

cards.front: How does Don John's plot create dramatic irony for the audience in Acts 2-3?
cards.answer: The audience knows the gulling is benign and Don John's plot is a malicious fabrication, so they feel both comic pleasure and growing dread.

cards.front: Why is Margaret's role in the window scene ambiguous?
cards.answer: Shakespeare never explains whether she knowingly helped Borachio deceive Claudio, and she is never punished for it.

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson gives as gaining from hyperinflation in 1923.
cards.answer: People with debts / Businesspeople and industrialists with physical assets / Foreign visitors with hard currency / Shrewd speculators
items: Businesspeople and industrialists with physical assets

cards.front: Name the three effects of the Ruhr occupation on German society and economy given in the lesson.
cards.answer: 150,000 Germans expelled from homes / Factories and mines seized / German economy ground to a halt
items: German economy ground to a halt

cards.front: How did German government policy during the First World War lay the roots of hyperinflation?
cards.answer: The government borrowed heavily and printed money to fund the war instead of raising taxes, increasing money in circulation without increasing goods.

cards.front: Why did the increase in money supply after the First World War cause prices to rise?
cards.answer: The amount of money in circulation increased massively but the amount of goods available did not, so prices rose.

cards.front: Name the three groups of characters Syal uses to populate Tollington.
cards.answer: The nosy neighbours / The struggling families / The men who drink at the pub while women hold everything together
items: The men who drink at the pub while women hold everything together

cards.front: What three things do the early comic episodes show Meena doing?
cards.answer: Steals the charity tin and lets another child take the blame / Tells outrageous stories to get attention / Navigates the village's social minefield with bravado and desperation
items: Steals the charity tin and lets another child take the blame
Tells outrageous stories to get attention
Navigates the village's social minefield with bravado and desperation

cards.front: Why does Meena feel embarrassed by the Aunties' gatherings?
cards.answer: She sees them through English eyes and cringes at how different they seem, not yet realising this is a source of strength.

cards.front: How does Syal's early comic writing serve a serious purpose in the novel?
cards.answer: It makes Meena sympathetic to the reader, so the later darker themes of racism and betrayal hit with greater emotional impact.

title: Spitalfields: site introduction and Huguenot weavers
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three streets the lesson says Huguenot weavers settled along in Spitalfields.
cards.answer: Fournier Street / Princelet Street / Elder Street

cards.front: Name the three regions of France the lesson says most Huguenot migrants came from.
cards.answer: Normandy / Poitou / Loire Valley

cards.front: Why did Parliament fund the building of Christ Church Spitalfields?
cards.answer: To assert the Church of England's presence in a district full of foreign Protestants, as a statement of permanence and prosperity.

cards.front: Why is Brick Lane Jamme Masjid described as the most useful building for studying this site?
cards.answer: Because it embodies four different migrant communities using the same building in the same street across three centuries.

title: Core Beliefs: Six Articles and the Five Roots
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the five beliefs that both Sunni and Shi'a Muslims hold in common.
cards.answer: Tawhid (oneness of Allah) / Prophethood of Muhammad / The Qur'an as final revealed scripture / The five daily prayers / Expectation of a Day of Judgement
items: The Qur'an as final revealed scripture
Expectation of a Day of Judgement

cards.front: Which five beliefs does Surah 4:136 explicitly name?
cards.answer: Allah / His angels / His books / His messengers / The Last Day

cards.front: Why do Sunni Muslims reject the Shi'a doctrine of the Imamate?
cards.answer: Sunnis believe the community should be guided by the consensus of scholars and the Sunnah, not a hereditary line of infallible Imams.

cards.front: How does the belief in Al-Adl shape the Shi'a understanding of suffering?
cards.answer: Since Allah cannot act unjustly, suffering and hardship are understood as purposeful tests rather than random events.

cards.front: Why does HMS Thunder Child's destruction of two tripods matter, given the tripods' usual power?
cards.answer: It shows individual courage can briefly overcome even overwhelming Martian technology, before the ship is overwhelmed.

cards.front: How does Wells show that class distinctions collapse during the London exodus?
cards.answer: A fine carriage becomes no better than a cart, and the strong take from the weak regardless of wealth.

title: Collectivisation and the War on the Kulaks
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four methods the lesson gives for how peasants resisted collectivisation.
cards.answer: Slaughtered their livestock / Buried grain / Broke tools / Fled to the cities

cards.front: Why did Stalin abandon the NEP and launch the Great Turn in 1928?
cards.answer: The 1927 grain procurement crisis meant peasants were not delivering enough grain, and Stalin needed grain to feed cities and fund industrialisation.

cards.front: How did the famine of 1932-33 come about?
cards.answer: Sown area and grain output collapsed, yet the state raised procurement quotas to fund industrial imports, causing famine.

cards.front: Why did agricultural output remain poor even though collectivisation gave the state political control?
cards.answer: Peasant resistance like livestock slaughter and disrupted farming meant grain output did not regain 1928 levels for decades.

cards.front: Name the four discoveries Galileo made with his telescope from 1609.
cards.answer: Phases of Venus / Four moons of Jupiter / Mountains and craters on the Moon / Sunspots
items: Mountains and craters on the Moon

cards.front: Name three advantages of reflecting telescopes over refractors given in the lesson.
cards.answer: No chromatic aberration / Mirrors can be made much larger / Shorter tube lengths / Lower cost per unit aperture
items: Mirrors can be made much larger

cards.front: Why does the human eye struggle to see faint astronomical objects compared to a telescope?
cards.answer: Its pupil is only about 7 mm wide, limiting light collected, and it cannot accumulate light over time like a camera.

cards.front: Why is there a practical maximum useful magnification for any telescope?
cards.answer: Beyond about 2x the aperture in mm, the image becomes too dim and blurred by atmospheric turbulence to show more detail.

title: Restoring Royal Authority: The Hundred Rolls and Quo Warranto
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What four things did Hundred Rolls commissioners ask local juries about in every hundred?
cards.answer: Missing royal lands / Sheriffs taking bribes / Lords running private courts / Liberties claimed without permission

cards.front: Name the three things the Hundred Rolls findings directly shaped, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: First Statute of Westminster (1275) / Statute of Gloucester (1278) / The Quo Warranto inquiries

cards.front: Why did many barons struggle to answer the Quo Warranto justices when challenged over their liberties?
cards.answer: They often had no charter because the rights had simply been exercised for so long that everyone had stopped asking by what authority.

cards.front: Why did Edward I compromise with the Statute of Quo Warranto instead of stripping barons of their liberties completely?
cards.answer: He could not afford a new civil war, so barons kept most rights while the crown still asserted all jurisdiction came from it.

cards.front: Name the three eras of poetic form the Time and Place anthology spans.
cards.answer: Romantic formal structures / Literary Heritage verse / contemporary free verse

cards.front: Which three poets use quatrains (4-line stanzas) in the anthology?
cards.answer: Blake ("London") / Thomas ("Adlestrop") / Davidson ("In Romney Marsh")

cards.front: Why does Blake use four quatrains instead of a sonnet in "London"?
cards.answer: The tight rhymed stanzas hold his anger in, offering control where a sonnet's form would suggest praise.

cards.front: How does the structure of Thomas's "Adlestrop" reflect its meaning?
cards.answer: It expands from a specific train platform to "all the birds of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire," widening the focus outward.

cards.front: Name the three sounds that break the 'peculiar, intense silence' at Eel Marsh House.
cards.answer: The bumping of a rocking chair / A child crying / The sound of the pony and trap
items: The bumping of a rocking chair
The sound of the pony and trap

cards.front: What items does Hill list inside the preserved nursery?
cards.answer: A small bed / A chest of toys / A child's chair / Clothes

cards.front: Why does crossing the causeway make Arthur's situation a 'point of no return'?
cards.answer: The causeway is only passable at low tide, so once the tide rises Arthur is trapped on the island with no escape.

cards.front: How does Hill's language show Arthur's psychological deterioration by Chapter 8?
cards.answer: His sentences become shorter and more fragmented compared to the measured, professional prose of earlier chapters, showing his mind under siege.

title: Black Power, the Panthers and the 1968 Olympics
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five 'survival programmes' the Black Panthers ran for their communities.
cards.answer: Free Breakfast for Children / Free health clinics / Sickle-cell anaemia testing / Free legal aid / Escort services for the elderly / Liberation Schools

cards.front: Why did SNCC activists break with nonviolent direct action by 1966?
cards.answer: The 1964 and 1965 Acts had not touched ghetto poverty, racist policing or Northern segregation, so activists concluded nonviolence alone could not deliver freedom.

cards.front: Name the four different ways characters in Journey's End cope with fear.
cards.answer: Stanhope uses alcohol / Osborne uses routine and calm / Trotter uses food and humour / Hibbert tries to escape

cards.front: What four things does each paragraph of a modern-text essay need, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: A point / A quotation (embedded) / Analysis of language / A link to context (AO3)

cards.front: How does Osborne demonstrate heroism in Journey's End?
cards.answer: Osborne shows calm decency and willingly leads the dangerous raid despite knowing the risk, making heroism about willingness not fearlessness.

cards.front: Why is Trotter's focus on the next meal seen as a form of heroism?
cards.answer: His determination to focus on food rather than fear is a survival strategy that keeps him and others grounded.

cards.front: How does the relationship between monastics and lay Buddhists sustain Buddhism?
cards.answer: Monastics provide teaching and spiritual merit while lay people provide material support, an interdependence sustaining Buddhism for over 2,500 years.

cards.front: Why must monks remain in their monastery during Vassa?
cards.answer: Vassa runs during the monsoon season so monks can focus on intensive meditation and study without travelling.

cards.front: Why does Sallust describe Sempronia's crimes using the word 'virilis' (manly)?
cards.answer: Because Sallust saw boldness as a male virtue, so he could not simply call her actions bold without marking them as unnatural for a woman.

cards.front: How does Virgil's introduction of Camilla as 'an Amazon' before naming her shape how readers judge her?
cards.answer: It signals immediately that she should be read as a legendary warrior-woman type, not an ordinary woman, before her name is even given.

cards.front: Why does Livy present Tullia driving her chariot over her father's corpse as shocking?
cards.answer: Because she deliberately chose that route over a longer one, showing disregard for family duty and horrifying even her own household gods.

cards.front: According to the lesson, why do Sempronia's talents fail to redeem her in Sallust's account?
cards.answer: Because Sallust judges her against feminine virtues like decus and pudicitia, which she lacked, so her talents become evidence of moral danger instead of praise.

cards.front: Name the three British garrisons besieged by Boer forces from late 1899.
cards.answer: Ladysmith / Mafeking / Kimberley

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four factors let the Boers fight so effectively early in the war?
cards.answer: Experienced farmers who knew the landscape / Skilled horsemen and marksmen / Equipped with modern Mauser rifles / Used guerrilla tactics to hit supply lines and retreat
items: Experienced farmers who knew the landscape
Used guerrilla tactics to hit supply lines and retreat

cards.front: Why did Kitchener introduce scorched earth tactics and concentration camps against the Boers?
cards.answer: To defeat the guerrilla campaign by denying Boer commandos food and support from farms and civilians.

cards.front: Why did British attitudes towards the war shift by 1901-1902?
cards.answer: Hobhouse's report exposing camp death rates caused public outcry, converting many moderates to criticism of the war.

title: Musical Devices and Cadences: The Composer's Toolkit
subject: music-eduqas

cards.front: Besides naming the cadence type, what four effects does the lesson say you should describe in an exam answer?
cards.answer: Final / Unfinished / Surprising / Gentle

cards.front: Why does a pedal note create tension in a passage of music?
cards.answer: It sustains a note in the bass while the harmony above changes, and the tension is released when the harmony matches the pedal note again.

cards.front: Why is the 'and He shall reign for ever and ever' passage in Handel's Hallelujah Chorus described as imitation rather than strict canon?
cards.answer: Because the parts diverge and combine freely rather than copying one another exactly all the way through.

cards.front: Name the five levels in the hierarchy of control measures, from most to least effective.
cards.answer: Elimination / Substitution / Engineering controls / Administrative controls / PPE

cards.front: Name three hazards mentioned during machining operations such as turning, milling and drilling.
cards.answer: Sharp swarf can cut skin / Swarf can enter eyes / Rotating chuck can catch loose clothing
items: Rotating chuck can catch loose clothing

cards.front: Why is risk assessed using both likelihood and severity rather than either alone?
cards.answer: Risk is likelihood multiplied by severity, so a hazard needs both factors judged together to decide how much control it needs.

cards.front: Why should engineering controls and administrative controls be described before PPE when explaining how to reduce a risk?
cards.answer: PPE only protects the wearer and doesn't remove the hazard, so engineering and administrative controls must be tried first as they are more effective.

cards.front: Name the three methods the lesson gives for sustainable forest management.
cards.answer: Selective logging / Replanting with native species / FSC certification

cards.front: Name the three types of alternative livelihood the lesson gives that let people earn money without clearing forest.
cards.answer: Ecotourism / Sustainable farming (agroforestry, shade-grown coffee, cacao) / Indigenous land rights

cards.front: Why does illegal wildlife and timber trade continue despite CITES?
cards.answer: Enforcement is patchy, so illegal logging and wildlife smuggling remain billion-pound criminal industries even though CITES lists species and requires permits.

cards.front: Why can REDD payments fail to actually protect threatened forest?
cards.answer: Monitoring is weak, so some payments go to areas that were never under threat, and political change can reverse progress.

cards.front: Name the three sinners the Porter imagines admitting to 'hell-gate', and the crime each represents.
cards.answer: A farmer who hoarded grain (self-interest) / An equivocator who committed treason (deception) / A tailor who stole cloth (theft)

cards.front: Name the three things 'innocent sleep' is said to represent in the play.
cards.answer: Innocence / Peace / The natural order

cards.front: Why is the floating dagger Macbeth sees before the murder deliberately ambiguous?
cards.answer: It could be a supernatural sign sent by the witches or a hallucination born from Macbeth's own guilty conscience, and either reading supports the play's themes.

cards.front: Why does Macbeth's language shift from the Latinate word 'incarnadine' to the blunt phrase 'making the green one red'?
cards.answer: The shift from elaborate Latinate language to blunt Anglo-Saxon words mirrors how horror strips away Macbeth's eloquence.

title: Restoration Stage, Coffee Houses and Women in Public Life
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three named Restoration comedy plays the lesson gives, with their authors.
cards.answer: The Man of Mode by Etherege (1676) / The Country Wife by Wycherley (1675) / The Way of the World by Congreve (1700)
items: The Man of Mode by Etherege (1676)
The Way of the World by Congreve (1700)

cards.front: Name the four examples the lesson gives of women's increased public visibility in Restoration England.
cards.answer: actresses became celebrities / female playwrights and poets earned by writing / women published in print on religion / royal mistresses exerted political influence at court
items: female playwrights and poets earned by writing
women published in print on religion
royal mistresses exerted political influence at court

cards.front: Why did women start playing female roles on the English public stage from December 1660?
cards.answer: Charles II's second royal letter, issued in 1662, made it explicit that women's parts were to be played by women instead of boys.

cards.front: Why is Restoration women's status described as a tension between visibility and law?
cards.answer: Women gained visible roles as actresses, writers and royal mistresses, but coverture still barred married women from owning property or suing independently.

cards.front: Give the reactivity series of metals listed in the lesson, from most to least reactive (11 items).
cards.answer: Potassium / Sodium / Calcium / Magnesium / Aluminium / Carbon / Zinc / Iron / Hydrogen / Copper / Silver / Gold

cards.front: Why is gold found in the Earth's crust as an uncombined element rather than as an ore?
cards.answer: Gold is very unreactive, so it does not readily react with other substances to form compounds.

cards.front: In the industrial purification of copper by electrolysis, why does the impure copper anode lose mass while the pure copper cathode gains mass?
cards.answer: The impure copper anode dissolves into the solution as ions, while pure copper is deposited onto the cathode.

cards.front: Why does iron displace copper from copper sulfate solution?
cards.answer: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from its salt solution.

title: The First New Deal: Hundred Days and the Alphabet Agencies
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six main alphabet agencies of the First New Deal (by their initials).
cards.answer: CCC / AAA / FERA / TVA / NRA / PWA

cards.front: Which three agencies fall under Roosevelt's 'Relief' and 'Reform' categories in the three Rs grouping?
cards.answer: FERA and CCC (Relief) / TVA (Reform) / FDIC under Glass-Steagall (Reform)

cards.front: Why did Roosevelt declare a four-day bank holiday on taking office in March 1933?
cards.answer: To stop the banking panic by closing every bank so inspectors could check their books before reopening only sound ones.

cards.front: How did the Emergency Banking Act and Glass-Steagall together restore confidence in banks?
cards.answer: They ensured only solvent banks reopened and insured deposits, so people trusted their money would still be there.

title: Migrants In & Out: Huguenots, Highland Clearances & Ulster
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six counties where land was confiscated for the Ulster Plantation.
cards.answer: Armagh / Cavan / Coleraine (later Londonderry) / Donegal / Fermanagh / Tyrone

cards.front: Name the three places in England where Huguenots settled and built up trades.
cards.answer: Spitalfields / Canterbury / Norwich

cards.front: Why did Britain welcome Huguenot refugees in 1685 when it had earlier expelled other groups?
