cards.answer: It began as a practical workaround because recording clean sound in controlled studio conditions was beyond the movement's tiny budgets.

title: Living through the Blitz: shelters, disasters and daily life
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three Tube stations the lesson gives as examples of direct hits that killed shelterers.
cards.answer: Balham (October 1940) / Bank (January 1941) / Marble Arch

cards.front: What four pieces of evidence does the lesson give showing London leisure continued during the Blitz?
cards.answer: Windmill Theatre stayed open / Cinema attendance rose / Dancehalls ran most nights / Proms continued at the Albert Hall
items: Proms continued at the Albert Hall

cards.front: How did the crush at Bethnal Green Tube station actually start on 3 March 1943?
cards.answer: A woman tripped on wet steps after a rocket-battery test was misheard as a bomb, and the crowd behind kept pushing.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say morale 'bent badly in places but did not break' during the Blitz?
cards.answer: Because fewer than 5% of Londoners evacuated long-term and work and absenteeism levels stayed largely under control despite low points.

cards.front: Vegetarian and vegan diets require careful planning to avoid deficiencies in which three nutrients?
cards.answer: Vitamin B12 / Iron / Calcium

cards.front: Name the three categories of alcohol misuse the lesson distinguishes.
cards.answer: Binge drinking / Alcohol abuse / Dependence

cards.front: Why does over-nutrition increase the risk of health problems?
cards.answer: Excess calories or saturated fat increase the risk of obesity, cardiovascular disease, and Type 2 diabetes.

cards.front: Why is muscle-strengthening activity especially important in adulthood and later adulthood?
cards.answer: It counters the natural decline in muscle mass that occurs with age.

title: Spring Offensive, Hundred Days and Armistice
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five German offensives Ludendorff launched between March and July 1918.
cards.answer: Michael (Somme) / Georgette (Lys) / Blücher (Aisne) / Gneisenau (Matz) / Friedensturm (Marne)

cards.front: Name the five interlocking factors the lesson says broke Germany in 1918.
cards.answer: failed Spring Offensive / American manpower arriving / Allied combined-arms learning curve / British naval blockade / German internal collapse

cards.front: Why did the Spring Offensive's stormtrooper tactics fail strategically despite early success?
cards.answer: Infiltrating troops outran their horse-and-foot-supplied logistics and could not be reinforced, while Ludendorff missed key objectives like Amiens.

cards.front: How did Foch's role as Allied Generalissimo help defeat Germany in the Hundred Days?
cards.answer: His strategic coordination let the Allies attack Germany at multiple points simultaneously, never letting German reserves rest.

cards.front: Name the three example activities the lesson gives for active learning in concrete operational children.
cards.answer: Counting blocks / Sorting shapes / Running simple experiments

cards.front: Name the three learning styles that Willingham's research tested against meaningful learning.
cards.answer: Visual / Auditory / Kinaesthetic

cards.front: Why can praising a pupil's fixed ability harm their future learning?
cards.answer: It can make pupils avoid difficult tasks in case failure exposes a lack of talent.

cards.front: Why does praising effort and strategy help pupils cope with setbacks?
cards.answer: It encourages pupils to keep trying after setbacks and to see mistakes as part of learning.

cards.front: Name the three pieces of evidence the lesson gives that reveal the private man behind Darcy's public mask.
cards.answer: Mrs Reynolds's testimony / The Pemberley visit / His secret rescue of Lydia

cards.front: Name the judgement failure or success the lesson assigns to each of the five characters: Elizabeth, Darcy, Jane, Mr Bennet, Mrs Bennet.
cards.answer: Elizabeth judges too quickly / Darcy judges by class / Jane judges too generously / Mr Bennet judges accurately but refuses to act / Mrs Bennet judges entirely by wealth
items: Mr Bennet judges accurately but refuses to act
Mrs Bennet judges entirely by wealth

cards.front: Why does Elizabeth believe Wickham's account of Darcy?
cards.answer: His story confirms her existing prejudice against Darcy.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Bennet behave in her loud, marriage-obsessed way?
cards.answer: Her behaviour is driven by genuine fear of poverty under the entailment.

cards.front: Name the three training seasons that most competitive sports are divided into.
cards.answer: Pre-season / Competition season / Post-season

cards.front: Name the five key strategies the lesson gives for preventing injury.
cards.answer: Thorough warm-up before exercise / Avoiding over-training with appropriate rest / Wearing appropriate clothing and footwear / Using taping or bracing on vulnerable joints / Maintaining hydration throughout training
items: Using taping or bracing on vulnerable joints

cards.front: Why is altitude training more beneficial for a marathon runner than for a 100m sprinter?
cards.answer: The marathon relies entirely on aerobic respiration needing oxygen delivery, whereas the sprint relies on the anaerobic ATP-PCr system, not oxygen.

cards.front: Why should stretches be eased into slowly rather than bounced?
cards.answer: Bouncing a stretch activates the stretch reflex, which risks causing muscle tears.

cards.front: Name the four ways to fix a cash-flow problem that the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Re-schedule payments / Arrange an overdraft / Reduce cash outflow / Increase cash inflow

cards.front: Name the four rows found in a cash-flow forecast.
cards.answer: Cash inflows / Cash outflows / Net cash flow / Opening and closing balances

cards.front: Why can't a structural cash-flow problem be solved by borrowing more?
cards.answer: Because outflows stay consistently higher than inflows, so any extra debt just keeps growing instead of fixing the gap.

cards.front: Why is an overdraft a good fix for a one-off cash-flow dip, like a customer paying late?
cards.answer: It's a short-term, flexible bank facility designed to cover temporary shortfalls until cash comes back in.

cards.front: Why does the Creature murder William Frankenstein?
cards.answer: William rejects and insults it, and reveals the Frankenstein name, sparking rage as revenge against Victor.

cards.front: Why does Victor destroy the unfinished female creature?
cards.answer: He fears the two creatures breeding into a 'race of devils' and cannot control what the independent female might do.

title: Parish reaction and the Prayer Book Rebellion
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four demands made in the rebels' Articles during the Prayer Book Rebellion.
cards.answer: Restoration of the Latin mass / Communion in one kind / Reservation of the sacrament / Revival of the Six Articles

cards.front: Name the four regions where resistance to Reformation change was strongest.
cards.answer: Devon / Cornwall / Yorkshire / Lancashire

cards.front: Why did the government require clergy to preach from approved homilies instead of their own sermons?
cards.answer: It was a way of controlling what theological content parishioners heard, directing it from the centre rather than letting priests choose.

cards.front: Why was the Prayer Book Rebellion about more than just the language of church services?
cards.answer: It was also a defence of a whole material culture of religion, including beloved imagery, that was being destroyed.

title: Characters: Fogg, Passepartout and a Cast of Many
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name four of the minor roles the eight-actor ensemble plays in Around the World in 80 Days.
cards.answer: Reform Club wager-makers / Suez customs official / Bombay merchant / Ship captains / Yokohama acrobats

cards.front: Why does the comedy between Fogg and Passepartout collapse if either performer copies the other's energy level?
cards.answer: Their comedy depends entirely on contrast, so Fogg energetic or Passepartout restrained removes the gap that creates the humour.

cards.front: How does typical proxemic positioning between Fogg and Passepartout reinforce their status difference?
cards.answer: Fogg is placed upstage centre or slightly elevated while Passepartout stays downstage centre nearer the audience, showing status and identification.

cards.front: Why does Inspector Fix create dramatic irony in the play?
cards.answer: The audience knows Fogg is innocent while Fix wrongly believes he is guilty, generating both tension and comedy from that gap.

title: Market Failure & the Misallocation of Resources
subject: economics-aqa

cards.front: The lesson gives three government tools to tackle market failure — name them.
cards.answer: Direct state provision / Subsidies for merit goods / Taxes or regulation on demerit goods
items: Taxes or regulation on demerit goods

cards.front: Why can a lighthouse beam not be switched off just for ships that haven't paid?
cards.answer: Because the good is non-excludable, so it is impossible to stop any ship from consuming the beam once it is provided.

cards.front: Why does an information gap between a policyholder and insurer distort the private health insurance market?
cards.answer: The consumer knows more about their own health risk than the insurer, so the insurer cannot price the policy accurately.

title: Magna Carta and the Limits of Kingship, 1215
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four failures of King John that the lesson lists as building baronial anger before 1215.
cards.answer: Lost Normandy and Anjou by 1204 / Taxed barons heavily through scutage / Quarrelled with Pope Innocent III / Defeated by France at Bouvines in 1214
items: Defeated by France at Bouvines in 1214

cards.front: Why did Stephen Langton use Henry I's 1100 coronation charter as a template for Magna Carta?
cards.answer: It had already limited royal powers, giving the barons an existing precedent to demand John confirm similar rights.

cards.front: Why did Magna Carta survive in the long term despite being annulled within ten weeks in 1215?
cards.answer: Henry III's regents reissued it in 1216 and 1217 to win loyal support, and Henry confirmed it again in 1225 for a tax.

cards.front: Name the four values of military heroism celebrated in Greek and Roman culture.
cards.answer: Courage / Endurance / Loyalty to comrades / Willingness to die for one's community
items: Willingness to die for one's community

cards.front: Why did Leonidas send away the allied troops but stay to fight at Thermopylae?
cards.answer: When Ephialtes showed the Persians a path around the pass, Leonidas chose to remain with his Spartans and fight to the death rather than retreat.

cards.front: How did the Spartan festival at Thermopylae help preserve the warrior ideal?
cards.answer: An annual festival with athletic contests for boys honoured the fallen, keeping the memory of their heroic death alive.

cards.front: How does the Simonides inscription at Thermopylae reinforce Tyrtaeus's message?
cards.answer: It declared the dead lay there in obedience to Sparta's words, permanently reminding people of the duty to die rather than retreat.

cards.front: Name the three unrequited loves that make up the love triangle in Twelfth Night.
cards.answer: Orsino pines for Olivia / Olivia pursues Cesario / Viola adores Orsino

cards.front: How does Orsino unconsciously notice Viola's femininity while she is disguised as Cesario?
cards.answer: He praises Cesario's smooth, rubious lip and small pipe like a maiden's organ, unknowingly describing Viola's female features.

cards.front: Why is the ending of Twelfth Night's love triangle left ambiguous rather than fully resolved?
cards.answer: Because it's unclear if Olivia loves Sebastian for himself or because he resembles Cesario, so the relationships still rest on illusion.

title: Growing Opposition: Stamp Act to Boston Tea Party, 1765–73
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four Coercive Acts that colonists nicknamed the Intolerable Acts (1774).
cards.answer: Boston Port Act / Massachusetts Government Act / Administration of Justice Act / Quartering Act

cards.front: Besides taxation, what other grievances fed the Stamp Act crisis, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Trial without jury in vice-admiralty courts / Threat to freedom of the press / Right of assemblies to vote their own taxes / Frontier anger over the Proclamation Act of 1763 / Merchant frustration with the Sugar Act of 1764
items: Trial without jury in vice-admiralty courts
Threat to freedom of the press
Right of assemblies to vote their own taxes
Frontier anger over the Proclamation Act of 1763
Merchant frustration with the Sugar Act of 1764

cards.front: Why did the repeal of the Stamp Act in 1766 help cause later escalations like the Townshend crisis?
cards.answer: It taught colonists that boycotts and crowd action worked, so they reached for the same toolkit when new duties came in 1767.

cards.front: Why did closing Boston harbour under the Boston Port Act backfire on Britain?
cards.answer: Meant to isolate Massachusetts from other colonies, it instead brought food, money and political support flowing in from across America.

title: Hormones: Adrenalin, Thyroxine and the Menstrual Cycle
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four glands (or organs) whose hormones control the menstrual cycle.
cards.answer: Pituitary gland (FSH and LH) / Ovaries (oestrogen) / Corpus luteum (progesterone)

cards.front: Why does adrenalin divert blood flow away from the digestive organs and towards the muscles?
cards.answer: Arterioles to digestive organs constrict while those to muscles dilate, redirecting blood to give muscles more oxygen and glucose for action.

cards.front: Why is the fight-or-flight response described as helping survival?
cards.answer: It increases the body's capacity for explosive physical activity by suppressing non-essential processes and redirecting resources to systems needed to fight or flee.

cards.front: How does oestrogen prevent more than one follicle maturing in the menstrual cycle?
cards.answer: Oestrogen inhibits further FSH release through negative feedback, stopping additional follicles from maturing.

cards.front: Name four details in the lesson that suggest Inspector Goole is not entirely human.
cards.answer: His name hints at 'ghoul' / He seems to know everything before asking / He appears just as Birling says people should look after themselves / He controls the pace of revelations in time / His prophecy of 'fire and blood and anguish' comes true
items: He seems to know everything before asking
He appears just as Birling says people should look after themselves
He controls the pace of revelations in time
His prophecy of 'fire and blood and anguish' comes true

cards.front: Why does Priestley show that moral authority trumps social authority in the Inspector's method?
cards.answer: The Inspector refuses to be intimidated by Birling's status, showing his power comes from truth, not money or title.

cards.front: Why is Gerald's 'rescue' of Eva Smith seen as problematic despite his genuine care?
cards.answer: The power imbalance meant Eva was destitute and Gerald wealthy, so she had no choice but to be grateful to him.

cards.front: What four features of Tollington does Syal describe when setting the scene?
cards.answer: The Big House / The yard / Mr Ormerod's corner shop / The wasteland where children play

cards.front: What four functions do Meena's lies serve in the novel, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: They are funny / They reveal her desperation for attention / They mirror the lies of adult society / They set up her move from lying to telling the truth
items: They reveal her desperation for attention
They mirror the lies of adult society
They set up her move from lying to telling the truth

cards.front: How do Mama and Papa Kumar show 'cultural adaptation without surrender'?
cards.answer: They take part in Tollington's community events while privately keeping their own Punjabi traditions, language and values.

cards.front: Why does Syal use the Aunties' and Uncles' gatherings at the Kumar house?
cards.answer: To contrast the warmth of Indian family culture with the emotional poverty of many Tollington households.

cards.front: Name the four basic file handling operations the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Open a file / Read from it / Write to it / Close it

cards.front: Why should you use a function rather than a procedure when calculating a total?
cards.answer: Because a function works out or looks up a value the rest of the program will use, sent back through return.

cards.front: Why are local variables usually the safer choice compared to global variables?
cards.answer: A local variable is sealed inside its own sub program so can't be changed by accident, keeping sub programs independent.

title: Technology of warfare: modern and nuclear
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three delivery systems Britain's nuclear deterrent has used, in order.
cards.answer: Aircraft-delivered bombs / Polaris submarine-launched missiles (1968–1996) / Trident system (today)

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four things must technology be integrated with to be effective in war?
cards.answer: Command / Logistics / Training / Strategy

cards.front: Why did the Chain Home radar network help Britain win the Battle of Britain?
cards.answer: It let controllers track incoming German aircraft and direct fighter squadrons to intercept them, so the RAF's thin fighter reserves could be used effectively against the larger Luftwaffe.

cards.front: Why did Britain decide to develop its own independent nuclear deterrent after 1945?
cards.answer: The Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb in 1949, so British leaders concluded an independent deterrent was essential for national security and great-power status.

cards.front: Name the six team sports listed in the lesson (Spanish terms).
cards.answer: el fútbol / el baloncesto / el voleibol / el rugby / el hockey / el cricket

cards.front: Name the five time expressions the lesson gives for describing how often you exercise.
cards.answer: Todos los días / dos veces a la semana / los fines de semana / después del instituto / por la mañana temprano

cards.front: Why do you use 'jugar a' for football but 'hacer' for swimming in Spanish?
cards.answer: Jugar a is used for ball/team sports, while hacer is used for individual activities like swimming.

cards.front: Why does the lesson recommend using 'no solo... sino también' in your writing?
cards.answer: Using connectives and complex structures like this lifts your writing to reach higher mark bands.

cards.front: Why did Lucretia stab herself according to Livy's account?
cards.answer: She refused to provide a precedent for unchaste Roman women, and her death forced the men to revolt against the Tarquins.

cards.front: Why is the Hegeso Stele useful alongside literary sources about Athenian wives?
cards.answer: It gives the literary ideal of the confined, respectable wife a visual presence, showing her wealth, dignity and domestic authority.

cards.front: Name the four disadvantages the lesson gives for intensive farming.
cards.answer: Welfare concerns / Disease risk / Environmental impact from concentrated waste / Not always linked to quality

cards.front: Why can intensive farming produce chicken so cheaply?
cards.answer: Broiler chickens raised intensively reach slaughter weight in as few as five to six weeks, driving down price.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say local food and organic food are the same thing?
cards.answer: A farm can be local but use synthetic pesticides, or organic but grown abroad and shipped to the UK.

cards.front: Why must fish farms be well-managed for aquaculture to be sustainable?
cards.answer: Poorly managed farms can cause water pollution and disease, even though farming fish reduces pressure on wild stocks.

cards.front: Name the three editing techniques D.W. Griffith helped codify in the 1910s.
cards.answer: Close-up to convey emotion / Cross-cutting between simultaneous events / Tracking shot following a character

cards.front: Name the five large studios that dominated Hollywood production by 1930.
cards.answer: MGM / Paramount / Warner Bros. / RKO / Fox

cards.front: Why did silent film directors use exaggerated gesture and chiaroscuro lighting?
cards.answer: Without dialogue, filmmakers needed exaggerated gesture and high-contrast lighting to communicate mood and emotion visually.

cards.front: Why did Los Angeles become the centre of world film production by 1930?
cards.answer: Californian light, varied landscapes, and distance from the eastern patent trusts controlling early cinema equipment attracted producers there.

title: The Norman monarchy and feudal power 1066-1154
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four things Domesday commissioners asked local juries about each piece of land.
cards.answer: Who held it before the Conquest (in King Edward's time) / Who holds it now / How many people lived there / What it was worth
items: Who held it before the Conquest (in King Edward's time)

cards.front: Why did William I order the Harrying of the North (1069-70)?
cards.answer: He deliberately destroyed crops, livestock and settlements to wipe out the economic base of northern rebellion.

cards.front: Why did Henry I issue the Charter of Liberties in 1100?
cards.answer: To secure baronial support after coming to power following his brother William II's sudden death in a hunting accident.

title: Neurons, Synapses and the Central Nervous System
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: What is the typical order neurons are activated in when responding to a stimulus (three-step sequence)?
cards.answer: Sensory neuron / Relay neuron / Motor neuron

cards.front: What are the five steps in the synaptic transmission sequence, from the signal arriving to the synapse clearing?
cards.answer: Action potential arrives at pre-synaptic neuron / Neurotransmitters are released / They cross the synapse / They bind to post-synaptic receptors causing excitation or inhibition / Reuptake clears the synapse
items: Action potential arrives at pre-synaptic neuron
They bind to post-synaptic receptors causing excitation or inhibition

cards.front: Why can a reflex, like pulling your hand off a hot pan, happen almost instantly without the brain?
cards.answer: The relay neurons involved are in the spinal cord, so the signal doesn't need to travel to the brain and back.

cards.front: How does a neuron 'decide' whether to fire an action potential?
cards.answer: It depends on the combined effect of all the excitatory and inhibitory signals it receives at that moment, not just one synapse.

title: Magnets, Magnetic Fields and the Motor Effect
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four rules given for magnetic field lines around a magnet.
cards.answer: Run from north to south outside the magnet / Closer lines mean stronger field / Field is strongest at the poles / Field lines never cross
items: Run from north to south outside the magnet
Field is strongest at the poles

cards.front: Name the three factors that affect the size of an induced potential difference.
cards.answer: Speed of movement / Strength of the magnetic field / Number of turns in the coil
items: Number of turns in the coil

cards.front: Why is an induced magnet always attracted to, and never repelled by, the magnet that magnetises it?
cards.answer: Its induced poles always arrange so that unlike poles face the permanent magnet, and unlike poles attract.

cards.front: How does a split-ring commutator keep a DC motor's coil spinning continuously?
cards.answer: It reverses the current through the coil every half turn, so the forces always act in the same rotational direction.

cards.front: Name the six main categories of media codes given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Camera / Layout / Colour / Typography / Language / Imagery

cards.front: What three conventions does a typical thriller poster use?
cards.answer: Dark colours / Large bold type / Single central figure in silhouette

cards.front: Why do genre conventions matter to audiences even though they make products predictable?
cards.answer: Audiences use conventions to decide whether to engage, acting as a contract between creator and audience about what to expect.

cards.front: How can a media product create a tense mood without using any dialogue?
cards.answer: By combining dark colours, fast-cut editing, minor-key music and tight close-up shots to build tension through codes alone.

cards.front: Name the three stages by which Stalin defeated his rivals between 1924 and 1929.
cards.answer: Stalin, Kamenev and Zinoviev beat Trotsky's Left Opposition (1925) / Stalin and Bukharin beat Kamenev and Zinoviev's United Opposition (1926–27) / Stalin turned on Bukharin's Right Opposition (1928–29)
items: Stalin, Kamenev and Zinoviev beat Trotsky's Left Opposition (1925)
Stalin and Bukharin beat Kamenev and Zinoviev's United Opposition (1926–27)
Stalin turned on Bukharin's Right Opposition (1928–29)

cards.front: How did Stalin use the General Secretaryship to control votes at party congresses?
cards.answer: The post controlled party appointments and membership records, letting him pack delegations with loyal supporters who voted his way.

cards.front: Why did Trotsky's Civil War record as founder of the Red Army actually work against him in the Politburo?
cards.answer: His military prestige raised fears of Bonapartism, that a charismatic general might replace the party with personal dictatorship.

cards.front: Name the two tasks a student can choose between in the short final part of the language paper.
cards.answer: Translate simple sentences from English into Latin / Recognise and explain grammar points in a Latin passage
items: Translate simple sentences from English into Latin
Recognise and explain grammar points in a Latin passage

cards.front: Give the four Latin words used in the lesson to show how Latin roots survive in English derivatives.
cards.answer: aqua (water) / scribo (write) / porto (carry) / audio (hear)

cards.front: Why is writing 'went' for advenit marked as unsafe?
cards.answer: Because advenit means 'arrived', a precise separate meaning from venio's 'come', so an approximate meaning is not accepted.

cards.front: How can spotting an English derivative help when reading an unseen Latin passage?
cards.answer: A familiar English word grown from a Latin root can help you recall or guess the meaning of an unfamiliar Latin word.

cards.front: Name the six benefits of market segmentation for a start-up given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Meeting specific customer needs / Increasing profits / Enabling targeted marketing / Improving customer retention / Growing market share / Matching product accurately to needs

cards.front: Why is age used to segment a market for products like mobility scooters or streaming gift cards?
cards.answer: Age shapes spending habits, product preferences and the channels through which customers can be reached.

cards.front: Why is location often the most practical first segmentation base for a small start-up?
cards.answer: A small start-up has limited resources, so it can only realistically reach and serve customers within a short travel radius or delivery area.

cards.front: Why is the chapter title 'Joshua' ironic in Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit?
cards.answer: Joshua is about conquering the Promised Land, but the chapter shows the church declaring Jeanette full of demons and locking her away.

cards.front: How does the novel's non-linear structure reflect Jeanette's own experience?
cards.answer: Her life breaks apart from the church's planned linear path, just as the narrative breaks apart and must be reassembled by the reader.

cards.front: What function do the fairy tale interludes serve beyond commenting on the plot?
cards.answer: They provide emotional distance, letting Winterson explore painful themes through allegory rather than direct narration.

cards.front: How does the fairy tale of the prince searching for a flawless wife connect to Jeanette's dilemmas?
cards.answer: The woman he beheads says perfection is balance not flawlessness, paralleling the church's false idea of a perfect life as a prison.

cards.front: Name the four psychological terms the lesson says Freud's theory gave lasting vocabulary to, still used today.
cards.answer: the unconscious mind / repression / wish fulfilment / manifest and latent content

cards.front: Why did Freud believe repressed material can resurface during dreaming?
cards.answer: Repression pushes disturbing material out of awareness but it stays active in the unconscious mind and finds another route to be expressed, which is dreaming.

cards.front: Why do critics say Freud's theory of dreaming is too reductionist?
cards.answer: It reduces every dream to one cause, a disguised repressed wish, ignoring other influences like brain activity during sleep.

cards.front: Name the three inputs used in break-even analysis.
cards.answer: Selling price per unit / Variable cost per unit / Total fixed costs

cards.front: Name the three lines shown on a break-even diagram.
cards.answer: Total revenue / Total costs / Fixed costs

cards.front: Why does a rise in variable costs push the break-even point to the right?
cards.answer: Contribution per unit falls, so the business needs more sales to cover its fixed costs.

cards.front: Why does the margin of safety shrink when fixed costs rise?
cards.answer: The break-even point moves right while sales stay the same, narrowing the gap between actual sales and break-even sales.

cards.front: Name the four human activities the lesson gives that raise greenhouse gas levels.
cards.answer: Burning fossil fuels / Deforestation / Agriculture (cattle and rice paddies) / Landfill sites

cards.front: Name the three sources of evidence the lesson gives for what the early atmosphere was like.
cards.answer: Analysis of ancient rocks / Volcanic emissions / Comparison with other planets

cards.front: How did the ozone layer forming allow life to move onto land?
cards.answer: As oxygen accumulated it formed the ozone layer, which blocked harmful ultraviolet radiation, allowing life to move onto land.

cards.front: Why is the average surface temperature of Earth warmer than it would be without greenhouse gases?
cards.answer: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the warm surface and re-emit it in all directions, trapping heat near Earth.

title: Themes: continuity and change in British warfare
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What four elements make up a strong thematic change essay structure?
cards.answer: A clear argument in the introduction about the extent of change / At least one paragraph per era with named evidence / A paragraph or sentences addressing continuity / A conclusion weighing change against continuity to reach a judgement
items: A clear argument in the introduction about the extent of change
At least one paragraph per era with named evidence
A paragraph or sentences addressing continuity
A conclusion weighing change against continuity to reach a judgement

cards.front: What four technologies did industrialisation produce in the modern period of British warfare?
cards.answer: The machine gun / The tank / The aircraft / The nuclear weapon

cards.front: Why did the tank fail to be decisive in 1916 but became decisive by 1918?
cards.answer: In 1916 it was used in small numbers without effective tactics, but by 1918 doctrine had caught up with the technology.

cards.front: Why has the Royal Navy been continuously maintained by successive governments for five centuries?
cards.answer: Because all governments, regardless of political allegiance, recognised sea power as essential to an island nation.

cards.front: Name the eight types of PPE listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Disposable aprons / disposable gloves / rubber gloves / face masks / hairnets or hygiene hats / overalls / overshoes / surgical garments / scrubs

cards.front: Name the eight personal hygiene measures the lesson lists for care workers.
cards.answer: Hair tied back or covered / open wounds covered / no jewellery / no nail polish / correct hand washing routine / regular showering and hair washing / regular brushing of teeth / appropriate use and disposal of tissues, antiseptic wipes and hand sanitiser

cards.front: Why must open wounds on a care worker be covered?
cards.answer: An uncovered wound can harbour infection and introduce bacteria to a service user through direct contact.

cards.front: Why is incorrect disposal of clinical waste a serious infection risk in care settings?
cards.answer: It creates infection risks for staff, other residents and the wider community if hazardous waste isn't placed in correct containers.

cards.front: Name the five elements the lesson lists as equal 'languages' in total theatre.
cards.answer: Light / Sound / Movement / Spatial arrangement / Smell

cards.front: Name the three examples the lesson gives of Artaud's influence on contemporary practice.
cards.answer: Peter Brook's Theatre of Cruelty season at the RSC / Immersive theatre companies such as Punchdrunk / The physical theatre tradition more broadly
items: Peter Brook's Theatre of Cruelty season at the RSC
Immersive theatre companies such as Punchdrunk
The physical theatre tradition more broadly

cards.front: Why did Artaud believe theatre needed to shock its audience?
cards.answer: He believed Western culture had become anaesthetised, so shock broke people out of habitual numbness and forced them to feel and be present.

cards.front: How did Balinese dance theatre shape Artaud's approach to performance?
cards.answer: It showed him meaning conveyed through gesture, posture and rhythm without words, convincing him theatre should prioritise the physical body over text.

title: Texture and Sonority in Chamber Music
subject: music-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three common accompaniment patterns the lesson gives for filling out homophonic texture.
cards.answer: Broken-chord Alberti bass / Steady block chords / Repeated rhythmic figure

cards.front: Why do composers often use unison writing at dramatic openings?
cards.answer: Several instruments playing identically creates a powerful, focused sound that projects further and reinforces tone rather than competing.

cards.front: How does the pizzicato ostinato at the start of the Debussy String Quartet second movement build texture?
cards.answer: A plucked rhythmic pattern is established first, then further pizzicato and bowed layers are gradually added, thickening the texture.

cards.front: How does Schubert keep the Trout Quintet's theme and variations movement homophonic while still varying it?
cards.answer: The tune passes between instruments and accompaniment patterns change character each variation, but one melody stays clearly supported throughout.

title: Sociological Theories of the Role of Education
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four functions the functionalist perspective says education performs for society.
cards.answer: Transmitting shared norms and values / Creating social cohesion / Teaching specialist skills / Allocating individuals to roles meritocratically

cards.front: Why do Marxists like Bowles and Gintis argue the hidden curriculum benefits capitalism?
cards.answer: It teaches obedience and acceptance of hierarchy, preparing working-class pupils for routine employment while convincing them their position is earned, not structural.

cards.front: How does the interactionist perspective differ from macro perspectives in studying education?
cards.answer: It examines micro-level classroom processes, like teacher labelling and the self-fulfilling prophecy, rather than macro-level functions of society.

cards.front: Name the four hand stitching techniques described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Running stitch / Backstitch / Slip stitch / Pad stitch

cards.front: Name the four edge finishing techniques described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pinking shears / Zigzag stitch / Overlocking / Binding

cards.front: How does a domestic sewing machine form a lockstitch?
cards.answer: A hook in the bobbin case catches the upper thread and loops it around the bobbin (lower) thread.

cards.front: Why must upper and lower thread tension be balanced on a sewing machine?
cards.answer: Because uneven tension between the two threads causes loops or puckering in the stitching.

cards.front: Name the three main drivers of uneven development at the global scale.
cards.answer: International trade / Multinational companies / Tourism

cards.front: What five benefits do MNCs bring to host LICs and NICs?
cards.answer: Jobs / Training / Technology / Infrastructure / Tax revenue

cards.front: Why do HICs and NICs earn more from trade than LICs that export primary products?
cards.answer: HICs and NICs export manufactured goods and services which earn higher, steadier prices than primary products, whose prices swing wildly.

cards.front: Why did EU sugar subsidies hurt African cane sugar growers?
cards.answer: The subsidies kept European beet sugar artificially cheap, so African cane growers struggled to compete on price.

cards.front: Name the four key lifestyle factors identified in the specification.
cards.answer: Nutrition / Physical activity / Smoking / Substance misuse

cards.front: Name the three substances named under substance misuse.
cards.answer: Alcohol / Cannabis / Opiates (e.g. heroin)

cards.front: Why do smokers often feel more anxious even though they believe smoking relieves stress?
cards.answer: The nicotine addiction cycle actually increases anxiety between cigarettes, and worrying about health consequences adds further stress.

cards.front: Why does a lack of physical activity increase the risk of depression and anxiety?
cards.answer: Prolonged inactivity worsens mood and limits social opportunities, and is linked to higher rates of depression and anxiety.

cards.front: Name the five stages of a life cycle assessment (LCA), in order.
cards.answer: Raw material extraction / Processing & manufacture / Distribution & transport / Use & maintenance / End-of-life disposal

cards.front: Name the three main sources of textile fibres.
cards.answer: Animal sources / Vegetable sources / Chemical/synthetic sources

cards.front: Why does recycled paper have lower quality than paper made from fresh wood pulp?
cards.answer: Because each recycling cycle re-pulps the waste paper and shortens the cellulose fibres.

cards.front: Why can a 'biodegradable' polymer still cause a hidden environmental problem?
cards.answer: It may only break down under industrial composting conditions, not in a home compost bin.

title: Themes: Love, Fate, Honour, Youth and Age
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: How might a lighting designer use a gobo to communicate the theme of fate across the play?
cards.answer: Project star patterns that appear soft and warm in the balcony scene but cold and hard-edged in the tomb.

cards.front: How might costume design make the feud visible to the audience from the opening scene?
cards.answer: Give each family a distinct colour palette so the audience can read the familial divide at a glance.

cards.front: Name the two directorial interpretations the lesson gives for staging fate in Romeo and Juliet.
cards.answer: Fate is absolute / Fate is the product of choices
items: Fate is the product of choices

cards.front: Why is treating Romeo and Juliet as primarily a love story a misconception, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It underemphasises the feud, patriarchal power and fate, which are systems that destroy the lovers' real love.

cards.front: Name the four stages of a material's life the lesson says its ecological footprint tracks.
cards.answer: Extraction / Processing / Transportation / Wastage and pollution

cards.front: What three countries does the lesson give as the main sources of lithium for batteries?
cards.answer: Australia / Chile / Argentina

cards.front: Why does growing cotton contribute to a large ecological footprint?
cards.answer: Growing cotton uses large amounts of water and pesticides, and shipping it worldwide adds carbon emissions.

cards.front: Why do most polymers add significantly to landfill and pollution?
cards.answer: Polymers are made from crude oil and most do not biodegrade, so they build up in landfill.

cards.front: Name the three things Mickey has none of after losing his factory job.
cards.answer: No qualifications / No savings / No prospects

cards.front: Name three things the energetic child Mickey did in Act 1, contrasted with his hollow adult self.
cards.answer: Played cowboys / Made blood pacts / Laughed at everything

cards.front: Why is Mickey sent to prison after the robbery, even though he didn't shoot anyone?
cards.answer: He is sentenced simply for being present at the robbery, not for pulling the trigger himself.

cards.front: Why does Russell suggest the Eddie and Linda affair would never have happened?
cards.answer: If Mickey had received proper mental health support, a stable job, and hope, the affair would not have occurred.

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why Holderness erodes so fast.
cards.answer: Weak boulder clay with no cement / Long North Sea fetch bringing destructive waves / Shallow offshore zone keeps wave energy high
items: Weak boulder clay with no cement
Long North Sea fetch bringing destructive waves
Shallow offshore zone keeps wave energy high

cards.front: Name the four hard engineering strategies used on the Holderness coast.
cards.answer: Sea walls / Rock armour / Groynes / Gabions

cards.front: Why is defending the entire 61 km Holderness coast with hard engineering not a viable option?
cards.answer: It would cost about £370 million to build, deflects wave energy onto neighbouring sections, and blocks sediment reaching Spurn Head, for low-value land.

cards.front: How does longshore drift keep erosion happening at Holderness after material falls from the cliff?
cards.answer: Longshore drift carries fallen material south at about 1.5 metres a day, leaving the cliff base exposed for the next wave attack.

cards.front: Name the five personal factors the lesson identifies as shaping engagement in sport.
cards.answer: Gender / Age / Socio-economic group / Ethnicity / Disability

cards.front: Name the five well-developed competitive pathways for disability sport given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Paralympic sport / Wheelchair basketball / Boccia / Goalball / Sitting volleyball

cards.front: How has increased media coverage of women's sport helped raise female participation?
cards.answer: It raised the profile and aspirational value of female sport, making it more visible and appealing.

cards.front: Why might people in ethnically diverse urban areas face facility-based barriers to sport participation?
cards.answer: Such areas are often urban and may have fewer open green spaces or high-quality sports facilities than suburban or rural areas.

cards.front: How does training raise a supermarket checkout worker's productivity?
cards.answer: Training lets them supervise four self-service tills instead of one, quadrupling their personal output.

cards.front: Why does a risk-bearing economy of scale lower a large firm's costs?
cards.answer: Operating across several markets means poor performance in one product line is offset by others, reducing overall uncertainty.

cards.front: Why can a clinometer reading be accurate but still unreliable?
cards.answer: Because it may only be correct if used by one particular person, so results are not consistent if repeated by others.

cards.front: Why is primary data limited even though it matches your specific question?
cards.answer: Because it is restricted to the time and weather conditions of the single day it was collected.

cards.front: In the Norfolk coastline worked example, what three reasons support recommending managed retreat?
cards.answer: Long-term cost is lower / Cliffs are eroding too fast for hard defences / A salt marsh would form behind the new shoreline
items: Cliffs are eroding too fast for hard defences
A salt marsh would form behind the new shoreline

cards.front: Name the three metals the lesson describes as reacting vigorously with cold water.
cards.answer: Potassium / Sodium / Calcium

cards.front: What three observations can show that a displacement reaction has occurred?
cards.answer: Colour change / Solid deposited / Temperature rise

cards.front: Why do copper, silver and gold not react with dilute acids?
cards.answer: They are below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so they do not lose their electrons readily enough.

cards.front: Why does calcium produce a cloudy solution when reacting with water, unlike sodium?
cards.answer: Calcium hydroxide has limited solubility, so it does not fully dissolve, making the solution cloudy.

title: The Nature of G-d and the Divine Presence
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the five key attributes of G-d given in the Key Fact, besides All-powerful, All-good, All-knowing and Everywhere.
cards.answer: One / Creator / Law-Giver / Judge / Eternal

cards.front: Name the three types of Jewish response the lesson gives to the problem of evil and suffering.
cards.answer: Human free will allows moral evil / G-d's justice works over longer timescales than humans perceive / Some suffering remains beyond full human understanding
items: Human free will allows moral evil
G-d's justice works over longer timescales
Some suffering is beyond human understanding

cards.front: Why is the universe described as depending entirely on G-d in Judaism?
cards.answer: Because Genesis 1:1 states G-d created the heavens and the earth, showing the physical universe originates from and depends on G-d.

cards.front: How does the mainstream rabbinic view of the Shekinah differ from the Kabbalistic view?
cards.answer: Mainstream rabbis see the Shekinah as simply another way of speaking about G-d's presence, while Kabbalists see it as a distinct emanation of G-d descending to dwell on Earth.

cards.front: What three things should a strong introduction to a thematic change essay do, in two to three sentences?
cards.answer: Directly address the question / State your overall argument / Briefly signpost the eras you will cover
items: Briefly signpost the eras you will cover

cards.front: Why does discipline count as a continuity across all three eras of warfare?
cards.answer: Warfare creates fear, confusion and exhaustion that push soldiers to act self-protectively, and only discipline overrides this and keeps them fighting collectively.

title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four gases the lesson gives specific tests for.
cards.answer: Hydrogen / Oxygen / Carbon dioxide / Chlorine

cards.front: Name the three examples of formulations given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Medicines / Paints / Alloys

cards.front: How can you identify an unknown substance using chromatography?
cards.answer: Compare its R_f value to known reference values, or run known substances alongside it and see if spots line up exactly.

cards.front: Why do different substances travel different distances up chromatography paper?
cards.answer: Because each substance has different solubility in the solvent, so more soluble substances are carried further.

cards.front: Name the three key phrases the lesson highlights from the Carew murder scene.
cards.answer: 'Trampled' / 'Ape-like fury' / 'Bones were audibly shattered'

cards.front: According to 'Why These Chapters Matter', what three 'wrong details' train the reader to distrust surfaces?
cards.answer: The tidy street with one wrong door / The respectable Jekyll with one dubious beneficiary / The quiet night with a moonlit murder
items: The tidy street with one wrong door
The respectable Jekyll with one dubious beneficiary
The quiet night with a moonlit murder

cards.front: How does Stevenson use reflected horror in Enfield's account of the girl's trampling to make Hyde disturbing?
cards.answer: He shows the violence through the witnesses' reactions rather than physical detail, making Hyde feel more disturbing than explicit description could.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson avoid giving a clear physical description of Hyde in Chapters 1-2?
cards.answer: Using indirect characterisation, Hyde is felt rather than seen, echoing Victorian anxieties about degeneration and hidden vice beneath respectability.

cards.front: Why does Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking scene show that guilt cannot be suppressed forever?
cards.answer: It structurally reverses her earlier composure, moving from controlled denial in Act 2 to helpless, observed suffering in Act 5.

cards.front: How does Macbeth's death in the final battle complicate the audience's view of him?
cards.answer: He refuses to surrender and dies fighting bravely, restoring some Act 1 heroism so he seems neither fully heroic nor fully villainous.

title: Resource Management: Food, Water & Energy in the UK
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the three water quality problems the lesson says put pressure on UK water companies.
cards.answer: Agricultural run-off / Sewage discharges / Microplastics

cards.front: What are the four parts of the UK's current electricity energy mix given in the lesson?
cards.answer: Renewables (over 40%) / Natural gas (around 30-35%) / Nuclear (around 12-15%) / Imports and other via interconnectors

cards.front: Why does the UK rely on water transfer schemes to meet demand?
cards.answer: Most rainfall falls on the north and west, but two-thirds of the population lives in the drier south and east.

cards.front: Why is natural gas still the largest single source of UK electricity despite renewables growth?
cards.answer: Gas-fired 'peaking' power stations are used to fill gaps in supply when wind generation drops.

cards.front: Name the five ways the lesson says humans use animals.
cards.answer: Food / Clothing / Medical research / Entertainment / Companionship

cards.front: Name the four practical religious responses to environmental issues given in the lesson.
cards.answer: A Rocha's conservation projects / Church of England's net zero by 2030 pledge / Islamic Relief's environmental programmes / Islamic Declaration on Global Climate Change (2015)
items: Church of England's net zero by 2030 pledge
Islamic Declaration on Global Climate Change (2015)

cards.front: Why do some Christians, particularly Quakers, oppose animal experimentation?
cards.answer: Because it causes unnecessary suffering, and they believe stewardship means protecting all of God's creatures.

cards.front: Under what condition does the Catholic Church say animal experimentation is morally acceptable?
cards.answer: If it stays within reasonable limits and contributes to caring for or saving human lives.

cards.front: Name the three ways Golding embeds nuclear anxiety directly into Lord of the Flies.
cards.answer: Nuclear war causes the evacuation / Piggy refers to 'the atom bomb' / The 'beast from air' is a dead parachutist
items: The 'beast from air' is a dead parachutist

cards.front: In Ballantyne's The Coral Island, name the three British boys shipwrecked on the tropical island.
cards.answer: Ralph / Jack / Peterkin

cards.front: Why does the boys' destruction of the island mirror the wider Cold War context of the novel?
cards.answer: Golding suggests human nature is constant: adults destroy the world through nuclear war while children destroy their island through savagery.

cards.front: Why does Simon die after freeing the dead parachutist's lines?
cards.answer: Simon symbolically confronts the truth of human evil, but the other boys are too far gone and kill him before he can share it.

cards.front: What three stages of order does the classic Shakespearean comedy structure follow in Twelfth Night?
cards.answer: Initial order disrupted (shipwreck, disguise) / Confusion escalates (love triangle, Malvolio's gulling) / Harmony restored (revelations, marriages)

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare's ending to Twelfth Night feel 'not entirely comfortable' despite the comic resolution?
cards.answer: Malvolio exits vowing revenge and Antonio is left isolated, showing not everyone benefits from the comic ending.

cards.front: How does Olivia's behaviour at the start of the play show her trapped in an extreme emotional state?
cards.answer: She has locked herself away in mourning for her dead brother, vowing to reject all suitors for seven years.

cards.front: Why was Viola's disguise as Cesario seen as a bold transgression by Elizabethan audiences?
cards.answer: She crosses both gender and class boundaries by dressing as a male courtier, defying sumptuary laws and gender norms.

cards.front: Name the three components every homeostatic control system has.
cards.answer: Receptor / Coordination centre / Effector

cards.front: What two responses does the body use to cool down when body temperature rises too high?
cards.answer: Vasodilation / Sweating

cards.front: How does sweating cool the body down?
cards.answer: Sweat evaporates from the skin surface, taking energy (heat) from the skin and cooling the body.

cards.front: Why are hormonal responses better suited than nervous responses for controlling blood glucose and water balance?
cards.answer: Hormonal responses are slower but longer-lasting, making them well-suited for regulating sustained processes.

cards.front: Name the six steps in the lesson's step-by-step formation of a corrie.
cards.answer: Snow accumulates in a sheltered hollow / Snow compacts into glacier ice / Rotational slip grinds the floor down / Backwall attacked by freeze-thaw and plucking / Lip erodes less due to lower ice pressure / Ice melts and basin fills to form a tarn
items: Snow accumulates in a sheltered hollow
Rotational slip grinds the floor down
Backwall attacked by freeze-thaw and plucking
Lip erodes less due to lower ice pressure
Ice melts and basin fills to form a tarn

cards.front: Why does a glacier carve a U-shaped valley instead of the V-shape a river creates?
cards.answer: A glacier fills the whole valley and erodes the floor and both sides at once, planing off interlocking spurs, unlike a river which only erodes its narrow channel.

cards.front: Why does bulldozing at a glacier's snout lead to till building up as moraine?
cards.answer: Material scraped up or freeze-thaw shattered onto the glacier is pushed ahead like a bulldozer blade and accumulates at the snout as moraine.

cards.front: Why is plucking most effective on the downstream side of a rock obstacle?
cards.answer: Pressure is lower there, so meltwater refreezes around jointed bedrock, allowing the glacier to tear away whole blocks as it moves on.

cards.front: Name the three key components whose I–V characteristic shapes you need to know.
cards.answer: Ohmic resistor / Filament lamp / Diode

cards.front: Name the three uses of an NTC thermistor given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Temperature sensors / Fire alarms / Thermostat circuits

cards.front: Why is current not 'used up' as it flows around a circuit?
cards.answer: Charge flows continuously around the closed circuit; energy is transferred from the charge carriers, not the current itself.

cards.front: Why is household wiring connected in parallel rather than series?
cards.answer: So each appliance receives the full 230 V supply and can be switched on or off independently.

cards.front: Name the four types of love the lesson identifies on the love spectrum in Romeo and Juliet.
cards.answer: Petrarchan (Romeo/Rosaline) / Mutual (Romeo/Juliet) / Physical/bawdy (Mercutio/Nurse) / Conditional (Capulet)

cards.front: According to the lesson, what should each paragraph of a close extract analysis follow?
cards.answer: Point / Quotation / Analysis of technique / Effect on audience

cards.front: Why does Romeo kill Tybalt after Mercutio's death?
cards.answer: Honour culture shames him for passivity, so he kills Tybalt to restore his masculine identity.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare leave the fate versus free will debate in the play?
cards.answer: He shows both cosmic destiny (star-cross'd lovers, the failed letter) and deliberate choices, leaving the question unresolved.

cards.front: Name the three main types of hazard a tropical cyclone brings.
cards.answer: High winds / Intense rainfall / Storm surge

cards.front: Name the three factors that make some places more vulnerable to cyclones than others.
cards.answer: Physical factors / Social factors / Economic factors

cards.front: Why does storm surge usually cause more deaths than a cyclone's winds?
cards.answer: It causes a sudden, widespread rise in sea level that floods coastal communities over a large area.

cards.front: Why did Cyclone Nargis kill an estimated 138,000 people in Myanmar in 2008?
cards.answer: The military government delayed international aid, worsening the disaster's impact on a vulnerable population.

cards.front: Name the six structural disadvantages the lesson says caused Mickey's depression.
cards.answer: Poverty / A failing school / A dead-end factory job / Redundancy / Sammy's criminal influence / A prison sentence

cards.front: Which four perspectives does the cross-cutting scene of the affair's revelation show colliding?
cards.answer: Linda's desperation / Eddie's guilt / Mrs Lyons's malice / Mickey's shattering realisation

cards.front: Why does Mickey's rage at the Town Hall land on his mother rather than on Eddie?
cards.answer: His fury is not about Linda or Eddie but about the life he was denied because of class.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Johnstone reveal that Mickey and Eddie are twins at the Town Hall?
cards.answer: In desperation she hopes the truth will stop the violence, but instead it destroys Mickey.

cards.front: Why does Tommy work feverishly on his tiny animal drawings after Ruth's death?
cards.answer: He believes the drawings will prove to Madame that he and Kathy have souls and deserve a deferral.

cards.front: How does the act of narrating her story give Kathy a form of resistance?
cards.answer: By telling her story, Kathy asserts that her life mattered, despite having no control over her fate.

cards.front: What are the three possible causes of an outlier in a dataset?
cards.answer: A genuine extreme value / A measurement or data entry error / A genuinely different subgroup
items: A measurement or data entry error

cards.front: What three things should you do when commenting on an outlier in an exam question?
cards.answer: Identify the outlier's approximate value / Suggest if it's genuine or an error / Comment on its effect on averages
items: Suggest if it's genuine or an error
Comment on its effect on averages

cards.front: Why is the median often a more representative average than the mean for UK household income data?
cards.answer: Income is positively skewed, so a small number of very high earners pull the mean upwards above the median.

cards.front: Why is the production process stopped and investigated if a sample mean falls outside the action lines? (Higher)
cards.answer: Because a result that far from the target would be very unusual if the process were running correctly.

cards.front: Name the three stages of destruction across the first three stanzas of 'The Destruction of Sennacherib'.
cards.answer: Stanza 1: army charges, glittering and powerful / Stanza 2: the Angel of Death breathes on the foe / Stanza 3: the army is found dead the next morning
items: Stanza 1: army charges, glittering and powerful
Stanza 2: the Angel of Death breathes on the foe
Stanza 3: the army is found dead the next morning

cards.front: What three different scales of destruction do Byron, Carson and Clarke each present in their poems?
cards.answer: Byron: annihilation of an entire army / Carson: one explosion shattering a single street / Clarke: the severing of the umbilical cord
items: Byron: annihilation of an entire army
Carson: one explosion shattering a single street
Clarke: the severing of the umbilical cord

cards.front: Why does Byron present the Assyrian army's arrival in vivid colour before switching to pale, lifeless imagery?
cards.answer: The contrast between vibrant life ('purple and gold') and sudden death makes the destruction feel swift and absolute.

cards.front: Why does Clarke call the umbilical cord a 'rope' rather than a cord in 'Catrin'?
cards.answer: Calling it a 'rope' suggests something stronger and more combative, like a tug-of-war, fitting the battle imagery of birth.

title: Legal Ages and the Three UK Legal Systems
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the five rights a person gains at age 18 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (full legal adulthood).
cards.answer: Vote in UK general elections / Sit on a jury / Buy alcohol and tobacco / Enter into a contract independently / Join the armed forces without parental consent
items: Join the armed forces without parental consent

cards.front: Name the four things a 16-year-old in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is allowed to do.
cards.answer: Consent to medical treatment / Leave school / Work full-time / Join the armed forces with parental consent
items: Join the armed forces with parental consent

cards.front: Why did Scotland set its age of criminal responsibility higher than England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
cards.answer: Scotland's higher threshold reflects a philosophy that younger children cannot fully understand the consequences of their actions.

cards.front: Why does the UK have three distinct legal systems?
cards.answer: Scotland kept its own legal system at the 1707 Acts of Union, Northern Ireland developed separately, and 1997-98 devolution reinforced these distinctions.

title: Meditation, the Three Marks and the Three Jewels
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why does clinging to impermanent things cause suffering, according to anicca?
cards.answer: We treat impermanent things as if they will last, so we suffer when they inevitably change or end.

cards.front: How does mettābhāvanā meditation relate to the teaching of anatta?
cards.answer: It breaks down the mental barrier between 'self' and 'other' by extending loving-kindness outward to all beings.

cards.front: Why is direct insight through vipassanā considered important for enlightenment?
cards.answer: It lets the meditator directly experience the impermanent, unsatisfying and selfless nature of reality, not just understand it as a concept.

cards.front: What are the three distinct roles of the Three Jewels in Buddhism?
cards.answer: Buddha shows liberation is achievable / Dhamma is the path and teachings guiding practitioners / Sangha is the community that supports and preserves the teachings
items: Dhamma is the path and teachings guiding practitioners
Sangha is the community that supports and preserves the teachings

cards.front: Name the four occupation zones the Allies divided Germany into after 1945.
cards.answer: American / British / French / Soviet

cards.front: What were the five categories Germans were classified into under the Fragebogen system?
cards.answer: Major offenders / Offenders / Lesser offenders / Followers / Exonerated

cards.front: Why was de-Nazification effectively wound down in the Western zones by 1948-51?
cards.answer: Courts were overwhelmed by cases, witnesses died or became unavailable, and rebuilding the economy became more urgent as the Cold War intensified.

cards.front: Why did Stalin's Berlin Blockade fail?
cards.answer: The Western Allies supplied West Berlin by air for nearly a year via the Berlin Airlift, defeating Stalin's attempt to cut off the city.

cards.front: Name the five key sequences the lesson identifies for micro/representation analysis of The Wave.
cards.answer: Opening lesson on autocracy / White-shirt uniform-adoption sequence / School playground wave-chant scene / Late-night graffiti tagging sequence / Closing assembly-hall reveal

cards.front: What three social conditions does the lesson say make young people vulnerable to conformity in The Wave?
cards.answer: The teacher's charisma / The students' longing for belonging / The school as a laboratory of controlled social pressure
items: The school as a laboratory of controlled social pressure

cards.front: Why does Breuer hold an extended locked-off wide shot during the closing assembly-hall reveal instead of using fast editing?
cards.answer: The sustained duration forces the spectator to observe the group's uniformity without the kinetic excitement that made it appealing earlier.

cards.front: How does the sound design in the playground wave-chant scene create 'dual coding' of the group's energy?
cards.answer: The diegetic chant codes communal joy while the layered non-diegetic score codes the same moment as ominous, warning the audience.

cards.front: Why is Shylock's legal position in the trial described as sound?
cards.answer: The bond was signed willingly, and Venetian law must uphold contracts or the city's commercial reputation will collapse.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare show prejudice exists in the court itself, before Shylock even arrives?
cards.answer: The Duke calls Shylock 'an inhuman wretch' while speaking to Antonio before Shylock is called into court.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare give Antonio no triumphant speech after being saved from the trial?
cards.answer: His silence may speak louder than words, since he has watched the destruction of his enemy despite claiming to value mercy.

cards.front: Name the three group roles Kelly shows in DNA, according to the lesson's mapping onto the Stanford Prison Experiment.
cards.answer: Leader who cannot cope (John Tate) / Controlling power figure (Phil) / Passive bystanders (Richard, Danny, Lou)

cards.front: Name the two dramatic techniques the lesson says Kelly uses throughout DNA.
cards.answer: Fragmented, overlapping dialogue / Minimal stage directions

cards.front: Why does the group in DNA stay together, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: They are bound not by loyalty or friendship but by shared guilt and fear after their crime against Adam.

cards.front: Why does Leah fail to stop what happens to Adam despite recognising it is wrong?
cards.answer: Her moral awareness never turns into action, so she stays complicit like the watching audience.

title: The Great Terror, the NKVD and the Show Trials
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four methods the lesson says were used to force confessions from Show Trial defendants.
cards.answer: Beaten / Denied sleep / Threatened with arrest of wives and children / Promised a confession would save their families
items: Threatened with arrest of wives and children
Promised a confession would save their families

cards.front: Name the three Gulag camp locations or projects mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Kolyma / Vorkuta / White Sea–Baltic Canal

cards.front: Why did the 1937–38 purge of the Red Army officer corps weaken Soviet performance when Operation Barbarossa began in 1941?
cards.answer: Most senior marshals, generals and corps commanders had been executed, so the army was led by hastily promoted commanders with little senior experience.

cards.front: Why were the diplomatic corps and Western journalists invited to attend the Moscow Show Trials?
cards.answer: So the trials could be reported abroad as proof of the regime's impartiality.

cards.front: Name the four Italian trading cities' role and the three difficulties the crusader states faced (structural problems listed in the lesson).
cards.answer: Tiny Western settler population / Scarce military manpower / Dependence on Italian trading cities for supply / Weak feudal levy forces / Poor coordination between separate states
items: Dependence on Italian trading cities for supply

cards.front: Why did the crusader states rely on castles and diplomacy rather than pure military force to survive?
cards.answer: They could not match Muslim forces militarily, so they built strong stone castles and made alliances exploiting divisions among Muslim neighbours.

cards.front: Why did Muslim neighbours pose less of a threat to Outremer in its early decades?
cards.answer: The Seljuk empire was fragmenting into rival states and the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt was also weakened.

cards.front: Why did tension arise between the Latin Church and Eastern Christian communities in Outremer?
cards.answer: The Latin Church claimed authority over Eastern clergy, replacing Orthodox patriarchs and treating Eastern Christians as second-class.

cards.front: Name the three wrongs the lesson says Rochester committed that led to his punishment.
cards.answer: He lied / He attempted bigamy / He kept a woman imprisoned in his attic
items: He kept a woman imprisoned in his attic

cards.front: What three things does Jane bring with her when she arrives at Ferndean, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Her own money / Her own family connections / Her own fully formed identity

cards.front: Why does hearing Rochester's voice pull Jane away from St John's proposal?
cards.answer: It reasserts the claims of emotion and desire over duty and cold reason, pulling her back towards Rochester.

cards.front: How does Rochester's suffering after the fire make a marriage of equals possible?
cards.answer: His blindness and mutilation diminish and humble him, stripping away the power that once made him Jane's superior.

cards.front: Name the seven ways of working named for UK businesses.
cards.answer: Full-time / Part-time / Temporary / Working whilst mobile / Flexible working / Working from home / Self-employed

cards.front: Why do large, safety-critical organisations like the NHS tend to use tall structures?
cards.answer: Because clear lines of responsibility matter more than speed for these organisations.

cards.front: Why does poor delegation cause mistakes and resentment?
cards.answer: Because the manager gives a task without the authority to decide or without proper training.

cards.front: Name the five main renewable energy sources the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Wind / Solar / Tidal / Hydroelectric / Biomass

cards.front: Name the six factors designers consider when choosing an energy source for a product.
cards.answer: Power requirement / Portability / Environmental impact / Cost / Availability / Reliability

cards.front: How does a nuclear power station use fission to generate electricity?
cards.answer: Splitting uranium atoms releases heat, which produces steam that drives turbines connected to generators.

cards.front: Why is biomass considered carbon neutral?
cards.answer: The plants burned as fuel absorbed CO2 while growing, offsetting the CO2 released when they are burned.

title: The Question of God and the Problem of Evil
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the three core divine attributes the lesson gives as forming the classical theistic view of God.
cards.answer: Omnipotence (all-powerful) / Omniscience (all-knowing) / Omnibenevolence (all-loving/all-good)

cards.front: How does the logical problem of evil argue against God's existence?
cards.answer: If God is omnipotent he could stop suffering, if omnibenevolent he'd want to, yet suffering exists, so God isn't both or doesn't exist.

cards.front: How do humanists respond to suffering instead of praying for divine help?
cards.answer: They emphasise human responsibility, working through human action to reduce poverty, disease and injustice.

cards.front: Why do Muslims see trials and suffering as compatible with a merciful Allah?
cards.answer: They view suffering as a test of faith and a means of spiritual purification, not evidence of divine absence.

title: Increasing Water Supply: Strategies & Sustainable Futures
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four main strategies the lesson gives for increasing water supply.
cards.answer: Dams and reservoirs / Inter-basin water transfers / Desalination / Sustainable approaches (conservation, groundwater management, recycling)

cards.front: Name the three routes planned as part of the South–North Water Transfer Project.
cards.answer: Eastern Route / Central Route / Western Route

cards.front: Why is desalination not a suitable solution for a landlocked, low-income country?
cards.answer: It has no coast to draw seawater from and lacks the capital needed to build and run desalination infrastructure.

cards.front: How do johads raise groundwater levels in the Wakel River Basin?
cards.answer: They slow monsoon run-off, spread it over a wide area and let it percolate slowly into the ground, recharging the aquifer.

cards.front: What four key dramatic devices does the lesson identify in the play?
cards.answer: Asides / Dramatic irony / Disguise / The ring as a symbol

cards.front: Why does Shylock switch between prose and verse in the play?
cards.answer: The shift between prose and verse shows his adaptability and signals changes in tone and social register.

cards.front: Why does Act 5's lightness feel forced rather than natural after the trial?
cards.answer: The trial's intense human grievances cannot be resolved by comic conventions like marriages and moonlight.

cards.front: How does gold represent two opposing ideas in the play?
cards.answer: Gold signifies true love, as when Bassanio wins Portia, and false judgement, as with Morocco's casket mistake.

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why athletes use PEDs.
cards.answer: Financial rewards / Competitive pressure / Fear of falling behind rivals / National expectation

cards.front: Name the five reasons the lesson gives against using PEDs.
cards.answer: Health risks / Ban from sport / Reputational damage / Acting as a negative role model / Unfair advantage over clean competitors
items: Acting as a negative role model

cards.front: How does blood passporting help catch dopers?
cards.answer: It tracks an athlete's biological markers over time, revealing patterns of doping even when no specific substance is found in a single test.

cards.front: Why was swimmer Sun Yang given an eight-year ban?
cards.answer: For refusing to cooperate with anti-doping testers, not for a positive test itself; the ban was later revised on appeal.

title: Case Study: Liverpool and the Irish in the 19th Century
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why Liverpool became the main entry point for Irish migration.
cards.answer: Cheap short sea crossing from Ireland / Port already tied to Atlantic and imperial trade / Docks needed unskilled labour
items: Cheap short sea crossing from Ireland
Port already tied to Atlantic and imperial trade

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives for why Irish identity persisted in Liverpool into the 20th century.
cards.answer: Ongoing migration into the early 1900s / Catholic Church as active institution / Sectarian violence with the Orange Order / Tightly clustered dock economy communities
items: Sectarian violence with the Orange Order

cards.front: Why does the lesson warn against assuming all Famine migrants who landed in Liverpool stayed there?
cards.answer: Many travelled onward almost immediately to Manchester, Glasgow or transatlantic ships, so the 22% figure only reflects those too poor or sick to move on.

cards.front: Why did the Workhouse Test Order fail to control Irish relief demand in Liverpool?
cards.answer: It required migrants to enter the workhouse to qualify for relief, but the system was overwhelmed by the sheer number of penniless applicants.

cards.front: What three reasons does the lesson give for why Muslim scholars might accept contraception within marriage?
cards.answer: pregnancy would harm the mother's health / the family cannot afford more children / it would protect existing children's welfare
items: pregnancy would harm the mother's health
the family cannot afford more children
it would protect existing children's welfare

cards.front: Why do some Muslim scholars oppose contraception?
cards.answer: Because they believe children are a blessing from Allah and humans should not interfere with God's will.

cards.front: Why do Humanists support same-sex relationships and LGBTQ+ equality?
cards.answer: They base morality on human rights, happiness and the harm principle, and see no harm in consenting same-sex relationships.

cards.front: How do liberal Protestants justify sex outside marriage within committed relationships?
cards.answer: They interpret the Bible in its historical context and accept sex within committed, loving relationships even without marriage.

cards.front: Why does the Inspector show Eva's photograph to only one character at a time?
cards.answer: To control who speaks and stop the family from collaborating on a shared story.

cards.front: Why does Priestley make Sheila's motive for getting Eva sacked vanity rather than malice?
cards.answer: To show that even thoughtless, unintentional use of class privilege can destroy a working-class life.

title: Robust Programming: Validation, Authentication and Testing
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three validation checks the lesson identifies as required.
cards.answer: Minimum length check / Empty string (presence) check / Range check

cards.front: Name the three types of test data used when testing a program.
cards.answer: Normal (typical) data / Boundary (extreme) data / Erroneous data

cards.front: Why do systems often limit the number of login attempts in an authentication routine?
cards.answer: To prevent someone trying thousands of username/password combinations to gain unauthorised access.

cards.front: How does the authentication routine decide whether to grant access?
cards.answer: It compares the entered username and password to the stored values, and if both match it sets access to true.

cards.front: Name the four demands Austria-Hungary's ultimatum made of Serbia on 23 July 1914.
cards.answer: Suppress anti-Austrian publications / Dissolve nationalist societies / Dismiss named officials / Allow Austrian officials to investigate on Serbian soil
items: Allow Austrian officials to investigate on Serbian soil

cards.front: Name the four deeper causes of the First World War that the lesson says had been building for two decades.
cards.answer: The alliance system / Anglo-German naval rivalry / Slav nationalism in Austria-Hungary / Militarisation of European planning

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Sarajevo was the trigger rather than the cause of the First World War?
cards.answer: Deeper causes like the alliance system, naval rivalry, Slav nationalism and militarisation had already been building for two decades before the assassination.

cards.front: Why couldn't diplomacy stop the slide into war during the July Crisis?
cards.answer: Tight mobilisation timetables forced quick action, Germany and Russia lacked a direct telephone link, and both sides assumed the worst of each other.

cards.front: Name the five key production systems the lesson describes in modern manufacturing.
cards.answer: CAD (computer aided design) / CAM (computer aided manufacture) / FMS (flexible manufacturing systems) / JIT (just in time) / Lean manufacturing

cards.front: Name the three sustainable design methods the lesson gives for reducing environmental impact.
cards.answer: Using recycled materials / Designing for disassembly so parts can be reused / Minimising packaging
items: Designing for disassembly so parts can be reused
