cards.front: Why must a method justification link back to the enquiry question in two parts?
cards.answer: You must state what the method measures and how that measurement directly answers the question, not just describe the method.

title: Road to the Six Day War, 1964–67
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What four consequences did the Samu raid have, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: King Hussein humiliated / Palestinians on West Bank rioted / Egypt accused of hiding behind UNEF / All three front-line states pushed closer to war
items: Egypt accused of hiding behind UNEF
All three front-line states pushed closer to war

cards.front: Why did Nasser act on the Soviet warning about Israeli troop movements in May 1967 even though it was false?
cards.answer: He could not risk pan-Arab opinion accusing him of abandoning Syria, even though he couldn't verify the intelligence.

cards.front: Why did the closure of the Straits of Tiran make war more likely in the longer term?
cards.answer: It escalated Arab confidence and pulled Jordan into the 30 May defence pact, making the West Bank a battlefield.

cards.front: Why did the dissolution of the monasteries (1536-40) strengthen Parliament's role in protecting the Protestant settlement?
cards.answer: It redistributed Church land to the gentry, giving them a financial stake in Protestantism and in Parliament defending it.

cards.front: Why could Elizabeth I not simply stop the 'Puritan choir' MPs from raising Church discipline bills?
cards.answer: She could veto the bills themselves but had no power to stop MPs from raising them in the first place.

cards.front: What three aspects does the lesson compare between Dickinson's and Hannah's poems?
cards.answer: Tone / Voice / Form

cards.front: Why does Dickinson's simple hymn metre create an unsettling effect in 'I started Early – Took my Dog'?
cards.answer: Because its nursery-rhyme-like, song-like rhythm contrasts with the disturbing content of the speaker being pursued by the sea.

cards.front: Why is the distance between Hannah and her persona essential for the satire in 'Postcard from a Travel Snob' to work?
cards.answer: The reader must recognise Hannah is mocking, not endorsing, the speaker, so the self-important voice exposes the speaker's own arrogance.

cards.front: Name the six causes the lesson gives for rising poverty in Elizabethan England.
cards.answer: Population growth / Rising prices / Sheep enclosures replacing arable farming / Dissolution of the monasteries / Bad harvests in the 1580s / Demobilisation of soldiers

cards.front: Name the three currents the lesson gives for why attitudes to the poor began to soften.
cards.answer: Towns pioneering local schemes / Protestant clergy preaching about the poor / Visibility of unemployed able-bodied men
items: Protestant clergy preaching about the poor

cards.front: How did enclosure reduce the number of labouring jobs on the land?
cards.answer: One shepherd could manage land that had previously employed a dozen ploughmen.

cards.front: Why did price inflation hit wage labourers hardest?
cards.answer: Because their wages rose much more slowly than the rising cost of bread.

cards.front: Name the four zones in Mumbai's urban land-use pattern, moving from the coast inland.
cards.answer: Central Business District (Nariman Point and Fort) / Inner city (older industry and Dharavi) / Suburbs (e.g. Bandra and Andheri) / Urban-rural fringe (new airport and satellite towns)
items: Central Business District (Nariman Point and Fort)
Urban-rural fringe (new airport and satellite towns)

cards.front: Name the three types of work the lesson says pull migrants to Mumbai.
cards.answer: Textiles / Construction / Domestic service

cards.front: Why can bulldozers clear slum neighbourhoods in Mumbai with little notice?
cards.answer: Many slum residents have insecure property rights, so they have no legal protection against eviction.

cards.front: Why is there such stark inequality within Mumbai?
cards.answer: Skilled, English-speaking workers gained far more from growth than unskilled migrants, and peninsula land scarcity pushed property prices to extreme levels, excluding the poor.

cards.front: Why is mass conserved in a sealed container during a reaction?
cards.answer: Nothing can enter or leave the system, so no atoms are created or destroyed.

cards.front: How do you find the empirical formula of magnesium oxide experimentally?
cards.answer: Heat magnesium in a crucible, use the mass increase as oxygen mass, divide masses by Ar and simplify the ratio.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says to consider when comparing the injury risk of different sporting activities.
cards.answer: Contact level / Speed of movement / Use of implements / The natural environment involved

cards.front: Name the four categories of equipment discussed as extrinsic factors affecting injury risk.
cards.answer: Protective equipment / Performance equipment / Clothing / Footwear

cards.front: Why does an excessively hard artificial playing surface increase the risk of stress fractures and shin splints?
cards.answer: A hard surface increases ground-reaction forces on the joints, raising the risk of stress fractures and shin splints.

cards.front: How can a hostile crowd increase injury risk during a match?
cards.answer: A hostile crowd can increase a performer's anxiety, which in turn can lead to reckless play and injury.

cards.front: What four push factors from rural Maharashtra and Bihar drive migration to Mumbai?
cards.answer: Small landholdings / Drought / Low rural wages / Limited rural healthcare

cards.front: What four downsides of the informal economy in Mumbai does the lesson give?
cards.answer: Workers earn very little / Conditions are dangerous / Tax revenue is missed / Women exposed to harassment

cards.front: Why do some Londoners move out of the city in their thirties?
cards.answer: High housing costs push people out when they start families.

cards.front: How does the informal economy help new arrivals in Mumbai?
cards.answer: It provides cheap goods and services and creates work for new arrivals who would otherwise be unemployed.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says subroutines make programs easier.
cards.answer: Easier to write (tackle one task at a time) / Easier to test (check each block in isolation) / Easier to reuse (call the same subroutine many times) / Easier to maintain (change one block without breaking others)
items: Easier to write (tackle one task at a time)
Easier to test (check each block in isolation)
Easier to reuse (call the same subroutine many times)
Easier to maintain (change one block without breaking others)

cards.front: What three steps does the lesson say to follow when asked to write a subroutine?
cards.answer: Start with the signature (name and parameters) / Write the body / Add RETURN at the end if it is a function
items: Start with the signature (name and parameters)
Add RETURN at the end if it is a function

cards.front: In a banking app, how does making the balance a local variable make it easier to find bugs than using a global variable?
cards.answer: Only the subroutine that owns the local variable can change it, so any fault is isolated to that one subroutine.

cards.front: How do local variables let a hundred users run the same login check at once without interfering with each other?
cards.answer: Each user gets their own isolated local copy of the username and password that only exists while that subroutine runs.

title: Health, Disease and the Immune System
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four non-specific first-line defences the body uses against pathogens.
cards.answer: Skin / Mucus and cilia in respiratory tract / Stomach acid / Tears and saliva
items: Mucus and cilia in respiratory tract

cards.front: Name the four non-communicable diseases the lesson gives as examples.
cards.answer: Cardiovascular disease / Type 2 diabetes / Cancer / Asthma

cards.front: How does the inflammatory response help fight infection at the site of damage?
cards.answer: Damaged cells release chemicals that dilate and make blood vessels more permeable, increasing blood flow and letting white blood cells migrate into the tissue faster.

cards.front: How do antibodies help destroy pathogens once they bind to antigens?
cards.answer: They clump pathogens together for easier destruction, neutralise toxins, and mark pathogens for engulfment by phagocytes.

cards.front: Name the three components of a lever system in the body, arranged around the pivot.
cards.answer: Fulcrum (the joint) / Load (the resistance) / Effort (the muscular force)

cards.front: Why does a first-class lever like the triceps extending the elbow give mechanical advantage or disadvantage depending on arm lengths?
cards.answer: Because the fulcrum sits between load and effort, so whichever arm (effort or load) is longer relative to the other determines the outcome.

cards.front: Why can a javelin thrower accelerate the javelin to high speed with only a short muscular contraction?
cards.answer: The long lever of the arm magnifies the small movement of the muscle into greater speed and range at the hand.

cards.front: Why is heading a football classed as a first-class lever action?
cards.answer: Because the fulcrum, the atlanto-occipital joint, lies between the effort (neck muscles behind it) and the load (face and forehead in front).

cards.front: Why is UK shoe size classed as discrete data even though it is a numerical measurement?
cards.answer: Shoe sizes are a labelling convention with genuine gaps between values (e.g. no size 7.3), unlike a truly continuous measurement.

cards.front: Why can distinguishing the effect of one variable be difficult with multivariate data?
cards.answer: If variables like revision and sleep both increase together, it's hard to tell which one caused the change in outcome.

cards.front: Name the two further types the lesson gives within qualitative data.
cards.answer: Categorical data / Ordinal data

cards.front: Name the two further types the lesson gives within quantitative data.
cards.answer: Discrete data / Continuous data

title: Improving Processes: Metals, LCAs and Recycling
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the six factors that a life cycle assessment (LCA) considers.
cards.answer: Energy consumption at each stage / Raw material use / Water use / Emissions to air and water / Waste produced / Potential for recycling or reuse

cards.front: Name the four factors that affect decisions about whether to recycle a material.
cards.answer: Cost of collection and sorting / Energy needed to process recycled material compared to making new material / Market value of the recycled product / Public willingness to separate and recycle materials
items: Energy needed to process recycled material vs new material
Market value of the recycled product
Public willingness to separate and recycle

cards.front: Why is electrolysis used to extract aluminium instead of reduction with carbon?
cards.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot displace it from its oxide, meaning electrolysis must be used instead.

cards.front: Why should LCA evidence be evaluated critically rather than accepted at face value?
cards.answer: LCAs involve subjective judgement on hard-to-quantify factors, and companies sometimes use selective LCA data to support marketing claims.

cards.front: Name the five uses of glucose produced by photosynthesis in a plant.
cards.answer: Respiration / Starch storage / Cellulose for cell walls / Amino acids and proteins / Lipids for energy storage

cards.front: Name the three main factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
cards.answer: Light intensity / Carbon dioxide concentration / Temperature

cards.front: Why does the rate of photosynthesis eventually level off as light intensity keeps increasing?
cards.answer: Because carbon dioxide concentration or temperature becomes the limiting factor, so extra light no longer increases the rate.

cards.front: Why does the rate of photosynthesis decrease at temperatures below the enzyme's optimum?
cards.answer: Molecules have less kinetic energy, so they collide less frequently with enzyme active sites, slowing the reaction.

cards.front: Name the five dry cooking methods the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Roasting / Baking / Grilling / Frying / Dry-frying

cards.front: Name the five moist cooking methods the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Boiling / Steaming / Poaching / Braising / Stewing

cards.front: Why does over-working a pastry dough make it tough and chewy instead of short and crumbly?
cards.answer: Over-working activates the gluten network too strongly, producing a tough, chewy result instead of a short, crumbly texture.

cards.front: Why does a meringue foam collapse if fat gets into the egg whites?
cards.answer: Fat destroys the protein film that wraps around and stabilises the tiny air bubbles, causing the foam to collapse.

cards.front: Name the four things Prospero uses magic to control in Act 1, Scene 2, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Creates the storm / Puts Miranda to sleep / Summons and threatens Ariel / Punishes Caliban with cramps

cards.front: Why does Prospero keep interrupting his story to ask Miranda if she is listening?
cards.answer: It reveals his need for control, even over the narrative of his own suffering.

cards.front: Why is the word 'profit' in Caliban's line about learning language considered bitterly ironic?
cards.answer: Because the only profit his colonisation gained him is the ability to curse and voice his dispossession.

cards.front: Why does Prospero eventually have to give up his magic by the end of the play, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because his controlling use of magic isolates him and prevents genuine human connection, so he must trust relationships instead.

title: Modern policing, the death penalty and the Bentley case
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three types of exemption a WWI tribunal could grant to a Conscientious Objector.
cards.answer: Absolute exemption (rare) / Conditional exemption (alternative civilian work) / Non-combatant service (RAMC or Non-Combatant Corps)

cards.front: Name the five non-custodial sentencing options that existed in Britain by 2000, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Probation / Community service / Suspended sentences / Fines / Electronic tagging

cards.front: How did the alleged words 'Let him have it, Chris' make Bentley legally guilty of murder?
cards.answer: The Crown argued they were an instruction to shoot, making Bentley guilty of murder under joint enterprise even though Craig fired the shot.

cards.front: Why did the Bentley case not lead straight to the abolition of the death penalty in 1953?
cards.answer: It took twelve more years, further controversial executions like Ruth Ellis, and four attempts by Silverman before Parliament abolished capital punishment in 1965.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says you should annotate in an unseen poem.
cards.answer: Language / Structure / Form

cards.front: Name the three common mistakes the lesson warns against in unseen poetry answers.
cards.answer: Retelling the poem / Feature-spotting / Ignoring form and structure

cards.front: How does the 'How' stage of the What-How-Why method work?
cards.answer: You quote the poet's specific words and analyse them closely, looking at word choices, sounds, rhythms and patterns.

cards.front: Why should you summarise a poem's message in one sentence before writing your response?
cards.answer: It keeps your response focused, so every paragraph you write connects back to that central interpretation.

cards.front: Name the four explanations contemporaries gave for the cause of the 1665 plague.
cards.answer: Miasma (bad air) / Divine punishment for sin / The comet of 1664 / Unusual conjunctions of the planets

cards.front: Why did the Bills of Mortality probably underestimate the true number of plague deaths in 1665?
cards.answer: Families bribed searchers to record other causes to avoid shutting up, and Dissenters and Jews were buried outside the parish system.

cards.front: How did William Mompesson's response to plague in Eyam differ from the usual reaction to outbreaks?
cards.answer: He persuaded villagers to quarantine themselves voluntarily rather than flee, to avoid infecting neighbouring villages.

cards.front: Why did the practice of shutting up houses in 1665 probably increase deaths?
cards.answer: It kept infected families sealed inside together for forty days, so they often died together rather than escaping infection.

cards.front: Name the four types of research businesses combine with location factors when actually deciding where to locate.
cards.answer: Customer demographics / Planning permission / Transport access / Rival activity

cards.front: Name the four business types and the location factor each weighs most heavily, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Service businesses – proximity to market / Materials-heavy manufacturers – availability of materials / Warehouses/fulfilment centres – costs and motorway access / Knowledge-based businesses – availability of labour
items: Warehouses/fulfilment centres – costs and motorway access

cards.front: Why is the location decision described as an operations decision first and foremost?
cards.answer: Because it affects how the business produces, supplies and serves customers every single day.

cards.front: How does being close to suppliers improve a factory's operations?
cards.answer: It creates shorter supply chains, giving faster restocking and more reliable delivery to the business's own customers.

cards.front: Name the five main material categories covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Papers and boards / Timbers / Metals / Polymers / Textiles

cards.front: Name the three alloys named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Brass / Stainless steel / High speed steel (HSS)

cards.front: Why is plywood strong in all directions?
cards.answer: Because it is made from layers of veneer glued together at right angles to each other.

cards.front: Why is copper used for electrical wiring and plumbing?
cards.answer: Because copper is an excellent electrical conductor.

title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the six features of the alveoli that make gas exchange efficient.
cards.answer: Large total surface area / moist walls only one cell thick / short diffusion distance / large capillary network / large blood supply / maintained concentration gradient (high O2, low CO2)
items: Moist walls only one cell thick
Maintained concentration gradient (high O2, low CO2)

cards.front: Name the four lung volumes shown on a spirometer trace at rest.
cards.answer: Inspiratory reserve volume / tidal volume / expiratory reserve volume / residual volume

cards.front: How do the intercostal muscles help cause inhalation at rest?
cards.answer: They contract to raise the rib cage upward and outward, increasing chest cavity volume and lowering lung air pressure so air rushes in.

cards.front: Why can't you increase oxygen delivery to muscles just by trying harder to breathe?
cards.answer: Diffusion rate depends on surface area and concentration gradients, which effort alone cannot increase, though exercise raises breathing rate and opens more capillaries.

cards.front: Name the four social engineering techniques described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Phishing / Pretexting / Baiting / Vishing

cards.front: Name the three types of hacker in the colour-coded classification.
cards.answer: White hat / Black hat / Grey hat

cards.front: Why does stealing intellectual property damage a business's competitive advantage?
cards.answer: Competitors can replicate the stolen designs or research without the original investment, destroying the creator's market edge.

cards.front: Why can a business struggle to recover even after a data breach is technically fixed?
cards.answer: Customers lose confidence and partners withdraw, causing lasting reputational damage beyond the initial technical problem.

cards.front: Name the four human activities the lesson identifies as reducing biodiversity.
cards.answer: Deforestation / Pollution / Global warming / Overexploitation

cards.front: Name the five strategies the lesson gives for maintaining biodiversity.
cards.answer: Breeding programmes for endangered species / Protection of rare habitats / Reintroduction of hedgerows and field margins / Seed banks / Reducing deforestation and carbon emissions
items: Reintroduction of hedgerows and field margins

cards.front: How does deforestation reduce biodiversity?
cards.answer: Clearing forests for agriculture and building destroys habitats, reducing the space and resources available for species.

cards.front: How do decomposers release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere?
cards.answer: They break down dead organic material from dead organisms and release CO2 through respiration.

cards.front: Name the three predictions Birling makes that turn out to be wrong (his dramatic irony).
cards.answer: The Titanic is 'unsinkable' / There will be no war / Prosperity will keep 'steadily increasing'

cards.front: Name the three things Sheila does by the end of the play that show her transformation.
cards.answer: Returns the engagement ring / Defies her parents / Adopts the Inspector's moral perspective

cards.front: Why is Mrs Birling arguably more culpable than any other character in the play?
cards.answer: She represents institutional failure, corrupting the charity that was Eva's last safety net with class prejudice, causing her death.

cards.front: Why does Priestley make Eric more sympathetic than his parents despite his terrible crimes?
cards.answer: Because Eric accepts what he has done, unlike his parents who try to escape blame and refuse responsibility.

cards.front: Name the three structural causes the lesson gives for the early West being hard to police.
cards.answer: Distance from federal authority / Transient seasonal populations / Absence of women, families and settled property
items: Absence of women, families and settled property

cards.front: What four types of authority does the lesson list as covering law and order in the early West?
cards.answer: Town marshals / Sheriffs / US marshals / Vigilance committees

cards.front: Why did the misconception that 'Westerners were just lawless criminals' fail to explain frontier violence?
cards.answer: The same men were respectable at home; what changed was the absence of sheriffs, courts, jails and property lines restraining behaviour.

cards.front: Why was federal authority so thin in the early West even though marshals existed?
cards.answer: Government was tiny, telegraph and railroad had not reached the frontier, so a marshal with few deputies had to enforce huge territories alone.

title: The 6Cs — Qualities of a Service Practitioner
subject: health-social-care-ocr

cards.front: Name the nine person-centred values that are separate from the 6Cs.
cards.answer: Individuality / Choice / Rights / Independence / Privacy / Dignity / Respect / Partnership / Encouraging decision making

cards.front: Why is naming a 6C as if it were one of the nine person-centred values a mistake in an exam answer?
cards.answer: The 6Cs are the practitioner's own qualities, while the nine values are principles of care delivery for the service user, so they are different lists.

cards.front: Name the six threats to food security given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Increasing birth rate / Changing diets (more meat) / New pests and pathogens / Environmental change / Cost of agricultural inputs / Conflicts

cards.front: Name the four farming techniques the lesson gives for improving food security sustainably.
cards.answer: Biological control / Genetically modified crops / Hydroponics / Reducing food waste

cards.front: Why do rising fuel, fertiliser and seed costs threaten food security?
cards.answer: Rising prices of agricultural inputs affect farmers' ability to produce food.

cards.front: Why is mycoprotein production more efficient than rearing livestock for food?
cards.answer: The fungus grows and is harvested rapidly, and needs less land and water than livestock farming.

cards.front: Name the six types of financial information the lesson lists for measuring performance.
cards.answer: Revenue / Costs / Profit and loss / Gross and net margins / Average rate of return / Cash flow figures

cards.front: What are the four steps the lesson gives for structuring a synoptic answer?
cards.answer: Identify at least two functions involved / Link them together / Use the numbers given / Make a supported judgement
items: Identify at least two functions involved

cards.front: Why would the vegan sausage roll launch have stalled if finance underestimated demand?
cards.answer: Finance would have run out of cash to pay for ingredients, causing the launch to stall halfway through January.

cards.front: Why is financial information described as a feedback loop between the four functions?
cards.answer: Only financial data can confirm whether marketing, operations or pricing claims actually worked, showing what to adjust next.

cards.front: Name the three assumptions Sandra holds when she first arrives at Mrs Rutter's cottage.
cards.answer: Old ladies are kind / Boys like Kerry are undesirable / The world is readable by its surface appearances
items: The world is readable by its surface appearances

cards.front: Why does Kerry not undergo the same moral revelation that Sandra does?
cards.answer: He simply knows immediately that leaving the airman to die was wrong, unlike Sandra, whose moral understanding develops more slowly.

cards.front: How does Mrs Rutter's character subvert traditional expectations of elderly women?
cards.answer: She appears to be a gentle, nurturing grandmother figure but is shown to be capable of cruelty and feels no remorse about it.

cards.front: Name Piaget's four stages of cognitive development, in order.
cards.answer: Sensorimotor / Pre-operational / Concrete operational / Formal operational

cards.front: Why does a pre-operational child say there is more water after it's poured from a short wide glass into a tall thin one?
cards.answer: They lack conservation, so they judge quantity by appearance (height) rather than understanding the amount stayed the same.

cards.front: Why do concrete operational children struggle with a logic puzzle that has no physical objects?
cards.answer: Their logical thinking only works when applied to real, tangible objects, not to purely abstract or hypothetical reasoning.

cards.front: Name the four key themes the lesson identifies in Blood Brothers.
cards.answer: Class and Inequality / Nature vs Nurture / Superstition and Fate vs Free Will / Violence
items: Superstition and Fate vs Free Will

cards.front: What four-part pattern should each body paragraph of a modern text essay follow?
cards.answer: Point / Evidence / Analysis / Context

cards.front: Why does Russell use superstition as a theme in Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: It acts as a metaphor for the false explanations society uses to justify inequality, while class remains the real cause.

cards.front: Why does Mickey become violent in Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: Not because he is a bad person but because the class system has left him with nothing, driven by poverty and desperation.

cards.front: Name the four contact forces listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Friction / Air resistance / Tension / Normal contact force

cards.front: Name the three non-contact forces listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Gravitational force / Electrostatic force / Magnetic force

cards.front: Why does a book resting on a table stay still?
cards.answer: Its weight acting downwards and the normal contact force acting upwards are equal, giving a zero resultant force.

cards.front: How do you find the resultant of two forces that don't act along the same line using a scale drawing?
cards.answer: Draw the forces as arrows tip-to-tail to scale; the resultant runs from the start of the first to the end of the second; measure its length and angle.

cards.front: Name the three things Hitler did to secure the two-thirds majority needed to pass the Enabling Act.
cards.answer: Arrested Communist deputies / Intimidated Social Democrat deputies / Secured Catholic Centre Party support

cards.front: Name the three institutions whose collaboration helped the Nazis consolidate power in 1933.
cards.answer: The army / Civil servants / The Catholic Church

cards.front: How did the army's oath of loyalty on 2 August 1934 make it harder for officers to resist Hitler later?
cards.answer: It bound soldiers personally to Hitler himself rather than to Germany or the constitution, making resistance psychologically and legally harder.

cards.front: Why did the Catholic Church sign the Concordat with Hitler in July 1933?
cards.answer: To gain legal protection for the Church in exchange for accepting Nazi political supremacy and withdrawing from politics.

title: Engineering Maths II — Areas, Volumes, Estimation & Scale
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four length unit conversions given in the lesson.
cards.answer: 1 m = 1000 mm / 1 km = 1000 m / 1 foot = 12 inches / 1 inch ≈ 25.4 mm

cards.front: What are the four common engineering drawing scales given in the lesson?
cards.answer: 1:1 full size / 1:2 half size / 1:10 one tenth of real size / 2:1 twice real size

cards.front: Why can the cylinder volume formula be applied to any prism shape?
cards.answer: Because it is the area of the constant cross-section multiplied by the length, which works for any prism.

cards.front: How can an engineer quickly estimate the cost of materials before ordering?
cards.answer: Round all values to one or two significant figures, calculate mentally, then refine with a calculator if needed.

cards.front: Why does Papa never complain about the racism he faces?
cards.answer: He chooses dignity and grace over confrontation, representing the resilience of the immigrant experience.

cards.front: How does Mama represent the cost of immigration?
cards.answer: She has sacrificed her homeland, community and cultural context for her family's future, and feels homesick.

cards.front: Name the five key indicators of substance misuse problems given in the lesson.
cards.answer: using more or larger amounts over time / unable to stop despite wanting to / neglecting responsibilities like work or family / needing more for the same effect (tolerance) / withdrawal symptoms when not using
items: using more or larger amounts over time
unable to stop despite wanting to
neglecting responsibilities like work or family
needing more for the same effect (tolerance)

cards.front: What are the UK CMO physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19-64?
cards.answer: 150 minutes moderate activity per week / or 75 minutes vigorous activity / strength-building activity 2+ days per week / reduce extended sitting time

cards.front: Why are lifestyle indicators useful alongside physiological readings like high blood pressure?
cards.answer: They reveal the causes behind abnormal readings, so health professionals can recommend specific, targeted actions for improvement.

cards.front: Why do health professionals ask how many cigarettes a smoker has per day and for how long?
cards.answer: This data helps calculate the level of health risk and how urgently the person needs to quit.

cards.front: Name the seven variables Townsend's deprivation index scored households on.
cards.answer: Diet / Fuel / Clothing / Housing / Health / Education / Social activities

cards.front: Name the three industries the lesson says were relocated to South and East Asia due to globalisation.
cards.answer: Car production / Steel production / Textile production

cards.front: Why do lone parents face a high risk of poverty?
cards.answer: They combine childcare responsibility with a single, often part-time or lower-paid, income, worsened by the gender pay gap and childcare costs.

cards.front: How does the cycle of deprivation reinforce poverty across generations?
cards.answer: Poor childhood health limits educational attainment, which restricts employment prospects, which creates low income and material deprivation for the next generation.

title: The failure of Weimar democracy and Hitler's appointment
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three layers of cause the lesson gives for the failure of Weimar democracy.
cards.answer: Structural causes / Long-term causes / Contingent causes

cards.front: What four structural causes does the lesson give for Weimar's weakness?
cards.answer: Treaty of Versailles / Article 48 emergency provision / Proportional representation causing fragmented Reichstags / Survival of anti-democratic elites

cards.front: Why did Schleicher's attempt to govern as Chancellor in December 1932 fail within four weeks?
cards.answer: His plan to split Strasser's Nazi wing failed, he had no Reichstag majority, and trade unions distrusted an aristocratic general.

cards.front: Why did the Preussenschlag of July 1932 matter for Nazi power?
cards.answer: It destroyed the largest democratic stronghold and removed the SPD-controlled police force resisting Nazi street violence.

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives that determine different interest rates.
cards.answer: Risk of the borrower defaulting / Time period of the loan / Competition and the base rate

cards.front: Why do longer-term loans often carry higher interest rates?
cards.answer: The lender's money is tied up for longer and faces greater uncertainty, so they charge more.

cards.front: Why might a very low interest rate fail to stimulate borrowing and investment after a financial crisis?
cards.answer: Banks may become unwilling to lend for fear of bad debts, so low rates don't lead to more borrowing.

cards.front: How does the Bank of England's base rate affect the rates commercial banks offer?
cards.answer: It acts as a benchmark, so when it rises or falls commercial banks typically adjust their mortgage, savings and loan rates accordingly.

cards.front: Name the five methods the lesson gives for reducing unwanted energy transfer from buildings.
cards.answer: Low thermal conductivity materials (foam/fibreglass/trapped air) / Double glazing / Cavity wall insulation / Loft insulation / Reflective surfaces to reduce radiation

cards.front: Name the three steps the lesson gives for measuring the density of a liquid.
cards.answer: Place measuring cylinder on balance and zero it / Pour in the liquid and read mass and volume / Use ρ = m/V
items: Place measuring cylinder on balance and zero it
Pour in the liquid and read mass and volume

cards.front: Why does increasing the temperature of a gas at constant volume increase its pressure?
cards.answer: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, hitting the walls more frequently and with greater force.

cards.front: Why does heating a substance not always raise its temperature?
cards.answer: If the substance is changing state, the energy is used to break bonds between particles instead of raising temperature.

title: The Berlin Blockade, Airlift and the Birth of NATO
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the twelve countries that signed the North Atlantic Treaty in 1949.
cards.answer: USA / Canada / Britain / France / Italy / Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Portugal
items: Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Portugal

cards.front: Why did Stalin blockade Berlin in 1948?
cards.answer: He saw the new Western currency as building a working West German economy that would draw East Germans toward the Western system, so he cut off access to force the West out.

cards.front: How did the Berlin Blockade lead to the permanent division of Germany?
cards.answer: Once Stalin tried to starve out West Berlin, no Western leader would trust the Soviet zone, so the Western zones became West Germany and the Soviet zone became East Germany.

title: Terror, the Three and Five Antis, and the Hundred Flowers, 1951-57
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three tools/methods the CCP used during these mass campaigns of 1950-57.
cards.answer: public denunciation / mass meetings / struggle sessions

cards.front: Why did local cadres end up denouncing large numbers of people during the 1950-52 terror campaign?
cards.answer: Local cadres met quotas, as each county was expected to identify a set proportion of 'enemies'.

cards.front: Why might the early stages of the Hundred Flowers Campaign have been a genuine reform rather than a trap, according to Dikötter and Spence?
cards.answer: Mao expected only mild criticism, was alarmed by the volume received, and reframed it as a trap afterwards.

cards.front: How did the Five Antis Campaign change China's economy by 1956?
cards.answer: Almost all private industry and commerce had been absorbed into the state or into joint state-private enterprises.

cards.front: Name the five fundamental tasks the lesson says the operating system handles.
cards.answer: Manages the CPU / Allocates RAM to running programs / Controls input and output devices / Manages the file system / Provides the user interface

cards.front: Name the five examples of utility software given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Anti-malware software / Disk defragmenters / File compression tools / Backup software / Disk cleanup tools

cards.front: How does firmware prepare a computer when it first starts up?
cards.answer: Firmware such as BIOS/UEFI runs a Power-On Self Test before handing control over to the operating system.

cards.front: Why is specialist software usually more expensive than general applications software?
cards.answer: It is developed for a narrower market with specific requirements and usually requires specialist training to use.

title: Racial policy: Nazi treatment of the Jews to 1939
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five stages of escalating persecution of Jews the lesson traces from 1933 to 1938.
cards.answer: 1933 boycott of Jewish businesses / Professional exclusions from jobs / Nuremberg Laws (legal racial separation) / Aryanisation of businesses / Kristallnacht violence

cards.front: Why did the 1933 boycott of Jewish businesses only last one day?
cards.answer: Because of international criticism and because many Germans did not observe it.

cards.front: Why did the international community's reaction to Kristallnacht encourage further Nazi persecution?
cards.answer: Because it produced only expressions of horror with no sanctions or military threat, signalling the regime could act with impunity.

cards.front: How did Hitler's ideas in Mein Kampf justify Nazi persecution of Jews?
cards.answer: He argued Jews were a separate, inferior race responsible for Germany's 1918 defeat and the evils of communism and capitalism.

cards.front: The lesson gives four recognised routes into manumission. Name all four.
cards.answer: Being included in the census as free / Being freed by a magistrate (manumissio iusta) / Being named as free in an owner's will / Being declared free before the owner's friends
items: Being included in the census as free
Being freed by a magistrate (manumissio iusta)
Being named as free in an owner's will
Being declared free before the owner's friends

cards.front: Why did service to the Roman state as a public slave sometimes lead to freedom faster than private slavery?
cards.answer: Public slaves like Scipio's captured workers were promised freedom if they actively helped provide equipment for war.

cards.front: Why did King Philip of Macedon praise the Romans for their manumission system, and where was he wrong?
cards.answer: He praised them for making slaves citizens who could hold important positions, but freedmen could not actually hold public office.

cards.front: Name the four common timber defects described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Knots / Shrinkage and warping / Shakes / Fungal attack

cards.front: Name the four types of manufactured board named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Plywood / MDF / Chipboard / Hardboard

cards.front: Why is balsa classed as a hardwood even though it feels soft?
cards.answer: Because hardwood/softwood is a botanical classification based on the tree (balsa comes from a deciduous tree), not physical hardness.

cards.front: Why do manufactured boards overcome most of the defects found in solid timber?
cards.answer: Their manufacturing process removes directional grain dependence, large knots and growth-related stresses that cause defects.

cards.front: Name the three experimental designs described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Independent groups / Repeated measures / Matched pairs

cards.front: Name the three types of experiment based on setting described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Laboratory experiment / Field experiment / Natural experiment

cards.front: Why can experiments establish cause and effect, unlike other methods?
cards.answer: Because they directly manipulate one variable while keeping everything else constant, then measure its effect on another variable.

cards.front: Why is a natural experiment lower in control than laboratory or field experiments?
cards.answer: Because the researcher does not choose the IV, so participants cannot be randomly allocated to conditions.

title: Worsening Relations: Taxation, Plot of 1212 and Bouvines 1214
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three things broke the relationship between John and the barons between 1212 and 1215?
cards.answer: Relentless financial pressure / A baronial plot John never forgave / The catastrophe of Bouvines in July 1214
items: A baronial plot John never forgave
The catastrophe of Bouvines in July 1214

cards.front: Beyond scutage, name the four ways the lesson says John exploited feudal incidents.
cards.answer: Charging punitive reliefs on inheritance / Selling heiresses to the highest bidder / Forcing widows to pay fines to avoid remarriage / Auctioning wardships of orphaned heirs
items: Selling heiresses to the highest bidder
Forcing widows to pay fines to avoid remarriage

cards.front: According to modern historians like W. L. Warren, why did the barons actually rebel against John?
cards.answer: Not because he was a bad administrator but because he was a good one whose methods were arbitrary and squeezed them harder than any king before.

cards.front: Why did John's southern advance towards Bouvines fail before the main battle even happened?
cards.answer: His advance stalled at the siege of La Roche-aux-Moines because his Poitevin allies refused to fight a pitched battle.

title: Glaciated Uplands: Economic Activity, Conflict & Tourism
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four main economic activities in glaciated uplands like the Lake District.
cards.answer: Tourism / Farming / Forestry / Quarrying

cards.front: Name the three types of environmental impact of tourism listed for the Lake District.
cards.answer: Footpath erosion / Water pollution from boats and camping / Disturbance of ground-nesting birds
items: Water pollution from boats and camping

cards.front: Why does sheep grazing on the Lake District fells matter for tourism?
cards.answer: Sheep grazing keeps the fell slopes open; without it they would revert to scrub and woodland, losing the scenery tourists visit for.

cards.front: Why did mid-20th century conifer plantations in the Lake District cause controversy?
cards.answer: Non-native Sitka spruce was planted in geometrical blocks, which was seen as visually intrusive and damaging to biodiversity.

cards.front: Name the five 'Giant Evils' Beveridge identified in his 1942 report.
cards.answer: Want / Disease / Ignorance / Squalor / Idleness

cards.front: Name the six industries nationalised by Attlee's government (1945-51).
cards.answer: Coal / Railways / Electricity / Gas / Steel / Bank of England

cards.front: Why was Britain's entry into the EEC in 1973 controversial for parliamentary sovereignty?
cards.answer: EEC membership meant Community law was superior to Acts of Parliament in areas like trade, agriculture and competition.

cards.front: Why did the Conservatives keep the NHS and most nationalised industries after returning to power in 1951?
cards.answer: Keeping them suggested the welfare settlement had wide public support across the political spectrum.

cards.front: What three drawbacks of celluloid film stock does the lesson give as limitations directors faced?
cards.answer: Expensive to buy / Expensive to process / Limited in quantity (finite takes)

cards.front: What three visual qualities does the lesson give as the recognisable look of DV footage?
cards.answer: Specific colour response / Softness / Visible grain in low light

cards.front: Why did digital cinematography change the economics and culture of film production?
cards.answer: Digital sensors recorded to memory cards or hard drives, footage could be reviewed instantly, and takes were essentially free.

cards.front: Why did Tangerine (2015) have its distinctive intimate, close-up visual look?
cards.answer: The iPhone's wide-angle lens made faces fill the frame, backgrounds fall into soft-focus, and the camera move through streets with immediacy.

title: Interpreting Data on Participation and Performance
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the four steps of the method for interpreting data in an exam question.
cards.answer: Read / Compare / Calculate / Explain

cards.front: Name the four main formats for presenting data given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Table / Bar chart / Line graph / Pie chart

cards.front: Why does simply copying numbers from a table or graph fail to earn marks on an interpret-data question?
cards.answer: Because reading off figures shows the data but does not compare, calculate or explain what the pattern means.

cards.front: Why must both axes on a bar chart or line graph always be labelled?
cards.answer: So the variable being measured and its unit are clear, showing what the category and value axes represent.

title: Social Challenges in Africa & South Asia
subject: geography-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four main social challenges the lesson identifies for sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
cards.answer: Getting girls through school / Ending child labour / Supporting refugees / Reducing infant mortality

cards.front: What six stubborn reasons does the lesson give for girls dropping out of school?
cards.answer: School fees / Cost of uniforms and books / Long unsafe walks to class / Lack of girls' toilets / Early marriage / Assumption boys' education is more valuable
items: Assumption boys' education is more valuable

cards.front: Why does educating girls tend to lower infant mortality in the next generation?
cards.answer: Better-educated mothers are more likely to vaccinate children, less likely to die in childbirth, and less likely to lose a baby in its first year.

cards.front: Why is child labour so hard to tackle even though it harms children?
cards.answer: It is woven into household survival, as families depend on children's income and a missed school year often means missing school forever.

cards.front: Name the three pillars of Stresemann's 1923-24 economic recovery.
cards.answer: Ending passive resistance in the Ruhr / Replacing the mark with the Rentenmark / Negotiating the Dawes Plan for US loans
items: Ending passive resistance in the Ruhr
Replacing the mark with the Rentenmark
Negotiating the Dawes Plan for US loans

cards.front: Name four terms Germany was forced to accept in the Treaty of Versailles.
cards.answer: Accept sole war guilt / Pay reparations of 132 billion gold marks / Lose 13% of territory and 10% of population / Reduce army to 100,000 men
items: Pay reparations of 132 billion gold marks
Lose 13% of territory and 10% of population

cards.front: Why did hyperinflation in 1923 destroy trust in the Weimar Republic?
cards.answer: It wiped out savings and ruined people on fixed incomes, generating deep distrust of democracy's ability to manage the economy.

cards.front: Why did the Wall Street Crash of 1929 destroy Weimar democracy's stability?
cards.answer: American banks recalled loans to Germany, causing businesses to collapse and unemployment to soar, destroying the fragile economic consensus.

cards.front: What are the three offences under the Computer Misuse Act 1990?
cards.answer: Unauthorised access to computer material / Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences / Unauthorised modification of computer material
items: Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences

cards.front: What three rights does GDPR give individuals over their personal data?
cards.answer: Right to access data held about them / Right to correct inaccurate data / Right to request deletion (right to be forgotten)
items: Right to access data held about them
Right to request deletion (right to be forgotten)

cards.front: Why is the monitoring of individuals an ethical issue rather than just a legal one?
cards.answer: Something can be legal yet still ethically questionable, so an employer legally reading staff emails without telling them can still breach trust.

cards.front: Why do companies need strong security as well as privacy protections when collecting personal data?
cards.answer: Collecting large amounts of data creates a responsibility to protect it, and poor security can cause breaches exposing people to identity theft, fraud and harassment.

cards.front: Name the four items offered before a shrine or Buddha image during puja.
cards.answer: Flowers / Candles or lamps / Incense / Food and water

cards.front: Name the three Tibetan Buddhist devotional practices mentioned alongside malas.
cards.answer: Prostrations / Mandala offerings / Prayer wheels

cards.front: Why do Buddhists bow during puja?
cards.answer: Bowing is an act of respect for the Buddha as teacher, cultivating humility and reducing pride, not worship of a god.

cards.front: Why is Samatha meditation seen as a foundation for other types of meditation?
cards.answer: It calms and steadies the mind through concentration, and without this tranquillity insight meditation is difficult to develop.

title: Learning Theories: Mindset and Learning Styles
subject: psychology-ocr

cards.front: Why do fixed-mindset learners avoid challenges and give up when work gets difficult?
cards.answer: Because failure feels like proof of a permanent limit, threatening their belief that ability is fixed.

cards.front: Why can praising a child for being 'clever' backfire, according to Dweck?
cards.answer: It signals intelligence is fixed and must be protected, making the child avoid risky, difficult work.

cards.front: What did Blackwell et al. (2007) find happened to fixed-mindset students' maths grades over the transition to secondary school?
cards.answer: Their achievement levelled off into a flat trajectory over that period.

cards.front: According to Willingham, why does teaching for meaning beat teaching for style?
cards.answer: Information connected to what a learner already understands is remembered far better than information merely matched to their preferred format.

cards.front: Name the three German adverbs used to show how much you like an activity, from least to most.
cards.answer: gern (like doing) / lieber (prefer doing) / am liebsten (like doing most of all)
items: am liebsten (like doing most of all)

cards.front: What are the six present tense verb endings used for regular German verbs like spielen?
cards.answer: -e / -st / -t / -en / -t / -en

cards.front: How do you form the present tense of a regular German verb such as spielen?
cards.answer: Remove -en from the infinitive to get the stem (spiel-), then add the correct ending for the subject.

cards.front: How does using weil or obwohl to give a reason change the word order of a German sentence?
cards.answer: The verb moves to the end of the clause, which is called subordinate word order.

cards.front: Name the four types of sentence available to Youth Courts for offenders aged 10-17.
cards.answer: Youth cautions / Referral orders / Youth rehabilitation orders / Detention and training orders

cards.front: Name the four main types of sentence available to courts.
cards.answer: Custodial sentence / Community order / Fines / Conditional discharge

cards.front: Why can higher levels of policing in an area make crime appear more concentrated there than it really is?
cards.answer: More policing leads to more recorded offences in that area, which can make crime seem concentrated when the reality may be more complex.

cards.front: Why do official crime statistics undercount offences like domestic violence and sexual offences?
cards.answer: Underreporting means these offences are often not reported to police, so they are missed from recorded crime figures.

cards.front: Name the three lean techniques beyond JIT that the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Kaizen / 5S / Cell production

cards.front: What do the five S's stand for in the 5S lean technique?
cards.answer: Sort / Set / Shine / Standardise / Sustain

cards.front: How does lean production help stop faulty cars being made at Toyota's Burnaston plant?
cards.answer: Workers can stop the line if they spot a defect, preventing faulty cars travelling further down the process.

cards.front: Why is flow production's set-up cost very high compared to its running cost?
cards.answer: It needs a continuous assembly line built for huge standardised volumes before any low-cost units can be made.

title: Passchendaele and the Tactical Learning Curve
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six combined-arms tactics the BEF was using by the end of 1917.
cards.answer: Predicted artillery fire / Sound-ranging / Aerial reconnaissance / Platoon-level infantry organisation / Mass tank attacks / More accurate creeping barrage

cards.front: Why was aerial photography important for artillery attacks by 1917?
cards.answer: It produced detailed trench maps that let artillery fire accurately without registering shots in advance and giving away the attack.

cards.front: Name the five steps the lesson gives for drawing a geological cross-section from map data.
cards.answer: Draw a line along the section / Mark where boundaries cross the line / Read dip angle and direction at symbols / Project each boundary down at that dip angle / Connect projected boundaries between units
items: Draw a line along the section
Mark where boundaries cross the line
Read dip angle and direction at symbols
Project each boundary down at that dip angle

cards.front: Why did the unconformity at Siccar Point convince James Hutton the Earth was immeasurably old?
cards.answer: The nearly 65-million-year gap between the tilted and horizontal beds showed far more time had passed than any biblical timescale allowed.

cards.front: Name the three main types of waste/excess substances the kidneys filter from the blood to form urine.
cards.answer: Urea / Excess water / Excess mineral ions (such as sodium)

cards.front: According to the lesson, what are the four drawbacks of dialysis compared with a transplant?
cards.answer: Time-consuming / Requires repeated sessions / Restricts diet and quality of life / Does not cure kidney failure
items: Restricts diet and quality of life

cards.front: How are nephron tubule cells adapted to maximise selective reabsorption?
cards.answer: They have microvilli to increase surface area and many mitochondria to provide energy for active transport.

cards.front: Why is dialysis fluid carefully formulated to contain the correct concentrations of glucose and mineral ions?
cards.answer: So that glucose and mineral ions are not lost from the blood by diffusion during dialysis.

cards.front: Name the six key themes that every Anita and Me exam question connects to.
cards.answer: Identity / Racism / Friendship / Family / Class / Growing Up

cards.front: What five-part pattern does a strong comparative paragraph follow?
cards.answer: Point about the studied text / Quotation + AO2 analysis / Comparison with unseen text / Quotation + AO2 analysis / Link to context (AO3)

cards.front: Why does Syal argue that the community's silence is as damaging as racism itself?
cards.answer: Because that silence enables racism to continue unchallenged at every level, from casual comments to violent attacks.

cards.front: Why is Tollington's class status significant for the novel's class theme?
cards.answer: The Kumars are middle-class in education and aspiration but live in working-class Tollington, showing class intersecting with race.

cards.front: Name the six tools an IDE typically includes.
cards.answer: Code editor / Syntax error detection / Debugger / Breakpoint / Variable watch / Memory inspector

cards.front: Name the five compilation stages in order.
cards.answer: Lexical analysis / Syntax analysis / Semantic analysis / Code generation / Code optimisation

cards.front: Why does an interpreted program run more slowly than a compiled program?
cards.answer: Because an interpreter translates each line every time the program runs, instead of translating once beforehand like a compiler.

cards.front: Why are logic errors the hardest type of error to find?
cards.answer: Because the program runs without crashing and appears to work, even though it produces the wrong result.

cards.front: Name the three market data signals the lesson gives that tell a business when the marketing mix needs to change.
cards.answer: Changes in demand / Changes in market share / Effect of promotion on sales

cards.front: Why did the coffee chain's sales settle at £210,000 a week after its Instagram campaign ended, rather than dropping back to £200,000?
cards.answer: The campaign created a small lasting lift in sales even after the spending stopped.

cards.front: Why did Debenhams' marketing mix stop being integrated?
cards.answer: Its place (mainly high-street stores) fell behind as rivals invested in e-commerce, so only three Ps kept moving forward.

cards.front: Why would it be a problem if ASOS ran TV adverts aimed at over-60s while keeping its other Ps the same?
cards.answer: The promotion channel would not match the target customer the other three Ps were designed for, breaking the mix.

cards.front: Name the three components in a series circuit whose resistance and voltage give the equipment needed for the I-V characteristic practical, plus what the voltmeter connects across.
cards.answer: Variable resistor in series / Ammeter in series / Power supply / Voltmeter connected in parallel across the component
items: Voltmeter connected in parallel across the component

cards.front: Why does the resistor with the larger resistance get a bigger share of the voltage in a series circuit?
cards.answer: Because voltage is shared between components in proportion to their resistance, so a larger resistance takes a greater share.

title: Early modern crime: heresy, treason and witchcraft
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three new categories of crime that defined the early modern period.
cards.answer: Heresy / Vagabondage / Witchcraft

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives for the surge in English witchcraft prosecutions.
cards.answer: Religious anxiety after the Reformation / Fear of social disorder and bad harvests / The printing press spreading sensational stories / James I's personal interest via Daemonologie
items: Fear of social disorder and bad harvests
The printing press spreading sensational stories
James I's personal interest via Daemonologie

cards.front: Why did the dissolution of the monasteries (1536–41) contribute to the rise in vagabondage?
cards.answer: It closed the largest providers of poor relief almost overnight, leaving more people homeless and jobless.

cards.front: Why were most people accused of witchcraft poor, elderly, single women?
cards.answer: They were the people most easily suspected by their neighbours.

cards.front: What three factors does personal space vary with, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Culture / Gender / Social status

cards.front: Why does eye contact matter for regulating conversation?
cards.answer: We use gaze to signal when we are ready to speak, want the other to continue, or are handing over our turn.

cards.front: Why do people from different cultures read the eyes or mouth differently when judging emotion, according to Yuki?
cards.answer: If NVC were entirely innate everyone would read the same features the same way, so the difference shows cultural learning shapes interpretation.

cards.front: What four main things does the biosphere provide for people, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Food / Medicine / Building materials / Fuel

cards.front: Name the four types of UK terrestrial ecosystem given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Moorland / Heathland / Woodland / Wetland

cards.front: Why do mountainsides show the same sequence of biomes as travelling from the equator to the poles?
cards.answer: Every 100m of altitude is roughly equivalent to moving 100km polewards, so height recreates the global climate pattern in miniature.

cards.front: Why is the biosphere described as a regulator as well as a resource?
cards.answer: Plants remove CO2 and release oxygen and water vapour, so damaging ecosystems releases stored carbon and reduces the planet's ability to recycle gases.

title: Characters: Mercutio, Tybalt and the Nurse
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the three ways Mercutio, Tybalt and the Nurse each directly cause the tragedy.
cards.answer: Mercutio's death provokes Romeo to kill Tybalt / Tybalt's aggression causes Romeo's banishment / The Nurse's betrayal pushes Juliet to the Friar's plan
items: Mercutio's death provokes Romeo to kill Tybalt
The Nurse's betrayal pushes Juliet to the Friar's plan

cards.front: Why does it matter that Mercutio is neither a Montague nor a Capulet when he dies?
cards.answer: His death can't be blamed on either family, showing that the feud itself, not one side, kills him.

cards.front: Why does the Nurse tell Juliet to marry Paris after Romeo's banishment?
cards.answer: She prioritises Juliet's physical safety and social security over romantic love, seeing it as practical advice.

cards.front: Name the three character pairings the lesson gives to show Shakespeare's deliberate contrasts.
cards.answer: Beatrice and Hero / Benedick and Claudio / Don Pedro and Don John

cards.front: The lesson lists three stages of Beatrice's language across the play — what are they?
cards.answer: Witty prose in Acts 1-2 / Dignified verse after the gulling / Raw, violent anger in Act 4

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Hero stays almost silent during the church scene?
cards.answer: Because patriarchy silences women, giving her no language to defend herself against the accusation.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Benedick's failed love poem in Act 5 Scene 2 is endearing rather than embarrassing?
cards.answer: Because it shows a prose speaker stepping outside his comfort zone into verse, proving his love is genuine even though clumsy.

cards.front: Name the three main parts of a sperm cell.
cards.answer: Head containing the nucleus / Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy / Tail (flagellum) for propulsion
items: Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy

cards.front: Name the four stages a fertilised egg goes through from zygote to implantation.
cards.answer: Cleavage (repeated division) / Morula (solid ball of cells) / Blastocyst (hollow ball with fluid cavity) / Implantation into the endometrium

cards.front: How is the sex of a baby determined at fertilisation?
cards.answer: The egg always contributes an X chromosome; a Y sperm makes a male (XY) embryo, an X sperm makes a female (XX) embryo.

cards.front: Why does menstruation happen if fertilisation does not occur?
cards.answer: Progesterone and oestrogen levels fall, causing the thickened uterine lining to break down and be shed.

title: Trophic Levels and Transfer of Biomass
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why biomass is lost between trophic levels.
cards.answer: Not all parts of organisms are eaten (e.g. roots, bones, feathers) / Material lost in excretory products (faeces, urine, carbon dioxide) / Biomass used in respiration, released as heat
items: Not all parts of organisms are eaten (e.g. roots, bones, feathers)
Material lost in excretory products (faeces, urine, carbon dioxide)
Biomass used in respiration, released as heat

cards.front: Name the three intensive farming methods the lesson gives for increasing energy transfer efficiency to animals.
cards.answer: Restricting movement / Controlling temperature / Using high-energy feeds

cards.front: How does controlling temperature in factory farming increase energy efficiency?
cards.answer: Heated or insulated buildings mean animals lose less energy keeping warm, so more energy goes into growth.

cards.front: Why does a human get less energy from eating grain-fed meat than from eating the grain directly?
cards.answer: Eating the animal adds an extra trophic level, so about 90% of the grain's energy is lost before it reaches the human.

title: Crime, Punishment and the Aims of Justice
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four main aims of punishment given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Justice / Retribution / Deterrence / Reformation

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why most Humanists oppose capital punishment.
cards.answer: Execution is irreversible / Miscarriages of justice cannot be corrected / Evidence for deterrence is weak
items: Miscarriages of justice cannot be corrected

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching call the death penalty 'inadmissible' even though it accepts the state's right to defend society?
cards.answer: Because the death penalty attacks human dignity, according to the Catechism of the Catholic Church.

cards.front: Why does ahimsa make capital punishment a problem for many Hindus?
cards.answer: Because taking a life, even a criminal's, creates negative karma, so many Hindus see it as wrong.

title: Peterloo, the Great Reform Act and Chartism, 1819-1858
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six demands of the People's Charter (1838).
cards.answer: Votes for all adult men / Secret ballots / Equal-sized constituencies / Paid MPs / No property qualification for MPs / Annual parliaments

cards.front: What three pressures forced parliamentary reform onto the agenda by the late 1820s/early 1830s, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Catholic Emancipation in 1829 / July Revolution in France, 1830 / Riots in Bristol, Nottingham and Derby, 1831
items: Riots in Bristol, Nottingham and Derby, 1831

cards.front: Why did the government use repression rather than reform after Peterloo in 1819?
cards.answer: The government was terrified of a French-style revolution, so it pushed through the Six Acts to restrict radical activity instead of conceding reform.

cards.front: Why did the 1832 Reform Act lead working-class radicals to form Chartism?
cards.answer: The Act only gave the vote to the middle class, betraying working men who had marched and petitioned but remained excluded.

cards.front: Name the five common social indicators of development given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Life expectancy / Infant mortality / Literacy rate / Mean years of schooling / Access to clean water

cards.front: Name the four extra indicators the lesson gives for measuring inequality and poverty beyond GDP and HDI.
cards.answer: Gini coefficient / Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI) / Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) / Gender Inequality Index

cards.front: Why do countries with persistently low Corruption Perceptions Index scores develop more slowly?
cards.answer: Economic gains get captured by elites and public services collapse, which slows broader development.

cards.front: Why do geographers usually combine several development indicators rather than rely on just one?
cards.answer: A single indicator gives only a partial picture, so combining measures reveals what each one misses.

cards.front: Name six situations the lesson gives when parents should seek medical attention for a sick child.
cards.answer: High fever not responding to paracetamol/ibuprofen / Under three months with any fever / Difficulty breathing / Unusually pale, limp or unresponsive / Rash or persistent vomiting / Illness lasting longer than expected
items: High fever not responding to paracetamol/ibuprofen
Under three months with any fever

cards.front: Why does a non-blanching rash appear in meningococcal disease?
cards.answer: It is caused by bleeding under the skin from septicaemia, which is why it does not fade under pressure.

cards.front: Why can mumps cause orchitis?
cards.answer: Mumps causes swelling of the parotid glands and can also cause testicular swelling (orchitis) in post-pubertal males.

cards.front: Name the four purposes the lesson gives for why Orwell wrote Animal Farm.
cards.answer: To warn against totalitarianism / To show how propaganda enables dictatorship / To criticise the complacency of the masses / To satirise the Soviet Union specifically
items: To show how propaganda enables dictatorship
To criticise the complacency of the masses
To satirise the Soviet Union specifically

cards.front: How does Squealer's use of language help the pigs stay in power?
cards.answer: He manipulates language, rewriting the commandments and distorting the truth, showing that controlling language means controlling thought.

cards.front: Why does Orwell criticise the ordinary animals' behaviour in Animal Farm?
cards.answer: Their failure to question authority lets the pigs seize power unchecked, suggesting ordinary people must stay vigilant.

title: Vikings, Anglo-Saxons and the Danelaw, c800–c1066
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three pull factors the lesson gives for Vikings settling in Britain.
cards.answer: Fertile land / Weak political resistance after Anglo-Saxon infighting / Coastline studded with rich monasteries
items: Weak political resistance after Anglo-Saxon infighting

cards.front: Name the three areas of lasting Viking impact on England the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Language / Law / Economy

cards.front: Why did Old English and Old Norse mingle rather than clash?
cards.answer: Because Anglo-Saxons and Vikings both spoke languages from the same Germanic family.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to treat Anglo-Saxons as the original 'native' population set against foreign Vikings?
cards.answer: Anglo-Saxons were themselves migrants who arrived from Germany and Denmark in the fifth and sixth centuries, only becoming 'British' later.

cards.front: The lesson names seven key attributes of Allah among the 99 names — what are they?
cards.answer: Tawhid (Oneness) / Omnipotent (Al-Qadir) / Benevolent / Fair and Just (Al-'Adl) / Transcendent / Immanent

cards.front: Why do Muslims regard polytheistic religions as committing shirk, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because dividing divine power and worship among several beings contradicts the reality of Allah's unique oneness.

title: Cinematography: Shot, Angle, Movement and Lighting
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five core shot distances the lesson identifies, from closest to furthest.
cards.answer: extreme close-up / close-up / medium shot / long shot / extreme long shot

cards.front: Name the four camera angles the lesson describes.
cards.answer: high angle / low angle / Dutch tilt / aerial shot

cards.front: Why is the medium shot the most common distance for dialogue scenes?
cards.answer: It shows characters from the waist up, which feels like a natural conversational distance.

cards.front: How does handheld camerawork affect the spectator during action scenes?
cards.answer: It introduces tremor and unpredictability, placing the spectator in nervous proximity to the action.

title: The Citizen and the State: A Thematic Toolkit, c1170-Present
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the seven factors AQA tests across this unit.
cards.answer: War / Religion / Chance / Government / Communication / The economy / Ideas

cards.front: Name the four question types always asked, in order, on Paper 2 Section A.
cards.answer: 8-mark how useful is the source / 8-mark explain the significance / 8-mark explain two ways similar or different / 16-mark factors essay
items: 8-mark explain two ways similar or different

cards.front: How did the Black Death (1348–49) make the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 possible?
cards.answer: It reshaped the labour market, creating the conditions that allowed the revolt to happen.

cards.front: How did the First World War affect women's suffrage?
cards.answer: The war accelerated the granting of women's suffrage in 1918.

title: Contemporary Music Videos: Stormzy and Justin Bieber
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the two well-known media texts that Superheroes references through intertextuality.
cards.answer: Toy Story (Buzz Lightyear carrying Woody) / The Matrix (Neo's telekinetic powers)

cards.front: Name the three ways Superheroes challenges stereotypes about Black British family and identity, according to the lesson's key fact.
cards.answer: Rashford shirt challenges football stereotypes / father doing his daughter's hair challenges fatherhood stereotypes / protest scene reflects Black Lives Matter and Covid-19
items: father doing his daughter's hair challenges fatherhood stereotypes
protest scene reflects Black Lives Matter and Covid-19

cards.front: Why does Superheroes use a soft pink sky and gold highlights on the bones of characters?
cards.answer: The pink sky suggests optimism, while gold highlights reflect the song's lyrics about courage and inner strength.

cards.front: Why did the director choose Adidas tracksuit costume for the boy in Superheroes?
cards.answer: To echo the style of Stormzy's earlier Sounds of the Skeng video, giving the character authenticity for a young audience.

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three rights does an advocate help uphold for a service user?
cards.answer: Right to choice / Right to consultation / Right to dignity

cards.front: Name the four types of service user the lesson gives as needing special methods of communication.
cards.answer: A person who is profoundly deaf / A person with a learning disability / A patient with little English / A resident who is blind
items: A person who is profoundly deaf
A person with a learning disability

cards.front: Why should a practitioner arrange a qualified BSL interpreter instead of using gestures or written notes for a Deaf patient?
cards.answer: BSL is a full language with its own grammar, so without an interpreter the patient may consent to a procedure they haven't fully understood, risking their health and rights.

cards.front: Why does Hassan need a professional interpreter at every clinical appointment?
cards.answer: Without one he cannot describe his symptoms accurately, consent meaningfully to treatment, or understand his care plan.

title: Solo Artists 1990 to Now: Producers, Studio Technology and the Streaming Era
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the four studio techniques the lesson gives as examples of technology used as a compositional tool.
cards.answer: Programmed beats / Sampling / Layering / Pitch correction

cards.front: What three steps does the lesson recommend for answering exam questions on any strand of pop?
cards.answer: Name the convention you can hear / place it in its decade or genre / give specific musical evidence from the excerpt
items: Place it in its decade or genre

cards.front: Why did the solo artist's image become as important as the music itself from the 1990s onwards?
cards.answer: Image, music videos and choreography became central to marketing, so musical decisions were often made with visual performance and media impact in mind.

cards.front: How does pitch correction technology affect a vocal by the 2000s?
cards.answer: It adjusts a vocal so it sits perfectly in tune, and can also be used deliberately to create a robotic vocal timbre.

title: Formation of Planetary Systems and Gravitational Forces
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: The lesson gives three effects of tidal forces in the Solar System. Name them.
cards.answer: Ring systems / Tidal heating / Synchronous rotation

cards.front: Name the two impact effects the lesson describes on planets' axial tilt or spin.
cards.answer: Uranus knocked onto its side / Venus spinning retrograde

cards.front: Why does the Moon always show the same face to Earth?
cards.answer: Earth's tidal forces gradually slowed the Moon's rotation until it matched its orbital period, causing synchronous rotation.

cards.front: Why has Mars lost most of its original atmosphere over billions of years?
cards.answer: Mars has a relatively low escape velocity (5.0 km/s), so gas molecules exceeding this speed gradually escaped into space over geological time.

cards.front: Name the three types of legitimate authority identified by Weber.
cards.answer: Traditional authority / Charismatic authority / Rational-legal authority

cards.front: Name the four examples of informal power given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Economic power (employer dismissing/rewarding workers) / Social influence through cultural or media prestige / Patriarchal power within families / Social closure by status groups
items: Social influence through cultural or media prestige

cards.front: Why is a popularly elected Prime Minister's authority rational-legal rather than charismatic?
cards.answer: Because their power rests on formal electoral rules and constitutional office, not on personal devotion from followers.

cards.front: How can a monarch hold charismatic authority alongside traditional authority?
cards.answer: If followers are personally devoted to the monarch as an individual, this creates charismatic authority existing alongside their inherited traditional authority.

cards.front: Name the five items that made up a hoplite's panoply, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Hoplon (large round shield) / Doru (spear) / Helmet (usually Corinthian type) / Breastplate (thorax or linothorax) / Bronze greaves

cards.front: Why did poorer Athenian citizens gain political influence when Athens built its fleet to fight Persia at Salamis?
cards.answer: They rowed the triremes in the large fleet, which gave them a claim to political influence they had never previously held.

cards.front: Why did Greek helmet designs become more open later in the fifth century BC?
cards.answer: City-states began valuing better hearing and awareness in larger, more complex battles over the full protection of enclosed helmets.

cards.front: Name the five personality traits Priestley establishes for the Birlings and Gerald at the start of Act 1.
cards.answer: Arthur: pompous and self-important / Sybil: cold and class-conscious / Sheila: light-hearted but shows flashes of intelligence / Eric: nervous and drinks too much / Gerald: polished and well-connected
items: Sheila: light-hearted but shows flashes of intelligence
Eric: nervous and drinks too much

cards.front: What three things does Birling dismiss or boast about in his speech just before the Inspector arrives?
cards.answer: Dismisses community as 'nonsense' / Mocks the possibility of war / Boasts the Titanic is 'unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable'
items: Boasts the Titanic is 'unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable'

cards.front: Why does Birling's use of the word 'awkward' reveal his selfishness?
