cards.answer: It reduces the profound moral question of caring for others to a matter of minor inconvenience, showing he can't think beyond his own comfort.

cards.front: Why did Birling sack Eva Smith from his factory?
cards.answer: She was one of several workers who asked for a pay rise, so he sacked the ringleaders, including her, to stop further demands.

cards.front: Name the four features shared by Shakespeare's late romances.
cards.answer: Fathers separated from children / Sea voyages / Apparent loss followed by miraculous reunion / Endings that favour forgiveness over revenge
items: Apparent loss followed by miraculous reunion
Endings that favour forgiveness over revenge

cards.front: Name the three plots to seize power by force in The Tempest.
cards.answer: Antonio overthrowing Prospero / Antonio and Sebastian plotting to murder Alonso / Caliban, Stephano and Trinculo plotting to murder Prospero
items: Antonio and Sebastian plotting to murder Alonso
Caliban, Stephano and Trinculo plotting to murder Prospero

cards.front: How does Shakespeare undercut Gonzalo's idealistic commonwealth speech in Act 2?
cards.answer: Antonio and Sebastian mock him throughout, and the play shows that power struggles and treachery persist even on the island.

cards.front: Why does Prospero abruptly end the wedding masque in Act 4?
cards.answer: Because he suddenly remembers Caliban's conspiracy to murder him.

cards.front: Name the four key locations where the British sector saw major engagements on the Western Front.
cards.answer: The Ypres salient / The Somme / Arras / Cambrai

cards.front: Name the five stages of the chain of evacuation, in order from the battlefield.
cards.answer: Stretcher bearers / Regimental Aid Post / Dressing stations / Casualty Clearing Stations / Base hospitals

cards.front: Why was wound infection such a constant danger in Flanders and the Somme?
cards.answer: The farmland soil was heavily manured, so shrapnel drove bacteria deep into wounds.

cards.front: How did soldiers catch trench fever?
cards.answer: It was spread by body lice that infested soldiers' clothing and bedding.

cards.front: Name the four attempted overthrows of the Weimar Republic between 1919 and 1923.
cards.answer: Spartacist uprising, January 1919 / Kapp Putsch, March 1920 / Erzberger assassination, 1921 / Munich Putsch, November 1923

cards.front: Why did the Spartacist uprising of January 1919 fail?
cards.answer: It lacked majority support, the SPD opposed it, and the far smaller Spartacist force was crushed by the well-armed Freikorps.

cards.front: How did Hitler's trial after the Munich Putsch help him despite his defeat?
cards.answer: A sympathetic judge let him give long speeches reported nationally, giving him a platform and a light sentence.

cards.front: Why did the army refuse to stop the Kapp Putsch in 1920?
cards.answer: General von Seeckt said the army would not fire on fellow soldiers, so it refused to act against the Ehrhardt Brigade.

cards.front: Name the four natural resources the lesson says gave the United States a head start before the First World War.
cards.answer: Coal / Iron / Oil / Timber

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson says did not share in the 1920s economic boom.
cards.answer: Farmers / Black Americans / Recent immigrants / Unskilled industrial workers

cards.front: How did the self-reinforcing 'virtuous circle' drive the 1920s consumer boom?
cards.answer: Higher factory productivity lowered prices, letting more people buy goods, which raised output and gave more workers wages to spend.

cards.front: Why did the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 end up damaging the American economy in the longer term?
cards.answer: It protected American industry short-term but raised duties so high it damaged international trade, contributing to later economic fragility.

cards.front: Name the three topics Leah talks about in her monologues to Phil.
cards.answer: Bonobos (peaceful apes) / The nature of happiness / What it means to be alive
items: What it means to be alive

cards.front: Name the three behaviours the group shows while panicking in the wood.
cards.answer: Argue / Blame each other / Talk over one another

cards.front: Why did Phil's cover-up plan go wrong in Act 2?
cards.answer: Cathy took DNA from a real postman instead of a stranger, so police matched an innocent man fitting Brian's description and arrested him.

cards.front: How does Phil's silence during Leah's monologues affect her role as the play's conscience?
cards.answer: His refusal to respond reduces Leah to a voice heard by the audience but ignored by the one person she wants to reach.

cards.front: Name the ten forms of media that use sound creation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: radio broadcasts / movies / TV shows / video games / advertisements / jingles / podcasts / animations / theatre / installations

cards.front: Why must dialogue sometimes be re-recorded using ADR?
cards.answer: Because if on-set recording is unusable, actors re-record their lines in a studio to replace it.

cards.front: What three refusals show Jane Eyre asserting her independence in the novel?
cards.answer: Refuses to become Rochester's mistress / Refuses St John Rivers's loveless proposal / Only marries Rochester as his equal
items: Refuses St John Rivers's loveless proposal
Only marries Rochester as his equal

cards.front: What features make Thornfield Hall a classic Gothic setting?
cards.answer: Grand and isolated / Locked rooms / Mysterious laughter from the attic / A fire in Rochester's bed / A secret that threatens everyone

cards.front: Why does Jane refuse to become Rochester's mistress even though she loves him?
cards.answer: Because it would mean sacrificing her moral autonomy for comfort, which she will not accept.

cards.front: How does Jane's inheritance let her return to Rochester out of love rather than need?
cards.answer: Her £20,000 inheritance gives her financial independence, so she chooses to return out of love, not economic necessity.

title: Beliefs about Death and the Afterlife
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three Christian afterlife beliefs given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Heaven / Hell / Purgatory

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say Islamic burial involves, reflecting belief in akhirah?
cards.answer: Body washed and shrouded / Buried promptly / Placed facing Makkah

cards.front: Why is Jewish burial traditionally preferred over cremation?
cards.answer: Because it expresses the hope of resurrection reflected in Jewish belief about the afterlife.

cards.front: How does the Buddhist candle-flame analogy explain rebirth without a fixed soul?
cards.answer: Something is transmitted from one life to the next, but it is neither the same flame nor a completely different one, showing kamma carries forward without an unchanging soul.

title: Vietnam protests, Great Society and Nixon's America
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the five key pieces of Great Society legislation the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Medicare and Medicaid / Elementary and Secondary Education Act / Voting Rights Act / Housing Act / Immigration and Nationality Act

cards.front: What three cover-up actions did Nixon take during Watergate, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Paying hush money / Ordering the CIA to obstruct FBI investigations / Firing the special prosecutor
items: Ordering the CIA to obstruct FBI investigations

cards.front: Why did Johnson announce in March 1968 that he would not seek re-election?
cards.answer: The Tet Offensive destroyed his war claims and he faced a serious challenge in his own party's primaries.

cards.front: Why did Nixon's Family Assistance Plan fail to become law?
cards.answer: Conservatives thought it too generous while liberals thought it too stingy and feared it would undermine union wages.

cards.front: Name the three rules the lesson gives for forming a Relativsatz (relative clause).
cards.answer: Relative pronoun must match the noun's gender (der/die/das) / Always place a comma before the relative pronoun / The verb goes to the end of the clause
items: Relative pronoun must match the noun's gender (der/die/das)
Always place a comma before the relative pronoun
The verb goes to the end of the clause

cards.front: Name the three common adjectives the lesson gives that add an Umlaut in the comparative.
cards.answer: alt → älter / jung → jünger / groß → größer

cards.front: Why should you use a wide variety of personality adjectives instead of repeating 'nett' in your writing or speaking?
cards.answer: Using varied vocabulary rather than repeating one word shows range, which earns credit for vocabulary variety.

cards.front: How do you form a comparative adjective in German to compare two people's personalities?
cards.answer: Add -er to the adjective and follow it with als (than), e.g. lustiger als.

cards.front: What four conditions must line up for a tropical cyclone to form?
cards.answer: Sea-surface temperature above 26.5°C / Warm ocean air rising rapidly / Low vertical wind shear / Coriolis effect giving spin

cards.front: What four ways can wealthier countries prepare for tropical cyclones, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Hurricane-resistant building codes / Early-warning satellite systems / Mass-evacuation transport networks / Well-equipped emergency services

cards.front: Why is the eye of a tropical cyclone eerily calm?
cards.answer: Air is sinking in the eye, warming by compression, so cloud evaporates and skies briefly clear.

cards.front: Why did poorer Black neighbourhoods in New Orleans struggle to evacuate before Hurricane Katrina?
cards.answer: They had less car ownership, making evacuation before the storm much harder.

cards.front: Why does Brontë make Jane wander the moors starving and destitute after leaving Thornfield?
cards.answer: To strip Jane of everything so Brontë can test whether her principles can sustain her with nothing else.

cards.front: How does St John Rivers differ from Brocklehurst as a religious character?
cards.answer: St John genuinely practises his ascetic faith, unlike the hypocritical Brocklehurst, but his devotion is life-denying.

title: Medicines, Monoclonal Antibodies and Lifestyle Disease
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three phases of clinical trials described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Phase I: small number of healthy volunteers to test safety / Phase II: patients test effectiveness and side effects / Phase III: large-scale randomised controlled trial
items: Phase I: small number of healthy volunteers to test safety
Phase II: patients test effectiveness and side effects
Phase III: large-scale randomised controlled trial

cards.front: Name the three uses of monoclonal antibodies given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pregnancy testing / Cancer diagnosis / Cancer therapy

cards.front: Why can preclinical testing not fully predict how a drug will affect humans?
cards.answer: Because it only tests cells, tissues and animals, not humans, so it filters dangerous compounds but can't guarantee human safety.

cards.front: Why do stents give only temporary relief for cardiovascular disease?
cards.answer: They mechanically prop open the narrowed artery but don't stop fatty plaque building up in other vessels, so disease can still progress.

title: Moments, Levers, Gears and Momentum Changes
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name three examples of levers given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Crowbar / Wheelbarrow / Scissors

cards.front: Name four car safety features that reduce collision force, given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Crumple zones / Seat belts / Airbags / Cycle helmets

cards.front: Why does a small gear driving a large gear increase the turning moment?
cards.answer: The larger gear has a bigger radius, so the force acts at a greater distance from the axle.

cards.front: In an explosion where objects start at rest, why do they move in opposite directions with equal and opposite momenta?
cards.answer: Because total momentum before the explosion is zero, so momentum must stay zero after, requiring equal opposite momenta.

title: Stellar Evolution: Birth, Life and Death of Stars
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six stages in the lifecycle of a Sun-like (low-mass) star, in order.
cards.answer: Nebula / Protostar / Main-sequence star / Red giant / Planetary nebula / White dwarf

cards.front: Name the two pieces of evidence for black holes given, besides X-ray binaries.
cards.answer: Gravitational lensing / Supermassive black holes at galaxy centres
items: Supermassive black holes at galaxy centres

cards.front: Why does a red giant form once hydrogen runs out in a Sun-like star's core?
cards.answer: Core fusion stops so the core contracts and heats under gravity, while the outer layers expand and cool from shell fusion around it.

cards.front: Why does a massive star's core collapse into a black hole rather than a neutron star?
cards.answer: If the collapsing core exceeds about 3 solar masses, even neutron degeneracy pressure cannot resist gravity, so it collapses into a black hole.

cards.front: Name the five main formation routes for minerals given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Crystallisation from a melt / Metamorphic recrystallisation / Evaporation / Precipitation from pore waters / Deposition from hydrothermal fluids

cards.front: Name the three temperature zones of hydrothermal fluids and what each deposits.
cards.answer: High temperature deposits gold and tungsten / Mid temperature deposits copper and lead sulphides / Coolest deposits carbonates
items: High temperature deposits gold and tungsten
Mid temperature deposits copper and lead sulphides

cards.front: Why do minerals like chlorite, mica and garnet appear in a mudstone that has undergone deep regional metamorphism?
cards.answer: Increasing temperature and pressure make original clay minerals break down and atoms reorganise into new minerals stable under the new conditions.

cards.front: Why is a silica-cemented sandstone harder and less permeable than a calcite-cemented one?
cards.answer: The type of cement precipitated from pore waters affects rock strength and permeability, and silica cement binds grains more strongly than calcite.

title: Telescopes Across the Spectrum and in Space
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the two main atmospheric windows that let radiation reach ground level.
cards.answer: Optical window (visible light) / Radio window (1 mm to 10 m)

cards.front: What four things does infrared astronomy reveal, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Molecular clouds and protostars hidden by dust / Starburst galaxies emitting mainly infrared / Thermal glow of brown dwarfs / Thermal glow of exoplanets
items: Molecular clouds and protostars hidden by dust

cards.front: Why is dust largely transparent to infrared telescopes but blocks visible light?
cards.answer: Dust absorbs visible light but is largely transparent in infrared, letting infrared telescopes see through it.

cards.front: Why do X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors instead of normal mirrors?
cards.answer: X-rays only bounce off mirrors at very shallow angles, so mirrors must be angled to reflect them.

title: Discipleship: The Call, the Cost and Living It Today
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four types of soil/ground in the Parable of the Sower (Mark 4:1-20).
cards.answer: The path – no response / Rocky ground – initial enthusiasm withers / Thorny ground – choked by wealth and worries / Good soil – bears fruit
items: Thorny ground – choked by wealth and worries

cards.front: Name the three modern Christians studied as examples of costly discipleship.
cards.answer: Dietrich Bonhoeffer / Oscar Romero / Mother Teresa

cards.front: Why were the disciples unable to drive out the spirit from the boy in Mark 9:14-29?
cards.answer: Because they relied on their own authority instead of prayer; Jesus says 'this kind can come out only by prayer.'

cards.front: Why is Peter's denial of Jesus in Mark 14:66-72 significant for understanding discipleship?
cards.answer: Because Peter, despite confidently declaring Jesus the Messiah, denied him under pressure, showing discipleship depends on grace, not strength.

cards.front: Name the three features used to compare RAM and ROM.
cards.answer: Whether it is volatile / Whether it can be written to / What it stores
items: Whether it can be written to

cards.front: How does a computer use ROM and RAM to start up?
cards.answer: The CPU runs the bootstrap instructions stored in ROM, which test the hardware and copy the operating system from secondary storage into RAM.

cards.front: Why is RAM usually much larger than ROM?
cards.answer: RAM must hold everything currently in use, while ROM only needs enough room for a small boot-up program.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that affect the rate of decomposition.
cards.answer: Temperature / Moisture / Oxygen / Surface area

cards.front: Name the three things gardeners do when composting to speed up decomposition.
cards.answer: Shred material / Turn compost heaps regularly / Keep it moist and warm

cards.front: Why does rising atmospheric CO2 cause ocean acidification?
cards.answer: Oceans act as a carbon sink, dissolving CO2 from the atmosphere, and rising CO2 levels increase ocean acidity.

cards.front: Why do waterlogged landfill sites produce methane instead of CO2?
cards.answer: Without oxygen, decomposition occurs anaerobically, which is slower and produces methane rather than CO2.

cards.front: Name the four stages covered by a life cycle assessment (LCA).
cards.answer: Raw material extraction / Manufacture and transportation / Use by the consumer / Disposal or recycling

cards.front: Why should measurements be checked regularly during manufacture rather than only at the end?
cards.answer: So small errors are spotted and corrected before they build up into large errors that cannot be fixed later.

cards.front: Why is it better to explain why a material or tool was chosen rather than just listing what was used?
cards.answer: Justifying the choice shows more understanding and is what lifts the quality of the answer.

cards.front: How is accuracy different from quality when checking a finished prototype?
cards.answer: Accuracy is how closely it matches the working drawing and specification, while quality also includes finish, assembly and how well it performs.

cards.front: Name the four environmental problems the lesson links to rapid urbanisation.
cards.answer: Increased traffic / Air pollution / Water shortages / Waste-disposal problems

cards.front: Name the four contemporary challenges the lesson says Lagos faces.
cards.answer: Housing shortages and spreading informal settlements / Traffic congestion / Waste collection problems / Flooding
items: Housing shortages and spreading informal settlements

cards.front: Why have some megacities, like Tokyo, stopped growing or started shrinking?
cards.answer: Because birth rates in these cities have fallen.

cards.front: Why is urbanisation happening fastest in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia?
cards.answer: Because populations there are young and rural-to-urban migration is high.

title: Pilgrimage, Catholic Social Teaching and Mission
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four pilgrimage sites specified in this unit.
cards.answer: Jerusalem / Lourdes / Rome / Walsingham

cards.front: What three purposes does the Catholic funeral rite serve?
cards.answer: Communion with the deceased through prayer / Supporting the bereaved community / Proclaiming eternal life and the resurrection
items: Communion with the deceased through prayer
Proclaiming eternal life and the resurrection

cards.front: Why are many Protestants sceptical about the practice of pilgrimage?
cards.answer: The Reformation rejected the idea that visiting a physical place earns spiritual merit, teaching instead that God can be encountered anywhere.

cards.front: How does Pope Francis link mission (proclamation) and social action in Evangelii Gaudium?
cards.answer: He insists authentic faith always involves a deep desire to change the world, so proclaiming the Gospel and serving the poor cannot be separated.

cards.front: Why does Macbeth order the murder of Macduff's family even though Macduff has already fled?
cards.answer: Emboldened by false confidence from the prophecies, Macbeth acts on impulsive cruelty with no strategic purpose.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare stage the killing of Lady Macduff's young son on stage?
cards.answer: To maximise audience horror and destroy remaining sympathy for Macbeth, so the audience supports Malcolm and Macduff's overthrow.

cards.front: Name the five areas of public debate about crime covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Concerns over violent crime / Sentencing / Treatment of young offenders / The prison system / Media coverage of crime

cards.front: Name the four goals of sentencing debated by sociologists.
cards.answer: Retribution / Deterrence / Rehabilitation / Incapacitation

cards.front: Why do Marxists argue that focusing public debate on violent street crime is misleading?
cards.answer: It diverts attention from corporate and state harms like unsafe workplaces, pollution and financial misconduct, which may cause more damage overall.

cards.front: How does the functionalist perspective explain public concern about violent crime?
cards.answer: It serves an integrative function, where collective outrage, law enforcement and sentencing reinforce shared values and social solidarity.

cards.front: Name the five categories of characters covered by standard ASCII's 128 codes.
cards.answer: Upper-case letters A-Z / Lower-case letters a-z / Digits 0-9 / Punctuation and special symbols / Control characters

cards.front: Name the three common Unicode encodings the lesson describes.
cards.answer: UTF-8 / UTF-16 / UTF-32

cards.front: Why did extended ASCII cause compatibility problems between different computer systems?
cards.answer: Different manufacturers implemented the extra codes 128-255 differently, so the same code could mean a different character on different systems.

cards.front: Why does mojibake (garbled text) appear when a file is opened?
cards.answer: It happens when a file saved in one encoding is opened assuming a different encoding, so bytes are misread as the wrong characters.

cards.front: Name the six key themes of A Christmas Carol identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Redemption / Social responsibility / Family / Isolation / Poverty / The spirit of Christmas

cards.front: What five items should a 5-minute extract-question plan list?
cards.answer: Extract thesis / Two methods from the extract / Two supporting moments from other staves / Context strand / Closing argument
items: Two supporting moments from other staves

cards.front: Why is embedding a short quotation inside your own sentence stronger than dropping in a long block quote?
cards.answer: It lets you pick a single word or short phrase and analyse it closely, rather than just describing what is said.

cards.front: Why does Dickens present Scrooge's loneliness as a self-imposed penalty?
cards.answer: Because his isolation, shown through the word "solitary", is a punishment he brought on himself through his own chosen behaviour.

title: Mountain Men, the Donner Party and the Mormon Trek
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four US states where the Mormons faced persecution before settling in Salt Lake Valley.
cards.answer: New York / Ohio / Missouri / Illinois

cards.front: Name the three differences the lesson gives for why the Mormons succeeded where the Donner Party failed.
cards.answer: Leadership / Planning / Geography

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the Donner disaster was not just about freak weather?
cards.answer: The storm was the final blow, but the real danger came from earlier choices: trusting an untested guidebook, taking the cutoff, losing weeks in the Wasatch, and splitting the train in the desert.

cards.front: Why did neighbouring communities react violently to the early Mormons?
cards.answer: Their distinct beliefs and practice of polygamy outraged neighbours, while their political and economic power frightened them.

cards.front: Name the four steps used to extract DNA from strawberries.
cards.answer: Mash the fruit / Add salt water and washing-up liquid / Filter the mixture / Layer ice-cold ethanol on top
items: Add salt water and washing-up liquid

cards.front: Name the four potential applications of the Human Genome Project mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Identifying genes linked to diseases / Developing personalised medicines / Understanding human evolution and migration / Creating genetic tests for inherited condition risk
items: Creating genetic tests for inherited condition risk

cards.front: How does fertilisation determine whether a baby is male or female?
cards.answer: Eggs always carry an X chromosome; if an X-carrying sperm fertilises it the offspring is female, if a Y-carrying sperm does it's male.

cards.front: Why are salt water and washing-up liquid added when extracting DNA from strawberries?
cards.answer: They break open the fruit's cells so that the DNA inside is released.

cards.front: Name the three things Japanese Buddhist memorial services are held on after a death.
cards.answer: The seventh day / The forty-ninth day / The death anniversary each year

cards.front: Name the three things loved ones do at a dying Buddhist's bedside to support their mental state.
cards.answer: Recite texts / Chant / Create a calm and focused environment
items: Create a calm and focused environment

cards.front: Why is cremation the traditional funeral practice in most Theravada Buddhist communities?
cards.answer: It follows the example of the Buddha, whose own body was cremated after his parinibbana.

cards.front: Why does Parinirvana Day remind Buddhists of impermanence?
cards.answer: Even the Buddha, who had attained Enlightenment, still died, showing all conditioned existence is transient.

title: Analysing Performers: Vocal and Physical Choices
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Why does a sudden drop in volume followed by a shout create impact for an audience?
cards.answer: Dropping to near-inaudible draws the audience forward physically, so a sudden shout after quiet becomes a physical shock.

cards.front: Why does a performer freezing mid-action in a tableau grab audience focus?
cards.answer: Stillness contrasts with surrounding chaotic movement, so every audience member's eye is drawn immediately to the frozen performer.

cards.front: Name the three broad categories of contraception methods described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Barrier methods / Hormonal methods / Natural/other methods

cards.front: Name the four female causes of infertility the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Problems with ovulation e.g. PCOS / Blocked or damaged fallopian tubes / Endometriosis / Age-related decline in egg quality

cards.front: Why does copper in the IUD prevent pregnancy?
cards.answer: Copper ions are toxic to sperm.

cards.front: Why does sickle cell disease cause pain and anaemia?
cards.answer: A mutation in the haemoglobin gene produces abnormally shaped red blood cells that block blood vessels.

cards.front: Name the four areas of life the lesson says Shari'ah covers.
cards.answer: Worship (ibadat) / Relationships and family (muamalat) / Criminal law (uqubat) / Social ethics

cards.front: Give three subtle forms of shirk the lesson describes, beyond idol worship.
cards.answer: Trusting or fearing humans over Allah / Following desires as if divine commands / Giving devotion owed to Allah to humans / Hidden shirk: acting for human approval
items: Trusting or fearing humans over Allah
Following desires as if divine commands
Giving devotion owed to Allah to humans
Hidden shirk: acting for human approval

cards.front: Why does the golden calf story in Surah 7:148-150 count as shirk?
cards.answer: The Israelites worshipped a created, speechless idol that could not guide or help them, instead of the invisible eternal God.

cards.front: Why do atheists and Humanists say laws should not come from Shari'ah?
cards.answer: They argue laws should come from democratic consent and human reason, not divine revelation, and question if God's command alone justifies law.

title: Origins of the Universe, the Sanctity of Life and Abortion
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five things Genesis 1-2 describes God creating in stages.
cards.answer: Light / Land / Sea / Plants / Animals

cards.front: In the abortion debate, name the four viewpoints the lesson says show sanctity of life in action.
cards.answer: Pro-life Christians defend the unborn as made in God's image / Pro-choice Christians may apply situation ethics to hard cases / Non-religious critics focus on a woman's right to choose / Christians respond by reasserting all human life has God-given worth
items: Pro-life Christians defend the unborn as made in God's image
Pro-choice Christians may apply situation ethics to hard cases
Non-religious critics focus on a woman's right to choose
Christians respond by reasserting all human life has God-given worth

cards.front: Why do some Christians see a conflict between the Big Bang theory and Genesis?
cards.answer: They read Genesis literally as a six-day creation, which conflicts with the Big Bang's account of the universe's origin.

cards.front: Why do most Christians reject treating the universe purely as a commodity?
cards.answer: The universe is God's creation reflecting his goodness, so exploiting it dishonours his ownership and ignores humanity's responsibility to care for it.

cards.front: Name the five market segmentation bases named in the specification.
cards.answer: Age / Gender / Income / Location / Lifestyle

cards.front: Why does a business use market segmentation instead of trying to please every customer?
cards.answer: Trying to be cheapest, most luxurious, most ethical and most convenient at once means being none of them well.

cards.front: Why do businesses often combine more than one segmentation base, as Boots does?
cards.answer: Combining bases like age, gender, income and location gives a sharper, more detailed picture of the customer than one base alone.

cards.front: How can segmentation let a smaller firm compete with bigger businesses?
cards.answer: By owning one tight segment rather than fighting across the whole market against giants.

title: Characters and Relationships: Proctor, Abigail, Elizabeth
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three men through whom Miller shows Abigail's only routes to power in Salem.
cards.answer: Parris (her uncle and protector) / Proctor (her former lover) / The court

cards.front: Why does Judge Danforth refuse to admit the trials are unjust?
cards.answer: He has already signed death warrants, so admitting error would mean admitting he has murdered innocent people.

cards.front: Why does Miller make Rebecca Nurse one of the accused?
cards.answer: Her piety and community standing make her the most improbable of the accused, making the court's injustice most damning.

cards.front: Name the five steps for structuring a strong modern-text essay response given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Engage with the quotation / Explore the theme across the play / Embed context throughout / Analyse dramatic techniques / Write precisely
items: Explore the theme across the play

cards.front: Name the three levels at which prejudice operates in Refugee Boy.
cards.answer: Personal / Institutional / Societal

cards.front: How does the play show that identity is constructed by others as much as by the individual?
cards.answer: Alem is the same person wherever he is, but is treated differently depending on who defines him — rejected by Ethiopia and Eritrea, seen as an outsider in England.

cards.front: Why does the asylum tribunal fail to represent true justice in the play?
cards.answer: It follows legal rules, but those rules cannot fully account for human suffering, making the process feel cold, impersonal and arbitrary.

title: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle: Reviewing the Whole Investigation
subject: statistics-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five stages of the Statistical Enquiry Cycle in order.
cards.answer: Planning / Sourcing Data / Processing and Presenting Data / Interpreting Results / Communicating Findings and Evaluating

cards.front: Name the three parts a full-mark evaluation point must have.
cards.answer: Identify the weakness at a named stage / Explain why it undermines the conclusion / Suggest a specific improvement
items: Identify the weakness at a named stage
Explain why it undermines the conclusion

cards.front: Why does a bigger symbol in a pictogram mislead a reader, even if the key is correct?
cards.answer: Because a reader may judge the area of the symbol rather than reading the key, making the value look bigger than it is.

cards.front: Why can't a vague hypothesis be tested properly during planning?
cards.answer: Because it has no measurable variables, so no data collection method can confirm or reject it.

cards.front: Name the four research methods the lesson says sociologists use to research education.
cards.answer: Observation (participant or non-participant) / Interviews (structured or unstructured) / Questionnaires / Secondary data (official statistics, league tables, Ofsted reports)
items: Secondary data (official statistics, league tables, Ofsted reports)

cards.front: Name the three key ethical issues in sociological research on education.
cards.answer: Informed consent / Confidentiality / Harm to participants

cards.front: Why can requiring parental written consent introduce class bias into a study's sample?
cards.answer: It may reduce the sample to pupils whose parents are engaged and able to respond, excluding others.

cards.front: Why might a headteacher acting as gatekeeper limit how representative research data is?
cards.answer: Headteachers may only allow observation of 'good' lessons, so the data does not represent everyday school life.

cards.front: The lesson gives four corporate/business terms the Headmaster uses to describe education. Name them.
cards.answer: results / shelf / display / selling points

cards.front: What three steps does Irwin's method involve for arguing against the obvious?
cards.answer: Find a proposition / invert it / look around for proofs

cards.front: Why did the Headmaster fail to act on Hector's inappropriate behaviour until it became a problem?
cards.answer: He knew about it but only acted once it became publicly embarrassing, caring about institutional reputation rather than child protection.

cards.front: Why does Bennett draw a parallel between Irwin's intellectual and sexual dishonesty?
cards.answer: Irwin performs heterosexuality by hiding his attraction to Dakin just as he performs historical argument without genuine conviction.

cards.front: Name the four main factors that shape where a business locates.
cards.answer: Proximity to the market / Proximity to labour / Proximity to materials / Proximity to competitors

cards.front: Name the four elements of the marketing mix (the four Ps).
cards.answer: Product / Price / Promotion / Place

cards.front: Why might a business choose to locate near its competitors, like car dealerships?
cards.answer: Clustering together can attract more customers to the area, although it also intensifies rivalry between the businesses.

cards.front: Why did some businesses lose sales when shoppers shifted to buying groceries online during lockdowns?
cards.answer: Because they could not adjust their 'place' strategy to sell online, so more agile rivals took their customers.

title: Case Study: Development in an Emerging Country (India)
subject: geography-edexcel-b

cards.front: Name the four megacities the lesson gives for India and their roles.
cards.answer: Mumbai - financial / Delhi - political / Bengaluru - IT / Kolkata - cultural-historical

cards.front: Name the four countries the lesson gives as India's largest sources of FDI.
cards.answer: Singapore / USA / Mauritius / Japan

cards.front: Why has India's rural-urban migration happened as the economy has grown?
cards.answer: Rapid economic change has drawn tens of millions of people from farms to cities as jobs shifted to industry and services.

cards.front: How has India's demographic profile changed as its economy has developed?
cards.answer: Fertility fell from 5.4 to 2.0 and life expectancy rose from 41 to 70 as the country urbanised and grew economically.

cards.front: Name the three isotope pairs used in radiometric dating.
cards.answer: Uranium-238 to lead-206 / Potassium-40 to argon-40 / Carbon-14 to nitrogen-14

cards.front: Why is radioactive decay considered a reliable geological clock?
cards.answer: Because it happens at a fixed, predictable rate regardless of temperature, pressure or chemical environment.

cards.front: Why can't carbon-14 be used to date material older than about 50,000 years?
cards.answer: After about 10 half-lives so little carbon-14 remains that measurements become unreliable.

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say shaped the real Salem witch trials, besides superstition?
cards.answer: Land disputes between families / Social tensions between settlers and newcomers / Vulnerability of people at the social margins
items: Social tensions between settlers and newcomers
Vulnerability of people at the social margins

cards.front: How did Puritan theology make the witch trials logically coherent within the community's own belief system?
cards.answer: Puritans believed one sinner could bring divine punishment on everyone, so private behaviour became a legitimate public concern.

cards.front: Why did Miller use a small number of specific historical details rather than a fully period-accurate set for The Crucible?
cards.answer: A fully period-specific design risks letting the audience distance themselves historically instead of seeing the pattern across time.

cards.front: How did Puritan dress visually reinforce the community's culture of conformity and surveillance?
cards.answer: Puritan dress was deliberately plain and uniform, so in a community where everyone looked alike, any deviation became visible.

cards.front: Name the three parts of the Apollo spacecraft.
cards.answer: Command Module / Service Module / Lunar Module

cards.front: Name the four challenges of crewed deep-space missions the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Radiation exposure beyond the magnetosphere / Bone, muscle and cardiovascular changes from microgravity / Psychological isolation over months or years / Life-support systems must be highly reliable with minimal resupply
items: Bone, muscle and cardiovascular changes from microgravity
Psychological isolation over months or years
Life-support systems must be highly reliable with minimal resupply

cards.front: Why are fly-by missions used for distant targets instead of orbiters?
cards.answer: Because the fuel cost of slowing down to enter orbit around a distant target would be too high.

cards.front: Why can a human geologist identify interesting rocks much faster than a robotic rover?
cards.answer: Astronauts can make real-time decisions on the spot, while rovers face communication delays of minutes to hours.

cards.front: Why does deforming a solid always need at least two forces?
cards.answer: A single force just accelerates the object; changing its shape needs two opposite forces acting on it.

cards.front: Why can a stretched spring return to its original shape when the force is removed?
cards.answer: Stretching pulls particles apart, increasing attractive forces, which restore the original arrangement if not overstretched.

cards.front: Why does bending a paperclip until it stays bent show plastic deformation?
cards.answer: The force is large enough that particles permanently slip past each other into new positions and don't return.

cards.front: Name the two precautions the lesson gives for accurately investigating Hooke's law.
cards.answer: Use a set square or pointer at eye level to reduce parallax error / Remove loads gently afterwards to check for permanent deformation
items: Use a set square or pointer at eye level to reduce parallax error
Remove loads gently afterwards to check for permanent deformation

cards.front: Why does incongruence lead to low self-esteem, according to Rogers?
cards.answer: A large gap between self-image and ideal self causes anxiety and low self-worth, blocking self-actualisation.

cards.front: Why might a child with an anxious temperament and critical upbringing develop especially low self-esteem?
cards.answer: Their innate anxious nature and repeated criticism from experience reinforce each other, lowering self-esteem further.

cards.front: Why must the existential self develop before the categorical self?
cards.answer: A child cannot categorise itself until it first understands it exists as a separate self to be categorised.

title: Form and Methods: Monologue, Movement and Season
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four children whose monologues open a seasonal section, and where each is set.
cards.answer: Rosie in Berlin / Pip in the garden / Mark remembering the gum tree / Ben remembering his parents dancing

cards.front: Name the six seasonal sections in the order given by the world premiere's printed synopsis.
cards.answer: Winter (London) for Rosie / Summer (Adelaide) as the family gathers / Autumn for Pip / Winter for Mark / Spring for Ben / final Summer in which Rosie leaves and Fran dies
items: final Summer, Rosie leaves and Fran dies

cards.front: Why did Bovell write the four children's monologues instead of naturalistic dialogue scenes?
cards.answer: Because collaborating with physical theatre company Frantic Assembly meant monologues suited a more physical, abstract, movement-based staging better.

cards.front: How did the production use a harness to stage the opening midnight phone call knocking Bob off balance?
cards.answer: A hidden harness let the performer fall slowly forward at about forty-five degrees and return upright, as if the earth tilted.

cards.front: Name the seven types of low-rise building given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Residential / Commercial / Industrial / Agricultural / Community / Religious / Recreational

cards.front: What four design priorities does the lesson give for industrial buildings?
cards.answer: Large clear floor areas / High eaves heights / Heavy-duty floor slabs for forklifts and racking / Good loading facilities like dock levellers and roller shutter doors
items: Heavy-duty floor slabs for forklifts and racking
Good loading facilities like dock levellers and roller shutter doors

cards.front: Why can a single building fall into more than one building-type category, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Buildings often combine uses, like a hotel that is commercial but also has recreational and community facilities within it.

cards.front: Why has the UK housing shortage created strong demand for residential construction?
cards.answer: Population growth, longer life expectancy and more single-person households increase demand while planning restrictions, land costs and worker shortages limit supply.

title: The Origins of the Weimar Republic 1918–19
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three things did the armistice of 11 November 1918 require Germany to do?
cards.answer: Withdraw troops from occupied territories / Surrender its navy and heavy weapons / Allow Allied forces to occupy the Rhineland
items: Surrender its navy and heavy weapons
Allow Allied forces to occupy the Rhineland

cards.front: What five strengths did the Weimar Constitution have?
cards.answer: Universal suffrage for men and women over 20 / A Bill of Rights protecting individual freedoms / President directly elected by the people / Reichstag could pass laws and government was accountable to it / Länder kept local powers
items: Universal suffrage for men and women over 20
A Bill of Rights protecting individual freedoms
President directly elected by the people
Reichstag could pass laws and government was accountable to it

cards.front: How did the mutiny at Kiel turn into a full-scale revolution across Germany?
cards.answer: Workers and soldiers formed councils like the Russian soviets and seized control of cities such as Hamburg, Bremen and Munich, demanding peace and change.

cards.front: Why had political change become inevitable in Germany by October 1918?
cards.answer: Germany faced military defeat, mass starvation from the British blockade, and collapsing morale among soldiers and civilians all at once.

cards.front: Name the three developments the lesson gives that deepened American disillusionment with the Vietnam War.
cards.answer: Television coverage of the war / The Tet Offensive (1968) / The My Lai massacre revelation (1969)

cards.front: Why did the Korean War (1950-53) count as a direct application of containment?
cards.answer: UN forces, mainly American, fought to stop communist North Korea from conquering South Korea, resisting communist expansion by force.

cards.front: Why was NATO founded in April 1949?
cards.answer: To formalise Western defence by committing members to treat an attack on any one member as an attack on all.

cards.front: Name the four sources of background radiation the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Radon gas from granite rocks / Cosmic rays from space / Radioactive isotopes in food and water / Radiation from medical procedures
items: Radioactive isotopes in food and water

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives that determine how severe a radiation health risk is.
cards.answer: Type of radiation (ionising ability) / Half-life of the isotope / Whether it's irradiation or contamination

cards.front: Why does a gamma source pose an external irradiation risk even from a distance?
cards.answer: Gamma rays have low ionising ability but high penetrating power, needing thick lead or concrete to block them, so they pass easily through air to the body.

cards.front: Why do control rods keep a nuclear fission chain reaction steady?
cards.answer: Control rods absorb neutrons so that on average only one neutron from each fission goes on to cause the next fission.

title: In Paris With You — James Fenton
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name the three famous Paris landmarks the speaker says they will skip in the poem.
cards.answer: The Louvre / Notre Dame / The Champs Elysées

cards.front: Name the four other anthology poems the lesson compares with 'In Paris With You'.
cards.answer: Lochhead's 'I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine' / Browning's 'Now' / Jordan's 'Poem for My Love' / Antrobus's 'The Perseverance'
items: Lochhead's 'I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine'

cards.front: Why does the speaker dismiss the Louvre, Notre Dame and the Champs Elysées in one breath?
cards.answer: Naming and rejecting all three shows he has no interest in tourism; the person in front of him matters more than the city's monuments.

cards.front: How does the closing refrain let the speaker admit happiness without using the word 'love'?
cards.answer: By ending stanzas on 'I'm in Paris with you', presence and place replace the romantic vocabulary he claims to distrust.

cards.front: Why do most psychologists reject strict linguistic determinism?
cards.answer: People can think thoughts for which they have no word and then coin a new word, which would be impossible if language fully controlled thought.

cards.front: Why is it hard to test Vygotsky's claim about when thought and language merge?
cards.answer: Very young children cannot easily report on their own thinking, making the exact age and process difficult to test directly.

title: Diurnal Motion, Circumpolarity and Observing Conditions
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three key moments in a star's path across the sky each day.
cards.answer: Rising / Upper transit (culmination) / Lower transit

cards.front: According to the lesson, where does a star rise depending on its declination (three cases)?
cards.answer: Dec = 0° rises due east / Positive declination rises north of east / Negative declination rises south of east
items: Positive declination rises north of east
Negative declination rises south of east

cards.front: Why is lower transit invisible for stars that rise and set, unlike circumpolar stars?
cards.answer: For stars that rise and set, lower transit occurs below the horizon, so it cannot be seen.

cards.front: Why is Arcturus (Dec +19°11′) not circumpolar as seen from Edinburgh (56°N)?
cards.answer: Its declination of 19° is less than the circumpolar limit at 56°N, which is 34°, so it rises and sets.

title: Challenges for Religion in a Secular Society
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: What three types of secularisation does the lesson describe?
cards.answer: Institutional secularisation (laws, schools, hospitals no longer religiously controlled) / Individual secularisation (ethical decisions made without religious teaching) / Cultural secularisation (religious symbols/festivals become commercial)
items: Institutional secularisation (laws, schools, hospitals no longer religiously controlled)
Individual secularisation (ethical decisions made without religious teaching)

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say Humanists UK has campaigned for?
cards.answer: Removal of bishops from the House of Lords / An end to compulsory acts of worship in schools / Inclusive sex education
items: Removal of bishops from the House of Lords
An end to compulsory acts of worship in schools

cards.front: Why are religious organisations not required to conduct same-sex marriages in Britain?
cards.answer: When same-sex civil marriage was legalised in 2014, religious organisations were given an explicit exemption from having to conduct them.

cards.front: Why does therapeutic gene editing receive more religious support than 'designer baby' selection?
cards.answer: Therapeutic gene editing corrects inherited diseases, whereas selecting non-medical traits treats embryos as raw material and undermines their dignity.

cards.front: Name the five stratigraphic principles used together to build a sequence of geological events.
cards.answer: Superposition / Original horizontality / Lateral continuity / Cross-cutting relationships / Included fragments

cards.front: Name three way-up structures the lesson gives for working out which way up a tilted rock sequence originally was.
cards.answer: Graded bedding / Cross-bedding / Mudcracks

cards.front: Why can mudcracks be used to tell which way up a rock sequence originally formed?
cards.answer: Mudcracks only form at an exposed surface, so they show which side of the bed was on top.

cards.front: Why does uniformitarianism let geologists interpret rocks formed millions of years ago using processes seen today?
cards.answer: Because the laws of physics and chemistry do not change, past processes followed the same rules as present-day ones.

cards.front: Name the four irregular adjectives given in the lesson, showing their feminine forms.
cards.answer: bon → bonne / beau → belle / nouveau → nouvelle / vieux → vieille

cards.front: What are the three past participle agreement endings for the perfect tense with être, based on the subject?
cards.answer: add -e for feminine subject / add -s for masculine plural subject / add -es for feminine plural subject

cards.front: Why do verbs like aller and sortir use être instead of avoir in the perfect tense?
cards.answer: Because they belong to a group of verbs of movement that use être as the auxiliary verb instead of avoir.

cards.front: How does the feminine form of an adjective ending in -eux change, such as ennuyeux?
cards.answer: Adjectives ending in -eux change to -euse in the feminine, so ennuyeux becomes ennuyeuse.

title: Russia in 1917: Empire at Breaking Point
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three crises collided in Russia by February 1917?
cards.answer: Military disaster on the Eastern Front / Peasant land hunger since the 1861 Emancipation / Strike wave in Petrograd over food and fuel
items: Military disaster on the Eastern Front
Peasant land hunger since the 1861 Emancipation
Strike wave in Petrograd over food and fuel

cards.front: What three groups of ministers did Tsarina Alexandra replace at speed in just over a year?
cards.answer: Four prime ministers / Five interior ministers / Three war ministers

cards.front: Why could a concentrated urban working class bring down the tsar while a scattered peasantry could not?
cards.answer: Workers were packed into a few Petrograd districts, so when Putilov workers struck, half of working Petrograd joined within days.

cards.front: Why did rumours about Rasputin damage the dynasty more than his actual influence did?
cards.answer: His real power over policy was modest, but public belief he was the Tsarina's lover and choosing ministers destroyed the dynasty's respectability.

title: Photosynthesis, Limiting Factors and the Inverse Square Law
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four ways leaves are adapted to maximise photosynthesis, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Broad, flat surface area for light / Thin leaf so CO2 diffuses short distance / Network of veins for water and glucose transport / Waxy cuticle that is transparent and waterproof
items: Broad, flat surface area for light
Thin leaf so CO2 diffuses short distance
Network of veins for water and glucose transport
Waxy cuticle that is transparent and waterproof

cards.front: Name the five uses of glucose in plants given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Respiration for energy / Converted to starch for storage / Producing cellulose for cell walls / Making amino acids and proteins with nitrates / Producing lipids for storage
items: Making amino acids and proteins with nitrates

cards.front: Why does the waxy cuticle on a leaf's upper surface being transparent help photosynthesis?
cards.answer: Being transparent lets light pass through it so it can still reach the chloroplasts.

cards.front: Why should you repeat each distance measurement at least three times in the light intensity core practical?
cards.answer: Repeating and calculating a mean reduces the effect of anomalous results.

cards.front: Name the four groups Michael Harrington identified as living in poverty amidst plenty in 1950s America.
cards.answer: Rural poor of Appalachia / Elderly Americans on fixed incomes / African Americans excluded from the boom / Urban workers left behind by change
items: African Americans excluded from the boom
Urban workers left behind by change

cards.front: Why did the GI Bill end up reinforcing racial segregation in housing?
cards.answer: Banks refused mortgages and universities denied admission to Black veterans, so white veterans alone gained access to all-white suburbs.

cards.front: How did the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956 change American life?
cards.answer: It built over 41,000 miles of motorway linking cities, deepening car dependency and shifting retail and jobs to the suburbs.

cards.front: Why did unemployment disappear in the USA during the Second World War?
cards.answer: Millions of Americans joined the armed forces while defence industries absorbed the rest of the workforce.

title: Al-Qaeda: Aims, Beliefs and Bin Laden
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What four aims did bin Laden state for al-Qaeda?
cards.answer: Remove Western/American troops from Saudi Arabia and the Muslim world / Topple corrupt Arab governments, starting with Saudi Arabia and Egypt / Destroy Israel / Restore a unified Islamic caliphate under strict Wahhabism
items: Remove Western/American troops from Saudi Arabia and the Muslim world
Topple corrupt Arab governments, starting with Saudi Arabia and Egypt
Restore a unified Islamic caliphate under strict Wahhabism

cards.front: What three attacks before 9/11 established al-Qaeda as a global threat?
cards.answer: East African embassy bombings, 7 August 1998 / Failed Millennium plot at Los Angeles airport, December 1999 / USS Cole bombing, 12 October 2000
items: Failed Millennium plot at Los Angeles airport, December 1999

cards.front: Why did the 9/11 Commission conclude pre-2001 warnings about al-Qaeda were missed?
cards.answer: The failures were of imagination, structure and information sharing rather than effort — agencies were watching for a different kind of attack.

cards.front: How did al-Qaeda's structure make it both hard to destroy and capable of major attacks?
cards.answer: It was decentralised enough to survive losing any single cell, yet coordinated enough to plan a synchronised four-airliner attack.

title: The Origin of Evil and Suffering
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What three qualities must God have for the problem of evil to arise as a challenge?
cards.answer: omnipotent (all-powerful) / omniscient (all-knowing) / omnibenevolent (perfectly good)

cards.front: What three gunas does the Bhagavad Gita describe, where dominance of the lower ones leads to suffering?
cards.answer: goodness / passion / ignorance

cards.front: Why does the free-will defence struggle to explain natural evil such as earthquakes and disease?
cards.answer: Natural evil is not caused by human choices, so blaming misuse of free will fails to account for it.

cards.front: Why do critics find the soul-making theodicy morally troubling?
cards.answer: It seems to require extreme suffering to be justified by the spiritual growth it produces, which many find unacceptable.

cards.front: Name the three main differences the lesson gives between the Roman matrona and the Athenian kyria.
cards.answer: attended dinner parties with husbands / could receive academic education / greater legal independence under sine manu
items: greater legal independence under sine manu

cards.front: Why did Lucretia stab herself even though she was raped against her will?
cards.answer: Because in Roman thinking her chastity belonged to her male relatives, so her violation had to be cleansed by death despite her innocence.

cards.front: Why does the Laudatio Turiae complicate the simple picture of Roman women as passive and voiceless?
cards.answer: It shows a real wife exercising loyalty, bravery and practical influence, publicly valued and praised by her husband.

cards.front: Name the six religious traditions covered in this lesson's teaching on sexual ethics and contraception.
cards.answer: Christianity / Judaism / Islam / Hinduism / Sikhism / Buddhism

cards.front: Why does an agunah in Orthodox Judaism remain unable to remarry?
cards.answer: Because Orthodox divorce requires the husband to issue the get and a woman cannot obtain one unilaterally, so refusal leaves her chained.

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching in Humanae Vitae reject artificial contraception?
cards.answer: Because it breaks the God-given link between the unitive and procreative dimensions of sex, which must remain open to new life.

cards.front: Why is natural family planning permitted by the Catholic Church while artificial contraception is not?
cards.answer: Because tracking fertility cycles works with the body's natural processes rather than against them, unlike artificial contraception.

title: The League's 1920s Record: Successes and Failures
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three 1920s disputes the lesson lists as League successes.
cards.answer: Aaland Islands (1921) / Upper Silesia (1921) / Bulgaria (1925)

cards.front: Name four humanitarian achievements of League agencies in the 1920s described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Nansen passports for stateless refugees / Repatriating about 425,000 prisoners of war / Fighting typhus and cholera epidemics / ILO securing 17 labour conventions

cards.front: Why could the League resolve the Aaland Islands and Upper Silesia disputes but not Vilna or Corfu?
cards.answer: Aaland and Upper Silesia involved small, cooperative states, while Vilna and Corfu involved a great power or one backed by a great power, which the League couldn't force to comply.

cards.front: Why did the League's agencies' humanitarian work survive into the 1945 United Nations even though the League's political system failed?
cards.answer: Agencies like the refugee commission, Health Committee and ILO achieved durable practical results, so they outlived the political League and formed the UN's foundation.

cards.front: Name the four guerrilla tactics the lesson gives for how the Vietcong fought.
cards.answer: Ambushes / Booby traps / Hit-and-run raids / Underground tunnel network at Cu Chi
items: Underground tunnel network at Cu Chi

cards.front: What three factors does the lesson say made continued US involvement in Vietnam untenable by 1973?
cards.answer: Domestic political pressure / The Tet Offensive's psychological impact / Credibility damage from My Lai and the Pentagon Papers
items: Credibility damage from My Lai and the Pentagon Papers

cards.front: Why did the Tet Offensive shatter American public confidence even though it was militarily repulsed?
cards.answer: Westmoreland had assured the public the war was being won, so the offensive proved the enemy was far from defeated.

cards.front: Why was it so difficult for US forces to identify the enemy in Vietnam?
cards.answer: Vietcong fighters were indistinguishable from civilians, making identification of the enemy extremely difficult.

cards.front: Name the five strong structural points the lesson lists for writing about structure in the exam.
cards.answer: The three unities / The lighting shift / The doorbell / The act-ending cliffhangers / The cyclical ending

cards.front: How does Act 1 end on a cliffhanger?
cards.answer: It ends with the Inspector beginning to question Gerald, keeping the audience engaged into the next act.

cards.front: Why is Mrs Birling's demand to 'make an example' of Eva's child's father dramatically ironic?
cards.answer: Because the father she is unknowingly condemning is her own son, Eric.

cards.front: Why is the audience's knowledge of the two world wars a form of dramatic irony in the play?
cards.answer: The 1945 audience knows the Birlings' confident 1912 world will be destroyed, undercutting their assertions that all is well.

cards.front: Name the five factors the lesson gives for choosing a supplier.
cards.answer: Price / Quality / Reliability / Delivery speed / Payment terms

cards.front: Name the five impact criteria the lesson gives for logistics and supply decisions.
cards.answer: Time / Length of supply chain / Reliability of supply / Costs / Customer service

cards.front: Why does delivery speed matter more for bakeries and florists than for other businesses?
cards.answer: Their products have short shelf-lives, so slow delivery leaves shelves empty or goods spoiled before sale.

cards.front: How do long payment terms, like 60 days credit, help a buyer's cash flow?
cards.answer: They let the business sell goods and collect cash before paying the supplier, acting like an interest-free loan.

title: Space Physics: The Solar System and Beyond
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four types of small bodies (other than the planets) listed as part of our solar system.
cards.answer: Dwarf planets / Moons / Asteroids / Comets

cards.front: What are the two independent pieces of evidence given for the Big Bang theory?
cards.answer: Red-shift of distant galaxies / Cosmic microwave background radiation

cards.front: Why does a comet move fastest at perihelion (closest to the Sun)?
cards.answer: Because the gravitational pull from the Sun is strongest when the comet is closest to it.

cards.front: Why do scientists think dark matter exists in galaxies?
cards.answer: Stars at the edges of galaxies rotate faster than expected, suggesting galaxies contain much more mass than we can see.

title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: What four factors can be altered to change the rate of a chemical reaction?
cards.answer: Temperature / Concentration of solutions (or pressure of gases) / Surface area of solid reactants / Using a catalyst
items: Concentration of solutions (or pressure of gases)

cards.front: What three methods can be used to measure the rate of a reaction?
cards.answer: Collecting gas in a syringe or over water / Measuring mass loss on a balance / Timing a colour change (e.g. disappearing cross)
items: Collecting gas in a syringe or over water
Measuring mass loss on a balance
Timing a colour change (e.g. disappearing cross)

cards.front: Why does increasing temperature or concentration change the steepness of a rate graph but not the final volume of gas produced?
cards.answer: The same amount of reactant is used, so the same total gas forms, just faster; only the rate changes.

cards.front: Why does increasing the amount of reactant increase the total volume of gas produced on a rate graph?
cards.answer: More reactant means more product can form before the reaction finishes, increasing the total gas volume.

cards.front: Name the four persuasion techniques Lady Macbeth uses on Macbeth in Act 1, Scene 7.
cards.answer: Questions his manhood / Accuses him of cowardice / Presents a practical plan / Uses the image of killing her own child
items: Uses the image of killing her own child

cards.front: Name the three things a wife was expected to do in Jacobean England, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Obey her husband / Manage the household / Bear children

cards.front: Why is Lady Macbeth's manipulation of Macbeth so effective?
cards.answer: She exploits the Jacobean equation of masculinity with violence, appealing only to his pride and shame, not reason or morality.

cards.front: Why would Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me here' speech have unsettled a Jacobean audience?
cards.answer: Women were expected to be gentle, obedient and maternal, so her rejection of femininity for cruelty seemed deeply unnatural.

cards.front: Name the four types of diagnostic technology the lesson gives that let doctors see inside the body without surgery.
cards.answer: X-rays / CT scans / MRI scans / Ultrasound

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why penicillin took so long to develop.
cards.answer: Fleming lacked chemistry skills to purify it / Funding was limited in the 1930s Depression / Only WWII gave the motivation and funding for mass production
items: Fleming lacked chemistry skills to purify it
Funding was limited in the 1930s Depression
Only WWII gave the motivation and funding for mass production

cards.front: Why did the experience of the Second World War create strong public support for a free NHS?
cards.answer: The government had organised emergency healthcare during the war, and the 1942 Beveridge Report had called for a welfare state.

cards.front: How were antibiotics like penicillin different from earlier 'magic bullets' like Salvarsan and Prontosil?
cards.answer: Antibiotics were natural substances made by moulds or fungi that could kill a wide range of bacteria, unlike targeted magic bullets.

title: The Depression and the rise of the Nazis, 1928-1932
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What did Hitler offer to the six different audiences he appealed to, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Unemployed: jobs, food, dignity / Middle class: protection from Communism, order / Farmers: subsidies and protectionism / Industrialists: end to union militancy, rearmament / Nationalists: revision of Versailles / Everyone: Volksgemeinschaft
items: Middle class: protection from Communism, order
Industrialists: end to union militancy, rearmament

cards.front: Why did the Wall Street Crash cause a severe economic collapse in Germany specifically?
cards.answer: American banks called in loans that had funded German industry under the Dawes Plan, reversing the flow of borrowed US capital almost overnight.

cards.front: Why did Bruning's deflation policy make the Depression worse rather than better?
cards.answer: Cutting wages, benefits and spending while six million were unemployed caused more starvation, which fuelled more political extremism.

cards.front: Why were middle-class Germans willing to vote Nazi even though many did not love Hitler?
cards.answer: Fear of a Bolshevik revolution, fuelled by Bruning's austerity, SA street violence and the rising KPD, made an authoritarian regime seem the only way to restore order.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson gives to increase the strength of an electromagnet.
cards.answer: Increasing the current / Increasing the number of turns in the coil / Using a soft iron core
items: Increasing the number of turns in the coil

cards.front: Name four applications of electromagnets given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Scrapyard cranes / Electric bells / Relays / Loudspeakers / MRI scanners

cards.front: Why is an induced magnet always attracted to the permanent magnet that magnetises it, never repelled?
cards.answer: Because the induced poles always form so that unlike poles face the permanent magnet, causing attraction.

cards.front: How does a split-ring commutator keep a DC motor spinning continuously?
cards.answer: It reverses the current direction through the coil every half turn, keeping the forces pushing in the same rotational direction.

title: The First Crusade: Antioch and Jerusalem
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six leaders of the First Crusade army mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Godfrey de Bouillon / Baldwin / Bohemond of Taranto / Tancred / Raymond of Toulouse / Robert of Normandy

cards.front: Name the three hardships the crusaders suffered during the eight-month Siege of Antioch.
cards.answer: Famine killed thousands / Desertion was a constant problem / Foraging parties were ambushed by Seljuk relief forces
items: Foraging parties ambushed by Seljuk forces

cards.front: Why did the crusaders defeat Kerbogha's much larger relief army outside Antioch in June 1098?
cards.answer: Kerbogha's coalition was fragile because individual Muslim commanders had their own rivalries and withdrew during the battle.

cards.front: How did having no single commander affect the First Crusade's campaign?
cards.answer: It weakened coordination among the leaders but also stopped the whole crusade collapsing when any one leader failed.

cards.front: Name the three laws the lesson calls the legal spine of apartheid.
cards.answer: Population Registration Act (1950) / Group Areas Act (1950) / Bantu Education Act (1953)

cards.front: Why did the apartheid government create the Bantustans and strip citizenship via the 1970 Act?
cards.answer: It let the government claim it wasn't oppressing South African citizens, since black residents were legally citizens of foreign homelands instead.

cards.front: How was the Suppression of Communism Act (1950) used to silence opposition to apartheid?
cards.answer: It defined 'communist' broadly to include anyone advocating racial equality, letting the government ban the ANC, unionists and liberals as criminals.

cards.front: Name the five standard stock forms that metals are supplied in, as described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sheet / Bar (flat/square) / Rod (round bar) / Tube / Angle

cards.front: Name the four methods the lesson gives for protecting metals from corrosion.
cards.answer: Galvanising / Powder coating / Painting / Anodising

cards.front: Why does the green patina that forms on copper actually protect it?
cards.answer: The patina is a layer of copper carbonate that protects the underlying metal from further corrosion.

cards.front: Why is recycling aluminium preferred over producing virgin aluminium from bauxite?
cards.answer: Recycling aluminium uses only around 5% of the energy needed to smelt virgin aluminium from bauxite.

cards.front: Name the six classic examples of high-risk foods given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cooked poultry / Cooked rice / Custards and cream-based desserts / Soft cheeses / Cooked shellfish / Egg-based dishes such as quiche

cards.front: Name the three ways given to control enzymic browning in fruit.
cards.answer: Adding acids like lemon juice / Blanching with heat / Covering to minimise oxygen exposure

cards.front: Why is a cooled cooked chicken breast left at room temperature considered higher-risk than raw chicken about to be roasted?
cards.answer: The cooked breast will be eaten as-is, so any bacteria multiplying in the danger zone go straight into the body, unlike raw chicken which will still be cooked.

cards.front: Why can vacuum-packed meat still carry a food safety risk?
cards.answer: Some bacteria are anaerobic and grow without oxygen, so removing air doesn't stop them multiplying if temperature control fails.

title: Magna Carta and the emergence of Parliament 1199-1399
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Why did King John face rebellion from his barons by 1215?
cards.answer: He raised taxes beyond feudal custom, took hostages, manipulated royal courts and lost Normandy, damaging baronial estates.

cards.front: Why did John seek papal annulment of Magna Carta soon after sealing it?
cards.answer: He wanted to escape its limits on his power, so he had Pope Innocent III annul it in August 1215.

cards.front: How did Edward I's Model Parliament of 1295 shape later constitutional practice?
cards.answer: By requiring representative consent for taxation, it built the convention that taxation needed approval from a representative body.

cards.front: Why is Richard II's deposition in 1399 constitutionally significant?
cards.answer: Parliament formally approved it, showing kingship could be conditional on good governance rather than absolute.

cards.front: Name the three different forms in which an algorithm can be expressed.
cards.answer: Pseudo-code / Flowchart / Actual program code

cards.front: Name the four sub-problems the NHS GP appointment booking system is decomposed into.
cards.answer: Patient login / Show available slots / Book slot / Send confirmation

cards.front: Why does a sat-nav system abstract away road surface physics, the Highway Code and car mechanics?
cards.answer: Keeping only position, destination, road connections and speeds means less detail to process, so routes are calculated faster and more clearly.

cards.front: How is abstraction applied in the school login system algorithm?
cards.answer: It ignores how passwords are stored, the server's operating system and network details, keeping only username, password, stored credentials and match/no-match.

cards.front: Name the three men who destroy Hero at the wedding, with the phrase each uses.
cards.answer: Claudio - 'rotten orange' / Don Pedro - 'common stale' / Leonato - 'Do not live'

cards.front: Why does Friar Francis plan to announce Hero has died?
cards.answer: To make Claudio feel remorse and, if the truth emerges, allow Hero to be restored; if not, hidden in a convent.

cards.front: Why does Beatrice say 'O God, that I were a man!' instead of confronting Claudio herself?
cards.answer: As a woman she cannot challenge Claudio to a duel, so gendered constraints force her to rely on Benedick to act.

cards.front: Why does Leonato's shift in Act 5 Scene 1 not undo the damage of his earlier reaction?
cards.answer: His initial wish for Hero's death cannot be unsaid, showing patriarchal reflexes are destructive even when later regretted.

cards.front: Name the six fundamental operations that flowchart programs can implement.
cards.answer: Input/output / Counting / Branching / Testing a condition / Time delay / Loop

cards.front: In the pedestrian crossing flowchart, list the steps in order from START to the loop back point.
cards.answer: Turn GREEN LED on / Is button pressed? / Turn GREEN LED off, RED LED on / Wait 5000 ms / Turn RED LED off
items: Turn GREEN LED off, RED LED on

cards.front: Why does a light-sensor circuit include a Schmitt inverter before the microcontroller input pin?
cards.answer: Without it, a slowly-rising LDR voltage could put the input pin at an ambiguous logic level, causing unpredictable behaviour.

cards.front: How does a flowchart implement a counting operation?
cards.answer: A process block increments or decrements a variable each time the program passes through it, and a decision block tests if it reached a target.

title: The Periodic Table and Its Patterns
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the three uses of noble gases given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Argon in welding (shields weld from oxygen) / Helium in balloons and airships / Neon in lighting
items: Argon in welding (shields weld from oxygen)

cards.front: Give the four coloured transition metal compounds/ions named in the lesson and their colours.
cards.answer: Copper compounds are blue or green / Iron(II) compounds are pale green / Iron(III) compounds are orange-brown
items: Copper compounds are blue or green

cards.front: How does chlorine water added to potassium bromide solution show a displacement reaction?
cards.answer: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from the salt, turning the solution orange.

cards.front: Why do elements in the same period of the periodic table differ from each other despite being neighbours?
cards.answer: Periods share the same number of electron shells, but each element has a different number of outer electrons, giving different properties.

title: Signed Binary, Addition, Subtraction and Shifts
subject: computer-science-eduqas

cards.front: How does a processor perform binary subtraction (A − B) without a separate subtraction circuit?
cards.answer: It adds A to the two's complement of B, turning subtraction into addition.

cards.front: What does a logical shift right do to the MSB, and why is this different from an arithmetic shift?
cards.answer: It always inserts 0 into the MSB, not preserving sign, since it's used for unsigned numbers.

title: Effectiveness, Opposition and the Second New Deal
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three directions from which opposition to the New Deal came.
cards.answer: The Supreme Court / Congressional Republicans / Radical critics

cards.front: Name the three parts of the Second New Deal package of 1935.
cards.answer: Wagner Act (union rights) / Social Security Act (pensions, insurance, aid) / WPA (work for 8.5 million)

cards.front: Why did Roosevelt propose the 1937 court-packing plan?
cards.answer: Because the Supreme Court had struck down the NRA and AAA, so he wanted extra justices to outvote the conservative bloc blocking New Deal laws.

cards.front: Why did political pressure push Roosevelt to launch the Second New Deal in 1935?
cards.answer: Court strikes against the NRA and AAA, radical critics' popularity, and the approaching 1936 election convinced Roosevelt he needed bolder, more redistributive reforms.

cards.front: Why does Golding have Roger throw stones to miss in Chapter 4 but kill Piggy in Chapter 11?
cards.answer: It shows Roger's progression from restrained by civilisation's taboo to committing deliberate murder once that taboo is destroyed.

cards.front: Why does Piggy still carry the conch to Castle Rock even though the tribe no longer respects it?
cards.answer: Piggy believes the conch still commands authority, showing his continued faith in rules and democracy even as they collapse.

cards.front: What three things does Ralph weep for at the novel's end (three things named in the lesson)?
cards.answer: The end of innocence / The darkness of man's heart / The fall through the air of the true, wise friend called Piggy
items: The fall of the wise friend Piggy

title: Stars, Galaxies and the Big Bang
