subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the four types of object the lesson says space telescopes can detect that ground telescopes can't (blocked by Earth's atmosphere).
cards.answer: Infrared / Ultraviolet / X-ray / Microwave

cards.front: Why does gravity provide a centripetal force for orbiting planets without changing their speed?
cards.answer: Gravity continuously changes a planet's direction of travel, keeping it in a circular path, but doesn't change its speed.

cards.front: How does a cloud of gas and dust heat up enough to start nuclear fusion when a star forms?
cards.answer: Gravity compresses the cloud, doing work on it so particles collide more forcefully, raising the core temperature until fusion begins.

cards.front: Why can't a massive star's core release energy once it has fused elements up to iron?
cards.answer: Iron cannot release energy through fusion, so the core can no longer balance gravity and collapses catastrophically.

cards.front: What are the three genotype ratios produced from a Bb × Bb cross?
What three arguments does the lesson give about embryo screening?
cards.answer: it prevents suffering / it is unethical to select embryos / it could lead to designer babies
items: it is unethical to select embryos
it could lead to designer babies

cards.front: How does cystic fibrosis affect the body?
cards.answer: It causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system.

cards.front: How does the Y chromosome cause a baby to develop as male?
cards.answer: It carries the SRY gene, which triggers male development.

cards.front: Name the four rules of binary addition given in the lesson.
Name the four SI decimal units of data storage used on this course, smallest to largest, and what each equals.
cards.answer: kilobyte (kB) = 1,000 bytes / megabyte (MB) = 1,000 kilobytes / gigabyte (GB) = 1,000 megabytes / terabyte (TB) = 1,000 gigabytes

cards.front: Why do computers store and process all data as binary rather than another number system?
cards.answer: A transistor is either conducting electricity or not, and this two-state physical reality maps perfectly onto binary's two digits.

cards.front: Why can a right binary shift by 1 lose information from a number?
cards.answer: It performs integer division by 2, so any remainder is lost as the last bit shifts beyond the boundary.

title: From Diem to Tonkin: US Steps into Vietnam, 1954-64
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: According to the domino theory, which four Southeast Asian states would fall to communism in sequence after South Vietnam?
cards.answer: Laos / Cambodia / Thailand / Burma

cards.front: Name three features of Diem's government that made it structurally weak in rural South Vietnam.
cards.answer: Reversed land reform for landlords / Catholic-Mandarin regime alienated Buddhist peasants / Nepotistic rule via brother Nhu's secret police / Preferential treatment for Catholic refugees
items: Nepotistic rule via brother Nhu's secret police

cards.front: Why did Diem's reversal of land reform help the Vietcong recruit peasants?
cards.answer: Bringing back fled landlords and reimposing rents on tenant farmers gave the Vietcong a ready-made recruitment programme among angry peasants.

cards.front: Why did the 1963 self-immolation of Thich Quang Duc damage Diem internationally?
cards.answer: Photographs of the monk's protest against Buddhist repression were printed on front pages worldwide, destroying Diem's remaining international standing.

cards.front: Name the four things Athena does to help Odysseus in the Odyssey.
cards.answer: Engineers his release from Calypso's island / Guides Telemachus on his journey / Gives Odysseus his beggar's disguise / Intervenes in the battle of Book 22
items: Engineers his release from Calypso's island
Intervenes in the battle of Book 22

cards.front: Name the three things Poseidon does to stop Odysseus getting home.
cards.answer: Destroys his ships / Strands him on distant islands / Stirs up deadly storms

cards.front: Why is Polyphemus presented as the worst possible host in the Odyssey?
cards.answer: He eats his guests instead of feeding them, dismisses the gods who protect xenia, and ignores reciprocal obligation.

cards.front: Why does Homer treat Circe's hospitality as improving over time?
cards.answer: Odysseus's resistance transforms her from a hostile host into a genuine one who gives a year of hospitality, restores his crew and vital information.

cards.front: What four things does ATP energy power in cells, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Muscle contraction / Nerve impulse transmission / Protein synthesis / Active transport

cards.front: The lesson describes three stages in how mitochondria's function was discovered over time — name them in order.
cards.answer: Observation of structure under light microscopes / Experimental isolation to find function / Detailed biochemical analysis of reaction steps
items: Observation of structure under light microscopes
Detailed biochemical analysis of reaction steps

cards.front: Why do cristae increase the rate of aerobic respiration in mitochondria?
cards.answer: The cristae are folds in the inner membrane that increase the surface area for aerobic respiration reactions to take place.

cards.front: Why must yeast fermentation avoid having too much oxygen present?
cards.answer: Too much oxygen switches yeast to aerobic respiration, which reduces the ethanol yield.

title: Mechanical Systems: Motion, Linkages and Cams
subject: engineering-aqa

cards.front: Name the four types of motion that mechanical systems use.
cards.answer: Rotary motion / Linear motion / Reciprocating motion / Oscillating motion

cards.front: Name the four named cam profiles covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pear cam / Eccentric (circular) cam / Snail (drop) cam / Heart cam

cards.front: How does a crank and slider mechanism turn rotary motion into reciprocating motion?
cards.answer: A rotating crank pin is connected to a slider by a connecting rod, so as the crank rotates the slider moves back and forth.

cards.front: Why is the cam profile in an aero-engine fuel valve unit machined to very tight tolerances?
cards.answer: Because any deviation in the profile changes the valve timing, which affects the engine's thrust output.

cards.front: Name the four types of erosion the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Abrasion / Hydraulic action / Attrition / Solution

cards.front: Name the four types of transport the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Traction / Saltation / Suspension / Solution

cards.front: Why does freeze-thaw weathering break rock apart?
cards.answer: Water seeps into cracks, freezes overnight, expands by about 9%, and prises the rock apart.

cards.front: Why do hard rocks like those in the Pennines stand higher than surrounding land?
cards.answer: Harder rocks such as limestone and Millstone Grit resist weathering more, so they weather slower and stand higher.

title: Organic Chemistry: Hydrocarbons, Alcohols and Polymers
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the six main fractions crude oil is separated into by fractional distillation.
cards.answer: Refinery gases / Petrol (gasoline) / Kerosene / Diesel / Fuel oil / Bitumen

cards.front: Name the first four alkanes in order.
cards.answer: Methane / Ethane / Propane / Butane

cards.front: Why are alkenes far more reactive than alkanes?
cards.answer: The C=C double bond is a site of high electron density, so molecules like hydrogen, water or bromine can add across it, breaking the bond.

cards.front: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous to breathe in?
cards.answer: It is a toxic, colourless, odourless gas that binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen from being transported around the body.

cards.front: Name the four great Anglo-Saxon earldoms that existed before William reduced the power of earls.
cards.answer: Wessex / Mercia / Northumbria / East Anglia

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says the feudal system worked through to give William control.
cards.answer: Homage / Knight service / Forfeiture

cards.front: Why did William need to appoint regents to govern England?
cards.answer: Because William spent roughly half his reign in Normandy, so trusted men had to govern England in his absence.

cards.front: Why did William's system of using regents create a risk for him?
cards.answer: A regent who abused his power could cause resentment and rebellion, as Odo of Bayeux later proved.

cards.front: What three classical authors did Elizabethan grammar school students study?
cards.answer: Plutarch / Cicero / Seneca

cards.front: Name the four key contextual threads for exam analysis of Julius Caesar given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Roman republican ideal against absolute power / Elizabethan succession crisis and fear of instability / the divine right debate over legitimacy of power / Shakespeare's use of Plutarch for historical authority
items: Roman republican ideal against absolute power
Elizabethan succession crisis and fear of instability
the divine right debate over legitimacy of power
Shakespeare's use of Plutarch for historical authority

cards.front: How did Shakespeare turn Plutarch's biography into a gripping political thriller?
cards.answer: He compressed timelines, invented dialogue, and gave far more dramatic weight to moments like the soothsayer's warning.

cards.front: Why did Rome share power between two consuls rather than one ruler?
cards.answer: Power was deliberately shared between two annually elected consuls to prevent any one person becoming a king.

cards.front: Name the five xerophyte adaptations for reducing water loss given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Thick waxy cuticle / Reduced or modified leaves (spines) / Sunken stomata / Rolled leaves / Water storage tissue

cards.front: Name the three hydrophyte adaptations given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Aerenchyma (air spaces) / Broad flat floating leaves / Flexible stems

cards.front: Why does a root bend downward in response to gravity (positive gravitropism)?
cards.answer: Auxin accumulates on the lower side, but root cells are sensitive to it, so high auxin inhibits elongation there, bending the root down.

cards.front: How does rolling its leaves inward help marram grass reduce water loss?
cards.answer: Rolling leaves inward traps humid air inside the leaf, reducing the humidity gradient and slowing water vapour loss.

title: The Alliance System and Splendid Isolation
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three bilateral agreements the lesson says formed the Triple Entente.
cards.answer: Franco-Russian Alliance (1894) / Entente Cordiale (1904) / Anglo-Russian Convention (1907)

cards.front: Why did Italy's commitment to the Triple Alliance stay shallow?
cards.answer: Many Italians saw Austria-Hungary as the hereditary enemy for controlling Italian-speaking lands like Trento and Trieste.

cards.front: How did the alliance system raise, rather than lower, the risk of war by 1914?
cards.answer: Once both blocs were locked in, a small incident could trigger a chain reaction as mobilisation timetables left diplomacy only days to defuse crises.

cards.front: What four theatrical spectacles does Prospero stage on the island?
cards.answer: The storm / The masque / The harpy banquet / The spirits

cards.front: What three roles does the Epilogue simultaneously perform?
cards.answer: A character's plea / An actor's curtain call / A playwright's farewell

cards.front: Why does Prospero's magic move Antonio emotionally but fail to make him genuinely repent?
cards.answer: Art can move people emotionally but cannot change their fundamental nature, shown by Antonio never apologising despite Prospero's illusions.

cards.front: How does the play's tight structure of the unities reflect Prospero's control over the island?
cards.answer: The single overarching plan within one place and short time mirrors Prospero's orchestration, making others seem like performers hitting his marks.

cards.front: Name the four categories that hospitality and catering provision is split into.
cards.answer: Commercial residential / Commercial non-residential / Non-commercial residential / Non-commercial non-residential

cards.front: Name the four examples the lesson gives of non-commercial residential provision.
cards.answer: Hospitals, hospices and care homes / Boarding schools, colleges and university residences / Prisons / Armed forces
items: Boarding schools, colleges and university residences

cards.front: Why can achieving a Michelin star or AA rosettes be expensive for a restaurant to maintain?
cards.answer: Staff must be highly trained, ingredients must be top quality, and facilities must be immaculate.

cards.front: Why does a higher hotel or restaurant rating often let a business charge more?
cards.answer: Ratings give customers confidence in quality, so a higher rating attracts wealthier clientele willing to pay more.

cards.front: The lesson groups electronic system components into three jobs. Name them.
cards.answer: Sensing what is happening / Controlling what happens next / Producing an output

cards.front: Name the three control devices between the sensor and output described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Switch / Transistor / Resistor

cards.front: Why must a resistor connected to an LED have exactly the right value, not too low or too high?
cards.answer: Too little resistance damages the LED, while too much resistance makes the output too dim or weak.

cards.front: Why can a transistor let a weak sensor signal control a powerful output like a motor or bright lamp?
cards.answer: A small current or voltage at one connection switches a much larger current, controlling power the sensor alone couldn't drive.

title: SQL: Retrieving Data with SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the six comparison operators the lesson gives for use in a WHERE clause.
cards.answer: = (equal) / <> (not equal) / (greater than) / = (greater than or equal to)

cards.front: Why must you write Students.student_name instead of just student_name in a two-table query?
cards.answer: TableName.ColumnName notation avoids ambiguity when the same column name appears in both tables.

cards.front: Why does the WHERE clause in a two-table query set Students.student_id = Enrolments.student_id?
cards.answer: This matches the primary key in one table to the foreign key in the other, effectively joining the tables.

title: Performance Interpretation: Playing Mickey at Seven and Twenty-Five
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four physical vocabulary choices the lesson gives for playing the adult Mickey at twenty-five.
cards.answer: Higher, contracted posture with shoulders forward / Slower, heavier gait / Reduced range of gesture / Vacancy behind the eyes
items: Higher, contracted posture with shoulders forward

cards.front: Why does invading personal space signal childhood when playing Mickey at seven?
cards.answer: Children are not yet socialised into adult rules about personal space, so leaning in close reads instantly as childlike to an audience.

cards.front: How does adult Edward's clear, measured, authoritative vocal delivery affect Mickey even though Edward means only warmth?
cards.answer: It marks Edward's class privilege, making Mickey feel excluded and patronised despite Edward's genuine affection for him.

cards.front: How does Ralph betray Piggy's trust in Chapter 1?
cards.answer: He reveals Piggy's hated nickname to the other boys after Piggy specifically asked him not to.

cards.front: Why does enthusiasm for shelter-building and the fire fade by Chapter 3?
cards.answer: Hunting offers immediate, exciting satisfaction, while maintaining the fire and shelters is boring and requires discipline and sacrifice.

cards.front: Name the five stages of Macbeth's character arc across the play.
cards.answer: Loyal warrior / Tempted nobleman / Guilt-stricken murderer / Paranoid tyrant / Nihilistic villain

cards.front: What three pieces of evidence support reading Macbeth as a tragic hero deserving pity?
cards.answer: He hesitates / He feels guilt / He recognises what he has lost
items: He recognises what he has lost

cards.front: Why don't the witches' prophecies actually create Macbeth's ambition?
cards.answer: They reveal an ambition that already existed within him, shown by the phrase 'horrid image' in Act 1 Scene 3.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare bring Banquo's ghost back in Act 3 Scene 4?
cards.answer: To make Banquo the play's symbol of inescapable guilt and of legitimate succession through his descendants.

cards.front: Name the three targets the lesson gives that Vikings attacked far inland in Britain.
cards.answer: Lindisfarne / York / London

cards.front: Name the three Anglo-Dutch Wars periods given in the lesson.
How did Nelson's tactics at Trafalgar differ from the traditional line of battle?
cards.answer: He attacked in two columns perpendicular to the enemy line, cutting it in three and forcing close-quarters fighting where British gunnery won.

cards.front: Why did the Spanish Armada suffer its greatest losses in 1588?
cards.answer: As it tried to return home around Scotland and Ireland, storms wrecked about 63 ships, far more than were lost in battle.

cards.front: Name the three sterilisation methods the lesson gives for treating potable water.
cards.answer: Chlorine / Ozone / Ultraviolet (UV) light

cards.front: Name the five stages of sewage treatment described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Screening and grit removal / Primary sedimentation / Biological treatment / Secondary sedimentation / Final filtration and sterilisation

cards.front: Why is chlorine most commonly used to sterilise water in the UK?
cards.answer: It is effective, cheap, and continues to kill bacteria as water travels through the distribution network.

cards.front: Why is desalination essential in arid countries but not usually needed in the UK?
cards.answer: Desalination uses lots of energy and is expensive, whereas the UK has enough rainfall for cheaper fresh water treatment.

title: UK Population Distribution & a Major UK City
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four things that make Manchester an important city within the UK, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Major financial centre (Spinningfields) / Home to four universities including University of Manchester / Manchester Airport, third-busiest in the UK / BBC's second hub at MediaCityUK
items: Home to four universities including University of Manchester
Manchester Airport, third-busiest in the UK

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why Manchester became 'Cottonopolis'.
cards.answer: Wet climate suited cotton spinning / Fast-flowing Pennine streams powered mills / Coal from Lancashire fed steam engines
items: Coal from Lancashire fed steam engines

cards.front: How does cumulative causation explain why London and the south-east became so densely populated?
cards.answer: A navigable Thames and fertile lowlands helped a financial centre grow, which then attracted jobs, transport links and universities, drawing in more people.

cards.front: Why did the Manchester Ship Canal help Manchester's development?
cards.answer: Opened in 1894, it let ocean-going ships reach Manchester directly, bypassing Liverpool and boosting trade.

cards.front: Name the four festivals covered in this lesson on Spanish festivals.
cards.answer: Las Fallas / La Tomatina / Semana Santa / El Día de los Muertos

cards.front: What four things are ofrendas decorated with during El Día de los Muertos?
cards.answer: photographs / flowers (marigolds/cempasúchil) / candles / favourite foods of the deceased

cards.front: How does El Día de los Muertos combine two different cultural traditions?
cards.answer: It combines indigenous Aztec traditions with Catholic beliefs brought by Spanish colonists.

cards.front: Why is El Día de los Muertos a joyful celebration rather than a sad one?
cards.answer: It celebrates the lives of family members who have died, and Mexicans believe their spirits return to visit.

title: Sources of Authority and Muslim Identity
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four architectural features of a mosque given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Mihrab (prayer niche facing Makkah) / Minbar (pulpit for Friday sermons) / Minaret (tower for call to prayer) / Area for wudu (ritual washing)

cards.front: Name the four main Sunni legal schools of Shari'ah Law.
cards.answer: Hanafi / Maliki / Shafi'i / Hanbali

cards.front: Why did the Sunni-Shi'a split over religious authority arise after the Prophet's death?
cards.answer: Shi'a Muslims believe Ali and the Ahl-ul-Bayt were the divinely appointed rightful authorities, while Sunnis respect Ali as a caliph but not divinely appointed.

cards.front: Why was ibn al-Arabi's concept of wahdat al-wujud (Unity of Being) controversial?
cards.answer: It suggested all existence reflects Allah's being, which some orthodox scholars felt blurred the distinction between Creator and creation.

title: Civil Rights: Segregation, Martin Luther King and the 1964 Act
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four civil-rights leaders the lesson says mattered only because mass action made their leadership consequential.
cards.answer: Martin Luther King / Malcolm X / Rosa Parks / Stokely Carmichael

cards.front: Name the three US Civil Rights Acts passed between 1964 and 1968.
cards.answer: Civil Rights Act, 1964 / Voting Rights Act, 1965 / Fair Housing Act, 1968

cards.front: Why did President Eisenhower send federal troops to Little Rock in 1957?
cards.answer: Governor Faubus used the National Guard to block the Little Rock Nine, so Eisenhower sent paratroopers to enforce desegregation.

cards.front: Why did Congress pass the 1964 Civil Rights Act?
cards.answer: Televised images of Bull Connor's police using dogs and fire hoses on child protestors in Birmingham shocked the nation and pushed Congress to act.

cards.front: Name the three narrative techniques the lesson says Wells uses in The War of the Worlds.
cards.answer: Journalistic register / Direct address / Scientific language for the Martians

cards.front: Name the five escalating threats that structure Book 1 of The War of the Worlds.
cards.answer: Cylinder / Heat-Ray / Tripods / Black Smoke / Exodus

cards.front: Why does the pacing change so dramatically between Book 1 and Book 2 of The War of the Worlds?
cards.answer: Book 1 is fast-paced action showing public spectacle, while Book 2 slows to show private, claustrophobic psychological survival.

cards.front: How does the structural mirroring of Book 1 expanding and Book 2 contracting reflect Wells's argument?
cards.answer: Book 1's escalating threats mirror growing public crisis, while Book 2's shrinking setting mirrors the shift to private survival.

cards.front: Name the seven operations the lesson says cover the whole string/random topic.
cards.answer: .length / .substring(x, i) with .left(i) and .right(i) / .upper / .lower / + for joining / ASC(...) and CHR(...) / random(min, max)

cards.front: Why does random(1,7) or random(0,6) break a six-sided dice program instead of causing an error?
cards.answer: Because random is inclusive of both ends, so those ranges give seven possible outcomes instead of six, silently giving wrong results.

cards.front: How can arithmetic on a character code shift a letter along the alphabet?
cards.answer: Because character codes run in order, adding to a code with ASC and converting back with CHR moves to the next letter.

cards.front: Why does word.substring(3,4) on 'Programming' give 'gram' rather than stopping at index 4?
cards.answer: Because the second argument is a count of characters taken from the start index, not a stopping index, so it takes indexes 3 to 6.

title: Cinema, TV and screen entertainment from 1920
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three Ealing comedy films the lesson gives as examples from the late 1940s and early 1950s.
cards.answer: Passport to Pimlico (1949) / Kind Hearts and Coronets (1949) / The Lavender Hill Mob (1951)

cards.front: Why did British cinema admissions fall so sharply between 1946 and 1970?
cards.answer: Television was free at the point of use, available at home, and offered a growing range of content, making it more convenient than cinema.

cards.front: How did cinema survive despite losing audiences to television?
cards.answer: It differentiated itself with large screens, better sound, and blockbuster films that could not be replicated at home.

cards.front: Name the six fixed costs the lesson gives as typical for a start-up.
cards.answer: Rent / Insurance / Advertising / Salaries / Utilities / Loan interest

cards.front: Name the three rearranged formulas the lesson says to practise for calculation questions.
cards.answer: Find selling price (Revenue ÷ Quantity sold) / Find quantity sold (Revenue ÷ Selling price) / Find variable cost per unit (Total variable costs ÷ Quantity produced)
items: Find variable cost per unit (Total variable costs ÷ Quantity produced)

cards.front: Why is flour a variable cost for a baker who makes more loaves?
cards.answer: Because making twice as many loaves means using twice as much flour, so the cost rises directly with output.

cards.front: Why is it useful for a start-up to identify a loss early?
cards.answer: It helps the entrepreneur decide whether to adjust prices, cut costs, or both before the problem grows.

title: Immigration: Windrush, race riots and Enoch Powell
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson names three groups whose hostility Caribbean migrants faced in Britain. What were they and how did each act?
cards.answer: Landlords who refused rooms to Black tenants / Employers who paid lower wages / Neighbours who objected to their presence
items: Landlords who refused rooms to Black tenants
Neighbours who objected to their presence

cards.front: The lesson lists five types of institutions migrant communities built for themselves. What were they?
cards.answer: Temples / Mosques / Churches / Social clubs / Newspapers

cards.front: Why was the Commonwealth Immigrants Act 1968 seen by critics as racially discriminatory?
cards.answer: It targeted East African Asians who held British passports by requiring them to prove a 'substantial connection' with Britain before entry.

cards.front: Why did the reaction to Powell's 1968 speech reveal a gap between politicians and the public?
cards.answer: Heath sacked Powell for the speech, yet opinion polls showed over 70% of the public agreed with his concerns about immigration.

title: Cold War, IRA and the wars on terror
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four IRA attacks described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Guildford pub bombings (1974) / Birmingham pub bombings (1974) / Brighton hotel bomb (1984) / Canary Wharf bomb (1996)

cards.front: Name the four key figures involved in the Good Friday Agreement given in the lesson.
cards.answer: John Hume (SDLP) / Gerry Adams (Sinn Féin) / David Trimble (Ulster Unionist Party) / Mo Mowlam (Secretary of State)

cards.front: Why did the Army's relationship with nationalist areas in Northern Ireland deteriorate after 1969?
cards.answer: Troops initially welcomed as protection against loyalist attacks saw relations with nationalist communities rapidly worsen after deployment.

cards.front: Why did the 7/7 bombings prompt debate about British foreign policy?
cards.answer: The bombers were inspired by al-Qaeda ideology, raising questions about links between the Iraq War and domestic terrorist recruitment.

title: The Second Cold War: Afghanistan & Reagan’s SDI
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four punitive measures Carter took against the USSR after the invasion of Afghanistan.
cards.answer: Withdrew SALT 2 from Senate consideration / Imposed a grain embargo on the USSR / Increased US defence spending / Boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics
items: Imposed a grain embargo on the USSR

cards.front: What are the two historian views on whether SDI helped end the Cold War?
cards.answer: SDI pressured the USSR into arms reduction talks it couldn't afford to match / The Cold War ended due to Soviet internal weakness and Gorbachev's reforms, not SDI
items: SDI pressured the USSR into arms reduction talks it couldn't afford to match
The Cold War ended due to Soviet internal weakness and Gorbachev's reforms, not SDI

cards.front: Why did Brezhnev send Soviet troops into Afghanistan in 1979?
cards.answer: He feared that if the communist government fell, it would encourage anti-Soviet movements in the USSR's own Muslim-majority Central Asian republics.

cards.front: How did Reagan's increased defence spending aim to defeat the Soviet Union?
cards.answer: He believed the USA could outspend the USSR in an arms race, forcing it to choose between military spending and economic collapse.

title: Fort Laramie 1851 and the Indian Wars 1862-1867
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four pressures the lesson gives for why the 1851 Fort Laramie concentration policy failed.
cards.answer: Senate cut annuity from fifty to ten years / no Plains nation was a single political body / growing settler pressure from Pike's Peak gold rush / 1861 Treaty of Fort Wise stripped Cheyenne/Arapaho land
items: Senate cut annuity from fifty to ten years
no Plains nation was a single political body
growing settler pressure from Pike's Peak gold rush
1861 Treaty of Fort Wise stripped Cheyenne/Arapaho land

cards.front: Name the three consequences the lesson gives for the 1862-67 Indian Wars.
cards.answer: trust between Plains nations and government collapsed / US Army grew to 25,000 men west of the Mississippi by 1869 / eastern public opinion split over Sand Creek
items: trust between Plains nations and government collapsed
US Army grew to 25,000 men west of the Mississippi by 1869
eastern public opinion split over Sand Creek

cards.front: Why did the 1862 Dakota War break out in Minnesota?
cards.answer: Annuity payments were months late, the harvest had failed, and starving Dakota were told to eat grass, so four young men killed settlers, sparking a wider uprising.

cards.front: How did Fetterman's Trap happen on 21 December 1866?
cards.answer: Fetterman's detachment chased a Lakota decoy party led by Crazy Horse over a ridge into an ambush of 1,500-2,000 warriors, killing all 81 men.

title: The Elizabethan theatre and attitudes towards it
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three connected factors the lesson gives for why Elizabethan theatre boomed.
cards.answer: Noble patronage protecting actors from vagrancy laws / Rise of a paying urban audience with disposable income / Elizabeth's personal taste for plays at court
items: Noble patronage protecting actors from vagrancy laws
Rise of a paying urban audience with disposable income
Elizabeth's personal taste for plays at court

cards.front: What four reasons did the City of London Corporation give for banning public playhouses?
cards.answer: Spread plague by drawing crowds / Attracted pickpockets, prostitutes and brawlers / Pulled apprentices away from honest work / Encouraged immorality
items: Pulled apprentices away from honest work

cards.front: Why did the Privy Council sometimes order playhouses closed during serious plague outbreaks?
cards.answer: Partly to control infection by stopping crowds gathering, and partly to placate the City of London and the Puritans.

cards.front: How did royal licensing by the Master of the Revels from 1581 protect acting companies?
cards.answer: A licensed play could not be banned by the City of London Corporation, so licensing shielded companies as well as censoring them.

title: Culture and fashion in Edwardian Britain
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four major authors the lesson credits with publishing important works during the Edwardian period (1890–1914).
cards.answer: Thomas Hardy / George Bernard Shaw / H.G. Wells / Beatrix Potter

cards.front: Why did Thomas Hardy stop writing novels after 1896?
cards.answer: He gave up fiction following the hostile reception to his novel Jude the Obscure.

cards.front: Why did women's fashion shift towards straighter, less restrictive styles by around 1907–1910?
cards.answer: Partly due to the suffragette movement's critique of restrictive clothing, and partly the rise of active leisure like cycling and golf.

cards.front: Name the three common mistakes the lesson warns about when calculating image file size.
cards.answer: Forgetting to multiply by colour depth / Leaving the answer in bits when bytes are asked for / Dividing by 1,000 instead of 8 to convert bits to bytes
items: Forgetting to multiply by colour depth
Leaving the answer in bits when bytes are asked for
Dividing by 1,000 instead of 8 to convert bits to bytes

cards.front: Name the three problems the lesson says happen when there aren't enough bits to represent data accurately.
cards.answer: Colour banding in images / Quantisation noise in sound / Lost high-frequency detail from low sample rate
items: Lost high-frequency detail from low sample rate

cards.front: Why does increasing colour depth allow more possible colours per pixel?
cards.answer: Colour depth is the number of bits per pixel, and the number of possible colours equals 2 to the power of that bit count.

cards.front: Why does a lower sample rate cause loss of high-frequency detail in a recorded sound?
cards.answer: Fewer samples per second means rapid wave variations happen faster than the gaps between samples, so they get missed.

title: Stock Control and Working with Suppliers
subject: business-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three types of stock a manufacturing business might hold.
cards.answer: Raw materials / Work in progress / Finished goods

cards.front: Name the four key values shown on a bar gate stock graph.
cards.answer: Maximum stock level / Minimum stock level / Re-order level / Re-order quantity

cards.front: Why might a business using just-in-time stock control miss out on volume-purchase discounts?
cards.answer: It orders smaller quantities more frequently instead of buying in bulk, so it misses discounts for large orders.

cards.front: How can poor supply chain decisions, like relying on a single supplier, affect a business?
cards.answer: They raise costs, create delays and damage the business's reputation.

title: Staging and Design: Sea, State Apartment and Searchlight
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four specific choices the lesson says should be specified when designing cold lighting for the North Korea scenes.
cards.answer: Which lantern type (profile spot or Fresnel) / What intensity (e.g. 70%) / What colour gel (e.g. Full C.T. Blue) / What directional angle (e.g. steep top-light)
items: Which lantern type (profile spot or Fresnel)
What colour gel (e.g. Full C.T. Blue)

cards.front: Name the three elements the lesson gives as North Korea's design vocabulary.
cards.answer: Flat, harsh overhead light / Institutional walls / Absence of the natural world

cards.front: Why does the play use a minimalist set instead of a naturalistic one?
cards.answer: The play spans 24 years and two countries, so a realistic set would need constant scene changes that would fatally slow its momentum.

cards.front: Why does the sound designer move the sea sound from binaural speakers to a mono centre speaker as the play progresses?
cards.answer: To suggest the sea has retreated into memory, marking how far Hanako has moved from her original loss.

cards.front: According to mainstream Islamic scholarship, what four conditions must be met for armed (Lesser) Jihad to be legitimate?
cards.answer: Declared by legitimate authority / Must be the last resort / Civilians and non-combatants must be protected / Must cease when the enemy seeks peace
items: Civilians and non-combatants must be protected
Must cease when the enemy seeks peace

cards.front: In classical Islamic jurisprudence, what three circumstances allow Lesser Jihad to be waged?
cards.answer: Muslim community under attack / Innocent people being oppressed / Evil cannot be removed by other means
items: Evil cannot be removed by other means

cards.front: Why do Sunni and Shi'a Muslims mark Ashura in such different ways?
cards.answer: For Shi'a it mourns Hussayn's martyrdom at Karbala, while for Sunni it marks Moses's rescue from Pharaoh, so Sunni Muslims fast instead.

cards.front: Why do Sunni Muslims not observe Eid-ul-Ghadeer?
cards.answer: They do not share the Shi'a belief that Muhammad designated Ali as his rightful successor at Ghadir Khumm.

title: Violence, War and Just War Theory
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the four causes of terrorism the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Political grievances / Economic marginalisation / Cultural humiliation / Extremist ideologies claiming divine sanction

cards.front: What three extra criteria did later Catholic tradition add to Aquinas's conditions for a just war?
cards.answer: Last resort / Proportionality / Reasonable chance of success

cards.front: What does jus in bello mean and how does it differ from the criteria for going to war?
cards.answer: Jus in bello means even a just war must be fought justly, sparing non-combatants and avoiding disproportionate destruction.

cards.front: How does Islamic teaching balance the sanctity of life with the right to self-defence?
cards.answer: Islam teaches life is sacred and unlawful killing is a serious sin, but recognises defending the community against aggression as legitimate.

title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the five stages a Bill passes through in each House of Parliament.
cards.answer: First Reading / Second Reading / Committee Stage / Report Stage / Third Reading

cards.front: What four ways does the lesson give for citizens to engage with the legislative process?
cards.answer: Writing to their MP / Giving evidence to a committee / Petitioning Parliament / Joining campaigns to influence a Bill
items: Joining campaigns to influence a Bill

cards.front: Why is Second Reading described as the most politically significant early stage of a Bill?
cards.answer: It is the first vote on whether the Bill's broad aims are worthwhile, so whips work hard to secure their party's votes.

cards.front: Why can the Lords only delay a Finance Bill for one month, unlike other Bills?
cards.answer: This gives the Commons much stronger control over financial legislation than over other types of Bill.

cards.front: Name the four comparison partner poems the lesson pairs with 'Venus's-flytraps'.
cards.answer: Out, Out— (Frost) / Cold Knap Lake (Clarke) / My First Weeks (Olds) / Theme for English B (Hughes)

cards.front: Name the three juxtapositions the lesson says the whole poem is built from.
cards.answer: Play beside danger / Love beside violence / Sweetness beside death

cards.front: Why does the poem end on overheard family secrets rather than the flowers?
cards.answer: It shows the flowers are a way into the poem's real subject: a child gathering fragments of an adult world he's too young to understand.

cards.front: How do the poem's short, blunt sentences with mid-line full stops reflect the boy's mind?
cards.answer: They make statements land abruptly and images collide, imitating how ideas crash together in a five-year-old's thinking.

title: Tests for Ions, Gases and Chromatography
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four hydroxide precipitate colours the lesson gives for identifying metal ions with sodium hydroxide (excluding aluminium).
cards.answer: Copper - blue precipitate / Iron(II) - green precipitate / Iron(III) - brown (rust-coloured) precipitate / Calcium - white precipitate

cards.front: How can you distinguish an aluminium hydroxide precipitate from a magnesium hydroxide precipitate using excess sodium hydroxide?
cards.answer: Excess sodium hydroxide dissolves the aluminium hydroxide precipitate but does not dissolve the magnesium hydroxide precipitate.

cards.front: In paper chromatography, why do some components travel further up the paper than others?
cards.answer: Components that are more soluble in the solvent travel further up the paper.

cards.front: How is ammonia gas detected in the test for ammonium ions?
cards.answer: Damp red litmus paper held near the gas turns blue because ammonia is an alkaline gas.

title: The Dignity of Human Life and Religious Freedom
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six humanitarian organisations the lesson gives as examples of religious groups acting on human dignity.
cards.answer: World Jewish Relief and HIAS / Islamic Relief and Muslim Aid / Ramakrishna Mission / Khalsa Aid / Karuna Trust / Christian charities and advocacy organisations

cards.front: How did Sikh legal cases in Britain illustrate tension with Article 18 of the UDHR?
cards.answer: Cases over wearing the kara and turban in schools and workplaces tested religious freedom against institutional rules, mostly resolved in favour of accommodation.

cards.front: Why do Humanists argue that human rights should not be based on religion?
cards.answer: They ground dignity in every person's capacity to reason, feel, and flourish, so rights don't depend on religious belief and must be universal.

cards.front: Why is Article 18 of the UDHR especially significant for Jewish people, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because Jewish history is shaped by persecution, making the protection of religious freedom particularly resonant for Jews.

title: Sedimentary Rocks and Environments of Deposition
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four clastic sedimentary rocks in order from coarsest to finest grain size.
cards.answer: Breccia / Conglomerate / Sandstone / Shale

cards.front: In the Carboniferous cyclothem, name the repeating sequence of beds from bottom to top.
cards.answer: Limestone / Shale / Sandstone / Seat earth (fossil soil) / Coal

cards.front: Why do well-rounded, frosted sandstone grains suggest a desert (aeolian) origin?
cards.answer: Grains are rounded and frosted by long transport and constant collisions carried by wind in a desert environment.

cards.front: Why does grain size in a graded bed fine from base to top?
cards.answer: A turbidity current drops its sediment load as it slows, so heaviest grains settle first and finer particles settle last.

title: Worship at Home and the Mandir
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four places where Hindus worship, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: the home shrine / the mandir (temple) / outdoors/natural shrines / the space of the heart

cards.front: Name the sequence of offerings made to the deity during puja.
cards.answer: water for washing / flowers / incense / food (prasad) / a flame / cloth

cards.front: Why do worshippers remove their shoes before entering a mandir?
cards.answer: As a sign of respect, signalling that they are entering sacred ground.

cards.front: How is puja understood as a 'sacred transaction' between worshipper and deity?
cards.answer: The devotee offers love and honour through offerings, and the deity offers blessing and presence in return.

title: Lanfranc and the Reform of the English Church
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three functions Lanfranc's Church reforms created or revived: synods, archdeacons and Church courts.
cards.answer: Revived regular synods / Developed the office of archdeacon / Separated Church courts from secular courts
items: Separated Church courts from secular courts

cards.front: Why did Lanfranc replace almost all Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans by 1080?
cards.answer: To put Norman voices in royal council, shire courts and coronations, giving political control alongside doctrinal reform.

cards.front: Why did the 1075 Council of London move sees like Sherborne and Selsey into towns?
cards.answer: Because bishops belonged where Norman castles, courts and markets were concentrated, not remote Anglo-Saxon religious sites.

cards.front: Why were the new Norman cathedrals politically significant as well as religious?
cards.answer: Their huge size and Romanesque style made Norman authority visible from miles away, like castles asserting conquest.

title: The road to war with Spain, 1569–87
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four strands the lesson identifies in the breakdown of Anglo-Spanish relations (1569–87).
cards.answer: Political – Mary's execution and rival claims to the throne / Religious – Protestant England versus Catholic Spain after 1570 / Commercial – privateering and clashes in the Atlantic / Military – English troops in the Netherlands from 1585 and the Cadiz raid in 1587
items: Political – Mary's execution and rival claims to the throne
Religious – Protestant England versus Catholic Spain after 1570
Commercial – privateering and clashes in the Atlantic
Military – English troops in the Netherlands from 1585 and the Cadiz raid in 1587

cards.front: What three reasons did the lesson give for Elizabeth worrying about a Spanish-controlled Netherlands?
cards.answer: It sat just across the Channel from Kent / Spanish armies there could ferry to England / Suppressing Protestantism there weakened her own position
items: It sat just across the Channel from Kent
Spanish armies there could ferry to England
Suppressing Protestantism there weakened her own position

cards.front: Why did the 1570 papal bull Regnans in Excelsis worsen Anglo-Spanish relations?
cards.answer: It excommunicated Elizabeth and absolved Catholics of allegiance to her, recasting any Catholic monarch's duty as removing her.

cards.front: Why did Mary, Queen of Scots' execution in February 1587 remove Philip's diplomatic restraint?
cards.answer: Mary had been Catholic Europe's legitimate alternative ruler, so her death removed Philip's remaining reason to hold back from war.

title: Warming Her Pearls — Carol Ann Duffy
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name the four other cluster poems the lesson compares with 'Warming Her Pearls'.
cards.answer: Looking at Your Hands (Martin Carter) / Poem for My Love (June Jordan) / Flirtation (Rita Dove) / The Perseverance (Raymond Antrobus)

cards.front: Which three short phrases from 'Warming Her Pearls' does the lesson suggest memorising for the exam?
cards.answer: Next to my own skin / my slow heat entering each pearl / I feel their absence and I burn
items: my slow heat entering each pearl
I feel their absence and I burn

cards.front: Why does the maid's desire in 'Warming Her Pearls' surface through her body rather than her words?
cards.answer: She has no socially acceptable language for what she feels, so desire is displaced onto objects and bodily sensation like warmth and blushing.

cards.front: How does the poem's final line depend on it being a dramatic monologue?
cards.answer: Staying entirely inside the maid's private voice lets Duffy reveal a confession she could never say aloud to her mistress.

cards.front: Name the five key themes of Macbeth summarised in the lesson.
cards.answer: Ambition / Appearance vs Reality / Guilt and Conscience / Kingship and Tyranny / Gender and Masculinity

cards.front: Name the five physical signs of guilt the lesson lists as evidence guilt cannot be suppressed.
cards.answer: The dagger hallucination / Sleeplessness ("Macbeth does murder sleep") / Blood Neptune's ocean cannot wash / Banquo's ghost / Lady Macbeth's obsessive hand-washing

cards.front: Why does Macbeth compare life to "a poor player" that "struts and frets his hour upon the stage"?
cards.answer: The theatre metaphor reduces life to a bad performance — brief, meaningless and forgotten — showing the spiritual cost of his crimes.

cards.front: Why is Malcolm's description of the Macbeths as "this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen" reductive?
cards.answer: It strips away Macbeth's complexity, agonised conscience and soliloquies, simplifying him into a villain to legitimise Malcolm's own claim to the throne.

cards.front: Name the four poems the lesson gives as comparison partners for The Perseverance.
cards.answer: Warming Her Pearls / Dusting the Phone / Morning Song / Love After Love

cards.front: Name the four short quotations the lesson says to have ready if The Perseverance is explored alone.
cards.answer: man overstanding / overstanding / serves / perseverance

cards.front: Why does the poem shift noticeably between its second and third stanzas?
cards.answer: It moves from steady description to something less certain, reflecting how the relationship resists a tidy resolution.

cards.front: Why does the word 'perseverance' appear in lowercase within the poem itself?
cards.answer: It presents perseverance not as a grand or heroic title but as an ordinary quality practised quietly, again and again.

cards.front: Name the four elements of the marketing mix a business may need to change when selling in a new country.
cards.answer: Product (reformulated for taste) / Price (repriced for incomes) / Place (distributed differently) / Promotion (different language/channels)

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why multinationals are attracted to a country.
cards.answer: Lower labour costs / Proximity to raw materials / Access to large consumer markets

cards.front: Why have some businesses reversed offshoring and reshored production closer to home?
cards.answer: Supply chain disruptions revealed the vulnerability of long global supply lines.

cards.front: Why do trade blocs create barriers for businesses in countries outside the bloc?
cards.answer: Trade blocs remove internal tariffs only between members, so non-member countries face higher barriers selling inside the bloc.

title: The Saar, Rearmament and the Stresa Front 1935
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four key episodes of 1935 in the order they happened.
cards.answer: Saar plebiscite (January) / Conscription and Luftwaffe announced (March) / Stresa Front formed (April) / Anglo-German Naval Agreement (June)

cards.front: Give the three reasons the Stresa Front looked like a strong deterrent on paper.
cards.answer: Britain had the largest navy in the world / France had the largest army in western Europe / Italy bordered Germany at the Brenner Pass
items: Britain had the largest navy in the world
France had the largest army in western Europe
Italy bordered Germany at the Brenner Pass

cards.front: Why did Britain agree to the Anglo-German Naval Agreement even though it undermined the Stresa Front?
cards.answer: Britain judged German rearmament was happening anyway, so it was more practical to cap it by treaty than let it run unrestricted.

cards.front: Why did bilateral diplomacy work in Hitler's favour in the 1930s?
cards.answer: It let deals be made quickly with a willing partner, presented as a compromise, bypassing League unanimity and cutting across collective Allied policy.

title: Using Data in Physical Activity and Sport
subject: physical-education-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five normative categories used to classify Cooper 12-minute run results for 16-year-old males, from lowest to highest.
cards.answer: Poor ( 2,800 m)

cards.front: What three things must be included when describing a trend from a graph or table?
cards.answer: State the trend / Quote a figure with units / State a conclusion

cards.front: Why is a decrease in time counted as an 'improvement' when calculating percentage change for a time-based fitness test?
cards.answer: For time-based tests a lower score is better, so a reduction in time represents an improvement in performance.

cards.front: Why should you read the full data set before drawing a conclusion about a single data point, such as a score drop in week 8?
cards.answer: A single drop might be caused by overtraining or illness rather than a genuine decline, so the whole data set gives proper context.

cards.front: Name the four factors that influence BMR.
cards.answer: Body size / Age / Sex / Hormones

cards.front: Name the five life stages nutritional needs change across.
cards.answer: Toddlers / Teenagers / Early adulthood / Middle adulthood / Late adulthood

cards.front: Why does a consistent positive energy balance lead to weight gain?
cards.answer: Eating more energy than is burned means the excess energy is stored in the body as adipose tissue.

cards.front: Why do protein needs stay high, or even rise slightly, in late adulthood even though energy needs fall?
cards.answer: To help maintain muscle mass and support immune function as activity and overall energy needs decrease.

cards.front: Name the three muscle roles the lesson says OCR requires for movement analysis.
cards.answer: Agonist / Antagonist / Fixator

cards.front: Why must every joint be controlled by at least two muscles working in opposite directions?
cards.answer: Muscles can only pull, not push, so an opposing muscle is needed to reverse or allow the movement.

cards.front: Why do the roles of the biceps and triceps reverse during elbow extension in a press-up?
cards.answer: The triceps becomes the agonist by contracting to extend the elbow, while the biceps becomes the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening.

cards.front: Why do muscle fibres contain lots of mitochondria?
cards.answer: Mitochondria produce ATP through aerobic respiration, supplying energy for sustained muscular contraction during exercise.

cards.front: Name Merton's five modes of adaptation to strain.
cards.answer: Conformity / Innovation / Ritualism / Retreatism / Rebellion

cards.front: Why does Merton's strain theory say working-class people are more likely to turn to crime?
cards.answer: They share the same success goals as everyone else but face greater structural barriers to legitimate means, creating strain to deviate.

cards.front: How does Cohen's status frustration explain non-instrumental crime like vandalism?
cards.answer: Boys who fail by mainstream standards form subcultures that invert mainstream values, gaining status and prestige rather than material reward.

cards.front: Why did Durkheim believe a society with no crime at all would be unhealthy?
cards.answer: It would have become so rigid and repressive that even minor non-conformity would be treated as a serious offence.

title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three uses of noble gases given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Helium in balloons and airships / Neon in advertising signs / Argon in light bulbs and welding
items: Argon in light bulbs and welding

cards.front: Name the three properties of transition metals given in the lesson that alkali metals do not typically share.
cards.answer: High melting points / High density / Coloured compounds and can be catalysts
items: Coloured compounds and can be catalysts

cards.front: How do sodium and water react to form sodium hydroxide?
cards.answer: Sodium reacts with water to produce sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

cards.front: Why did chemists arrange elements by atomic weight before atomic number was known?
cards.answer: Protons and neutrons had not yet been discovered, so atomic weight was the property used to order elements.

cards.front: Name the four types of factory-produced toys that became available in Victorian Britain.
cards.answer: Tin trains / Mechanical toys / Wooden building blocks / Porcelain dolls

cards.front: What four factors drove the shift from outdoor to indoor, screen-based children's leisure by the 2000s?
cards.answer: Technology / Rising parental anxiety / Traffic / The entertainment industry targeting children as consumers
items: The entertainment industry targeting children as consumers

cards.front: How did video games change the nature of children's play?
cards.answer: Play became more solitary and screen-based, and extended into adulthood in a way traditional toys did not.

cards.front: Why did the children's comics industry grow in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries?
cards.answer: It grew alongside mass literacy, as the 1870 Education Act brought compulsory schooling for all children.

title: Pressure Groups, Trade Unions and Civil Society
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the six tactics the lesson gives that pressure groups, unions and charities use to influence policy.
cards.answer: Writing to MPs and ministers / Presenting evidence to select committees / Organising demonstrations and marches / Running media campaigns / Using social media to mobilise supporters / Commissioning research to build evidence
items: Using social media to mobilise supporters

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says civil society organisations give citizens a voice.
cards.answer: Direct advocacy to MPs and ministers / Public campaigns to shape opinion / Evidence to parliamentary committees / Running services showing unmet need
items: Direct advocacy to MPs and ministers

cards.front: Why might having insider status limit a pressure group's influence, even though it gives access to government?
cards.answer: Formal access can mean the group compromises its goals in exchange for being included in consultation.

cards.front: Why can outsider pressure groups sometimes succeed in forcing government action despite lacking formal access?
cards.answer: A well-organised campaign with broad public support and media coverage can pressure a government to act.

cards.front: Name the three angels the lesson identifies as particularly significant in Islam, with their roles.
cards.answer: Jibril – angel of revelation / Mika'il – angel of sustenance and mercy / Izra'il – angel of death
items: Mika'il – angel of sustenance and mercy

cards.front: List the four stages in the sequence of Islamic eschatology after death.
cards.answer: Death and Barzakh / Resurrection / Judgement / Jannah or Jahannam

cards.front: Why does the angel Izra'il matter as a reminder to Muslims about death?
cards.answer: Because he takes the soul at the appointed moment, showing that death is controlled by Allah rather than by chance.

cards.front: How do most Sunni theologians reconcile Allah's foreknowledge with genuine human free will?
cards.answer: They teach that divine foreknowledge and genuine human free will coexist, though how this is possible remains a theological mystery.

cards.front: Name the three types of visitors Scrooge rejects in Stave 1.
cards.answer: His nephew Fred / Two charity collectors / Marley's ghost (warning him)

cards.front: Why does Dickens keep the office 'cold, bleak, biting' and give Cratchit only a tiny fire?
cards.answer: It shows Scrooge's miserliness causing real suffering to real people, not just atmosphere.

cards.front: Why does Dickens allude to Hamlet at the start of the novella?
cards.answer: Just as Shakespeare's audience must believe the old king is dead before his ghost appears, readers must accept Marley's death for the ghost's appearance to work.

cards.front: Why does Dickens make Scrooge such a repellent character by the end of Stave 1?
cards.answer: So the reader actively wants him to change, making his later redemption arc satisfying.

cards.front: Give the order of the 12 key metals (and reference elements) in the reactivity series, most to least reactive.
cards.answer: Potassium (K) / Sodium (Na) / Calcium (Ca) / Magnesium (Mg) / Aluminium (Al) / Carbon (C) / Zinc (Zn) / Iron (Fe) / Hydrogen (H) / Copper (Cu) / Silver (Ag) / Gold (Au)

cards.front: What two changes can you observe when iron is placed into copper sulfate solution?
cards.answer: Iron becomes coated with reddish-brown copper / Blue colour of the solution fades
items: Iron becomes coated with reddish-brown copper
Blue colour of the solution fades

cards.front: Why is limestone added to a blast furnace?
cards.answer: Limestone removes acidic impurities like silica by forming molten slag.

cards.front: How does bioleaching recover metal from the leachate produced by bacteria?
cards.answer: Scrap iron is added to the leachate to displace the less reactive metal, such as copper, from solution.

cards.front: Name the four types of strategy used to balance development and conservation in cold environments.
cards.answer: Technology / Governments / International agreements / Conservation groups

cards.front: Give the three reasons the lesson gives for the wilderness value of cold environments.
cards.answer: Scientific value / Aesthetic value / Ethical value

cards.front: Why is infrastructure so expensive to build and maintain in Svalbard's permafrost landscape?
cards.answer: Heat from buildings or pipelines melts permafrost ice, turning solid ground into unstable mud (thermokarst), causing subsidence and costly repairs.

cards.front: How does the 1920 Svalbard Treaty create tension between Norway's development goals and conservation?
cards.answer: It gives Norway sovereignty but grants all signatory nations equal commercial rights, so Norway cannot unilaterally end other nations' operations like Russian coal mining.

title: The CPU and Von Neumann Architecture
subject: computer-science-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five registers built into the CPU (not what they store, just their names).
cards.answer: Program Counter (PC) / Memory Address Register (MAR) / Memory Data Register (MDR) / Current Instruction Register (CIR) / Accumulator (ACC)

cards.front: Name the three levels of cache memory, from smallest/fastest to largest.
cards.answer: L1 cache / L2 cache / L3 cache

cards.front: Why does the CPU check cache before going to RAM?
cards.answer: Because accessing RAM takes far longer than accessing the CPU's own circuits, so cache stores frequently used data close by to cut waiting time.

cards.front: Why does a full RAM cause a computer to slow down significantly?
cards.answer: If RAM fills up, the operating system uses part of the slower secondary storage as virtual memory, causing a big performance drop.

cards.front: Name the five ethical guidelines the BPS requires for research.
cards.answer: Informed consent / Right to withdraw / Confidentiality / Protection from harm / Debrief

cards.front: Name the four ways researchers control extraneous variables, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Standardised procedures / Random allocation / Controlled settings / Matched pairs or repeated measures designs
items: Matched pairs or repeated measures designs

cards.front: How does a biased sample affect the external validity of a study?
cards.answer: A biased sample reduces external validity because it limits how well the results can generalise to the target population.

cards.front: Why is the debrief especially important when a study has used deception?
cards.answer: Because deception withheld the true purpose to prevent demand characteristics, so the debrief must fully explain this afterwards and allow withdrawal of data.

cards.front: Why does the discovery of Dunsey's skeleton force Godfrey to confess to Nancy?
cards.answer: The skeleton confirms Dunsey stole the gold and links the crime back to Godfrey's hidden past, forcing his secret marriage and Eppie's parentage into the open.

cards.front: How does Eliot use language differences to show the class divide between Eppie and Godfrey?
cards.answer: Eppie speaks in working-class dialect while Godfrey speaks formally and educatedly, showing her identity is rooted in her upbringing, not blood.

title: Planning and Evaluating a Citizenship Action
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the six stages of a citizenship action investigation, in order.
cards.answer: Decide the question or issue / Carry out initial research using primary and secondary sources / Plan the action / Take the action / Assess the impact / Evaluate the whole process
items: Carry out initial research using primary and secondary sources

cards.front: What five things should a good plan for a citizenship action include?
cards.answer: A clear aim / The method (what you will actually do) / Who you will work with / A realistic timeline and resources/permissions needed / How you will measure whether it worked
items: The method (what you will actually do)
A realistic timeline and resources/permissions needed
How you will measure whether it worked

cards.front: Why do strong citizenship investigations use both primary and secondary sources?
cards.answer: Primary sources show what those directly affected think and experience, while secondary sources provide context, background and comparison.

cards.front: Why does evaluating a citizenship action require honesty?
cards.answer: Because not all actions achieve their intended aim, and recognising this and explaining why is itself good citizenship thinking.

cards.front: Why is the Holocaust scene morally uncomfortable in The History Boys?
cards.answer: It exposes that Irwin's contrarian method produces smart answers on demand rather than genuine belief, applied to a subject that resists inversion.

cards.front: How does Bennett use the motorbike crash to deny the audience moral closure?
cards.answer: Hector's death freezes him as a beloved teacher, avoiding questions about prosecution, while Irwin survives diminished, preventing a clear judgement.

cards.front: Why does the Headmaster force Hector out once he discovers the abuse?
cards.answer: He exploits it as a pretext because he cannot measure the value of general studies, not out of concern for the boys.

cards.front: How does Irwin respond when Scripps challenges his relativism in the Holocaust lesson?
cards.answer: He avoids defending truth and instead tells them to distance themselves, saying 'this is history'.

cards.front: Name the three ways Roman culture reacted to powerful women, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Idealised women who exercised power invisibly / Feared women who sought visible political power / Demonised foreign women who wielded power on their own terms
items: Idealised women who exercised power invisibly
Feared women who sought visible political power
Demonised foreign women who wielded power on their own terms

cards.front: Name the three sources of power that made Cleopatra a formidable independent ruler.
cards.answer: A large army / Great wealth / Strategic control of Egypt's grain supply
items: Strategic control of Egypt's grain supply

cards.front: Why did Octavian present his war against Antony and Cleopatra as a war against a foreign queen rather than a civil war?
cards.answer: So he could present his victory as defending Rome against an alien threat, not admit it was a civil war between Roman generals.

cards.front: How did Agrippina the Younger allegedly secure her son Nero's succession, according to Tacitus?
cards.answer: By poisoning her husband Claudius to clear the way for Nero to become emperor.

cards.front: Name the five fields in the Car record example from the lesson.
cards.answer: make / model / reg / price / noOfDoors

cards.front: Name the seven string operations covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Length / Position / Substring / Concatenation / Character to character code / Character code to character / String conversion

cards.front: Why does POSITION("London", "n") return 2?
cards.answer: Because indexing starts at 0, so the first "n" is the third character, giving index 2.

cards.front: Why is RANDOM_INT(1, 6) useful for a dice simulator?
cards.answer: It generates an unpredictable value within the range 1 to 6 inclusive, matching a dice roll.

title: Sources of Data on Crime and the Dark Figure
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three types of crime the lesson gives as examples of invisible crime.
cards.answer: Domestic abuse / Environmental crime / White-collar and corporate crime in private settings
items: White-collar and corporate crime in private settings

cards.front: Name the two main reasons the lesson gives for why the dark figure of crime exists.
cards.answer: Crimes are not reported to police / Reported crimes are not always recorded
items: Crimes are not reported to police
Reported crimes are not always recorded

cards.front: Why does the Crime Survey for England and Wales usually record higher crime levels than police-recorded statistics?
cards.answer: It captures crimes experienced by victims even when they were never reported to the police.

cards.front: Why is environmental crime considered invisible crime?
cards.answer: It lacks obvious individual victims who can report it to the police.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why sorting matters.
cards.answer: Unlocks binary search / Makes data easier to present to users / Prerequisite for many other algorithms
items: Makes data easier to present to users

cards.front: Name the six features the lesson uses to compare bubble sort and merge sort.
cards.answer: Worst-case complexity / Strategy / Memory use / Ease of implementation / Performance on small lists / Performance on large lists

cards.front: Why does merge sort split a list all the way down until every sub-list has one item?
cards.answer: Because a single-item list is always sorted by definition, giving a guaranteed sorted starting point for merging.

cards.front: Why might bubble sort be preferred over merge sort when sorting a small list?
cards.answer: Bubble sort's performance is acceptable on small lists, whereas merge sort's splitting overhead may not be worth it.

cards.front: Name the four structures blood/urine pass through in order from the kidney to leaving the body (via the renal vein and ureter/bladder/urethra route).
cards.answer: Renal artery into kidney / Ureter to bladder / Bladder stores urine / Urethra expels urine

cards.front: Why do large molecules like proteins and red blood cells stay in the blood during ultrafiltration?
cards.answer: They are too big to pass through the capillary walls into the Bowman's capsule.

cards.front: How does dialysis fluid prevent useful substances like glucose being lost from the blood?
cards.answer: Dialysis fluid has the same concentration of glucose and mineral ions as normal blood, so none diffuses out.

cards.front: Why does drinking a lot of water lead to large volumes of dilute urine? (Higher tier)
cards.answer: Osmoreceptors detect diluted blood, less ADH is released, tubules become less permeable, so less water is reabsorbed.

cards.front: Name the three examples the lesson gives of long-lived data structures designed around the sorting trade-off.
cards.answer: Phone books / Dictionaries / Sorted database indexes

cards.front: Why does binary search stop working correctly if the list isn't sorted first?
cards.answer: Comparing the target to the midpoint gives no information about which half to discard, so the halving strategy breaks down entirely.

cards.front: Why does an array let binary search jump straight to the midpoint each time?
cards.answer: An array lets you read any index directly, so binary search can jump straight to any position in the data.

cards.front: Why does Claudio believe Don John's lie at the masked ball so easily?
cards.answer: His trust is fragile and built on surfaces, so one sentence from a known villain destroys it instantly.

cards.front: How does Benedick's failed love poem in Act 5 Scene 2 show his change?
cards.answer: He switches from prose to clumsy verse, comically but genuinely trying to express love in an unnatural language.

cards.front: Name the two parallel tracks of deception Shakespeare establishes by the end of Act 2.
cards.answer: Benign deceptions leading to love / Malicious deceptions leading to destruction

title: The Provisional Government and Dual Power
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four decisions that ruined the Provisional Government, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Continuing the war (the failed June Offensive) / Deferring land reform to the Constituent Assembly / Postponing Constituent Assembly elections / Arming the Bolsheviks during the Kornilov Revolt
items: Continuing the war (the failed June Offensive)
Deferring land reform to the Constituent Assembly
Arming the Bolsheviks during the Kornilov Revolt

cards.front: Why did the Kornilov Revolt collapse within days without a fight?
cards.answer: Railway and telegraph workers stalled his troop trains, his soldiers deserted, and the Petrograd Soviet's armed Red Guards were ready to defend the city.

cards.front: Why did Kerensky end up trusted by neither the left nor the right by autumn 1917?
cards.answer: He repressed the Bolsheviks after the July Days but then armed and released them during the Kornilov Revolt, constantly switching sides while trying to balance liberals and revolutionaries.

title: Context: Japan, North Korea and the Real Abductions
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four features the lesson gives describing Japan as the Cold War regional contrast to North Korea.
cards.answer: American ally / Functioning democracy / Rapidly expanding economy / Constitutionally pacifist

cards.front: Name the three features the lesson gives describing North Korea's political context in the late 1970s/early 1980s.
cards.answer: Tightly closed state / No diplomatic relations with Japan / Led by Kim Il-sung

cards.front: Why must a director avoid staging the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration scene as a happy ending?
cards.answer: Because the Declaration gave the family confirmation, not return - North Korea declared Megumi Yokota dead, a claim her family and government contested.

cards.front: Why does the audience's knowledge that the abductions really happened matter for how The Great Wave works as documentary theatre?
cards.answer: Because knowing the events actually happened amplifies the emotional impact beyond what a purely fictional story could achieve.

cards.front: Name the five family forms identified by sociologists as making up UK family diversity.
cards.answer: Nuclear family / Extended family / Reconstituted family / Lone parent family / Single sex family

cards.front: Name the five types of family diversity identified by the Rapoports.
cards.answer: Organisational diversity / Cultural diversity / Social class diversity / Life cycle diversity / Cohort diversity

cards.front: Why is it an overstatement to say the nuclear family is dying out in the UK?
cards.answer: ONS data shows the nuclear family remains the most common family form; other forms have simply grown in proportion alongside it.

cards.front: How did the kibbutz challenge the usual assumption about family life?
cards.answer: It shared property and child rearing collectively across the whole community, challenging the assumption that child rearing is always a private family function.

title: Marriage, Sexual Relationships and Family in Islam
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four purposes of marriage given for Islamic marriage.
cards.answer: Companionship and emotional fulfilment / Procreation / Strengthening the ummah / Channelling sexual desire within Allah's approved framework
items: Channelling sexual desire within Allah's approved framework

cards.front: Name the four schools of Sunni law that all agree mut'ah (temporary marriage) is forbidden.
cards.answer: Hanafi / Maliki / Shafi'i / Hanbali

cards.front: Why does Surah 4:3 limit a man to only one wife in some cases, despite permitting polygyny?
cards.answer: It states that if a man fears he cannot treat multiple wives justly, he should marry only one.

cards.front: Why is the extended family model traditionally preferred in Islamic teaching over the nuclear family?
cards.answer: It better reflects Islamic values of kinship solidarity, providing mutual support and ensuring elderly members are cared for within the family.

cards.front: Name the three steps used in systematic sampling.
cards.answer: Calculate the sampling interval k (population size ÷ sample size) / Choose a random start between 1 and k / Select every k-th member after that start
items: Calculate the sampling interval k (population size ÷ sample size)
Choose a random start between 1 and k
Select every k-th member after that start

cards.front: Name the three techniques the lesson gives for achieving random selection.
cards.answer: Assigning numbers and using a random number generator / Shuffling a pack of cards / Rolling dice
items: Assigning numbers and using a random number generator

cards.front: Why is quota sampling still susceptible to bias even though it matches population proportions?
cards.answer: Because selection within each quota is done by convenience rather than randomly, so it suffers the same biases as opportunity sampling.

cards.front: Why can a biased sample from opportunity or judgement sampling still be useful?
cards.answer: For exploratory research it gives a quick first look to identify variables worth studying, even though results may not represent the wider population.

cards.front: Name the three assessment objectives (AOs) tested by the Never Let Me Go exam question.
cards.answer: AO1 (your response) / AO2 (language, form and structure) / AO4 (spelling, punctuation and grammar)

cards.front: Name the three stages of a clone's fixed life path in the novel.
cards.answer: Childhood at an institution like Hailsham / A period as a carer / Their own donations until they complete
items: Childhood at an institution like Hailsham
Their own donations until they complete

cards.front: Why does Ishiguro's understated, restrained style make events like Tommy's death more powerful?
cards.answer: It forces the reader to supply the emotional response the narrator withholds, creating a gap between what is said and what is felt.

cards.front: Why is the clones' total lack of rebellion disturbing according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It shows people can be conditioned to accept even unjust fate, mirroring how oppressed groups internalise the values of those exploiting them.

cards.front: What four specific physical demands does Blackman's portrait of parenting focus on?
cards.answer: Nappies / Milk / Sleep deprivation / Managing a reactive but non-verbal ten-month-old
items: Managing a reactive but non-verbal ten-month-old

cards.front: Why is caring for Emma at ten months old especially hard for Dante?
cards.answer: She is old enough to have strong preferences and reactions but too young to communicate them in words.

cards.front: How does the novel's climax show masculine social expectations becoming lethal?
cards.answer: The dual-narration structure brings Dante's and Adam's storylines together in violence, showing the pressure of expectation turn deadly.

title: Business Ownership and Sources of Capital
subject: cambridge-nationals-enterprise-and-marketing

cards.front: Name the six sources of start-up capital the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Own savings / Friends and family / Loans / Crowdfunding / Grants / Business angels

cards.front: What four factors determine which source of capital an entrepreneur should choose?
cards.answer: How much capital is needed / How quickly it is needed / How much control they'll give up / What obligations come with the money
items: How much control they'll give up
What obligations come with the money

cards.front: Why do banks see sole traders as higher risk when lending?
cards.answer: Because sole traders have unlimited liability and limited access to finance, making banks less willing to lend.

cards.front: Why might one partner in a standard partnership be forced to pay a debt they had no involvement in creating?
cards.answer: Because standard partners share unlimited liability, so all partners are personally responsible for any debt any partner creates.

title: Dietary Laws and Rites of Passage
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: What four features make land animals, fish and birds kosher or not, according to the lesson?
