cards.answer: split hooves and chew the cud (land animals) / fins and scales (fish) / birds of prey forbidden, domestic birds permitted / all insects prohibited
items: split hooves and chew the cud (land animals)
birds of prey forbidden, domestic birds permitted

cards.front: Name the four steps in Jewish burial rites described in the lesson.
cards.answer: washing and purifying the body (tahara) / dressing in simple white shrouds / burial within 24 hours / seven-day mourning period (shiva)

cards.front: How does a shochet slaughter an animal to make it kosher?
cards.answer: A trained shochet uses a single, swift cut to the throat with a perfectly smooth blade to minimise suffering and ensure rapid blood loss.

cards.front: Why does Judaism insist on burial rather than cremation?
cards.answer: Out of respect for the body created in G-d's image and in anticipation of bodily resurrection.

cards.front: Name the three characters the lesson gives as examples of managing their public reputation in The Crucible.
cards.answer: Reverend Parris (as minister) / Danforth (as incorruptible judge) / Abigail (as chosen witness of God)

cards.front: How might a director use tableau to stage the moment Abigail points and accuses in Act 3?
cards.answer: Freeze the whole cast in a fixed image at the point of accusation, showing the court collapsing into one collective response rather than individuals.

cards.front: How might a lighting designer use colour contrast to stage the hypocrisy theme across court and private scenes?
cards.answer: Use cold blue-white light for court scenes to feel institutional and inhuman, and warm amber side-light for private moments to feel human.

cards.front: Why might a Brechtian director use direct address in the courtroom scenes of The Crucible?
cards.answer: To force the audience to recognise themselves as the jury of history rather than passively watching, keeping critical distance instead of emotional immersion.

title: Ideas of Englishness and Britishness over time
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson gives as evidence that Britishness was racialised despite Commonwealth citizens being legally British.
cards.answer: The 1958 riots / "No Coloured" signs in lodging houses / Enoch Powell's 1968 speech

cards.front: Name the three developments the lesson gives that changed Britain's political geography in the late 1990s.
cards.answer: Scottish Parliament with tax-varying powers / Welsh Assembly with secondary legislative powers / Good Friday Agreement power-sharing executive in Northern Ireland
items: Welsh Assembly with secondary legislative powers
Good Friday Agreement power-sharing executive in Northern Ireland

cards.front: Why did the arrival of Caribbean and South Asian migrants in the 1950s reveal a contradiction in British identity?
cards.answer: They were legally British Commonwealth citizens who had often served in WWII, but in practice found Britishness was racialised and exclusionary.

cards.front: Why was the Life in the UK test seen as controversial?
cards.answer: Critics noted many long-term British residents would fail it, suggesting it measured a particular version of Britishness rather than lived belonging.

title: Energy in Motion — Crumple Zones and Momentum
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the three vehicle safety features the lesson says work by increasing collision time (other than crumple zones).
cards.answer: Airbags / Seatbelts / Cycle helmets and padded sports equipment
items: Cycle helmets and padded sports equipment

cards.front: Why does braking distance increase with the square of speed?
cards.answer: Because kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, so more energy must be removed by braking as speed rises.

cards.front: Why do sudden braking forces on vehicle occupants become very large during a crash?
cards.answer: Large deceleration means large negative acceleration, and since F = ma, this produces a very large force.

cards.front: In the worked example where a 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s collides and sticks to a stationary 1 kg trolley, why does kinetic energy fall from 9 J to 6 J? (HT)
cards.answer: The 3 J difference converts to thermal energy and sound, even though momentum stays conserved.

cards.front: Name the four scales of production the lesson describes for polymer manufacturing.
cards.answer: One-off production / Batch production / Mass production / Continuous production

cards.front: Name the three thermosetting polymer products the lesson gives as examples sent to landfill or incineration at end of life.
cards.answer: Urea formaldehyde electrical fittings / Melamine worktops / Phenol formaldehyde saucepan handles

cards.front: Why is expanded polystyrene (EPS) rarely recycled?
cards.answer: Its low density makes transporting it for recycling uneconomical.

cards.front: Why does 'wish-cycling' harm the recycling system?
cards.answer: Putting non-recyclable items in the recycling bin causes entire batches of recyclate to be rejected.

title: The Making of a Roman Hero
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three things Latin writers repeatedly link heroism to.
cards.answer: Physical courage in the face of death / Willingness to sacrifice comfort or life for the state / A sign that the gods support the hero's cause
items: Physical courage in the face of death
Willingness to sacrifice comfort or life for the state
A sign that the gods support the hero's cause

cards.front: Why was delivering the Second Philippic so dangerous for Cicero?
cards.answer: Antony later allied with Octavian and Lepidus and put Cicero's name at the head of a list of enemies who could be killed on sight.

cards.front: Why does Livy mention the two soldiers who briefly stood with Horatius before he sent them away?
cards.answer: It shows they stayed only from shame, not orders, making Horatius's isolated stand against the whole enemy army seem even more remarkable.

title: The Battle of Hastings: Historic Environment 2027
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three divisions of William's army at Hastings, by nationality and position.
cards.answer: Bretons on the left / Normans in the centre / French and Flemish on the right
items: French and Flemish on the right

cards.front: Name the five battlefield features the lesson says you must pair with a consequence for the 16-mark question.
cards.answer: The crest / The marshy flanks / The slope / The low ground / The site's position astride the London road
items: The site's position astride the London road

cards.front: Why did William need to force a quick battle rather than wait through the winter?
cards.answer: His army risked disease and storm damage to his ships, and every week of delay let Harold gather more men.

cards.front: Why did the Battle of Hastings last from morning until dusk, unusually long for a medieval battle?
cards.answer: The ridge and marshy flanks let the shield wall hold, stopping Norman cavalry, archers and infantry combining effectively against it.

cards.front: The lesson gives four broad themes of rights covered by the UNCRC. Name all four.
cards.answer: Survival rights / Development rights / Protection rights / Participation rights

cards.front: According to the lesson, who do the Geneva Conventions protect?
cards.answer: Wounded and sick soldiers / Prisoners of war / Civilians in occupied territories

cards.front: Why did the Human Rights Act 1998 make it easier for UK citizens to challenge human rights violations?
cards.answer: Before 1998 citizens had to take cases all the way to the Strasbourg court, which was slow and expensive, but the Act allows cases to be heard in UK courts.

cards.front: Why do critics argue that international human rights agreements are not always effective?
cards.answer: They rely on states' willingness to comply, powerful states can resist enforcement, and the UN Security Council veto can block action against allies.

title: Juno: Tonal Comedy and the Indie Voice
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three techniques give Juno's dialogue its stylised, mannered quality?
cards.answer: Invented slang / Literary allusions / Comic hyperbole

cards.front: Why did Reitman rely on long, static-camera dialogue scenes rather than visual effects or music to carry Juno's emotional weight?
cards.answer: He trusted Cody's script, letting the writing do work that big-budget films would typically offload onto visual effects or music.

cards.front: Why does Reitman avoid reaction-shot close-ups in the Loring living-room first-meeting scene?
cards.answer: So the audience isn't pushed towards a predetermined emotional reading, letting them interpret the scene themselves, creating a non-judgemental feel.

title: The Nature of God and the Trinity
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four 'omni' attributes the lesson gives to describe God's nature.
cards.answer: Omnipotence / Omnibenevolence / Omniscience / Omnipresence

cards.front: Name the three persons of the Trinity the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Father / Son / Holy Spirit

cards.front: Why do Christians say humans have inherent dignity that cannot be taken away by poverty, failure or sin?
cards.answer: Because every person is made in the image of God (imago Dei), so all human life has inherent dignity.

cards.front: How does the Trinity provide a model for human relationships, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Since God exists as three persons in loving community, humans made in his image are fundamentally relational too.

title: Research Design, Sampling and Types of Data
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: What are the seven stages in the research design sequence, in order?
cards.answer: Aim / Hypothesis / Method choice / Sampling / Pilot study / Main data collection / Analysis

cards.front: Name the five main sampling methods described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Random sample / Systematic sample / Stratified sample / Quota sample / Snowball sample

cards.front: Why might a systematic sample introduce bias?
cards.answer: If the sampling frame has a repeating pattern at the same interval as the selection gap, that pattern skews who gets chosen.

cards.front: Why do interpretivists prefer qualitative data over quantitative data?
cards.answer: Because understanding social behaviour requires grasping the subjective meanings behind participants' actions, which numbers cannot capture.

cards.front: Name the four forms evangelism takes for Catholics in Britain today, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Inviting friends and neighbours to Mass / Running faith exploration courses like RCIA / Speaking openly about faith in workplaces and schools / Engaging in dialogue with people of other faiths
items: Inviting friends and neighbours to Mass
Running faith exploration courses like RCIA
Speaking openly about faith in workplaces and schools
Engaging in dialogue with people of other faiths

cards.front: Name the four things SVP members (Vincentians) do for the people they serve.
cards.answer: Visit people in homes, hospitals and care homes / Offer practical help like food, clothing and furniture / Befriend the lonely and isolated / Run projects for the homeless and unemployed
items: Visit people in homes, hospitals and care homes
Offer practical help like food, clothing and furniture
Run projects for the homeless and unemployed

cards.front: Why do Vincentians sit with the people they help rather than just delivering goods?
cards.answer: Because they treat each person as Christ, forming a personal relationship rather than simply distributing goods, grounded in Matthew 25:40.

cards.front: Why does Pax Christi see disarmament as a moral requirement rather than a political preference?
cards.answer: Because it flows from the sanctity of human life and Jesus's command to love one's enemy (Matthew 5:44).

cards.front: Name the four specific animals Clarke lists as victims of the Gulf oil spill in 'Lament'.
cards.answer: Green turtle / Cormorant / Dugong and dolphin / Whale

cards.front: How does the structure of 'Lament' widen as the poem progresses?
cards.answer: It moves from a single turtle, through named and unnamed people, to wider groups of animals and the whole scorched landscape.

cards.front: Why does Clarke name only the civilian Ahmed while leaving combatants unnamed in 'Lament'?
cards.answer: Giving one civilian a name while leaving soldiers, gunsmiths and armourers anonymous shifts sympathy toward those displaced rather than those fighting.

cards.front: Why does Clarke include figures like the 'boy fusilier' and 'farmer's sons' in the litany of 'Lament'?
cards.answer: They show war draws in the naive and unwilling for ordinary reasons, complicating who deserves blame.

cards.front: Name the seven main characters examined in this lesson on Coram Boy.
cards.answer: Meshak / Otis Gardiner / Alexander Ashbrook / Aaron / Melissa / Thomas Ledbury / Sir William Ashbrook

cards.front: Why does Thomas Ledbury's death during the rescue of Aaron and Toby matter to the novel?
cards.answer: It is one of the novel's most shocking moments, and his reliable decency throws the dysfunction of other characters into sharp relief.

cards.front: How does the pairing of Melissa and Mrs Lynch develop Gavin's themes?
cards.answer: Both are women caught in systems that exploit them, yet Melissa is a victim while Mrs Lynch is a willing accomplice, testing themes from multiple angles.

title: Explaining Depression: Genes and Cognitive Theory
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Why does having a negative attribution style make setbacks feel permanent and unavoidable?
cards.answer: It blames setbacks on internal, stable and global causes, so the person feels it's their fault, will always happen, and ruins everything.

cards.front: Why does twin study evidence suggest genes play a role in depression?
cards.answer: Identical twins, who share all their genes, are more likely to both develop depression than non-identical twins, who share only some genes.

cards.front: Why is Caspi et al. (2003) only correlational evidence rather than proof genes cause depression?
cards.answer: It only identifies a relationship between the gene, stress and depression, so it cannot prove the gene causes it.

title: Dawud, Maryam, Isa and the Mission of Muhammad
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four miracles the lesson says Isa performed.
cards.answer: Healing the blind / Healing the leper / Raising the dead / Breathing life into clay birds

cards.front: What three ways does the lesson say different Muslim communities today interpret 'calling to Islam'?
cards.answer: Personal moral example / Formal da'wah (invitation) / Social justice work as witness

cards.front: Why does the Qur'an say Dawud's victory over Jalut (Goliath) belonged to Allah, not to Dawud's own courage?
cards.answer: The verse says they were routed 'by Allah's leave', showing victory comes from Allah and Dawud was merely a willing instrument.

cards.front: Why is it significant that the infant Isa speaks from the cradle in Islamic tradition?
cards.answer: It shows that even as a newborn, Isa affirms he is a servant and prophet of Allah, not divine.

title: Formatting Output: .format, Alignment, Width and Precision
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four common mistakes with formatted output that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Too few values for placeholders raises IndexError / Forgetting the colon after the opening brace / Using type d on a real number / Expecting quotation marks to appear in printed output
items: Too few values for placeholders raises IndexError
Forgetting the colon after the opening brace
Using type d on a real number
Expecting quotation marks to appear in printed output

cards.front: Why does right-aligning a fixed-width numeric column keep the digits lined up under each other?
cards.answer: Right-aligning within a fixed width means every value ends at the same column, whatever the number of digits it has.

cards.front: Why is a format placeholder with .2f safer than round() for displaying money?
cards.answer: A .2f placeholder always shows exactly two digits, whereas round() does not force a trailing zero to appear.

cards.front: Name the three stages of morality in the stage theory of morality.
cards.answer: Pre-conventional morality / Conventional morality / Post-conventional morality

cards.front: Name the three areas of development that Willingham's strategies support.
cards.answer: Cognitive strategies / Physical strategies / Social strategies

cards.front: Why does Willingham think skills like critical thinking can't be taught separately from factual content?
cards.answer: Because thinking processes are always about something specific, so without factual knowledge in long-term memory there's nothing to apply thinking skills to.

cards.front: Why is Willingham's theory difficult to test scientifically?
cards.answer: Because practice and effort are difficult to measure precisely.

cards.front: What three actions in the lesson show Dunsey Cass's selfish, villainous nature?
cards.answer: Blackmails his brother Godfrey / Kills Godfrey's horse Wildfire in a drunken accident / Steals Silas's gold on impulse
items: Kills Godfrey's horse Wildfire in a drunken accident

cards.front: Why is Dunsey's death in the stone-pit described as an act of moral justice?
cards.answer: He falls into the quarry while carrying the stolen gold and isn't found for sixteen years, symbolising how greed destroys those who pursue it.

cards.front: How does Eliot use Eppie's hair to show the gold-to-child substitution?
cards.answer: Silas first mistakes Eppie's golden hair for his returned gold, then realises she is alive, marking the novel's turning point.

cards.front: Name the several factors the lesson gives for why Cabinet support for Thatcher collapsed so rapidly in 1990.
cards.answer: Poll Tax made Conservatives deeply unpopular / MPs in marginal seats feared losing seats / European question created ministers willing to act against her / Howe's speech made dissent respectable / individual consultations revealed private willingness for her to go
items: Poll Tax made Conservatives deeply unpopular
MPs in marginal seats feared losing seats
European question created ministers willing to act against her
individual consultations revealed private willingness for her to go

cards.front: Why did Geoffrey Howe's resignation speech accelerate Thatcher's political collapse?
cards.answer: It broke the convention of Cabinet loyalty, made dissent respectable, and directly prompted Heseltine's leadership challenge within days.

cards.front: Why did Thatcher decide not to contest the second ballot of the 1990 leadership election?
cards.answer: After consulting Cabinet ministers individually, she found most believed she could not win a second round.

cards.front: Why was the Community Charge widely seen as unfair?
cards.answer: It charged every adult the same flat amount regardless of income, so a wealthy owner paid the same as a low-paid worker.

cards.front: Name the four common rainforest sustainable management strategies given in the lesson.
cards.answer: National Parks / Agro-forestry / Selective logging / Ecotourism

cards.front: What are the three zones within Costa Rica's Tortuguero National Park?
cards.answer: Strict no-entry zone for nesting turtles / Buffer zone for guided tourism / Outer zone of low-impact farming
items: Strict no-entry zone for nesting turtles

cards.front: Why does keeping forest standing pay better than clearing it for cattle in Costa Rica?
cards.answer: A forest acre earns about US$300/year from ecotourism, compared with only US$60/year from cattle grazing.

cards.front: Why can National Parks fail to actually protect an ecosystem even though they exist on paper?
cards.answer: They can be 'paper parks' lacking enough rangers to enforce protection, letting illegal logging continue inside reserves.

cards.front: Name the seven main anti-hooliganism strategies the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: All-seater stadia / Segregation of fans / Alcohol restrictions / Early kick-offs / Improved security and CCTV / Banning orders / Education and campaigns

cards.front: Why do the home team win more often than the away team in football?
cards.answer: Players feed off crowd energy, officials may be subconsciously influenced, and away teams face the psychological burden of hostile noise.

cards.front: How does deliberate crowd hostility disrupt an away penalty-taker?
cards.answer: Abuse from the crowd is a form of deliberate psychological disruption designed to increase pressure and harm performance.

cards.front: Name the three early modern migrant groups that dominate England's history c1500–c1700.
cards.answer: Flemish and Walloon Protestant refugees from the 1560s / Huguenots fleeing France after 1685 / Africans documented in parish, court and household records
items: Flemish and Walloon Protestant refugees from the 1560s
Africans documented in parish, court and household records

cards.front: Name the three continuities the lesson gives between medieval and early modern migration to England.
cards.answer: The legal label of 'alien' survived from medieval England / The south-east remained the main entry route / Economic skills like weaving and finance drew migrants in
items: The legal label of 'alien' survived from medieval England
The south-east remained the main entry route
Economic skills like weaving and finance drew migrants in

cards.front: Why did Huguenot weavers in Spitalfields build tall houses with broad upper-floor windows?
cards.answer: To let in the light needed to work the patterned brocades and damasks they specialised in.

cards.front: Why did Sandwich's town authorities defend the Flemish and Walloon strangers' right to trade despite guild resentment?
cards.answer: Because the strangers generated customs revenue and tax for the town.

cards.front: Name the four negative human impacts on ecosystems given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Deforestation / Pollution (air and water) / Over-exploitation (overfishing/over-hunting) / Introduction of invasive species

cards.front: What three assumptions must hold for the capture-recapture method to give an accurate population estimate?
cards.answer: Marked individuals mix back into the population / Marking doesn't affect survival or behaviour / Population size stays stable (no births, deaths, immigration, emigration)
items: Marked individuals mix back into the population
Marking doesn't affect survival or behaviour
Population size stays stable (no births, deaths, immigration, emigration)

cards.front: Why does random quadrat sampling avoid bias?
cards.answer: Because the researcher does not choose where the quadrats are placed, so results aren't influenced by their choices.

cards.front: How does environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling detect species without seeing them?
cards.answer: Scientists collect water or soil samples and analyse DNA traces left behind by organisms to detect their presence.

cards.front: What four levels does the Inspector function on in the play?
cards.answer: A detective figure uncovering truth / A moral judge forcing confrontation with guilt / A mouthpiece for Priestley's socialist beliefs / A supernatural or symbolic presence
items: A moral judge forcing confrontation with guilt
A mouthpiece for Priestley's socialist beliefs

cards.front: Why does Priestley make Mrs Birling's rejection of Eva especially damning?
cards.answer: She chairs the Brumley Women's Charity Organisation, so the person meant to help the vulnerable is the one who turns Eva away.

cards.front: How does Eric's family environment contribute to his weakness?
cards.answer: His family values respectability over honesty, so he cannot be honest with his father when in trouble.

cards.front: Why is Birling's line about minding his own business important to Priestley's message?
cards.answer: It represents the capitalist creed of selfish individualism that Priestley wants to dismantle through the play.

cards.front: What are the four stages of Beatrice's character arc across the play?
cards.answer: Witty independence (Act 1) / Vulnerability in the gulling scene (Act 3) / Fury at Hero's shaming (Act 4, 'Kill Claudio') / Genuine love partnership with Benedick (Act 5)

cards.front: Name the five ways the lesson says the characters embody the play's themes.
cards.answer: Beatrice = wit as defence + genuine passion / Benedick = performed misogyny transformed by tested love / Claudio = conventional love's fragility / Hero = patriarchy's silencing of women / Don John = the danger of deception without conscience
items: Beatrice = wit as defence + genuine passion
Benedick = performed misogyny transformed by tested love
Don John = the danger of deception without conscience

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present Beatrice's scorn for love as a defence mechanism rather than a genuine belief?
cards.answer: An earlier exchange with Don Pedro shows she was hurt before, so she now uses scorn to protect herself.

cards.front: How does Claudio's story let Shakespeare criticise conventional Elizabethan courtship as a whole system?
cards.answer: Love based on appearance and arranged through intermediaries has no resilience, showing it's a failure of the social system, not just Claudio personally.

cards.front: Name the three social factors that shape collective behaviour in crowds.
cards.answer: Social loafing / Deindividuation / Culture

cards.front: How does social loafing dilute individual moral responsibility in a crowd?
cards.answer: In larger groups each person feels their contribution matters less, so no one feels personally accountable for the group's actions.

cards.front: How does culture affect collective behaviour in crowds?
cards.answer: Culture shapes learned norms and expectations for gatherings, affecting how orderly crowds are and how much people conform to the crowd.

cards.front: Name the 6 conditional tense endings used for -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
cards.answer: -ía / -ías / -ía / -íamos / -íais / -ían

cards.front: Name the 8 irregular verbs the lesson gives with irregular stems in the conditional tense.
cards.answer: tener / poder / querer / hacer / ir / ser / salir / poner

cards.front: How is the conditional tense formed for regular verbs like hablar, comer and vivir?
cards.answer: Add the endings -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían directly to the infinitive.

cards.front: How do irregular verbs like tener and poder change in the conditional tense?
cards.answer: They drop the -e- or -i- from the infinitive, sometimes adding -d-, before adding the normal conditional endings.

cards.front: Name the four trophic levels in a food chain, in order from base to top.
cards.answer: Producer / Primary consumer (herbivore) / Secondary consumer (carnivore) / Tertiary consumer (top predator)

cards.front: Name the three types of adaptations organisms can have, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Structural / Behavioural / Functional

cards.front: In the grass → rabbit → fox → eagle food chain, why does removing the fox reduce plant cover?
cards.answer: Without the fox, rabbit numbers increase, and the larger rabbit population over-grazes the grass, reducing plant cover.

cards.front: Why do predator and prey populations rise and fall in cycles in a stable ecosystem?
cards.answer: More prey lets predators increase, but this raises predation so prey fall, causing predators to fall too, letting prey recover again.

cards.front: Name the three concepts the lesson identifies about how family relationships have changed.
cards.answer: Child-centred families / Boomerang children / Sandwich generation

cards.front: Why did Parsons argue segregated conjugal roles were functionally efficient for modern industrial society?
cards.answer: Because paid work often required geographical mobility, so one partner needed to stay home and maintain it while the other moved for work.

cards.front: Why does Oakley argue the 'New Man' is more a cultural ideal than a sociological reality?
cards.answer: Because despite more men taking paternity leave, daily routine domestic tasks like cooking, cleaning and managing schedules still fall mainly on women.

cards.front: Why has the number of boomerang children increased in the UK?
cards.answer: High property prices mean many people in their twenties and thirties cannot afford to live independently, forcing them back to the parental home.

title: Types and Causes of Sports Injuries
subject: cambridge-nationals-sport-science

cards.front: Name the four types of acute skin damage covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Abrasions (grazes) / Cuts and lacerations / Contusions (bruises) / Blisters

cards.front: Why must a suspected fracture or dislocation not be manipulated in the field?
cards.answer: Because handling by non-experts risks further damage, so the injury must be immobilised and the athlete referred straight to emergency services.

cards.front: Why do contact sports like rugby union and American football have strict return-to-play protocols after concussion?
cards.answer: Because repeated concussive and sub-concussive blows are linked to Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy, so no athlete with suspected concussion should return in the same session.

title: Plot and Structure: Two-Act Working-Class Tragedy
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three life stages the two acts of Blood Brothers move through, with the ages the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Childhood (around age seven) / Adolescence (around age fourteen) / Adulthood (around age twenty-five)

cards.front: Name the four design choices the lesson suggests for staging the play's circular structure.
cards.answer: Single fixed platform re-dressed for each stage / Blood-red lighting wash repeated at start and end / Muted adult costumes vs bright child costumes / Toy gun for children vs real gun for adults
items: Single fixed platform re-dressed for each stage
Blood-red lighting wash repeated at start and end
Muted adult costumes vs bright child costumes
Toy gun for children vs real gun for adults

cards.front: Why does Russell have the Narrator use direct address rather than staying neutral?
cards.answer: It stops the audience being swept along emotionally, reminding them the story is about a social and political system, not just a personal one.

cards.front: How do performers physically show the twins are seven years old rather than twenty-five?
cards.answer: As children they use a lower centre of gravity, exaggerated limb co-ordination and impulsive energy; as adults their weight feels heavier and speech slower.

cards.front: Name the five components of fitness tested by speed, power, agility, balance and reaction time tests, along with their test names.
cards.answer: Speed - 30-metre sprint / Power - vertical jump/Sargent jump / Agility - Illinois agility run / Balance - stork stand / Reaction time - ruler drop test

cards.front: Why is the one-rep max test hard to standardise safely?
cards.answer: The participant must lift to their absolute maximum, raising injury risk, and testers may judge 'full range of motion' differently.

cards.front: Why can the ruler drop test give a falsely fast reaction time score?
cards.answer: If the tester gives a visual cue like a finger movement before releasing, the participant reacts to the cue rather than the drop.

cards.front: Why must testing conditions be standardised before comparing results to normative data tables?
cards.answer: Any change in warm-up, equipment, time of day or examiner technique threatens reliability, which then makes the comparison invalid.

cards.front: Name the four musical elements the lesson says composers manipulate to build character and tension.
cards.answer: Instrumentation / Dynamics / Harmony / Rhythm

cards.front: What quick test does the lesson give for telling if music in a film is source (diegetic) music?
cards.answer: Character on screen could hear it / Character might react to it / e.g. dancing to it / e.g. turning down a radio
items: Character on screen could hear it

cards.front: Why does a gradual crescendo build tension before a climax or jump scare?
cards.answer: It controls dynamics directly, building anticipation as the sound gets louder towards the dramatic moment.

cards.front: How does the minor key and heavy brass in the Imperial March create a sense of menace?
cards.answer: The minor key, heavy low brass, simple repeated rhythmic motif and loud dynamic combine to represent power and menace.

cards.front: Name the four 'Enemies' on Jeanette's mother's list.
cards.answer: The Devil (in his many forms) / Next Door / Sex (in its many forms) / Slugs

cards.front: How does Winterson's deadpan delivery turn Jeanette's deafness into black comedy?
cards.answer: The whole church decides the silent child is in a state of rapture and agrees nobody should speak to her, masking genuine neglect as comedy.

cards.front: Why does fire imagery carry contradictory meaning in the novel?
cards.answer: Fire represents both the mother's passionate faith and the church's destructive judgment, seen in hellfire sermons and the Holy Spirit's 'burning'.

cards.front: Why does Winterson describe Jeanette's love for Melanie in physical terms?
cards.answer: She insists on the body's validity, making love real and immediate rather than abstract, against the church's view of the body as sinful.

cards.front: Name the three items Scrooge's servants stole from him and sold to Old Joe.
cards.answer: Bed curtains / his shirt / buttons from his coat

cards.front: Name the three emotions the lesson says match Scrooge's journey through the Past, Present and Yet to Come ghosts.
cards.answer: Nostalgia (Past) / guilt (Present) / terror (Yet to Come)

cards.front: How does the silence of the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come affect Scrooge and the reader?
cards.answer: Its silence forces Scrooge and the reader to interpret the visions themselves, making the experience more psychologically intense.

cards.front: Why does Dickens juxtapose Scrooge's unmourned death with Tiny Tim's death?
cards.answer: To show wealth without compassion leads to spiritual death, while love and generosity even in poverty create a meaningful life.

title: Civil Wars in England, Scotland and Ireland 1642-1651
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four ways ordinary communities were burdened during the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.
cards.answer: Sieges / Requisitioning / Heavy taxation / Quartering of soldiers

cards.front: How did the Scottish Bishops' Wars lead directly to the English Civil War?
cards.answer: Charles I's prayer book triggered war with Scotland, forcing him to recall Parliament, which then challenged his power and caused the English conflict.

cards.front: Why was the New Model Army's cavalry discipline decisive at Naseby?
cards.answer: It was trained to maintain formation after charging instead of galloping off to plunder like earlier Parliamentary horse.

cards.front: Why did Colonel Pride's soldiers exclude Presbyterian MPs from Parliament in December 1648?
cards.answer: Army leaders were convinced Charles would never accept a lasting settlement, so they purged MPs likely to negotiate with him, leaving the Rump Parliament to try him.

cards.front: Name the four examples of duality Stevenson uses beyond Jekyll himself.
cards.answer: London divided into wealthy squares and slums / Jekyll's house has a grand front and sinister back / The novella's structure is split between investigation and confession / Minor characters like Utterson and Enfield lead double lives
items: London divided into wealthy squares and slums
Jekyll's house has a grand front and sinister back
The novella's structure is split between investigation and confession
Minor characters like Utterson and Enfield lead double lives

cards.front: Name the four secrets kept by major characters in the novella.
cards.answer: Jekyll hides his experiment / Lanyon seals his letter / Utterson refuses to speak about the window incident / Enfield agrees never to discuss the trampling
items: Utterson refuses to speak about the window incident
Enfield agrees never to discuss the trampling

cards.front: Why does Hyde's violence escalate as the novella progresses?
cards.answer: Repression stores up dangerous urges instead of removing them, and each indulgence intensifies rather than satisfies Hyde's desires, causing escalating violence.

cards.front: Why is Lanyon destroyed even though he never carries out an experiment himself?
cards.answer: He is destroyed simply by witnessing Jekyll's transgression, showing there is no safe position in the science-versus-morality debate.

cards.front: According to the lesson, what are the five qualities of a strong analysis response?
cards.answer: Clear thematic statement in the opening line / 2-3 quotations analysed in depth / At least one structural observation / A personal response beyond generic statements / A coherent argument that develops throughout
items: Clear thematic statement in the opening line
A personal response beyond generic statements
A coherent argument that develops throughout

cards.front: What are the five self-assessment questions to ask after writing a practice response?
cards.answer: Did I state the theme clearly? / Did I analyse language and structure? / Did I explain effects, not just name techniques? / Did I compare methods where required? / Did I stay within my target time?
items: Did I state the theme clearly?
Did I analyse language and structure?
Did I explain effects, not just name techniques?
Did I compare methods where required?
Did I stay within my target time?

cards.front: Why should you read a second poem 'through the lens' of the first when comparing?
cards.answer: Because the poems are chosen for comparison because they connect, so your job is to find that connection and show how each poet approaches it differently.

cards.front: How does a strong comparison response explain the difference between two poems on the same theme?
cards.answer: It explains how the same theme is treated differently because the poets use different methods.

cards.front: Name the four interconnected reasons the lesson gives for why the Spanish Armada failed.
cards.answer: English ship design and gunnery / Failure of the plan to join with Parma / English fireships at Calais / Storms that scattered the fleet
items: Failure of the plan to join with Parma

cards.front: Name the three Channel skirmishes fought between the English and Spanish fleets from 31 July to 6 August 1588.
cards.answer: Plymouth, 31 July / Portland Bill, 2 August / Isle of Wight, 3-4 August

cards.front: Why couldn't the Armada wait safely off the Flemish coast for Parma's barges to be ready?
cards.answer: There was no deep-water port on the Flemish coast where the large Spanish galleons could shelter while waiting.

cards.front: How did the English fleet's tactics avoid letting Spain force a close-quarters fight?
cards.answer: They used longer-range gunfire to fight at a distance, harassed the formation, and attacked from the rear using the wind.

title: Network Security and the TCP/IP Model
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four network security methods described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Authentication / Encryption / Firewalls / MAC address filtering

cards.front: How does TCP ensure data arrives correctly at the Transport layer?
cards.answer: It breaks data into packets, numbers them, checks they all arrive, and requests any lost packet again.

cards.front: Why do layered security measures give stronger protection than one measure alone?
cards.answer: Each layer compensates for the weaknesses of the others, e.g. a firewall can't stop an attacker with valid credentials but authentication can.

title: Columbus Reaches the Americas: Tainos, Caribs and La Navidad
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says the Tainos lacked compared to Europeans.
cards.answer: No iron tools or weapons / No horses / No wheels / No immunity to European diseases

cards.front: Name the four crops the Tainos farmed.
cards.answer: Cassava / Sweet potato / Maize / Tobacco

cards.front: Why did Columbus build La Navidad at that particular spot on Hispaniola?
cards.answer: The Santa María wrecked there on Christmas Eve 1492, and Columbus saw this as providence, using its timbers to build a fort.

cards.front: Why did the trade of gold ornaments for European trinkets bewilder the Spanish?
cards.answer: The Spanish did not realise how rare and ritually valuable items like hawk's bells, beads and cloth were to Taino communities.

title: The Covenant and Jewish Moral Principles
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five commandments of the Decalogue that Jews class as duties to the Almighty.
cards.answer: I am the Lord your God / No other gods or idols / No misuse of the divine name / Keep Shabbat / Honour your father and mother
items: I am the Lord your God
No misuse of the divine name

cards.front: Name the five commandments of the Decalogue that Jews class as duties to other people.
cards.answer: No murder / No adultery / No theft / No false testimony / No coveting

cards.front: How does Orthodox Judaism's application of Pikuach Nefesh differ from Reform Judaism's?
cards.answer: Orthodox applies it strictly, only when there is a genuine immediate threat to life, whereas Reform applies it more broadly, including to mental health.

cards.front: How does free will make obedience to the Mitzvot meaningful in Jewish theology?
cards.answer: The Almighty does not compel obedience, so humans can choose righteousness or sin, making obedience meaningful and disobedience culpable.

title: Exoplanets, Habitable Zones and the Search for Life
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three Solar System moons the lesson gives as potential life candidates.
cards.answer: Europa / Enceladus / Titan

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson states astrometry and radial velocity together can determine about a planet.
cards.answer: Minimum mass (radial velocity) / True mass (astrometry) / Full 3D orbit (astrometry)

cards.front: Why does the radial velocity method only give a planet's minimum mass rather than its true mass?
cards.answer: It measures the star's wobble along our line of sight, so it cannot directly determine the planet's radius or true mass.

cards.front: Why do red dwarf stars have habitable zones located very close to the star?
cards.answer: Because red dwarfs are cooler and less luminous, so the zone where liquid water can exist lies much nearer to the star.

title: The Five Year Plans and Soviet Society
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What were the three core aims Stalin set out for industrialisation?
cards.answer: Build heavy industry / Achieve autarky / Prepare for war

cards.front: Name the three ways Soviet workers' lives were controlled or made harsher under the Plans.
cards.answer: Lateness over 20 minutes criminalised / Internal passports restricted movement / Wages tied to output via piece-rates
items: Wages tied to output via piece-rates

cards.front: Why is the Stakhanov coal-cutting record described as 'engineered' rather than a fair record?
cards.answer: He had teams clearing the coal away for him, making the output look like one man's work.

cards.front: Why do historians say the Five Year Plans were a triumph of headline numbers but a failure of living standards?
cards.answer: Tonnage and output soared, but quality was poor, quotas were falsified, and consumer goods stayed scarce throughout the 1930s.

cards.front: Name the four functions of political parties in a democracy given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Give voters clear policy choices / Recruit and train politicians / Organise debate in Parliament / Provide an organised Opposition

cards.front: Name the two main policies Reform UK has campaigned on, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Lower taxes / Stricter immigration controls

cards.front: Why do left-wing and right-wing parties disagree on economic policy?
cards.answer: Left-wing parties favour state intervention and redistribution while right-wing parties favour free markets, lower taxes and personal responsibility.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say political parties and pressure groups are the same thing?
cards.answer: Parties field candidates and seek to win elections and govern, while pressure groups try to influence government without seeking power themselves.

title: Modern policing: specialisation, technology and community
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three main ways British police forces responded to new challenges in the twentieth century.
cards.answer: New technologies / Specialist units / Community-based approaches (from the 1980s)

cards.front: Name the three specialist police units named in the lesson, with the years they were set up.
cards.answer: Special Branch (1883) / Flying Squad (1919) / Serious Fraud Office (1987)

cards.front: Why did the introduction of the 999 system change public expectations of policing?
cards.answer: It seemed revolutionary at the time, creating a lasting public assumption that police would respond rapidly to calls.

cards.front: Why did Neighbourhood Watch schemes work best in stable, owner-occupied suburban areas?
cards.answer: Residents knew each other well, making it easier to recognise strangers and cooperate, unlike transient high-turnover urban areas.

cards.front: Name the three pieces of Greek hoplite equipment shown on the Triptolemos Painter kylix.
cards.answer: Round shield / Spear / Close-fitting helmet

cards.front: Name the three items of eastern dress shown on the Persian figure on the Triptolemos Painter kylix.
cards.answer: Sleeved tunic / Trousers / Soft Phrygian cap

cards.front: Why did the Athenian army march straight back to Athens after winning at Marathon?
cards.answer: The Persian fleet was sailing round the coast to attack Athens, so they had to man the walls before it arrived.

cards.front: How did the Athenian wings defeat the Persian centre after it had pushed back the weakened Greek middle?
cards.answer: The victorious wings wheeled inward and attacked the Persian centre from both sides, causing it to collapse.

cards.front: Name the five main poetic forms found across the Conflict anthology.
cards.answer: Ballad / Dramatic monologue / Free verse / Blank verse / Song/chant

cards.front: Name the three poems in the Conflict anthology written in free verse.
cards.answer: Belfast Confetti / Poppies / War Photographer

cards.front: Why does Tennyson use a modified ballad form with a driving dactylic rhythm in The Charge of the Light Brigade?
cards.answer: To create the energy and momentum of a cavalry charge.

cards.front: Why does Wordsworth choose blank verse for The Prelude extract?
cards.answer: Unrhymed iambic pentameter creates a continuous, elevated tone suited to the sublime encounter with nature.

title: Context: Blackman, Cooke and the Politics of Adaptation
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: What are the three key decisions Cooke made as adaptor of Noughts & Crosses?
cards.answer: Compress the sprawling narrative into a tight two-act structure / Foreground the dual-narrator device as the play's central formal innovation / Specify projection, soundscape and minimal staging instead of a naturalistic set
items: Compress the sprawling narrative into a tight two-act structure
Foreground the dual-narrator device as the play's central formal innovation
Specify projection, soundscape and minimal staging instead of a naturalistic set

cards.front: Why did Cooke's choice of a thrust stage suit the play's direct-address narration?
cards.answer: It gave the sections where Sephy and Callum step forward to speak to the audience a physical intimacy a proscenium stage might not achieve.

cards.front: Why does the play use speculative fiction rather than a real historical setting to explore racial injustice?
cards.answer: Setting it in an alternate world creates distance from one specific historical injustice, letting the play speak to multiple contexts and inviting audiences to notice the mapping onto their own world.

cards.front: The lesson names four things good design must balance. What are they?
cards.answer: How it looks / How it works / What it is made of / How much it costs to make
items: How much it costs to make

cards.front: At the decline stage, what three options does a business have for the product?
cards.answer: Refresh it one more time / Sell it off at a discount / Withdraw it and redirect resources
items: Sell it off at a discount

cards.front: Why has Cadbury's Dairy Milk stayed in maturity instead of declining since 1905?
cards.answer: Constant refreshes like Fruit & Nut, Caramel and Oreo versions have repeatedly pulled it back from the edge of decline.

cards.front: Why did Blockbuster Video decline into closure by 2013?
cards.answer: It could not refresh its DVD rental product to compete once streaming became available.

title: Anti-Slavery, Anti-Corn Law, and Reform Campaigners, c1780-1846
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: The lesson gives four things anti-slavery and the Anti-Corn Law League had in common. What are they?
cards.answer: Organised outside Parliament / Used mass petitioning / Relied on lecturers and pamphlets / Framed their case as moral even when economic interests were at stake
items: Framed their case as moral even when economic interests were at stake

cards.front: What three factors does the lesson add to explain how pressure groups won change without the vote?
cards.answer: Religion / Communication / The role of the individual

cards.front: Why did Robert Peel finally push through repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846?
cards.answer: The Irish Famine of 1845-46 raised the political cost of high bread prices to breaking point, forcing Peel to split his party and repeal them.

cards.front: How did Chadwick's 1842 report change the debate on public health?
cards.answer: It showed disease in industrial cities cost more in lost labour than sanitation would cost, changing the terms of debate.

cards.front: Name the four stages in the sequence from 1950 redistribution to 1956 collective ownership.
cards.answer: 1950 redistribution to poor peasants / 1951–52 voluntary Mutual Aid Teams / 1953–54 lower-stage cooperatives / 1955–56 higher-stage cooperatives

cards.front: Why did Mao accelerate cooperation with his 1955 'Socialist High Tide' speech?
cards.answer: He believed the masses were ready, feared a return of rich-peasant power, and wanted higher grain output for industry.

cards.front: How did land reform bind peasants to the CCP through more than just receiving land?
cards.answer: Speak bitterness meetings made peasants denounce and often help kill landlords, creating shared guilt as well as shared gain.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says De Waal presents Maureen.
cards.answer: Sensory language / Cultural identity / Patience / Limitations

cards.front: Name the three behaviours Leon shows in Part 2 of My Name is Leon.
cards.answer: Stealing / Lying / Occasional violence

cards.front: Why does the restrained, careful way Leon is told about the separation make the scene more devastating?
cards.answer: Because Leon's silence and confusion speak louder than tears would, so the calm, restrained language makes it more devastating.

cards.front: How does De Waal use the missed and dwindling contact visits structurally in My Name is Leon?
cards.answer: As contact fades the reader feels Leon's grip on his family loosening, showing the system erasing the sibling bond through process, not cruelty.

cards.front: Name the six key characteristics of embedded systems given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dedicated function / Real-time operation / Low power consumption / Low cost / High reliability / Compact size

cards.front: Name the three safety-critical embedded system examples the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Pacemakers / Anti-lock braking systems (ABS) / Fly-by-wire flight control systems

cards.front: Why must a car's ABS release the brakes within milliseconds of detecting wheel lock-up?
cards.answer: Because any longer and the response would be too late to prevent a skid, so it fails to do its job.

cards.front: Why are embedded chips built as a System on a Chip (SoC) rather than spread across a motherboard?
cards.answer: Because embedded systems must fit inside small host devices, so their components are integrated onto a single chip.

title: Early Models of the Solar System
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three astronomical distance units the lesson describes for measuring different scales of space.
cards.answer: Astronomical unit (AU) / Light-year (l.y.) / Parsec (pc)

cards.front: What three reasons does the lesson give for why the geocentric model survived for about 1,400 years?
cards.answer: It was mathematically sophisticated and matched observations / It had philosophical authority from Aristotle / Stellar parallax was too small to detect, seeming to support it
items: It was mathematically sophisticated and matched observations
It had philosophical authority from Aristotle
Stellar parallax was too small to detect, seeming to support it

cards.front: Why does the position of the north celestial pole shift over thousands of years?
cards.answer: Because of precession, the slow wobble of Earth's rotation axis over a 26,000-year cycle, which makes the pole migrate around the sky.

cards.front: Why do calendars based on lunar months need extra months added periodically (intercalation)?
cards.answer: Because the lunar month (about 29.5 days) doesn't divide evenly into the solar year (about 365.25 days), so extra months keep the calendar aligned with the seasons.

title: Case Study: A Dynamic UK City (Birmingham)
subject: geography-edexcel-b

cards.front: Name the four zones in Birmingham's urban structure, from centre outwards.
cards.answer: CBD / Inner city / Suburbs / Urban-rural fringe

cards.front: What three migrant groups does the lesson identify as shaping Birmingham's population since 1948?
cards.answer: Caribbean families from 1948 / South Asian families from the 1960s / EU migrants after 2004

cards.front: Why do land values fall so sharply from Birmingham's CBD to its suburbs?
cards.answer: Retail and business demand for space is highest in the centre, so competition pushes rents and land values down with distance from the CBD.

cards.front: How did the closure of factories in Birmingham's inner city help cause inequality with the suburbs?
cards.answer: Factory closures like Longbridge removed most jobs from the inner ring, while suburbs gained new jobs from car-friendly retail and tech parks.

title: The Nature of Allah, Tawhid and the Qur'an
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three dimensions of tawhid in Islamic theology.
cards.answer: Tawhid al-rububiyya (oneness of lordship) / Tawhid al-uluhiyya (oneness of right to worship) / Tawhid al-asma wa-l-sifat (oneness of names and attributes)
items: Tawhid al-uluhiyya (oneness of right to worship)
Tawhid al-asma wa-l-sifat (oneness of names and attributes)

cards.front: Name four occasions when the Shahadah is spoken, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Whispered to a newborn at birth / Recited in the call to prayer / Spoken by converts entering Islam / Ideally the last words before death
items: Whispered to a newborn at birth
Recited in the call to prayer
Ideally the last words before death

cards.front: Why does Islamic art favour calligraphy and geometric patterns instead of figurative images?
cards.answer: Because the prohibition on images, rooted in tawhid, stops any object being associated with Allah, guarding against shirk.

cards.front: Why is shirk considered the most serious sin in Islam?
cards.answer: Because it directly violates tawhid and is the one sin the Qur'an indicates cannot be forgiven if not repented.

title: A Major UK City: Site, Structure & Functions
subject: geography-edexcel-a

cards.front: Name the four concentric zones of urban structure in Birmingham.
cards.answer: Central Business District (CBD) / Inner city / Suburbs / Urban-rural fringe

cards.front: Name the four layers of Birmingham's connectivity.
cards.answer: Road / Rail / Air / Digital

cards.front: How did Birmingham's location and resources make it the natural hub of the Industrial Revolution's metalworking trade?
cards.answer: Its central location, nearby coalfields and a canal network linking it to the Mersey, Severn and Thames made it the natural hub.

cards.front: Why does Birmingham's CBD contain both the oldest historic buildings and the newest skyscrapers?
cards.answer: Because central land is recycled most aggressively, so old buildings get replaced with new skyscrapers over time.

title: Context: Liverpool, Thatcher and the Working-Class Musical
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three Thatcherite economic policies described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Reduction of state support for industry / Weakening of trade union power / Emphasis on individual aspiration over collective provision
items: Reduction of state support for industry
Emphasis on individual aspiration over collective provision

cards.front: Name the four things that make up Mickey's downfall in the play's final act, coherent with the Thatcherite context.
cards.answer: Unemployment / Depression / Bank robbery driven by financial desperation / Imprisonment
items: Bank robbery driven by financial desperation

cards.front: Why does the same event of factory closures affect Mickey and Edward so differently?
cards.answer: Mickey's working-class upbringing exposes him to the economic collapse, while Edward's middle-class education and university path insulate him from it.

cards.front: Why might a lighting designer shift from warm tungsten tones to cooler, harsher lighting across a production of Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: To use colour temperature as a visual metaphor for the worsening political and economic climate of the 1980s.

title: From Wall Street Crash to Depression America
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four main causes the lesson gives for the Depression slump.
cards.answer: Over-production by industry / Under-consumption from 1920s inequality / Speculation on the stock market / Bank failures

cards.front: Name the four Depression-era nicknames or terms the lesson gives for poverty and Hoover-blaming.
cards.answer: Hoovervilles / Hoover blankets / Hoover flags / Okies

cards.front: Why did falling share prices in 1929 lead to a spiral of factory layoffs?
cards.answer: When share-buyers stopped spending, factories cut production and laid off workers, so unemployed workers stopped buying and more factories cut production.

cards.front: Why was 1929's stock market crash able to drag down the whole economy rather than staying contained?
cards.answer: Most Americans had little spare cash due to inequality, and over-production, bank failures and the Hawley-Smoot Tariff all multiplied the damage.

cards.front: Name the four ways German school life differs from the UK, according to the lesson's Kulturzone section.
cards.answer: No school uniform / Classes last 45 minutes / Pupils stay in same room, teachers move / Must repeat year if you fail two subjects
items: Pupils stay in same room, teachers move
Must repeat year if you fail two subjects

cards.front: Why does 'halb sechs' mean 5:30 and not 6:30 in German?
cards.answer: Because halb means 'half to' the next hour, not 'half past', so it counts down to six.

cards.front: Why does the verb come straight after 'Montags' in 'Montags habe ich Englisch'?
cards.answer: Because German follows the verb-second rule, so the verb stays in position 2 even when a time phrase starts the sentence.

cards.front: Why do 'du' and 'er/sie' forms of finden add an extra e, as in 'du findest'?
cards.answer: Because finden's stem ends in -d, so an extra e is added before the ending.

title: The Four Yogas, Pilgrimage and Hindu Charities
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four sites of India's Char Dham pilgrimage circuit.
cards.answer: Badrinath / Dwarka / Puri / Rameshwaram

cards.front: Name the four sacred river sites where the Kumbh Mela is held.
cards.answer: Prayagraj (Allahabad) / Haridwar / Nashik / Ujjain

cards.front: How does the jnana yoga technique of 'neti, neti' work to reveal Brahman?
cards.answer: It systematically negates everything that is not Brahman, until only Brahman remains, showing atman and Brahman are one.

cards.front: Why is bathing at the sacred confluence during the Kumbh Mela believed to be spiritually beneficial?
cards.answer: Bathing there at the auspicious time is believed to wash away all sin and help the atman's journey towards liberation.

cards.front: The lesson names four types of imagery pattern used across the Relationships poems. What are they?
cards.answer: Pathetic fallacy / Sensory imagery / Domestic imagery / Natural imagery

cards.front: Why does the enjambment in 'My Last Duchess' disguise the rhyme of the heroic couplets?
cards.answer: It makes the speech sound natural while keeping poetic control, mirroring the Duke's smooth exterior hiding his violent interior.

cards.front: Why does the shortened fourth line in each stanza of 'La Belle Dame Sans Merci' matter?
cards.answer: It creates a halting, incomplete rhythm that mirrors the knight's interrupted happiness.

cards.front: Name the four ways a plant uses the glucose it makes in photosynthesis.
cards.answer: Respiration for energy / Starch storage / Cellulose for cell walls / Amino acids and proteins

cards.front: Why does the rate of photosynthesis increase as temperature rises, up to the optimum?
cards.answer: Enzyme and substrate molecules move faster, increasing their collision rate and so speeding up the reaction.

cards.front: Why do leaves appear green?
cards.answer: Chlorophyll mainly absorbs red and blue light, so green light is reflected rather than absorbed.

title: The Great Leap Forward and the famine
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three items peasants melted down in backyard furnaces to meet steel quotas.
cards.answer: Farming tools / Cooking pots / Door hinges

cards.front: Name the three features of daily life in the people's communes described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Private plots abolished / Meals eaten in communal canteens / Told they were 'eating from the same big pot'
items: Told they were 'eating from the same big pot'

cards.front: Why did the 1958 harvest rot in the fields?
cards.answer: Agricultural labour had been diverted away from farming to the steel-smelting campaign, leaving no one to bring in the crops.

cards.front: Why did the Great Leap Forward continue for three more years after Peng Dehuai was purged?
cards.answer: His purge showed that even senior officials who questioned Mao's policies risked destruction, so no one dared criticise the policy further.

cards.front: Name the four logic gates you must know for your exam.
cards.answer: NOT / AND / OR / XOR

cards.front: Why is the output 0 only in rows 2, 4 and 6 of the truth table for (A AND B) OR (NOT C)?
cards.answer: Because the output is 0 only when A·B equals 0 and C equals 1 (so NOT C is also 0).

cards.front: Why must input combinations in a truth table be listed in binary counting order (000, 001, 010...)?
cards.answer: To guarantee that every possible combination of inputs is covered without any being missed.

cards.front: Name the five techniques the lesson gives for stiffening papers and boards.
cards.answer: Lamination / Encapsulation / Corrugation / Adding extra layers or ribs / Sandwich construction

cards.front: Name the five ways the lesson gives for reinforcing textiles.
cards.answer: Ribs and boning / Lamination / Embedded composite materials / Stay stitching / Interfacing

cards.front: Why does a bent shelf crack on its underside first if the material is too weak?
cards.answer: The underside is in tension while the top is in compression, so if the material can't resist both at once it cracks on the tension side first.

cards.front: Why can a steel case around an electronic component cause problems with a signal?
cards.answer: The metal case sits close to the circuit and can accidentally shield or interfere with the signal.

title: Brigham Young and the Mormon Migration
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why the Mormons faced hostility in the East before moving West.
cards.answer: Believed they were God's gathered people / Voted as a political bloc / Refused to mix religion and the state / A minority practised polygamy from the late 1830s
items: Believed they were God's gathered people
Refused to mix religion and the state
A minority practised polygamy from the late 1830s

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why the Mormons succeeded where other migrant groups failed.
cards.answer: Leadership / Unity / Geography

cards.front: Why did the Mormon Trail have a lower death rate than secular trails like the Oregon and California Trails?
cards.answer: Companies stayed together, cared for the sick collectively, shared tools and livestock, and planted crops to feed later groups.

cards.front: Why did relations between Deseret and the US federal government worsen after the settlement was built?
cards.answer: Polygamy, theocratic government, and the Saints' refusal to obey federal officials steadily damaged relations with Washington.

cards.front: Name the five activities the lesson gives as examples of 'on peut + infinitive' in town.
cards.answer: faire du shopping (go shopping) / aller au cinéma (go to the cinema) / manger au restaurant (eat at a restaurant) / se promener dans le parc (walk in the park) / visiter des musées (visit museums)
items: aller au cinéma (go to the cinema)
manger au restaurant (eat at a restaurant)
se promener dans le parc (walk in the park)

cards.front: Name the six negative adjectives the lesson gives for describing a town.
cards.answer: ennuyeux/ennuyeuse (boring) / bruyant(e) (noisy) / sale (dirty) / pollué(e) (polluted) / démodé(e) (old-fashioned) / il n'y a rien à faire (nothing to do)
items: il n'y a rien à faire (nothing to do)

cards.front: How do you say you cannot do something in your town and give a reason why, in French?
cards.answer: Use on ne peut pas + infinitive plus parce qu'il n'y a pas de..., e.g. On ne peut pas nager parce qu'il n'y a pas de piscine.

cards.front: How is la banlieue (the suburbs) described as a compromise between la ville and la campagne?
cards.answer: It is less noisy than the city but more practical than the countryside.

cards.front: Name the three main rites of the Lupercalia described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Goats sacrificed at the Lupercal / Noble boys touched with bloodied knife then wiped clean, forced to laugh / Luperci running near-naked striking bystanders with goat-hide strips
items: Noble boys touched with bloodied knife then wiped clean, forced to laugh
Luperci running near-naked striking bystanders with goat-hide strips

cards.front: Why did young married women let the Luperci strike them during the Lupercalia?
cards.answer: They believed the blows would help them conceive and deliver safely.

cards.front: Why did some Roman men view the December Bona Dea rite with suspicion?
cards.answer: Because upper-class women met at night to drink wine and dance unsupervised, without men present.

cards.front: Why did Julius Caesar divorce his wife after the 62 BC Bona Dea scandal?
cards.answer: Because a man had disguised himself as a woman to infiltrate the secret rite at his house, and it was ruled sacrilege.

title: Cell Structure and How We Know It
subject: science-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the three internal structures revealed by electron microscopy that light microscopes could not resolve.
cards.answer: Mitochondrial cristae / Structure of ribosomes / Double membrane of the nucleus

cards.front: Why does the folded inner membrane of the mitochondrion make aerobic respiration more efficient?
cards.answer: The folds (cristae) greatly increase the surface area available for respiration enzymes, speeding up energy transfer.

cards.front: Why can the cell wall stop a plant cell bursting when water enters by osmosis?
cards.answer: It provides structural strength around the cell membrane, keeping the cell turgid instead of bursting.

cards.front: Why does the nuclear membrane keep pores to let genetic instructions out to the ribosomes?
cards.answer: It keeps genetic material separate from the cytoplasm while still allowing DNA instructions to be copied and sent to ribosomes for protein synthesis.

cards.front: Name the three things that are true about a reaction at dynamic equilibrium.
cards.answer: Forward rate equals reverse rate / Concentrations of reactants and products stay constant / Reaction has not stopped
items: Concentrations of reactants and products stay constant

cards.front: Why is the temperature used in the Haber process a compromise?
cards.answer: Lower temperature would give a higher yield but the reaction rate would be too slow.

cards.front: How does an iron catalyst affect the yield of ammonia in the Haber process?
cards.answer: It speeds up the reaction without changing the yield.

cards.front: Name the three types of soldiers that made up Tudor armies for overseas campaigns like Henry VIII's expeditions to France.
cards.answer: Retained household troops / Contract soldiers hired for a campaign / Impressed men
items: Contract soldiers hired for a campaign

cards.front: Name the four historical periods the lesson identifies, each with its own way of recruiting soldiers.
cards.answer: Medieval: feudal obligation and religious duty / Early modern: professional armies / Industrial: propaganda and conscription / Modern: voluntary professional force
items: Medieval: feudal obligation and religious duty

cards.front: Why did the Pals Battalions system mean heavy casualties hit individual communities especially hard?
cards.answer: Because men from the same town or workplace enlisted and served together, so battalion losses fell disproportionately on one community.

cards.front: Why did press ganging largely disappear after the Napoleonic Wars ended in 1815?
cards.answer: Because voluntary enlistment and improved pay made forced recruitment unnecessary once Britain returned to peacetime.

cards.front: How does Victor's failure to protect Elizabeth mirror his failure with the Creature?
cards.answer: In both cases his self-absorption blinds him to an obvious threat, leading to destruction.

cards.front: Why does Walton turn the ship back at the end of the novel?
cards.answer: His crew demand it, and he yields, heeding the warning Victor gave but could not follow himself.

cards.front: Name the four motives the lesson gives for Iago's actions against Othello.
cards.answer: Professional jealousy over Cassio's promotion / Sexual jealousy over suspected cuckolding / Racial hatred / General Schadenfreude

cards.front: Name the four techniques the lesson gives for how Iago manipulates others.
cards.answer: Soliloquy sharing plans with audience / Insinuation without direct accusation / Weaponising truth / Exploiting each character's weakness

cards.front: How does Othello's suicide give him back a kind of agency, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: He becomes judge, executioner and condemned in one gesture, refusing to let Venetian justice define his ending.

cards.front: Why does Roderigo keep helping Iago despite his suspicions, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: His desire for Desdemona overrides his judgment every time, despite flickering awareness he is being manipulated.

cards.front: Name the four conditions the Qur'an sets for declaring a lesser jihad.
cards.answer: Must be defensive / Declared by legitimate authority / Use proportionate force / Avoid harming non-combatants

cards.front: Name the three types of Muslim women's clothing described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Hijab - covers hair and neck / Niqab - covers face except eyes / Burkha - full body covering with mesh over eyes
items: Burkha - full body covering with mesh over eyes

cards.front: Why does the belief in akhirah motivate Muslims to act justly and generously in this life?
cards.answer: Because Muslims know they will be held accountable for their choices on the Day of Judgement.

cards.front: How does the mosque embody the concept of ummah?
cards.answer: It hosts Qur'an classes, Eid gatherings, marriages, funerals and welfare support, uniting the global Muslim community in faith.

cards.front: Name the three steps of Iago's method for destroying Cassio and Othello, as given in the lesson's Key Fact.
cards.answer: Get Cassio drunk and disgraced / Advise Cassio to seek Desdemona's help / Present their innocent meetings as an affair
items: Advise Cassio to seek Desdemona's help
Present their innocent meetings as an affair

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why Othello accepts the handkerchief as 'ocular proof'.
cards.answer: He trusts Iago absolutely / It touches his insecurities about being an outsider / Jealousy has already corrupted his judgment
items: It touches his insecurities about being an outsider
Jealousy has already corrupted his judgment

cards.front: Why is Act 3 Scene 3 called the play's pivotal scene?
cards.answer: It is the longest scene in the play, where Iago plants suspicion through insinuation and turns Othello against Desdemona.

cards.front: How does Iago use insinuation rather than direct accusation to provoke Othello in Act 3 Scene 3?
cards.answer: He says little, feigns reluctance to speak, and echoes Othello's own words back as suspicious questions, making Othello imagine the worst.

cards.front: Name the four physical changes the lesson gives for pregnancy in adulthood.
cards.answer: Blood volume increases 40-50% / Uterus expands from pear-size to full-term / Weight increases by 10-12 kg / Major hormonal and cardiovascular changes
items: Uterus expands from pear-size to full-term

cards.front: Name the three cardiovascular and respiratory changes the lesson gives for later adulthood.
cards.answer: Heart muscle weakens slightly / Blood vessels lose elasticity / Lung capacity reduces

cards.front: Why can delays in fine motor development in childhood lead to a referral to an occupational therapist?
cards.answer: Delays in fine motor development can indicate conditions such as dyspraxia, prompting practitioners to refer the child.

cards.front: Why do older adults tire more quickly with exertion?
cards.answer: The heart muscle weakens slightly, blood vessels lose elasticity, and lung capacity reduces, lowering stamina.

title: Factors Affecting Food Choice & Sensory Evaluation
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four control factors needed to set up a proper sensory test, for full marks.
cards.answer: Defined method (preference, ranking or profiling) / Samples coded to prevent bias / Controlled environment (no competing aromas, consistent lighting, palate-cleansing water) / Results recorded on a standard proforma
items: Controlled environment (no competing aromas, consistent lighting, palate-cleansing water)
Results recorded on a standard proforma

cards.front: Name the four senses, beyond taste and smell, involved in evaluating food.
cards.answer: Texture (mechanoreceptors) / Sound / Appearance / Taste and smell combine to give flavour
items: Taste and smell combine to give flavour

cards.front: Why is 'I asked my friends if they liked it' not valid sensory evaluation?
cards.answer: It describes informal opinion, without a defined method, coded samples, controlled environment or standard recording, so bias distorts results.

cards.front: Why might a working parent choose a ready meal over a slow-cooked stew, even knowing the stew is more nutritious?
cards.answer: Time and lifestyle pressures, such as arriving home late, make convenience more important than nutritional value at that moment.

cards.front: Name the three overlapping groups that made up the Iraqi insurgency.
cards.answer: Sunni Ba'athist remnants / Foreign jihadists (al-Qaeda in Iraq) / Shia militias linked to Iran

cards.front: Name the two attacks the lesson cites as global blowback from the Iraq War, before the 2007 surge.
cards.answer: 2004 Madrid train bombings / 2005 London bombings (7/7)

cards.front: How did the CPA's May 2003 orders help create the insurgency?
cards.answer: De-Ba'athification and disbanding the army removed a generation of Sunni Arabs from public life, creating a pool of trained, humiliated recruits.

cards.front: Why did the 2007 surge succeed in reducing civilian deaths?
cards.answer: It paired extra troops with a counter-insurgency doctrine protecting civilians, while the Sunni Awakening turned Anbar tribes against al-Qaeda in Iraq.

title: The Atom Bomb, Ideologies, and the Iron Curtain
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six areas the Red Army occupied by the end of 1945, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Poland / Hungary / Romania / Bulgaria / Eastern Germany / Parts of Czechoslovakia and Austria

cards.front: What four features did the lesson give for US-style capitalism and liberal democracy?
cards.answer: Free elections / Multi-party politics / Freedom of the press / Competing private businesses

cards.front: Why did the Yalta promise of free elections in Eastern Europe end up broken by 1948?
cards.answer: Elections between 1945 and 1948 were rigged or manipulated so local communist parties took power in every Soviet-occupied state.

cards.front: Why did Stalin barely react when Truman mentioned the new weapon at Potsdam?
cards.answer: Soviet intelligence had already penetrated the Manhattan Project years earlier, so Stalin already knew the bomb existed.

cards.front: Name the five groups the lesson says Hitler tailored his promises to.
cards.answer: The unemployed / The middle classes / Farmers / Industrialists / Nationalists

cards.front: Name the five propaganda techniques Goebbels used, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Mass rallies / Posters and leaflets / Radio / Scapegoating / Crafting Hitler's image

cards.front: How did the SA's street violence help the Nazis' rise to power?
cards.answer: Their violence made it seem the Weimar Republic was collapsing into chaos, so people believed only the Nazis could restore order.

cards.front: Why did Hitler keep his core message of national renewal deliberately vague?
cards.answer: So he could tell each audience what it wanted to hear, offering something for everyone without alienating potential supporters.

title: Editing: Cuts, Continuity, Pace and Visual Effects
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why does breaking the 180-degree rule disorient the spectator?
cards.answer: Characters appear to have switched sides of the frame without moving, breaking the spectator's spatial orientation.

cards.front: How does cross-cutting build tension in a chase-or-rescue sequence?
cards.answer: Cutting faster between pursuer and escaper as the strands converge makes the spectator experience mounting tension neither strand alone creates.

title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that affect the resistance of a wire.
cards.answer: Length of the wire / Cross-sectional area / Material / Temperature

cards.front: In a series circuit, name the three rules the lesson gives for current, potential difference and resistance.
