Solid white board header card with UV spot varnish for visibility

cards.front: Why does a paper mill run as a continuous 24-hour process rather than stopping and starting?
cards.answer: It runs constantly to justify the energy cost of maintaining the operating temperatures needed for the process.

cards.front: How does NFC paper let a smartphone read product information without any visible electronics?
cards.answer: A thin conductive antenna and chip are embedded within the paper sheet, letting a phone read data simply by tapping the packaging.

title: The Magisterium, Sacred Art and Catholic Funeral Rites
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three principal rites that make up the Catholic Order of Christian Funerals in Britain.
cards.answer: The vigil (prayer service the evening before) / The funeral Mass / The rite of committal at the graveside or crematorium
items: The vigil (prayer service the evening before)
The rite of committal at the graveside or crematorium

cards.front: What five key symbols are used in the Catholic funeral rite?
cards.answer: The Paschal Candle / Sprinkling the coffin with holy water / A white pall over the coffin / A copy of the Gospels or a cross on the coffin / The use of incense
items: Sprinkling the coffin with holy water
A white pall over the coffin
A copy of the Gospels or a cross on the coffin

cards.front: Why is the Paschal Candle used at both baptisms and funerals?
cards.answer: Baptism begins a person's share in Christ's paschal mystery, which death completes, so the same candle marks both stages of passing from death to life.

cards.front: How did Vatican II's Sacrosanctum Concilium reform the celebration of the Mass?
cards.answer: It permitted the Mass to be celebrated in vernacular languages instead of Latin and emphasised the active participation of all the faithful.

cards.front: What four qualities did the gods each give to Pandora, according to Hesiod?
cards.answer: Beauty / Charm / Cunning / Deceit

cards.front: In the Iliad's 'viewing from the walls' scene, which four Greek leaders does Helen identify to Priam?
cards.answer: Agamemnon / Odysseus / Ajax / Idomeneus

cards.front: Why did Zeus send Pandora to humanity?
cards.answer: Zeus was angry that Prometheus had stolen fire for humanity, so he sent Pandora as punishment.

cards.front: Why did Medea kill her own children?
cards.answer: To punish Jason as deeply as possible for abandoning her to marry a Greek princess.

cards.front: Name the three key waveform properties described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Amplitude / Frequency / Periodic time

cards.front: Why can a noisy digital signal be restored to a clean signal, but a noisy analogue signal cannot?
cards.answer: Digital signals have only two states, so if a noisy signal is clearly above the threshold it can be regenerated to a clean 1, unlike continuous analogue signals.

cards.front: Why does converting an analogue signal to digital introduce quantisation error?
cards.answer: Because the continuous analogue signal is approximated using discrete steps when converted, causing a small quantisation error.

title: Search and Destroy, My Lai and Protest
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three structural problems that caused search-and-destroy to fail.
cards.answer: Vietcong chose when and where to fight (80% of engagements enemy-initiated) / Cleared ground was simply re-occupied once US units left / Body-count metric corrupted reporting
items: Vietcong chose when and where to fight (80% of engagements enemy-initiated)
Cleared ground was simply re-occupied once US units left

cards.front: What three things does the lesson give for why US public opinion turned so hard against the war?
cards.answer: Nightly TV footage of the 'living-room war' / The Tet Offensive contradicting official optimism / The 1971 Pentagon Papers revealing government lies
items: Nightly TV footage of the 'living-room war'
The Tet Offensive contradicting official optimism
The 1971 Pentagon Papers revealing government lies

cards.front: How did the draft make the Vietnam War personal for many young Americans?
cards.answer: Young men were called up, disproportionately working-class and African American, while wealthier students could defer through college.

cards.front: Why is Vietnam described as the first 'living-room war'?
cards.answer: TV crews followed combat units and networks broadcast nightly footage of body bags, burning villages and wounded marines into American homes.

title: Narrative Structure: Plot, Story and Three-Act Form
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the seven character roles ('spheres of action') Propp identified in Russian folk tales.
cards.answer: Hero / Villain / Donor / Helper / Dispatcher / Princess / False hero

cards.front: Why does disrupting cause and effect (jumping scenes with no explained connection) affect the spectator?
cards.answer: It makes the spectator aware of the narration itself, which can feel disorienting or thought-provoking depending on the filmmaker's intent.

cards.front: How should Todorov's or Propp's models be used to get analytical credit, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: By pinning the theory to a named moment in the film and explaining specific filmic choices, not describing the theory abstractly.

title: Time Series, Trends and Rates of Change
subject: statistics-aqa

cards.front: Name the four steps the lesson gives for interpreting a time series graph.
cards.answer: State the overall trend / Identify any seasonal pattern / Note any unusual features / Quantify where possible

cards.front: Name the four specific rate measures the lesson says are used in real UK contexts.
cards.answer: Birth rate / Death rate / House price change / Unemployment rate

cards.front: Why doesn't a rise in the number of deaths necessarily mean mortality is getting worse?
cards.answer: The population may have grown or aged, so the death rate is needed to put the change in proportion.

cards.front: How does a cyclic trend differ from a seasonal trend?
cards.answer: A cyclic trend rises and falls over a longer, less regular timescale, unlike a seasonal trend which repeats at a fixed calendar point.

title: Fats, Fruit & Vegetables and Raising Agents
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: Name the four functional properties of fats and oils identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Shortening / Aeration / Plasticity / Emulsification

cards.front: Name the four types of raising agent covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Chemical / Mechanical / Steam / Biological

cards.front: Why must water only be added after the fat has been rubbed into the flour when making shortcrust pastry?
cards.answer: If water is added before the fat coats the flour, gluten begins developing immediately, making the pastry tough instead of short.

cards.front: Why is butter at room temperature (around 18–20°C) ideal for creaming?
cards.answer: Cold butter cannot trap air efficiently, while very warm butter releases the trapped air before the cake sets.

title: Medieval warfare: knights, archers and the feudal army c1250–c1500
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three battles the lesson gives where mounted French knights charged into a wall of English arrows.
cards.answer: Crécy (1346) / Poitiers (1356) / Agincourt (1415)

cards.front: How were the Scottish schiltrons at Falkirk eventually destroyed?
cards.answer: Not by horsemen but by English longbowmen, who shot the schiltrons apart from a safe distance.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the longbow alone should not be credited with winning Agincourt?
cards.answer: It worked alongside funnel terrain, deep mud, French command failures and Henry V's choice to fight on a narrow front between two woods.

cards.front: How did gunpowder cannon and the longbow together squeeze the mounted knight from two sides?
cards.answer: Cheap missile troops broke up cavalry charges while cannon broke the castle walls that had been the knight's refuge.

title: Homesteaders, Railroads and the Closing Frontier
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four big farming problems the lesson gives for settlers on the Great Plains.
cards.answer: Lack of timber / Lack of water / Tough sod / Crop failure from drought or pests
items: Crop failure from drought or pests

cards.front: Name the four big solutions the lesson gives to the Plains farming problems.
cards.answer: Sod homes / Windmill-pumped wells / John Deere's steel plough / Dry farming with drought-resistant wheat

cards.front: Why did railroad companies advertise the West and run cheap emigrant trains for settlers?
cards.answer: They calculated that filled-up land along the line meant freight to ship in both directions, and they profited from selling land to settlers.

cards.front: How did barbed wire bring about the end of the open range cattle system?
cards.answer: Cheap, mass-producible barbed wire let homesteaders fence their fields, enclosing the once-unfenced grassland from the mid-1870s onward.

cards.front: Name the five Ks that Khalsa Sikhs commit to wearing.
cards.answer: kesh (uncut hair) / kangha (small comb) / kara (steel bracelet) / kaccha (modest undergarment) / kirpan (small sword)

cards.front: Name the three practical expressions of equality in Sikh life given in the lesson.
cards.answer: sangat (equal congregation) / langar (community kitchen) / sewa (selfless service)

cards.front: Why is the Guru Granth Sahib treated as if it were a living being in the gurdwara?
cards.answer: Because it holds the eternal authority of a living Guru, so it is honoured like royalty: bowed to, fanned, and ceremonially put to rest at night.

cards.front: Why are Sikhs cremated rather than buried after death?
cards.answer: Cremation symbolises the soul's release from the cycle of rebirth, as the body returns to the elements while the soul journeys toward liberation.

cards.front: Name all four benefits for service users given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Standardisation of care / Improved quality of care / Maintains or improves quality of life / Supports service users to develop their strengths
items: Maintains or improves quality of life
Supports service users to develop their strengths

cards.front: How does applying the value of individuality lead to improved quality of care for a service user?
cards.answer: A practitioner asks about preferences, history and culture, shaping a care plan that genuinely fits the person, giving better health outcomes.

cards.front: How does the value of individuality support a practitioner's skill development?
cards.answer: Recognising each service user has unique communication needs pushes practitioners to learn new skills, such as Makaton or sign language.

cards.front: Name the four upland areas the lesson gives as examples of high ground in the UK.
cards.answer: Scottish Highlands / Lake District / Snowdonia / Pennines / Dartmoor

cards.front: Name the four processes the lesson gives that shape UK landscapes on top of the underlying geology.
cards.answer: Past glaciation / ongoing weathering / slope processes / centuries of human activity

cards.front: Why do hard rocks like granite and slate form upland areas in the UK?
cards.answer: They resist erosion better than surrounding rocks, so softer rock wears away while the hard rock stays standing.

cards.front: Why does upland Britain run roughly NW-SE?
cards.answer: Ancient mountain-building (the Caledonian and Variscan orogenies) folded rocks along this line, forming a geological backbone, while younger rocks stayed flatter.

cards.front: Name the three economic forces the lesson says influence almost every business decision.
cards.answer: Interest rates / Level of employment / Consumer spending

cards.front: Name the three examples of automation firms use to cut wage costs given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Self-checkout tills at Tesco / Order-at-table apps at Wetherspoon / AI chatbots for customer service

cards.front: How can rising interest rates end up reducing employment and incomes?
cards.answer: Rising rates slow spending, which reduces demand, which can reduce employment, weakening incomes and cutting spending further.

cards.front: Why might a business automate jobs when it is struggling to recruit staff?
cards.answer: Automation replaces some jobs, saving on rising wage costs while filling gaps left by hard-to-recruit vacancies.

cards.front: Why is the moral ending of Twelfth Night unbalanced regarding Malvolio and his tormentors?
cards.answer: Malvolio suffers while Maria and Sir Toby are rewarded with marriage, creating a moral asymmetry between victim and pranksters.

cards.front: How does Feste's mock examination of Malvolio show irony in the Sir Topas scene?
cards.answer: Malvolio answers Feste's questions about Pythagoras correctly and coherently, yet Feste still declares him mad.

cards.front: Name the four fields where nanoparticles are applied, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Sunscreen / Medicine / Electronics / Catalysis

cards.front: Name the three example alloys given in the lesson, with their components.
cards.answer: Steel (iron + carbon) / Brass (copper + zinc) / Bronze (copper + tin)

cards.front: In the worked example, why does splitting a large cube into smaller cubes increase the surface area to volume ratio?
cards.answer: Cutting into smaller cubes increases total surface area while total volume stays the same.

cards.front: How does a composite material achieve properties that neither of its components has alone?
cards.answer: It combines materials so each contributes its best property, exploiting the stiffness of the fibres and toughness of the polymer matrix.

cards.front: How does Orwell contrast the setting with Clover's feelings after the executions?
cards.answer: He sets her silent despair against a clear spring evening and a farm that has never looked more desirable, heightening the tragedy.

cards.front: Why does Squealer say 'Beasts of England' must be banned?
cards.answer: He claims the song is no longer necessary because the Rebellion is complete and the better society it promised has been achieved.

title: Interpreting Data on Health and Participation
subject: physical-education-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five common errors the lesson identifies in data interpretation questions.
cards.answer: Describing a trend without quoting figures / Quoting figures without interpretation / Making claims beyond the data / Forgetting units on calculations / Confusing percentage point with percentage change
items: Describing a trend without quoting figures
Confusing percentage point with percentage change

cards.front: Why does the worked example suggest sport participation declines as socio-economic status decreases?
cards.answer: Higher costs like club fees, equipment and transport, plus less flexible working hours for lower-income groups, act as barriers.

cards.front: Why can't you claim a policy caused a change in participation just because the data shows a trend?
cards.answer: Data can show trends and suggest explanations, but you cannot state a cause definitively unless the data explicitly shows it.

title: Theme for English B — Langston Hughes
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name the three short quotations from 'Theme for English B' worth memorising for part b) analysis.
cards.answer: "true" / "instructor" / "I hear New York too"

cards.front: Which four other anthology poems does the lesson suggest comparing with 'Theme for English B'?
cards.answer: 'Holy Thursday' / 'Cold Knap Lake' / 'Tea With Our Grandmothers' / 'Venus's-flytraps'

cards.front: Why does Hughes use alliteration in the phrase 'Bessie, bop, or Bach'?
cards.answer: It links a blues singer, jazz and classical music through their shared 'b' sound, showing his tastes can't be sorted into racial categories.

cards.front: How does the poem's free verse form reflect the speaker's writing process?
cards.answer: Lines of very different lengths capture the drifting, thinking voice of someone composing the assignment aloud.

title: Young King Henry and the Rise of Wolsey
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three main aims Henry VIII had as a young king.
cards.answer: Military glory in France / A male heir to secure the dynasty / Personal control without doing daily admin
items: A male heir to secure the dynasty
Personal control without doing daily admin

cards.front: What four factors does the lesson give for why Wolsey rose so fast?
cards.answer: Sheer administrative ability / He understood and flattered Henry / Independent clerical income / No powerful family to rival the king
items: No powerful family to rival the king

cards.front: Why did Henry VIII need someone like Wolsey to manage his government?
cards.answer: Henry preferred hunting, jousting and music to daily administration, so he needed someone else to do the detailed work of ruling.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Wolsey was not simply Henry's puppet?
cards.answer: Wolsey shaped foreign policy, drove the Eltham Ordinances and ran the law courts on his own initiative, while Henry only set broad goals.

title: The Mitzvot and Key Moral Principles
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the three prohibitions that Pikuach Nefesh cannot override, even to save a life.
cards.answer: Murder / Sexual immorality / Idol worship

cards.front: Why do ethical Mitzvot require people to treat others with dignity, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because all humans are created in the image of G-d, so they deserve dignity and fair treatment.

cards.front: How does Judaism resolve the tension between Divine Providence and human free will?
cards.answer: Thinkers like Maimonides argue G-d's foreknowledge does not cancel human freedom, even though this is hard to fully explain.

cards.front: Name the four phases of clinical trials described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Phase 1: healthy volunteers, test safety / Phase 2: patients, initial effectiveness evidence / Phase 3: large-scale comparison against best treatment / Phase 4: post-approval surveillance in general population
items: Phase 3: large-scale comparison against best treatment
Phase 4: post-approval surveillance in general population

cards.front: Why is a placebo control essential in a clinical trial?
cards.answer: It separates the true drug effect from the placebo effect, since belief in receiving treatment alone can improve symptoms.

cards.front: Why has the pipeline for new antibiotics slowed in recent decades?
cards.answer: Because development costs are high but commercial returns are lower than for drugs used long-term, discouraging investment.

cards.front: Why does post-approval surveillance (Phase 4) matter even after a drug is approved?
cards.answer: It can detect rare side effects that were too uncommon to appear during clinical trials, once the drug is used by the wider population.

cards.front: How does becoming a mother change identity in Duffy's "Before You Were Mine"?
cards.answer: The mother's glamorous, independent past self was surrendered and replaced by belonging to her child.

cards.front: Why does the son's memory in "Walking Away" still "gnaw" at Day-Lewis eighteen years on?
cards.answer: The pain of watching his son separate from him remains permanent even after many years.

cards.front: How does the verb "stumbling" create the reversal in Heaney's "Follower"?
cards.answer: It transfers from the clumsy child following his father to the now ageing, dependent father following his son.

cards.front: Why is the reversal in "Follower" described as both tender and uncomfortable?
cards.answer: Heaney remembers his own loving devotion as a child but feels frustration at his father now being burdensome.

cards.front: Name the first six of the Seven Commandments (excluding 'All animals are equal').
cards.answer: Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy / Whatever goes upon four legs or has wings is a friend / No animal shall wear clothes / No animal shall sleep in a bed / No animal shall drink alcohol / No animal shall kill any other animal
items: Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy
Whatever goes upon four legs or has wings is a friend
No animal shall sleep in a bed
No animal shall kill any other animal

cards.front: Why does Squealer say the pigs must have the milk and apples?
cards.answer: He claims the pigs need them because they do 'brainwork' and warns Jones would come back if the pigs failed.

cards.front: How does the speed of the Rebellion parallel the October Revolution?
cards.answer: Both happened quickly and with relatively little resistance, as Jones's neglect let the animals seize power easily, mirroring the Bolsheviks' seizure of power.

cards.front: Name the two weaknesses the lesson gives for using ARR to judge an investment.
cards.answer: Ignores timing of returns / Based on forecasts that may be wrong / ignores risk
items: Based on forecasts that may be wrong / ignores risk

cards.front: Name the three strengths the lesson gives for the ARR method.
cards.answer: Simple to calculate and explain / Gives a percentage comparable to interest rates / Uses the full life of the project
items: Gives a percentage comparable to interest rates
Uses the full life of the project

cards.front: Why does a healthy margin of safety help protect a business?
cards.answer: It gives a cushion so sales can fall (from bad weather, new rivals or lower demand) before the business starts losing money.

cards.front: Why is a 30% ARR on a risky project considered worse than a 15% ARR on a safe project?
cards.answer: Because ARR ignores risk, so a high return on a reckless venture can be worse than a lower return on a safe one.

cards.front: The lesson names three types of characters Delaney included that were rarely seen on stage before. What are they?
cards.answer: a single mother / a mixed-race relationship / a gay man

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three options did women like Helen have in 1950s Britain?
cards.answer: marriage / factory work / dependence on men

cards.front: How does Helen's reliance on men throughout the play reflect the lesson's context on 1950s women?
cards.answer: It reflects the limited options available to working-class women in the 1950s, who could rely only on marriage, factory work, or dependence on men.

cards.front: Why is Jo's line 'I'm not just talented, I'm geniused' significant in terms of context?
cards.answer: It represents a new generation of women refusing to accept the limited options available to working-class women in the 1950s.

cards.front: The lesson gives three reasons the division of labour raises output for firms. What are they?
cards.answer: Workers become highly skilled at the task / Less time wasted switching between tasks / Machinery designed for repetitive jobs
items: Workers become highly skilled at the task
Less time wasted switching between tasks

cards.front: Name the four functions of money given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Medium of exchange / Store of value / Unit of account / Standard of deferred payment

cards.front: Why can a region become vulnerable if it relies heavily on specialising in one industry?
cards.answer: If demand for its main product collapses, workers have narrow skills, firms have few alternative markets, and the region can decline long-term.

cards.front: Why does money remove the need for a double coincidence of wants?
cards.answer: Everyone accepts money, so a seller doesn't need to want what the buyer produces, only the money itself.

cards.front: How does Austen show Darcy's pride and Elizabeth's prejudice feeding each other?
cards.answer: Darcy's pride causes Elizabeth's prejudice, and her prejudice then reinforces her resistance to seeing his true character.

cards.front: Why does Jane and Bingley's relationship break down despite their genuine connection?
cards.answer: External forces (Darcy and Bingley's sisters) separate them because one or both lack strength to resist social pressure.

cards.front: Why does the moors sequence strip Jane of money, shelter, identity and status?
cards.answer: To reduce her to her most basic self, proving her worth doesn't depend on Thornfield or Rochester.

cards.front: Why must Diana and Mary Rivers work as governesses?
cards.answer: Their family lost its money, mirroring Jane's own situation and showing poverty doesn't diminish worth.

title: Video Games: Fortnite — Industry and Audience
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three examples the lesson gives of Fortnite's cross-media collaborations to stay in the news.
cards.answer: Avengers: Infinity War segment with Marvel / Godzilla tie-in / Promotion by celebrities Drake and Ben Simmons
items: Avengers: Infinity War segment with Marvel
Promotion by celebrities Drake and Ben Simmons

cards.front: How does Fortnite's technological convergence work across devices?
cards.answer: It can be played on consoles, PCs, laptops, smartphones and tablets, and players can switch device mid-game without interruption.

cards.front: Why does Fortnite appeal to a wider audience than realistic violent games like Call of Duty?
cards.answer: Its unrealistic, cartoon-style violence and focus on construction alongside combat draw in younger and more diverse players.

cards.front: Why is Fortnite seen as an example of active audience theory?
cards.answer: Gameplay is interactive and collaborative, letting players deconstruct and rebuild environments and design content, encouraging creativity over passive consumption.

cards.front: Why must vague specification criteria like 'the product must be strong' be avoided?
cards.answer: Vague criteria cannot be tested objectively, so they produce vague evaluation and no clear basis for deciding if the design succeeds.

cards.front: Why does a stacking toy specification need both quantitative and qualitative criteria?
cards.answer: A toy passing all quantitative tests but looking unappealing won't sell, and one looking perfect but failing strength tests is unsafe, so both are needed.

cards.front: Name the four physical properties the lesson gives that distinguish transition metals from Group 1 metals.
cards.answer: Higher melting points / Harder and stronger / Much denser / Less reactive

cards.front: Name the four uses of nanoparticles given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Medicine (wound dressings) / Sunscreens / Electronics / Catalysis

cards.front: Why does cutting a material into smaller cubes increase its total surface area for the same volume?
cards.answer: Splitting a solid into smaller pieces exposes more surface for the same total volume, increasing the surface area to volume ratio.

cards.front: Why are nanoparticle catalysts more effective than bulk catalysts using the same mass of material?
cards.answer: Their very high surface area to volume ratio means more surface is exposed for reactions, so less material is needed.

cards.front: Name the four advantages of technology given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Communicate easily with people worldwide / Useful for homework research / Stay in touch with family and friends / A good way to have fun
items: Stay in touch with family and friends
A good way to have fun

cards.front: Name the four disadvantages of technology given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Too much time in front of the screen / Cyberbullying is a serious problem / Bad for health, not enough exercise / Risk of addiction
items: Too much time in front of the screen
Bad for health, not enough exercise

cards.front: Why does French use both 'pour' and 'afin de' when giving purpose sentences in French exams?
cards.answer: Both mean 'in order to' and take an infinitive, but using both shows you can vary your language.

cards.front: Why can the French word 'portable' cause confusion, and how do you make its meaning clear?
cards.answer: 'Portable' alone can mean phone or laptop; 'mon portable' usually means phone, while 'un ordinateur portable' specifically means laptop.

cards.front: Give the two main types of source used to study insula life.
cards.answer: Material remains (Insula of Diana) / Literary descriptions (Juvenal and Petronius)

cards.front: Why did fires spread so rapidly through the upper floors of a Roman insula?
cards.answer: There was no running water upstairs, no kitchens so residents cooked on open braziers, and buildings were partly built of timber.

cards.front: Why was the ground floor of an insula usually used for shops and taverns rather than housing?
cards.answer: Ground level with street frontage was the most accessible and commercially valuable space, so landlords rented it for business.

cards.front: Why is material evidence like the Insula of Diana limited on its own for understanding insula life?
cards.answer: It shows building design, scale and materials but cannot reveal daily experience like noise, smells or social tensions.

cards.front: Name the three models of atomic structure the lesson describes in order of development.
cards.answer: Thomson's plum pudding model / Rutherford's nuclear model (dense positive nucleus) / Bohr's model (electrons in fixed energy levels/shells)
items: Bohr's model (electrons in fixed energy levels/shells)

cards.front: Name the three sources of error in density experiments given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Reading the measuring cylinder at an angle (parallax error) / Not drying the object before measuring mass / Air bubbles clinging to the object during displacement
items: Reading the measuring cylinder at an angle (parallax error)
Not drying the object before measuring mass
Air bubbles clinging to the object during displacement

cards.front: Why did the alpha particle scattering experiment cause the plum pudding model to be abandoned?
cards.answer: Most alpha particles passed straight through but some deflected or bounced back, showing atoms have a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus, which plum pudding couldn't explain.

cards.front: Why does density drop dramatically when water boils to steam?
cards.answer: Mass stays the same but the volume increases enormously as particles spread far apart, so the density decreases greatly.

title: The Gurdwara, Langar and Daily Worship
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five prayers that make up the Nitnem.
cards.answer: Japji Sahib (morning) / Jaap Sahib (morning) / Tav-Prasad Savaiye (morning) / Sodar Rahiras Sahib (evening) / Kirtan Sohila (bedtime)

cards.front: Name the three forms Nam Japna can take.
cards.answer: Silent personal meditation / Recitation during daily prayers / Communal singing of hymns (kirtan)

cards.front: Why was the langar instituted by the Sikh Gurus?
cards.answer: As a direct rejection of the caste system, dissolving social distinctions by having everyone eat together on the floor.

cards.front: How does the Harmandir Sahib's care for the Guru Granth Sahib show it is treated as a living presence?
cards.answer: It is placed there through the day with hymns sung almost continuously, then carried by palanquin to rest each night and returned at dawn.

title: Visual Illusions and Gregory's Constructivist Theory
subject: psychology-aqa

cards.front: Name the six illusions the lesson uses as evidence for Gregory's constructivist theory.
cards.answer: Ponzo illusion / Müller-Lyer illusion / Rubin's vase / Necker cube / Kanizsa triangle / Ames Room

cards.front: Why does perception flip between two interpretations in Rubin's vase and the Necker cube?
cards.answer: The brain cannot settle on one best-guess for figure and ground (or which face is front), so it alternates between equally plausible interpretations.

cards.front: Why is top-down processing harder to study scientifically than bottom-up processing?
cards.answer: It is difficult to isolate the effect of prior knowledge because everyone's past experience differs.

title: A female ruler: Parliament, marriage and the succession
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What three drawbacks did each of Elizabeth's potential marriage matches bring, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Catholic husband risked the religious settlement / Foreign prince risked drawing England into wars / Domestic noble risked civil war between rival factions
items: Catholic husband risked the religious settlement
Domestic noble risked civil war between factions

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth use marriage negotiations as a diplomatic tool rather than aiming to actually marry?
cards.answer: While Spain and France believed she might wed their candidate, neither dared invade, so delay bought safety.

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth call Parliament rarely and limit what it discussed?
cards.answer: She needed Parliament for taxation and law but disliked its Protestant views and pressure over marriage and the succession, so she restricted its role.

title: Benefits to Health & Wellbeing When Rights Are Maintained
subject: health-social-care-ocr

cards.front: Name the four main benefits produced when rights are maintained, as grouped in the lesson.
cards.answer: Empowerment / High self-esteem / Needs being met / Trust

cards.front: Why does trust depend particularly on confidentiality and protection from abuse and harm?
cards.answer: Knowing personal information stays private and staff are properly trained reassures the service user that providers have their best interests in mind.

cards.front: How does a lack of equal treatment affect a service user's self-esteem?
cards.answer: Without equal treatment, self-esteem drops and the service user may feel worthless or discriminated against.

cards.front: Why does a breach of confidentiality lead to worse clinical outcomes?
cards.answer: Breaching confidentiality destroys trust, so the service user may withhold health information from practitioners, worsening clinical outcomes.

cards.front: Name the three components whose I-V characteristics you need to investigate.
cards.answer: Fixed resistors / Filament lamps / Diodes

cards.front: What equipment do you connect to investigate a component's I-V characteristics?
cards.answer: Variable resistor / Ammeter / Power supply / Voltmeter (in parallel across the component)

cards.front: Why does total resistance decrease when more resistors are added in parallel?
cards.answer: Because adding more resistors in parallel gives the current more paths to flow through.

cards.front: Why does the total current from the battery increase when more resistors are added in parallel?
cards.answer: Adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance, which increases the total current from the supply.

cards.front: Name the four key terms studied in social influence.
cards.answer: Obedience / Conformity / Deindividuation / Bystander effect

cards.front: Name the five ways the lesson suggests blind obedience can be reduced.
cards.answer: Exposure to a disobedient role model / Education about situational pressures / Encouraging personal responsibility / Removing anonymity / Allowing time for reflection
items: Exposure to a disobedient role model

cards.front: How does having to answer publicly rather than privately affect conformity?
cards.answer: Giving an answer publicly increases conformity because people fear standing out or being judged if they disagree with the majority.

cards.front: How does feeling anonymous in a crowd lead to deindividuation?
cards.answer: Wearing similar clothing or a mask, or being in darkness or noise, makes people feel anonymous, reducing their sense of personal accountability.

title: African Americans before Brown v Board
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the two practices the lesson gives that caused housing and employment inequality for African Americans outside the South.
cards.answer: Restrictive covenants in housing deeds / Redlining by banks and insurers

cards.front: Why did Southern states target graduate and professional education first, rather than school segregation, in the NAACP's early legal strategy?
cards.answer: Because inequality of facilities was starkest there and courts were more likely to be receptive to challenges.

cards.front: How did Massive Resistance show the gap between the Brown ruling and daily reality in the South?
cards.answer: Southern states signed the Southern Manifesto and Virginia closed schools, so by 1964 fewer than 2% of Black students attended desegregated schools.

title: Religion and race: the Bible Belt and the KKK
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five groups the lesson says the 1920s Klan targeted.
cards.answer: Black Americans / Catholics / Jews / Immigrants / Trade unionists

cards.front: Name the five areas of public life the lesson says Jim Crow laws segregated.
cards.answer: Schools / Transport / Restaurants / Hospitals / Courtrooms

cards.front: Why did the Scopes Trial embarrass William Jennings Bryan and fundamentalism?
cards.answer: The trial was broadcast live on radio, letting millions hear Darrow cross-examine Bryan, who struggled to answer questions about the age of the Earth.

cards.front: Why did the 1920s Klan attract millions of members across the North, Midwest and South?
cards.answer: It appealed to working-class white Protestants who felt threatened by immigration, urbanisation and social change.

cards.front: Name the three main ways the lesson says humans modify UK ecosystems.
cards.answer: Mechanised farming and fishing for food / Wind farms and fracking for energy / Reservoirs and water transfer schemes for water
items: Mechanised farming and fishing for food
Wind farms and fracking for energy
Reservoirs and water transfer schemes for water

cards.front: Name the four factors that govern where UK wind farms are located.
cards.answer: Physical geography (wind, seabed, upland exposure) / Planning policy (excludes areas of outstanding natural beauty) / Grid connection (proximity to high-voltage cables) / Public acceptance
items: Planning policy (excludes areas of outstanding natural beauty)

cards.front: Why was fracking at Preston New Road paused in the UK?
cards.answer: It caused small earthquakes up to 2.9 magnitude and faced intense local opposition.

cards.front: Why did building reservoirs like Kielder Water and the Lake District reservoirs harm the environment?
cards.answer: They flooded valleys, displaced communities and altered downstream river flow.

cards.front: Why must a designer avoid internal corners and recesses when designing for finishing processes?
cards.answer: Internal corners and recesses trap residues and prevent even coating, spoiling the finish.

cards.front: Why is injection moulding uneconomical for a 50-unit batch prototype but viable for 100,000 units per year?
cards.answer: The expensive mould tool cost can only be recovered when spread across a very large production run.

cards.front: Why does forming a sheet metal part by bending require the designer to account for spring-back?
cards.answer: Forming deforms material without removing it, and the metal partially returns towards its original shape after bending.

title: Chemical Equations and Conservation of Mass
subject: science-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the four state symbols used in chemical equations and what each means.
cards.answer: (s) solid / (l) liquid / (g) gas / (aq) dissolved in water

cards.front: Why must a symbol equation be balanced when a word equation does not need to be?
cards.answer: Symbol equations show the actual ratio of atoms reacting, so both sides must have equal atom numbers to obey conservation of mass.

cards.front: How do you work out the formula of an ionic compound like Al2O3 from the ion charges?
cards.answer: You combine ions in whatever ratio makes the total positive and negative charge cancel out, e.g. Al3+ and O2- combine 2:3.

cards.front: [HIGHER] Why do electrolysis reactions use half-equations showing electrons instead of a normal balanced equation?
cards.answer: Because each half-equation shows electrons gained or lost at one electrode, and must balance for both atoms and charge.

cards.front: Name the five central themes this lesson identifies in Much Ado About Nothing.
cards.answer: Deception and Noting / Honour and Shame / Love and Gender / Wit and Language / Appearance versus Reality

cards.front: What are the three steps for structuring a theme-based Shakespeare essay?
cards.answer: Extract analysis / Whole-play links / Evaluate

cards.front: Why is Benedick's challenge to Claudio described as the play's most significant act?
cards.answer: He chooses Hero's word over male loyalty, breaking the honour code and redefining honour as moral courage rather than reputation.

cards.front: Why is Claudio and Hero's love fragile compared to Beatrice and Benedick's?
cards.answer: It is based on visual attraction and convention, so a false appearance created by Don John's trick can destroy it.

cards.front: Name the five types of home given in the lesson, with their French words.
cards.answer: une maison (individuelle) - detached house / un appartement - flat/apartment / une maison jumelée - semi-detached house / une maison mitoyenne - terraced house / une ferme - farm/farmhouse

cards.front: Name the four forms of 'il y a' given in the lesson for different tenses/negatives.
cards.answer: il y a - there is/are / il y avait - there was/were / il y aura - there will be / il n'y a pas de - there is no/isn't any
items: il y aura - there will be
il n'y a pas de - there is no/isn't any

cards.front: Why do adjectives like grand, petit, beau, joli and vieux come before the noun in French, unlike most adjectives?
cards.answer: They are common adjectives that the lesson states come before the noun, while most other adjectives come after it.

cards.front: Why is 'une grande cuisine' spelled with 'grande' but 'un petit jardin' spelled with 'petit'?
cards.answer: Adjectives must agree with the noun's gender, so they change form for feminine nouns like cuisine and masculine nouns like jardin.

title: Ethics in Sport: Sportsmanship, Gamesmanship and Deviance
subject: physical-education-ocr

cards.front: Name the four examples of deviant behaviour given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Using performance-enhancing drugs / Deliberately injuring an opponent / Match-fixing / Persistent verbal abuse of officials

cards.front: Name three golf etiquette customs the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Repair divots / Rake bunkers / Maintain silence when others are playing
items: Maintain silence when others are playing

cards.front: Why does a win-at-all-costs culture lead to deviant behaviour in sport?
cards.answer: Because winning is prioritised above all other values by athletes, coaches, clubs or the media, gradually eroding ethical boundaries.

cards.front: How do financial incentives amplify a win-at-all-costs culture in elite sport?
cards.answer: Prize money, sponsorship and status attached to winning create intense pressure on performers to succeed at any cost.

cards.front: Name the four periods the thematic study of migration covers.
cards.answer: Medieval, c800-c1500 / Early modern, c1500-c1700 / Industrial, c1700-c1900 / Modern, c1900-present

cards.front: Name the five turning points the lesson lists for the migration thematic study.
cards.answer: 1290 expulsion / 1685 Huguenot wave / 1905 Aliens Act / 1948 British Nationality Act / 1962 Commonwealth Immigrants Act

cards.front: Why does the 1290 expulsion of England's Jewish population mix several key factors together?
cards.answer: It combined institutions (a royal decree from Edward I), religion (Christian hostility) and economics (royal debts owed to Jewish lenders).

cards.front: Why does the 1948 British Nationality Act mix several key factors together?
cards.answer: It combined institutions (Parliament passing the Act) with end-of-Empire politics and post-war labour shortages.

cards.front: Name the five aspects of Elizabethan society the lesson says you must understand as context for Romeo and Juliet.
cards.answer: Attitudes to love / Marriage / Family honour / Gender roles / Religion

cards.front: What three things does Juliet's refusal to marry Paris challenge at once, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Patriarchal authority / Religious expectations / Family honour

cards.front: Why is Romeo's love for Rosaline described as performative rather than genuine?
cards.answer: He speaks in contradictory oxymorons like 'loving hate', showing he is performing the role of a lover rather than truly feeling love.

cards.front: Why does Romeo and Juliet's secret marriage act as a trap as well as a bond?
cards.answer: Marriage was a sacred, unbreakable sacrament, so once secretly married Juliet was already wed before God and could not marry Paris.

title: Birmingham, Washington and the Civil Rights Act, 1963-64
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Why did King and Wyatt Tee Walker choose Birmingham as the 1963 campaign target?
cards.answer: They expected police commissioner Bull Connor to react with public violence, forcing the country to see what segregation actually was.

cards.front: Why did Freedom Summer deliberately recruit mainly white Northern student volunteers?
cards.answer: Organisers knew violence against Black activists alone was ignored, but violence against white students would generate national news.

cards.front: How did the murder of the three Freedom Summer volunteers help the civil rights movement, despite no murder convictions at the time?
cards.answer: It put the lack of Black voting rights in the national news and led to the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party's convention challenge.

cards.front: Name the three things the 1964 Civil Rights Act banned segregation in.
cards.answer: Public accommodations / Federally funded programmes / Employment

title: The Impact of War on Others
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three poems in the lesson about war's impact on people beyond the battlefield, and their poets.
cards.answer: Poppies by Jane Weir / War Photographer by Carole Satyamurti / What Were They Like? by Denise Levertov
items: What Were They Like? by Denise Levertov

cards.front: Why does the photographer in Satyamurti's War Photographer find 'the reassurance of the frame' fragile?
cards.answer: Because the photographs later force the photographer to confront what they witnessed, even in the safety of the darkroom.

cards.front: How does the word 'crimped' in Poppies add to the poem's meaning?
cards.answer: It suggests the poppy is carefully handmade, fragile and easily damaged, mirroring the mother's fragile emotions.

cards.front: Name the three skills the lesson says Cromwell learned working on Wolsey's monastery project.
cards.answer: How to value monastic property / How to draft Acts of Parliament / How to manage royal commissioners on the ground
items: How to draft Acts of Parliament
How to manage royal commissioners on the ground

cards.front: Name the three offices/roles Cromwell held by 1535 that let him run government from one desk.
cards.answer: Principal Secretary / Master of the Rolls / Vicegerent in Spirituals

cards.front: How did Cromwell's statutory argument let Henry get his annulment without going through Rome?
cards.answer: Parliament could declare England a self-sufficient empire whose king answered to no foreign prince, so no English court needed papal permission on the marriage.

cards.front: Why did Henry promote Cromwell so quickly through 1530–1533?
cards.answer: Cromwell's promotions tracked his usefulness, offering Henry a route to the annulment via statute that Wolsey, More and the bishops could not provide.

title: Circuit Symbols, Voltage and Current Rules
subject: electronics-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four test instruments the lesson says you need to know how to connect and use.
cards.answer: Voltmeter / Ammeter / Logic probe / Oscilloscope

cards.front: Name the three types of waveform a signal generator produces.
cards.answer: Sine wave / Square wave / Triangular wave

cards.front: Why does a voltmeter have very high input resistance?
cards.answer: So it draws negligible current, meaning it doesn't affect the circuit it's measuring.

cards.front: Why can setting a multimeter to the wrong mode damage it?
cards.answer: On the current setting it has almost zero resistance, so connecting it in parallel across a supply can damage it.

cards.front: In the truth table for (A AND B) OR (NOT C), why is the output True whenever C is False?
cards.answer: When C is False, NOT C is True, so the OR output is True regardless of A and B.

cards.front: Why does a bank transfer example use AND rather than OR to check authentication and funds?
cards.answer: Because both conditions (authenticated AND sufficient funds) must hold for the transfer to be authorised.

cards.front: Name the four potential benefits of autonomous vehicles given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Reduced road accidents caused by human error / Improved mobility for people who cannot drive / Smoother traffic flow / Reduced need for parking in cities
items: Reduced road accidents caused by human error
Improved mobility for people who cannot drive
Reduced need for parking in cities

cards.front: Name the three main categories of environmental impact of digital technology.
cards.answer: Manufacturing / Energy consumption in use / Disposal

cards.front: Why is hacking a serious risk for autonomous vehicles?
cards.answer: Because the vehicle is essentially a computer on wheels, hacking could let someone manipulate it remotely, creating a physical safety risk.

cards.front: How does manufacturing electronic devices harm the environment?
cards.answer: Mining metals like lithium and cobalt for devices causes habitat destruction, water pollution and carbon emissions, even before use.

title: English sailors: Hawkins, Drake, Raleigh and exploration
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four connected reasons the lesson gives for why the Roanoke colony failed.
cards.answer: Site poorly chosen with shallow inlets / Arrived too late to plant crops / Violent breakdown with the Algonquian / War with Spain took ships away
items: Site poorly chosen with shallow inlets
Arrived too late to plant crops
War with Spain took ships away

cards.front: Name the three trading companies the lesson lists as part of England's wider sea power.
cards.answer: Muscovy Company (1555) / Levant Company (1581) / East India Company (1600)

cards.front: Why did the second Roanoke colony's food supply break down into violence with the Algonquian?
cards.answer: The colonists became dependent on the Algonquian for food after arriving too late to plant their own crops.

cards.front: Why is Hawkins's redesign of the navy from 1577 seen as his most lasting contribution?
cards.answer: His race-built galleons — lighter, faster and more heavily gunned — were the ships that defeated the Armada eleven years later.

title: Act 3: Eric, the Speech & the Twist
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name the three people or things Mrs Birling deflects blame onto in Act 3.
cards.answer: Eva Smith ('she had only herself to blame') / Eric ('I didn't know — I didn't understand') / The Inspector (calling his manner 'rude and assertive')
items: Eva Smith ('she had only herself to blame')
Eric ('I didn't know — I didn't understand')
The Inspector (calling his manner 'rude and assertive')

cards.front: Name the three steps the older generation take to prove Inspector Goole wasn't real.
cards.answer: Gerald meets a police sergeant who knows no such inspector / Birling rings the chief constable to confirm it / Gerald rings the infirmary and no girl has died
items: Gerald meets a police sergeant who knows no such inspector
Birling rings the chief constable to confirm it
Gerald rings the infirmary and no girl has died

cards.front: Why does the lesson describe Eric's alcoholism as 'a product of privilege'?
cards.answer: He drinks because he can afford to, nobody in the family holds him accountable, and his father's emotional distance leaves him without guidance.

cards.front: Why does the Inspector's phrase 'millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths' matter?
cards.answer: It elevates Eva Smith from an individual victim into a symbol representing all working-class people.

cards.front: Name the three steps to measure the density of a liquid.
cards.answer: Measure mass of empty measuring cylinder / Pour in liquid and measure total mass / Read volume at bottom of meniscus, then apply ρ = m/V
items: Measure mass of empty measuring cylinder
Pour in liquid and measure total mass
Read volume at bottom of meniscus, then apply ρ = m/V

cards.front: Why does a liquid have a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
cards.answer: Particles are close together but the weaker forces between them let them slide past each other, so they flow into the container's shape while staying close together.

cards.front: Why does pressure in a fluid increase with depth?
cards.answer: A deeper column of fluid has more fluid weight above it, pressing down and increasing the force on any surface at that depth.

cards.front: Why is the density of a gas much lower than the same substance as a liquid?
cards.answer: Gas particles are very widely spaced compared to liquid particles, so the same mass occupies far more volume, making density about a thousand times lower.

cards.front: Name the stages of Mickey's decline that Russell shows across the play.
cards.answer: Energetic teenager / Factory worker / Unemployed man / Criminal / Prisoner / Medicated shell of himself

cards.front: Why does Russell shift from upbeat songs to sombre ones as the play moves into adolescence and adulthood?
cards.answer: The musical form compresses emotion in ways dialogue cannot, and the darkening songs mirror the play's darkening tone.

cards.front: Why does Mickey's childhood admiration for Eddie turn into toxic resentment in adulthood?
cards.answer: Class inequality destroys Mickey's self-esteem, friendships and mental health, curdling his harmless admiration into resentment.

cards.front: Name the three things self-management programmes help individuals do.
cards.answer: Identify triggers for substance use / Develop coping strategies / Set goals for reducing or stopping use
items: Set goals for reducing or stopping use

cards.front: Name the two types of therapy for addiction described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Aversion therapy / Self-management programmes

cards.front: How does social learning theory explain why people imitate peers who use substances?
cards.answer: Observing peers use substances and seeing them rewarded socially or through pleasure increases the likelihood of imitation.

cards.front: Why might combining aversion therapy with self-management programmes be more effective than using either alone?
cards.answer: Aversion therapy works quickly but may not stop relapse, while self-management is more comprehensive, so combining both improves outcomes.

cards.front: Name the four Catholic grievances in Northern Ireland listed by the lesson.
cards.answer: Discrimination in council housing allocation / Gerrymandered electoral boundaries / Discrimination in employment / Special powers act allowing detention without trial
items: Special powers act allowing detention without trial

cards.front: Why did the march in Londonderry/Derry on 5 October 1968 mark the start of the Troubles?
cards.answer: The RUC attacked the march with batons and it was filmed and broadcast, shocking British and international audiences.

cards.front: Why did internment in 1971 fail to suppress the IRA?
cards.answer: It used outdated intelligence, arrested mostly Catholics with no paramilitary links, which fuelled anger and swelled IRA recruitment.

cards.front: Why did the Sunningdale power-sharing executive collapse in 1974?
cards.answer: Unionists opposed the Irish dimension and the Ulster Workers' Council general strike brought Northern Ireland to a standstill, forcing its collapse.

cards.front: Name the three addition reactions alkenes undergo, given in the lesson (with hydrogen, water, and bromine).
cards.answer: With hydrogen to produce an alkane / With water/steam to produce an alcohol / With bromine to produce a dibromo compound
items: With hydrogen to produce an alkane
With water/steam to produce an alcohol
With bromine to produce a dibromo compound

cards.front: Why are alkenes more reactive than alkanes?
cards.answer: Because alkenes have a C=C double bond that can open up and react with other atoms.

cards.front: Why don't alkanes decolourise bromine water?
cards.answer: Because alkanes have no double bonds for bromine to add across.

cards.front: Why is the reaction of ethanol with sodium less vigorous than sodium with water?
cards.answer: The lesson states this reaction is less vigorous than sodium reacting with water.

title: Identity and Diversity in the UK
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: What four levels does the lesson say shape a person's identity?
cards.answer: Individual level / Group level / National level / Global level

cards.front: Which religions does the lesson name as practised in the UK, alongside a growing group with no religion?
cards.answer: Christianity / Islam / Hinduism / Sikhism / Judaism / Buddhism

cards.front: Why does the lesson say identity is not fixed?
cards.answer: It shifts over time as a person's circumstances, relationships and experiences change.

cards.front: Why does having multiple identities not mean someone is disloyal to the UK?
cards.answer: Because these identities reinforce rather than compete with one another in most people's experience.

title: Christian Beliefs: God, Creation and Jesus
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six events in the sequence of Jesus' last days given in Luke 22–24.
cards.answer: Last Supper / Betrayal and arrest in Gethsemane / Trial before High Priest and Pilate / Crucifixion on Golgotha / Burial / Resurrection
items: Trial before High Priest and Pilate

cards.front: How does substitutionary atonement explain how the cross achieves salvation?
cards.answer: Jesus took humanity's punishment for sin in their place.

cards.front: How does the moral influence theory explain how the cross achieves salvation?
cards.answer: The cross shows God's love so powerfully that it draws humanity to repentance.

cards.front: Name the four monosyllabic adjectives given in the lesson that gain an umlaut in the comparative.
cards.answer: warm → wärmer / kalt → kälter / gesund → gesünder / scharf → schärfer

cards.front: Name the five key past participles for food verbs given in the lesson.
cards.answer: essen → gegessen / trinken → getrunken / bestellen → bestellt / kochen → gekocht / finden → gefunden

cards.front: Why does the conjugated verb move to the end of the clause when you use weil or obwohl?
cards.answer: Because weil and obwohl are subordinating conjunctions, and both send the conjugated verb to the end of their clause.

cards.front: How does the word order work when you combine a comparative with weil, e.g. 'weil es süßer als Brot ist'?
cards.answer: The verb still moves to the end of the clause, even when there is a comparative plus als phrase before it.

cards.front: Name the three things monasteries provided for the poor, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Food at the gate / Beds in the guesthouse / Prayers for the dead

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why some people supported the dissolution.
cards.answer: Gentry buying cheap monastic land / Protestants saw monasteries as superstitious and wasteful / Towns repurposed buildings as schools or civic halls / Lollard communities in Kent and Essex welcomed removal of idolatry
items: Protestants saw monasteries as superstitious and wasteful
Towns repurposed buildings as schools or civic halls
Lollard communities in Kent and Essex welcomed removal of idolatry

cards.front: Why did the Pilgrimage of Grace fail despite having 30,000-40,000 supporters?
cards.answer: It lacked a noble military commander willing to take the field, as the northern earls were reluctant to commit to treason.

cards.front: Why could Mary I not restore the monasteries during her Catholic restoration of 1554-1555?
cards.answer: The monastic land had already been sold to new owners, who refused to give it back.

title: Measuring Development: GNI, HDI & the DTM
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the five social indicators of development given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Infant mortality / Life expectancy / Literacy rates / Doctors per 1,000 people / Access to safe water

cards.front: Name the five stages of the Demographic Transition Model in order.
cards.answer: High fluctuating / Early expanding / Late expanding / Low fluctuating / Decline

cards.front: Why is HDI more useful than GNI per head alone for measuring development?
cards.answer: HDI shows whether a country's wealth is actually being turned into better health and education, not just income.

cards.front: Why does Stage 5 of the DTM create a problem for a country?
cards.answer: Birth rate falls below death rate, so the population shrinks and ages, leaving fewer workers to support many pensioners.

title: Revelation, Visions and Miracles in Islam
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What three grounds do Atheists and Humanists give for challenging Islamic claims about the Qur'an and visions?
cards.answer: Beauty or complexity isn't evidence of divine authorship / All religions claim unique authority, so claims cancel out / Visions may have natural psychological explanations
items: Beauty or complexity isn't evidence of divine authorship
All religions claim unique authority, so claims cancel out
Visions may have natural psychological explanations

cards.front: What three responses do Muslims give to atheist and humanist challenges about the Qur'an?
cards.answer: The inimitability challenge has stood 1,400 years unanswered / Its consistency and preservation are themselves remarkable / The transformation it produces in believers is evidence of a real source
items: The inimitability challenge has stood 1,400 years unanswered
Its consistency and preservation are themselves remarkable
The transformation it produces in believers is evidence of a real source

cards.front: Why is the Islamic understanding of the Qur'an fundamentally different from most Christian understandings of the Bible?
cards.answer: Muslims believe the Qur'an is the direct speech of Allah himself, not a book written about God by humans.

cards.front: Why don't Muslims automatically accept every claimed vision or true dream as genuine divine communication?
cards.answer: Scholarly tradition requires such experiences to be consistent with the Qur'an and Sunnah before they are accepted as real.

cards.front: Name the nine criteria Aitchison uses to judge whether a communication system is a language.
cards.answer: Semanticity / Displacement / Arbitrariness / Productivity / Cultural transmission / Spontaneous usage / Turn-taking / Duality / Structure dependence

cards.front: Name the three animal communication examples the lesson uses to show shared function with human language.
cards.answer: Vervet monkeys' alarm calls for different predators / Bees' dance movements showing food source location / Bird song to attract mates or defend territory
items: Vervet monkeys' alarm calls for different predators
Bees' dance movements showing food source location
Bird song to attract mates or defend territory

cards.front: Why do most animal communication systems lack duality and structure dependence?
cards.answer: Animal signals function as a single whole rather than being built from smaller meaningless units combined by grammar rules.

cards.front: Why is cultural transmission limited in most animal communication systems?
cards.answer: Animal calls are largely instinctive and consistent across the species rather than learned from a particular community.

title: The English Revolution: Civil War, Regicide and Republic, 1642-1660
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four interlocking causes of the English Revolution given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Ideas: Divine Right vs Parliament's consent / Religion: Laudian reforms vs Puritan reformers / Money: ship money and the Personal Rule / Political crisis: Grand Remonstrance and failed arrest of Five Members
items: Ideas: Divine Right vs Parliament's consent
Religion: Laudian reforms vs Puritan reformers
Money: ship money and the Personal Rule
Political crisis: Grand Remonstrance and failed arrest of Five Members

cards.front: Name the four demands set out in the Levellers' 1647 Agreement of the People.
cards.answer: Manhood suffrage (excluding servants and beggars) / Regular elections / Religious liberty / Equality before the law

cards.front: Why did the New Model Army become a political force after the First Civil War ended in 1646?
cards.answer: Soldiers were owed back pay and many were Puritans with strong religious convictions, leading to radical movements like the Levellers.

cards.front: Why did the army decide Charles I could not be trusted alive in 1648?
cards.answer: Charles started a Second Civil War from his prison at Carisbrooke by plotting with the Scots, angering the army.

cards.front: What four steps does the lesson recommend when reading a graph or chart in a business question?
cards.answer: Read the title and axis labels / Check the units on each axis / Identify the trend before stating values / Note any anomalies and their possible cause
items: Read the title and axis labels
Check the units on each axis
Identify the trend before stating values
Note any anomalies and their possible cause

cards.front: Name the four main categories of data a business uses to understand performance, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Financial data / Marketing data / Market data / Data from graphs and charts

cards.front: Why can having access to more data actually lead to worse or slower business decisions?
cards.answer: Too much data without the ability to filter and interpret it causes 'analysis paralysis', delaying decisions while more information is gathered.

cards.front: How can national market data mislead a business about its own position?
cards.answer: National market size figures may not accurately represent the specific niche or region the business actually operates in.

cards.front: What are the three types of plate boundary described in the lesson?
cards.answer: Convergent boundary / Divergent boundary / Conservative boundary

cards.front: Name the five volcanic hazards the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Lava flows / Ash falls / Pyroclastic flows / Lahars / Toxic gases

cards.front: Why are shallow earthquakes usually more damaging than deep ones?
cards.answer: Because they occur under 70 km deep, so their energy reaches the surface concentrated rather than spread out.

cards.front: Why is basaltic volcanic activity rarely deadly compared to andesitic eruptions?
cards.answer: Basaltic magma is fluid and produces gentle lava flows, while andesitic magma is sticky, trapping gas that builds up into explosive eruptions.

title: The Grand Alliance & the Origins of the Cold War
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What four things did the 'Big Three' agree at the Yalta Conference in February 1945?
cards.answer: Divide Germany into four zones of occupation / Hold free elections in liberated countries / Set up the United Nations / Allow the USSR to enter the war against Japan
items: Divide Germany into four zones of occupation
Hold free elections in liberated countries
Allow the USSR to enter the war against Japan

cards.front: According to the lesson, in what three ways did the atomic bomb transform superpower relations?
cards.answer: Gave the USA a nuclear monopoly / Truman used it for atomic diplomacy / Stalin accelerated the Soviet nuclear programme
items: Gave the USA a nuclear monopoly
Truman used it for atomic diplomacy
Stalin accelerated the Soviet nuclear programme

cards.front: Why did the Grand Alliance break down once Nazi Germany was defeated?
cards.answer: The shared enemy holding the alliance together disappeared, letting the deep ideological differences between capitalism and communism resurface and drive the powers apart.

cards.front: Why did Stalin want a buffer zone of friendly states in Eastern Europe?
cards.answer: Because the USSR had suffered around 27 million deaths in the war and Stalin wanted to prevent any future invasion.

cards.front: Name the four individual responses the lesson gives for reducing a consumer's ecological footprint.
cards.answer: Choosing seasonal local food / Eating less meat / Repairing rather than replacing electronics / Reducing fast-fashion buys

cards.front: Name the four government responses the lesson gives for tackling consumer environmental impact.
cards.answer: Carbon taxes / Plastic bag charges / Mandatory recycling / Right-to-repair laws

cards.front: Why does e-waste still end up in places like Ghana or Nigeria despite stricter international rules?
cards.answer: The Basel Convention has reduced flows, but poor recycling infrastructure means much e-waste still ends up where it shouldn't.

cards.front: How do HIC consumer choices reshape environments in LICs, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Through palm-oil deforestation, food-mile emissions and shipped e-waste, connecting supermarket choices to ecosystems on the other side of the world.

title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four consequences of global warming given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sea level rise / More extreme weather events / Changes to ecosystems and species distribution / Impacts on agriculture
items: Changes to ecosystems and species distribution

cards.front: Name the five ways the lesson gives to reduce a carbon footprint.
cards.answer: Use renewable energy / Improve energy efficiency / Carbon capture and storage / Reduce meat consumption / Reduce travel

cards.front: How did the oceans form from Earth's early atmosphere?
cards.answer: Water vapour in the early atmosphere condensed as the Earth cooled, forming the oceans.

cards.front: How did the ozone layer form and why was this important for life?
cards.answer: As oxygen levels increased, the ozone layer formed, shielding life on Earth from UV radiation.

title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the four atomic models covered in the lesson, in the order they were proposed.
cards.answer: Dalton's solid sphere model (1803) / Thomson's plum pudding model (1897) / Rutherford's nuclear model (1909) / Bohr's electron shell model (1913)

cards.front: Name the three types of particles that make up an atom.
cards.answer: Protons / Neutrons / Electrons

cards.front: Why did Rutherford's gold foil results show that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus?
cards.answer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, but some bounced back, showing a small, dense, positively charged region.

cards.front: Why don't neutrons affect an atom's chemical properties?
cards.answer: Neutrons are neutral particles with no charge, so they only add mass and aren't involved in chemical bonding.

title: The Depression and the rise of the Nazis 1929-1933
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the five intersecting factors the lesson gives for Hitler's rise to power.
cards.answer: The Depression (economic) / Failure of parliamentary government (political) / The divided left (party politics) / Nazi propaganda (movement strength) / Elite miscalculation by Hindenburg and von Papen (individual decisions)
items: Elite miscalculation by Hindenburg and von Papen (individual decisions)

cards.front: Name the three scapegoats the lesson says Nazi propaganda offered voters.
cards.answer: Jews / Marxists / The 'November criminals'

cards.front: Why did the collapse of the Grand Coalition in March 1930 end parliamentary government in Germany?
cards.answer: The SPD and Centre Party could not agree on funding unemployment benefits, so from then Germany was ruled by presidential decree under Article 48.

cards.front: Why did Germany's conservative elite support Hitler's appointment as Chancellor in January 1933?
cards.answer: The KPD's growth terrified them, so they believed they could use Hitler as a weapon against communism and then control him.

title: Pioneer Farmers, the Journey West and the Miners
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four types of hardship/danger the lesson gives for pioneers on the trail.
cards.answer: Disease (cholera, typhoid, dysentery) / Accidents (children run over, drownings, gunshots) / Weather (hailstorms, lightning, blizzards) / Oxen stampedes

cards.front: Name the two push factors and two pull factors the lesson gives for pioneer farmers going west.
cards.answer: Soil exhaustion in the east / The 1837 Panic (banking crisis) / Fertile Willamette Valley land / Free or cheap land

cards.front: Why did the Donner Party get trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in 1846?
cards.answer: They took an untested shortcut from a guidebook that cost about a month, so they reached the mountains just as heavy snow hit the passes.

cards.front: Why did the Gold Rush speed up calls for a transcontinental railroad?
cards.answer: Because the months-long sea route around Cape Horn was no longer fit for purpose given the huge numbers travelling to California.

cards.front: Name the three examples of juxtaposition the lesson gives from Julius Caesar.
cards.answer: Brutus's prose beside Antony's verse / Portia's courage beside Calpurnia's fear / conspirators' idealism beside triumvirate's ruthlessness

cards.front: Why does Antony's funeral speech overpower Brutus's, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Antony's verse gives his words musical, emotional power that overwhelms the reasoned appeal of Brutus's plain prose.

cards.front: How does dramatic irony make Brutus's decision to spare Antony land more powerfully?
cards.answer: The audience knows sparing Antony and letting him speak will be catastrophic, so each misjudgement carries force Brutus cannot see.

cards.front: How does the crowd's behaviour reveal the play's political message about democracy?
cards.answer: Their fickleness shows democracy is only as stable as the people's judgement, which a skilled speaker can manipulate.

title: Treating Depression and Addiction: CBT and Drugs
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four lenses used to evaluate treatments for depression and addiction.
cards.answer: Validity / Reliability / Generalisability / Ethics

cards.front: How does behavioural activation help treat depression in CBT?
cards.answer: It gradually reintroduces activities the person has withdrawn from because of low mood.

cards.front: Why can CBT's effects outlast a course of medication?
cards.answer: Because CBT teaches skills the client can keep using after treatment ends.

title: Kingship, Succession and Ruling England in Richard's Absence
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five reasons the lesson gives for why royal government did not collapse during Richard's ten-year absence.
cards.answer: Strong existing institutions from Henry II / Hubert Walter's outstanding administration / Eleanor of Aquitaine as political fixer / John's failed 1191-94 power grab united barons / Pope and Archbishop anchored Richard's legitimacy
items: Strong existing institutions from Henry II
Eleanor of Aquitaine as political fixer
John's failed 1191-94 power grab united barons
Pope and Archbishop anchored Richard's legitimacy

cards.front: Name the four tasks the sheriff performed in each shire, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Collected royal revenues / Banked money at the Exchequer / Presided over the shire court / Led the county levy in arms
items: Led the county levy in arms

cards.front: Why did Richard sell offices, charters and castles soon after becoming king in 1189?
cards.answer: He needed money quickly to fund his crusade, so he raised cash by selling offices, charters and castles.

cards.front: Why did John's 1191-94 attempt to seize power actually help hold Richard's government together?
cards.answer: It gave the loyal barons a clear enemy to unite against, pushing them to defend Richard's government.

cards.front: Name the four forces the lesson gives for the growth of spectator sport in Victorian Britain.
cards.answer: Industrialisation creating concentrated working-class populations / Railways enabling travel to away matches / Legal reforms giving workers free time / Codification of rules by educated men
items: Railways enabling travel to away matches
Legal reforms giving workers free time
Codification of rules by educated men

cards.front: How did the 1885 legalisation of professional football change who could play the sport?
cards.answer: It opened the game to working-class players who could not afford to play as unpaid amateurs.

cards.front: How did the 1992 Premier League TV deal change English football?
cards.answer: Selling broadcast rights to Sky Sports raised wages sharply, brought overseas players, and turned clubs into global commercial brands.

cards.front: Why did the Football League's growth lead clubs to build enclosed grounds?
cards.answer: So they could charge admission to matches and use the income to fund their activities.

cards.front: What three stages make up the novel's Bildungsroman arc, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Innocence — the early comic chapters / Experience — the racism, the betrayal, the broken leg / Maturity — the break with Anita and the grammar school place
items: Experience — the racism, the betrayal, the broken leg
Maturity — the break with Anita and the grammar school place

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say Meena has that Anita does not?
cards.answer: A loving family / A rich cultural heritage / The intellectual ability to imagine a different future
items: The intellectual ability to imagine a different future

cards.front: Why does Syal present Anita's fate with sorrowful understanding rather than condemnation?
cards.answer: Because Anita is shaped by her environment — the neglect, poverty and lack of aspiration in the Rutter family, showing class harms as much as racism.

cards.front: Why is Meena's rejection of Anita described as self-assertion rather than anger?
cards.answer: Because it is a quiet, decisive choice to stop seeking validation from someone who will never truly offer it.

cards.front: Name the six output devices listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Lamp / LED / Buzzer / Solenoid / Motor / Servo / Loudspeaker

cards.front: Name the three common errors students make with block diagrams.
cards.answer: Mixing up stages / Inventing blocks not needed / Omitting the transducer driver

cards.front: Why does the security light example use an AND gate rather than a single sensor?
cards.answer: The light must only turn on when it is dark AND movement is detected, so the AND gate output is HIGH only when both sensor inputs are HIGH.

cards.front: Why would a designer use a latch instead of a simple logic gate for an output that must stay on?
cards.answer: A latch holds its output HIGH or LOW until told to change, so the output stays on even after the trigger signal is removed.

cards.front: Name the three types of evidence for evolution given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Fossil record / Comparative anatomy / DNA analysis

cards.front: List the four steps of Darwin's theory of natural selection.
cards.answer: Individuals show variation / Individuals compete for limited resources / Best suited survive and reproduce / Advantageous alleles passed to offspring

cards.front: Why did dark peppered moths become more common during the Industrial Revolution?
