cards.answer: Health / Fitness / Exercise / Performance

cards.front: Why can someone be very fit but not fully healthy, using the gymnast example from the lesson?
cards.answer: An elite gymnast may have excellent flexibility, endurance and body composition, yet suffer disordered eating or stress-related injury, compromising health despite high fitness.

cards.front: Why is fitness described as specific to the demands of the activity, rather than being one fixed quality?
cards.answer: Because different environments demand different abilities, so a sprinter needs explosive power and speed while a marathon runner needs cardiovascular endurance.

cards.front: Name the five principles of training the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Specificity / Progressive overload / Reversibility / Variance (tedium) / Individual needs

cards.front: Name the three overtraining injuries the lesson gives as common examples.
cards.answer: Stress fractures / Tendinopathy / Muscle strains

cards.front: Why can changing the Type variable in FITT create a different physiological adaptation?
cards.answer: Switching training method, such as from continuous running to interval training, recruits the anaerobic energy system more heavily.

cards.front: Why does rest allow fitness improvements to happen after training?
cards.answer: During exercise muscle fibres are micro-damaged, and it is during recovery that the body repairs and strengthens them, producing adaptation.

cards.front: Name the four other resistive/analogue sensing types described besides the LDR and thermistor.
cards.answer: Pressure sensor (force-sensitive resistor) / Moisture sensor (copper tracks) / Sound sensor (electret microphone + amplifier) / Potentiometer (variable resistor)

cards.front: Why does an LDR as R1 with a fixed resistor as R2 give a LOW V_out in the dark?
cards.answer: In the dark the LDR's resistance is large, so most of the supply voltage drops across R1, leaving little across R2.

cards.front: Why should you write a one-line logic check before drawing a sensing circuit that must trigger when warm?
cards.answer: It confirms whether placing the thermistor as R1 makes V_out rise with heat, preventing the common orientation mistake.

cards.front: Why is a pulse generator never placed in the sensor position of a voltage divider?
cards.answer: It is used purely as a timing input feeding a clock, not to sense a physical quantity via resistance change.

title: The Boom: Consumerism, Mass Production and Republican Policy
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three Republican policies the lesson says powered the Boom.
cards.answer: Laissez-faire (minimal government interference) / High tariffs like Fordney–McCumber / Low taxation on the rich

cards.front: Name the five industries the car boom pulled along with it, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Steel / Rubber / Glass / Leather / Paint

cards.front: How did Mellon's tax cuts and the Fordney–McCumber Tariff together set up the Wall Street boom?
cards.answer: Tariffs and tax cuts meant factories sold more and profits rose, leaving shareholders spare cash to invest in the stock market.

cards.front: Why did advertising in the 1920s change from describing products to selling feelings?
cards.answer: Advertisers used psychologists and new techniques to sell how a product would make buyers feel modern, attractive and successful.

cards.front: Name the four features that always describe a Newton's third law force pair.
cards.answer: Same type of force / Act on two different objects / Equal in magnitude / Opposite in direction

cards.front: Why does an object moving in a circle at constant speed still count as accelerating?
cards.answer: Its direction is constantly changing, so its velocity changes even though its speed stays the same.

cards.front: Why is a loaded trolley harder to push than an empty one?
cards.answer: The loaded trolley has a larger inertial mass, so a larger force is needed to produce the same acceleration.

cards.front: Why does mass stay the same everywhere while weight changes?
cards.answer: Mass is scalar and constant, but weight depends on gravitational field strength, which varies from place to place.

cards.front: Name the four different verb patterns Spanish uses to express weather.
cards.answer: hace (for most expressions) / llueve/nieva (standalone verbs) / hay (for fog and storms) / está (for cloudy)

cards.front: Name the six subject pronouns given in the past continuous conjugation table.
cards.answer: yo / tú / él/ella / nosotros / vosotros / ellos/ellas

cards.front: Why does the model past holiday paragraph combine the preterite and imperfect tenses?
cards.answer: The preterite (fui) shows completed actions while the imperfect (hacía, nadábamos) gives ongoing descriptions, combining them for richer writing.

cards.front: How does combining the past continuous with the preterite improve writing, as in 'Estaba tomando el sol cuando empezó a llover'?
cards.answer: The past continuous sets the scene of what was happening, then the preterite shows the sudden action that interrupted it.

cards.front: Name the four features that typically define Victorian adventure fiction as a genre.
cards.answer: Western protagonist tested by ingenuity and stoicism / loyal, comic companion providing audience's emotional reaction / series of exotic locations each with distinctive character / resolution confirming the protagonist's superiority through success
items: Western protagonist tested by ingenuity and stoicism
loyal, comic companion providing audience's emotional reaction
series of exotic locations each with distinctive character
resolution confirming the protagonist's superiority through success

cards.front: What three facts can a student draw on to explain how historical context shapes a director's choices for the India scenes?
cards.answer: Verne wrote these scenes from a colonial gaze / Eason adapted the play for a post-colonial 21st-century audience / physical theatre allows critical handling without pausing the adventure
items: Verne wrote these scenes from a colonial gaze
Eason adapted the play for a post-colonial 21st-century audience
physical theatre allows critical handling without pausing the adventure

cards.front: Why does Fogg's devotion to his schedule carry deeper cultural meaning rather than just being a personality quirk?
cards.answer: It satirises Victorian industrial modernity, where standardised time, telegraph speed and timetable precision had become a cultural value.

cards.front: How does Eason's physical-theatre form comment on the colonial-adventure genre it adapts?
cards.answer: By making the ensemble's construction of the story visible, it invites the audience to watch storytelling as storytelling rather than be absorbed uncritically into the colonial adventure.

title: The Sun: Structure, Fusion and Atmosphere
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the Sun's four internal regions from centre outwards.
cards.answer: Core / Radiative zone / Convective zone / Photosphere

cards.front: Which layer of the Sun dominates when observing in visible light, UV, and X-rays respectively?
cards.answer: Visible light: photosphere / Ultraviolet: chromosphere / X-rays: corona

cards.front: Why does energy take around 100,000 years to travel from the Sun's core to its surface?
cards.answer: Photons are repeatedly absorbed and re-emitted by plasma particles on their way outward, slowing their journey enormously.

cards.front: Why do bright granules and dark intergranule lanes appear on the photosphere?
cards.answer: Bright granules are tops of rising hot plasma columns and dark lanes are cooler plasma sinking back down in the convective zone.

cards.front: Why might an entrepreneur work long hours for little or no immediate return even after their business survives its early stages?
cards.answer: The business may go months without generating enough revenue to pay the owner a salary.

cards.front: How can financial reward include more than just the annual profit an entrepreneur earns?
cards.answer: It also includes the long-term value built up in a business that can eventually be sold.

cards.front: Name the three sealed documents featured in the novella's structure.
cards.answer: Jekyll's will / Lanyon's letter / Jekyll's own statement

cards.front: What three purposes does the multiple-narrator structure serve in the novella?
cards.answer: Creates suspense / mirrors the theme of concealment / suggests identity is never fully knowable
items: suggests identity is never fully knowable

cards.front: How does London's day/night contrast mirror Jekyll and Hyde's duality?
cards.answer: By day London's streets are busy and respectable, like Jekyll; by night they turn threatening and strange, like Hyde.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson shift to first-person narration in Jekyll's final statement?
cards.answer: The shift forces the reader into Jekyll's mind, creating uncomfortable intimacy so we understand him, not just judge him.

title: Causes of the Hundred Years' War
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four aims the lesson gives for Edward III at the start of the war.
cards.answer: Secure Aquitaine against French encroachment / End French support for Scotland / Demonstrate military prowess to the English nobility / Prospect of plunder, ransom and glory
items: Demonstrate military prowess to the English nobility
Prospect of plunder, ransom and glory

cards.front: Name the four underlying causes the lesson says shaped the whole Hundred Years' War.
cards.answer: Dynastic rivalry / Disputed territory / Scottish entanglement / French provocation

cards.front: Why did holding Aquitaine put English kings in an awkward position with France?
cards.answer: Holding Aquitaine made English kings feudal vassals of the French Crown, which caused problems when relations broke down.

cards.front: Why did Philip VI claim he had the right to confiscate Aquitaine in 1337?
cards.answer: Philip VI claimed Edward III had failed in his feudal obligations as a vassal for his French lands.

cards.front: Name the four situational influences on social behaviour covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Majority influence / Collective and crowd behaviour / Culture / Authority figures

cards.front: What three outfits did confederates wear in Bickman's 1974 study?
cards.answer: Everyday civilian clothing / A milkman's uniform / A security guard's uniform

cards.front: Why does a uniform increase obedience even when the wearer has no real power to reward or punish?
cards.answer: A uniform acts as a situational cue signalling legitimate authority, so people obey the appearance of authority itself.

cards.front: How does culture influence whether people act pro-socially or anti-socially?
cards.answer: Cultures emphasising collective wellbeing and cooperation encourage pro-social behaviour, while low trust in authority or others is linked to more anti-social behaviour.

title: Performance Interpretation: Comic Precision and Ensemble Trust
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four different roles the lesson gives as examples an actor might play across scenes in Around the World in 80 Days.
cards.answer: A Reform Club gentleman / An elephant's front legs / A Yokohama acrobat / A ship's captain

cards.front: What three vocal choices does the lesson's toolkit suggest for different minor roles (customs official, elephant-driver, Yokohama crowd)?
cards.answer: Clipped nasal RP with staccato rhythm for the customs official / Distinct tonal warmth and rhythmic pattern for the elephant-driver / Fragmented exclamatory sounds for the Yokohama crowd
items: Clipped nasal RP with staccato rhythm for the customs official
Distinct tonal warmth and rhythmic pattern for the elephant-driver
Fragmented exclamatory sounds for the Yokohama crowd

cards.front: Why does Fogg's refusal to react physically make the play's comedy work?
cards.answer: As the straight man, his deadpan stillness is the setup that allows everyone else's reactions to land as comedy.

cards.front: How does the lighting design isolate Fogg during the Reform Club wager?
cards.answer: A tight spotlight from above picks out his face and pocket watch while the ensemble is lit in a cooler, softer flood, drawing the audience's eye to him.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says Victorian women could not do in the 1840s.
cards.answer: Vote / Attend university / Enter most professions

cards.front: Name the three Gothic conventions the lesson says Brontë uses in Jane Eyre.
cards.answer: The red-room at Gateshead / The mysterious third floor at Thornfield / The figure of Bertha Mason
items: The mysterious third floor at Thornfield

cards.front: How does the red-room foreshadow Bertha Mason's imprisonment?
cards.answer: Both are enclosed spaces where women are locked away by patriarchal authority, Jane by Mrs Reed and Bertha by Rochester.

cards.front: Why was the governess position socially isolating in Victorian society?
cards.answer: Governesses were educated but paid so poorly they had no independence, too genteel to eat with servants yet not treated as family equals.

title: Life in Stalin's USSR by 1941: Workers, Women and Minorities
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four rewards top Stakhanovite performers received under Stalin's USSR.
cards.answer: Cash bonuses / Larger flats with own kitchens / Holiday vouchers to Black Sea sanatoria / Access to closed shops
items: Holiday vouchers to Black Sea sanatoria

cards.front: Name the four things the 1936 Family Code did to family life in the USSR.
cards.answer: Banned abortion / Made divorce expensive and bureaucratic / Restored awards for mothers of large families / Criminalised male non-payment of child support
items: Restored awards for mothers of large families
Criminalised male non-payment of child support

cards.front: Why did ordinary Soviet workers have to work harder after the Stakhanovite movement began?
cards.answer: Stakhanovite record performances were used to raise official production norms higher across whole industries.

cards.front: Why did the Soviet regime roll back family policy from 1936 despite promoting women's work?
cards.answer: It was both ideological, showing the regime as morally conservative before the war, and demographic, since famine, Terror and falling births had cut the population.

cards.front: Name the four main trap types described for oil and gas.
cards.answer: Anticline traps / Fault traps / Unconformity traps / Salt dome traps

cards.front: Name the three rock types that must be present together for a commercial oil deposit.
cards.answer: Source rock / Reservoir rock / Cap rock

cards.front: Why can a rock be highly porous but still impermeable, like pumice?
cards.answer: Its pores are numerous but not well-connected, so fluids cannot flow through them easily.

cards.front: Why are unconventional shale source rocks unsuitable for conventional extraction, requiring fracking instead?
cards.answer: Shale is too impermeable for hydrocarbons to flow to a well without artificially fracturing it first.

title: The Dhamma and the Three Marks of Existence
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the Five Aggregates (skandhas) that Theravada Buddhism says make up what we call the 'self'.
cards.answer: Form / Sensation / Perception / Mental formations / Consciousness

cards.front: Why is understanding dependent arising considered essential to liberation in Buddhism?
cards.answer: It dismantles the illusion that things, including the 'self', are solid, permanent and separate from everything else.

cards.front: Why does dependent arising lead to dukkha (unsatisfactoriness)?
cards.answer: Because we keep trying to find lasting satisfaction in impermanent things and a non-existent fixed self, we experience unsatisfactoriness.

title: Anglo-German Rivalry: Weltpolitik and the Naval Race
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five German colonial territories mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cameroon / German East Africa (Tanzania) / South-West Africa (Namibia) / Togo / Pacific islands

cards.front: Why was Germany's colonial empire modest and often unprofitable by 1900?
cards.answer: Germany was a latecomer to imperialism, so the world's best colonial territory was already taken by Britain, France and Russia.

cards.front: How do historians differ over Kaiser Wilhelm II's personal responsibility for Anglo-German rivalry?
cards.answer: Clark argues structural rivalry mattered more than Wilhelm's outbursts, while older accounts emphasise his erratic temperament; the truth is probably both.

cards.front: Name the four ferrous metals listed in the specification.
cards.answer: Cast iron / Low carbon steel / High carbon steel / Stainless steel

cards.front: Name the four smart materials specified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Shape memory alloy / Thermochromic pigment / Photochromic pigment / Quantum Tunnelling Composite

cards.front: Why does stainless steel resist corrosion so well?
cards.answer: Its chromium content forms a self-healing protective oxide layer on the surface.

cards.front: How does shape memory alloy (Nitinol) behave when heated above its transition temperature?
cards.answer: It deforms when cold but returns to its pre-set shape once heated above the transition temperature.

cards.front: Name the three things President Johnson announced in his televised address on 31 March 1968.
cards.answer: Partial halt to bombing of North Vietnam / Opening to peace talks / Decision not to seek re-election
items: Partial halt to bombing of North Vietnam

cards.front: Name the three events that shaped the 1968 election after Johnson withdrew from the race.
cards.answer: Robert Kennedy assassinated in June / Democratic Convention in Chicago dissolved into riots / Nixon won the November election narrowly
items: Democratic Convention in Chicago dissolved into riots
Nixon won the November election narrowly

cards.front: How did the siege of Khe Sanh help the Tet Offensive attackers elsewhere in South Vietnam?
cards.answer: It tied down US marine forces for 77 days, stopping them responding faster to the city attacks.

cards.front: How did the Cronkite report affect Johnson's political position?
cards.answer: Cronkite declared the war 'mired in stalemate', reportedly prompting Johnson to say he had lost middle America.

cards.front: Name the four types of radioactive emission the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Alpha / Beta / Gamma / Neutron emission

cards.front: Name the four scientists/models involved in the historical development of the atomic model, in order.
cards.answer: Dalton - solid sphere / Thomson - plum pudding / Rutherford - nuclear model / Chadwick - neutron

cards.front: How did the results of the Rutherford-Geiger-Marsden gold foil experiment show that the atom has a nucleus?
cards.answer: Most alpha particles passed straight through but some deflected sharply and a few bounced back, showing a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.

cards.front: Why is gamma radiation the most penetrating but least ionising type of radiation?
cards.answer: Ionising power and penetrating power are inversely related, so the weakly ionising gamma rays pass through most material instead of being absorbed.

cards.front: What three tactics does Lady Macbeth use to manipulate Macbeth in Act 1 Scene 7?
cards.answer: Attacks his masculinity / Uses the infanticide image / Presents a practical plan to frame the guards
items: Presents a practical plan to frame the guards

cards.front: What three reasons does Macbeth give against killing Duncan in his Act 1 Scene 7 soliloquy?
cards.answer: Duncan is his kinsman / Duncan is his subject / Duncan is his guest/host

cards.front: Why does the witches' second prophecy make the third seem inevitable to Macbeth?
cards.answer: Because the first title is already true and the second is confirmed within minutes by Ross, so the pattern makes kingship seem certain too.

cards.front: How does the power dynamic between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth change across the play?
cards.answer: Lady Macbeth starts dominant and controls Macbeth, but by Act 3 he acts without her and by Act 5 she is destroyed by guilt, reversing their roles.

title: Choosing Devices and Distribution Channels for an Audience
subject: it-ocr

cards.front: Name the four types of accessibility need covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Motor accessibility / Visual accessibility / Hearing accessibility / Cognitive accessibility

cards.front: Name the four advantages given for a smartphone as a device.
cards.answer: Portable / Always connected / Push notifications reach users instantly / Wide adoption

cards.front: Why might a phone call or printed material sometimes be more accessible than a digital channel for older adults?
cards.answer: Older adults may have lower digital literacy, prefer larger text and simpler navigation, and be less likely to have high-speed broadband.

cards.front: Why can complex menus and jargon-heavy text be a barrier for cognitive accessibility?
cards.answer: They may be barriers for users with learning difficulties or limited IT literacy, making content harder to understand and navigate.

title: Western, Russian and Regional Interests in the Gulf
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three overlapping interests the lesson says drove outside involvement in the Gulf.
cards.answer: Oil supply (Hormuz, OPEC) / Cold War alignments (Soviet-Iraqi arms ties, US-Saudi defence links) / Pull of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict
items: Cold War alignments (Soviet-Iraqi arms ties, US-Saudi defence links)

cards.front: Why did Saddam Hussein want oil prices to stay high in 1989-90?
cards.answer: He needed high prices to pay off Iraq's $80 billion war debt from the Iran-Iraq war.

cards.front: Why did Saddam misjudge how outside powers would react to invading Kuwait?
cards.answer: He thought the USA was distracted by Eastern Europe and the USSR weakened by Afghanistan, underestimating that a threat to Gulf oil would unite outside powers.

title: Why Europeans sailed: motives for the voyages of discovery
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three technological advances that made long ocean voyages possible.
cards.answer: The caravel / The magnetic compass / The astrolabe

cards.front: Why did sailors use dead reckoning alongside the astrolabe in the 1490s?
cards.answer: Longitude could not be calculated accurately, so sailors combined starting point, estimated speed and compass bearing to guess position.

cards.front: How did Columbus end up reaching the Americas instead of Asia?
cards.answer: He believed the westward distance to Asia was shorter than it actually was, so he accidentally landed in the Americas.

cards.front: Why did the fall of Constantinople in 1453 push Spain and Portugal towards sea exploration?
cards.answer: It blocked reliable overland trade to Asia, giving them an economic motive to find alternative sea routes instead.

title: The Roaring Twenties and Republican prosperity
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three Republican presidents who governed the US during the 1920s and their years in office.
cards.answer: Harding (1921–23) / Coolidge (1923–29) / Hoover (1929–33)

cards.front: Name the five groups the lesson identifies as excluded from 1920s prosperity.
cards.answer: Farmers facing falling crop prices / Coal and textile workers in declining industries / African Americans facing segregation and discrimination / Recent immigrants in low-wage factory jobs / The roughly 40% of Americans living in poverty
items: Coal and textile workers in declining industries
African Americans facing segregation and discrimination
Recent immigrants in low-wage factory jobs
The roughly 40% of Americans living in poverty

cards.front: Why did trade union membership fall sharply during the 1920s?
cards.answer: Employers used court injunctions, the threat of replacement workers, and company unions to undermine collective bargaining.

cards.front: Why was the economic growth of the 1920s built on a risky foundation?
cards.answer: Wages didn't rise fast enough, so spending relied on credit while margin buying pushed stock prices above real company value.

title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
subject: physical-education-ocr

cards.front: Name the six features that make alveolar gas exchange efficient.
cards.answer: Large surface area / Moist thin walls (one cell thick) / Short diffusion distance / Large capillary network / Large blood supply / Maintained concentration gradient

cards.front: During intense exercise, what happens to the rib cage on the inhale to move air faster?
cards.answer: Accessory muscles, the pectorals, help elevate the rib cage further and faster than at rest.

cards.front: Why doesn't breathing harder alone increase the surface area available for gas exchange?
cards.answer: Diffusion rate is limited by fixed alveolar surface area and concentration gradients, which effort cannot change directly.

cards.front: How does exercise increase the effective surface area for gas exchange at the alveoli?
cards.answer: More capillaries open up around active alveoli during exercise, increasing the surface area available for exchange.

cards.front: Name the four layers the speaker removes in 'Honour Killing', in order.
cards.answer: The coat (nationality) / The veil (religion) / The silks and jewellery (family/dowry) / The skin, flesh and bone (the body)
items: The skin, flesh and bone (the body)

cards.front: Why does Dharker's title 'Honour Killing' mislead the reader about the poem's content?
cards.answer: It suggests violent death, but the poem is really about a woman killing off imposed identities to reclaim her own honour.

cards.front: How does the structure of 'Honour Killing' enact its argument about identity?
cards.answer: Destructive verbs like 'taking off' shift to active, creative verbs like 'making, crafting, plotting', showing loss of imposed identity leading to self-invention.

cards.front: How does enjambment in 'Honour Killing' reflect the poem's central metaphor?
cards.answer: Lines running on without pause, as in 'the face, the flesh, / the womb', mimic peeling back one layer to reveal another underneath.

cards.front: Name the five key methods Wells uses that the lesson lists for analysis.
cards.answer: First-person narration / Scientific register / Imperial analogy / Documentary realism / Anti-climactic ending

cards.front: Why is ignoring AO3 a mistake when analysing War of the Worlds?
cards.answer: Wells wrote the novel specifically to critique imperialism, so context is essential to understanding it.

cards.front: Why does Ralph feel a 'little fall of the heart' about his own filthy appearance in Chapter 7?
cards.answer: He realises he now sees his dirty, uncivilised state as normal and no longer minds it, showing civilisation slipping away unnoticed.

cards.front: Why do Ralph and Piggy deny their involvement after Simon's murder?
cards.answer: Their guilt makes them deny responsibility, showing how the mob absorbed even good people into collective violence.

cards.front: Name the four conditions from Surah 4:69–110 used to judge whether a modern conflict is a just war.
cards.answer: Just cause / Declared by legitimate authority / Last resort / Avoid harming non-combatants

cards.front: Why do most Muslims argue that WMD are unacceptable, based on Surah 5:32?
cards.answer: WMD cause indiscriminate mass killing that cannot separate combatants from innocent civilians, conflicting with the sanctity of every innocent life.

cards.front: How do Muslims respond to the claim that religion itself causes conflict and terrorism?
cards.answer: They argue most 'religious' conflicts are really driven by politics, land or power, and terrorism distorts genuine Islamic teaching.

title: Resistors in Series and Parallel; the E24 Series
subject: electronics-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four things represented by the multiplier exceptions and colours (gold and silver) on a resistor band, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Gold = ×0.1 multiplier / Silver = ×0.01 multiplier / Gold = ±5% tolerance / Silver = ±10% tolerance

cards.front: Why does connecting resistors in parallel always reduce the total resistance below the smallest individual resistor?
cards.answer: Parallel resistors provide additional current paths, so the total resistance falls below any single resistor's value.

cards.front: What should you do if the calculated power dissipated in a resistor exceeds its power rating?
cards.answer: Choose a higher-rated resistor with the same resistance value.

cards.front: Name the three anthology poems the lesson pairs with 'Cousin Kate' for comparison.
cards.answer: Sonnet 29 (Elizabeth Barrett Browning) / Kamikaze (Beatrice Garland) / Catrin (Gillian Clarke)

cards.front: How does the dramatic monologue form in 'Cousin Kate' shape the reader's view of the speaker?
cards.answer: Because Kate never replies, we only hear the speaker's version, making her bitterness and self-justification feel raw and immediate.

cards.front: Why is the speaker's disgrace in 'Cousin Kate' described as unfair by Rossetti?
cards.answer: The speaker and Kate did nothing very different, yet society judges them oppositely, calling Kate pure and the speaker unclean.

cards.front: Why is a nested for loop needed to traverse a 2D list?
cards.answer: The outer loop gives each row as a list, and the inner loop processes each value within that row.

cards.front: Why must the field order of a record always be documented with a comment?
cards.answer: Because fields are accessed by index, not by name, so there's no other way to know what each position represents.

cards.front: Name the three things about Mickey's life that fascinate Eddie when they first meet.
cards.answer: His swearing / His street games / His ability to play outside unsupervised
items: His ability to play outside unsupervised

cards.front: What three purposes does Russell's use of comedy in the childhood scenes serve?
cards.answer: Establishes the boys' genuine affection and compatibility / Lowers the audience's guard before foreshadowing hits / Reflects working-class humour as a survival mechanism
items: Establishes the boys' genuine affection and compatibility
Lowers the audience's guard before foreshadowing hits
Reflects working-class humour as a survival mechanism

cards.front: Why does Russell present childhood as a time of freedom and equality for Mickey and Eddie?
cards.answer: Because class does not divide them as children, so they can be friends and share games, jokes and secrets.

cards.front: Why is the pun in Mickey's slang phrase 'dead funny' significant?
cards.answer: 'Dead' is casual slang meaning 'very', but the audience hears it as a reminder of the boys' fate.

cards.front: Name the five reasons the lesson gives for why people smoke, in Spanish.
cards.answer: Te hace sentir más adulto / Me relaja / Me da confianza / Todos en mi clase fuman / Se burlan de mí si no fumo
items: Se burlan de mí si no fumo

cards.front: Name the five smoking-related health effects given in Spanish in the lesson.
cards.answer: cáncer de pulmón / cáncer de garganta / dolor en el pecho / tos del fumador / mala circulación

cards.front: Why does Felipe think smoking is harmless, according to the reading practice text?
cards.answer: He smokes with friends because it makes him feel more grown-up and believes he can quit easily.

cards.front: Why did Maripi's grandfather suffer from lung cancer, according to the reading practice text?
cards.answer: He smoked when he was young, which caused him to suffer from lung cancer.

cards.front: What four effects does a rise in the bank rate have, according to the lesson's chain of effects?
cards.answer: Mortgages and loans cost more / Saving becomes more attractive / Business investment falls / Consumer credit becomes more expensive

cards.front: What four limitations of monetary policy does the lesson identify?
cards.answer: Works with a time lag / High household/firm debt limits effect / Global shocks push up inflation anyway / QE risks increasing asset price inequality
items: Global shocks push up inflation anyway
QE risks increasing asset price inequality

cards.front: Why is the Monetary Policy Committee kept independent of the government?
cards.answer: To stop politicians ordering rate cuts for short-term political gain, which could cause long-term inflation damage.

cards.front: Why does quantitative easing risk widening inequality?
cards.answer: QE pushes up asset prices like property and shares, benefiting people who already own assets more than those who don't.

cards.front: Why did the usurpation of Prospero as Duke of Milan matter so much to a Jacobean audience?
cards.answer: Because overthrowing a rightful duke was seen as a crime against the natural order, like regicide in Macbeth.

cards.front: How does Prospero maintain control over the different characters on the island?
cards.answer: He controls Ariel with a promise of freedom, Caliban with threat of punishment, and the nobles through magic.

cards.front: Name the four standard surface preparation steps carried out before any coating is applied.
cards.answer: Degrease (solvent or alkali wash) / Abrade (grit-blast or sandpaper for a mechanical key) / Rinse / Dry
items: Abrade (grit-blast or sandpaper for a mechanical key)

cards.front: What three questions should you ask to choose the right surface finish for a product?
cards.answer: What material is the workpiece? / What environment will it face? / What is the production volume?

cards.front: Why does a small scratch or chip in a paint coating lead to a widening area of rust?
cards.answer: Bare metal is exposed to moisture, and corrosion undercuts the surrounding paint from underneath, spreading the failure zone.

cards.front: Why is electroplating an economical way to coat components with expensive metals like gold or platinum?
cards.answer: The plated layer is extremely thin (1–50 μm), so very little of the costly metal is needed to cover the surface.

cards.front: The lesson gives three examples of sensory receptors for different stimuli. What are they?
cards.answer: Light receptors in the eyes / Temperature receptors in the skin / Chemical receptors in the nose and tongue
items: Chemical receptors in the nose and tongue

cards.front: Name the three ways given to improve the reliability of the ruler drop reaction time test.
cards.answer: Repeat at least five times and take a mean / Discard anomalous results / Ensure the same person drops the ruler each time
items: Repeat at least five times and take a mean
Ensure the same person drops the ruler each time

cards.front: Why do synapses only let impulses travel in one direction?
cards.answer: Neurotransmitters are only released from one side of the synapse and receptor molecules are only present on the other side.

cards.front: How does the type of response produced by the nervous system differ from that of the endocrine system?
cards.answer: The nervous system gives fast, short-lived, precise responses using electrical impulses, while the endocrine system gives slower, longer-lasting, widespread responses using hormones.

cards.front: Name the six bandit and monster encounters shown on the outer ring of the Theseus Kylix.
cards.answer: Kerkyon / Prokrustes / Skiron / Bull of Marathon / Sinis / Krommyonian Sow

cards.front: What three similarities did Plutarch note between Theseus and Romulus in his Parallel Lives?
cards.answer: Uncertain births / Both unified scattered communities into one city / Both committed acts of violence overshadowing achievements
items: Both unified scattered communities into one city
Both committed acts of violence overshadowing achievements

cards.front: Why did Romulus end up killing Remus?
cards.answer: They disputed which hill to build the city on and argued over omens — Romulus saw twelve vultures, Remus six — leading to the killing.

cards.front: Why did the Athenians see the olive tree's regrowth after 480 BC as significant?
cards.answer: After the Persians burned Athens, the sacred olive tree sprouted new shoots the next day, a sign of Athena's undying protection.

title: Notting Hill: Black Activism and the Mangrove
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four overlapping strands of Black activism in Notting Hill between 1958 and 1971.
cards.answer: Claudia Jones's West Indian Gazette (1958) / The indoor Caribbean Carnival (1959) / The Mangrove Restaurant (from 1968) / The Black Panthers and Mangrove Nine trial (1971)
items: The Black Panthers and Mangrove Nine trial (1971)

cards.front: Why did Frank Crichlow and his customers organise the August 1970 protest march?
cards.answer: Because the Mangrove had been raided by police nine times in eighteen months with no drugs found, which was seen as targeted harassment.

cards.front: How did the defence in the Mangrove Nine trial use jury selection to challenge racism?
cards.answer: They challenged 63 potential jurors over their understanding of 'black power', leaving two Black jurors on the panel of twelve.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to say the Notting Hill Carnival began only in 1966?
cards.answer: Because its political and cultural source was Claudia Jones's 1959 indoor Caribbean Carnival, which the 1966 street festival inherited from.

cards.front: Why do the animals confess to crimes they did not commit in Chapter 7?
cards.answer: They are terrified of Napoleon's dogs, showing terror aims at submission rather than justice.

cards.front: Why can't the animals challenge the changes made to the commandments?
cards.answer: They can barely read, showing lack of education is used as a tool of oppression.

cards.front: Why does Napoleon ban 'Beasts of England' after the executions?
cards.answer: It reminded animals of the original revolutionary vision, exposing the gap between promise and reality.

cards.front: Name the three-step pattern the lesson gives for how commandments get changed.
cards.answer: Pigs commit a forbidden act / Animals check the commandment / Commandment has been altered to permit it
items: Commandment has been altered to permit it

title: Malcolm X, Black Power and radical movements
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the two fundamental points on which Malcolm X and King differed, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Malcolm X rejected integration and wanted separate Black institutions / Malcolm X advocated self-defence while King insisted on non-violence

cards.front: Why was Martin Luther King Jr in Memphis when he was assassinated in April 1968?
cards.answer: He was supporting striking Black sanitation workers, showing he was linking civil rights with economic justice.

cards.front: How did the methods used by COINTELPRO against the Black Panthers break the law?
cards.answer: It used illegal surveillance, informants and forged letters to cause internal conflict, and cooperated with police in violent raids, which the Church Committee found unlawful.

cards.front: Why did Malcolm X break with the Nation of Islam in 1964?
cards.answer: He discovered Elijah Muhammad's personal misconduct, and his pilgrimage to Mecca broadened his view of race.

cards.front: The lesson names twelve core Olympian gods, plus Hades sometimes as a thirteenth. Name six of the twelve.
cards.answer: Zeus / Hera / Demeter / Poseidon / Hephaistos / Apollo

cards.front: The lesson gives symbols for several Olympians. Which symbol identifies each of these four gods: Athena, Apollo, Ares, Demeter?
cards.answer: Athena - owl, helmet, olive branch / Apollo - lyre and laurel wreath / Ares - spear and helmet / Demeter - sheaf of wheat

cards.front: Why was Hades not usually counted among the twelve Olympians?
cards.answer: Although brother to Zeus and Poseidon, he lived in the underworld rather than on Mount Olympus.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say it is a mistake to think the Greek gods were morally perfect?
cards.answer: Gods like Zeus and Hera behaved badly, so they were worshipped from respect and fear, not because they were good.

title: Types of School and Alternative Provision
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: Name the six main types of school in the UK, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: State-maintained primary and secondary schools / Comprehensive schools / Grammar schools / Academies / Free schools / Private (independent) schools

cards.front: Name the four sociological perspectives on school diversity covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Functionalist / Marxist / Feminist / New Right

cards.front: Why do critics argue that grammar schools entrench class inequality?
cards.answer: Middle-class families can afford private tuition to prepare children for the eleven-plus, while working-class families typically cannot.

cards.front: Why do Marxist sociologists say home schooling is not a neutral alternative to school?
cards.answer: It requires significant parental time and resources, often a non-working parent, making it more accessible to middle-class families.

title: Bystander Behaviour and Piliavin's Subway Study
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Why were passengers more likely to leave the carriage the longer a Piliavin trial went on without anyone helping?
cards.answer: Without help occurring, passengers were more likely to leave rather than assist, showing reduced willingness to intervene over time.

cards.front: How can safety campaigns use knowledge of diffusion of responsibility to increase helping?
cards.answer: By telling bystanders directly that they personally should act, rather than assuming someone else will help.

cards.front: Name the three reasons mitosis is important for organisms.
cards.answer: Growth / Repair / Asexual reproduction

cards.front: Name the three types of stem cell and where each is found.
cards.answer: Embryonic stem cells - found in early embryos / Adult stem cells - found in adult tissues e.g. bone marrow / Meristems - found at plant root and shoot tips
items: Embryonic stem cells - found in early embryos
Adult stem cells - found in adult tissues e.g. bone marrow
Meristems - found at plant root and shoot tips

cards.front: Why is a malignant tumour more dangerous than a benign one?
cards.answer: A malignant tumour can spread to other parts of the body, whereas a benign tumour stays in one place.

cards.front: Why do plants continue growing for their entire lifespan?
cards.answer: Meristem cells at root and shoot tips can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the plant's life.

cards.front: Name the two pieces of legislation used to repress the Highlands after Culloden.
cards.answer: Disarming Act (1746) / Heritable Jurisdictions Act (1747)

cards.front: Why did the Jacobite army retreat from Derby in December 1745 instead of marching on London?
cards.answer: Charles's council of war voted against continuing, fearing government forces closing in from the south and west.

cards.front: How did the Heritable Jurisdictions Act (1747) lead to the Highland Clearances?
cards.answer: It abolished chiefs' power to hold their own courts, so stripped chiefs needed new income and converted estates to sheep farming, evicting tenants.

cards.front: Why did the Seven Years War contribute to the American War of Independence within a generation?
cards.answer: The war roughly doubled Britain's public debt, forcing new taxation including taxes on the American colonies.

cards.front: Name the three purposes of the family given in Christian teaching from Ephesians 6:1-4.
cards.answer: Procreation / Security / Education

cards.front: Name three practical ways the local parish supports families, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Sunday schools and youth groups / Marriage or new-baby preparation classes / Counselling for couples / Food banks and welfare support

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church teach that artificial contraception is not permitted within marriage?
cards.answer: Because Humanae Vitae teaches every act of sexual intercourse in marriage should remain open to new life.

cards.front: Why do Christians disagree about whether same-sex sexual relationships are acceptable?
cards.answer: Traditional teaching holds sex belongs only between a man and woman in marriage, while others judge relationships by love and commitment rather than marital status or gender.

cards.front: Name the three internal sources of finance the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Retained profit / Selling unwanted assets / Owner's savings

cards.front: The lesson gives four factors that decide which finance source suits a business. What are they?
cards.answer: How much is needed / How quickly it's needed / How long it's needed for / How established the business is

cards.front: Why might family and friends be a risky source of finance despite often being interest-free?
cards.answer: Arguments over repayment can wreck the personal relationship between the owner and the lender.

cards.front: Why is a mortgage's interest rate usually lower than a normal bank loan?
cards.answer: Because the property acts as security, so it can be repossessed if repayments are missed.

title: The Six Beliefs, the Five Roots, the Nature of Allah and Risalah
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six beliefs of Sunni Islam.
cards.answer: Allah / Angels (Malaikah) / Books (Kutub) / Prophets (Risalah) / Day of Judgement (Akhirah) / Divine decree (al-Qadr)

cards.front: Name the five roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi'a Islam.
cards.answer: Tawhid / 'Adl / Nubuwwah / Imamah / Mi'ad

cards.front: Why do Sevener and Twelver Shi'a Muslims both still hold Imamah despite disagreeing about the Imams?
cards.answer: They disagree only on the number and identity of the Imams, but both accept the principle that leadership passed to Muhammad's family.

cards.front: Why is Risalah so important for Muslims today?
cards.answer: It provides the direct link between Allah's will and human life, making the Qur'an and Islamic guidance possible, and gives Muslims role models for persevering through hardship.

title: Sacraments, the Mass and Catholic Prayer
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What three parts make up the Liturgy of the Eucharist in the Mass?
cards.answer: Offertory (bread and wine brought forward) / Eucharistic Prayer (priest consecrates bread and wine) / Holy Communion (congregation receives)
items: Eucharistic Prayer (priest consecrates bread and wine)

cards.front: What two types of prayer, beyond the Lord's Prayer, does Catholic tradition practise?
cards.answer: Set (formulaic) prayer / Informal (extempore) prayer

cards.front: Why do most Protestant churches recognise only two sacraments instead of seven?
cards.answer: Because only baptism and the Lord's Supper were explicitly commanded by Jesus with a physical element.

cards.front: Why do Catholics call the Eucharist the 'source' and 'summit' of Christian life?
cards.answer: Source means all Catholic spiritual life flows from the Mass; summit means everything is directed back towards it.

title: Spain in 1490: Crusading Spirit and Foreign Ambitions
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four Portuguese exploration milestones down the African coast given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cape Bojador in 1434 / Cape Verde in 1444 / The Equator by the 1470s / Cape of Good Hope in 1488

cards.front: Name the four spices the lesson says made up the wealthiest trade in the world.
cards.answer: Pepper / Cloves / Cinnamon / Nutmeg

cards.front: Why did the end of the Reconquista push Spain towards overseas ventures?
cards.answer: It freed thousands of soldiers and hidalgos trained only for war and conquest, with no enemy left to fight.

cards.front: How did the crusading spirit link conquest to future ventures like Columbus's voyage?
cards.answer: It held that fighting unbelievers earned salvation and lawful spoils, so gold from new lands could fund another holy war.

title: Industrial Britain: Irish, Scottish and Eastern European migrants
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four urban areas where Irish communities concentrated in industrial Britain.
cards.answer: Liverpool / Manchester / Glasgow / London's East End

cards.front: Name the three types of cultural institutions Eastern European Jewish immigrants built in London's East End.
cards.answer: Synagogues / Yiddish theatres / A thriving press

cards.front: Why did Scottish migrants generally face less hostility than Irish migrants in industrial Britain?
cards.answer: Shared Protestantism, the Act of Union (1707) and legal British citizenship reduced the discrimination Scottish workers faced.

cards.front: Why was the Aliens Act 1905 directed primarily at the Eastern European Jewish community?
cards.answer: They were arriving in large numbers, generating a tabloid-driven debate about overcrowding and alien influence in the East End.

cards.front: Name the four impulsive decisions the lesson says Romeo makes that drive the plot.
cards.answer: Attending the Capulet ball / Marrying Juliet within hours / Killing Tybalt in rage / Drinking poison too early

cards.front: Name the three foil pairings the lesson gives to show how Shakespeare sharpens character contrast.
cards.answer: Mercutio vs Romeo / Tybalt vs Benvolio / Nurse vs Juliet

cards.front: Why does Mercutio's death act as the play's turning point?
cards.answer: It removes the play's comic energy and replaces it with tragedy, suggesting even wit cannot survive the feud.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare give Tybalt a flat, unchanging character?
cards.answer: His unchanging hatred serves a structural purpose as the catalyst that triggers the crisis and Romeo's banishment.

cards.front: Name the four main methods of collecting primary data given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Experimental / Simulation / Questionnaire / Observation

cards.front: What three limitations does the lesson give for secondary data?
cards.answer: May not measure exactly what you need / Variable definitions may have changed / Source must be acknowledged and quality assessed
items: May not measure exactly what you need
Source must be acknowledged and quality assessed

cards.front: Why can observer presence be a problem when using observation to collect primary data?
cards.answer: Because the observer's presence can influence the behaviour being watched, so it may not show what people actually do.

cards.front: Why can sensitive topics like income or health lead to biased survey results?
cards.answer: People may give socially desirable answers rather than honest ones, or refuse to answer, creating response or non-response bias.

title: 'Invisible Mass of the Back Row' — Claudette Williams
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why is Hortense's punishment described as a particularly pointed injustice?
cards.answer: She is punished for thinking and asking a fair question, not for misbehaving, showing the classroom silences critical thought.

cards.front: Why does the ending in England matter for the theme of voice?
cards.answer: It is the moment Hortense is finally listened to, after researching Black history herself and answering with real evidence.

cards.front: Name the three forces the lesson says have built up the UK's landscape over time.
cards.answer: Geology / Past climate processes (especially glaciation) / Human activity

cards.front: Name the four post-glacial processes the lesson says are still shaping the UK's landscape today.
cards.answer: Weathering (e.g. freeze-thaw) / Mass movement (landslides, mudflows, rockfalls) / Rivers re-carving valleys / Coastal erosion by the sea

cards.front: Why does the South Downs cross-section show chalk as a high ridge with a hollowed-out clay vale (the Weald) beneath it?
cards.answer: Chalk is resistant and stands up as a ridge, while the weaker underlying gault clay is more easily worn down into a vale.

cards.front: Why are the 'wild' moors of the Yorkshire Dales and Lake District largely treeless?
cards.answer: Uplands were cleared for sheep grazing, and livestock keep trees from regrowing, leaving open moorland.

cards.front: Name the four entertainments the lesson says the wealthy enjoyed at court.
cards.answer: Elaborate banquets / Hunting / Jousting / Masques

cards.front: Name the five Elizabethan playhouses mentioned in the lesson, in order of building.
cards.answer: The Theatre (1576) / The Curtain (1577) / The Rose (1587) / The Swan (c.1595) / The Globe (1599)

cards.front: Why did Puritans object to bear-baiting and cock-fighting?
cards.answer: They worried these sports encouraged idleness and gambling and drew people away from church, not out of concern for the animals.

cards.front: How did Elizabethan plays show where a scene was set without any scenery?
cards.answer: Location was established through the actors' words and the audience's imagination, since there was no scenery.

cards.front: What are the six stages of the boy's argument that Blake gives one stanza each to in 'The Schoolboy'?
cards.answer: Joy / Misery / Exhaustion / The bird question / The appeal to parents / The warning about ruined harvest

cards.front: Why does Blake use agricultural imagery like 'buds are nip'd' in the final stanza to warn parents?
cards.answer: Because damage happens now but its consequence, the harvest failing, only appears later, showing harm to a child stays hidden until too late.

cards.front: Why does Blake widen his imagery from one unhappy boy to nature's whole yearly cycle in the closing stanzas?
cards.answer: To move from a single boy's personal complaint to a universal warning, making the protest feel bigger than one child's tantrum.

title: Exploration, Drake's circumnavigation and the Virginia colony
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four motives the lesson gives for Elizabethan exploration.
cards.answer: expand trade beyond northern Europe / attack Spanish shipping for gold and silver / search for a north-west passage to Asia / patriotic and religious wish to challenge Spain
items: attack Spanish shipping for gold and silver
search for a north-west passage to Asia
patriotic and religious wish to challenge Spain

cards.front: Name the five causes the lesson gives for the failure of the 1585 Roanoke settlement and its 1587 successor.
cards.answer: colonists were soldiers not farmers / killing of Wingina ended Indigenous co-operation / Roanoke Island had a poor harbour / relief fleet diverted to fight Spain / White's return delayed by the Armada
items: killing of Wingina ended Indigenous co-operation
Roanoke Island had a poor harbour
relief fleet diverted to fight Spain
White's return delayed by the Armada

cards.front: Why did English trade need to expand into new markets in the 1560s?
cards.answer: Religious wars in the Netherlands disrupted the Antwerp cloth market, so merchants sought new outlets like the Baltic, Mediterranean, Russia and West Africa.

cards.front: How did new technology make longer Elizabethan sea voyages possible?
cards.answer: Galleons with longer, lower hulls, astrolabes and quadrants for measuring latitude, accurate charts and logbooks let captains plan long ocean voyages confidently.

cards.front: Name the four measures the lesson says almost every colonial protest after 1763 was a direct consequence of.
cards.answer: Proclamation Act / Sugar Act / Stamp Act / standing army of 10,000 troops

cards.front: Why did winning the French and Indian War actually weaken Britain's position in America?
cards.answer: It removed the French threat binding colonies to Britain, added frontier costs Britain couldn't afford, and left debt London wanted colonies to pay.

cards.front: Why did Britain issue the Proclamation Act of 1763?
cards.answer: To buy time and reduce frontier defence costs after Indigenous attacks, by banning settlement west of the Appalachians.

cards.front: Why did the Lenape fight alongside the French at the Battle of the Monongahela?
cards.answer: To defend their way of life, which was threatened far more by British settlement than by a French garrison.

cards.front: Name the three Black rock and roll artists the lesson mentions who were paid less than their white counterparts.
cards.answer: Chuck Berry / Little Richard / Fats Domino

cards.front: Name the three legal milestones for women's rights listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Equal Pay Act (1963) / Civil Rights Act (1964) banned sex discrimination / Roe v Wade (1973) legalised abortion
items: Civil Rights Act (1964) banned sex discrimination

cards.front: How did television help rock and roll create the first teenage mass market?
cards.answer: It reached nearly 90% of American homes by 1960, giving rock and roll national reach and a mass teenage audience.

cards.front: Why is the Stonewall uprising seen as different from earlier police raids on gay bars?
cards.answer: Patrons fought back instead of submitting to arrest as had been customary, sparking days of resistance that galvanised the gay rights movement.

cards.front: Name the four ways the Inspector's identity has been interpreted in the play.
cards.answer: A ghost or ghoul / A time traveller / A divine or moral agent / A dramatic device

cards.front: Name the five one-dimensional ways each Birling family member sees Eva Smith.
cards.answer: Birling: a troublesome worker / Sheila: a rival / Gerald: a pretty mistress / Mrs Birling: a dishonest applicant / Eric: a girl he used

cards.front: Why does Priestley use the metaphor of a 'body' to describe society?
cards.answer: A body is an interconnected system where if one part suffers all suffer, arguing against Birling's individualism.

cards.front: Why does the Inspector remain powerful even though his police credentials turn out to be false?
cards.answer: His authority is moral rather than institutional, coming from the truth he represents rather than his rank.

cards.front: Name the three non-negotiable features of a top-band 16-mark essay.
cards.answer: An argument (thesis stated upfront) / Precise evidence (names, dates, acts, statistics) / A substantiated overall judgement (weighed conclusion)

cards.front: In a 16-mark essay, what paragraphs should you include besides the introduction and conclusion?
cards.answer: At least two paragraphs arguing one side / One paragraph engaging with the counter-argument
items: At least two paragraphs arguing one side
One paragraph engaging with the counter-argument

cards.front: Why does writing three pages of description without arguing a position cap an essay in the middle band?
cards.answer: Because it fails to construct a substantiated judgement, which requires arguing a position and weighing evidence, not just describing it.

cards.front: In the worked example, why does the essay argue the Second World War was more important than the New Deal for economic change?
cards.answer: Because by 1944 unemployment fell below 2% and GDP roughly doubled, achieving genuine full employment the New Deal had not.

title: The Role of the Media and a Free Press
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: What three types of information can lawfully be restricted (censored) in the UK, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Details that would prejudice a fair trial / Information that would endanger national security / Material that incites hatred or violence
items: Details that would prejudice a fair trial
Information that would endanger national security
Material that incites hatred or violence

cards.front: What three responsibilities does the media have, alongside its right to report?
cards.answer: Be accurate / Respect personal privacy / Avoid defamation

cards.front: Why is the media sometimes called the 'Fourth Estate'?
cards.answer: Because, alongside Parliament, the executive and the judiciary, it is seen as a pillar of democratic accountability.

cards.front: Why did the Leveson Inquiry recommend independent regulation of the press?
cards.answer: Because of widespread concern about journalistic practices, including phone hacking and invading the privacy of crime victims.

cards.front: Name the four main barriers to entry described in the lesson.
cards.answer: High start-up costs / Economies of scale / Patents and legal protection / Brand loyalty and switching costs

cards.front: Name the four powers the CMA has to deal with dominant firms.
cards.answer: Investigate mergers creating dominant firms / Break up companies abusing market power / Impose fines for cartels or anti-competitive behaviour / Order access to a dominant firm's infrastructure
items: Break up companies abusing market power
Impose fines for cartels or anti-competitive behaviour
Order access to a dominant firm's infrastructure

cards.front: Why do economies of scale create a catch-22 barrier to entry for new firms?
cards.answer: A new entrant has higher average costs than the incumbent but cannot grow to match its scale until it attracts customers away from the cheaper incumbent.

cards.front: Why does a single rural internet provider have little incentive to improve its service?
cards.answer: Residents have no alternative network, so they must pay the provider's price or go without, removing competitive pressure to improve.

title: The First World War and the Fall of the Tsar
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why Russian sea routes failed to support wartime industry.
cards.answer: Baltic closed by Germany / Black Sea closed by Ottoman Turkey (late 1914) / Only Vladivostok and Murmansk-Archangel left, the latter iced over half the year
items: Black Sea closed by Ottoman Turkey (late 1914)
Only Vladivostok and Murmansk-Archangel left, the latter iced over half the year

cards.front: Name the four key events, in order, of the eight days from 23 February to 2 March 1917 (Old Style) that ended Romanov rule.
cards.answer: Women's bread strike begins in Vyborg / Volynsky Regiment mutinies and joins protesters / Petrograd garrison mutinies and Duma forms Provisional Committee / Nicholas II abdicates
items: Women's bread strike begins in Vyborg
Volynsky Regiment mutinies and joins protesters
Petrograd garrison mutinies and Duma forms Provisional Committee

cards.front: Why did Russian soldiers sometimes go to the front with only one rifle between two men?
cards.answer: Russian industry produced barely a fifth of the rifles the army needed in 1915, causing severe shortages.

cards.front: Why was Nicholas II's decision to take personal command of the army in September 1915 politically disastrous?
cards.answer: It meant every subsequent defeat was blamed personally on him, since he had taken direct responsibility for the war.

title: Stamford Bridge & the Battle of Hastings
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: The lesson gives five reasons for William's victory at Hastings. What are they?
cards.answer: William's skilled leadership and adaptable tactics / Norman combined use of archers, infantry and cavalry / Harold's exhausted and weakened army / Bad luck and timing over the wind change / Harold's death ending English morale
items: William's skilled leadership and adaptable tactics
Norman combined use of archers, infantry and cavalry
Bad luck and timing over the wind change

cards.front: The lesson describes four stages of the Battle of Hastings, from morning to evening. What are they?
cards.answer: Morning: Norman attacks repelled / Midday: rumour of William's death / Afternoon: feigned retreats / Evening: Harold's death

cards.front: Why did Harold have to disband his fyrd in September 1066?
cards.answer: Supplies were running low and the fyrd's period of service had expired, forcing Harold to send them home.

cards.front: Why did the Battle of Gate Fulford force Harold to march north?
cards.answer: Gate Fulford destroyed Edwin and Morcar's northern army, so Harold had to bring his own troops to face Hardrada, leaving the south undefended.

cards.front: Name the six qualities the lesson gives for a bad friend (ein schlechter Freund).
cards.answer: ungeduldig — impatient / eifersüchtig — jealous / ärgerlich — annoying / negativ — negative / langweilig — boring / gemein — mean

cards.front: Name the five things the lesson says a strong paragraph about your best friend should include.
cards.answer: Name and how long known / Their personality / What they look like / Why they're a good friend (weil) / A balanced detail (obwohl/trotzdem)

cards.front: How does using denn differ from using weil when giving a reason in German?
cards.answer: Denn is a coordinating conjunction so the verb stays in its normal position, unlike weil which sends it to the end.

cards.front: Why does the verb come immediately after trotzdem in a sentence?
cards.answer: Trotzdem is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it starts a new sentence and the verb follows straight after it.

cards.front: Name the three British taxes on the American colonies that provoked colonial anger, in order.
cards.answer: Stamp Act 1765 / Townshend duties 1767 / Tea Act 1773

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why Jamestown survived its disastrous start.
cards.answer: Leadership of John Smith / Corn supplied by the Powhatan Confederacy / Tobacco introduced by John Rolfe
items: Corn supplied by the Powhatan Confederacy

cards.front: Why did indentured servitude decline in the colonies by 1700?
cards.answer: As tobacco profits rose, planters increasingly preferred enslaved labour, which had no contract and no end-date.

cards.front: How did the 1783 loss of the American colonies affect the future direction of the British Empire?
cards.answer: It shifted British attention to Asia, Australia and Africa, creating a 'second empire' based on commerce and military rule rather than settlement.

cards.front: Name the three stages of escalating violence that open Act 1, Scene 1.
cards.answer: Servants trade insults and fight / Tybalt enters with characteristic aggression / The Prince threatens death for further disturbance
items: The Prince threatens death for further disturbance

cards.front: Name the three qualities Romeo's sun metaphor associates with Juliet in the balcony scene.
cards.answer: Warmth / Life / Light

cards.front: Why does the Prince's death threat create dramatic tension throughout the play?
cards.answer: Every later act of violence now risks execution, so when Romeo kills Tybalt, his banishment feels both merciful and devastating.

cards.front: Why does Friar Lawrence's plan for the secret marriage prove naive?
cards.answer: Because the marriage is secret, no one knows about it, so it cannot end the feud, and Romeo cannot explain his change to Tybalt.

cards.front: What three reinforcing factors does the lesson give for why Kim Il Sung invaded South Korea?
cards.answer: Korean nationalism (belief force was needed for reunification) / Military superiority (Soviet tanks, planes, trained troops) / US signals (Acheson placing Korea outside the defence perimeter)
items: Korean nationalism (belief force was needed for reunification)
Military superiority (Soviet tanks, planes, trained troops)
US signals (Acheson placing Korea outside the defence perimeter)

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say helped UN forces hold the Pusan Perimeter?
cards.answer: US air superiority / Fresh divisions arriving from Japan / North Korea's over-extended supply lines

cards.front: Why did Truman decide the US had to respond to the North Korean invasion?
cards.answer: Because it was the first test of containment in Asia, and inaction would encourage aggression and confirm Republican claims he was weak.

cards.front: Why did Korea matter to Washington in 1950 despite being strategically marginal?
cards.answer: After 'losing China', Truman could not afford to lose Korea too, and the Cold War atmosphere made it look like a Soviet test of Western will.

cards.front: Name the three defining traits the lesson gives for Jo's character.
cards.answer: Resilience / Directness / Vulnerability

cards.front: Why does Jo struggle to accept help, even when Geof or the Boy offer it?
cards.answer: Her emotional armour, formed as a survival mechanism from years of neglect, makes her mock or deflect care instead of accepting it.

cards.front: Why is Peter described as the play's least sympathetic character?
cards.answer: He is brash and hostile, treats Helen as a convenience rather than a person, and calls Jo ugly, showing he sees women as objects.

cards.front: Why does Geof's departure from the play feel painful despite his kindness?
cards.answer: He leaves quietly without drama after Helen's homophobic bullying destroys his bond with Jo, showing kindness isn't enough to protect him.

cards.front: Name the four 3D printing (additive manufacturing) processes described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) / Stereolithography (SLA) / Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) / Selective Laser Melting (SLM)

cards.front: Name the four disadvantages of CAM given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Very high capital costs for equipment / Significant set-up time needed / Production stops entirely if machine breaks down / Maintenance needs specialist engineers with high salaries
items: Very high capital costs for equipment
Production stops entirely if machine breaks down
Maintenance needs specialist engineers with high salaries

cards.front: How does CAM help reduce material waste in manufacturing?
cards.answer: Toolpaths can be optimised by software to minimise material removed, and consistent machine operation causes fewer rejected parts.

cards.front: Why might CAM be uneconomical for making just one part or a very small batch?
cards.answer: The time and cost of programming the toolpath and setting up the workpiece may exceed the time a skilled craftsperson would take to make it by hand.

title: Contemporary Music Videos: Lizzo and Taylor Swift
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four areas of the theoretical framework both videos are analysed through.
cards.answer: Media language / Representation / Media industries / Audiences

cards.front: Name the five settings the Man visits during his day in The Man.
cards.answer: Subway / Office / Park / Yacht / Tennis court

cards.front: How does the camerawork in The Man signify the Man's assumed dominance?
cards.answer: It consistently centres the Man in the frame and positions him higher than the women around him, especially on the yacht.

cards.front: Why do the colour palette and lighting shift during Good as Hell?
cards.answer: They become more positive as the storylines improve, reinforcing the song's message of recovery and confidence.

cards.front: Besides reactivity, name the four other properties of materials that the lesson says can change at the nanoscale.
cards.answer: Melting point / Electrical and thermal conductivity / Colour / Catalytic activity

cards.front: Name the five uses of nanoparticles given in the lesson's key fact summary.
cards.answer: Sunscreens (UV absorption) / Wound dressings (antibacterial silver nanoparticles) / Self-cleaning glass (photocatalysis) / Drug delivery (targeted medicine) / Electronics (smaller transistors)

cards.front: Why can gold nanoparticles appear red or purple instead of the usual yellow of bulk gold?
cards.answer: Their electrons interact with light differently depending on the particle's size, changing the colour observed.

cards.front: Why might banning a nanotechnology before there is enough evidence still cause harm?
cards.answer: It removes potential benefits like better medicines or sun protection and may push users towards alternatives with their own risks.

cards.front: Name the three regions the text says Britain recruited workers from after WWII to fill labour shortages.
cards.answer: India / Pakistan / the Caribbean

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says Meena is surrounded by at home that reflect her family's Punjabi culture.
cards.answer: Punjabi language / food / music / values

cards.front: Why did Britain recruit workers from former colonies like India, Pakistan and the Caribbean after WWII?
cards.answer: To fill labour shortages in the country after the war.

cards.front: How does Syal show the same racist anger as Powell's speech without naming him in the novel?
cards.answer: Through Sam Lowbridge's outburst at the village fete, revealing the racism simmering beneath 'polite' village life.

cards.front: Why did strict Victorian respectability lead to a culture of hypocrisy?
cards.answer: Any improper behaviour could ruin a man's reputation, so many Victorians lived respectably in public but indulged privately.

cards.front: How does Jekyll's experiment challenge Victorian religious ideas about good and evil?
cards.answer: It suggests evil lives inside every person rather than being an external force resisted through willpower and faith.

title: The War at Sea: Jutland, U-boats and Convoys
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three British battlecruisers that blew up at Jutland when shells hit their magazines.
cards.answer: HMS Indefatigable / HMS Queen Mary / HMS Invincible

cards.front: What were the three decisive effects of the war at sea named by the lesson?
cards.answer: Blockade starved Germany of food and morale / U-boat campaign drew the USA into the war / Convoys contained U-boats and got the American army over safely
items: Blockade starved Germany of food and morale
U-boat campaign drew the USA into the war
Convoys contained U-boats and got the American army over safely

cards.front: Why did the 'cruiser rules' make it hard for a U-boat to attack safely?
cards.answer: Surfacing to warn a merchant crew before sinking their ship meant the submarine lost its main advantage of stealth.

cards.front: Why did Jellicoe refuse to chase the German fleet at night after Jutland?
cards.answer: He knew a single torpedo hit on the British flagship could change the strategic balance of the whole war.

title: Diem, the Vietcong and Civil War in the South
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says Diem's regime alienated rural South Vietnam.
cards.answer: Land policy reversing Vietminh reforms / Reliance on his own family and Catholics / Strategic Hamlets programme from 1962
items: Reliance on his own family and Catholics

cards.front: Name the three aims of the Vietcong (NLF) given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Overthrow Diem's regime / Expel American influence / Reunify Vietnam under Hanoi's leadership

cards.front: Why did the Strategic Hamlets programme push many peasants to join the Vietcong?
cards.answer: Forced relocation broke ancestral ties to village land and was enforced brutally, driving many peasants to join the Vietcong.

cards.front: How did the political chaos after Diem's fall help the Vietcong grow?
cards.answer: South Vietnam had seven different governments in 1964 alone, creating instability that let the Vietcong expand unchecked.

cards.front: Name the three key employer duties in relation to PPE.
cards.answer: Assess whether PPE is needed / Select the correct PPE for the task / Train and supervise employees in correct use, storage and maintenance
items: Select the correct PPE for the task
Train and supervise employees in correct use, storage and maintenance

cards.front: How is each of gas, water and electricity isolated before work starts on site?
cards.answer: Electricity: switch off at consumer unit, lock-out/tag-out / Gas: turn off at meter or isolation valve / Water: close the relevant stop valve
items: Electricity: switch off at consumer unit, lock-out/tag-out
Gas: turn off at meter or isolation valve
Water: close the relevant stop valve

cards.front: Why is scaffold inspected at least every seven days when used for work at height?
cards.answer: The lesson requires regular inspection by a competent person before and during use, with scaffold inspected at least every seven days.

cards.front: How can an un-isolated gas pipe cause danger if it is cut during work?
cards.answer: It will release gas that can build up in the area and ignite.

cards.front: Name the four wastage processes the lesson gives for cutting metals and timber.
cards.answer: Sawing / Drilling / Milling / Turning

cards.front: Name the three deforming processes the lesson gives for shaping polymers.
cards.answer: Vacuum forming / Blow moulding / Injection moulding / Extrusion

cards.front: Why do textiles use a wider tolerance (10–15 mm seam allowance) than metal engineering components (±0.01 mm)?
cards.answer: Fabric garment construction needs looser seam allowances, while engineering parts need very tight tolerances to ensure interchangeability.

cards.front: Why do timber joinery products need wider tolerances (around ±1 mm) than metal components?
cards.answer: Wood is a natural material that expands and contracts with humidity, so frames need clearance gaps for seasonal movement.

title: Bonding, Structure and Why Properties Differ
subject: science-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the four types of bonding this lesson uses to explain material properties.
cards.answer: Ionic / Covalent (simple or giant) / Polymer / Metallic

cards.front: What three things should you identify when explaining a property using structure and bonding?
cards.answer: The type of structure / The relevant force or bond / How much energy is needed to overcome it
items: How much energy is needed to overcome it

cards.front: Why do metals have high tensile strength?
cards.answer: The sea of delocalised electrons holds the positive ion lattice strongly, and the ions can slide without breaking the overall bond.

cards.front: Why does graphene have exceptionally high tensile strength?
cards.answer: Every bond in its covalent network would have to be broken to tear the material.

cards.front: Name the five social groups the specification identifies for studying engagement patterns.
cards.answer: Gender / Race and religion (including culture) / Age / Family and friends (peers) / People with a disability

cards.front: Name the five cross-cutting factors that affect engagement across multiple social groups.
cards.answer: Role models / Media coverage / Accessibility / Attitudes / Education

cards.front: Why do older adults often face barriers to sport participation?
cards.answer: Declining physical capacity, higher injury risk, fewer accessible facilities and reduced social networks after retirement or bereavement discourage participation.

cards.front: Why do family commitments particularly reduce adult female participation in sport?
cards.answer: Childcare and caring responsibilities fall disproportionately on women, reducing the leisure time they have available for sport.

title: Buddhist Worship: Temples, Puja, Death Rites and Festivals
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four items typically offered during Theravada puja.
cards.answer: Flowers (impermanence) / Incense (spread of good reputation) / Candles or lamps (wisdom) / Prostrations before the buddharupa

cards.front: What are the three Theravada practices that structure the monastic calendar?
cards.answer: Vassa (Rain Retreat) / Kathina (robe offering) / Uposatha days (precept-keeping)

cards.front: Why do Buddhist offerings of flowers, incense and candles not count as gift transactions?
cards.answer: They are symbolic acts that cultivate the offering of oneself to the path, not gifts exchanged with a deity.

cards.front: Why is the body often cremated in Theravada death rituals?
cards.answer: Cremation reflects the teaching that the body is impermanent (anicca).

title: Stave 2: The Ghost of Christmas Past
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four memories the Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge, in order.
