cards.answer: Childhood loneliness at school / Fan's love and arrival to bring him home / Fezziwig's generosity at the party / Belle's rejection of Scrooge
items: Fan's love and arrival to bring him home

cards.front: Why does Dickens show Scrooge as a lonely schoolboy left behind at Christmas?
cards.answer: To generate sympathy, showing his isolation came from a painful upbringing rather than just his personality.

cards.front: Why does Dickens place Belle's rejection as the final memory in Stave 2?
cards.answer: Because it is the most painful memory, and it drives Scrooge to try to extinguish the spirit's light.

title: Christian Morality, the Church and Worship
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three broad Christian groupings that are significant in Britain.
cards.answer: Roman Catholicism / Anglicanism (Church of England/Wales) / Non-conformist churches (e.g. Methodists, Baptists, Pentecostals)

cards.front: What five things does the Lord's Prayer cover as a model for prayer?
cards.answer: praise / submission / daily needs / forgiveness / protection from evil

cards.front: How does a situational approach to Christian ethics decide the right action?
cards.answer: It holds that the right action depends on the situation, with the only absolute rule being to act with agapé, working out the most loving choice each time.

cards.front: Why does the Lord's Prayer link receiving God's forgiveness with forgiving others?
cards.answer: Christians understand receiving God's forgiveness and extending forgiveness to others as inseparably linked, shown by asking God to forgive as we forgive others.

title: Film Music: Creating Mood, Time and Place
subject: music-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says composers typically build tension across a cue.
cards.answer: Rising pitch / Thickening texture / Increasing dynamics / Mounting dissonance

cards.front: Name the four stages of the typical climax-and-resolution shape the lesson describes in exam extracts.
cards.answer: Calm thin opening / Thickening middle section / Climax with full orchestration / Calm consonant closing passage

cards.front: Why does the Phrygian mode often suggest Spanish or Middle Eastern settings in film music?
cards.answer: Its distinctive flattened second degree sounds unfamiliar to Western listeners, evoking those regions.

cards.front: Why did Jarre use wide, sparse string writing in Lawrence of Arabia's Main Title?
cards.answer: Avoiding a busy texture leaves space for the listener to imagine an enormous, empty desert landscape.

cards.front: What four things does Odimba establish through Act 1's exposition?
cards.answer: Setting / Relationships / Tension / Tone

cards.front: Name the four functions of Princess's imagination described in Act 1.
cards.answer: Coping mechanism / Dramatic device / Thematic statement / Audience connection

cards.front: Why does Mavis initially refuse to let Wendell into the house but accept Lorna?
cards.answer: Mavis rejects Wendell over his past and absence, but accepts Lorna, letting Princess and Lorna bond over shared identity.

cards.front: Why does Junior feel torn between belonging and exclusion in Act 1?
cards.answer: As a Jamaican-British teenager he understands the racism around him but feels British society won't fully accept him, creating tension.

title: Jesus as Messiah, Son of Man and the Baptism
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three different Jewish groups and their differing Messiah expectations described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pharisees wanted a teacher to purify the law / Zealots wanted a military revolutionary / Essenes wanted a priestly Messiah from Levi
items: Pharisees wanted a teacher to purify the law
Essenes wanted a priestly Messiah from Levi

cards.front: Give the three explanations Christian traditions offer for why a sinless Jesus was baptised.
cards.answer: Solidarity with sinful humanity / Submitting to fulfil all righteousness / A public commissioning for ministry

cards.front: Why did Isaiah 53's 'suffering servant' change how early Christians understood the Messiah?
cards.answer: It showed the Messiah could fulfil God's purposes through self-giving suffering rather than military conquest, so Christians saw Jesus in it.

cards.front: Why is the baptism narrative seen as a historical problem from a non-religious perspective?
cards.answer: John's baptism implied Jesus needed to repent of sin, which contradicts the Christian claim that Jesus was sinless.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why Britain could no longer fund Greece and Turkey by 1947.
cards.answer: Coal shortages / A brutal winter / The cost of empire

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says Marshall aid achieved in Western Europe.
cards.answer: Rebuilt Western European industry / Restored trade between countries / Gave moderate parties something to point to against communists
items: Gave moderate parties something to point to against communists

cards.front: Why did US officials see Greece and Turkey as strategically crucial in 1947?
cards.answer: If Greece fell to communism Turkey would follow, giving the Soviet navy access to the Mediterranean and oil-rich states beyond.

cards.front: Why did Truman argue that economic aid alone would not defeat communism?
cards.answer: Because hungry people believed in whichever system kept them fed, not in democracy simply because it promised freedom.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why Nigeria matters globally.
cards.answer: Oil (major producer/supplier) / Culture (Afrobeats and Nollywood) / Demographics (fast-growing population)

cards.front: Name the three ethnic groups that dominate Nigeria's population.
cards.answer: Hausa-Fulani (north) / Yoruba (south-west) / Igbo (south-east)

cards.front: How is climate change affecting Nigerian farmers?
cards.answer: It is making the north drier, increasing desertification, while southern rainfall becomes heavier and less predictable, hitting farmers hardest.

cards.front: Why has oil wealth in the Niger Delta also caused problems for local communities?
cards.answer: Pollution from oil spills and gas flaring has damaged local fisheries and farmland despite making Nigeria wealthy on paper.

cards.front: What three priorities does Ralph establish as leader in the early chapters?
cards.answer: Build shelters / Maintain a signal fire / Establish rules

cards.front: What three physical traits does the text give for Piggy when he first appears?
cards.answer: Overweight / Asthmatic / Wears thick spectacles

cards.front: Why is Ralph's rational leadership shown to be fragile compared to Jack's?
cards.answer: He lacks rhetorical skill, loses his train of thought, needs Piggy to think, and lacks charisma, unlike Jack's visceral authoritarian appeal.

cards.front: Why is Piggy marginalised by the other boys despite being intelligent?
cards.answer: The boys mock his weight, asthma and lower-class accent, and Ralph betrays his trust by revealing his nickname.

cards.front: Name the three processes the lesson says representation is built through.
cards.answer: Selection / Construction / Mediation

cards.front: Why might a charity advert and a tabloid front page represent the same social group in opposite ways?
cards.answer: They select different images to suit their purpose: the charity emphasises vulnerability to encourage donations, the tabloid emphasises threat to sell papers.

cards.front: How can a news photograph construct a protest as either peaceful or violent?
cards.answer: By selecting a single moment out of thousands of possible moments to represent the whole event.

cards.front: Name the four stages of the Athenian wedding ritual described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dedication of toys/hair to Artemis / Bathing in sacred water / Torch-lit procession to husband's house / Anakalypteria (veil-lifting)

cards.front: Why did Athenian citizenship law make men so concerned about their wives' fidelity?
cards.answer: Because a child needed both parents to be Athenian citizens to inherit citizen rights, so only a legitimate wife could produce citizen sons.

cards.front: Why were girls a significant economic commitment for poorer Athenian fathers?
cards.answer: Because fathers had to pay a dowry to secure a daughter's marriage, and poorer families struggled to afford this.

cards.front: Why did the husband continue sleeping in communal quarters after a Spartan wedding?
cards.answer: The couple did not live together immediately; he stayed in communal quarters and visited his wife secretly for a time.

cards.front: Name the four main design tools the exam requires you to know.
cards.answer: Flow chart / Mind map / Visualisation diagram / Wireframe

cards.front: Give three advantages of using a flow chart to plan a process.
cards.answer: Clear visual representation of logic / Easy for technical and non-technical stakeholders to follow / Standard symbols understood internationally / Helps identify missing steps or infinite loops
items: Easy for technical and non-technical stakeholders to follow
Helps identify missing steps or infinite loops

cards.front: Why are wireframes often used as the first design step in a project?
cards.answer: Because they are quick to produce and cheap to revise before more detailed design work begins.

cards.front: Why might a hand-drawn flow chart become a problem when a design changes?
cards.answer: Because updating a hand-drawn chart is time-consuming compared with editing a software version.

cards.front: Why should a beginner programmer choose a block-based editor or flowchart rather than a text-based language?
cards.answer: They are more accessible because block-based editors prevent syntax errors and flowcharts make program logic immediately visible.

cards.front: In a temperature alarm flowchart, why does the arrow loop back to the sensor-reading step when the answer to the decision is 'no'?
cards.answer: So the program keeps repeating the check, continually monitoring the temperature until the condition becomes true.

cards.front: Name the three types of blood cells produced in red bone marrow and what each one does.
cards.answer: Red blood cells carry oxygen to working muscles / White blood cells fight infection / Platelets trigger clotting to stop bleeding
items: Red blood cells carry oxygen to working muscles
Platelets trigger clotting to stop bleeding

cards.front: Name the six movements the ball-and-socket shoulder joint allows.
cards.answer: Flexion / Extension / Abduction / Adduction / Rotation / Circumduction

cards.front: Why does the hinge joint at the knee suit the repetitive action of running?
cards.answer: It only allows flexion and extension, which matches the repetitive straightening action needed in running.

cards.front: Why do endurance athletes rely heavily on red blood cell production?
cards.answer: Greater numbers of red blood cells means more oxygen can be transported to muscles during prolonged exercise.

cards.front: Name the four physical activities Spartan girls trained in as part of the agoge.
cards.answer: Running / Wrestling / Discus throwing / Javelin throwing

cards.front: What two reasons does the lesson give for why Spartan women came to own so much land?
cards.answer: Male citizen population declined from war losses, leaving estates to female heirs / Women needed to manage estates while husbands were away on campaign
items: Male citizen population declined from war losses, leaving estates to female heirs
Women needed to manage estates while husbands were away on campaign

cards.front: Why did Athens and Sparta give women such different roles, even though both used women to serve the state?
cards.answer: Athens needed women to produce legitimate heirs and keep the household stable, requiring seclusion; Sparta needed strong warriors, requiring physical training and independence.

cards.front: Why should Spartan women's freedom not be seen as a belief in gender equality?
cards.answer: Their freedom existed because the state trained and managed them to serve its military needs, not because Sparta valued equality.

cards.front: Name the four people who provide Victor with a loving, privileged upbringing in Geneva, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: His affectionate parents / Elizabeth Lavenza (childhood companion) / Henry Clerval (best friend)

cards.front: How does Professor Krempe's treatment of Victor differ from Professor Waldman's at Ingolstadt?
cards.answer: Krempe dismisses the alchemists Victor admires as charlatans and humiliates him publicly, while Waldman praises modern chemistry and inspires Victor's ambition.

cards.front: Why does Shelley describe Waldman's language about science as an act of 'penetration' and 'violation'?
cards.answer: It frames science as forcing nature to reveal her hidden secrets rather than working with her, foreshadowing Victor's destructive ambition.

cards.front: Name the five categories hardware is divided into.
cards.answer: Computing devices / Input devices / Output devices / Storage devices / Internal components

cards.front: Name the four most common types of computing device given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Desktop computer / Laptop computer / Tablet / Smartphone

cards.front: Why does a cooling system matter for a CPU?
cards.answer: It prevents overheating, which would otherwise cause the processor to slow down or fail.

cards.front: Why is upgrading RAM often the most cost-effective way to improve an older computer's performance?
cards.answer: The CPU can only use data in RAM, so more RAM lets more programs run at once without slow swapping to storage.

title: The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five key rituals of the Hajj described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Circling the Ka'bah seven times (tawaf) / Walking seven times between Safa and Marwa / Standing in prayer at Arafah / Throwing stones at three pillars in Mina / Sacrificing an animal (qurbani)
items: Walking seven times between Safa and Marwa
Throwing stones at three pillars in Mina

cards.front: Name the four things Muslims must abstain from during the Ramadan fast between dawn and sunset.
cards.answer: Food / Drink, including water / Smoking / Sexual relations

cards.front: Why does Sawm require fasting during Ramadan, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It builds self-discipline, creates empathy with the hungry, shows gratitude for Allah's provision, and increases spiritual focus.

cards.front: How does the state of ihram during Hajj show equality among Muslims?
cards.answer: Ihram removes all distinctions of wealth, nationality, and status, with everyone dressed the same way.

cards.front: Name the seven types of barrier the lesson identifies to health and social care access.
cards.answer: Physical barriers / Sensory disability barriers / Social and cultural barriers / Language and speech barriers / Geographical barriers / Resource barriers / Financial barriers

cards.front: Name the five types of personal obstacle the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Emotional and psychological obstacles / Time constraints / Availability of resources / Unachievable targets / Lack of support

cards.front: Why do resource barriers cause long waiting lists at a service?
cards.answer: The service provider lacks enough staff, equipment or facilities to meet demand, so appointments and waiting lists build up.

cards.front: How do social and cultural barriers stop people accessing services?
cards.answer: Lack of awareness, differing cultural beliefs, stigma around issues like mental health, and fear of losing independence put people off using services.

cards.front: Name the five lustre types the lesson describes for minerals.
cards.answer: Metallic / Vitreous or glassy / Pearly / Silky / Dull or earthy

cards.front: Name the four everyday tools used to test mineral hardness, in order of increasing hardness.
cards.answer: Fingernail / Copper coin / Steel file / A harder mineral

cards.front: Why does calcite fizz when dilute hydrochloric acid is dropped on it?
cards.answer: Calcite is calcium carbonate, and the acid decomposes it, releasing carbon dioxide gas as it reacts.

cards.front: Why does quartz appear in several different colours even though it is one mineral?
cards.answer: Tiny amounts of impurities present during crystallisation change quartz's appearance without changing what mineral it is.

cards.front: Name the three groups of reasons the lesson gives for why people stay in hazard zones.
cards.answer: People don't choose to be there / The benefits outweigh the risks / They trust they can manage the danger
items: People don't choose to be there
They trust they can manage the danger

cards.front: Name the four benefits the lesson gives that attract people to hazard zones despite the risks.
cards.answer: Fertile volcanic soil / Economic opportunities / Tourism revenue / Geothermal energy

cards.front: Why are eruptions at constructive margins gentle rather than explosive?
cards.answer: The plates slide apart smoothly and the magma is runny basalt, so lava flows steadily rather than exploding.

cards.front: Why do continental-continental collisions like India and Eurasia form mountains but no volcanoes?
cards.answer: Neither plate is dense enough to subduct, so the rock buckles upwards instead of melting in the mantle.

title: Mechanical Calculations: Gears, Pulleys and Mechanical Advantage
subject: engineering-aqa

cards.front: Name the two main types of bearing the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Plain (journal) bearing / Ball (rolling) bearing

cards.front: Why does a bicycle use a small front chainring and large rear sprocket in low gear for going uphill?
cards.answer: This gear ratio makes pedalling easier by increasing torque at the wheel, though it reduces speed.

cards.front: How does a ball bearing reduce friction compared with a plain bearing?
cards.answer: It uses rolling contact from steel balls instead of sliding contact, which dramatically reduces friction, heat and energy loss.

cards.front: Why is a gear train with a ratio greater than 1 used for a winch or robot arm?
cards.answer: It reduces output speed but multiplies torque, giving the high torque at low speed these machines need.

cards.front: Name the three key body systems affected by the short-term effects of exercise.
cards.answer: Cardiovascular system / Cardio-respiratory system / Muscular-skeletal system

cards.front: Why does losing too much fluid through sweat make it harder for the heart to work?
cards.answer: Sweating reduces blood volume, which makes it harder for the heart to maintain cardiac output.

cards.front: How is lactic acid cleared from the body during recovery after exercise?
cards.answer: Increased breathing and blood flow deliver extra oxygen used to convert lactic acid back into glucose in the liver (Cori cycle).

cards.front: Why does blood flow shift towards working muscles and away from organs like the digestive system during exercise?
cards.answer: Vessels to working muscles vasodilate while vessels to less active organs vasoconstrict, directing blood where it's needed most.

cards.front: Name the five common mistakes to avoid in the Part 1 comparison essay.
cards.answer: Writing two separate essays / Retelling the poem / Spotting techniques without explaining effect / Forgetting AO3 / Choosing a weak comparison poem

cards.front: What are the five parts of the recommended comparative paragraph structure?
cards.answer: Point about both poets / Evidence from Poem A / Link to Poem B / Evidence from Poem B / AO3 context

cards.front: Why should context (AO3) be integrated into your analysis rather than given as a separate paragraph?
cards.answer: Because context is worth marks only when woven into the comparative analysis, not bolted on as a separate section.

cards.front: Why does simply spotting a technique without explaining its effect earn almost no marks?
cards.answer: Because naming a technique like alliteration alone shows no understanding; you must explain what effect it creates.

title: Reactions to the Treaty and the Wider Settlement
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three structural weaknesses that undermined the peace settlement from the start.
cards.answer: USA walked away / Russia was excluded / Germany treated as defeated outlaw

cards.front: Name the four ethnic groups the lesson says Yugoslavia bound together.
cards.answer: Serbs / Croats / Slovenes / different religions and scripts

cards.front: Why was Japan offended at the Paris peace conference?
cards.answer: Its proposed clause on racial equality was rejected, even though it gained former German Pacific islands as mandates.

cards.front: Why did Britain, unlike France, worry the Treaty of Versailles was too harsh on Germany?
cards.answer: Lloyd George privately predicted the harsh terms would cause another war within a generation.

title: Hercules and Cacus: The Battle and the Whole-Narrative Answer
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: What three things does a strong evaluative answer need to include as evidence, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: One piece of evidence from an early section / One piece of evidence from the battle itself / One piece of evidence from what happens afterwards
items: One piece of evidence from an early section
One piece of evidence from the battle itself
One piece of evidence from what happens afterwards

cards.front: When analysing the effect of Virgil's language, what three steps should you follow?
cards.answer: Quote the Latin / Give a short translation / Explain what that choice of words does to the reader
items: Explain what that choice of words does to the reader

cards.front: How did Cacus try to hide Hercules' stolen cattle before the battle began?
cards.answer: He dragged the cattle backwards into his cave by their tails so any tracks pointed the wrong way.

cards.front: Why did Cacus's trick of hiding the cattle in his cave fail?
cards.answer: One of the captured cows lowed from deep inside the cave, giving away the hiding place.

cards.front: Name the four everyday tensions the domestic arguments in Scenes 1–4 are built around.
cards.answer: Respectability / Education / Money / Demands from Jamaica

cards.front: What four converging crises drive the acceleration of Scenes 5–8?
cards.answer: Del at Mai's / Enid searching for her / Brod's revelation / The final reconciliation

cards.front: Why does Pinnock structure the play with slow domestic scenes before a crisis breaks it open?
cards.answer: It reflects how cultural conflict in immigrant families often simmers beneath ordinary life for years before a crisis forces it into the open.

cards.front: Why does Pinnock reveal Enid's backstory and Del's pregnancy gradually rather than all at once?
cards.answer: Gradual revelation and foreshadowing engage the audience as active interpreters, rewarding close attention to dialogue and behaviour.

cards.front: Name the seven regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, in order from longest to shortest wavelength.
cards.answer: Radio waves / Microwaves / Infrared / Visible light / Ultraviolet / X-rays / Gamma rays

cards.front: Name the four ways a material can interact with an EM wave, as described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Absorption / Transmission / Reflection / Refraction

cards.front: Why does a higher frequency EM wave always have a shorter wavelength in a vacuum?
cards.answer: Because v = fλ applies and speed is fixed in a vacuum, so frequency and wavelength must be inversely related.

cards.front: How does a receiver aerial pick up radio waves?
cards.answer: Radio waves reaching the aerial induce oscillations, an alternating current, in the aerial circuit at the wave's frequency.

cards.front: Name the four abiotic factors the lesson lists that affect where organisms live.
cards.answer: Light intensity / Temperature / Moisture level / Soil pH and mineral content

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says energy is lost at each trophic level.
cards.answer: Movement / Keeping warm / Other metabolic reactions

cards.front: Why is decomposition faster in warm, moist conditions?
cards.answer: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down matter faster when conditions are warm, moist and aerobic.

cards.front: How does golden rice help combat vitamin A deficiency?
cards.answer: It has been genetically modified to produce beta-carotene, which is a source of vitamin A.

cards.front: Name the four main categories of reasons for crime given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Poverty and upbringing / Mental health and addiction / Greed and hate / Opposition to unjust laws

cards.front: Name the three types of crime covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Hate crimes / Theft / Murder

cards.front: How can causing suffering ever be justified according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It can be justified if it leads to a greater good, such as a doctor's painful surgery saving a life or a parent disciplining a child.

cards.front: Why does Islam see greed as wrong?
cards.answer: Because greed goes against the principle of zakah, which requires Muslims to share their wealth with those in need.

cards.front: Name the three stress management techniques used to reduce over-arousal.
cards.answer: Deep breathing / Mental rehearsal / visualisation / Positive self-talk

cards.front: Name three techniques coaches use to increase arousal in an under-aroused athlete.
cards.answer: Energetic music / Team talks raising emotional intensity / Fast-paced warm-up drills / Raising the perceived stakes

cards.front: Why does over-arousal cause a basketball player to miss free throws after dominating a physical post-up battle?
cards.answer: High arousal that helps gross, physical skills disrupts the fine motor control needed for the precise free throw technique.

cards.front: Why might an experienced elite athlete have a higher optimal arousal threshold than a beginner in the same sport?
cards.answer: They have built mental skills to channel arousal into performance, so they can tolerate higher activation before over-arousing.

cards.front: What three things does the Prologue reveal to the audience before the play begins?
cards.answer: Where the play is set (fair Verona) / What the central conflict is (the feuding households) / How the play ends (the lovers' deaths)
items: Where the play is set (fair Verona)
What the central conflict is (the feuding households)
How the play ends (the lovers' deaths)

cards.front: What three comic elements appear at the start of the play before it shifts into tragedy?
cards.answer: Witty servants / Love at first sight / A secret wedding

cards.front: Why did Shakespeare rely so heavily on language to create atmosphere in Romeo and Juliet?
cards.answer: Elizabethan theatre had no elaborate sets, electric lighting or many props, so language had to create atmosphere, location and emotion.

cards.front: Why is Romeo and Juliet's secret marriage more than just a romantic act?
cards.answer: It is an act of rebellion against their families and the patriarchal system that controlled women's lives.

cards.front: Name the four stages of the emotional arc Sissay builds in the opening scenes of Refugee Boy.
cards.answer: Warmth (father-son bond) / Unease (audience senses something wrong) / Shock (discovery of the letter) / Isolation (Alem alone in a foreign country)
items: Isolation (Alem alone in a foreign country)

cards.front: How does Sissay use physical staging to convey Alem's isolation without dialogue?
cards.answer: He uses visual storytelling, like an empty room and a letter on a pillow, to show isolation without words.

cards.front: Name the four pressures the lesson gives for why traditional UK industry declined.
cards.answer: Cheaper foreign competition / Outdated machinery lowering productivity / Resource exhaustion (coal running out) / Government policy (closures and reduced subsidies)

cards.front: Name the four sectors of the economy described in the lesson, with a UK example of each.
cards.answer: Primary - UK fishing / Secondary - JCB diggers in Staffordshire / Tertiary - London banking / Quaternary - Cambridge biotech

cards.front: Why did remaining UK coal become more expensive to mine by the 1980s?
cards.answer: Easy-to-mine coal seams had run out, so extracting the rest cost more than importing coal from abroad.

cards.front: Why did unemployment and low wages persist in former mining and steel towns even years after decline?
cards.answer: They lost their main single employer with no comparable replacement, and new service jobs were often located far away in London or the south-east.

cards.front: The lesson says the pigeon represents three things about Harri's life on the estate — what are they?
cards.answer: His innocence / His loneliness / The fragility of life on the estate
items: The fragility of life on the estate

cards.front: Why does Harri smash-fail the fire alarm during his gang initiation test?
cards.answer: The glass will not break, so he runs away, showing his moral compass resists gang pressure.

cards.front: Why does Kelman treat the desensitisation of estate residents as itself a form of violence?
cards.answer: When people can walk past bloodstains without flinching, something essential in their humanity has been destroyed.

cards.front: Why does Kelman refuse to present Harri's death as inevitable or deserved?
cards.answer: It is the direct result of a system that failed to protect him, not a natural consequence of his innocence.

cards.front: Name the four key quotations the lesson gives for the theme of ambition.
cards.answer: vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself / Unsex me here / fruitless crown and barren sceptre / signifying nothing

cards.front: How does Macbeth's guilt after Duncan's murder affect him, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It is visceral and overwhelming, shown by the dagger hallucination and unwashable blood, but it doesn't stop him killing again.

cards.front: How much of an extract-based Shakespeare answer should focus on the printed passage itself?
cards.answer: Roughly half, spent on close language analysis, with the other half linking to the wider play.

cards.front: Why is Duncan's excessive trust presented as his flaw in the play?
cards.answer: Because he trusts Macbeth's outward appearance, failing to see the deceptive reality, which leads to his murder.

cards.front: Name the four themes explored in 'My Polish Teacher's Tie'.
cards.answer: Identity / Class / Belonging / Language

cards.front: What three qualities does Dunmore give Carla as narrator?
cards.answer: Observant / Intelligent / Self-aware

cards.front: How does class function as the story's 'structural antagonist' rather than through open conflict?
cards.answer: It works through erasure — the canteen worker is functionally invisible to teaching staff, an unconscious but effective form of social violence.

cards.front: How does the story's climax differ from a typical dramatic confrontation?
cards.answer: It is a quiet, understated, private claiming of identity rather than a dramatic clash, making Carla's self-assertion more credible and powerful.

title: Engineering Drawing — Orthographic, Isometric & Sectional Views
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five BS 8888 line types used in engineering drawings.
cards.answer: Continuous thick line / Continuous thin line / Thin dashed line / Thin chain line / Thick chain line

cards.front: Why must engineering drawings always show a projection symbol in the title block?
cards.answer: Because BS 8888 permits both first-angle and third-angle projection, so the symbol shows which layout is used to avoid misreading dimensions.

cards.front: Why do circles appear as ellipses in isometric projection?
cards.answer: Because lengths are only drawn true to scale along the three axes, so curved features must be constructed indirectly by plotting points.

cards.front: Why is a sectional view used instead of just dashed lines to show an internal bore?
cards.answer: Because internal features like bores are hard to describe with dashed lines alone, so cutting through the object shows them more clearly.

cards.front: Name the three elite private schools the History Boys compete against for Oxbridge places.
cards.answer: Eton / Harrow / Winchester

cards.front: Name the three assessment objectives credited on the drama question.
cards.answer: AO1 / AO2 / AO4

cards.front: Why does Irwin call Oxbridge 'a monument to social inequality'?
cards.answer: Because Oxbridge has historically favoured wealthy, privately educated students over state-school candidates like the History Boys.

cards.front: Why did the subjective Oxbridge interview process favour privileged candidates?
cards.answer: Interviewers could select on 'potential' or personality, which favoured candidates coached since childhood in performing intelligence.

title: Searching Algorithms: Linear and Binary Search
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three conditions the lesson gives for when to use binary search.
cards.answer: Dataset is large / Data is already sorted or sorted once and searched many times / Fast repeated look-ups are a priority
items: Data is already sorted or sorted once and searched many times
Fast repeated look-ups are a priority

cards.front: Why did linear search need 6 comparisons to find 23 in the 9-item sorted list, while binary search only needed 3?
cards.answer: Linear search checks items one by one from the start, but binary search halves the search area each comparison, reaching the target much faster.

cards.front: ASCII's 128 codes are split into which five groups of characters?
cards.answer: upper-case English alphabet / lower-case English alphabet / digits 0-9 / punctuation marks / control characters

cards.front: What four things can ASCII not represent because it only has 128 codes?
cards.answer: accented letters (é, ñ, ü) / Chinese or Arabic script / mathematical symbols beyond basic operators / emoji

cards.front: Why does sorting text by character code put 'Z' before 'a'?
cards.answer: All upper-case codes (65-90) are numerically lower than all lower-case codes (97-122), so 'Z' sorts before 'a'.

cards.front: Why might sorting strings numerically place "10" before "9"?
cards.answer: Comparison happens character by character, and '1' (code 49) is less than '9' (code 57), so "10" sorts first.

title: Urban Greening, Brownfield Sites & Quality of Life
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: What four things did the Salford Quays Regeneration Project aim to do?
cards.answer: Clean up the contamination / Build new homes / Attract employers / Create public space

cards.front: Name the four principles of sustainable urban living given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Energy and water conservation in homes / Recycling waste rather than landfill / Creating green space for residents / Transport designed to reduce private car use
items: Energy and water conservation in homes
Transport designed to reduce private car use

cards.front: Why is building on brownfield sites more expensive than building on greenfield sites?
cards.answer: Contaminated soil must be cleaned, old foundations broken up, and homes built more compactly.

cards.front: How does reducing the number of car journeys improve life in a city like Manchester?
cards.answer: Lower traffic volume means lower emissions, lower noise, safer streets and more space for trees and cafés.

cards.front: Name the four main stages a life cycle assessment covers.
cards.answer: Extracting and processing raw materials / Manufacturing the product / Using the product (including transport) / Disposing of the product at end of life
items: Disposing of the product at end of life

cards.front: Give the four reasons the lesson gives for percentage yield often being less than 100%.
cards.answer: Incomplete reactions / Side reactions / Product lost during purification / Reversible reactions not going to completion
items: Reversible reactions not going to completion

cards.front: Why is recycling aluminium particularly worthwhile?
cards.answer: Extracting aluminium from bauxite by electrolysis is very energy-intensive, but recycling it uses only about 5% of that energy.

cards.front: Why are life cycle assessments considered partly subjective?
cards.answer: Some impacts, like noise or visual pollution, are hard to quantify, so different analysts weight factors differently and reach different conclusions.

cards.front: The lesson names five uses of drones. What are they?
cards.answer: Parcel delivery / Agricultural monitoring / Search-and-rescue operations / Film-making / Infrastructure inspection

cards.front: What four examples of Green IT practices does the lesson give?
cards.answer: Energy-efficient server hardware / Renewable-powered data centres / Device recycling programmes / Power-saving settings on consumer hardware

cards.front: Why have jobs in manufacturing, retail checkout and telephone directories shrunk?
cards.answer: Automation and digital systems have taken over these roles.

cards.front: Why has online shopping had a mixed effect on road traffic?
cards.answer: It lowers personal car use since people don't visit shops, but increases delivery van traffic to bring goods to them.

cards.front: Name the three fundamental types of plate boundary described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Divergent boundaries / Conservative boundaries / Convergent boundaries

cards.front: Name the three-part sequence of ocean floor topography from the ridge to the trench.
cards.answer: Mid-ocean ridge / Abyssal plain / Trench

cards.front: How does subduction lead to the formation of andesitic magma?
cards.answer: The descending slab releases water, which rises into the mantle wedge, lowers its melting point, and causes partial melting that enriches the magma in silica.

cards.front: Why does the ocean floor get deeper as you move away from a mid-ocean ridge?
cards.answer: As the crust moves away from the ridge it ages, cools and contracts, causing it to sink and deepen towards the abyssal plain.

cards.front: Name the three main types of ionising radiation emitted by unstable nuclei.
cards.answer: Alpha particles / Beta particles / Gamma rays

cards.front: Name the three natural sources of background radiation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Radon gas from rocks / Cosmic rays from space / Radioactive materials in food and building materials
items: Radioactive materials in food and building materials

cards.front: Why are swallowed or inhaled alpha sources especially dangerous, even though alpha is stopped by skin?
cards.answer: Alpha particles are the most ionising type of radiation, so once inside the body they cause more damage to living cells.

cards.front: Why is contamination generally considered more dangerous than irradiation?
cards.answer: The radioactive material stays on or inside the person, giving continuous exposure that cannot be stopped by moving away.

cards.front: After Bassanio chooses the lead casket correctly, what three things does Portia commit to him?
cards.answer: Herself / her wealth / her household

cards.front: Why does the Prince of Arragon's failure with the silver casket punish his character flaw?
cards.answer: He chooses silver reasoning he 'deserves' Portia, revealing arrogance, and finds a portrait of a fool inside, punishing his self-importance.

cards.front: Why can Portia only use her intelligence to save Antonio by disguising herself as a man?
cards.answer: Venetian and Elizabethan society excluded women from the courtroom, so she must become a man to argue the case.

cards.front: What three functions does code-switching serve in Leave Taking?
cards.answer: Characterisation / Thematic (patois vs standard English tension) / Dramatic (exposes Enid's contradiction)

cards.front: Why does the audience hear irony when Enid argues for English respectability?
cards.answer: Because she makes the argument in Jamaican patois, so the audience hears the contradiction she is living.

cards.front: Name the four ways De Waal presents Leon's bond with Jake in Part 1.
cards.answer: Physical closeness / Responsibility / Promises / Leon's identity

cards.front: Give three signs of Carol's deterioration described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Stops cooking / Sleeps for days / Brings home frightening men / Disappears leaving children alone

cards.front: How does De Waal use tactile language to show love between Leon and Jake?
cards.answer: She uses words like 'warm,' 'soft,' and 'tucked in' to show love expressed through touch rather than words.

cards.front: Why does the bureaucratic language of social services create a power imbalance for Leon?
cards.answer: Words like 'placement' and 'permanency' describe devastating changes he doesn't understand, leaving him no voice in decisions about his life.

title: Characters: Jo, Helen, Geof, Peter and the Boy
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the six stages of Jo's arc across the play, from Christmas engagement to the final curtain.
cards.answer: Engaged to the Boy at Christmas / Abandoned when his naval tour ends / Pregnant and working two jobs alone / Sharing a flat with Geof / Refusing Geof's marriage proposal / Alone again as her labour begins
items: Engaged to the Boy at Christmas
Abandoned when his naval tour ends
Pregnant and working two jobs alone
Alone again as her labour begins

cards.front: Name the three relationships the lesson says you should track across the play.
cards.answer: Jo and Helen / Jo and Geof / Helen and Peter

cards.front: Why does Jo refuse Geof's proposal of marriage?
cards.answer: She tells him she chose him partly because he will not try to start a romance with her.

cards.front: Why does Helen's marriage to Peter collapse?
cards.answer: Their marriage collapses because of another woman, and it is over by the final scene.

title: Nuclear Radiation: Uses, Fission and Fusion
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three categories of nuclear waste described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Low-level waste / Intermediate-level waste / High-level waste

cards.front: Name the four safety precautions the lesson gives for handling radioactive materials.
cards.answer: Keep exposure time short / Maximise distance from source / Use shielding / Monitor exposure with dosimeters

cards.front: Why does gamma radiotherapy aim beams at a tumour from multiple angles?
cards.answer: To concentrate the radiation dose on the cancer while minimising damage to healthy tissue.

cards.front: How does a thickness monitor detect if a material becomes too thick during manufacturing?
cards.answer: If the material gets too thick, less radiation passes through to the detector, triggering an adjustment.

cards.front: Name the four documents in Jekyll and Hyde that contain and control crucial information.
cards.answer: Jekyll's will / Hyde's forged letter / Lanyon's sealed letter / Jekyll's full statement

cards.front: What five things does Utterson find when he searches Hyde's ransacked Soho rooms?
cards.answer: Good paintings / fine wine / silver cutlery / ransacked drawers / a pile of burnt papers

cards.front: Why does the London fog serve a dual purpose in Jekyll and Hyde?
cards.answer: Literally it blocks characters' sight of the truth about Jekyll, while symbolically it represents Victorian society valuing appearances over reality.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson's three-narrator structure suggest full knowledge of human duality cannot be survived?
cards.answer: Each narrator gets closer to the truth but is more damaged: Utterson never fully understands, Lanyon dies, and Jekyll is destroyed.

title: Transformers, Power Transmission and Moments Drill
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Why does stepping voltage down at a substation cause a big increase in current?
cards.answer: Since power (V×I) is conserved, decreasing voltage by a factor increases current by the same factor.

cards.front: How does a transformer keep power constant while changing voltage?
cards.answer: It doesn't create energy; it exchanges it between voltage and current, so as voltage rises current falls proportionally, keeping Vp×Ip = Vs×Is.

cards.front: Why does Jane refuse to become Rochester's mistress despite loving him?
cards.answer: She chooses principle over feeling, believing laws and principles exist precisely for moments of temptation like this.

cards.front: Why does Brontë make Jane leave Thornfield with no money or help from Rochester?
cards.answer: Her independence would be worthless if funded by the man she refuses, so moral agency must be material as well as spiritual.

cards.front: Name the five processes within schools that the lesson says affect educational achievement.
cards.answer: Streaming / Setting / Mixed ability teaching / Labelling / Self-fulfilling prophecy

cards.front: Name the four sociological perspectives the lesson gives on processes within schools.
cards.answer: Functionalist / Interactionist / Marxist / Feminist

cards.front: How does being placed in a low stream or set affect a pupil's own aspirations?
cards.answer: Teachers give less challenging work and lower expectations, so the pupil internalises the 'low ability' label and lowers their own aspirations.

cards.front: Why did Willis argue that the lads' rebellion still prepared them for working-class jobs?
cards.answer: Their resistance to school authority, experienced as freedom, prepared them for manual labour just as effectively as conformity would have.

title: The Oneness of Humanity and Equality
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three composers included in the Guru Granth Sahib whose castes/backgrounds show its teaching of equality.
cards.answer: Kabir, a low-caste weaver / Sheikh Farid, a Muslim mystic / Ravidas, a leatherworker of very low caste
items: Ravidas, a leatherworker of very low caste

cards.front: How did Guru Gobind Singh's founding of the Khalsa in 1699 abolish caste hierarchy?
cards.answer: He chose the Panj Pyare from different castes and initiated them as equals, then gave all Sikhs shared names instead of caste surnames.

title: Religion at Home and Honouring the Dead
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three annual Roman festivals connected to the dead.
cards.answer: Parentalia / Feralia / Lemuria

cards.front: What three limits did the Twelve Tables place on funerals (besides banning burial in the city)?
cards.answer: Funeral expenses were capped / Women forbidden from tearing cheeks or crying loudly / No gold buried with a corpse except dental work
items: Women forbidden from tearing cheeks or crying loudly
No gold buried with a corpse except dental work

cards.front: In Plautus's Pot of Gold, why did the Lar Familiaris decide to reward the owner's daughter with hidden gold?
cards.answer: Because she alone still brought daily offerings of incense, wine and flowers, showing faithful devotion to him.

cards.front: Why did some Romans inscribe curses on their tombs, like that of Caius Tullius Hesper?
cards.answer: To protect the grave from being robbed or damaged by threatening anyone who disturbed it with suffering.

title: The Social Learning Theory of Criminality
subject: psychology-ocr

cards.front: Name the three factors that make a child more likely to identify with a role model.
cards.answer: Role model is the same sex as them / Role model is high in status / Role model is seen being rewarded for behaviour
items: Role model is the same sex as them
Role model is high in status
Role model is seen being rewarded for behaviour

cards.front: What are the four stages of the learning process in Social Learning Theory?
cards.answer: Identification with a role model / Observation and imitation of their behaviour / Reinforcement, vicarious or direct / Internalisation of the behaviour
items: Observation and imitation of their behaviour

cards.front: Why might Cooper and Mackie's (1986) lab findings not reflect children's everyday behaviour?
cards.answer: The free-play session took place in an artificial laboratory setting, so it may not show how children really behave day to day.

cards.front: How does Social Learning Theory suggest future offending could be reduced?
cards.answer: By reducing children's exposure to criminal role models and making sure anti-social behaviour is not rewarded.

cards.front: What three central elements does the novel's opening establish, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Pip's orphan vulnerability / The power of the class system / The connection between Pip and Magwitch
items: The power of the class system
The connection between Pip and Magwitch

cards.front: Why does Miss Havisham's plan to use Estella as revenge against men ultimately backfire?
cards.answer: She makes Estella so emotionally cold that Estella cannot love Miss Havisham either.

cards.front: How does Dickens show that violence in the Gargery household is cyclical?
cards.answer: Mrs Joe, who is violent towards Pip and Joe, is later attacked by Orlick and left brain-damaged.

title: Types of Retail Business and Activity
subject: l12-retail-business

cards.front: Name the eight main types of retailer given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Supermarket / Hypermarket / Department store / Convenience store / Specialist/independent / Discount/variety store / E-tailer / Market trader

cards.front: Why do discount and variety stores like Primark and Poundland rely on high footfall?
cards.answer: Their business model relies on selling high volumes of products at low prices with tight cost control.

cards.front: Why does e-commerce tend to lead to higher return rates for retailers?
cards.answer: Customers cannot physically inspect or try products before buying, so more items get sent back.

cards.front: Why can a global retailer like Amazon or IKEA achieve huge purchasing economies compared to a local independent shop?
cards.answer: Its large scale gives it much greater buying power than a local independent, though it must manage different markets and regulations.

title: Depression and Addiction: Symptoms and Impact
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four ICD symptoms of depression besides low mood and loss of interest.
cards.answer: Low energy and fatigue / Poor concentration / Disturbed sleep or appetite / Feelings of worthlessness or guilt

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why reported incidence of depression and addiction has risen.
cards.answer: Increased challenges of modern living / Increased recognition of symptoms / Lessening of social stigma

cards.front: Why does the ICD require several symptoms to occur together rather than just one?
cards.answer: This separates ordinary sadness, which everyone experiences, from clinical depression that affects a person's ability to function.

cards.front: Why can reduced face-to-face contact and constant connectivity increase risk of depression and addiction?
cards.answer: They can increase loneliness, which is a known risk factor for both depression and addictive behaviour.

cards.front: Name the seven sacraments recognised by the Catholic Church.
cards.answer: Baptism / Confirmation / Eucharist / Reconciliation / Anointing of the Sick / Holy Orders / Matrimony

cards.front: What are the three forms of popular piety described in the lesson?
cards.answer: The Rosary / Eucharistic adoration / The Stations of the Cross

cards.front: Why do most Protestant denominations recognise only two sacraments?
cards.answer: Because they see only Baptism and the Eucharist as clearly instituted by Christ in the Gospels.

cards.front: Why is the Eucharist called the 'source and summit of the Christian life'?
cards.answer: Because every part of Catholic life flows from the Mass and is directed back towards it.

title: Lollards, Luther and English criticism of the church
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Why did Henry VIII write the Assertio Septem Sacramentorum in 1521?
cards.answer: To attack Luther's ideas, which earned him the title 'Defender of the Faith'.

cards.front: Why did the Church's attempts to burn Tyndale's Bibles fail to stop them spreading?
cards.answer: Demand outstripped supply, so burning one edition simply created demand for the next.

cards.front: Why did word choices in Tyndale's translation matter to the Church?
cards.answer: He used words like 'congregation' instead of 'church', carrying Protestant theological meaning that challenged Catholic teaching.

cards.front: Why did the Richard Hunne case in 1514 increase anti-clerical feeling in London?
cards.answer: Londoners believed the Church had murdered Hunne while he awaited trial for heresy in the Bishop's prison.

cards.front: Name the five characters and the idea each one embodies in Lord of the Flies.
cards.answer: Ralph = democracy / Jack = dictatorship / Piggy = reason / Simon = spiritual truth / Roger = sadism

cards.front: Why is Ralph ultimately unable to stop civilisation collapsing on the island?
cards.answer: He lacks ruthlessness to enforce his rules, so he can only appeal and argue rather than compel obedience.

cards.front: Why does Jack succeed in gaining followers when Ralph struggles to keep them?
cards.answer: Jack offers immediate rewards like meat, excitement and protection from the beast, understanding people follow strength, not rules.

cards.front: How does the decline of the signal fire reflect the boys' journey in the novel?
cards.answer: Its decline mirrors their descent into savagery, and its abandonment marks the present's triumph over hope of rescue.

title: Challenges to the settlement: Puritans and Catholics
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three features of the Church did Puritans want removed, according to the lesson's Key Fact?
cards.answer: Vestments / Ornaments / Bishops

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth's government toughen its treatment of Catholics after 1570?
cards.answer: The Pope's 1570 bull, the 1571 Ridolfi plot, and fear that Catholic loyalty meant disloyalty to England pushed the shift.

cards.front: Why were the Earls of Northumberland and Westmorland already alienated from Elizabeth's government before 1570?
cards.answer: They lost influence at court to reformers like Cecil, and their remote northern lands with Catholic tenants were hard to control.

title: Lenin, Trotsky and the October Revolution
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three Bolshevik strengths the lesson gives for why they won in 1917.
cards.answer: A clear popular slogan no rival could match / A tightly disciplined party that could act fast / Trotsky's organisational skill with the Military Revolutionary Committee
items: A clear popular slogan no rival could match
A tightly disciplined party that could act fast
Trotsky's organisational skill with the Military Revolutionary Committee

cards.front: Name the three groups the Bolsheviks used to seize key buildings on the night of 24-25 October.
cards.answer: Kronstadt sailors / Bolshevik Red Guards from the factories / Pro-Bolshevik units of the Petrograd garrison
items: Bolshevik Red Guards from the factories
Pro-Bolshevik units of the Petrograd garrison

cards.front: Why did the slogan 'Peace, Land, Bread' work so well for the Bolsheviks in 1917?
cards.answer: Peace appealed to war-weary soldiers and cities, Land to peasants wanting noble estates broken up, Bread to workers facing inflation, and no other party offered all three.

cards.front: Why was the Bolshevik party so effective in 1917 despite its small size in April?
cards.answer: Discipline meant central committee decisions bound every cell, Pravda repeated consistent slogans, and agitators gave trained answers, so they acted while rivals debated.

cards.front: What four arguments does the lesson give in favour of marriage?
cards.answer: Shows a serious commitment / Important tradition in many cultures / Gives legal security to the couple / A beautiful celebration of love
items: Gives legal security to the couple

cards.front: What four arguments does the lesson give against marriage?
cards.answer: Not necessary to be happy / Costs a lot of money / Many marriages end in divorce / PACS is simpler to choose

cards.front: Why is it useful to be able to argue both sides of the marriage debate in a writing task?
cards.answer: Because it shows you can construct a balanced response, which is key for higher-level writing tasks.

cards.front: Why might a couple in France choose a PACS instead of marriage?
cards.answer: It gives many of the same legal rights as marriage but is simpler and cheaper to arrange.

cards.front: Why is the handwriting on Hyde's forged letter actually the same as Jekyll's?
cards.answer: Because Jekyll wrote it himself as Hyde, so the writer of both is literally the same person.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson set Jekyll's cabinet above the dissecting theatre inside a layered house?
cards.answer: The layered house mirrors a mind with a respectable surface, a working intellect, and a hidden appetite locked away.

cards.front: Why do Utterson and Enfield leave the window scene in silence?
cards.answer: Stevenson uses their silence to show there is nothing respectable Victorian gentlemen can say about what they saw.

cards.front: How do Chapters 5-8 change Stevenson's technique compared to earlier chapters?
cards.answer: He switches from planting clues to accumulating them until the reader can no longer resist the conclusion.

title: Short and Long Term Effects of Exercise
subject: physical-education-ocr

cards.front: Why does lactic acid production increase during high-intensity exercise?
cards.answer: Because exercise intensity rises beyond the aerobic threshold, so the body supplements aerobic energy with anaerobic pathways.

cards.front: How does capillarisation improve resistance to fatigue?
cards.answer: New capillaries increase oxygen delivery and speed up waste removal, letting muscles delay lactic acid accumulation and sustain effort longer.

cards.front: What are the three rules of kashrut given in the lesson?
cards.answer: Only permitted animals may be eaten (chew cud + split hooves; fins + scales) / Kosher slaughter (shechita) that minimises suffering, with blood drained / Complete separation of milk and meat
items: Only permitted animals may be eaten (chew cud + split hooves; fins + scales)
Kosher slaughter (shechita) that minimises suffering, with blood drained
Complete separation of milk and meat

cards.front: What three things characterise the Ten Days of Awe between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur?
cards.answer: Intense prayer / Repentance / Acts of tzedakah

cards.front: Why must blood be drained from meat before it is eaten under kashrut?
cards.answer: Because Jewish teaching holds that 'the life of the flesh is in the blood' (Leviticus 17:11).

cards.front: Why can Yom Kippur not atone for sins between people without further action?
cards.answer: Yom Kippur atones for sins between humans and God, but sins between people must first be addressed by seeking forgiveness from those harmed.

cards.front: What are the four key events through which Catholics understand redemption?
cards.answer: The life of Jesus / The death of Jesus on the cross / The resurrection / The ascension
items: The death of Jesus on the cross

cards.front: According to the Council of Chalcedon, the two natures of Jesus exist in what four ways?
cards.answer: Without confusion / without change / without division / without separation

cards.front: Why do Catholics see the whole life of Jesus, not just his death, as redemptively significant?
cards.answer: His miracles reveal the coming Kingdom of God and his teachings show its values, so imitating him is part of being saved.

cards.front: How does baptism relate to grace in Catholic teaching?
cards.answer: Baptism removes original sin and begins the life of grace, which the Eucharist then nourishes and sustains.

cards.front: Name the three pillars that Anglo-Saxon kingship rested on.
cards.answer: Hereditary descent / Military leadership/prowess / The Church's sanction through coronation

cards.front: Besides providing a warrior, name the three local roles thegns performed for the king.
cards.answer: Sat on local courts / Collected royal taxes / Enforced the king's peace in their shires
items: Enforced the king's peace in their shires

cards.front: How did Cnut's reign show that Anglo-Saxon kingship was defined by behaviour rather than blood?
cards.answer: Although a Danish conqueror, he governed as an English king by issuing law codes, building churches and ruling through the Witan.

cards.front: Why did Æthelred II earn the nickname 'the Unready'?
cards.answer: Because he was unable to halt Viking raids, though 'Unready' actually mistranslates the word meaning 'ill-advised'.

title: Dramatic Methods: The Narrator and the Songs
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: According to the lesson's Key Fact, what four things does the Narrator do throughout Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: Breaks the fourth wall / Addresses the audience directly / Uses the language of superstition and fate / Reappears at key moments of transition
items: Uses the language of superstition and fate
Reappears at key moments of transition

cards.front: The lesson corrects a misconception that the Narrator is neutral. What three staging choices show he is threatening instead?
cards.answer: Dark costume / Still and predatory physicality / Controlled, low-pitched vocal quality

cards.front: Why does Mrs Lyons introduce the 'shoes on the table' superstition to Mrs Johnstone?
cards.answer: It is a manipulation device using a familiar working-class taboo to bind Mrs Johnstone to silence.

cards.front: Why does 'Tell Me It's Not True' function as a lament rather than a prayer at the play's close?
cards.answer: It is sung with full knowledge the ending is true, so the audience's shared knowledge strips it of hope, leaving only grief.

title: The Cabal, Party Politics and Rule Without Parliament
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five members of the Cabal ministry (1668–1674) whose initials gave it its nickname.
cards.answer: Clifford / Arlington / Buckingham / Ashley / Lauderdale

cards.front: Name the two reasons Charles II could afford to rule without Parliament from 1681.
cards.answer: Booming customs and excise revenue / French subsidy of around £385,000 from Louis XIV
items: French subsidy of around £385,000 from Louis XIV

cards.front: Why did the discovery of the Rye House Plot in 1683 help Charles II tighten his grip on local government?
cards.answer: It let him press legal challenges to borough charters much harder and purge Whig sympathisers from the corporations.

cards.front: Why did Charles II deliberately keep the five Cabal ministers divided rather than letting them act as a unified team?
cards.answer: So that no single one of them could dominate government or gain too much power over him.

cards.front: Name the four cardinal virtues in Catholic virtue ethics.
cards.answer: Courage / Justice / Prudence / Temperance

cards.front: Name the five seasons of the Catholic liturgical calendar that shape parish life.
cards.answer: Advent / Christmas / Lent / Easter / Ordinary Time

cards.front: Why do Catholics offer Masses for the dead?
cards.answer: Because of belief in purgatory — prayers of the living and the offering of the Mass can benefit souls being purified before heaven.

cards.front: Why is regular confession seen as supporting growth in virtue?
cards.answer: Because it is a practice that helps develop humility and honesty, two virtues essential for moral development.

cards.front: According to the lesson, name the six adaptations endurance athletes gain the most improvement in.
cards.answer: Cardiac hypertrophy / Increased stroke volume / Bradycardia / Increased vital capacity / Alveolar capillarisation / Lactic acid tolerance

cards.front: According to the lesson, name the three main adaptations resistance athletes (e.g. weightlifters) gain from training.
cards.answer: Pronounced muscle hypertrophy / Increased bone density / Stronger tendons and ligaments

cards.front: How does regular weight-bearing exercise increase bone density?
cards.answer: Repeated mechanical loading stimulates osteoblasts to lay down extra mineral in the bone.

cards.front: How does endurance training increase muscular endurance?
cards.answer: It improves the muscles' mitochondrial density and glycogen storage capacity, letting them sustain repeated contractions longer without fatiguing.

cards.front: What four things does Richard report about the group's fragmentation to Phil in Act 4 of DNA?
cards.answer: John Tate joined the Jesus Army / Brian is heavily medicated and may be sectioned / Danny hates his dentist work experience / Cathy is running things and cut off a finger
items: John Tate joined the Jesus Army
Brian is heavily medicated and may be sectioned
Danny hates his dentist work experience
Cathy is running things and cut off a finger

cards.front: Why does Phil's plan in Act 3 mark a moral escalation from his plan in Act 1?
cards.answer: In Act 1 his plan was deception that harmed no one physically, but in Act 3 he implies ordering Adam's murder, a far darker step.

cards.front: Why is it ironic that Cathy is the one 'running things' by Act 4 of DNA?
cards.answer: The character who showed the least remorse and enjoyed the violence most is the one who thrives, while others are damaged.

title: Types of Chemical Reactions and Electrolysis
subject: science-ocr

cards.front: Name the three key acid reactions given in the lesson that produce a salt.
cards.answer: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen / Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide / Acid + alkali → salt + water
items: Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide

cards.front: Name the three ways given in the lesson to measure pH.
cards.answer: Universal indicator / pH meter / Litmus paper

cards.front: Why can't solid ionic compounds be electrolysed?
cards.answer: Their ions are held in fixed positions within the lattice, so they cannot move to carry the electrical current.

cards.front: Why does hydrogen form at the cathode instead of the metal during electrolysis of an aqueous solution?
cards.answer: Hydrogen forms instead of the metal when the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions are reduced instead.

cards.front: Name the four key Space Race achievements given in the lesson, in order.
cards.answer: Sputnik satellite launched (1957) / Yuri Gagarin first human in space (1961) / NASA receives massive US investment / USA lands on the Moon (1969)
items: Yuri Gagarin first human in space (1961)

cards.front: Why did the USSR crush the Hungarian uprising in 1956?
cards.answer: Hungary tried to leave the Warsaw Pact, so Soviet tanks intervened to maintain control over its satellite states.

cards.front: Why did MAD (Mutually Assured Destruction) make direct war between the superpowers less likely?
cards.answer: Both sides had nuclear arsenals capable of devastating retaliation, so any first strike would trigger destruction for the attacker too.

cards.front: Why did the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979) put such strain on the USSR?
cards.answer: The nine-year war killed around 15,000 Soviet soldiers and vast numbers of Afghans, worsening existing Soviet economic strain.

title: Waterloo 1815 and Balaclava 1854: leadership, technology and reporting
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three episodes at Balaclava that Britain remembers.
cards.answer: The 'Thin Red Line' of the 93rd Highlanders / The Charge of the Heavy Brigade / The Charge of the Light Brigade
items: The 'Thin Red Line' of the 93rd Highlanders
The Charge of the Heavy Brigade
The Charge of the Light Brigade

cards.front: At Waterloo, what were the three combined arms roles used together?
cards.answer: Infantry squares to defeat cavalry / Cavalry counter-charges to break enemy infantry / Artillery to soften both
items: Cavalry counter-charges to break enemy infantry

cards.front: Why did Wellington use reverse-slope tactics at Waterloo?
cards.answer: He placed infantry just behind the ridge crest so French artillery could not target them and French troops could not see them until crossing the ridge.

cards.front: Why would the Charge of the Light Brigade have been destroyed regardless of the era's weapons technology?
cards.answer: Riding over a mile down a valley with enemy batteries firing from three sides would have been ruinous in any period, whatever the guns' design.

cards.front: Name the six types of accommodation vocabulary given in the lesson.
cards.answer: das Hotel – hotel / die Pension – guest house/B&B / die Jugendherberge – youth hostel / der Campingplatz – campsite / die Ferienwohnung – holiday apartment / das Ferienhaus – holiday home

cards.front: Name the seven hotel facilities (Einrichtungen) listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: der Aufzug – lift / der Swimmingpool – swimming pool / das Restaurant – restaurant / der Parkplatz – car park / die Klimaanlage – air conditioning / kostenloses WLAN – free Wi-Fi / die Rezeption – reception

cards.front: Why is 'Ich möchte' preferred over 'Ich will' when booking a hotel room in German?
cards.answer: Because möchte (would like) is more polite than will (want) and shows good language skills.

cards.front: How are German compound nouns like 'das Einzelzimmer' formed, and which part decides the gender?
cards.answer: They are formed by joining words together, and the last word in the compound determines its gender.

cards.front: What four things do top-band 12-mark decision essay answers do?
cards.answer: Weigh costs and benefits / Use evidence from the booklet / Balance opposing views / Reach a clearly justified conclusion

cards.front: What three types of information should you look for in the resources booklet?
cards.answer: Quantitative data like graphs and numbers / Qualitative data like quotes and photographs / Spatial information on maps
items: Quantitative data like graphs and numbers
Qualitative data like quotes and photographs

cards.front: In the Amazon worked example, why might a student justify choosing ecotourism with selective logging over the other two options?
cards.answer: Ecotourism aligns Indigenous, environmental and economic interests, but only works if backed by enforcement and infrastructure.

cards.front: Why might linking Amazon deforestation to UK flood risk strengthen a decision essay?
cards.answer: Deforestation contributes to climate change, which can increase UK flood risk, showing the decision's wider consequences.

cards.front: Name the six main types of media product identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Moving image / Audio / Publishing and print / Interactive / Games / Audio-visual

cards.front: Give the three examples of audio-visual products named in the lesson.
cards.answer: TV adverts / Corporate videos / Online tutorials

cards.front: How does the way audiences use content differ between the television and film sector and the web and app sector?
cards.answer: TV and film content is broadcast to passive viewers who watch, while web and app products are actively navigated and controlled by users.

cards.front: Why can the same organisation be described using both a sector and a product type, such as an advertising agency making a TV commercial?
cards.answer: The sector shows the industry area the organisation belongs to, while the product type shows the format of the content it creates, so both apply separately.

title: Forces in Action: Springs, Hooke's Law and Moments
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four examples of levers given in the lesson (other than a crowbar).
cards.answer: Scissors / Tweezers / Bottle opener / Wheelbarrow

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson gives to improve accuracy when investigating Hooke's Law.
cards.answer: Take repeated readings and calculate the mean / Read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax / Ensure the spring hangs freely without touching the stand
items: Take repeated readings and calculate the mean
Read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax
Ensure the spring hangs freely without touching the stand

cards.front: Why must two opposing forces be applied to deform an object, rather than just one?
cards.answer: A single force would just accelerate the object (Newton's Second Law), so two opposing forces are needed to cause deformation.

cards.front: In the see-saw example, why must the heavier adult sit closer to the pivot than the lighter child to balance it?
cards.answer: Since moment = force × distance, a larger force needs a smaller distance to produce the same moment as a smaller force at a larger distance.

cards.front: Name the four reforms Dubček introduced during the Prague Spring.
cards.answer: Relaxed censorship for greater free speech / Allowed other political parties alongside the Communist Party / Introduced elements of a market economy / Strengthened trade links with the West
items: Relaxed censorship for greater free speech
Allowed other political parties alongside the Communist Party
Introduced elements of a market economy
Strengthened trade links with the West

cards.front: What four reasons does the lesson give for why the USSR feared the Prague Spring?
cards.answer: Domino effect to other satellite states / Pressure from East Germany and Poland / Fear anti-Soviet ideas would spread / Fear trade links would pull Czechoslovakia towards the West
items: Domino effect to other satellite states
Pressure from East Germany and Poland
Fear trade links would pull Czechoslovakia towards the West

cards.front: Why did the UN fail to officially condemn the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia?
cards.answer: The United Nations debated the crisis, but the USSR used its veto to block any resolution.

cards.front: Why was Kennedy's 1963 'Ich bin ein Berliner' speech significant?
cards.answer: It was propaganda showing communism's failure, reassured West Berliners, and showed continued US commitment to Western Europe.

cards.front: Name the three main forms of sponsorship in sport described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Financial sponsorship / Clothing and equipment sponsorship / Facility sponsorship

cards.front: Name the four types of media that influence the commercialisation of sport.
cards.answer: Social media / The internet / Television / Newspapers and magazines

cards.front: How did social media change the relationship between athletes and fans compared to before?
cards.answer: Athletes can now communicate directly with fans and build personal brands, instead of their image being controlled by TV, newspapers and PR teams.

cards.front: Why does increased television coverage of a sport help attract sponsors?
cards.answer: Greater coverage raises the sport's profile and viewer numbers, which attracts sponsors wanting exposure to that larger audience.

title: Elizabeth I: background, character and the royal court
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four languages Elizabeth I read and wrote fluently, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Latin / Greek / French / Italian

cards.front: Which four royal palaces does the lesson name that the court moved between?
cards.answer: Whitehall / Greenwich / Hampton Court / Richmond

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth rely on image-making, such as her portraits, to rule?
cards.answer: She could not rely on a husband or a strong army to enforce her authority, so used image as a political tool.

cards.front: How did the patronage system stop ambitious nobles from uniting against Elizabeth?
cards.answer: Because she controlled rewards, ambitious men competed for her favour rather than challenging her authority, as long as rewards kept flowing.

cards.front: Name the four main ways the lesson says Christians worship.
cards.answer: Liturgical / Non-liturgical / Informal / Private

cards.front: The Lord's Prayer covers four things according to the lesson's Key Fact — what are they?
cards.answer: Praise of God / Submission to God's will / Requests for daily needs / Forgiveness

cards.front: Why do supporters value liturgical worship's use of a set lectionary?
cards.answer: Because readings follow a set pattern so all congregations worldwide hear the same Bible passages on the same day.

cards.front: Why does Quaker worship involve sitting in silence with no leader?
cards.answer: So there is no fixed structure, allowing God to communicate directly with individuals when they feel moved by the Holy Spirit.

title: Themes: continuity and change in twentieth-century Germany
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six turning points in German history from 1919 to 1991 that the lesson identifies as strongest candidates.
cards.answer: 1919 Treaty of Versailles/Weimar Constitution / January 1933 Hitler's appointment / 1945 total defeat and division / 1949 creation of two German states / 1963 Élysée Treaty / 1989–1990 fall of Wall and reunification

cards.front: Name the five distinct economic conditions Germany experienced between 1919 and 1991.
cards.answer: Weimar inflation, recovery, then Depression / Nazi rearmament recovery then war devastation / post-1945 total economic collapse / Wirtschaftswunder in the West vs planned economy in the East / 1990 merger of dynamic and declining economies
items: Nazi rearmament recovery then war devastation
Wirtschaftswunder in the West vs planned economy in the East
1990 merger of dynamic and declining economies

cards.front: Why was West Germany's democracy after 1949 able to survive economic downturns that would have destroyed Weimar's?
cards.answer: The Basic Law's structural safeguards embedded democracy so deeply it survived crises like the 1970s oil shock that Weimar could not withstand.

cards.front: Why is a change like 1945 or 1990 considered more significant than a single-track change in German history?
cards.answer: It transformed both Germany's internal situation and its external position simultaneously, making it harder to dismiss as less important.

title: The Rise of Trade Unions: Tolpuddle to New Unionism, 1834-1889
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What three phases did trade unionism develop through, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Tolpuddle (1834) showed state hostility / New Model Unions (1850s onwards) won legality and respectability / New unionism (1888-89) brought in unskilled workers
items: New Model Unions (1850s onwards) won legality and respectability
New unionism (1888-89) brought in unskilled workers

cards.front: The lesson gives four factors that come together in the story of trade unionism. What are they?
cards.answer: The economy / The role of the individual / Government / Communication

cards.front: Why did the Tolpuddle case backfire on the authorities?
cards.answer: The harsh transportation sentence provoked a national petition of 800,000 signatures and huge demonstrations, forcing the government to pardon the men.

cards.front: Why did New Model Unions win legal recognition and respectability by the 1870s?
cards.answer: Their high subscriptions, benefits and cooperation with employers made them respectable, winning the Trade Union Act 1871 and the 1875 Conspiracy Act.

cards.front: Why does the cyclical structure of 'When We Two Parted' make the speaker's grief feel unresolved?
cards.answer: The opening and closing 'silence and tears' show the pain has not diminished, trapping the speaker in the memory of loss.

cards.front: Why is the speaker in 'When We Two Parted' unable to publicly grieve?
cards.answer: Because the affair was secret, so the forced silence intensifies the emotional damage.

cards.front: How do the half-rhymes in 'When We Two Parted' reflect the speaker's grief?
