cards.answer: Half-rhymes like 'morning'/'warning' create a sense of incompleteness, reflecting the unfinished nature of the grief.

cards.front: Why does Dooley describe souls 'tapping out messages' in 'Letters from Yorkshire'?
cards.answer: It gives their spiritual bond a physical action, like a signal sent along a wire, showing connection can survive distance without technology.

title: Feudal England in 1189: Society, Towns and the Jewish Communities
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What were the four levels of England's feudal social pyramid in 1189, from top to bottom?
cards.answer: The king / Tenants-in-chief (barons and bishops) / Sub-tenants and knights / Unfree peasants

cards.front: What three ways did villein peasants pay rent to their lord?
cards.answer: Labour (week-work and boon-work) / In kind (eggs, hens, grain) / In cash

cards.front: Why did the king grant boroughs their charters of self-government?
cards.answer: In exchange for self-government, boroughs paid an annual farm to the exchequer and acted as a tax reserve for royal needs like crusades.

cards.front: Why was Richard I angry after the 1189-90 pogroms, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Not because Jews had died, but because his property, the Jewish community under royal protection, had been destroyed.

title: The End of Empire: Wars, Suez & Independence
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five African/Asian colonies (in order of independence, 1957-1963) the lesson traces through decolonisation.
cards.answer: Ghana, 1957 / Nigeria, 1960 / Sierra Leone, 1961 / Tanganyika, 1961 / Uganda, 1962 / Kenya, 1963

cards.front: What four conditions in Britain by 1945 left it unable to maintain the empire by force?
cards.answer: Debts more than twice yearly national income / Dependence on a large American loan / Still rationing food at home / A Labour government committed to the welfare state
items: Debts more than twice yearly national income
Dependence on a large American loan
A Labour government committed to the welfare state

cards.front: Why couldn't Britain defend the pound during the 1956 Suez Crisis without American help?
cards.answer: The Treasury lacked the funds to defend the pound alone, and Eisenhower withheld US help until British troops withdrew from Egypt.

cards.front: How did the 1943 Bengal famine kill at least three million Indians?
cards.answer: Churchill's government diverted food supplies to British troops during the Second World War, causing mass starvation in Bengal.

title: The Last Days of Jesus, Salvation and Atonement
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four interlocking concepts the lesson gives for Christian teaching on salvation.
cards.answer: Law / Sin / Grace / Spirit

cards.front: Name the three models of atonement the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Penal substitution / Moral influence/example theory / Christus Victor

cards.front: Why is the resurrection considered the foundation of Christian faith?
cards.answer: Without it the cross would just be a tragedy, and it shows death is not the final word for believers.

cards.front: How does the ascension prepare the disciples for their mission?
cards.answer: It leads into Pentecost, the coming of the Holy Spirit, and gives the disciples their commission to spread Jesus's message worldwide.

cards.front: What are the three sections of 'Odour of Chrysanthemums'?
cards.answer: Waiting for Walter / Arrival of the body / Washing of the body

cards.front: How does Lawrence use prose register to build up to the story's ending?
cards.answer: The cool, flat register of the waiting sections contrasts with the lyrical, interior prose of the final scene, making its emotion more powerful.

cards.front: How does Walter escape the pressures of the pit and home life?
cards.answer: Walter escapes through drink, while Elizabeth manages the house with an efficiency that displaces her feelings.

cards.front: Why does Lawrence use the chrysanthemum motif across the story?
cards.answer: It links love, birth and death, suggesting death was always present in the marriage and touched even its happy moments.

cards.front: Name the five workshop safety essentials the lesson gives for using machinery safely.
cards.answer: Wear appropriate PPE / Secure workpieces with clamps or vices / Never leave machines running unattended / Keep guards in place / No loose clothing, jewellery or untied hair
items: Secure workpieces with clamps or vices
No loose clothing, jewellery or untied hair

cards.front: Name the four hand tool categories the lesson groups by function, with one example each.
cards.answer: Marking and measuring - steel rule / Cutting - tenon saw / Shaping - chisels / Joining - clamps

cards.front: Why must work never be held by hand when using a pillar drill?
cards.answer: It must be secured with a machine vice or clamp because the drill needs precise vertical holes made safely, not held by hand.

cards.front: Why is laser cutting chosen for cutting or engraving sheet materials like acrylic or MDF?
cards.answer: Because a focused laser beam gives extremely high precision and clean edges with minimal kerf.

cards.front: Which four other anthology poems does the lesson compare with 'Happy Birthday Moon'?
cards.answer: Baby Song (Thom Gunn) / You're (Sylvia Plath) / Love (Kate Clanchy) / Prayer (Zaffar Kunial)

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say happened to Antrobus's debut collection The Perseverance?
cards.answer: Won the Ted Hughes Award / Won the Rathbones Folio Prize / Listed among the books of the year
items: Listed among the books of the year

cards.front: Why does Antrobus choose the pantoum form to write about a deaf child learning to speak?
cards.answer: Its circling, repeating lines imitate the halting, repetitive process of a child trying to say a word correctly for the first time.

cards.front: How does the poem's final repeated line show progress rather than mere repetition?
cards.answer: The line returns but a small change in punctuation shifts its meaning, showing father and son getting closer each time, not saying the same thing twice.

title: Yalta and Potsdam: Allies Become Rivals
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What did each of the Big Three want from the peace settlement at Yalta?
cards.answer: Stalin wanted permanent security on his western border / Roosevelt wanted the USSR in the UN and helping against Japan / Churchill wanted to limit Soviet influence in Europe
items: Stalin wanted permanent security on his western border
Roosevelt wanted the USSR in the UN and helping against Japan
Churchill wanted to limit Soviet influence in Europe

cards.front: What three explanations do historians give for the origins of the Cold War?
cards.answer: Stalin's expansion in Eastern Europe / Truman's atom-bomb diplomacy / Structural rivalry between two great powers with opposed ideologies
items: Structural rivalry between two great powers with opposed ideologies

cards.front: Why did the Potsdam reparations agreement leave Germany's two halves on different economic paths?
cards.answer: Each occupier took reparations from its own zone, so the Soviets stripped the east while the West rebuilt the industrial Ruhr.

cards.front: Why was Stalin not surprised when Truman mentioned a powerful new weapon at Potsdam?
cards.answer: Soviet spies had already alerted Stalin to the atomic bomb's existence before Truman told him.

cards.front: Name the three components that make up every homeostatic control system.
cards.answer: Receptors / Coordination centre / Effectors

cards.front: Name the three effector responses the body uses when it is too hot.
cards.answer: Blood vessels vasodilate / Sweat glands produce sweat / Body hairs lie flat

cards.front: How does sweating cool the body down?
cards.answer: Sweat evaporates from the skin surface, transferring heat energy away from the body.

cards.front: How does shivering help warm the body up?
cards.answer: Muscles undergo rapid involuntary contractions, generating heat from respiration in muscle cells.

title: 11 September 2001: The Attacks That Changed the World
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four countries the nineteen 9/11 hijackers came from.
cards.answer: Saudi Arabia / United Arab Emirates / Egypt / Lebanon

cards.front: Give the four locations struck or crashed into during the 9/11 attacks.
cards.answer: North Tower, World Trade Center / South Tower, World Trade Center / The Pentagon / A field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania

cards.front: Why did 9/11 become the most intimately documented atrocity of its time, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Mobile phones, then widespread, let trapped victims call relatives, and those voicemails were recovered and reconstructed by the 9/11 Commission.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to call 9/11 simply a 'Middle Eastern attack on America'?
cards.answer: The hijackers trained in Afghanistan, met in Malaysia, planned in Hamburg, learned to fly in Florida/Arizona and struck New York, Virginia and Pennsylvania, showing a transnational geography.

cards.front: Name the four towns where Huguenot refugees mainly settled in England.
cards.answer: London / Canterbury / Southampton / Norwich

cards.front: Name three fields the lesson credits Huguenot refugees with contributing skills to.
cards.answer: Silk-weaving / Silversmithing / Medicine

cards.front: Why did the arrival of the Palatines in 1709 provoke hostility despite them being fellow Protestants?
cards.answer: The sheer scale of arrivals strained charitable resources, and they had fewer skills and greater economic needs than Huguenots.

cards.front: Why were Huguenot silk-weavers sometimes resented by native English weavers in Spitalfields?
cards.answer: Native weavers resented the economic competition from Huguenots, leading to periodic riots.

cards.front: Name the five key causes of player violence given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Frustration / Rivalry and importance of the contest / Alcohol and drugs / Officiating decisions / Win-at-all-costs culture
items: Rivalry and importance of the contest

cards.front: Name the three actions national governing bodies (NGBs) can take in response to player violence.
cards.answer: Bans / Fines / Mandatory education programmes

cards.front: How can national governing bodies use rule changes to deter player violence?
cards.answer: They can introduce measures like sin bins or citing commissioners to deter violent conduct and protect the sport's reputation.

cards.front: Why is intimidation in a win-at-all-costs culture treated as deviance rather than gamesmanship?
cards.answer: Gamesmanship stays within the rules, but this intimidation exceeds the rules and risks injuring opponents, crossing ethical boundaries.

cards.front: Name the three narrative functions the lesson gives for Spider the dog.
cards.answer: Provides emotional companionship / Confirms the haunting is real / Creates vulnerability Arthur must protect

cards.front: How does Hill's changing prose style track Arthur's deterioration across the novel?
cards.answer: Prose moves from measured, controlled early chapters to fragmented, breathless writing at Eel Marsh House, ending quiet and broken.

cards.front: Why does Sam Daily break Crythin Gifford's code of silence to warn Arthur?
cards.answer: Because unlike the other townspeople, Sam values practical caution and cannot let Arthur walk into danger unwarned.

cards.front: Why does Mr Jerome fail to protect Arthur despite knowing about the curse?
cards.answer: He is overwhelmed by fear rather than malicious, and his silence makes him complicit through moral cowardice.

cards.front: Name the three macronutrients the lesson identifies as energy-providing nutrients.
cards.answer: Carbohydrates / Fats / Proteins

cards.front: Name the four functions of water in exercise given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Transporting nutrients and oxygen in the blood / Regulating body temperature through sweating / Lubricating joints / Removing waste products via urine
items: Transporting nutrients and oxygen in the blood

cards.front: Why doesn't carbohydrate loading benefit a sprinter in the 100m?
cards.answer: Their event lasts under 15 seconds and relies mainly on the ATP-PC system, not the glycogen stores that carb loading maximises.

cards.front: Why doesn't eating extra protein alone make an athlete more muscular?
cards.answer: Protein only supplies amino acids for repair; without resistance training as the stimulus, excess protein is simply excreted as urea, not built into muscle.

title: Sitcom Option: Modern Family and Friends
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three narrative strands resolved by the end of the set episode of Modern Family.
cards.answer: Dunphy family using Alex's illness to their advantage / Jay reacting to his new neighbours / Lily calling her friend Tom a "weirdo"
items: Dunphy family using Alex's illness to their advantage
Jay reacting to his new neighbours
Lily calling her friend Tom a "weirdo"

cards.front: Name the three US networks that Modern Family was pitched to.
cards.answer: CBS / NBC / ABC

cards.front: Why did NBC reject Modern Family when it was pitched to them?
cards.answer: NBC was already committed to other mockumentary sitcoms, The Office and Parks and Recreation.

cards.front: How does Modern Family show Steve Neale's idea that genres repeat conventions but also vary them?
cards.answer: It repeats sitcom staples like home settings and stereotyped characters, but varies them through mockumentary hybridity such as characters breaking the fourth wall.

cards.front: Name the three stages of the triangular trade Britain ran, as described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Manufactured goods to West Africa / Enslaved Africans to the Americas / Colonial produce back to Britain

cards.front: What four things does the lesson say slave-trade profits funded the building of in Britain?
cards.answer: Churches / Country houses / Banks / Public institutions

cards.front: Why was the Somerset case (1772) widely but incorrectly seen as making slavery illegal in England?
cards.answer: It only stopped Somerset being forcibly removed from England; enslaved people could still be held there and colonial slavery was unaffected.

cards.front: Why did the 1783 Zong court case not result in a murder trial for the 132 Africans killed?
cards.answer: The case was heard as an insurance dispute over the value of lost 'cargo,' not as a murder prosecution, which Granville Sharp failed to bring.

cards.front: Name the four 'king-becoming graces' that Malcolm lists in Macbeth.
cards.answer: Justice / Verity / Temperance / Mercy

cards.front: Name the four common pitfalls the lesson warns against in Shakespeare exam answers.
cards.answer: Retelling the story instead of analysing language / Bolting on context as a separate paragraph / Writing about only one scene instead of ranging across the play / Using vague phrases like 'this shows that'
items: Retelling the story instead of analysing language
Bolting on context as a separate paragraph
Writing about only one scene instead of ranging across the play
Using vague phrases like 'this shows that'

cards.front: Why does the lesson argue the witches do not create Macbeth's ambition?
cards.answer: His instant thought of murder straight after the prophecies shows the ambition already existed before the witches' encouragement.

cards.front: How does the horse metaphor in 'vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself' show ambition is self-destructive?
cards.answer: It suggests that reaching too far causes a fatal fall, presenting ambition as something that destroys itself.

cards.front: Name the three main global responses to uneven development given in the lesson.
cards.answer: International aid / The work of NGOs / Fair trade

cards.front: Name the three ways aid can flow between donor and recipient.
cards.answer: Bilateral aid / Multilateral aid / Voluntary aid

cards.front: Why can NGOs often work in remote villages or war zones where official aid agencies struggle?
cards.answer: Because NGOs are not run by governments, they can operate in places official agencies find difficult to reach.

cards.front: Why can aid create dependency rather than self-reliance in receiving countries?
cards.answer: Decades of aid without local capacity-building can leave countries relying on outside help instead of becoming self-reliant.

cards.front: What three signs suggest Jekyll has 'reformed' after the Carew murder in Chapters 5-6?
cards.answer: Resumes his charitable work / Becomes sociable / Seems healthier

cards.front: What three details create Gothic tension in the final scene at the laboratory door in Chapter 8?
cards.answer: Servants huddled in the hallway / The strange voice behind the door / Poole's whispered fear
items: The strange voice behind the door

cards.front: Why is Jekyll's apparent recovery after the Carew murder actually fragile?
cards.answer: He has not conquered Hyde, only stopped taking the potion, so the desire for Hyde remains and grows stronger the longer it is denied.

cards.front: Why is the window scene in Chapter 7 more disturbing than an explicit description would be?
cards.answer: Stevenson never explains what happened, leaving the reader to imagine Jekyll's transformation, which feels more terrifying than being shown it.

title: Wealth, Poverty and the Work of Faith Charities
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four key Gospel passages on wealth given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Luke 16:19-31 – rich man and Lazarus / Luke 12:13-21 – rich fool / Mark 10:21-31 – rich young man told to sell everything / Mark 12:41-44 – the widow's offering
items: Mark 10:21-31 – rich young man told to sell everything

cards.front: What are the three daily duties that Sikh sewa grows out of?
cards.answer: naam japna – remember God / kirat karo – work honestly / vand chhakna – share with others

cards.front: How does giving zakat purify a Muslim's wealth?
cards.answer: Giving 2.5% acknowledges that a portion of one's wealth belongs to the poor, purifying the rest as a religious duty rather than charity.

cards.front: How does attachment to wealth cause suffering according to Buddhism's Four Noble Truths?
cards.answer: Tanha, craving or attachment, treats wealth as a source of lasting happiness, which leads to dukkha, suffering.

title: Selection, Repetition and Iteration in Python
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three fundamental constructs that every program is built from.
cards.answer: Sequence / Selection / Iteration

cards.front: Name the three examples of nesting the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Loops nested inside loops / If statements nested inside loops / Multiple levels of elif in a condition
items: Multiple levels of elif in a condition

cards.front: How does Python decide which block runs in an if/elif/else chain?
cards.answer: It checks conditions top to bottom and executes the first block whose condition is True, skipping the rest.

cards.front: Why should you avoid breaking out of the middle of nested loops?
cards.answer: Each block should have a single entry and exit point; breaking out mid-loop makes code harder to trace, test and maintain.

cards.front: Name the five conservation strategies the lesson describes for protecting biodiversity.
cards.answer: Protected areas / Captive breeding programmes / Seed banks / Fishing quotas and logging regulations / Reforestation projects

cards.front: Name the four lines of evidence the lesson gives for evolution.
cards.answer: Fossil record / Comparative anatomy / DNA analysis / Peppered moth example

cards.front: Why did the dark (melanic) form of the peppered moth become more common during industrial pollution?
cards.answer: Soot darkened tree bark, making pale moths more visible to predators, so dark moths were better camouflaged and survived better.

cards.front: How does speciation lead to two populations becoming separate species?
cards.answer: Isolated populations face different environmental pressures and accumulate different mutations until they diverge too much to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says commercial media organisations can earn revenue.
cards.answer: Advertising / Sponsorship / Product placement

cards.front: Name the three examples the lesson gives of media funded by the voluntary or independent sector.
cards.answer: Community radio stations / Local community newspapers / Some investigative journalism outlets

cards.front: Why can the BBC invest in content that would be difficult to justify commercially?
cards.answer: Because it is funded by the licence fee rather than advertising, so it isn't dependent on maximising audience size.

cards.front: Why is balancing the free tier and paid tier a constant challenge for freemium media businesses?
cards.answer: They must keep the free tier attractive while still giving paying subscribers enough extra value to justify the subscription.

cards.front: Name the four types of movement mechanisms produce.
cards.answer: Linear motion / Rotary motion / Reciprocating motion / Oscillating motion

cards.front: Name the three types of cam follower the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Roller follower / Knife-edge follower / Flat follower

cards.front: How does a crank and slider mechanism convert rotary motion into reciprocating motion?
cards.answer: A rotating crank connects to a slider via a connecting rod, so as the crank turns full circles the slider moves back and forth in a straight line.

cards.front: Why is a V-belt used instead of a flat belt in a pulley system?
cards.answer: A V-belt grips the pulley more securely than a flat belt, reducing slipping.

title: Form and Methods: Thirty Scenes, Songs and Languages
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: What years does Act Two of The Empress jump between, in order?
Why does Act One repeatedly cut between Tilbury docks and Windsor Castle?
cards.answer: It invites the audience to compare Rani being dismissed with Abdul being welcomed into service on the same afternoon of empire.

cards.front: Why is every foreign phrase in the play's text printed with its English translation?
cards.answer: So a design or performance choice never needs to guess at translation, as the play already tells you what is being said and to whom.

cards.front: What are the three pillars of Sikhism that Guru Nanak intended the gurdwara to express?
cards.answer: Naam Japna (meditation on God's name) / Kirat Karni (honest work) / Vand Chakna (sharing with others)

cards.front: Why is the Guru Granth Sahib ceremonially 'put to rest' each night in the sukhasan room?
cards.answer: Because Sikhs treat it as a living presence, not a sacred object, so it is wrapped in cloth and rests like a person.

cards.front: How do the palki and takht together show the Guru Granth Sahib's status?
cards.answer: The canopy (palki) and throne (takht) together show the Guru Granth Sahib is a living, reigning Guru deserving royal honour.

cards.front: What three functions do the supporting characters Margot and Leon serve in the play?
cards.answer: Show diversity of response / Provide comic relief / Demonstrate solidarity

cards.front: Why did Wendell turn to crime?
cards.answer: Racist discrimination denied him the good job he was promised after serving in the English army, so crime was a response to systemic exclusion.

cards.front: How does Lorna's identity differ from Princess's?
cards.answer: Lorna, being mixed-race, feels she belongs nowhere fully, unlike Princess whose experience is specifically as a Black girl in 1960s Bristol.

cards.front: Why does Margot's help for Princess in Act 3 show solidarity is personal rather than political?
cards.answer: Margot shelters Princess after she runs away yet still dismisses the boycott campaign, so her care crosses race lines without changing her views.

title: Johnson's War: Tonkin and Rolling Thunder
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why Operation Rolling Thunder failed to break Hanoi.
cards.answer: Bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong was restricted / Aid from China and USSR replaced losses / North dispersed industry and dug shelters / Ho Chi Minh Trail could not be cut
items: Bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong was restricted
Aid from China and USSR replaced losses
North dispersed industry and dug shelters
Ho Chi Minh Trail could not be cut

cards.front: Name the four Vietcong guerrilla tactics the lesson gives that neutralised US technological superiority.
cards.answer: Moving at night / Mining trails / Setting bamboo punji-stick traps / Digging tunnel networks like Cu Chi
items: Digging tunnel networks like Cu Chi

cards.front: Why did Johnson pursue 'graduated escalation' rather than full-scale war or withdrawal in Vietnam?
cards.answer: He feared withdrawal would discredit US commitments worldwide but full-scale war would discredit him at home, so he used just enough force to try to win without provoking China.

cards.front: How did North Vietnam's workforce help the country survive the bombing of Rolling Thunder?
cards.answer: An estimated 500,000 workers, mainly women, repaired roads and bridges almost overnight, keeping supply routes open despite the bombing.

cards.front: What four-step pattern does Holmes's deductive method follow in these chapters?
cards.answer: Observe physical evidence / Eliminate impossibilities / Form a hypothesis / Test it

cards.front: What three investigative tools does Holmes use to track the killers?
cards.answer: His own deductive reasoning / Toby the dog / The Baker Street Irregulars

cards.front: Why are the Baker Street Irregulars useful to Holmes as informants?
cards.answer: They can go everywhere and overhear everyone without suspicion, because Victorian society largely ignored poor children.

cards.front: Why does Athelney Jones wrongly arrest Thaddeus Sholto?
cards.answer: Jones forms a theory of guilt from circumstantial evidence and motive, then looks for evidence to support it, instead of following the physical evidence.

title: Classification of Skills and Practice Structures
subject: physical-education-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three continua the lesson uses to classify skills.
cards.answer: Basic to complex / Open to closed / High to low organisation

cards.front: Name the four practice structures required for this unit.
cards.answer: Massed practice / Distributed practice / Fixed practice / Variable practice

cards.front: Why should a high-organisation skill like a golf swing be practised as a whole rather than in parts?
cards.answer: Breaking it into parts disrupts the timing and sequencing that make the skill effective, producing a disjointed movement.

cards.front: Why might fixed practice fail to prepare a performer for match conditions?
cards.answer: It rehearses the skill in exactly the same conditions each time, so it may not transfer to variable, changing match environments.

cards.front: Name the seven reasons the lesson gives for conducting fitness tests.
cards.answer: Identify strengths and weaknesses / Monitor improvement over time / Establish a baseline level of fitness / Inform training requirements / Compare against norms / Motivate athletes and set goals / Provide variety in training
items: Establish a baseline level of fitness

cards.front: Name the five limitations of fitness testing given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Not sport-specific / Don't replicate competitive conditions / Many tests are sub-maximal / Motivation affects results / Some tests need careful protocol

cards.front: Why might the Ruler Drop Test have lower validity for a goalkeeper's dive?
cards.answer: It only tests a hand catching a falling ruler, not the reactive whole-body movement needed for a dive.

cards.front: How can a coach improve the reliability of a fitness test?
cards.answer: By standardising conditions (same time of day, warm-up, equipment, instructions) and taking multiple trials.

cards.front: Name the eight stakeholder groups identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Shareholders / Employees / Customers / Managers / Suppliers / Local community / Pressure groups / Government

cards.front: Name the five ways the lesson says a local community is affected by a business.
cards.answer: Employment / Traffic / Noise / Pollution / Investment in local infrastructure

cards.front: Why do customers and shareholders often have conflicting objectives?
cards.answer: Customers want the lowest possible price while shareholders want the highest possible profit margin, so cutting prices to please customers reduces shareholder profit.

cards.front: Why can shareholders and managers conflict over how profit is used?
cards.answer: Shareholders want short-term profit and dividends, but managers may want to reinvest profit into growth that benefits them long-term, reducing immediate dividend payouts.

cards.front: Name the three components of a structured cool-down.
cards.answer: Gradual reduction in intensity / Maintained elevated breathing rate / Static stretching

cards.front: Why does DOMS actually occur, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It is caused by microscopic damage to muscle fibres and the associated inflammatory response, not solely lactic acid build-up.

cards.front: Why does heart rate start rising even before exercise begins?
cards.answer: The anticipatory rise is driven by adrenaline released in response to the prospect of exercise.

cards.front: Name the four sociological perspectives covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Functionalism / Marxism / Feminism / Interactionism

cards.front: Name the six structures of patriarchy identified by Walby.
cards.answer: Paid employment / Household production / Culture / Sexuality / Violence / The state

cards.front: Why did Davis and Moore argue that social inequality can be functional?
cards.answer: Higher rewards for more demanding roles act as incentives for talented individuals to train for them, filling important positions effectively.

cards.front: How does Bowles and Gintis's correspondence principle explain the role of schools in capitalism?
cards.answer: Schools match attitudes and behaviours like obedience, punctuality and deference to authority to those needed in the workplace, reproducing the workforce capitalism needs.

cards.front: Name the three stages of Macbeth's escalating violence given in the lesson, in order.
cards.answer: Duncan's murder (reluctant, political) / Banquo's murder (paranoid, independent) / Macduff's family (vindictive tyranny)

cards.front: Why does the king's healing touch of Edward the Confessor contrast with Macbeth's rule?
cards.answer: It symbolises legitimate, God-given kingship, unlike Macbeth's rule which has made Scotland itself sick.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare show Lady Macduff and her son in a tender domestic scene before the murderers arrive?
cards.answer: To make the massacre emotionally devastating and highlight the horror of murdering innocent children.

title: Kaiser Wilhelm and the difficulties of ruling Germany
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four powers the Kaiser held under the 1871 constitution.
cards.answer: Commanded the army / Controlled foreign policy / Appointed the Chancellor / Could dissolve the Reichstag

cards.front: What three approvals did a bill need before it became law in Imperial Germany?
cards.answer: Reichstag approval / Bundesrat approval / Kaiser's assent

cards.front: Why did real power shift towards the Kaiser after Bismarck was dismissed in 1890?
cards.answer: Bismarck's successors as Chancellor were weaker and more pliable, so decisions were increasingly taken by the Kaiser and a small circle of advisers.

cards.front: How could Prussia block reforms pushed by more liberal southern states like Bavaria?
cards.answer: Prussia held 17 of the Bundesrat's 58 seats, enough to veto constitutional changes, so its votes usually blocked their reforms.

cards.front: Name the six stages of the geographical enquiry process in order.
cards.answer: Pose questions / Collect evidence / Process and present / Analyse patterns / Draw conclusions / Evaluate

cards.front: Why is choosing a fair sample site location important in a river study of channel shape down a tributary?
cards.answer: Sites at intervals down a single tributary fairly test how channel shape changes with distance, while mixing rivers would mix variables and weaken conclusions.

cards.front: Name the three poems the lesson says 'Remains' pairs well with for comparison.
cards.answer: Kamikaze by Beatrice Garland / War Photographer by Carol Ann Duffy / Disabled by Wilfred Owen
items: War Photographer by Carol Ann Duffy

cards.front: What four stages of time does the structure of 'Remains' move through?
cards.answer: the shooting / daily patrols / being home on leave / sleepless nights

cards.front: How does the caesura in 'probably armed, possibly not' reflect the soldier's state of mind?
cards.answer: The pause mirrors his own uncertainty over whether the looter was a genuine threat, a doubt that haunts him.

cards.front: Why does Armitage write 'Remains' in loose, unrhymed, colloquial stanzas?
cards.answer: To mimic natural speech from the real soldier's testimony, making the horror feel like a confession rather than crafted poetry.

title: Classical Sociologists: Durkheim, Marx and Weber
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: According to the reliable pairing list, what four concepts are associated with Durkheim?
cards.answer: Social facts / Solidarity (mechanical/organic) / Anomie / Scientific method

cards.front: According to the reliable pairing list, what four concepts are associated with Marx?
cards.answer: Class conflict / Bourgeoisie/proletariat / False consciousness / Capitalism/means of production

cards.front: How did Marx argue the bourgeoisie exploit the proletariat?
cards.answer: By paying workers less than the full value of what they produce and keeping the difference as profit.

cards.front: Why did Durkheim warn that rapid social change increases crime and suicide?
cards.answer: Because it can produce anomie, a state of normlessness where the usual rules no longer hold.

title: The Internet: DNS, URLs and the Web Browser
subject: computer-science-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four main parts of a URL.
cards.answer: Protocol / Subdomain / Domain name / Path

cards.front: Name three things a web browser manages besides fetching and displaying pages.
cards.answer: Cookies / Browsing history / Cache of previously visited pages

cards.front: Why is DNS distributed across millions of servers worldwide rather than stored on one server?
cards.answer: So that no single server needs to know every domain name in the world.

cards.front: Why does a DNS lookup only need the domain name part of a URL, not the whole URL?
cards.answer: DNS converts a domain name into an IP address; the protocol and path aren't part of the DNS lookup.

cards.front: Name the four rival Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in Britain before the Viking raids began.
cards.answer: Northumbria / Mercia / East Anglia / Wessex

cards.front: What three reforms did Alfred make to Wessex's defences after Edington?
cards.answer: Built a network of fortified burhs / Redesigned the army so half fought half farmed / Ordered construction of larger ships
items: Built a network of fortified burhs
Redesigned the army so half fought half farmed

cards.front: Why did undefended monasteries look like an 'open vault' to Norse raiders?
cards.answer: Norse warriors did not share Christian taboos against attacking churches, so portable monastic wealth seemed easy plunder rather than sacred ground.

cards.front: How did religion end up uniting Anglo-Saxons and Danes rather than dividing them?
cards.answer: After Guthrum's baptism Norse settlers converted to Christianity, endowing churches and being buried in Christian cemeteries, making religion a shared glue.

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson gives as readers of financial statements, and what each checks them for.
cards.answer: Investors, before buying shares / Banks, before lending / Managers, to decide next year's strategy / Employees, to judge if jobs are safe
items: Managers, to decide next year's strategy
Employees, to judge if jobs are safe

cards.front: Name the four items the income statement structure runs through from top to bottom.
cards.answer: Revenue / Cost of sales / Gross profit / Other operating costs / Net profit

cards.front: Why does a falling gross profit margin over time suggest a problem?
cards.answer: It suggests rising supplier costs or price cuts that haven't been passed on to customers.

cards.front: Why can a business with a high gross profit margin still end up with a very low net profit margin, as with Burberry?
cards.answer: A high gross margin does not guarantee a high net margin because overheads can still eat most of the profit made on products.

cards.front: What three dimensions does exercise improve at the same time, according to the Key Fact?
cards.answer: Physical (heart, body systems, disease prevention) / Mental (stress reduction, hormones, emotional control) / Social (friendships, teamwork, community)

cards.front: Why does chronically elevated stress hormone levels harm the body?
cards.answer: Long-term high cortisol and adrenaline damage the cardiovascular system, suppress immunity and impair sleep.

cards.front: Why might low-intensity activities like yoga or walking groups produce greater wellbeing gains for some people than competitive sport?
cards.answer: They are more accessible, enjoyable and sustainable, so people keep doing them regularly, which is what matters.

cards.front: Name the three questions the lesson says you should ask yourself when choosing your comparison poem.
cards.answer: Which prepared poem connects to this theme? / Can I identify both similarities AND differences? / Can I discuss form and structure, not just language?
items: Which prepared poem connects to this theme?
Can I identify both similarities AND differences?
Can I discuss form and structure, not just language?

cards.front: Which three poems does the lesson pair together for the theme of power and control?
cards.answer: My Last Duchess / Valentine / The Manhunt

cards.front: Why does the lesson say to avoid choosing a comparison poem that is simply 'the same' as the named poem?
cards.answer: A poem with only similarities gives you less to say than one with interesting contrasts in method, tone or context.

cards.front: Why does the lesson warn against only discussing imagery when comparing two poems?
cards.answer: If your only point is about imagery, you are missing marks for comparing form, structure or voice.

cards.front: Name the four strategies the lesson gives for combating a sedentary lifestyle.
cards.answer: Increasing active transport / Taking regular breaks to move / Joining a local sports club / Using activity-tracking technology

cards.front: Why does hypertension increase the risk of stroke and kidney disease?
cards.answer: Hypertension damages arterial walls over time, increasing the risk of stroke, kidney disease and cardiovascular damage.

title: Food Processing, Production and Technological Developments
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: Name the four ways raw milk can be treated during primary processing to destroy bacteria.
cards.answer: Pasteurisation / UHT (ultra-heat treatment) / Sterilisation / Micro-filtration

cards.front: Name the three examples of secondary processing given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Flour into bread and pasta / Milk into cheese and yoghurt / Fruit into jams

cards.front: How does yeast make bread dough rise during breadmaking?
cards.answer: Yeast ferments sugars in the dough, producing carbon dioxide gas which causes the dough to rise.

cards.front: Why does cooking fruit with sugar preserve it as jam?
cards.answer: The high temperatures used destroy enzymes and most bacteria, preserving the jam for long-term storage.

cards.front: Name the four things you need to specify when booking a hotel room.
cards.answer: the type of room / the length of stay / any facilities you want / meals

cards.front: Name the four meal plan options given in the lesson.
cards.answer: breakfast included / half board / full board / all-inclusive

cards.front: Why does using je voudrais or j'aimerais improve your French writing?
cards.answer: Because they show you can use the conditional tense, which lifts your writing.

cards.front: How should you mix tenses when writing a hotel complaint letter?
cards.answer: Use the imperfect tense for descriptions, like the room was dirty, and the perfect tense for events, like I saw a fly.

cards.front: Name the four physical factors the lesson gives that increase flood risk.
cards.answer: Precipitation / Geology / Relief / Saturation

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says urbanisation increases flood risk.
cards.answer: Impermeable surfaces stop infiltration / Storm drains speed water to river / New housing on flood plains
items: Storm drains speed water to river

cards.front: Why does ground saturation increase flood risk, especially in November and December?
cards.answer: Ground already wet from previous rain cannot absorb more, so new rainfall runs straight off into the river.

cards.front: Why do farming practices increase how fast water reaches a river?
cards.answer: Heavy machinery compacts soil, autumn ploughing leaves bare fields exposed, and livestock paths channel runoff downslope.

cards.front: What five attractions did seaside resorts invest heavily in to attract visitors?
cards.answer: Piers / Promenades / Theatres / Bandstands / Amusement arcades

cards.front: What was the typical route of the eighteenth-century Grand Tour?
cards.answer: Paris / The Swiss Alps / Venice / Florence / Rome

cards.front: How did the expanding railway network transform British seaside resorts after the 1840s?
cards.answer: It made resorts reachable in hours from industrial cities, bringing day-trippers and week-long holidaymakers who had previously only had coach access.

cards.front: Why did British seaside resorts decline from the 1970s onwards?
cards.answer: They struggled to compete with foreign package holidays offering guaranteed sunshine, cheap wine and modern hotels abroad.

cards.front: Name the four Spanish structures given for saying what should or must be done to help the environment.
cards.answer: Se debe + infinitive / Deberíamos + infinitive / Hay que + infinitive / Es importante + infinitive

cards.front: Name the four 'fancy phrases' the lesson gives to elevate environment writing.
cards.answer: A pesar de eso / Estoy convencido/a de que / Deberíamos / Vale la pena mencionar que

cards.front: Why must you use multiple tenses when discussing environmental issues in Spanish?
cards.answer: Because you need to say what you do now (present), what you did (preterite), and what you will/should do (future/conditional).

cards.front: Why does the school mosaic paragraph about becoming a green school use present, preterite and near future together?
cards.answer: Because using present (hacemos), preterite (hicimos, plantamos) and near future (vamos a empezar) in one paragraph is exactly what a strong answer does.

cards.front: Name the six key themes covered in Macbeth for the exam.
cards.answer: Ambition / Guilt / Power and kingship / Supernatural / fate vs free will / Masculinity / Appearance vs reality

cards.front: Name the four parts of the model extract-analysis paragraph structure.
cards.answer: Point / Evidence / Analysis (AO2) / Development

cards.front: Why does Macbeth appeal to Neptune rather than the Christian God when describing his guilt?
cards.answer: Appealing to a pagan god rather than the Christian God shows Macbeth has put himself outside Christian grace.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare use Duncan's and Macbeth's rule to contrast legitimate and illegitimate power?
cards.answer: Duncan's gentle, God-ordained rule makes Scotland flourish, while Macbeth's tyranny makes it bleed, showing power gained by regicide is illegitimate.

cards.front: Name the five functions of water given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Transports nutrients and oxygen in the blood / Removes waste products (urea) via the kidneys / Regulates body temperature through sweating and breathing / Provides a medium for chemical reactions in cells / Lubricates joints
items: Transports nutrients and oxygen in the blood
Removes waste products (urea) via the kidneys
Regulates body temperature through sweating and breathing
Provides a medium for chemical reactions in cells

cards.front: Name the three complementary nutrient pairs the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Vitamin C and iron / Vitamin D and calcium / B vitamins working together

cards.front: Why is steaming vegetables preferable to boiling them for retaining vitamins?
cards.answer: Water-soluble vitamins like B vitamins and vitamin C can be lost in cooking water, and vitamin C is heat-labile, so steaming keeps more of them intact.

cards.front: Why are pregnant women advised not to eat liver?
cards.answer: Liver is rich in vitamin A, and excess vitamin A from such sources is toxic and teratogenic during pregnancy.

title: Modern punishment: rehabilitation, abolition and alternatives
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What three activities did community service require offenders to do, as given in the lesson?
cards.answer: Painting community halls / Maintaining parks / Working in charity shops

cards.front: Why did open prisons face criticism despite supporters' evidence in their favour?
cards.answer: Critics argued they were 'soft on crime', while supporters pointed to evidence they reduced reoffending compared to closed prisons.

cards.front: Why did short custodial sentences fall out of favour, leading to community service as an alternative?
cards.answer: They were expensive, disruptive to employment and housing, and widely seen as ineffective at reducing reoffending.

cards.front: How did borstals aim to reform young offenders differently from adult prisons?
cards.answer: Through a structured regime of education, vocational training, physical activity and discipline instead of punitive adult prison conditions.

cards.front: Name the three main stages of treating fresh water to make it potable.
cards.answer: Filtration / Sedimentation / Sterilisation

cards.front: Name the four stages of waste water treatment described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Screening / Sedimentation / Biological treatment / Disinfection

cards.front: Why is a coagulant like aluminium sulfate sometimes added during sedimentation?
cards.answer: It makes tiny particles clump together into larger flocs, which settle out more easily.

cards.front: Why must waste water be treated before being released into rivers or lakes?
cards.answer: Untreated waste water depletes dissolved oxygen, harms aquatic life, spreads disease and can contaminate drinking water sources.

cards.front: Name the five strategies the lesson gives for preventing human communicable diseases.
cards.answer: Vaccination / Hygiene and sanitation / Sterilisation of wounds / Contraception for STIs / Travel/movement restrictions

cards.front: Name the three traditional lab methods the lesson gives for identifying pathogens (before monoclonal antibodies).
cards.answer: Culturing samples on nutrient agar / Observing colonies under a microscope / Testing sensitivity to antimicrobials

cards.front: Why does the primary immune response allow symptoms to develop while the secondary response usually doesn't?
cards.answer: The primary response takes days to find the antigen and make antibodies, letting the pathogen replicate, whereas memory cells respond almost immediately.

cards.front: Why can herd immunity break down even if most people believe it protects them?
cards.answer: If enough individuals rely on others being vaccinated and skip vaccination themselves, immunity falls below the threshold needed, allowing outbreaks.

cards.front: Name the three timescales over which the lesson says energy demand varies.
cards.answer: Daily variation / Seasonal variation / Long-term trends

cards.front: Name the four non-renewable energy sources given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Coal / Oil / Natural gas / Nuclear (uranium and plutonium)

cards.front: Why does electricity demand peak in the morning and early evening?
cards.answer: People wake and use appliances in the morning, and cook and use lighting in the early evening.

cards.front: Why is nuclear waste seen as a long-term environmental problem even though nuclear power emits no CO₂?
cards.answer: Nuclear power creates radioactive waste that must be stored safely for very long periods.

title: The Permanent Indian Frontier and the First Fort Laramie Treaty
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three pressures the lesson gives for why the Permanent Indian Frontier failed by 1851.
cards.answer: Migration along the Oregon Trail from 1836 / Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) adding new territories / The 1849 California Gold Rush
items: Migration along the Oregon Trail from 1836
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) adding new territories

cards.front: Name four of the Indigenous nations who gathered at Fort Laramie in September 1851, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Lakota Sioux / Cheyenne / Arapaho / Crow

cards.front: Why did settlers and Plains nations clash along the trails in the years before 1851?
cards.answer: They competed over wood, water and grazing, and settlers brought disease and disturbed the buffalo herds.

cards.front: Why did US policy shift from separation to concentration by 1851?
cards.answer: Migration, new territory from Guadalupe Hidalgo, and the Gold Rush made the Permanent Indian Frontier unworkable, so reservations replaced separation.

cards.front: What three approaches have UK governments used to try to close the north-south divide?
cards.answer: Infrastructure projects (like HS2) / Regeneration projects (like Salford Quays) / Devolution to regional mayors and governments
items: Devolution to regional mayors and governments

cards.front: What overheating problems does London and the south-east face due to regional imbalance?
cards.answer: House prices push young workers out / Transport networks reach capacity / Green belt land under pressure for housing
items: House prices push young workers out
Green belt land under pressure for housing

cards.front: How does a new car factory opening in a town like Sunderland trigger a positive multiplier?
cards.answer: Direct jobs create spending in local shops, attract suppliers and more staff, and tax revenue funds services, expanding jobs and investment further.

cards.front: Why did London become a richer region than the north of England after the 1970s?
cards.answer: As northern industries like coal and steel collapsed, London reinvented itself as a global hub for finance, technology and creative industries.

title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four main factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction.
cards.answer: Temperature / Concentration (or pressure for gases) / Surface area / Catalysts

cards.front: Name the four practical methods used to measure the rate of a reaction.
cards.answer: Gas syringe / Displacement of water / Mass loss on a balance / Disappearing cross (with sodium thiosulfate)

cards.front: How does increasing pressure affect the rate of reaction between gases?
cards.answer: It pushes the gas particles closer together, so they collide more frequently, increasing the rate.

cards.front: How does a catalyst increase the proportion of successful collisions?
cards.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react successfully.

cards.front: Name the four key properties used to describe any wave.
cards.answer: Amplitude / Wavelength / Frequency / Period

cards.front: Why can light travel through a vacuum but sound cannot?
cards.answer: Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium, but sound is mechanical and needs particles of a medium to travel.

cards.front: Why does sound diffract noticeably around corners but light does not?
cards.answer: Sound's wavelength (0.1–10 m) is similar to gaps like doorways, while light's wavelength is millions of times smaller than everyday gaps.

cards.front: Why does a wave bend towards the normal when it enters a denser medium?
cards.answer: Refraction occurs because the wave slows down when it enters a denser medium, causing it to change direction towards the normal.

title: Radio: Desert Island Discs — Industry and Audience
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four gratifications the lesson gives for why audiences listen to Desert Island Discs.
cards.answer: Entertainment / Information / Social interaction / Personal identity

cards.front: Name the four things a Desert Island Discs castaway personally chooses (aside from the automatic Bible and Shakespeare).
cards.answer: Eight pieces of music / One book / One luxury item

cards.front: Why is the BBC classed as a conglomerate?
cards.answer: It owns commercial subsidiaries like BBC Studios alongside its public service divisions, operating across different markets.

cards.front: How does Desert Island Discs show radio converging with online platforms?
cards.answer: Over 2,400 episodes are available as podcasts via BBC Sounds or the BBC website, letting listeners access it on-demand.

title: Source skills for Kenilworth and the Reformation
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four source types given in this unit's key fact for investigating Kenilworth and the Reformation.
cards.answer: Pipe Rolls / Valor Ecclesiasticus / Churchwardens' accounts / Dugdale's engravings

cards.front: What four steps make a strong 10-mark source comparison answer for this unit?
cards.answer: Identify what Source A says / Identify what Source B says / Explain the similarity or difference using authorship, purpose, date and audience / Reach a supported conclusion about the investigation question
items: Explain the similarity or difference using authorship, purpose, date and audience
Reach a supported conclusion about the investigation question

cards.front: Why is the Valor Ecclesiasticus limited as a source despite being reliable for income figures?
cards.answer: It was produced for political purposes, to justify dissolution, so it does not record the human experience of monastic life.

cards.front: How can physical evidence at Kenilworth be used to check claims made in Pipe Roll entries about building work?
cards.answer: Archaeological survey and dendrochronology can show whether the surviving fabric actually matches the date the work was claimed.

cards.front: What three parts should a well-structured conclusion from retail data have?
cards.answer: Reference to specific figures / A reason explaining the trend or change / The business implication going forward
items: A reason explaining the trend or change

cards.front: Why should a retailer investigate an anomaly rather than ignore it?
cards.answer: Because it is an unexpected data point breaking the trend, so it may signal a specific cause like a competitor sale or closure needing explanation.

cards.front: Why does recognising seasonal patterns matter for a retail business?
cards.answer: It helps the business plan staffing, stock levels and promotions appropriately around predictable busy or quiet periods.

cards.front: Name the five reasons the lesson gives for why Catholics go on pilgrimage.
cards.answer: To be closer to God / To seek healing or forgiveness / To pray for others / To deepen their faith / To fulfil a vow

cards.front: Why did the Catholic Church historically prefer burial over cremation?
cards.answer: Burial more clearly symbolised the resurrection of the body and followed the example of Jesus, who was buried in a tomb.

cards.front: Why do priests wear white or gold vestments rather than black at a Catholic funeral?
cards.answer: The white or gold vestments reflect the resurrection hope at the heart of Catholic funerals, rather than mourning.

cards.front: Why do pilgrims walk the final mile to Walsingham barefoot?
cards.answer: It is a penitential act of devotion, following the example of medieval pilgrims and countless generations of believers.

title: The Royal Society, Pepys and the New Science
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four buildings the lesson says Christopher Wren designed alongside his scientific work.
cards.answer: Royal Observatory at Greenwich / Royal Hospital at Chelsea / Trinity College Library, Cambridge / New buildings at Kensington Palace and Hampton Court
items: New buildings at Kensington Palace and Hampton Court

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the Royal Society was not a government department?
cards.answer: Royal patronage gave it prestige only; fellows funded it themselves through weekly subscriptions, with no Treasury money involved.

cards.front: Why did Hooke and Newton clash bitterly in the 1680s?
cards.answer: Hooke believed Newton had used his earlier ideas about gravity's inverse-square law without giving him credit.

cards.front: Why did the Royal Society require fellows to repeat each other's experiments?
cards.answer: Because the Society held that scientific claims must be reproduced by others before being accepted as true.

title: Mountain Meadows and the Mormon Question
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four motives the lesson gives for the Mountain Meadows Massacre.
cards.answer: War hysteria over the approaching federal army / Suspicion the party was linked to Parley P. Pratt's murder / Greed for the wagon train's livestock and goods / Encouragement by militia leader John D. Lee
items: War hysteria over the approaching federal army
Suspicion the party was linked to Parley P. Pratt's murder
Greed for the wagon train's livestock and goods
Encouragement by militia leader John D. Lee

cards.front: Name the three escalating federal laws Congress used against Mormon polygamy.
cards.answer: 1862 Morrill Anti-Bigamy Act / 1882 Edmunds Act / 1887 Edmunds-Tucker Act

cards.front: How did the Mormon militia leadership cover up the Mountain Meadows Massacre for almost twenty years?
cards.answer: Militiamen swore a written oath of secrecy, and southern Utah leaders blamed the killings entirely on Paiute warriors.

cards.front: Why did Congress force Mormons to give up polygamy before allowing Utah statehood?
cards.answer: Federal policy treated plural marriage as a threat to family and the rule of law, so ending it became the price of full citizenship.

cards.front: Name the three contrasting character pairs Brontë uses to build her argument.
cards.answer: Rochester/St John (passion vs duty) / Jane/Helen (rebellion vs acceptance) / Brocklehurst/Miss Temple (hypocrisy vs integrity)

cards.front: Name the three minor characters used to develop Jane's story and what each shows.
cards.answer: Adèle Varens - contrasts with Jane's depth, satirises French vanity / Mrs Fairfax - warns Jane, represents conventional Victorian morality / Rosamond Oliver - shows St John sacrificing happiness for duty
items: Adèle Varens - contrasts with Jane's depth, satirises French vanity
Mrs Fairfax - warns Jane, represents conventional Victorian morality
Rosamond Oliver - shows St John sacrificing happiness for duty

cards.front: Why is Jane's role as both protagonist and narrator significant?
cards.answer: It gives her double authority — she controls pacing, addresses the reader directly, and shapes how we see every other character.

cards.front: Why can Bertha Mason be read as a victim rather than simply a monster?
cards.answer: She was brought from Jamaica, married for money, then locked away when inconvenient — a victim of patriarchy and colonialism.

cards.front: Name the four stages of the dramatic arc in Hobson's Choice and what happens in each.
cards.answer: Act 1: exposition, introducing characters and conflict / Act 2: rising action, Maggie and Willie build their business / Act 3: climax, Hobson's collapse and legal crisis / Act 4: resolution, new arrangement under Willie and Maggie
items: Act 1: exposition, introducing characters and conflict
Act 2: rising action, Maggie and Willie build their business
Act 3: climax, Hobson's collapse and legal crisis
Act 4: resolution, new arrangement under Willie and Maggie

cards.front: What three layers of symbolic meaning does the boot carry in Hobson's Choice?
cards.answer: Meritocracy - talent exists at every social level / Exploitation - Hobson profits from Willie's labour unfairly / Foundation of the new business on Oldfield Road
items: Meritocracy - talent exists at every social level
Exploitation - Hobson profits from Willie's labour unfairly
Foundation of the new business on Oldfield Road

cards.front: How does Brighouse use staging to mirror the characters' changing fortunes across the play?
cards.answer: Settings shift from Hobson's shop, to Willie's own cellar showing independence, to a diminished, dirty Act 4 living-room showing Hobson's decline.

cards.front: Why does Hobson's belief that he is in control build to a 'devastating reversal' by Act 4?
cards.answer: In every act events move further beyond Hobson's grasp, yet he assumes his authority is intact, until he must accept terms from those he dismissed.

cards.front: Name the three characters the lesson says experience internal conflict, and what each is torn between.
cards.answer: Romeo: love vs honour after Mercutio's death / Juliet: loyalty to Romeo vs grief for Tybalt / Friar: helping the lovers vs risk of his secret plans
items: Romeo: love vs honour after Mercutio's death
Juliet: loyalty to Romeo vs grief for Tybalt
Friar: helping the lovers vs risk of his secret plans

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present family love in Verona as actually being about control?
cards.answer: Capulet demands Juliet's obedience rather than asking what she wants, showing love is conditional on compliance.

cards.front: How does the feud corrupt relationships throughout the play, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It stops Romeo and Juliet being open, kills Mercutio, forces the Friar into secrecy, and turns Capulet into a tyrant.

cards.front: Name the five independent types of measurement the lesson gives as evidence for climate change.
cards.answer: Atmospheric gas records / Ice core chemistry / Satellite temperature data / Ocean heat content / Glacier retreat observations

cards.front: Name the four consequences of continued warming that the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Rising sea levels / Disruption to agriculture / Water shortages in vulnerable regions / More frequent extreme weather events

cards.front: Why does the Keeling Curve show a seasonal up-and-down oscillation each year?
cards.answer: It is caused by the annual growth cycle of plants in the northern hemisphere absorbing and releasing CO2.

cards.front: Why is deciding how to respond to climate change not a purely scientific question?
cards.answer: Because it involves weighing economic and social costs of acting against the costs of inaction, shaped by values and priorities.

cards.front: Name the five abiotic factors the lesson gives that shape ecosystem conditions.
cards.answer: temperature / rainfall / light intensity / pH / mineral availability

cards.front: Name the four limiting factors the lesson gives that keep a population at its carrying capacity.
cards.answer: food shortage / disease / predation / competition for space

cards.front: Why have grey squirrels displaced red squirrels from most of England and Wales?
cards.answer: Grey squirrels digest acorns more efficiently and carry squirrelpox virus without symptoms, which is fatal to red squirrels.

cards.front: How does removing a predator from a food web affect the level below its prey?
cards.answer: Without the predator, prey numbers increase, so they over-consume their own food source, causing it to decrease.

cards.front: Name the four aerobic activities the lesson gives as examples of low-to-moderate intensity exercise.
cards.answer: Distance running / Cycling / Swimming / Rowing at a steady pace

cards.front: Name the three high-intensity activities the lesson gives as examples of anaerobic exercise.
cards.answer: 100 m sprint / Maximal weightlifting effort / Final kick at the end of a race
items: Final kick at the end of a race

cards.front: Why can aerobic respiration sustain exercise for hours without causing fatigue?
cards.answer: Its products, carbon dioxide and water, are easily removed via the lungs and sweat, so no harmful waste builds up.

cards.front: Why does 'hitting the wall' happen during a marathon?
cards.answer: Glycogen stores become depleted, forcing an abrupt shift to fat-dominated metabolism, which cannot sustain marathon pace.

title: Themes: Race, Power, Love Across Lines
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the seven themes the lesson lists as running through Noughts and Crosses.
cards.answer: Racial hierarchy and its reversal / invisibility of privilege / segregation and systemic power / terrorism versus resistance / love across enforced lines / family loyalty versus political loyalty / education as gatekeeping

cards.front: Why did Blackman invent words like 'Cross', 'nought' and 'blanker' rather than using real racial terms?
cards.answer: To make the audience experience the language of hierarchy as a structural system rather than as a personal insult.

cards.front: How might a director use proxemics to show the change in Sephy and Callum's relationship over the play?
cards.answer: Early scenes show them moving freely into each other's space with childhood ease; later scenes charge the same movements with caution and risk.

cards.front: Why does Cooke's play refuse to simply endorse the Liberation Militia's violence?
cards.answer: Because the violence arises from genuine systematic oppression yet is also morally costly since innocent people are harmed, making it political tragedy not propaganda.

cards.front: Name the three questions the lesson says to ask yourself to identify a poem's theme.
cards.answer: What emotion does this poem evoke? / What question does it ask? / What does the speaker seem to feel?
items: What emotion does this poem evoke?
What does the speaker seem to feel?

cards.front: What four things should you look for when analysing love poetry, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: The speaker's attitude to love / Imagery of warmth versus coldness / Proximity versus distance / Whether the tone shifts positive to negative or vice versa
items: Whether the tone shifts positive to negative or vice versa

cards.front: How can a poem's structure show the decline of a relationship?
cards.answer: By beginning with joy and ending with loss, using the structure to chart the relationship's decline.

cards.front: Why does memory poetry create such emotional power?
cards.answer: Because of the tension between the speaker vividly remembering the past and knowing it cannot be recaptured in the present.

cards.front: Name the three contingent events the lesson gives for the shift from reconciliation to independence.
cards.answer: George III's refusal to receive the Olive Branch Petition / The Prohibitory Act of December 1775 / Publication of Paine's 'Common Sense' in January 1776
items: George III's refusal to receive the Olive Branch Petition
Publication of Paine's 'Common Sense' in January 1776

cards.front: Name the three things Paine's 'Common Sense' did that no previous patriot writer had done.
cards.answer: Attacked monarchy itself, not just ministers / Framed independence as common sense for a continent / Wrote in plain English for ordinary people
items: Attacked monarchy itself, not just ministers
Framed independence as common sense for a continent
Wrote in plain English for ordinary people

cards.front: Why did many colonists see the Prohibitory Act of December 1775 as the moment independence became inevitable?
cards.answer: It stopped trade with the colonies and authorised seizing American ships, putting them outside the king's protection.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to treat the Revolution as inevitable from 1765 onwards?
cards.answer: Because reconciliation efforts like the Declaration of Rights and Grievances, Galloway's near-successful plan and the Olive Branch Petition show reconciliation was still the majority position deep into 1775.

cards.front: Name the four dispositional factors studied in social influence.
cards.answer: Self-esteem / Locus of control / Morality / Authoritarian personality

cards.front: Name the three situational factors mentioned as examples that create the conditions for social influence.
cards.answer: Uniform / Group size / Culture

cards.front: Why does having an authoritarian personality make someone more likely to obey a harmful order?
cards.answer: Because challenging authority conflicts with their core values, so they obey without question even when the order is harmful.

cards.front: Why might someone with strong personal morality resist joining in antisocial crowd behaviour?
cards.answer: Strong moral reasoning makes them more likely to act pro-socially, such as helping a victim, even when the crowd is destructive.

cards.front: Name the three uses of nuclear radiation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Gamma rays - medical tracers and sterilising equipment / Beta radiation - thickness gauges / Alpha radiation - smoke detectors
items: Gamma rays - medical tracers and sterilising equipment

cards.front: Name the four precautions given for handling radioactive sources safely.
cards.answer: Keep sources in lead-lined containers / Use tongs to handle sources / Wear protective clothing / Minimise exposure time

cards.front: Why does beta decay increase the atomic number by 1 but leave the mass number unchanged?
cards.answer: A neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton, raising the proton count by one while the total nucleon count stays the same.

cards.front: Why is radioactive decay described as random?
cards.answer: You cannot predict when any particular unstable nucleus will decay.

title: Care Settings & The Rights of Service Users
subject: health-social-care-ocr

cards.front: Name the five rights of service users covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Choice / Confidentiality / Consultation / Equal and fair treatment / Protection from abuse and harm

cards.front: Name the eight health care settings listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dental practice / GP surgery / Health centre / Hospital / Nursing home / Opticians / Pharmacy / Walk-in centre

cards.front: Why does the right to consultation lead to better care plans?
cards.answer: It respects the service user as the expert on their own experience, so plans are more likely to be followed.

cards.front: Why is confidentiality important in building trust between a GP and patient?
cards.answer: Service users are more likely to disclose sensitive health information if they know it will be handled carefully.

cards.front: Name the three main types of chemical bond covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Ionic bonding / Covalent bonding / Metallic bonding

cards.front: Give the four examples of simple covalent molecules used in this lesson.
cards.answer: H2 (single bond) / O2 (double bond) / N2 (triple bond) / H2O and CO2

cards.front: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved but not when solid?
cards.answer: In solid ionic lattices the ions are fixed in position, but when molten or dissolved they are free to move and carry charge.

cards.front: Why are ionic compounds brittle?
cards.answer: Layers of ions shift under force so ions of the same charge line up and repel each other, shattering the lattice.

cards.front: Name the three dramatic effects the lesson gives for The Empress's episodic structure.
cards.answer: Prevents settling into one perspective / Mirrors the fragmented historical record / Creates pace and energy

cards.front: How does blending historical and fictional characters serve Gupta's purpose in The Empress?
cards.answer: Historical figures give the play authority and credibility, while fictional characters let her explore emotions the historical record doesn't capture.

cards.front: How does the contrast between staging spaces communicate theme in The Empress?
cards.answer: The cramped, dark spaces of Indian characters against Victoria's grand palace visualises the power imbalance at the heart of the play.

cards.front: Name the four main reasons the first day of the Somme went so wrong.
cards.answer: Bombardment failed to cut wire / Bombardment failed to destroy dugouts / Infantry advanced slowly at walking pace, heavily loaded / Creeping barrage used inconsistently
items: Infantry advanced slowly at walking pace, heavily loaded

cards.front: Why did Pétain rotate divisions through Verdun using the noria system?
cards.answer: So that no single unit was completely destroyed, allowing about three quarters of the French army to serve there without collapse.

cards.front: How did the launch of the Somme offensive affect the German attack at Verdun?
cards.answer: It forced Germany to thin out its Verdun assault by sending divisions north, weakening the bleeding strategy.

cards.front: Why is the significance of the Somme not seen as pure futility despite huge losses?
cards.answer: It drew German divisions from Verdun, helped remove Falkenhayn, and taught the British lessons used in 1917-18.

cards.front: Name the three parts of Nixon's strategy for extracting the US from Vietnam without an obvious defeat.
cards.answer: Train and equip the ARVN to do its own fighting / Widen the war into Cambodia and Laos to disrupt enemy sanctuaries / Open diplomatic channels with Hanoi's Soviet and Chinese backers
items: Train and equip the ARVN to do its own fighting
Widen the war into Cambodia and Laos to disrupt enemy sanctuaries
Open diplomatic channels with Hanoi's Soviet and Chinese backers

cards.front: Name the three events the lesson says played out on prime-time news during Nixon's presidency.
cards.answer: Kent State shootings / The Pentagon Papers leak (1971) / Conviction of Lieutenant Calley over My Lai
items: Conviction of Lieutenant Calley over My Lai

cards.front: Why did Nixon think Vietnamisation would defuse the anti-war movement?
cards.answer: It brought American troops home while keeping the war going, removing the anti-war movement's central grievance.

cards.front: How did Nixon's opening to China put pressure on North Vietnam?
cards.answer: By exploiting the Sino-Soviet split and improving ties with Beijing, Nixon made Hanoi fear China might favour better US relations over supporting it.

title: A Major City in a Developing or Emerging Country
subject: geography-edexcel-a

cards.front: What four things does the lesson say support Mumbai's connectivity to other places?
cards.answer: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport / Mumbai-Ahmedabad Highway / Mumbai Coastal Road / Mumbai Metro

cards.front: What four big challenges has rapid growth produced in Mumbai?
cards.answer: Overstretched infrastructure / Housing supply lagging behind demand / Informal employment dominating / Severe pollution

cards.front: Why is land in South Mumbai among the most expensive in the world?
cards.answer: Its original site was seven islands joined by reclamation, squeezing a huge population into a narrow north-south strip of land.

cards.front: Why does Mumbai's city structure form long zones instead of concentric rings?
cards.answer: Because Mumbai sits on a narrow peninsula, its shape forces growth into long zones running north-south rather than rings.

title: The Four Aims of Life, Dharma and Human Concerns
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the four principal yamas described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Ahimsa (non-violence) / Daya (compassion) / Dama (self-control) / Dana (generosity/giving)

cards.front: Name the four duties the Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1-3) assigns to each varna.
cards.answer: Brahmins cultivate purity and wisdom / Kshatriyas show courage and leadership / Vaishyas engage in trade and agriculture / Shudras serve the other varnas
items: Vaishyas engage in trade and agriculture

cards.front: How does Hindu teaching explain suffering through karma?
cards.answer: Suffering is the natural consequence of past actions working themselves out, not divine punishment or random cruelty, and should inspire compassion.

cards.front: Why do Hindu thinkers say the four Purusharthas are not really in tension?
cards.answer: Dharma regulates the pursuit of artha and kama so wealth and pleasure don't become ends in themselves, guiding life gradually towards moksha.

title: Evaluating Human Rights and Final Exam Skills
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three mistakes the lesson says cost the most marks on the 15-mark evaluation question.
cards.answer: Giving only one side / Using bullet points / Failing to reach a clear justified conclusion
items: Failing to reach a clear justified conclusion

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four things must be checked for accurate writing in the exam?
cards.answer: Use full sentences / End each sentence with a full stop / Capital letters for proper nouns / Be consistent with religious terms
items: End each sentence with a full stop

cards.front: Why does the lesson say bullet points hurt a 15-mark evaluation answer?
cards.answer: Bullet points leave no room for the evaluative language needed to reach higher marks.

cards.front: Why does the lesson recommend writing your conclusion first if you are running short on time?
cards.answer: An answer with a conclusion but a thin body scores higher than a detailed first paragraph with no conclusion.

title: Operation Desert Storm and the End of the 1991 War
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four Arab states/groups the lesson says celebrated Kuwait's liberation and Saddam's discrediting.
cards.answer: Egypt / Saudi Arabia / Syria / Smaller Gulf states

cards.front: Name the three states/groups the lesson says sided with Iraq during the 1991 war.
cards.answer: Jordan / Yemen / Palestine Liberation Organisation

cards.front: Why did the coalition achieve air supremacy over Iraq within days?
cards.answer: Iraq's Soviet-supplied air defences could not match stealth aircraft and electronic warfare, and many Iraqi pilots flew their planes to Iran rather than fight.

cards.front: Why did Israel not retaliate against the Iraqi Scud attacks?
cards.answer: Bush's administration begged Israel to hold back and sent Patriot batteries as a gesture, since Israeli retaliation might force Arab coalition members to leave.

title: The Great Depression and Hoover's response
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: What three structural weaknesses of the 1920s economy caused the Wall Street Crash, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Share speculation by buying on margin / Over-production in agriculture and industry / Consumer debt from the hire-purchase economy
items: Share speculation by buying on margin
Consumer debt from the hire-purchase economy

cards.front: What three actions did Hoover take to respond to the Depression, besides refusing direct relief?
cards.answer: Convened conferences urging voluntary wage maintenance / Increased federal public works spending / Created the RFC
items: Convened conferences urging voluntary wage maintenance

cards.front: How did the wave of bank failures between 1930 and 1933 lead to mass unemployment?
