cards.answer: Bank failures wiped out savings, so families cut spending, causing businesses to cut production and sack workers.

cards.front: Why did the Smoot-Hawley Tariff make the Depression worse?
cards.answer: It raised import taxes to record highs, provoking countries to impose retaliatory tariffs, collapsing American exports and shrinking world trade by 65%.

cards.front: Name the five economic factors the lesson says affect retailers.
cards.answer: Consumer disposable income / Employment and unemployment / Interest rates / Tax rates / Inflation

cards.front: Name the four business functions retailers must plan across to manage seasonality.
cards.answer: Stock planning / Staffing / Promotions and visual merchandising / Post-season sales periods

cards.front: Why can an unexpectedly cool summer create a risk for clothing and garden retailers?
cards.answer: They may be left overstocked with swimwear and barbecue equipment, which must be sold at discounted prices, reducing profitability.

cards.front: How does Black Friday help retailers prepare for the Christmas trading period?
cards.answer: Retailers offer deep discounts to drive footfall and online traffic, using the event to shift slow-moving stock ahead of Christmas.

cards.front: Name the seven consequences of a sedentary lifestyle given in the lesson.
cards.answer: overweight/obesity / coronary heart disease / high blood pressure / type 2 diabetes / osteoporosis / loss of muscle tone and poor posture / depression/anxiety
items: loss of muscle tone and poor posture

cards.front: Why does a diet high in saturated fat and refined sugar increase risk of coronary heart disease?
cards.answer: It raises LDL cholesterol, which contributes to atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease.

cards.front: How does long-term heavy alcohol consumption harm an athlete's fitness?
cards.answer: It damages the liver, raises blood pressure, causes weight gain and disrupts sleep, worsening recovery and fitness over time.

cards.front: Why is an overfat person not always the same as someone who is overweight?
cards.answer: Overweight is based on BMI, but a heavily muscled athlete can have a high BMI without having excess body fat.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson says decide the right scale of production.
cards.answer: Number of products needed / Acceptable unit cost / Level of customisation required / Available budget for tooling

cards.front: Name the four scales of production covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Prototype (one-off) / Batch (set quantity) / Mass (large volume on assembly line) / Continuous (24/7 non-stop)

cards.front: Why is the unit cost of prototype production so high?
cards.answer: Because tooling and labour costs are not spread across many products, only one item.

cards.front: How does injection moulding make identical polymer products at mass-production scale?
cards.answer: Molten polymer is forced into a mould, cooled and then ejected, with cycle times as short as 30 seconds.

title: The Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram and Variable Stars
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four main regions of stars shown on the H-R diagram.
cards.answer: Main sequence / Red giants / Supergiants / White dwarfs

cards.front: Name the three types of variable stars covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cepheid variables / Eclipsing binaries / Novae

cards.front: Why do more massive main-sequence stars have shorter lifetimes than the Sun despite having more hydrogen fuel?
cards.answer: They are far more luminous and burn their hydrogen fuel much faster, despite having more of it.

cards.front: How does a star's position on the H-R diagram change as it leaves the main sequence and becomes a red giant?
cards.answer: Its outer layers cool, moving it rightward, while its luminosity increases, moving it upward, becoming a red giant.

title: Hercules and Cacus: A Monster in the Cave
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three religious roles the lesson says were set up in Hercules's honour after Cacus's death.
cards.answer: Potitius as first founder and priest / the house of Pinarii as guardians of the rites / the Salii priests who sing Hercules's hymn
items: Potitius as first founder and priest
the house of Pinarii as guardians of the rites
the Salii priests who sing Hercules's hymn

cards.front: Name the three gruesome details Virgil gives about Cacus before the fight starts.
cards.answer: he breathes black fire from his mouth / decaying faces of victims hang on his doorposts / the ground outside is always warm with fresh blood
items: he breathes black fire from his mouth
decaying faces of victims hang on his doorposts
the ground outside is always warm with fresh blood

cards.front: Why does Virgil compare the opened-up cave to the underworld being uncovered to the light?
cards.answer: The extended comparison, borrowed from Homer, exaggerates the size of Cacus's lair and the scale of Hercules's achievement.

cards.front: Why does the lesson warn students to check for perfect passive participles like 'elisos' and 'raptos'?
cards.answer: They describe something already done to the noun before the main action, so reading them as active or present-tense changes the sentence's meaning.

cards.front: Why does Antony dismiss Lepidus as 'a slight unmeritable man, / Meet to be sent on errands'?
cards.answer: Antony sees Lepidus as a useful tool rather than an equal partner in the triumvirate.

cards.front: How does the formal farewell between Brutus and Cassius before Philippi contrast with their earlier quarrel?
cards.answer: Its calm formality shows their bond has survived the bitter strain of the Sardis quarrel.

cards.front: Name the six waves of international migration into Manchester described in the lesson, in order.
cards.answer: Irish migrants working in mills / Jewish refugees settling in Cheetham Hill / Caribbean migrants in the 1950s-60s / South Asian families in Rusholme and Longsight / EU migrants after 2004 / Refugees from Syria, Afghanistan and Ukraine
items: Jewish refugees settling in Cheetham Hill
South Asian families in Rusholme and Longsight
Refugees from Syria, Afghanistan and Ukraine

cards.front: Name the four areas the lesson says inequality cuts across in Manchester.
cards.answer: Housing / Education / Health / Employment

cards.front: How does the 'cycle of deprivation' work in Manchester's most deprived communities?
cards.answer: Low incomes lead to poor housing and poor health, which lead to poor educational outcomes, which lead back to low incomes.

cards.front: How has Manchester's growth increased pressure on the rural-urban fringe?
cards.answer: New estates and commuter villages spreading into farmland raise traffic and air pollution, destroy hedgerows and woodland, and lengthen commutes.

title: The Glorious Revolution and parliamentary monarchy
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Why did William III need to call Parliament every year after 1688?
cards.answer: He needed Parliament's money to fund his wars against Louis XIV of France.

cards.front: How did Robert Walpole hold power as First Lord of the Treasury without a formal Prime Minister title?
cards.answer: He managed Parliament through patronage, persuasion and political organisation rather than relying on royal favour.

cards.front: Why did Catholics and Jacobites see the events of 1688 as not 'glorious'?
cards.answer: It was the violent overthrow of the legitimate king by a foreign army funded by Dutch commercial interests.

cards.front: Name the two Palestinian factions the lesson gives as part of the PLO umbrella body.
cards.answer: Fatah, led by Arafat / the Marxist-Leninist PFLP

cards.front: Why did the Rabat resolution of 1974 matter for future negotiations over the West Bank?
cards.answer: It made the PLO the sole legitimate representative of Palestinians, so any Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank had to be negotiated with the PLO, not Jordan.

cards.front: Why was Hezbollah able to displace the PLO as the main symbol of resistance to Israel after 1982?
cards.answer: The 1982 invasion removed the PLO's mini-state and fighters from Lebanon, leaving a vacuum that Iranian-backed Hezbollah filled with attacks Israel had not anticipated.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to treat 'the PLO' and 'the Palestinians' as the same thing?
cards.answer: The PLO was an Arab-state-funded leadership based in Lebanon, not a government chosen by Palestinians in the West Bank or Gaza.

title: The Economic Climate and How Businesses Respond
subject: business-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six key economic factors the lesson identifies as affecting businesses.
cards.answer: Unemployment / Consumer income / Inflation / Interest rates / Government taxation / Exchange rates

cards.front: Name the four common business responses to economic change given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cutting costs / Changing prices / Diversifying into new markets or products / Delaying investment plans
items: Diversifying into new markets or products

cards.front: Why does high inflation create a dilemma for a business like a bakery?
cards.answer: Rising costs of wages, materials and energy force a choice between absorbing costs and losing profit, or raising prices and losing price-sensitive customers.

cards.front: How does a rise in VAT affect consumer demand for non-essential goods?
cards.answer: Raising VAT increases the effective price of goods, which can reduce consumer demand, particularly for non-essential items.

title: Themes: State Power, Identity, Family Loss
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four key moments in the play where a director should return to the 'wave' metaphor.
cards.answer: The opening storm / The moment of abduction / The arrival of official news / The final scene

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say the state's use of sound achieves in the soundscape of The Great Wave?
cards.answer: Drown out / Overwrite / Silence

cards.front: Why does a director use a tableau to stage the complicity between Kum-Chol and Hanako?
cards.answer: A frozen, ambiguous spatial arrangement communicates their shared but asymmetrical captivity more efficiently than dialogue could.

cards.front: How does the underscore in the teaching scenes signal Hanako's retained inner life, and what does its cutting out suggest?
cards.answer: A quiet fragmented Japanese folk melody, heard only by the audience, signals her inner life; its cutting out suggests she may be losing her former self.

cards.front: Name the three causes the lesson gives for the 2021 UK supply chain crisis.
cards.answer: Covid factory closures / shortage of shipping containers / Suez Canal blockage (Ever Given) / HGV driver shortages

cards.front: Name the three effects the lesson gives of high unemployment on UK businesses.
cards.answer: Sales fall as customers spend less / wage costs drop from more competition for jobs / government benefit spending rises
items: Sales fall as customers spend less
wage costs drop from more competition for jobs

cards.front: Why are luxury brands like Burberry hit hard when consumer income falls?
cards.answer: Their products are non-essential, so customers cut them first when money is tight.

cards.front: How did the 2021 global supply chain crisis affect UK car production?
cards.answer: A shortage of computer chips from Taiwan meant car makers could not get parts, stalling production.

cards.front: Why does the theft of Piggy's glasses symbolise more than just losing an object?
cards.answer: It represents the theft of rational thought and technology, as fire and power now belong entirely to Jack.

cards.front: Why does the conch shattering at Piggy's death matter symbolically?
cards.answer: Piggy and the conch represent belief in reason and self-government, so both being destroyed shows democracy has been annihilated.

cards.front: Why is the naval officer's rescue of Ralph described as deeply ironic?
cards.answer: He expects brave British boys but finds painted savages and murderers, showing the adult world he belongs to is equally uncivilised.

cards.front: Why does Ralph lose his innocence, according to the lesson's reading of the ending?
cards.answer: Not because he witnessed violence, but because he took part in it and realised he was capable of it himself.

cards.front: According to the lesson's Key Fact, name the three ways nuclear weapons violate just war theory.
cards.answer: Cannot be used proportionately / Inevitably target civilians (indiscriminate blast radius) / Long-term effects extend beyond the battlefield
items: Long-term effects extend beyond the battlefield

cards.front: Besides Islamic Relief Worldwide, name the three other religious organisations the lesson mentions that support victims of war.
cards.answer: Christian Aid / CAFOD / Muslim Aid

cards.front: How does mutually assured destruction (MAD) work as a nuclear deterrent?
cards.answer: If both sides have weapons capable of destroying each other, neither side risks starting a war since both would be destroyed.

cards.front: Why does the Qur'an's teaching on proportionate response make nuclear weapons incompatible with Islamic teaching?
cards.answer: Nuclear weapons are disproportionate and indiscriminate, and they kill innocent civilians, which Islam forbids.

cards.front: Give the six stages of Othello's verse-to-prose arc across the play, in order.
cards.answer: Controlled iambic pentameter (Acts 1–2) / Increasingly disturbed verse (Act 3) / Fragmented prose (Act 4) / Epileptic collapse (Act 4) / Restored verse in murder scene (Act 5) / Restored verse in final speech (Act 5)

cards.front: Name the six stages of the handkerchief's journey through different hands in Othello.
cards.answer: Desdemona drops it / Emilia finds it / Iago takes it / Cassio has it planted on him / Bianca copies it / Othello sees it as proof
items: Cassio has it planted on him

cards.front: How does the eavesdropping staging in Act 4 Scene 1 create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: Iago places Othello where he can see but not hear Cassio joking about Bianca, so Othello wrongly believes Cassio is laughing about Desdemona.

cards.front: Why does Iago speak prose with Roderigo but verse with Othello?
cards.answer: Iago adapts his register to each audience, lowering himself to Roderigo's level and matching Othello's noble speech to manipulate them both.

cards.front: Name the four sources of tension the lesson identifies building in Act 2.
cards.answer: Economic pressure / Family conflict / Racial hostility / Junior's radicalisation

cards.front: Why does Lorna face a crisis of belonging in Act 2?
cards.answer: As Wendell's mixed-race daughter, she is neither fully Black nor fully white and feels she does not belong anywhere.

cards.front: Why does Princess destroy her beauty pageant costumes in Act 2?
cards.answer: After racist bullying, it rejects white beauty standards and marks her loss of innocence as her ambition cannot survive contact with racism.

cards.front: Name the three Hobson daughters introduced in Act 1.
cards.answer: Maggie / Alice / Vickey

cards.front: Why does Brighouse present Hobson's authority as absurd from the start of Act 1?
cards.answer: Hobson lectures his daughters on respectability then goes drinking, showing he cannot manage his own behaviour despite claiming authority.

cards.front: Why is Mrs Hepworth's visit a pivotal moment in Act 1?
cards.answer: She publicly recognises Willie's talent and gives him her calling card, giving Maggie evidence that Willie's skill is being exploited.

cards.front: How does Willie first directly challenge Hobson's power in Act 1?
cards.answer: He warns Hobson that if he uses the belt, Willie will take Maggie and the two will set up on their own.

title: Dramatic Methods: Direct Address and Dual Narration
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: What three staging decisions must a performer make when shifting into direct address narration?
cards.answer: Decide where to stand / Decide how to orient their body relative to others / Decide how to signal the shift from character to narrator
items: Decide how to orient their body relative to others
Decide how to signal the shift from character to narrator

cards.front: Name the three sound techniques the lesson gives that a sound designer might use for the news bulletins.
cards.answer: Slightly distorted radio texture / Newsreader's RP accent contrasted with narrators' warmer tones / Fading-in sound cue bleeding across a lighting transition
items: Newsreader's RP accent contrasted with narrators' warmer tones
Fading-in sound cue bleeding across a lighting transition

cards.front: Why is it wrong to describe the narrators' speeches in Noughts and Crosses as soliloquies?
cards.answer: Soliloquies are internal thoughts overheard, but the narrators actively address and plead with the audience as witnesses.

cards.front: How does making full eye contact with audience members change the effect of direct address?
cards.answer: It makes the audience complicit rather than comfortable, reflecting a more confrontational political intent.

title: Narrative Theory: Propp, Todorov and Audience Engagement
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: What are Todorov's five stages of a narrative arc, in order?
cards.answer: Equilibrium / Disruption / Recognition / Repair / New equilibrium

cards.front: What three effects can non-linear narrative techniques create for audiences?
cards.answer: Mystery (seeing aftermath before cause) / Empathy (flashback gives backstory before a decision) / Complexity (simultaneous storylines that converge)
items: Empathy (flashback gives backstory before a decision)

cards.front: Why might a streaming drama use a cliff-hanger ending instead of giving closure?
cards.answer: It deliberately denies closure to compel audiences to keep watching the next episode, a commercial use of the enigma code.

cards.front: How can Propp's character functions be used to critique gender representation in a media narrative?
cards.answer: They give precise language to describe patterns like women only filling the passive princess role while men hold all hero and villain roles.

cards.front: Name the three separate conspiracies for power that run through the play.
cards.answer: Antonio overthrew Prospero in the past / Antonio and Sebastian plot against Alonso / Caliban, Stephano and Trinculo plot against Prospero
items: Antonio overthrew Prospero in the past
Antonio and Sebastian plot against Alonso
Caliban, Stephano and Trinculo plot against Prospero

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare change the outcome of the Antonio-Sebastian conspiracy compared to the similar plot in Macbeth?
cards.answer: Ariel prevents the murder, so the play moves towards forgiveness rather than revenge, reflecting Shakespeare's shift towards reconciliation in his late romances.

cards.front: How does Caliban's offer to serve Stephano reveal his vulnerability as a colonised subject?
cards.answer: By trading one master for another, he shows that the colonised subject cannot easily escape structures of servitude.

title: Themes: change and continuity in health and medicine
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name three examples of continuity given in the lesson that persisted across all three eras of British medical history.
cards.answer: Quarantine used against outbreaks / Herbal and alternative medicine / Reactive government response to crises / Health inequalities between rich and poor
items: Health inequalities between rich and poor

cards.front: Why did Lister's antiseptic surgery, despite being based on Pasteur's germ theory, face years of resistance from surgeons?
cards.answer: Germ theory was published in 1861 but established surgeons resisted applying it in practice for years afterwards.

cards.front: How did the printing press speed up the spread of Vesalius's corrections to Galen?
cards.answer: It allowed medical knowledge to spread rapidly, making Vesalius's corrections widely known within years rather than decades.

title: Royal Government and Finance under John
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five feudal incidents John could demand from his tenants-in-chief.
cards.answer: Relief / Wardship / Marriage / Escheat / Aids

cards.front: What were the three customary cases in which an 'aid' payment was due?
cards.answer: Ransom of the king / Knighting of his eldest son / Marriage of his eldest daughter

cards.front: Why did the loss of Normandy in 1204 make John's government in England more arbitrary?
cards.answer: With Normandy gone he had nowhere else to go, so he stayed in England and imposed rulings at close range without the buffer of distance.

cards.front: Why did John sell and unsell sheriffdoms more often than his predecessors?
cards.answer: Sheriffs bought their offices, so reselling them raised extra cash and let John rotate men he distrusted.

cards.front: Name the four pilgrimage sites the lesson identifies as important to Christians.
cards.answer: Jerusalem / Iona / Taizé / Walsingham

cards.front: Name the four stages of Holy Week the lesson gives, from Palm Sunday to Easter Sunday.
cards.answer: Palm Sunday / Last Supper on Maundy Thursday / Crucifixion on Good Friday / Easter Sunday

cards.front: Why is Easter treated as Christianity's central festival rather than Christmas?
cards.answer: Because Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 15 that if Christ was not raised, Christian preaching and faith are useless.

cards.front: Why do Baptists and many evangelical Christians baptise adults rather than infants?
cards.answer: They see baptism as a public declaration of personal faith, made by full immersion, rather than a means of removing sin.

cards.front: Why does Gerald leave to be alone for a while after confessing about Eva?
cards.answer: So he can avoid witnessing Mrs Birling's interrogation, meaning distance stops him truly being changed by the experience.

cards.front: Why does the Inspector let Mrs Birling demand harsh punishment for the father before revealing it is Eric?
cards.answer: So her own class prejudice traps her into publicly condemning her son, delivering dramatic justice she cannot retract.

cards.front: Name the three Norfolk events/moments that build its symbolic weight in Never Let Me Go.
cards.answer: The failed search for Ruth's possible / Tommy finding the replacement tape / Kathy at the wire fence in the final scene
items: The failed search for Ruth's possible
Kathy at the wire fence in the final scene

cards.front: Why does the loss and replacement of the Judy Bridgewater tape reinforce the novel's message?
cards.answer: The original held Kathy's real childhood feelings, but the replacement only holds the memory of them, showing what is lost cannot be truly recovered.

cards.front: Why does Ishiguro present Hailsham as both a paradise and a prison?
cards.answer: It gave the clones friendship and safety while conditioning them to accept organ donation, showing how people can feel nostalgic for institutions that harmed them.

cards.front: Why did the Gallery's campaign to prove the clones' humanity fail?
cards.answer: Because proof of humanity means nothing to a society that has decided it doesn't want to think about the clones' treatment.

title: Context: Jacobean World, James I & Witchcraft
subject: english-literature-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three unnatural events Ross and the Old Man describe in Act 2, Scene 4 after Duncan's murder.
cards.answer: The sun is blocked out ('dark night strangles the travelling lamp') / A falcon is killed by a mousing owl / Duncan's horses turn wild and eat each other
items: The sun is blocked out ('dark night strangles the travelling lamp')
A falcon is killed by a mousing owl
Duncan's horses turn wild and eat each other

cards.front: According to Jacobean belief under the 1604 Witchcraft Act, what three things were witches thought capable of doing?
cards.answer: Controlling the weather / Cursing livestock / Foretelling the future

cards.front: Why does the falcon being killed by a 'mousing owl' in Act 2, Scene 4 show divine anger at Duncan's murder?
cards.answer: The owl (lower in the Chain of Being) killing the noble falcon (representing Duncan) allegorises a lesser being destroying a greater one, showing God's anger.

cards.front: How does the failure of the Gunpowder Plot help explain why Macbeth's regicide must fail?
cards.answer: The Plot's failure was seen as divine intervention protecting the anointed king, so Macbeth's murder of Duncan must also be destroyed to reassure the audience regicide can never succeed.

title: The League of Nations in the 1920s
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four main bodies of the League of Nations' structure.
cards.answer: The Assembly / The Council / The Permanent Court of International Justice / The Secretariat
items: The Permanent Court of International Justice

cards.front: Give three areas of humanitarian or technical work the League achieved success in during the 1920s.
cards.answer: Refugee work via the Nansen passport / Improving working conditions (ILO) / Coordinating typhus outbreak responses / Monitoring slavery in territories
items: Refugee work via the Nansen passport

cards.front: Why was the Mosul Settlement of 1925 considered a success for the League?
cards.answer: The League settled the border dispute between Turkey and British-controlled Iraq over the oil-rich Mosul region by awarding it to Iraq.

cards.front: Why did the Corfu incident reveal a critical weakness in the League's authority?
cards.answer: The League had moral authority but no military force to compel powerful states like Mussolini's Italy to obey its rulings.

cards.front: Why did the Montgomery bus boycott put serious pressure on the city's bus company?
cards.answer: Black passengers provided around 70 per cent of its revenue, so their boycott caused serious financial losses.

cards.front: Why was Emmett Till's mother's decision to hold an open-casket funeral so significant?
cards.answer: It let published photographs of his body show the brutal reality of racial violence, shocking and energising the movement.

cards.front: Name the three ways the Montgomery Bus Boycott was significant beyond Montgomery, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Showed organised non-violent protest could succeed / Launched Martin Luther King Jr. as a national figure / Provided a model of protest copied across the South
items: Showed organised non-violent protest could succeed
Launched Martin Luther King Jr. as a national figure
Provided a model of protest copied across the South

cards.front: Name the six stages of designing a piece of sociological research, in order.
cards.answer: Aim/hypothesis / Operationalise key concepts / Choose method / Choose sampling strategy / Run a pilot study / Address ethical issues

cards.front: Name the five main sampling methods covered for studying school exclusion.
cards.answer: Random / Systematic / Stratified / Quota / Snowball

cards.front: Why might a researcher choose participant observation to study excluded pupils rather than a questionnaire?
cards.answer: Because the group is hard to reach and unlikely to respond to surveys, so observation generates rich qualitative data on natural behaviour.

cards.front: How does using mixed methods increase the validity of a study's findings?
cards.answer: Combining two methods allows triangulation, checking whether findings from one method are supported or contradicted by another.

title: The Hurt Locker: Bigelow's Iraq Thriller
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three production companies that produced The Hurt Locker.
cards.answer: Voltage Pictures / Grosvenor Park Media / Film Capital Europe Funds

cards.front: What three camera positions does the opening pre-credits disposal sequence cut between?
cards.answer: A wide overhead shot / an extreme telephoto close-up from a rooftop / rapid rack-focus pulls scanning for threats
items: an extreme telephoto close-up from a rooftop
rapid rack-focus pulls scanning for threats

cards.front: Why does Bigelow use long telephoto lenses during the bomb-disposal sequences?
cards.answer: To compress space and create distance, positioning the spectator as an anxious, helpless observer rather than a participant.

cards.front: Why does The Hurt Locker structure itself as escalating disposal episodes rather than building to one climax?
cards.answer: Because bomb disposal has no narrative finish line, so each episode resets tension instead of resolving it.

cards.front: Name the four stages of a device's environmental impact given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Manufacture (mining, fabrication emissions) / Energy consumption in use (data centres, devices, networks) / Replacement cycle (how often devices are upgraded) / Disposal (e-waste and toxic materials)
items: Energy consumption in use (data centres, devices, networks)
Replacement cycle (how often devices are upgraded)

cards.front: Name the four types of intellectual property protection covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Copyright / Patents / Trademarks / Licencing

cards.front: How do cooling systems in data centres add to environmental impact?
cards.answer: They are needed to stop equipment overheating, but they themselves consume additional electricity and water.

cards.front: Why can long, complex privacy policies undermine genuine user consent?
cards.answer: They can obscure the true scope of what data collection and use users are actually agreeing to.

cards.front: Name the three pieces of evidence the lesson pairs with the three eras of policing.
cards.answer: Tithing system (Saxon era) / Parish constable (Tudor era) / Metropolitan Police 1829 (modern era)

cards.front: What three things must a 16-mark thematic essay do?
cards.answer: Identify turning points / Identify continuities / Reach a substantiated conclusion

cards.front: How did the spirit of community-based enforcement survive after it was replaced?
cards.answer: It survived in the Peelian principle of 'policing by consent', even though community-based enforcement itself was replaced.

cards.front: How does the aim behind the Bloody Code connect to deterrence debates today?
cards.answer: Both share the same underlying purpose of punishment — deterring crime — linking the Bloody Code to modern deterrence debates.

cards.front: Name the four deliberate hardships the agoge used to toughen boys, according to the lesson's key fact.
cards.answer: Minimal food / Rough sleeping / Endurance tests / Organised fighting

cards.front: Name the five things a Spartan man had to contribute to his syssitia each month.
cards.answer: Barley meal / Wine / Cheese / Figs / A sum for condiments

cards.front: Why was helot labour essential to the Spartan warrior lifestyle?
cards.answer: Helots worked the land assigned to Spartiates, freeing them from manual labour so they could train as warriors continuously.

cards.front: Why did the Spartans reportedly declare war on the helots at the start of each year?
cards.answer: So that helot deaths, such as those during the krypteia, were technically not classed as murder.

cards.front: Name the three anti-heroes/villains covered in this part of the Heroes and Villains theme.
cards.answer: Sejanus, ambitious adviser (Tacitus) / Mezentius, cruel Etruscan king (Virgil) / Sempronia, dangerous noblewoman (Sallust)

cards.front: Name the three crimes Sallust lists for Sempronia using asyndeton.
cards.answer: Betrayed trust / Denied a debt under oath / Was party to murder

cards.front: Why does the villa Spelunca rockfall episode make Sejanus hard to judge as simply a villain?
cards.answer: His genuine physical bravery in shielding Tiberius sits uneasily alongside Tacitus's portrait of his secret ambition and flattery elsewhere.

cards.front: Why does Virgil use a rhetorical question instead of listing all of Mezentius's crimes?
cards.answer: It lets Virgil imply endless, unspeakable cruelty without needing to catalogue every crime in full.

cards.front: Name the three things Ed confesses to Christopher in Act 2.
cards.answer: Hiding the letters / Lying about Judy's death / Killing Wellington

cards.front: What five things does the lesson say make the journey to London terrifying for Christopher?
cards.answer: Crowds / Strangers / Unpredictable sensory environments / Trains / The Underground

cards.front: Why did Ed choose to tell Christopher his mother was dead rather than that she had left?
cards.answer: He wrongly believed saying she had died was kinder than telling Christopher she had chosen to leave him.

cards.front: How does Stephens contrast Judy's and Christopher's love when they reunite in London?
cards.answer: Judy shows emotional, demonstrative love by weeping and holding him, while Christopher's love is shown through competence and simply arriving.

cards.front: Name the four groups in the class pyramid of Russian society in 1894.
cards.answer: Nobility (about 1%) / Middle class (about 1.5%) / Urban proletariat (about 4%) / Peasants (over 80%)

cards.front: Name the three methods Witte used to fund and drive industrial growth.
cards.answer: Borrowed heavily from French banks / Introduced the gold standard in 1897 / High tariffs protecting Russian industry / High indirect taxes on vodka, sugar and matches
items: High indirect taxes on vodka, sugar and matches

cards.front: Why was modern farming almost impossible under the mir system?
cards.answer: Land was divided into narrow, scattered strips to share good soil fairly, blocking efficient modern farming methods.

cards.front: Why were Russia's new industrial cities a natural recruiting ground for revolutionary parties?
cards.answer: Workers faced brutal conditions, illegal trade unions, harsh policing by the Okhrana, and violent responses to organising, breeding resentment.

cards.front: Name the three main types of system software given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Operating system / Utility programs / Device drivers

cards.front: Name the three example utility programs described in the lesson.
cards.answer: File compression tool / Disk cleanup tool / Encryption software

cards.front: Why is antivirus software classed as system software rather than application software?
cards.answer: Because its purpose is to maintain the health of the system, not to help the user complete a personal task.

cards.front: Why does a compiled program run faster than an interpreted one once it is finished?
cards.answer: Because the whole program is translated to machine code in advance, so no further translation is needed at run time.

title: Vocal Music: Meeting Purcell and Queen
subject: music-edexcel

cards.front: Why does Purcell use long melismas in Music for a While?
cards.answer: To let the voice imitate the sustained, hypnotic effect of music charming pain away, especially on words about eternity, suffering or enchantment.

cards.front: How does multitrack recording let Queen build a denser texture than Purcell's live continuo?
cards.answer: It lets separate vocal and instrumental performances be recorded on individual tracks and combined, creating layers impossible in one live take.

cards.front: How does Brian May's guitar solo in Killer Queen create an orchestral tone?
cards.answer: By recording layered guitar tracks that combine to sound almost brass-like rather than a single guitar line.

cards.front: Name the four things a real fortress would have that Acton Burnell lacks.
cards.answer: A moat / A curtain wall of any strength / A gatehouse / Room for a garrison
items: A curtain wall of any strength

cards.front: In the exam answer, name the four features the lesson says to read as evidence about Edward's England.
cards.answer: Large windows and thin defences / The licence to crenellate / The barn parliament and statute / The builder's career

cards.front: Why did Edward grant licences to crenellate like Burnell's if they weren't needed for real defence?
cards.answer: By Edward's reign such licences were largely honours showing royal favour, so a licence said publicly that a man mattered to the king.

cards.front: Why did a merchants' debt law matter to a warrior king like Edward?
cards.answer: Edward's wars ran on credit from merchant-bankers, who would only lend and trade freely if debts could actually be collected, so the statute was war finance by other means.

title: Themes: Motherhood, Class, Race and Sexuality
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four everyday things Geof does that show him practically mothering Jo.
cards.answer: Cleans / Cooks / Pays rent / Sews a maternity dress

cards.front: How does the play's circular structure reinforce the theme of motherhood?
cards.answer: It opens with Helen and Jo arriving together and closes with Jo alone in the same flat, suggesting the pattern of neglect repeats.

cards.front: Why did the Lord Chamberlain's Office demand cuts to the language used about Geof?
cards.answer: Because every play had to be licensed before performance, and sex between men was a criminal offence at the time.

title: Focuses of Worship and the Murti
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the five focuses of Hindu worship covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: The many deities, the guru and elders / One God (personal or non-personal) / Holy land, hills and rivers / Sacred plants and animals / The murti as a representation of God
items: The many deities, the guru and elders
The murti as a representation of God

cards.front: What four things count as personal focuses of worship in Hindu practice?
cards.answer: Deities such as Vishnu, Shiva or Ganesha / The guru / The murti / Sacred places linked to a deity's story
items: Deities such as Vishnu, Shiva or Ganesha
Sacred places linked to a deity's story

cards.front: Why is worshipping many different deities not seen as contradictory in Hindu thought?
cards.answer: Because Hindu teaching holds that all deities are ultimately manifestations of the one Brahman.

cards.front: Why is Varanasi considered the most sacred city in Hinduism?
cards.answer: Because it lies on the Ganges and dying there is believed to bring moksha.

cards.front: Name the four criticisms intellectuals raised about the Party during the Hundred Flowers Campaign.
cards.answer: Party corruption / Privileges enjoyed by cadres / Poor treatment of intellectuals / Rigid application of Soviet-style policies

cards.front: What three methods did the Anti-Rightist Campaign use to enforce punishments?
cards.answer: Public denunciations / Political study sessions / Pressure on colleagues and family to denounce
items: Pressure on colleagues and family to denounce

cards.front: How did running the Anti-Rightist Campaign benefit Deng Xiaoping's later political career?
cards.answer: Running it efficiently with Mao's backing cemented his reputation as a loyal enforcer, aiding his rehabilitation after his own later purge.

cards.front: Why did the Anti-Rightist Campaign create a lasting chilling effect on Chinese intellectual life?
cards.answer: Intellectuals who avoided being labelled rightists learned that silence was safer than honest appraisal, so they stopped speaking out for a decade.

cards.front: Name the four safety features the lesson gives for protecting against mains electrical dangers.
cards.answer: Fuses in the live wire / Earth wires on metal-cased appliances / Circuit breakers / Double insulation on plastic-cased devices

cards.front: What are the potential differences between the three wire pairs in a plug (live-neutral, live-earth, neutral-earth)?
cards.answer: Live to neutral: about 230 V / Live to earth: about 230 V / Neutral to earth: about 0 V

cards.front: Why must a fuse be placed in the live wire rather than the neutral wire?
cards.answer: If it were in the neutral wire, a blown fuse would leave the live wire connected, so the casing could stay at 230 V, causing electrocution risk.

cards.front: Why does the UK use alternating current for its mains supply instead of direct current?
cards.answer: A.c. can be stepped up and down by transformers, which only work with a.c., allowing efficient high-voltage transmission and safe domestic use.

title: Plot and Structure: A Dystopian Two-Act Tragedy
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: What are the six stages of the play's structural arc, from the opening scene to the epilogue?
cards.answer: Opening beach scene (childhood) / School integration scenes / Family fractures / Liberation Militia sequences / Hostage scene (brief hope) / Execution and epilogue

cards.front: Why does the dual-narrator device create dramatic irony in Noughts & Crosses?
cards.answer: Because the audience often knows more about each character's private feelings than the other character does.

cards.front: Why does Cooke use episodic structure to adapt the novel for the stage?
cards.answer: It allows him to compress years of narrative into stage time using short scenes marked by sound and lighting transitions rather than elaborate set changes.

title: A Divided Society: Prohibition, Crime, the Klan and the Red Scare
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three types of campaigners who pushed for Prohibition.
cards.answer: Anti-Saloon League / Women's Christian Temperance Union / Evangelical Protestant churches

cards.front: Name the four groups the revived Ku Klux Klan targeted.
cards.answer: African-Americans / Catholics / Jews / Recent immigrants

cards.front: Why did Prohibition create a huge illegal alcohol economy?
cards.answer: Most Americans did not want to give up alcohol, and only about 1,500 federal agents could not police a country that refused to be policed.

cards.front: Why did the WASP backlash of Prohibition, the Klan and immigration laws happen in the 1920s?
cards.answer: Urbanisation and the 1920 census made growing numbers of immigrants, Catholics, Jews and Black southerners visible, threatening rural Protestant dominance, so it reached for laws to reverse this.

title: The Hate U Give: Issue-Led Indie
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five sequences the lesson identifies for micro-analysis in The Hate U Give.
cards.answer: Opening kitchen-table 'the talk' scene / Traffic-stop police-shooting sequence / Protest-and-tear-gas sequence / Kitchen confrontation with King / Closing house-fire and recovery sequence

cards.front: How does the framing at Williamson Prep dramatise Starr's code-switching, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: The camera frames Starr with more space around her and cooler light, keeping her at a slight remove from the other students to show displacement before she speaks.

cards.front: How does Tillman use the formal grammar of the opening kitchen-table scene to contain its political content?
cards.answer: Warm palette, close hand-held framing and ordinary diegetic sound with no score create domestic warmth that holds the politically weighty conversation, making it feel personal.

cards.front: Why does the lesson argue The Hate U Give's YA register itself counts as a political choice?
cards.answer: Tillman and Thomas deliberately chose accessibility to reach audiences that more formally challenging or prestige-positioned films could not.

title: The Skeletal System: Bones and Functions
subject: physical-education-ocr

cards.front: Name the six functions of the skeleton.
cards.answer: Support / Posture / Protection / Movement / Blood cell production / Storage of minerals

cards.front: How do muscles and bones work together to produce movement in sport?
cards.answer: Muscles contract and pull on bones, which act as levers, creating movement at joints.

cards.front: How does weight-bearing exercise affect bone strength over time?
cards.answer: Weight-bearing exercise stimulates bones to increase their mineral density, making them stronger over time.

cards.front: Name the three responses Hoover made to the Depression, according to the lesson's key fact.
cards.answer: 1930 Hawley–Smoot Tariff / 1932 Reconstruction Finance Corporation / Continued belief in rugged individualism

cards.front: Name the three academics in Roosevelt's 'Brain Trust' during the 1932 campaign.
cards.answer: Raymond Moley / Rexford Tugwell / Adolf Berle

cards.front: Why did the Hawley–Smoot Tariff backfire on American farmers?
cards.answer: Twenty-five trading partners retaliated with their own tariffs, so farmers lost overseas export markets while crop prices collapsed at home.

cards.front: Why did the nicknames 'Hoovervilles' and 'Hoover blankets' damage Hoover politically?
cards.answer: They turned an economic crisis into a personal verdict on Hoover, attaching his name directly to people's misery.

cards.front: Name the four details Ishiguro uses to build the reader's suspicions in 'A Family Supper'.
cards.answer: Mother's death from fugu / Watanabe's murder-suicide / Father's belief his wife's death was no accident / The model battleship and talk of the pilot's 'final weapon'
items: Father's belief his wife's death was no accident
The model battleship and talk of the pilot's 'final weapon'

cards.front: Name the three symbols the lesson identifies in 'A Family Supper'.
cards.answer: The fugu fish / The empty rooms of the house / The old well the narrator believed haunted
items: The empty rooms of the house
The old well the narrator believed haunted

cards.front: How does the narrator's tone contribute to the story's ambiguity?
cards.answer: His calm, matter-of-fact tone even describing his mother's death or Watanabe's killings means nothing is flagged as alarming, leaving the reader unsure if suspicions are reasonable.

cards.front: Why does Ishiguro's use of a limited first-person narrator suit the story's themes?
cards.answer: Because the story is about failed understanding, the reader only knows what the son knows, and the son cannot fully read his father's intentions.

cards.front: Name the six minerals covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Calcium / Iron / Sodium / Fluoride / Iodine / Phosphorus

cards.front: Name the five ways given to minimise vitamin loss when cooking vegetables.
cards.answer: Use the minimum water possible / Steam rather than boil / Use short cooking times / Prepare vegetables just before cooking / Avoid keeping cooked vegetables warm for long periods
items: Avoid keeping cooked vegetables warm for long periods

cards.front: Why does eating too much sodium increase the risk of stroke and heart disease?
cards.answer: Excess sodium raises blood pressure (hypertension), which increases the risk of stroke and coronary heart disease.

cards.front: Why don't fat-soluble vitamins need to be eaten every day?
cards.answer: They are stored in the liver and body fat, so the body can draw on reserves instead of needing daily intake.

cards.front: Name the three techniques Byron uses in 'When We Two Parted' to present heartbreak as inescapable and permanent.
cards.answer: Pathetic fallacy (cold dew) / Metaphor (cold kiss = dead love) / Cyclical structure (ending repeats beginning)

cards.front: How does the personification in the final lines of 'Love's Philosophy' work as an argument for love?
cards.answer: It makes nature itself ('sunlight clasps', 'moonbeams kiss') act out love, so nature argues that the beloved should kiss the speaker too.

cards.front: Why does the final word 'me' at the end of each stanza in 'Love's Philosophy' disrupt the poem's smooth, song-like rhyme scheme?
cards.answer: It breaks the flow because the speaker's personal desire suddenly interrupts the natural philosophy he has been building.

cards.front: How does Barrett Browning complicate the vine metaphor in Sonnet 29?
cards.answer: She asks the beloved to 'burst, shattered, everywhere' the vines, showing she wants the real person, not just her idealised thoughts of him.

cards.front: Name the three types of maps the lesson gives for presenting spatial fieldwork data.
cards.answer: Choropleth map / Flow-line map / Proportional symbols map

cards.front: Name the five skills the lesson says a hand-drawn map should show.
cards.answer: Title / Scale bar / North arrow / Key / Accurate labelling

cards.front: Why must the categories in a pie chart add up to 100%?
cards.answer: A pie chart shows shares of a whole, so its segments must represent parts of one total.

cards.front: How does evaluating fieldwork differ from describing it?
cards.answer: Describing states what happened, while evaluating judges whether the method or data was reliable.

cards.front: Name the three poems the lesson covers under 'Inner Conflict & Anger'.
cards.answer: A Poison Tree by William Blake / Extract from The Prelude 'Boating' by William Wordsworth / Cousin Kate by Christina Rossetti
items: A Poison Tree by William Blake
Extract from The Prelude 'Boating' by William Wordsworth

cards.front: Why does Blake describe watering the tree with tears and sunning it with smiles?
cards.answer: The nurturing natural imagery is ironic, showing how the speaker's dishonest kindness secretly feeds his toxic hidden anger.

cards.front: How does the boy's confidence change during the boat journey in The Prelude extract?
cards.answer: His joyful confidence is destroyed when the huge peak seems to pursue him, leaving him terrified and permanently haunted by nature's power.

cards.front: How does the lord's language show he treats the speaker as property in Cousin Kate?
cards.answer: Rossetti uses possessive similes like 'wore me like a silken knot' to show the lord treating her as a disposable object, not a person.

cards.front: Name the three types of force the lesson says police and army used against Soweto protesters.
cards.answer: Tear gas / Rubber bullets / Live ammunition

cards.front: As protests spread nationwide after Soweto, what three types of targets were attacked?
cards.answer: Schools burned / Government buildings attacked / Police stations stoned

cards.front: Why does the lesson describe the Afrikaans decree as the trigger, not the cause, of the Soweto uprising?
cards.answer: Black Consciousness ideas had circulated in schools for years and students formed an action committee before the march, showing deeper organisation behind it.

cards.front: How did the Soweto uprising change the ANC exile leadership's view of resistance inside South Africa?
cards.answer: It showed resistance inside the country was self-generating, not dependent solely on direction from Lusaka, reconnecting the internal and external movements.

cards.front: What three purposes does Meena's lying serve in the novel?
cards.answer: To get attention / To fit in / To protect herself from a painful reality
items: To protect herself from a painful reality

cards.front: Why does Papa's statement 'We are the British' matter in the novel?
cards.answer: It is factually true since the Kumars are British citizens, and also a quiet act of resistance against exclusion.

cards.front: Why is what Meena envies in Anita actually an illusion?
cards.answer: Anita's freedom is really neglect and her confidence is bravado masking insecurity, while her home life is loveless.

cards.front: How does the food contrast between the Kumar and Rutter households support the novel's themes?
cards.answer: Mama's rich, ritual-filled cooking shows warmth and cultural pride, while Anita's processed, joyless food reveals emotional neglect.

title: Planning Assets, Hardware, Software & File Management
subject: cambridge-nationals-creative-imedia

cards.front: Name the four things a creator should note about each asset during the planning stage.
cards.answer: what the asset is / whether it will be created, sourced from stock, or provided by client / who is responsible for obtaining or creating it / any legal considerations such as copyright or licence requirements
items: whether it will be created, sourced from stock, or provided by client
who is responsible for obtaining or creating it
any legal considerations such as copyright or licence requirements

cards.front: Name the six sub-folders a project's top-level folder structure might contain.
cards.answer: images / audio / video / graphics / exports / working-files

cards.front: Why is it important to list all required assets during the planning stage of a media project?
cards.answer: To prevent discovering at the editing phase that a critical file is missing, unavailable or in the wrong format.

cards.front: How can choosing the wrong software for an asset type affect the finished product?
cards.answer: It can lead to poor-quality outputs or unnecessary file conversions.

cards.front: Name the three ways fossils can be dated, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Position in rock layers (older strata lie deeper) / Radiometric dating techniques / Comparison with other fossils of known age
items: Position in rock layers (older strata lie deeper)
Comparison with other fossils of known age

cards.front: Name the five causes of extinction given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Climate change / New predators or competitors / New diseases / Habitat destruction / Catastrophic events

cards.front: Why is variation essential for natural selection to occur?
cards.answer: Without variation all individuals would respond identically to environmental pressures, leaving nothing for selection to act on.

cards.front: Why did the proportion of dark peppered moths increase during industrial pollution?
cards.answer: Soot darkened tree bark and killed lichens, so dark moths were better camouflaged, survived predation more and reproduced more.

cards.front: Name the eight A8 countries that joined the EU in May 2004.
cards.answer: Poland / Czech Republic / Slovakia / Hungary / Slovenia / Estonia / Latvia and Lithuania

cards.front: Why did the July 2005 London bombings intensify criticism of multiculturalism?
cards.answer: Three of the four bombers were British-born men of Pakistani heritage, fuelling arguments that 'parallel lives' had replaced integration.

cards.front: Why was the genuine refugee/economic migrant distinction used in 1990s asylum debates seen as legally uncertain?
cards.answer: Many people fleeing poverty were doing so because their states had failed to protect them from violence.

cards.front: How did Britain's approach to A8 migration differ from Germany and France, and what was the result?
cards.answer: Britain, Ireland and Sweden imposed no transitional restrictions, causing large, rapid migration mainly from Poland.

title: Area of Study 4: Western Classical Tradition since 1910 — Unfamiliar Listening
subject: music-aqa

cards.front: Name the four movements of Bartók's Hungarian Sketches set for study (movement 3 is not included).
cards.answer: An Evening in the Village / Bear Dance / Slightly Tipsy / Swineherd's Dance

cards.front: Name the three pieces given in the British strand.
cards.answer: Peterloo Overture (Arnold) / Song for Athene (Tavener) / An Orkney Wedding, with Sunrise (Maxwell Davies)
items: An Orkney Wedding, with Sunrise (Maxwell Davies)

cards.front: How does Reich's Music for 18 Musicians change over any five-minute stretch of listening?
cards.answer: It changes very little, and only very gradually, even across a five-minute listen.

cards.front: What four income categories does the World Bank use to classify countries by GNI per capita?
cards.answer: Low-income / Lower-middle income / Upper-middle income / High-income

cards.front: Besides GNI and HDI, what four other measures does the lesson mention for judging development?
cards.answer: Literacy rates / Doctors per 1,000 people / Infant mortality / Access to safe water

cards.front: Why can China be called the world's second-largest economy but only a middle-income country per person?
cards.answer: China's total GDP is huge because of its large population, but dividing by that population gives a much lower per-capita figure.

cards.front: Why can a country's GDP grow quickly while quality of life or the environment gets worse?
cards.answer: GDP only measures market output and ignores unpaid care work, subsistence farming and environmental damage.

title: Modern Britain: Wars, Empire's End and the Law, c1900–present
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four major migrant streams that shaped modern Britain, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: World War refugees / Commonwealth migrants (Caribbean, South Asia, East Africa) / EU migrants after 2004 / Asylum seekers throughout
items: Commonwealth migrants (Caribbean, South Asia, East Africa)

cards.front: Name the four Race Relations/anti-discrimination laws or bodies the lesson says developed alongside restriction laws.
cards.answer: 1965 Race Relations Act / 1968 Race Relations Act / 1976 Race Relations Act / Commission for Racial Equality

cards.front: Why did Caribbean migration to Britain grow steadily through the 1950s?
cards.answer: London Transport, the new NHS and British Rail actively recruited workers from Barbados, Jamaica and Trinidad.

cards.front: Why did the state gain more discretion over who could enter Britain between 1905 and 1939?
cards.answer: Wartime laws like the 1914 Aliens Restriction Act gave sweeping powers over 'enemy aliens', later extended into peacetime and visa requirements.

title: Holy Books, Angels, Predestination and Akhirah
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four earlier holy books Muslims believe Allah revealed before the Qur'an.
cards.answer: Tawrat / Zabur / Injil / Sahifah

cards.front: What is the sequence of events in Muslim teaching about Akhirah, from death onwards?
cards.answer: Death / Barzakh / Resurrection / Judgement of deeds / Jannah or Jahannam

cards.front: Why does belief in al-Qadr not remove a Muslim's moral responsibility for their actions?
cards.answer: Although Allah already knows what a person will choose, Muslims are still judged on the basis of their actual choices, not a fixed fate.

cards.front: How does Islamic teaching on judgement after death differ from Christian teaching?
cards.answer: Islam has no purgatory, only barzakh, and judgement rests on weighing deeds plus Allah's mercy rather than a mediating figure like Christ's atoning death.

title: Dramatic Methods: Cross-Cutting and Stage Directions
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three signals Turnly's stage directions combine to mark a leap in time between scenes.
cards.answer: A change in lighting state / A costume change visible to the audience / A change in the physical bearing of performers
items: A costume change visible to the audience
A change in the physical bearing of performers

cards.front: Name the three design approaches the lesson gives for realising the sea on stage in The Great Wave.
cards.answer: A soundscape of waves fading in and out / A lighting wash of shifting blue-grey / Gobos throwing fragmented water-light patterns
items: A soundscape of waves fading in and out
A lighting wash of shifting blue-grey

cards.front: Why is cross-cutting in The Great Wave described as a political act rather than just an editing device?
cards.answer: It refuses to let the audience follow only one storyline, forcing them to hold both in mind and creating dramatic irony and moral pressure.

cards.front: How can blocking at the start of a new scene signal that time has passed in The Great Wave?
cards.answer: Quick movement to a new position suggests arrival in a new moment, while stillness as lights rise signals the scene begins mid-thought.

title: Peasant discontent: long and short-term causes
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three long-term causes the lesson gives for the Peasants' Revolt.
cards.answer: Continued enforcement of serfdom / Statute of Labourers reversing wage gains / Decades of resentment over legal status vs economic reality
items: Statute of Labourers reversing wage gains
Decades of resentment over legal status vs economic reality

cards.front: Why did tension build between peasants and lords in the decades after the Black Death?
cards.answer: Peasants felt their labour had earned them freedom, but lords used the courts to keep enforcing serfdom against them.

cards.front: Why did ordinary taxation in this period fall especially heavily on the poorest?
cards.answer: Parliamentary subsidies were assessed on moveable goods, so poorer property-owners paid while the richest paid proportionally less.

cards.front: William James identified four features common to mystical experiences. Name them.
cards.answer: Noetic (conveys knowledge) / Transient (short-lived) / Passive (person feels acted upon) / Ineffable (impossible to put into words)

cards.front: Name the four forms of religious experience discussed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Conversion / Mystical experience / Charismatic and ecstatic experience / Visions

cards.front: How do believers respond to Hume's argument that belief in miracles is almost never justified?
cards.answer: They say his argument presupposes naturalism and begs the question, since if God exists, miracles are entirely possible.

cards.front: Why do non-believers think religious experiences reflect prior belief rather than objective reality?
cards.answer: Because experiences are shaped by culture — a Christian sees Jesus, a Muslim encounters Allah — suggesting belief shapes the experience.

cards.front: Name the five codes Barthes identified at work in narratives and texts.
cards.answer: Enigma code / Action code / Semantic code / Symbolic code / Referential code

cards.front: Name the three types of sign semioticians distinguish.
cards.answer: Iconic sign / Index sign / Symbolic sign

cards.front: Why do media producers use anchorage on an ambiguous image?
cards.answer: Because an image is polysemic and could be read in multiple ways, so text pins down the preferred meaning.

cards.front: What is a key limitation of the linear model of communication?
cards.answer: It implies a passive audience who simply receive meaning and ignores noise, mediation and context shaping understanding.

cards.front: Name the four areas the WJEC specification groups hospitality job roles into.
cards.answer: Front of house / Housekeeping / Kitchen brigade / Management

cards.front: Name the three management roles listed for a hospitality business.
cards.answer: Food and beverage manager / Housekeeping manager / Marketing manager

cards.front: Why is the kitchen brigade structure important in a busy restaurant serving hundreds of covers a night?
cards.answer: It prevents confusion and ensures dishes are prepared consistently, since everyone knows their role and who they report to.

cards.front: How do smaller kitchens adapt the traditional kitchen brigade hierarchy?
cards.answer: They use a simplified version, with the head chef taking on multiple senior roles instead of separate staff.

title: The Classical Concerto: Balance, Dialogue and the Rise of the Public Concert (1750-1820)
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the four instrument groups the lesson says were added to the Classical orchestra beyond Baroque strings and continuo.
cards.answer: Oboes / Bassoons / Horns / Timpani

cards.front: Why did the rise of public, ticketed concerts change how composers wrote for orchestras?
cards.answer: Bigger, mixed audiences and larger halls demanded music that could impress a paying public, so orchestras grew larger and more varied in timbre.

cards.front: Why do Classical concerto melodies typically end with an imperfect cadence followed by a perfect cadence?
cards.answer: Melodies use an antecedent phrase ending on an imperfect cadence balanced by a consequent phrase ending on a perfect cadence, like a question and answer.

cards.front: How do Classical dynamics differ from Baroque terraced dynamics in concertos?
cards.answer: Instead of sudden loud/soft blocks, Classical orchestras use gradual crescendos and diminuendos, giving phrases shape and drama within themselves.

cards.front: Name the five key threats to biodiversity given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Deforestation / Habitat destruction / Climate change / Pollution / Overexploitation

cards.front: Name the five kingdoms organisms are traditionally divided into.
cards.answer: Animals / Plants / Fungi / Protists / Prokaryotes (Bacteria)

cards.front: Why were dolphins historically classified as fish?
cards.answer: Their body shape resembled fish due to convergent evolution, before DNA evidence showed they are actually mammals.

cards.front: Why would a decline in UK pollinators threaten more than just the pollinators themselves?
cards.answer: Almost nine in ten flowering plant species depend on animal pollinators, so losing them would cascade through food chains, threatening crop yields and wild plants.

title: Methods of punishment: medieval to early modern
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson names four specific mutilations used in Anglo-Saxon punishment. What were they and which crimes did they punish?
cards.answer: Hands cut off for theft / Ears cut off for false witness / Tongues cut off for slander / Blinding for particularly serious offences
items: Ears cut off for false witness

cards.front: Name the three aims of punishment that stayed constant across the medieval and early modern periods.
cards.answer: Deterrence / Retribution / Incapacitation

cards.front: How did the wergild system help prevent blood feuds?
cards.answer: It gave families a cash compensation alternative to private revenge, so violence between families was not needed to settle a killing.

cards.front: Why did authorities make executions at Tyburn public spectacles?
cards.answer: The public nature of execution was deliberate, meant to demonstrate the power of the state and deter crime among onlookers.

cards.front: Name the six themes the lesson gives for pairing poems in a comparison essay.
cards.answer: Power of nature / Effects of conflict / Power and control / Identity and place / Memory and loss / Attitudes to war

cards.front: Which three poem pairings does the lesson recommend for the theme 'memory and loss'?
cards.answer: Poppies + Remains / The Prelude + Kamikaze / War Photographer + The Emigrée

cards.front: Why should you plan your exam time to leave a few minutes spare at the end?
cards.answer: Planning, writing and proofreading are all part of a strong response, so time must be saved for checking.

cards.front: Why does 'eyeballs prick with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers' show bitter irony in War Photographer?
cards.answer: It reflects Duffy's anger that society treats real human suffering as a momentary inconvenience rather than something to act on.

title: Binary, BCD and Decade Counters with 7-Segment Displays
subject: electronics-eduqas

cards.front: Which six segments are ON to display the letter 'A' on a 7-segment display?
cards.answer: a / b / c / e / f / g

cards.front: Which four segments are ON to display the letter 'C' on a 7-segment display?
cards.answer: a / d / e / f

cards.front: Why does a decade counter automatically reset after reaching binary 1001 (9)?
cards.answer: Internal logic detects the forbidden state above 9 and fires a reset pulse that clears all flip-flops back to 0000.

cards.front: How does wiring a chosen Q output to the 4017's reset pin (MR) create a modulo-N counter?
cards.answer: When that Q output goes HIGH it immediately triggers reset, so the counter only stably counts through the earlier states before starting again.

title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three types of blood vessel described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Arteries / Veins / Capillaries

cards.front: Name the four components that make up blood.
cards.answer: Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets / Plasma

cards.front: Why do red blood cells have a biconcave disc shape and no nucleus?
cards.answer: The biconcave shape increases surface area and having no nucleus allows the cell to carry more haemoglobin.

cards.front: Why are heart transplants a limited treatment option for coronary heart disease?
cards.answer: They are limited by the availability of donor hearts and the risk of the immune system rejecting the transplant.

title: Post-war problems and the Treaty of Versailles
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four types of burden the Treaty of Versailles placed on Germany.
cards.answer: Territorial losses / Military restrictions / Financial costs (reparations) / Moral burden (war guilt)

cards.front: Name the four territorial losses Germany suffered under the Treaty of Versailles.
cards.answer: Alsace-Lorraine to France / Saar coalfield to League of Nations control / Parts of Posen to Poland / All overseas colonies
items: Saar coalfield to League of Nations control

cards.front: Why did the Dolchstosslegende (stab-in-the-back myth) matter politically for Weimar Germany?
cards.answer: It transferred blame for losing the war from the generals, where it belonged, to the politicians who signed the armistice and Versailles.

cards.front: Why did Weimar governments print money instead of paying reparations through taxation in the early 1920s?
cards.answer: Paying meant accepting Versailles, raising taxes on the rich and losing voters, so governments printed money instead.

cards.front: During a football kick, name the four muscle actions the lesson describes happening in sequence.
cards.answer: Hip flexors swing thigh forward / Quadriceps extend the knee / Gastrocnemius plantar-flexes the ankle / External obliques rotate the trunk

cards.front: Why can cardiac muscle keep contracting without ever fatiguing, unlike skeletal muscle?
cards.answer: Its cells are interconnected so electrical signals spread instantly across the whole heart wall, producing a coordinated contraction resistant to fatigue.

cards.front: Why is smooth muscle non-striated while cardiac muscle is striated?
cards.answer: Cardiac muscle has the overlapping actin-myosin filament arrangement for fast, high force, while smooth muscle's filaments are irregular, giving slower, sustained contraction.

title: The end of prosperity: the Wall Street Crash, 1929
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Why did unequal distribution of wealth make overproduction worse in the 1920s?
cards.answer: The top 5% got a third of income, so tens of millions of farmers and unskilled workers had little money to buy the goods being produced.

cards.front: How did margin buying turn falling share prices into a self-reinforcing crash?
cards.answer: Falling prices triggered margin calls, forcing investors to sell shares to repay loans, which pushed prices down further.

cards.front: How did the Wall Street Crash lead to mass unemployment in America?
cards.answer: Banks facing ruin called in loans to businesses, which cut production and laid off workers, collapsing consumer spending.

cards.front: Name the four pathetic fallacy examples the lesson gives across the anthology.
cards.answer: Byron: cold dew = grief / Hardy: white sun = drained love / Sheers: storm = discord, calm = reconciliation / Shelley: sunlight/moonbeams personified as lover

cards.front: How does the loose, irregular form of 'Singh Song!' support its meaning?
cards.answer: The playful, varying line lengths and phonetic dialect mirror the joy and spontaneity of the relationship it describes.

title: The Norman Church, Lanfranc & the Domesday Book
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why the Church was essential to William's rule.
cards.answer: Educated administrators / Moral authority / A network of parish churches reaching every community
items: A network of parish churches reaching every community

cards.front: Name the four key areas of Church reform Lanfranc carried out.
cards.answer: Replacing English churchmen with Normans / Ending corruption (simony and pluralism) / Reorganisation of the Church hierarchy / Separating Church courts from secular courts
items: Separating Church courts from secular courts

cards.front: Why did Pope Alexander II support William's invasion of England?
cards.answer: Stigand's irregular, uncanonical position as Archbishop made the English Church seem corrupt, giving William religious justification for reform through conquest.

cards.front: How did the Domesday Book confirm feudal landholding?
cards.answer: Once ownership was recorded in Domesday it became legally fixed, settling disputes and stopping lords claiming more land than they were entitled to.

title: Tet, My Lai and the War at Home, 1968-70
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four events of 1968-70 that the lesson says broke the credibility of the Johnson administration and divided American society.
cards.answer: The Tet Offensive / Walter Cronkite's CBS broadcast / The My Lai Massacre / The Kent State shootings

cards.front: Name the four students killed in the Kent State shootings of 4 May 1970.
cards.answer: Allison Krause / Jeffrey Miller / Sandra Scheuer / William Schroeder

cards.front: Why did the Tet Offensive damage American public opinion even though it was a tactical US-South Vietnamese victory?
cards.answer: It so completely contradicted Westmoreland's 'light at the end of the tunnel' assurances that the gap between official optimism and televised reality opened the credibility gap.

cards.front: How did helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson Jr intervene during the My Lai massacre?
cards.answer: He landed between US troops and fleeing Vietnamese, ordered his crew to fire on their own side if they advanced, and rescued around eleven civilians.

cards.front: Name the six adverbs of frequency given for talking about how often you do hobbies in French.
cards.answer: toujours (always) / souvent (often) / quelquefois / parfois (sometimes) / de temps en temps (from time to time) / rarement (rarely) / ne…jamais (never)
items: de temps en temps (from time to time)

cards.front: Name the five opinion phrases given for saying how you feel about a free-time activity in French.
cards.answer: J'adore (I love) / J'aime (I like) / Je préfère (I prefer) / Je n'aime pas (I don't like) / Je déteste (I hate)

cards.front: How do you decide whether to use faire, jouer à or jouer de when talking about a hobby in French?
cards.answer: Use faire de for sports/activities, jouer à for games and team sports, and jouer de for musical instruments.

cards.front: How can you build a high-level sentence about a free-time activity for the writing or speaking exam?
cards.answer: Combine a time phrase, a frequency adverb, the activity, an opinion, and a reason introduced by parce que/car.

cards.front: Why does Clarke describe Catrin's birth using battle language like 'our first Fierce confrontation'?
cards.answer: To show that love and conflict are inseparable, even in the tender moment of birth.

cards.front: Why does Clarke leave the poem's ending argument unresolved?
cards.answer: To suggest the push and pull between a mother's need to protect and a daughter's need for independence is permanent.

cards.front: Name the three features of a sperm cell that adapt it for its function.
cards.answer: Acrosome with enzymes to penetrate egg / Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy / Long flagellum tail for swimming
items: Acrosome with enzymes to penetrate egg
Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy

cards.front: Name the two features of a muscle cell that adapt it for contraction.
cards.answer: Large numbers of mitochondria for ATP / Actin and myosin proteins that slide past each other
items: Large numbers of mitochondria for ATP
Actin and myosin proteins that slide past each other

cards.front: Why do root hair cells have long thin extensions?
cards.answer: To dramatically increase surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.

cards.front: Why can undifferentiated stem cells be risky if transplanted into a patient?
cards.answer: They could divide uncontrollably after transplantation, forming tumours.

cards.front: Name the three 'common mistakes' the lesson lists for comparison essays other than retelling the poem.
cards.answer: Writing about each poem separately / Dropping in context without connecting it / Choosing a poem you barely know
items: Dropping in context without connecting it
Choosing a poem you barely know

cards.front: Why should you prepare a comparison grid before the exam?
cards.answer: It lets you choose your comparison poem within 30 seconds of reading the question, leaving more time for writing.

cards.front: How should AO2 and AO3 be combined in a strong comparison essay?
cards.answer: They should be woven together in the same sentence, showing context explains why a poet makes a language choice.

cards.front: Name the three levels of the Edwardian class hierarchy described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Landed aristocracy (e.g. the Crofts) / Industrial capitalists (e.g. Birling) / The working class (e.g. Eva Smith)

cards.front: What three things does Priestley achieve by setting the play in 1912 instead of 1945?
cards.answer: Dramatic irony discredits Birling's capitalist worldview / The 1945 audience sees themselves reflected in the selfishness shown / Creates urgency that disasters will repeat if attitudes don't change
items: Dramatic irony discredits Birling's capitalist worldview
The 1945 audience sees themselves reflected in the selfishness shown
Creates urgency that disasters will repeat if attitudes don't change

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Eva Smith's death is a direct consequence of the class system?
cards.answer: As a working-class woman she depended entirely on her employers' goodwill, and every Birling systematically removed that goodwill, leading to her death.

cards.front: Why was the play's Moscow premiere in 1945 significant?
cards.answer: The Soviet Union was a socialist state, and its ideology aligned with Priestley's themes of collective responsibility and critique of capitalism.

title: Crime, Courts and Punishment in Edward's England
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five crimes classified as felonies in Edward I's England.
cards.answer: Murder / Robbery / Rape / Arson / Treason

cards.front: Name the three punishments used for petty offences (trespasses) in this period.
cards.answer: Fines / The pillory / The stocks

cards.front: Why did the Statute of Winchester require hedges and undergrowth near major roads to be cleared?
cards.answer: So that highwaymen had nowhere to hide, making roads safer for travellers.

cards.front: Why did English judges turn to trial by jury after 1215?
cards.answer: Because the Pope banned clergy from taking part in trial by ordeal, so jury trial replaced it.

title: The Social Construction of Crime and Deviance
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: Name the three dimensions across which the lesson says deviance is relative.
cards.answer: Time / Place / Situation

cards.front: Name the four sociological perspectives the lesson uses to explain the social construction of crime.
cards.answer: Functionalist / Marxist / Feminist / Interactionist

cards.front: Why did Durkheim argue that some level of crime is functional for society?
cards.answer: Punishing crime helps clarify the boundaries of acceptable behaviour and reaffirms a society's shared values.

cards.front: According to interactionists like Becker, how does an act become deviant?
cards.answer: An act is not deviant in itself; it becomes deviant only when someone with power successfully applies a label to it.

cards.front: Name the four common sample rates given in the lesson, with their uses.
cards.answer: 8,000 Hz - telephone / 22,050 Hz - radio quality / 44,100 Hz - CD audio / 48,000 Hz - professional video

cards.front: Why does a low sample rate like 8,000 Hz make audio sound tinny or robotic?
cards.answer: The measurements are too sparse to faithfully reproduce high frequencies in the original wave.

cards.front: How does increasing bit depth reduce quantisation error?
