cards.front: What four types of goods did the London docks handle that made them a key bombing target?
cards.answer: Food / Oil / Timber / Munitions

cards.front: Why did the East End suffer disproportionate damage compared to wealthier boroughs during the Blitz?
cards.answer: Dockers and factory workers had to live within walking distance of the docks and factories, so bombing the targets also destroyed the surrounding housing.

cards.front: Why couldn't water be used to fight fires started by incendiary bombs?
cards.answer: Magnesium sticks burned at roughly 2,200°C, so water could not put them out and only sand or smothering worked.

title: The Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan & Berlin Blockade
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three major consequences did the Berlin Blockade crisis produce?
cards.answer: Germany formally divided into FRG and GDR / NATO formed in April 1949 / Cold War division of Europe became permanent
items: Germany formally divided into FRG and GDR
Cold War division of Europe became permanent

cards.front: What three methods did Stalin use to install communist governments in Eastern Europe's satellite states?
cards.answer: Rigged elections / Intimidation / Presence of the Red Army

cards.front: How was Stalin able to block Western access to West Berlin in 1948?
cards.answer: West Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone, so Stalin could cut all road, rail and canal links into it.

cards.front: Why did the USA believe economic aid through the Marshall Plan would stop communism spreading?
cards.answer: The USA believed poverty and instability made countries vulnerable, since hungry, desperate people found communist ideas attractive.

title: Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide and Climate Feedbacks
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three types of proxy evidence geologists use to reconstruct CO2 levels beyond the 800,000-year ice core record.
cards.answer: Sediment cores / Carbon isotope ratios in fossil shells / Stomatal density of fossil leaves
items: Carbon isotope ratios in fossil shells

cards.front: Name the three negative feedbacks the lesson describes that remove CO2 from the atmosphere.
cards.answer: Chemical weathering of silicate rocks / Marine storage in shells and carbonate sediment / Subduction of carbon-rich ocean crust
items: Marine storage in shells and carbonate sediment

cards.front: Why does the water vapour feedback amplify warming?
cards.answer: Warming increases atmospheric water vapour, which is itself a greenhouse gas, causing further warming.

cards.front: Why did the Carboniferous coal measures help trigger glaciation?
cards.answer: Organic carbon was buried at an enormous rate, drawing down atmospheric CO2 and helping trigger the Carboniferous–Permian glaciation.

cards.front: Name the four features of every Newton's third law pair.
cards.answer: Act on two different objects / Are the same size / Act in opposite directions / Are the same type of force
items: Are the same type of force

cards.front: How does a rocket accelerate forwards even though Newton's third law forces are equal and opposite?
cards.answer: The rocket pushes gas backwards and the gas pushes the rocket forwards, but these forces act on different objects so the rocket can still move.

cards.front: Why does a skydiver reach a new, lower terminal velocity after the parachute opens?
cards.answer: Air resistance suddenly increases above weight causing deceleration, until the reduced speed makes air resistance balance weight again.

cards.front: Name the four things Native American boarding school children were forbidden to do at school.
cards.answer: Speak their native languages / Wear traditional clothing / Practise their religions / Keep their hair and given names
items: Keep their hair and given names

cards.front: Why were death rates high in Native American boarding schools?
cards.answer: Partly due to disease spreading in crowded conditions, and partly due to inadequate care.

cards.front: Why does the lesson call the 1920s boom a 'nation of contrasts' for Native Americans?
cards.answer: While Wall Street boomed, reservations remained in deep poverty, showing prosperity did not reach Native Americans.

cards.front: How did the Dawes Act's allotment system damage tribal life beyond taking land?
cards.answer: It destroyed communal economic and social structures without providing meaningful support for individual farming.

cards.front: Name the four poems given as comparison partners for Rita Dove's 'Flirtation'.
cards.answer: Robert Browning's Now / James Fenton's In Paris With You / John Keats's Bright Star / Liz Lochhead's I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine
items: James Fenton's In Paris With You
Liz Lochhead's I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says to read for when practising a comparison with an unseen poem.
cards.answer: ideas and attitudes each poem explores / tone and atmosphere each creates / effects of language and structure each poet chooses
items: ideas and attitudes each poem explores
effects of language and structure each poet chooses

cards.front: Why does Dove use enjambment across an early stanza break in 'Flirtation'?
cards.answer: It lets one idea flow into the next without a full stop, fitting a moment that is itself unresolved and still unfolding.

cards.front: How does sibilance and alliteration affect the atmosphere of 'Flirtation'?
cards.answer: They build a hushed, sensuous soundscape that matches the poem's quiet, night-time setting.

cards.front: Why does the gap between Siobhan's narration and Christopher's performance create meaning in the play?
cards.answer: Siobhan's compassionate reading of Christopher's stark, logical words reveals the emotional weight he cannot express himself.

cards.front: How did Stephens theatrically replace the novel's printed diagrams, maps and mathematical proofs?
cards.answer: He used video projections on the graph-paper set and had the ensemble physically enact Christopher's spatial reasoning.

cards.front: Why did Haddon present Christopher's perspective as the novel's lens in 2003?
cards.answer: To challenge readers to see neurotypical behaviour as strange rather than normal, against the deficit model of autism common then.

cards.front: Two heterozygous Bb parents have children. What are the three possible genotype ratios among the offspring?
Why are most human characteristics not controlled by a single gene?
cards.answer: Because most characteristics are polygenic, meaning they are controlled by several genes working together.

cards.front: Why is embryo screening during IVF considered controversial?
cards.answer: Some argue it prevents suffering by avoiding faulty alleles, while others think selecting embryos is unethical or could lead to designer babies.

cards.front: Name the three biographical connections between Dickens's own life and A Christmas Carol.
cards.answer: His father was imprisoned for debt / He worked in a factory as a child / He was driven to change conditions for the poor, especially children
items: His father was imprisoned for debt
He worked in a factory as a child
He was driven to change conditions for the poor, especially children

cards.front: Name the three Christmas traditions that became popular during the Victorian era.
cards.answer: Cards / Crackers / Christmas trees

cards.front: Why did Dickens decide to write a story instead of a political pamphlet about child labour?
cards.answer: He believed a novella could reach people's hearts and make his argument hit harder than statistics or a political essay ever could.

cards.front: How does the Ghost of Christmas Present challenge Scrooge's Malthusian view of the poor in Stave 3?
cards.answer: The Ghost throws Scrooge's own words about decreasing the 'surplus population' back at him, forcing him to confront the cruelty of his views.

cards.front: Name the five groups the lesson says are exempt from fasting during Ramadan.
cards.answer: Children / The elderly / Pregnant or nursing women / Travellers / Those who are seriously ill

cards.front: Name the five key rituals of Hajj the lesson lists as re-enacting Ibrahim's trials.
cards.answer: Wearing ihram / Circling the Ka'bah / Walking between Safa and Marwa / Standing at Arafat / Stoning the devil at Mina

cards.front: Why do pilgrims walk seven times between Safa and Marwa during Hajj?
cards.answer: It re-enacts Hajar's search for water for her son Isma'il.

cards.front: How is Khums split between recipients according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Half goes to needy descendants of the Prophet (sayyids) and half goes to the Imam or his representatives.

cards.front: What two threats does Macbeth identify about Banquo in Act 3, Scene 1?
cards.answer: Witches prophesied his descendants would be kings / He has a 'royalty of nature' and 'dauntless temper'
items: Witches prophesied his descendants would be kings
He has a 'royalty of nature' and 'dauntless temper'

cards.front: How does Macbeth manipulate the murderers he sends after Banquo?
cards.answer: He tells them Banquo is their enemy, manipulating them just as Lady Macbeth once manipulated him.

cards.front: Why does Fleance's escape devastate Macbeth even though Banquo is dead?
cards.answer: It keeps the witches' prophecy that Banquo's descendants will be kings possible, shattering his sense of security.

cards.front: Why does Lady Macbeth's attempt to cover for Macbeth at the banquet fail to restore order?
cards.answer: His public outburst at the ghost exposes his guilt in front of the nobles and destabilises his authority.

cards.front: Name the four bases found in DNA nucleotides.
cards.answer: Adenine (A) / Thymine (T) / Cytosine (C) / Guanine (G)

cards.front: Name the four potential applications of the Human Genome Project given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Identifying genes linked to inherited diseases / Developing personalised medicines / Understanding evolutionary relationships between species / Advancing forensic science
items: Identifying genes linked to inherited diseases

cards.front: Why is each gamete produced by meiosis genetically different from the others?
cards.answer: Meiosis involves shuffling of genetic material, so each gamete ends up with a different combination of alleles.

cards.front: Why does a zygote have the full set of 46 chromosomes?
cards.answer: It forms when two haploid gametes, each with 23 chromosomes, fuse together at fertilisation.

cards.front: Name the four atomic models, in order, that led to our current model of the atom.
cards.answer: Dalton's solid sphere model / Thomson's plum pudding model / Rutherford's nuclear model / Bohr's energy levels model

cards.front: State the maximum number of electrons that can occupy each of the first three electron shells.
cards.answer: First shell: 2 / Second shell: 8 / Third shell: 8

cards.front: Why does losing electrons turn an atom into a positive ion?
cards.answer: Because there are now more protons than electrons, giving the atom an overall positive charge.

cards.front: Why do elements in the same group of the periodic table react in similar ways?
cards.answer: Because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which determines how they react.

title: The end of austerity: 'never had it so good'
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three consumer goods the lesson says ordinary working people could newly afford in the 1950s.
cards.answer: Televisions / Washing machines / Cars

cards.front: Name the three types of school under the 1944 tripartite system.
cards.answer: Grammar school / Technical school / Secondary modern school

cards.front: Why did Beeching recommend closing many rural railway lines in his 1963 report?
cards.answer: Because many rural branch lines were lossmaking and it was cheaper to let cars and lorries carry passengers and freight.

cards.front: Why did critics argue the tripartite system should be replaced?
cards.answer: It locked children into a track at eleven, disadvantaged working-class pupils, and wasted talent.

title: Causes of war across the eras
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four recurring causes of war identified across British history in this lesson.
cards.answer: Religion / Politics / Nationalism / Ideology

cards.front: What three things did the Treaty of Versailles do to Germany?
cards.answer: Stripped it of territory / Imposed heavy reparations / Limited its armed forces

cards.front: How did nationalism act as both an aggressive and a defensive cause in the Second World War?
cards.answer: German nationalism drove aggressive territorial expansion, while British national identity motivated resistance to defend freedom and treaty commitments.

cards.front: Why had religion largely stopped being the main cause of large-scale war by the twentieth century?
cards.answer: Religion was displaced as the primary driver of war by nationalism and ideology, which became the dominant causes.

title: Looking at Your Hands — Martin Carter
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name the six key phrases the lesson says to learn exactly for 'Looking at Your Hands'
cards.answer: dear friend / looking at your hands / a room without a light / walking in the sun / fire / dream to change the world

cards.front: Why does Carter use participles in three successive lines of stanza three?
cards.answer: To suggest that dreaming of change and working for change are ongoing, unfinished processes rather than one-off gestures.

cards.front: How does the shift from stanza two to stanza three change the poem's sense of time?
cards.answer: It moves the poem out of memory of the past into a more immediate, ongoing present, mirroring change as continuous.

cards.front: Name the three main types of chemical bonding covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Ionic bonding / Covalent bonding / Metallic bonding

cards.front: Name the three types of covalent bond based on how many electron pairs are shared, with an example gas for each.
cards.answer: Single bond - one shared pair / Double bond - two shared pairs (e.g. O2, CO2) / Triple bond - three shared pairs (e.g. N2)
items: Double bond - two shared pairs (e.g. O2, CO2)
Triple bond - three shared pairs (e.g. N2)

cards.front: Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not, even though both are giant covalent structures made of carbon?
cards.answer: Graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon atom that can move and carry charge, but diamond uses all its electrons in bonding.

cards.front: Why does an ionic compound conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water but not when solid?
cards.answer: When molten or dissolved the ions are free to move and carry charge, but in a solid the ions are fixed in position.

cards.front: Name the four stages in the chain of scientists (hypothesis, observation, law, theory) that led from geocentric to heliocentric astronomy, in order.
cards.answer: Copernicus proposed a simpler heliocentric framework / Brahe provided precise observational data / Kepler found laws fitting the data using ellipses / Newton explained why those laws hold
items: Copernicus proposed a simpler heliocentric framework
Kepler found laws fitting the data using ellipses
Newton explained why those laws hold

cards.front: Why does a planet move faster near perihelion than near aphelion?
cards.answer: Kepler's Second Law means the Sun-planet line sweeps equal areas in equal times, so the planet must move faster when closer to the Sun.

cards.front: Why do Northern Hemisphere winters last slightly less time than summers?
cards.answer: Earth is near perihelion in January and moves faster there, so it covers that part of its orbit more quickly than the aphelion arc in summer.

cards.front: What happens to a satellite's orbit if its speed is too low or too high for its orbital radius?
cards.answer: Too slow and gravity pulls it inward so it spirals in or falls; too fast and it escapes gravity on a parabolic or hyperbolic path.

title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four core Jewish moral principles the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Tzedek (justice) / Tikkun olam (repair the world) / Tzedakah (charity) / Chesed (loving kindness)

cards.front: Give the three examples the lesson gives of chesed in British Jewish community life.
cards.answer: Weekly food bank / Visiting housebound elderly members / Clothing collections for asylum seekers

cards.front: Why does Judaism teach that Pikuach Nefesh overrides almost all the mitzvot?
cards.answer: Because every human being is created in the image of God (tzelem Elohim), reflecting the absolute sanctity of human life.

cards.front: How did Maimonides resolve the tension between free will and God's foreknowledge?
cards.answer: He taught that free will is given to every human being and that God's foreknowledge does not remove human moral responsibility.

title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
subject: english-literature-eduqas

cards.front: Why does the memory of the daffodils matter more than the original sighting in the poem?
cards.answer: Because the mind stores the moment and can replay it later to lift the speaker's spirits when tired or low.

cards.front: How does the simile 'lonely as a cloud' shape our first impression of the speaker?
cards.answer: It suggests he drifts freely and passively through the landscape, detached and alone, until the daffodils interrupt him.

cards.front: Why does Wordsworth compare the daffodils to the waves on the lake in stanza three?
cards.answer: To show the daffodils 'out-did' the sparkling waves in glee, proving they dominate the scene completely.

cards.front: Name the three anthology poems this lesson pairs with 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud' for comparison.
cards.answer: Heaney's 'Blackberry Picking' / Clarke's 'Catrin' / Blake's 'The Schoolboy'

title: British & International Cuisine and Sensory Evaluation
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: Name the five senses involved in tasting food.
cards.answer: Taste / Smell (aroma) / Sight / Touch and texture / Aroma

cards.front: Name the three types of grading test used in sensory evaluation.
cards.answer: Ranking test / Rating test / Profiling test

cards.front: Why does food taste bland when you have a blocked nose from a cold?
cards.answer: The olfactory receptor cells cannot detect the aromatic compounds in food, and smell contributes hugely to flavour.

cards.front: Why is asking a few friends 'what do you think?' not valid sensory evaluation?
cards.answer: Friends are socially biased, the sample is too small, conditions are uncontrolled, and the question is too vague for useful data.

title: Wall Street Boom and the Inequalities Beneath It
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says happened at once to cause the Wall Street boom.
cards.answer: Republican tax cuts left wealthy Americans with billions to invest / Mass production generated record corporate profits / New buying rules let small investors join in
items: Republican tax cuts left wealthy Americans with billions to invest
Mass production generated record corporate profits
New buying rules let small investors join in

cards.front: Name the five groups the lesson says the Boom left out.
cards.answer: Farmers (collapsing crop prices) / Sharecroppers (debt to landlords) / African-Americans (Jim Crow segregation) / Native Americans (reservations) / Unskilled industrial workers (wages rose far less than profits)
items: Unskilled industrial workers (wages rose far less than profits)

cards.front: Why did buying shares on the margin become dangerous if share prices fell?
cards.answer: The loan from the stockbroker still had to be repaid in full, even though the shares bought with it had lost value.

cards.front: Why did the Great Migration not bring full equality for African-Americans in northern cities?
cards.answer: Restrictive covenants enforced white-only neighbourhoods and trade unions refused black members, confining them to overcrowded areas and the lowest-paid jobs.

title: Global Food Insecurity: Surplus, Deficit & Impacts
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the six factors the lesson gives that commonly limit food production.
cards.answer: Climate / Technology / Pests and disease / Water stress / Conflict / Poverty

cards.front: Name the five impacts of food insecurity described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Famine / Undernutrition / Soil erosion / Rising prices / Social unrest

cards.front: How did rising meat consumption in China drive deforestation in Brazil's Cerrado?
cards.answer: China's meat consumption doubling required more grain imports for animal feed, raising demand for soya and causing forest clearance in Brazil's Cerrado.

cards.front: Why do conflict and food insecurity reinforce each other in the Sahel?
cards.answer: Climate-driven drought reduces pasture, pushing herders onto cropland and sparking clashes with farmers, while resulting conflict further disrupts food production.

title: Film Music: Borrowed Classics and Video Game Scores
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the three named game composers/teams from the lesson and one game each is linked with.
cards.answer: Koji Kondo – Super Mario Bros./Zelda / Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori – Halo / Jesper Kyd – Assassin's Creed
items: Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori – Halo

cards.front: Name the two main forms of adaptive/dynamic scoring described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Vertical layering / Horizontal re-sequencing

cards.front: Why do game composers write music in short repeatable loops and layers rather than one fixed cue?
cards.answer: Because the player controls pacing, so a composer never knows exactly when an event will happen or how long it lasts.

cards.front: How does the Halo theme's musical style suggest Master Chief's character?
cards.answer: Its Gregorian-style chant and ritualistic timbre over a rolling string ostinato suggest ancient duty and sacrifice, fitting the soldier-hero.

cards.front: Name the four arguments given in the lesson for wearing school uniform.
cards.answer: Cheaper than other clothes / Don't waste time choosing clothes / Gives a sense of belonging to a community / Dressed the same so less bullying
items: Gives a sense of belonging to a community
Dressed the same so less bullying

cards.front: Name the three arguments given in the lesson against wearing school uniform.
cards.answer: Not fashionable / Can't show your personality / Not comfortable especially when hot

cards.front: How does the article change after the negative expression 'il n'y a pas' in French?
cards.answer: The article changes to de/d' regardless of gender, e.g. il y a une piscine becomes il n'y a pas de piscine.

cards.front: Why do some students argue that wearing a uniform reduces bullying?
cards.answer: Because everyone is dressed the same way, so people are less likely to be bullied.

title: The Importance & Impact of Effective Communication
subject: health-social-care-ocr

cards.front: Name the four rights the lesson says are most directly protected by good communication.
cards.answer: Choice / Confidentiality / Consultation / Protection from abuse and harm

cards.front: Name the four specific impacts of poor communication given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Misunderstanding / Errors or danger to health / Distress if patronised / Failing to retain information when speech is too fast
items: Failing to retain information when speech is too fast

cards.front: Why does being well-informed make a service user safer, using the pharmacist example?
cards.answer: Explaining how to take medication, side effects and when to return means the patient understands and can manage their care safely.

cards.front: How can poor communication lead to a chain of PIES harms, using the discharge instructions example?
cards.answer: Speech too fast means instructions aren't understood, medication is taken incorrectly, health deteriorates, causing distress and then withdrawal from appointments.

cards.front: What is the typical three-step sequence of neurons when the body responds to a stimulus?
cards.answer: sensory neuron / relay neuron / motor neuron

cards.front: Why does too much excitation in the nervous system cause a seizure?
cards.answer: The nervous system depends on a balance between excitation and inhibition, and too much excitation over-stimulates neural activity, causing a seizure.

cards.front: How do SSRIs affect serotonin levels at the synapse?
cards.answer: SSRIs block the reuptake of serotonin, so it stays in the synapse longer and keeps stimulating the post-synaptic receptor.

cards.front: What is a weakness of Hebb's theory relating to when it was proposed?
cards.answer: Hebb proposed it before technology existed to observe synapses in living brains, so it was initially only theoretical.

cards.front: Name the three components involved in all homeostatic control systems.
cards.answer: Receptors / Coordination centres / Effectors

cards.front: Name the three organs the lesson gives as coordination centres.
cards.answer: Brain / Spinal cord / Pancreas

cards.front: Why does a shorter distance in the ruler drop test mean a faster reaction time?
cards.answer: The ruler falls for less time before being caught, so less distance means the person reacted quicker.

cards.front: Why is a stable internal environment essential for cells?
cards.answer: Cells need the right conditions to function properly, particularly for enzymes to work.

cards.front: Name the three common flat-roof finishes given in the lesson.
cards.answer: EPDM rubber-based sheeting / GRP fibreglass / Single-ply membranes

cards.front: Name the five cladding options given for a framed building's external skin.
cards.answer: Brick slips on backing board / Rendered blockwork / Profiled steel sheeting / Aluminium-faced insulated panels / Curtain walling

cards.front: How does a cavity wall keep a building warm and dry?
cards.answer: Two leaves of masonry with an insulated air gap between them stop rain crossing while the insulation reduces heat loss.

cards.front: Why is a ventilated void included beneath a suspended ground floor?
cards.answer: It prevents moisture building up under the floor, which would otherwise cause timber decay.

title: Pillow Talk and When Harry Met Sally: The Romantic Comedy
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why did the seductions in Pillow Talk have to be entirely verbal rather than physical?
cards.answer: The Hays Code prohibited explicit sexual content and required transgression to be punished, so desire was displaced into dialogue and split-screen choreography.

cards.front: How does the static two-shot framing in the Katz's Delicatessen scene affect representation of Sally?
cards.answer: It keeps both characters in frame together throughout, giving Sally equal screen presence rather than privileging Harry's reaction.

cards.front: Why does the camera movement change during Harry's run through Manhattan at the New Year's Eve climax?
cards.answer: The handheld urgency breaks the film's previously static visual register, signalling emotional urgency before returning to stillness for sincerity.

cards.front: What three elements does the lesson say every comparative paragraph needs, to avoid 'parallel description'?
cards.answer: A matched moment / A named difference / A contextual reason

cards.front: Name the four kinds of wartime roles the lesson says Soviet women took on.
cards.answer: Drove tractors / Ran lathes / Served as pilots in the 'Night Witches' bomber regiment / Worked as front-line snipers and medics
items: Served as pilots in the 'Night Witches' bomber regiment
Worked as front-line snipers and medics

cards.front: Name the three ethnic groups the lesson says were deported en masse during the war.
cards.answer: Volga Germans / Chechens and Ingush / Crimean Tatars

cards.front: Why did Stalin order 1,500 factories moved east of the Urals in 1941?
cards.answer: To move industry beyond the reach of German bombers so weapons production could continue safely.

cards.front: Why did the Battle of Stalingrad become the war's turning point?
cards.answer: A Soviet pincer, Operation Uranus, encircled the German Sixth Army, forcing its surrender and confirming Soviet military recovery.

cards.front: What four stages describe Antony's transformation across the play?
cards.answer: Apparent hedonism (Act 1) / Genuine grief (Act 3, Scene 1) / Devastating rhetoric (Act 3, Scene 2) / Ruthless political calculation (Act 4, Scene 1)

cards.front: Why does Caesar dismiss the threat he identifies in Cassius?
cards.answer: Because he believes himself invulnerable, so his insight into Cassius's danger is undermined by his own arrogance.

cards.front: Why is Octavius's final speech and rise to power ironic for an Elizabethan audience?
cards.answer: Because they knew Octavius became Augustus, showing the assassination destroyed the republic it was meant to save.

cards.front: How does Portia try to prove her constancy to Brutus?
cards.answer: She wounds herself to demonstrate she can bear pain and be trusted with his secret.

title: Trench Warfare on the Western Front
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three combined defensive advantages that caused the Western Front stalemate.
cards.answer: Machine guns firing 500 rounds a minute / Barbed wire belts slowing attackers / Pre-registered artillery destroying attacks
items: Machine guns firing 500 rounds a minute

cards.front: What four elements made up the BEF's 'steep learning curve' by 1918?
cards.answer: Creeping artillery barrages / Combined-arms tactics / Accurate counter-battery fire / Tanks and aircraft used together

cards.front: Why did cavalry become useless as a weapon of breakthrough on the Western Front?
cards.answer: Cavalry, the traditional arm of breakthrough, could not overcome entrenched infantry defended by machine guns and artillery.

cards.front: Why did poison gas rarely produce a decisive breakthrough on the Western Front?
cards.answer: Prevailing winds were unreliable and gas masks improved quickly, so gas caused suffering but not lasting advantage.

cards.front: Name the seven elements of non-verbal communication listed in the specification for care settings.
cards.answer: Adapting type/method to needs / Eye contact / Facial expressions / Gestures / Positioning (space, height, personal space) / Positive body language / Sense of humour

cards.front: Why must a practitioner's facial expressions be consistent with the tone of a service user's conversation?
cards.answer: Consistent, genuine expressions build trust, while mismatched ones (like smiling during distress) confuse and unsettle the service user.

cards.front: Why can overusing gestures during a conversation with a service user be a problem?
cards.answer: Exaggerated or theatrical gestures can feel condescending to the service user rather than supportive.

cards.front: The lesson identifies seven factors affecting life chances alongside social class. Name them.
cards.answer: Gender / Race and ethnicity / Sexuality / Age / Disability / Religion and belief

cards.front: How does the social model of disability explain the disability employment gap?
cards.answer: It argues inequalities come from social barriers, such as employer attitudes and inaccessible workplaces, rather than from impairment alone.

cards.front: Why are women more likely to experience poverty in old age despite living longer than men?
cards.answer: Career breaks reduce women's pension accumulation, leaving them with lower incomes than men in retirement.

cards.front: Name the six arithmetic operators covered in this lesson, with what each does.
cards.answer: + (add) / − (subtract) / * (multiply) / / (real division, decimal result) / DIV (integer division, whole quotient) / MOD (remainder after integer division)

cards.front: Name the six relational operators used for comparisons in conditions.
cards.answer: = (equal to) / ≠ (not equal to) / (greater than) / ≤ (less than or equal to) / ≥ (greater than or equal to)

cards.front: Why should you use a WHILE loop, not REPEAT...UNTIL, for reading GPS data while a car is moving?
cards.answer: The car might already be stopped when the program starts, so the loop body may never need to run, and only WHILE can skip it.

cards.front: In a nested IF checking for Pass (score ≥40) then Merit (score ≥70), why might a student wrongly output 'Merit'?
cards.answer: They check the inner condition without first confirming the outer IF's condition was also met.

cards.front: Name the five factors the lesson gives that increase thinking distance.
cards.answer: Tiredness / Alcohol / Drugs / Distractions / Higher speed

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that increase braking distance.
cards.answer: Higher speed / Wet or icy roads / Worn tyres / Worn or overheated brakes

cards.front: Why does a spacecraft drifting in deep space keep moving at the same velocity?
cards.answer: No force such as friction or air resistance acts on it to slow it down, not because a force keeps pushing it.

cards.front: Why are weight and normal contact force on a person NOT a Newton's Third Law pair?
cards.answer: Both forces act on the same object (the person), but a Third Law pair must act on two different objects.

title: Arguments Against the Existence of God
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three pieces of evidence the lesson gives that support the Big Bang theory.
cards.answer: Observed expansion of the universe / Cosmic microwave background radiation / Relative abundance of light elements

cards.front: Why does the free will defence fail to fully solve the problem of evil, according to the counter-argument in the lesson?
cards.answer: Free will explains moral evil but does not explain natural evil, since events like earthquakes and disease are not caused by human choice.

cards.front: Why does Richard Dawkins argue that evolution removes the need for a designer God?
cards.answer: Once complex life is explained through natural selection, the Design argument loses its force, so the universe is explicable through natural causes alone.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say science cannot disprove the existence of God?
cards.answer: Science only describes how the universe operates through natural processes and cannot disprove a being that exists outside or beyond the universe.

title: The Buddha, the Dhamma and the Three Marks of Existence
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Why did Siddhattha Gotama choose the Middle Way rather than luxury or extreme asceticism?
cards.answer: He found neither luxury nor extreme self-denial led to liberation, so he chose a balanced path between the two.

cards.front: Why does understanding dependent origination (paticca-samuppada) help end suffering?
cards.answer: If suffering arises from conditions, changing those conditions can end suffering, which is the logic behind Buddhist practice.

cards.front: How does the chariot analogy show that persons exist conventionally but not ultimately?
cards.answer: Removing each part leaves no chariot, showing 'chariot' and 'person' are labels for changing collections, not fixed eternal entities.

title: Family Life, Shabbat, Festivals and the Synagogue
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three stages of Jewish mourning described in the lesson.
cards.answer: shiva (seven days) / avelut (30 days then first year) / yahrzeit (annual memorial)

cards.front: Name the four synagogue features the lesson's Key Fact lists besides the ner tamid.
cards.answer: Ark (houses Torah scrolls, faces Jerusalem) / bimah (raised reading platform) / yad (Torah pointer) / menorah (seven-branched lampstand)

cards.front: Why is a glass broken at the end of a Jewish wedding ceremony?
cards.answer: It recalls the destruction of the Temple, showing that even joy is tempered by remembrance of loss.

cards.front: Why do Orthodox synagogues mark a girl's Bat Mitzvah differently from a boy's Bar Mitzvah?
cards.answer: Orthodox synagogues do not let women read the Torah, so it is marked with a talk or a ceremony outside the main service.

cards.front: What are the three ways the lesson says information can be encoded?
cards.answer: Visually (as an image) / Acoustically (as a sound or word in your head) / Semantically (by meaning)
items: Acoustically (as a sound or word in your head)

cards.front: Name the three types of long-term memory the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Episodic memory / Semantic memory / Procedural memory

cards.front: Why does surface encoding produce weaker memories than deep encoding?
cards.answer: Surface encoding just repeats information without thinking about its meaning, so it produces weaker memories that fade quickly, unlike deeper, meaningful encoding.

cards.front: Why can retrieval fail even when a memory has been stored?
cards.answer: Retrieval can fail because the right retrieval cue is missing, so without that trigger the stored memory stays out of reach.

title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What three things happen during the 'iddah waiting period after talaq?
cards.answer: Couple typically continues living under same roof / Husband continues financial support / Reconciliation is actively encouraged
items: Couple typically continues living under same roof

cards.front: What three rights did revelation at the time of Muhammad give women, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Right to inherit / Right to consent to their own marriage / Right to own property
items: Right to consent to their own marriage

cards.front: Why do mainstream scholars extend the 'azl reasoning to modern reversible contraception like the pill or condom?
cards.answer: Because the same underlying principle applies: spacing pregnancies for the health of the mother and stability of the family.

cards.front: Why is abortion treated more restrictively than reversible contraception in Islam?
cards.answer: It is not accepted as a method of contraception, and strict conditions apply after ensoulment, allowing termination only if the mother's life is at risk.

cards.front: What three false identities does the lesson identify as performances in Great Expectations?
cards.answer: Pip performing the gentleman / Estella performing the lady / Miss Havisham performing the jilted bride
items: Miss Havisham performing the jilted bride

cards.front: What three parts does the lesson say a strong analytical response needs?
cards.answer: A clear opening addressing the question / Analytical paragraphs with point, evidence, analysis, context / A brief conclusion returning to the question
items: A clear opening addressing the question
Analytical paragraphs with point, evidence, analysis, context
A brief conclusion returning to the question

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Pip is not a true gentleman despite Magwitch's money?
cards.answer: Magwitch's money bought clothes, education and manners but could not buy character, which comes only from within.

cards.front: How does guilt drive the plot of Great Expectations, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Guilt makes Pip help Magwitch escape, sends him back to the forge, and shapes his remorseful narration.

title: Historic environment: Policing in Liverpool c.1787-1900
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three specialist branches Liverpool Police developed during the Victorian era.
cards.answer: Detective branch (1844) / River police (1865) / Mounted division (1886)

cards.front: Why was Liverpool's pre-1836 watch and ward system unable to cope with the city's needs?
cards.answer: Because rapid population growth created a large, transient, impoverished dock community that overwhelmed the old elderly, poorly paid watchmen.

cards.front: Why did Liverpool's new police force suffer high staff turnover in its early years after 1836?
cards.answer: Because officer numbers and pay were low and discipline was poor, causing men to resign or be dismissed for drunkenness, bribery and other misconduct.

cards.front: Why does Dickens make the Ghost of Christmas Past's appearance ambiguous, with a child's face but white hair?
cards.answer: It reflects how memories of the past can be both clear and uncertain, joyful and painful.

cards.front: Why does Scrooge weep when he sees his lonely younger self at school?
cards.answer: It shows his childhood hope and imagination still exist within him, waiting to be reawakened.

cards.front: What three main medical uses does the lesson give for genetic testing?
cards.answer: Informing family planning / Assessing individual disease risk / Enabling personalised medicine

cards.front: How do GM mosquitoes reduce wild mosquito populations that spread malaria and dengue?
cards.answer: Male GM mosquitoes carrying a self-limiting gene mate with wild females, so offspring inheriting the gene do not survive to reproduce.

cards.front: Why did human insulin production using bacteria replace extracting insulin from animals?
cards.answer: Animal-sourced insulin sometimes caused immune reactions in patients, so genetically modified bacteria producing human insulin were used instead.

cards.front: Why can a genetic carrier of a recessive disease allele still have an affected child?
cards.answer: A carrier has one copy of the recessive allele and is unaffected, but can pass it on to a child who inherits two copies.

title: England in 1216: John's Death, Succession and William Marshal as Regent
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four castles that made up the network of loyalist-held territory in October 1216.
cards.answer: Dover / Windsor / Corfe / Nottingham

cards.front: What three immediate problems did the succession face after John's death?
cards.answer: Legal status of a child king needing a regent / Political legitimacy against Louis's rebel claim / Finance to pay mercenaries
items: Legal status of a child king needing a regent
Political legitimacy against Louis's rebel claim

cards.front: Why was nine-year-old Henry chosen as king rather than an adult Plantagenet?
cards.answer: No plausible adult Plantagenet candidate existed, so his weak personal authority but indisputable legitimacy was an asset against Louis's foreign claim.

cards.front: How did reissuing Magna Carta in November 1216 help the loyalist cause?
cards.answer: It stripped the rebels of their political programme, since Magna Carta was now the new king's own law, drawing wavering moderates back.

cards.front: Name the five planning elements that must be agreed before a recording session.
cards.answer: Time constraints/timeline / Session length / Agreed goals / Hardware/software requirements / Artist requirements

cards.front: Name the three rules of good file management given for a recording project.
cards.answer: Naming audio files clearly / Labelling folders by song/instrument/date / Naming projects with song title and date
items: Naming projects with song title and date

cards.front: How does recording each overdubbed part onto its own track help later in production?
cards.answer: It allows each part to be edited and mixed independently of the others.

cards.front: Why must audio files be kept within the project folder rather than moved or renamed outside the DAW?
cards.answer: If files are moved or renamed outside the DAW, the project loses its links and the audio goes missing.

cards.front: Name the four short quotable phrases the lesson says to learn exactly for 'Colonization in Reverse'.
cards.answer: de motherlan / bag an baggage / loyalty / tun history upside dung

cards.front: Name the three poems the lesson pairs with 'Colonization in Reverse' besides Flag and Papa-T.
cards.answer: Partition by Sujata Bhatt / Songs for the People by Frances E. W. Harper / We Lived Happily during the War by Ilya Kaminsky
items: Songs for the People by Frances E. W. Harper
We Lived Happily during the War by Ilya Kaminsky

cards.front: Why does Bennett use humour rather than anger to criticise empire in 'Colonization in Reverse'?
cards.answer: She lets the comedy of reversed history do the criticism, since Jamaican dialogue's nature is comedy and laughing stops people weeping.

cards.front: How does the structure of the poem build up to its punchline about reversed history?
cards.answer: Rhetorical pairing sets up comic opposites, exclamations in the fourth stanza speed up the excitement, building to 'tun history upside dung'.

cards.front: The lesson gives four different forms of silence in DNA. Name them.
cards.answer: Phil's silence is strategic / The group's silence is self-protective / Leah's silence is defeat / Adam's absence is imposed

cards.front: How does Kelly link Phil's leadership to Milgram's obedience experiment?
cards.answer: Phil acts like the authority figure in the white coat while the group act as willing participants, showing power flows to whoever seems most confident and competent.

cards.front: Why does the debate over whether Phil is a manipulator or a pragmatist remain unresolved in the play?
cards.answer: Phil never lies or flatters the group, but his calm authority still overrides their moral judgement, so the effect matches manipulation regardless of his intent.

cards.front: Why is a binary search much faster than a linear search on large sorted lists?
cards.answer: Because each comparison rules out half of the remaining items at once, instead of checking them one by one.

cards.front: Why might a linear search still be the sensible choice for a small or frequently changing data set?
cards.answer: Because sorting takes time and effort, and for small lists the speed gain from a binary search is too small to be worth it.

title: Sacred Texts, the Covenant and Jewish Identity
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the first five of the Ten Commandments, which Jewish tradition groups as duties to G-d.
cards.answer: I am the Lord your God / No other gods or images / Not misusing the divine name / Keeping Shabbat / Honouring parents
items: I am the Lord your God

cards.front: Name the second five of the Ten Commandments, which Jewish tradition groups as duties to other people.
cards.answer: No murder / No adultery / No theft / No false witness / No coveting

cards.front: Why is a yad used when reading from the Torah scroll?
cards.answer: So that human fingers never touch the sacred text, reflecting the Torah's highest status.

cards.front: Why does the Talmud preserve minority opinions and ongoing debate rather than settling every question?
cards.answer: Because it works on the principle that honest disagreement is itself sacred.

cards.front: Name the five types of internal force found in structural members.
cards.answer: Tension / Compression / Bending / Torsion / Buckling

cards.front: What five ports does a 5/2 directional control valve have?
cards.answer: One air inlet / Two cylinder ports / Two exhaust ports

cards.front: Why are dynamic loads often more damaging than static loads of the same size?
cards.answer: Because the rapid change in the load creates additional stress within the material.

cards.front: Why does a beam loaded in the middle have its top surface in compression and bottom surface in tension?
cards.answer: The load makes the beam curve (bend), squeezing the top surface and stretching the bottom surface.

title: The Nature of God & the Trinity
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four Christian responses to the problem of evil given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Free will / Life as a test / Part of God's plan / The Devil

cards.front: What are the three persons of the Trinity and their roles?
cards.answer: Father - creator and sustainer / Son - Jesus, became human to save humanity / Holy Spirit - God's presence active in the world
items: Son - Jesus, became human to save humanity
Holy Spirit - God's presence active in the world

cards.front: How does the free will response try to explain moral evil?
cards.answer: God gave humans freedom to choose how to live, and some choose to do wrong, causing moral evil.

cards.front: How does the story of Job explain suffering as part of Christian belief?
cards.answer: It shows God allows suffering to test whether people remain faithful, rewarding those who do.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives for why Hitler became Chancellor.
cards.answer: Failure of other chancellors (Brüning, von Papen, von Schleicher) / Von Papen's scheming and desire for revenge / Hindenburg's exhaustion with political instability / Nazis were the largest party in the Reichstag
items: Failure of other chancellors (Brüning, von Papen, von Schleicher)
Von Papen's scheming and desire for revenge
Nazis were the largest party in the Reichstag

cards.front: Why did von Schleicher's attempt to stay in power fail?
cards.answer: He tried to split the Nazis by offering Strasser a post, and Hindenburg refused his request to rule by decree, so he resigned.

cards.front: Name the four dietary changes recommended in the lesson for managing cardiovascular disease (CVD).
cards.answer: Replace saturated fats with unsaturated fats / Increase NSP intake / Reduce salt intake / Limit free sugars
items: Replace saturated fats with unsaturated fats

cards.front: Name the three haem iron food sources given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Red meat / Liver / Sardines

cards.front: Why is someone with iron deficiency anaemia advised not to drink tea or coffee with iron-rich meals?
cards.answer: Tannins in tea and coffee inhibit iron absorption, so drinking them alongside iron-rich meals reduces how much iron the body absorbs.

cards.front: Why can switching to unfortified almond milk cause someone with lactose intolerance to miss their calcium needs?
cards.answer: Unfortified almond milk contains far less calcium than cow's milk, so a fortified plant milk must be chosen to match cow's milk calcium levels.

cards.front: Name the five poems the lesson compares with Plath's 'You're'.
cards.answer: Baby Song by Thom Gunn / My First Weeks by Sharon Olds / Theme for English B by Langston Hughes / Happy Birthday Moon by Raymond Antrobus / Equilibrium by Theresa Lola
items: My First Weeks by Sharon Olds
Theme for English B by Langston Hughes
Happy Birthday Moon by Raymond Antrobus

cards.front: What five comparisons open the lesson's description of the unborn child in 'You're'?
cards.answer: clown / fish / turnip / prawn / eel

cards.front: How does 'You're' change the usual riddle poem tradition?
cards.answer: It removes the suspense of guessing by naming the subject in the title, so the poem's energy comes from tone instead.

cards.front: How does the poem's two-stanza structure show the passage of time?
cards.answer: The break falls after 'Farther off than Australia', but time passes through the dates buried in the list, not the stanza break.

cards.front: Name the four features of a manic episode in bipolar depression.
cards.answer: Abnormally elevated or irritable mood / Increased energy / Reduced need for sleep / Impulsive or risky behaviour

cards.front: Name the three parts of Beck's cognitive triad.
cards.answer: Negative view of the self / Negative view of the world / Negative view of the future

cards.front: How do SSRIs work to treat depression?
cards.answer: They block the reabsorption of serotonin after it crosses the synapse, increasing serotonin availability in the brain.

cards.front: Why is clinical depression treated as different from everyday sadness?
cards.answer: It is persistent and debilitating, significantly impairing how a person thinks, feels and functions, requiring professional assessment.

title: Program Structure, Data Types and Variables
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four primitive data types in Python.
cards.answer: Integer / Real / Boolean / Char

cards.front: Name the four techniques that make code easy to read.
cards.answer: Meaningful identifier names / Correct indentation / Useful comments / Consistent use of white space

cards.front: Why does "5" + "3" give "53" instead of 8 in Python?
cards.answer: Because input() returns a string by default, so + joins (concatenates) the strings instead of adding numbers.

cards.front: Why is a name like livesRemaining better than x or temp for a variable?
cards.answer: Meaningful identifier names make the variable's purpose clear, making code readable and maintainable, unlike vague single-letter names.

cards.front: What three main routes do UK firms use to compete internationally (other than cheap labour)?
cards.answer: Better designs / Higher quality products / Clever pricing that makes quality feel affordable
items: Clever pricing that makes quality feel affordable

cards.front: Name the four benefits of globalisation for UK businesses given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Access to larger markets / Lower costs from global supply chains / Specialisation (focus on what they do best) / Economies of scale from global volumes
items: Lower costs from global supply chains
Specialisation (focus on what they do best)
Economies of scale from global volumes

cards.front: Why did many British factories close in the 1990s and 2000s because of globalisation?
cards.answer: Asian manufacturers had much lower labour costs and undercut British factories on price, taking their business.

cards.front: How do global supply chains lower costs for UK firms?
cards.answer: Firms can buy materials like steel, circuit boards or packaging from whichever country offers the best price.

title: Energy Transforming Matter — States and Heating
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: In the school experiment to measure specific heat capacity, name the four quantities you record.
cards.answer: Current / Voltage / Time / Temperature rise

cards.front: Why does the sea help moderate coastal climates compared to inland areas?
cards.answer: Water's high specific heat capacity lets the sea absorb large amounts of energy in summer and release it slowly in winter.

cards.front: Why does density change when a substance changes state?
cards.answer: Mass stays the same during a change of state, but the volume usually changes, so density changes too.

title: What Were They Like? — Denise Levertov
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Why does Levertov use enjambment, e.g. 'There is an echo yet / of their speech which was like a song'?
cards.answer: It keeps images incomplete until the next line resolves them, echoing how the culture has been left unfinished.

cards.front: How does the structure of the poem's two halves change its pace?
cards.answer: Six hopeful questions crowd the opening, then six calm flat answers follow, shifting the pace from curiosity to horror.

cards.front: Why does the adjective 'burned' in 'laughter is bitter to the burned mouth' matter?
cards.answer: It turns a gentle image of laughter into a wound, showing how war has corrupted something once peaceful.

cards.front: Why does addressing the answers to 'Sir' create guilt in the reader?
cards.answer: It puts the reader in the questioner's position, someone who assumed a culture could be reduced to a checklist of facts.

title: Cortes and the Conquest of Mexico
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What six factors does the lesson give for what actually defeated the Aztec Empire?
cards.answer: Tlaxcalan alliance provided warriors and intelligence / Smallpox killed the Aztec leadership / Tribute system alienated subject peoples / Spanish steel, horses, crossbows and brigantines / La Malinche's linguistic and political skill / Cortes's leadership
items: Tlaxcalan alliance provided warriors and intelligence
Spanish steel, horses, crossbows and brigantines
La Malinche's linguistic and political skill

cards.front: Why did the Tlaxcalans agree to ally with Cortes against the Aztecs?
cards.answer: They were not Aztec subjects and resented Aztec tribute demands, so they saw Cortes as a way to fight Aztec rule.

cards.front: How did smallpox help the Spanish coalition win the war against the Aztecs?
cards.answer: It killed the new emperor Cuitlahuac and much of the Aztec leadership and army, buying the coalition time to regroup before the siege.

cards.front: Why did Cortes scuttle his ships at Vera Cruz?
cards.answer: To strand his men on the mainland so they could not change their minds and sail back to Cuba.

cards.front: Name the four features of ordinary estate life Kelman uses to show it is also Harri's home.
cards.answer: Neighbours who look out for each other / Children playing in stairwells / The market / The chicken shop
items: Neighbours who look out for each other

cards.front: What three stages does Jordan pass through in his gradual drift towards the Dell Farm Crew?
cards.answer: Vandalism / Stealing for the Crew / Carrying a knife

cards.front: Why does Harri's happiness on the estate make his eventual fate more devastating?
cards.answer: He is shown as a genuinely happy child who loves his flat, school and friends, not a child trapped in misery, so his danger feels crueller.

cards.front: Why does Harri's outsider status put him at risk on the estate?
cards.answer: Belonging on the estate requires knowledge of its codes that Harri, as a Ghanaian newcomer, does not yet have, leaving him exposed to danger.

cards.front: According to the novel's ending, name the two things that on their own are not enough for a good marriage.
cards.answer: Love alone (Lydia and Wickham) / Financial security alone (Charlotte and Collins)

cards.front: Why do Lydia and Wickham remain unhappily married?
cards.answer: Their passion faded quickly and Wickham's debts continue, showing marriage based on superficial attraction fails.

cards.front: How does Austen's moral vision balance class and personal merit?
cards.answer: She argues wealth and class aren't the problem, but snobbery and prejudice are; character should determine a person's worth.

cards.front: Name the four stages of Romeo's character arc given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Artificial Petrarchan lover / Genuine romantic / Impulsive killer / Tragic victim

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says every adult in the play fails the young.
cards.answer: The Friar gambles with their lives / The Nurse betrays Juliet's trust / Capulet exercises tyrannical control / The Prince's mercy creates conditions for disaster
items: The Friar gambles with their lives
The Prince's mercy creates conditions for disaster

cards.front: Why does Mercutio's death shift the play's tone from comedy to tragedy?
cards.answer: It shows that the feud destroys even someone who stands apart from both families, ending the play's earlier comic energy.

cards.front: How does the Nurse's advice to marry Paris accelerate the tragedy?
cards.answer: By betraying Juliet's trust, it forces Juliet to turn to the Friar and the sleeping potion instead.

title: Musical Forms and Devices: Hearing Structure — Binary, Ternary, Rondo, Variations, Strophic and Minuet and Trio
subject: music-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six ways the lesson says a variation might transform the theme in theme and variations.
cards.answer: Change the melody's decoration / Switch from major to minor / Alter the rhythm / Change the texture from simple to complex / Add new countermelodies / Shift the tempo and dynamics dramatically
items: Change the texture from simple to complex
Shift the tempo and dynamics dramatically

cards.front: Using the return of the opening tune, what five clues does the lesson give for identifying a structure in the exam?
cards.answer: No return signals binary / One return signals ternary or minuet and trio / Catchy tune repeated between episodes signals rondo / Same tune with same words-pattern signals strophic / Tune reappearing transformed signals theme and variations
items: One return signals ternary or minuet and trio
Catchy tune repeated between episodes signals rondo
Same tune with same words-pattern signals strophic
Tune reappearing transformed signals theme and variations

cards.front: Why does binary form give a forward-moving, one-directional feel?
cards.answer: Because section A modulates away from the home key and section B returns to the home key, but never brings back the opening melody, so it goes somewhere and stays there.

cards.front: Why does the return of A in ternary form feel like a satisfying homecoming?
cards.answer: Because section B usually changes key, mood, texture or instrumentation, so the return of the original opening material feels like coming home after contrast.

title: Comparing Films: Genre, Narrative, Context Side by Side
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three matched moments this unit uses for its comparative film pairs.
cards.answer: Genre conflict announced (Pillow Talk / When Harry Met Sally) / Rebellion staged for the spectator (Rebel Without a Cause / Ferris Bueller) / Alien first encountered (Invasion of the Body Snatchers / E.T.)
items: Genre conflict announced (Pillow Talk / When Harry Met Sally)
Rebellion staged for the spectator (Rebel Without a Cause / Ferris Bueller)
Alien first encountered (Invasion of the Body Snatchers / E.T.)

cards.front: Why is 'Invasion of the Body Snatchers has dark lighting but E.T. has warm lighting' too weak to count as a named difference?
cards.answer: It names a tonal contrast but not a specific technique, sequence or effect that could be analysed.

cards.front: Why did Nicholas Ray frame teen rebellion in Rebel Without a Cause as existentially costly?
cards.answer: The 1950s moral-panic context drove him to use CinemaScope dwarfing and dissonant scoring to show rebellion as costly.

cards.front: How should contextual knowledge be used in a comparative essay, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It should support the comparison within paragraphs, not be listed separately at the start or end.

cards.front: Name the four risk controls the lesson gives for fieldwork hazards.
cards.answer: Work in pairs / Keep below the high-water mark / Wear hi-vis / Carry a mobile phone

cards.front: Name the five fieldwork hazards listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Slippery rocks / Traffic / Cold water / Deep mud / Lone working in unfamiliar towns

cards.front: Why do most fieldwork enquiries combine both primary and secondary data?
cards.answer: Primary data answers your specific question, while secondary data provides the wider context that supports it.

cards.front: Why do pebbles become smaller and rounder further downstream?
cards.answer: This can be explained by attrition, where pebbles wear down as they collide with each other while being transported.

cards.front: Name the four key lifestyle risk factors for non-communicable disease given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Smoking / Poor diet high in saturated fat and sugar / Excessive alcohol consumption / Physical inactivity
items: Poor diet high in saturated fat and sugar

cards.front: What three types of treatment for cardiovascular disease does the lesson describe?
cards.answer: Lifestyle changes / Medical treatments / Surgical treatments

cards.front: How does angina occur?
cards.answer: A coronary artery becomes severely narrowed so the heart muscle receives insufficient oxygen during exertion, causing chest pain.

cards.front: How does a stroke occur?
cards.answer: The blood supply to the brain is interrupted by a clot or a burst blood vessel.

cards.front: Name the four key considerations the lesson gives for choosing a distribution platform.
cards.answer: Target audience / File formats the platform accepts / Cost to creator and audience / Accessibility

cards.front: Name the four accessibility features the lesson gives for digital distribution.
cards.answer: Subtitles or closed captions / Alt text for images / Colour contrast standards / Transcripts for audio content

cards.front: Why is app store distribution best suited to interactive products rather than videos or podcasts?
cards.answer: Because app stores are designed to distribute software-based interactive products like games and apps, not passive media.

cards.front: Why does an app often need two separate versions when distributed through app stores?
cards.answer: Because the app must be built to meet the different technical requirements of iOS and Android platforms.

cards.front: Why were Jews permitted to live in Venice despite being confined to a ghetto?
cards.answer: Their financial services were essential to Venice's economy, so the city depended on them despite hostility towards them.

cards.front: Why does Shylock's anger at Antonio go beyond just the economic rivalry?
cards.answer: Antonio has personally abused Shylock, calling him 'misbeliever, cut-throat dog' and spitting on his gaberdine.

title: Elizabeth's accession in 1558: a difficult inheritance
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four overlapping problems Elizabeth inherited in 1558.
cards.answer: Questions about her legitimacy and gender / Crown debt of around £300,000 / Deep religious division / Hostile France with troops in Scotland
items: Questions about her legitimacy and gender
Hostile France with troops in Scotland

cards.front: Name the four religious changes England went through in the twenty-five years before Elizabeth's accession.
cards.answer: Catholic under Henry VIII / Protestant under Edward VI from 1547 / Firmly Catholic again under Mary I from 1553 / Protestant again under Elizabeth
items: Firmly Catholic again under Mary I from 1553

cards.front: Why was marriage seen as the obvious solution to Elizabeth's succession problem, yet still dangerous?
cards.answer: Marriage could produce an heir and a male partner, but a foreign Catholic prince risked making England a satellite of Spain or France, while an English noble would unbalance the court.

cards.front: Why did the loss of Calais in 1558 matter so much to Elizabeth's new reign?
cards.answer: It proved France could push England back militarily and showed the war Mary I fought for Philip II had cost England territory for nothing.

title: Trophic Levels, Pyramids & the Carbon Cycle
subject: science-edexcel

cards.front: What three processes does the lesson give for how energy is lost between trophic levels?
cards.answer: Used for movement and other life processes / Lost as heat during respiration / Not all parts eaten (e.g. bones, shells, roots)
items: Used for movement and other life processes
Not all parts eaten (e.g. bones, shells, roots)

cards.front: What four processes make up the water cycle?
cards.answer: Evaporation / Transpiration / Condensation / Precipitation

cards.front: Why are pyramids of biomass almost always a true pyramid shape, unlike pyramids of numbers?
cards.answer: Because they show total mass, and biomass decreases at each trophic level as energy is lost, regardless of organism number or size.

cards.front: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels?
cards.answer: So much energy is lost at each level that by the fifth level too little remains to support a viable top predator population.

title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Why is the live wire dangerous even when an appliance switch is off?
cards.answer: Because the live wire is still at 230 V relative to earth, so touching it makes current flow through your body.

cards.front: Why must a switch always be connected in the live wire rather than the neutral wire?
cards.answer: So that when the switch is off, no current can reach the appliance at all.

cards.front: Name the three wires found in a UK three-pin plug.
cards.answer: Live wire / Neutral wire / Earth wire

title: Ohm's Law, Power and Energy in Circuits
subject: electronics-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four equations the lesson says run every circuit.
cards.answer: V = IR / P = IV / P = I²R / P = V²/R

cards.front: Why should you use P = V²/R instead of first finding the current when given voltage and resistance?
cards.answer: It avoids computing an unnecessary intermediate quantity, saving time and arithmetic.

cards.front: Why does a current of 50 A through a 470 Ω resistor in a battery circuit signal a calculation error?
cards.answer: It is physically unrealistic for such a circuit, showing the answer doesn't make sense.

cards.front: Name the four main stages of genetic engineering described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cut out the desired gene / Open the vector / Insert the gene into the vector / Transfer to host organism
items: Insert the gene into the vector

cards.front: How does the same restriction enzyme allow a gene to be inserted into a vector?
cards.answer: Using the same enzyme on both the gene and vector creates complementary sticky ends that pair up together.

cards.front: Why does inbreeding increase health problems in animals like flat-faced dog breeds?
cards.answer: Breeding only similar organisms narrows the gene pool, reducing genetic variation and causing health problems such as breathing difficulties.

cards.front: Why has genetically modified bacteria replaced pig or cow insulin for treating diabetes?
cards.answer: GM bacteria produce human insulin cheaply and reliably, avoiding the allergic reactions sometimes caused by animal insulin.

cards.front: Name the five types of employment contract used in the hospitality industry.
cards.answer: Casual / Full-time permanent (or temporary) / Part-time (or temporary) / Seasonal / Zero-hours

cards.front: Name the four main factors that affect supply and demand for staff in hospitality.
cards.answer: Peak times / Large events / Seasonal times / Location of the provision

cards.front: Why can offering lots of flexible contracts reduce service quality for an employer?
cards.answer: High staff turnover on flexible contracts means a lack of committed staff, which can reduce service quality.

cards.front: Why can flexible working boost an employee's income during busy periods?
cards.answer: Tips and overtime pay during busy periods can increase the amount an employee earns.

cards.front: Name the three UK/government approaches used to reduce regional differences in the UK.
cards.answer: Enterprise Zones / Transport investment (HS2, Crossrail, Northern Powerhouse Rail) / Regional development funding
items: Transport investment (HS2, Crossrail, Northern Powerhouse Rail)

cards.front: Name the three ways migration has reshaped the UK's population geography over the past 50 years.
cards.answer: Internal migration / International migration / Changing immigration policy

cards.front: Why did the UK become one of the world's largest destinations for foreign direct investment (FDI) from the 1980s onwards?
cards.answer: UK policy from the 1980s favoured free trade, privatisation of nationalised industries, and openness to foreign investment.

cards.front: Why do more people live in London than in the Scottish Highlands, according to population density figures?
cards.answer: London is part of the job-rich urban core with over 5,500 people per km2, while the Highlands are rural periphery with under 10.

cards.front: Name the four key forms the lesson identifies in the cluster.
cards.answer: Sonnet (Shelley) / Ballad (Wordsworth) / Free verse (Mundair, Robinson, Berry, Femi) / Apostrophe (Brontë)

cards.front: Name the four language techniques the lesson covers across the cluster.
cards.answer: Imagery / Metaphor and simile / Tone / Sound

cards.front: How does enjambment function in Liz Berry's 'Homing'?
cards.answer: It lets years of lost words spill out across line-ends, reflecting an overflow of emotion.

cards.front: How does Shelley's volta change the direction of 'England in 1819'?
cards.answer: It turns the poem's despair into revolutionary hope, pivoting the argument's tone.

cards.front: Name the four holy books (Kutub) that Muslims believe Allah revealed, in the order given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Qur'an / Torah (Tawrat) / Psalms (Zabur) / Gospel (Injil) / Scrolls of Abraham (Suhuf Ibrahim)

cards.front: Why does the story of Ibrahim being commanded to sacrifice Isma'il matter in Islam?
cards.answer: It showed Ibrahim's total faith and willingness to obey Allah completely, so Allah provided a ram instead.

cards.front: How does the Imamate show a key difference between Sunni and Shi'a Islam?
cards.answer: Shi'a Muslims believe leadership passed to divinely appointed, infallible Imams from Muhammad's family, while Sunnis followed elected caliphs and scholarly consensus.

cards.front: Why do Muslims treat the physical Qur'an with such great respect?
cards.answer: Because it is believed to be the literal, unchanged word of Allah, so it is kept on the highest shelf and hands are washed before reading it.

title: Notting Hill: Caribbean Culture and Self-Help
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five areas of London life where Caribbean migrants faced a colour bar in the 1950s.
cards.answer: Housing / Pubs / Dance halls / Banks / Many shops

cards.front: Name the four foods typically served at Caribbean cafes in Notting Hill in the 1950s.
cards.answer: Rice and peas / Curry goat / Jerk chicken / Saltfish fritters

cards.front: Why did the Metropolitan Police repeatedly raid shebeens in Notting Hill?
cards.answer: Shebeens were unlicensed, so police used drugs and licensing raids as a recurring pretext to enter Caribbean-run premises.

cards.front: Why did the order of payouts in a pardner scheme vary between members?
cards.answer: The order was negotiated by need, so a family needing a child's fare took an early payout while a house-deposit saver waited later.

cards.front: Why does rising onto your toes (plantar flexion) lift the whole body with relatively little calf muscle effort?
cards.answer: It is a second class lever with the effort arm longer than the load arm, giving mechanical advantage greater than 1.

cards.front: Why does a bicep curl need much more muscular effort than the weight being lifted?
cards.answer: The effort arm (elbow to biceps insertion) is much shorter than the load arm (elbow to hand), giving mechanical advantage less than 1.

cards.front: How do you work out which class a lever belongs to when labelling a diagram?
cards.answer: Find the joint (fulcrum) first, then the load, then where the muscle pulls (effort); whichever sits in the middle decides the class.

title: Karzai, Bonn and the Long Resurgence of the Taliban
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four overlapping problems the lesson says Karzai inherited after Bonn.
cards.answer: Warlordism / The opium economy / Corruption / Karzai's own lack of legitimacy

cards.front: Name the three regional warlords the US and Britain relied on outside Kabul, with their provinces.
cards.answer: Abdul Rashid Dostum in the north / Ismail Khan in Herat / Gul Agha Sherzai in Kandahar
items: Abdul Rashid Dostum in the north

cards.front: How did opium money help fuel the Taliban's resurgence?
cards.answer: Opium money paid for fighters, weapons and motorcycles, funding both warlords and the returning insurgency.

cards.front: How did the Karzai government's failures in the south help the Taliban regain support?
cards.answer: It failed to deliver justice, jobs or honest policing, so the Taliban filled the gap with shadow courts that paid villagers more reliably than the state.

cards.front: Why does Rosa use a quieter, warmer tone with Caitlin, who has an eating disorder?
cards.answer: A warm, quiet tone signals a safe space and avoids clinical formality that could feel dehumanising.

cards.front: Why can 'adapting communication' mean using more technical language, not simpler language?
cards.answer: Adaptation means meeting the person where they are, so oversimplifying can feel condescending to someone with a professional background.

cards.front: Give the number of shared electron pairs and molecule example for the three types of covalent bond described (single, double, triple).
cards.answer: Single bond - one shared pair (H2) / Double bond - two shared pairs (O=O) / Triple bond - three shared pairs (N≡N)

cards.front: Why do ions formed by ionic bonding end up stable?
cards.answer: Both ions gain full outer electron shells after electrons are transferred, making them stable.

cards.front: How does metallic bonding hold a metal structure together?
cards.answer: Delocalised electrons form a moving sea that creates strong electrostatic attraction to the positive metal ions.

cards.front: Why does Bennett link Hector's teaching method to his own coping mechanism?
cards.answer: Hector cannot express his feelings directly, so he channels his loneliness and failure through poetry and quotation instead.

cards.front: Why is Mrs Lintott's description of herself as 'confided in by all parties' significant?
cards.answer: It is an understatement showing she sees everyone's secrets but remains invisible and powerless in the male-dominated drama.

cards.front: Why does the Headmaster call Hector's abuse 'the odd grope'?
cards.answer: The euphemism minimises sexual abuse into a trivial inconvenience, showing he processes everything through institutional self-interest.

cards.front: Why is Posner's declaration 'I'm a Jew...I'm fucked' so powerful?
cards.answer: Its short, simple sentences gain power because they contrast with his usual hesitant, quiet register.

title: Themes across the period: continuity and change
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the seven major turning points the lesson identifies across 1929-2000.
cards.answer: 1933 New Deal / 1941 Pearl Harbor / 1954 Brown v Board / 1963-68 civil rights legislation / 1974 Nixon resignation / 1980-81 Reagan revolution / 1991 Gulf War/USSR dissolved

cards.front: Name the four political scandals the lesson describes as recurring features of the period.
cards.answer: Teapot Dome scandal / Watergate / Iran-Contra affair / Clinton's impeachment

cards.front: Why did Watergate mark a significant turning point in US politics?
cards.answer: It resulted in the first presidential resignation, testing whether constitutional checks could limit presidential power.

cards.front: How did the Second World War change American unemployment compared to the New Deal?
cards.answer: It delivered full employment the New Deal had not achieved, with unemployment below 2 per cent by 1944.

cards.front: Name the three men in Much Ado whose roles the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Don Pedro - the prince and leader / Claudio - his young, impressionable officer / Benedick - the witty, independent soldier
items: Don Pedro - the prince and leader

cards.front: How does Claudio's courtship of Hero follow the Elizabethan arranged marriage model?
cards.answer: He notices her beauty, asks Don Pedro to negotiate on his behalf, and the match is arranged through her father with little private conversation.

cards.front: Why is Don John's villainy considered unusual compared to characters like Shylock or Iago?
cards.answer: His villainy is notably unmotivated, driven only by a generalised desire to cause misery rather than a specific personal grievance.

cards.front: Name the three parallel trench lines that made up a mature trench system on the Western Front.
cards.answer: Front trench / Support trench / Reserve trench

cards.front: Name the five military technologies the lesson says transformed warfare on the Western Front.
cards.answer: Machine gun / Artillery / Poison gas / Tanks / Aircraft

cards.front: Why was it almost impossible to break through the front line on the Western Front?
cards.answer: Defensive firepower from machine guns and artillery hugely favoured defenders over attackers.

cards.front: Why did soldiers carry out the dawn 'stand-to' each day in the trenches?
