items: Desire for spiritual reward through the indulgence
Genuine devotion to the Holy Sepulchre

cards.front: Name the three social and secular motives the lesson gives for individuals joining the Crusades.
cards.answer: Prospect of land and wealth for younger sons / Desire for adventure and glory / Loyalty to lords who had taken the cross
items: Prospect of land and wealth for younger sons
Loyalty to lords who had taken the cross

cards.front: How did the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert create the crisis that led to the appeal for Western help?
cards.answer: It opened Anatolia to Seljuk settlement, cutting off Byzantine military recruitment and leaving Constantinople directly threatened.

cards.front: Why was Urban II's offer of a plenary indulgence at Clermont so compelling to medieval Christians?
cards.answer: It promised full remission of sins, removing the fear of penance or suffering in purgatory that medieval Christians dreaded most.

title: Settler Pressure: Railroads, Cattle, Gold and the Indigenous Plains
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three settler pressures (plus the underlying fourth) that combined to destroy Plains Indigenous life.
cards.answer: Railroads splitting herds and carrying hunters / Cattle industry taking grass and water / Gold strikes breaking treaty lines / US government reservation policy
items: Railroads splitting herds and carrying hunters
Cattle industry taking grass and water

cards.front: Name the three gold strikes that broke treaty lines with Plains nations.
cards.answer: Pike's Peak strike 1858-59 / Bozeman Trail goldfields 1862-63 / Black Hills strike 1874

cards.front: How did the completion of the First Transcontinental Railroad in 1869 damage the bison population?
cards.answer: It physically split the great buffalo herd into northern and southern populations that never recombined, making them easier to wipe out separately.

cards.front: Why did hunger from bison loss lead to a repeating cycle of conflict for reservation nations?
cards.answer: Hunger pushed nations off reservations to hunt on cattle land, that hunting caused conflict with ranchers and the army, and conflict justified further restrictions.

cards.front: Name the four things the UK Equality Act 2010 relates to that are mentioned in the lesson (grounds, protected characteristics count, and race/religion examples)
cards.answer: Makes discrimination illegal / Based on nine protected characteristics / Race is one protected characteristic / Religion is one protected characteristic

cards.front: Why did Dr B.R. Ambedkar convert to Buddhism in 1956?
cards.answer: He argued Buddhism rejected caste and offered genuine equality, unlike Hinduism's caste structures which he was critical of.

cards.front: How does the langar in a gurdwara express Sikh teaching on equality?
cards.answer: It is open to all regardless of background, practically showing that no one is superior to another in God's eyes.

cards.front: Why did Martin Luther King argue that unjust laws need not be obeyed?
cards.answer: Because unjust laws degrade human personality and contradict natural and divine law, as he argued in his Letter from Birmingham Jail.

title: Investigating the Ripper: detection, sources and the press
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three detective methods police used in the 1888 Whitechapel investigation.
cards.answer: Door-to-door witness interviews / Police sketches from descriptions / Photographing bodies at crime scenes

cards.front: Name the four things missing from detective work in 1888 that would exist later.
cards.answer: Fingerprinting / Blood-typing / Central database of suspects / Anything beyond a paper record system
items: Anything beyond a paper record system

cards.front: Why did door-to-door interviews in Whitechapel often fail to produce reliable evidence?
cards.answer: Residents in the lodging houses moved frequently, so witnesses could become untraceable within a week.

cards.front: Why is a Punch cartoon useful for a historian studying public attitudes to the police in 1888, despite being biased?
cards.answer: Its bias reflects public mood, which is exactly what an enquiry into attitudes towards the Met needs to capture.

cards.front: Name the four sampling methods this lesson covers.
cards.answer: Random sampling / Opportunity sampling / Self-selected (volunteer) sampling / Snowball sampling

cards.front: Name the three key ethical issues in psychological research identified in this lesson.
cards.answer: Lack of informed consent / Protection of participants / Deception

cards.front: Why can a large sample still be unrepresentative of its target population?
cards.answer: Because representativeness depends on how the sample is drawn, not just its size, so a large sample can still be biased if drawn badly.

cards.front: Why can random sampling still end up producing a biased sample?
cards.answer: Because a complete list of the population is often hard to obtain, and people who decline to take part can leave the final sample biased.

title: The Eternal Self, Samsara and Karma
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Why does maya keep the atman trapped in samsara, according to Shankara's rope-and-snake illustration?
cards.answer: Maya makes people mistake the material world for ultimate reality, causing attachment that binds the atman to the cycle of rebirth.

cards.front: Why does the Vishishtadvaita school teach that moksha is loving union with a personal God rather than realising identity with Brahman?
cards.answer: Vishishtadvaita holds the individual self is real and distinct from Brahman, so liberation means union, not dissolving into one reality.

cards.front: Name the three points on the play's spectrum of servitude, from willing to forced.
cards.answer: Ferdinand's willing service through love / Ariel's conditional service for promised freedom / Caliban's forced labour under threat of cramps
items: Ariel's conditional service for promised freedom
Caliban's forced labour under threat of cramps

cards.front: What five-step pattern should each paragraph of a Shakespeare essay follow?
cards.answer: Point / Quotation / Word-level analysis / Contextual link / Effect on audience

cards.front: Why does Prospero's own freedom depend on him forgiving his enemies?
cards.answer: He is trapped on the island by his need for revenge, so he can only leave once he lets go of resentment and chooses mercy.

cards.front: How does Caliban's characterisation challenge Prospero's claim that Caliban is a 'born devil'?
cards.answer: Caliban shows sensitive poetry and genuine love for the island, while privileged Antonio proves equally treacherous, questioning whether nature fixes character.

cards.front: Name the four poems the lesson pairs with 'Morning Song' for comparison.
cards.answer: Poem for My Love / The Perseverance / Lullaby / Looking at Your Hands

cards.front: Name the three sound images that frame 'Morning Song' from start to finish.
cards.answer: the baby's bald cry / silent listening (a far sea moves in my ear) / the baby's babbled notes
items: silent listening (a far sea moves in my ear)

cards.front: Why does Plath write 'Morning Song' in free verse using short three-line stanzas?
cards.answer: The loose, unpredictable form suits a speaker still working out her feelings in real time, not making a settled statement.

cards.front: How does the enjambment in 'Morning Song' reflect the speaker's night-time experience?
cards.answer: Frequent enjambment carries sentences across lines and stanzas, mimicking the broken, disturbed rhythm of a night spent listening for a cry.

title: Energetics, Reaction Profiles and Bond Energies
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Why does using a polystyrene cup give a more accurate reading when measuring energy changes in reactions?
cards.answer: It acts as an insulator, reducing heat loss to the surroundings.

cards.front: Why is the reaction between hydrogen and chlorine to form HCl exothermic?
cards.answer: More energy is released making the H–Cl bonds than is needed to break the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds.

title: Cells and Control: Mitosis, Stem Cells and the Brain
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four main phases of mitosis, in order.
cards.answer: Prophase / Metaphase / Anaphase / Telophase and cytokinesis

cards.front: Name the three therapeutic uses of stem cells given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Replacing damaged nerve cells in spinal injuries / Producing insulin-secreting cells for diabetes / Growing replacement tissue for burns patients
items: Replacing damaged nerve cells in spinal injuries
Growing replacement tissue for burns patients

cards.front: Why can plant cells differentiate throughout life while most animal cells cannot?
cards.answer: Plants have meristem tissue at root and shoot tips that keeps dividing and differentiating, unlike most animal cells which lose this ability after embryonic development.

cards.front: Why is the outer layer of the cerebral hemispheres deeply folded?
cards.answer: The folding of the cerebral cortex increases its surface area.

cards.front: How does Dickens use pathetic fallacy to show Scrooge's inner coldness in Stave 1?
cards.answer: The cold 'froze his old features, nipped his pointed nose, shrivelled his cheek', showing his inner coldness physically shapes his appearance.

cards.front: Why does Dickens have Fred act as a foil to Scrooge in Stave 1?
cards.answer: Fred's warmth and generosity, despite being poorer, make Scrooge's coldness and greed appear even more obvious by contrast.

cards.front: Why does Marley say his own chain was forged 'link by link, and yard by yard'?
cards.answer: The repetition emphasises the chain was built gradually over years through many small, selfish choices rather than one act.

cards.front: Why is it significant that Scrooge asks charity collectors 'Are there no prisons? And the Union workhouses?'?
cards.answer: It shows Scrooge believes prisons and workhouses are already sufficient provision for the poor, excusing him from helping further.

title: Wave Behaviour and the Wave Equation
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four measurable properties used to describe all waves.
cards.answer: Amplitude / Wavelength / Frequency / Period

cards.front: Why does sound travel faster in solids than in gases?
cards.answer: Particles in solids are more tightly bonded, so they can transmit compressions more rapidly than in gases.

cards.front: Why does a mechanical wave like sound need a medium to travel, unlike light?
cards.answer: Sound relies on particles vibrating to pass energy on, while electromagnetic waves like light need no particles to travel.

cards.front: How is the period of a wave related to its frequency?
cards.answer: Period and frequency are reciprocals, so period equals one divided by frequency.

cards.front: Name the four steps the lesson gives that Hitler used methodically to consolidate power from 1933-1934.
cards.answer: Reichstag Fire pretext to arrest communists / Enabling Act for legal dictatorship / Gleichschaltung dismantled independent institutions / Night of the Long Knives eliminated rivals and secured army loyalty
items: Reichstag Fire pretext to arrest communists
Night of the Long Knives eliminated rivals and secured army loyalty

cards.front: How did Hitler achieve the two-thirds majority needed to pass the Enabling Act?
cards.answer: He had communist deputies arrested and surrounded the Reichstag with SA stormtroopers to intimidate the remaining members.

cards.front: Why did the Night of the Long Knives secure the loyalty of the German army to Hitler?
cards.answer: It destroyed the SA's threat to the army and showed Hitler would protect the generals' institutional interests, so they accepted it.

cards.front: Why did Hitler pursue a 'legal revolution' rather than relying on raw force to seize power?
cards.answer: The failed Munich Putsch of 1923 taught him force alone was insufficient, so he used constitutional legitimacy to neutralise conservative resistance.

cards.front: Name the six general symptoms of food poisoning the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Nausea (feeling sick) / Vomiting / Diarrhoea / Stomach cramps and abdominal pain / Fever (raised body temperature) / Headache and general malaise

cards.front: Name the four groups at greater risk of serious complications from food poisoning.
cards.answer: Young children / Elderly people / Pregnant women / People with weakened immune systems

cards.front: Why do staphylococcus aureus symptoms appear much faster than campylobacter symptoms?
cards.answer: Staph toxin is already present in the food and acts quickly, whereas campylobacter bacteria must first establish infection in the gut, which takes longer.

cards.front: Why can raw vegetables carry e-coli even though they never touch meat?
cards.answer: They can be grown in soil that has been fertilised with animal manure, transferring the bacteria onto the vegetables.

cards.front: Name the four conditions needed for a tropical storm to form.
cards.answer: Ocean at least 26.5°C to about 50m depth / Unstable air that rises easily / Enough Coriolis effect (away from the equator) / Similar wind speeds from sea level upwards
items: Ocean at least 26.5°C to about 50m depth
Enough Coriolis effect (away from the equator)
Similar wind speeds from sea level upwards

cards.front: Name the three changes most scientists agree climate change will cause to tropical storms.
cards.answer: More intense storms (higher winds, more rain) / Storms reaching higher latitudes / Longer storm seasons
items: More intense storms (higher winds, more rain)

cards.front: How does the release of latent heat make a tropical storm intensify?
cards.answer: Condensing water vapour releases latent heat, warming surrounding air so it rises faster and draws in more warm air from the sea.

cards.front: Why must wind speed be similar from sea level upwards for a tropical storm to develop?
cards.answer: If wind speeds differ with height, the storm gets sheared apart before it can organise.

title: The Great Fire of London 1666: Disaster and Reconstruction
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things that made the 1666 Pudding Lane fire different from London's usual small fires.
cards.answer: A long dry summer had baked the timber houses / An unusually strong easterly wind / Densely packed riverside warehouses full of flammable goods
items: A long dry summer had baked the timber houses
Densely packed riverside warehouses full of flammable goods

cards.front: Besides houses and parish churches, name the buildings and structures destroyed in the Great Fire.
cards.answer: The Royal Exchange / The Guildhall / The Custom House / Three of the City's gates / Old St Paul's Cathedral

cards.front: Why did the fire spread so quickly once it took hold of a street of houses?
cards.answer: Houses were timber-framed, jettied with overhanging upper storeys, and packed tightly together (often thatched), so once one caught, the whole row went up.

cards.front: Why was Charles II and James's personal firefighting during the Great Fire politically important?
cards.answer: Their visible leadership fighting the fire won cheering crowds, unlike the royal absence during the Plague of the previous year.

title: Change & Inequality in a UK City
subject: geography-edexcel-a

cards.front: The lesson gives four pull factors drawing migrants to Birmingham. What are they?
cards.answer: Established family networks (chain migration) / Demand for low-cost labour in services/food processing / English-language universities / HS2 construction jobs
items: Demand for low-cost labour in services/food processing

cards.front: Name the four strands of Birmingham City Council's strategy to improve quality of life.
cards.answer: Affordable housing (e.g. Perry Barr) / Clean Air Zone / Education investment (school meals, apprenticeships) / Recycling, bus routes and housing retrofits
items: Recycling, bus routes and housing retrofits

cards.front: Why did Birmingham's Central Business District lose retail trade in the 1980s and 1990s?
cards.answer: Out-of-town centres like Merry Hill and Touchwood opened, drawing shoppers away with free parking and one-stop convenience.

cards.front: Why do inner-city wards like Sparkbrook have a much younger age structure than outer suburbs like Sutton Coldfield?
cards.answer: Post-war Commonwealth migration and chain migration brought younger working-age families into inner wards, while outer suburbs remain older.

cards.front: What are the five stages of the tragic five-act structure in Macbeth?
cards.answer: exposition (Act 1) / rising action (Act 2) / climax (Act 3, banquet) / falling action (Act 4) / catastrophe (Act 5)

cards.front: How does Shakespeare use metre to show Macbeth's psychological state in Act 5?
cards.answer: Macbeth increasingly breaks from regular iambic pentameter, signalling his psychological fragmentation.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare have the witches speak in trochaic tetrameter instead of iambic pentameter?
cards.answer: Its stressed-unstressed, four-beat rhythm sounds jagged and unnatural, like a chant or spell, unlike noble characters' controlled speech.

cards.front: How does the changing attitude to blood between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: Macbeth sees blood as permanent while Lady Macbeth thinks it easily washed away, but their positions reverse by Act 5.

title: Anglo-Saxon crime, communities and the wergild
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three categories of crime Anglo-Saxon law recognised, with an example of each.
cards.answer: Against the person (assault, murder) / Against property (theft, arson) / Against authority (treason, tax evasion)

cards.front: What corporal punishments does the lesson mention for Anglo-Saxon crimes not settled by wergild?
cards.answer: Branding / Flogging / Cutting off a hand for repeated theft
items: Cutting off a hand for repeated theft

cards.front: How did collective responsibility within a tithing force communities to police themselves?
cards.answer: If one member committed a crime, the rest of the tithing had to bring him to court or pay a heavy fine themselves.

cards.front: Why was the hue and cry not a uniform, nationwide police system?
cards.answer: Its success depended entirely on the local community's alertness and willingness to chase, so it worked better in tight villages than busy towns.

title: Government Intervention to Correct Market Failure
subject: economics-aqa

cards.front: Name the four main tools of government intervention used to correct market failure.
cards.answer: Indirect taxes / Subsidies / Regulation and legislation / Direct state provision

cards.front: What three reasons does the lesson give for why government intervention can lead to government failure?
cards.answer: Lack of information about the true cost / Unintended consequences of the policy / Regulatory capture by industry
items: Lack of information about the true cost

cards.front: How does regulation such as food labelling laws correct information failure?
cards.answer: It forces producers to disclose ingredients and nutrition, removing the information gap so consumers can choose based on true costs and benefits.

cards.front: Why can higher fuel taxes cause an unintended consequence for low-income rural families?
cards.answer: They have no alternative to driving, so the tax raises their costs without changing behaviour, making transport less affordable.

cards.front: Name the three Rivers siblings who live at Moor House and take Jane in.
cards.answer: St John / Diana / Mary

cards.front: Why does St John suppress his feelings for Rosamond Oliver?
cards.answer: He believes she is not 'suitable' for missionary work, so he denies his love for religious duty.

cards.front: How does Moor House differ from both Thornfield and Lowood for Jane?
cards.answer: It offers a middle ground, giving Jane equal female friendship and financial independence, unlike Thornfield's passion or Lowood's coldness.

cards.front: Why is St John's self-denial described as a form of violence rather than virtue?
cards.answer: He suppresses his own and Jane's natural feelings for religious duty, harming both their true natures.

title: Material Choices and Life Cycle Assessment
subject: science-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the four main categories of engineering materials.
cards.answer: Ceramics / Polymers / Composites / Metals

cards.front: List the four end-of-life outcomes for a product, from lowest to highest environmental impact.
cards.answer: Reuse / Recycling / Incineration with energy recovery / Landfill

cards.front: How does steel-reinforced concrete get strength in both tension and compression?
cards.answer: The steel gives it strength in tension while the concrete gives it strength in compression.

cards.front: Why might a paper bag have a bigger environmental impact than a plastic bag despite being biodegradable?
cards.answer: Making one paper bag uses more water and energy and produces more greenhouse gases during manufacture than a plastic bag.

cards.front: What four areas does a plasterer work on, according to the lesson's key fact?
cards.answer: External walls (render) / Internal walls and ceilings (wet plaster skim) / Internal stud walls (dry lining) / Heritage features (ornamental plasterwork)
items: Internal walls and ceilings (wet plaster skim)

cards.front: What five systems does a plumber install, according to the lesson's key fact?
cards.answer: Cold water / Hot water / Sanitation / Boilers / Central heating

cards.front: Why is it important for a floor layer to level the subfloor before laying tiles or carpet?
cards.answer: Because uneven subfloors cause tiles to crack and carpet to ripple over time.

cards.front: Why must electricians strictly follow safety regulations when working?
cards.answer: Because electrical faults are a leading cause of serious injury and fire on construction sites.

title: Jewish Practices: Worship, Shabbat and Kashrut
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What are the four Shabbat rituals the lesson gives for ushering in and observing the day?
cards.answer: Lighting two candles / Reciting Kiddush over wine / Sharing a double portion of challah bread / Synagogue attendance, family meals and rest
items: Sharing a double portion of challah bread
Synagogue attendance, family meals and rest

cards.front: What two rules does the lesson give for an animal's meat to be kosher?
cards.answer: Chews the cud and has split hooves / Slaughtered by shechitah with blood fully drained
items: Chews the cud and has split hooves
Slaughtered by shechitah with blood fully drained

cards.front: Why do observant Jewish households keep two separate sets of crockery and cutlery?
cards.answer: Because the Torah repeats three times that a kid must not be boiled in its mother's milk, requiring complete separation of meat and dairy.

cards.front: Why do Orthodox Jews observe kashrut according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because it is commanded by God in the Torah, needs no further justification, and sanctifies eating as an act of obedience.

cards.front: Name the six key criticisms of the family given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Social isolation of the nuclear family / Unrealistic idealisation concealing conflict and abuse / Loss of traditional functions / Dysfunctional families / Marital breakdown and empty shell marriages / Inferior status and role of women through unpaid domestic labour
items: Social isolation of the nuclear family
Unrealistic idealisation concealing conflict and abuse
Marital breakdown and empty shell marriages
Inferior status and role of women through unpaid domestic labour

cards.front: What three forms can marital breakdown take, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Legal divorce / Long-term separation / Empty shell marriage

cards.front: Why do feminist sociologists say the private nature of the family makes domestic violence hard for the state to tackle?
cards.answer: The family concentrates male authority over women and children in a private space that is difficult for the state to monitor or regulate.

cards.front: How did women entering paid employment affect their overall workload, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Women acquired a 'double shift' of paid work plus domestic labour, since housework did not adjust proportionately, so equality was not gained.

cards.front: Name the three sporting examples the lesson gives for movement in the transverse plane.
cards.answer: 360° ice spin / Discus thrower spinning before release / Figure skater pulling in arms to spin faster
items: Figure skater pulling in arms to spin faster

cards.front: List the three joint movements and the plane each occurs in, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Flexion/extension - sagittal plane / Abduction/adduction - frontal plane / Rotation at shoulder or hip - transverse plane
items: Rotation at shoulder or hip - transverse plane

cards.front: Why is running classed as sagittal-plane movement but a cartwheel is not?
cards.answer: Running only swings limbs forwards and backwards (sagittal plane), whereas a cartwheel moves the body sideways in the frontal plane.

cards.front: How is the shoulder movement during the pull phase of front crawl classified by joint action, plane and axis?
cards.answer: The shoulder moves backwards past the hip, which is extension, occurring in the sagittal plane around the transverse axis.

title: The Nature of God, Shekhinah and the Messiah
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four features of the Messianic age described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Ingathering of exiled Jews to Israel / Rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem / Universal recognition of the Almighty / The end of war and injustice
items: Ingathering of exiled Jews to Israel
Rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem
The end of war and injustice

cards.front: Why does Orthodox Judaism see the Shekhinah's absence today as significant?
cards.answer: Because the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE, and its absence marks divine distance until the Messiah comes and rebuilds it.

cards.front: Why do Jews believe the messianic age has not yet arrived?
cards.answer: Because the world still contains war, injustice and suffering, showing the promised era of peace has not been fulfilled.

cards.front: Name the four musical elements the lesson says composers manipulate to build character and tension.
cards.answer: Instrumentation / Dynamics / Harmony / Rhythm

cards.front: How does the lesson say you can tell if a piece of music in a film is source music (diegetic)?
cards.answer: If a character on screen could plausibly hear the music and react to it, such as dancing or turning down a radio.

cards.front: Why does dark, low brass instrumentation suggest menace to an audience?
cards.answer: Low brass and dark string writing are chosen by composers because that timbre suggests menace or power.

cards.front: How do John Williams's Imperial March and Force theme use contrasting musical elements to represent opposite characters?
cards.answer: The Imperial March uses minor key, heavy brass and loud dynamics for menace, while the Force theme uses major key, strings and a rising melody for heroism.

cards.front: Name the five reasons the lesson gives for why businesses identify and satisfy customer needs.
cards.answer: Provide a product customers will actually buy / Increase sales / Select the correct marketing mix / Avoid costly mistakes / Stay competitive against rivals
items: Provide a product customers will actually buy

cards.front: Why does identifying customer needs first reduce risk for a business?
cards.answer: Because it means the business only spends money developing and making products that the market actually wants to buy.

cards.front: Why does combining several segmentation bases, like Boots does, help a business more than using just one base?
cards.answer: Combining bases gives a much sharper picture of the customer than one base alone, sharpening the marketing mix for each group.

cards.front: Name the four key skills the lesson identifies for health and social care professionals.
cards.answer: Problem solving / Observation / Dealing with difficult situations / Organisation

cards.front: Name the four attributes the lesson identifies for health and social care professionals.
cards.answer: Empathy / Patience / Trustworthiness / Honesty

cards.front: How does the 'Communication' value in the 6 Cs benefit care?
cards.answer: Involving individuals and carers in decisions and truly listening builds trust, ensures they feel heard, and reduces misunderstandings.

cards.front: Why does honesty matter when caring for individuals?
cards.answer: Being truthful about condition, treatment options and prognosis builds trust and enables informed decision-making.

cards.front: Name the four common mistakes to avoid in the anthology comparison essay.
cards.answer: Writing about one poem then the other / Retelling the poem / Identifying techniques without explaining effect / Bolting on context as a separate paragraph
items: Writing about one poem then the other
Bolting on context as a separate paragraph

cards.front: Name the four weeks of the suggested poetry revision plan and their focus.
cards.answer: Week 1: re-read all poems and summarise / Week 2: practise pairings with comparison plans / Week 3: memorise quotations with flashcards / Week 4: write full timed essays
items: Week 1: re-read all poems and summarise
Week 2: practise pairings with comparison plans

cards.front: Why should you avoid retelling the poem in a comparison essay?
cards.answer: Because you should analyse what the poem means and how the poet achieves it, not describe what happens.

cards.front: Why is embedding context within analysis better than writing a separate context paragraph?
cards.answer: A separate context paragraph is 'bolting on' context, which the lesson identifies as a mistake; it should be embedded within the analysis instead.

title: Factors Affecting Achievement: Class, Ethnicity and Gender
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four material deprivation examples the lesson gives for working-class pupils.
cards.answer: overcrowded housing with no quiet study space / unable to afford uniform or equipment / needing a part-time job that reduces study time / parents unable to pay for private tuition
items: overcrowded housing with no quiet study space
unable to afford uniform or equipment
needing a part-time job that reduces study time
parents unable to pay for private tuition

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for girls' improved performance since the 1990s.
cards.answer: changes in female aspirations / growth in service-sector employment for women / curriculum reforms moving away from male-dominated content
items: growth in service-sector employment for women
curriculum reforms moving away from male-dominated content

cards.front: How does the crisis of masculinity explain some working-class boys' underachievement?
cards.answer: De-industrialisation removed traditional male manual jobs, so some boys saw academic effort as incompatible with masculine identity, associating it with femininity and passivity.

cards.front: How do Willis's 'lads' reproduce their class position through counter-school culture?
cards.answer: Working-class boys develop anti-school peer cultures that value manual labour over academic work, limiting their own qualifications despite appearing to choose freely.

cards.front: Name the four benefits of EU membership for trade that the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Tariff-free access to a huge pool of customers and suppliers / Common product standards mean no redesign needed for each country / Free movement of workers helps fill skill shortages / Foreign direct investment flows more easily across borders
items: Tariff-free access to a huge pool of customers and suppliers
Common product standards mean no redesign needed for each country
Free movement of workers helps fill skill shortages
Foreign direct investment flows more easily across borders

cards.front: Name the three trade-offs the lesson gives that come with EU membership.
cards.answer: Accepting common rules and regulations / Contributing to the EU budget / Allowing free movement of people

cards.front: Why does a 20% tariff on imported steel help UK steel producers compete?
cards.answer: It raises the price of foreign steel, making it more expensive than domestic steel so domestic producers can compete more easily.

cards.front: Why did British exporters face higher costs when the UK left the EU?
cards.answer: New customs checks and paperwork were introduced that had not previously existed, increasing costs for businesses trading with the EU.

cards.front: Name the two everyday uses of static electricity given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Electrostatic paint sprayers / Laser printers and photocopiers

cards.front: Name the two safety measures the lesson gives for dealing with static hazards.
cards.answer: Earthing fuel tankers before transfer / Wearing anti-static wristbands

cards.front: Why do fuel tankers get earthed before fuel is transferred?
cards.answer: Earthing connects the tanker to the ground via a conducting cable, letting built-up static charge flow away safely instead of sparking near flammable vapour.

cards.front: Why does a jumper crackle when you pull it over your head?
cards.answer: Different fabrics rub together, transferring electrons and creating regions of opposite charge, which attract and cause rapid discharge as small sparks and sounds.

cards.front: Name the seven areas of the catering kitchen workflow in order.
cards.answer: Delivery area / Staffing area / Wash area / Storage area / Preparation and cooking area / Serving area (the pass) / Washing/cleaning area

cards.front: In a restaurant, what six steps does the front of house workflow follow, from arrival to leaving?
cards.answer: Customer arrives at reception / Shown to their table / Receives menus / Places an order / Served food and drinks / Pays the bill

cards.front: Why do front of house and back of house staff have different dress codes?
cards.answer: Front of house wear smart uniforms to look professional and reflect the brand, while back of house wear protective clothing for hygiene and safety.

cards.front: Why can well-kept documentation help a business during an Environmental Health Officer inspection?
cards.answer: Records demonstrate legal compliance, which can help the business avoid prosecution or closure.

cards.front: Name the three things a strong conclusion must do in a 16-mark essay.
cards.answer: States your position clearly / Gives the most important single reason for that position / Explains why the counter-argument is ultimately less convincing
items: Gives the most important single reason for that position
Explains why the counter-argument is ultimately less convincing

cards.front: Name the four StudyVault rubric bands for extended responses.
cards.answer: Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging

cards.front: Why is simply covering 'both sides' of an argument not enough to reach the top band?
cards.answer: Because every piece of evidence must be weighed to build an argument, not just balanced description.

cards.front: Why was the Wall Street Crash judged more decisive than Nazi propaganda in the worked example on Hitler's rise?
cards.answer: It transformed the Nazi Party from under 3% of the vote in 1928 into the largest Reichstag party by 1932.

cards.front: Name the three Assessment Objectives (AOs) tested in the modern prose exam section.
cards.answer: AO1 - personal response with textual references / AO2 - analysis of language, form and structure / AO3 - context
items: AO1 - personal response with textual references
AO2 - analysis of language, form and structure

cards.front: Name the three types of workplaces families like the Kumars came to Britain to fill labour shortages in.
cards.answer: Factories / Foundries / The NHS

cards.front: Why did Powell's speech embolden characters like Sam Lowbridge to voice racism openly?
cards.answer: Syal shows how political rhetoric like Powell's speech gave ordinary people permission to be cruel and express racism openly.

cards.front: Why does the novel show immigrant families being blamed for the Black Country's economic decline?
cards.answer: Deindustrialisation caused hardship and loss of identity for white working-class communities, so this frustration was redirected onto immigrants as a scapegoat rather than the economic system.

cards.front: Name the five paragraphs of the recommended structure for a comparison essay.
cards.answer: Introduction with argument / Comparative point paragraph 2 / Comparative point paragraph 3 / Comparative point paragraph 4 / Conclusion on which poem is more effective
items: Conclusion on which poem is more effective

cards.front: List the four common mistakes the lesson warns against in comparison essays.
cards.answer: Writing about each poem separately / Superficial comparison / Context dump / Choosing a weak comparison poem

cards.front: Why does the integrated structure usually score higher than the block structure?
cards.answer: It weaves between both poems within each paragraph, making the comparison explicit rather than describing each poem separately.

cards.front: Why is context best woven into analysis rather than given its own paragraph?
cards.answer: Because context must serve the argument by explaining why poets took different approaches, not sit as unconnected biography or history.

cards.front: Name the three barriers to Jane and Rochester's union that the Thornfield fire destroys.
cards.answer: Legal barrier: Bertha dies / Social barrier: Rochester's power reduced by blindness / Class barrier: Jane's inheritance gives financial independence
items: Social barrier: Rochester's power reduced by blindness
Class barrier: Jane's inheritance gives financial independence

cards.front: Why does Rochester partially regain his sight at the end of the novel?
cards.answer: Some critics read it as a reward for his repentance, having learned humility, honesty and dependence after the fire.

title: The Collapse of the League: Manchuria and Abyssinia
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Why did Britain and France refuse to impose oil sanctions on Italy during the Abyssinian Crisis?
cards.answer: They were unwilling to push Mussolini into an alliance with Hitler, so excluded the materials Italy needed most.

cards.front: Why couldn't the League impose economic sanctions on Japan over Manchuria?
cards.answer: Japan was a permanent Council member, and the unanimity rule meant Japan would have had to vote to sanction itself.

cards.front: What three foreign policy moves did Hitler make within a year of the Abyssinian collapse?
cards.answer: Remilitarised the Rhineland (March 1936) / Formed the Rome-Berlin Axis (October 1936) / Concluded the League was a paper tiger
items: Concluded the League was a paper tiger

cards.front: Why does the narrator knock the curate unconscious in Book 2?
cards.answer: Because the curate's hysterical screaming risked alerting the Martians and endangering both their lives.

cards.front: How does the artilleryman's vision of survivors show eugenic thinking?
cards.answer: He plans to select only "able-bodied, clean-minded men" to survive, echoing eugenic ideas popular in Victorian Britain.

cards.front: Name five key facts the lesson gives about Britain's condition by 1918.
cards.answer: Women over 30 could vote / House of Lords lost its absolute veto / Old age pensions and national insurance existed / Britain had fought its most costly war / Boer War had exposed cracks in imperial confidence
items: House of Lords lost its absolute veto
Old age pensions and national insurance existed
Britain had fought its most costly war
Boer War had exposed cracks in imperial confidence

cards.front: How did the Second Boer War change British attitudes to empire?
cards.answer: Concentration camps, humiliating early defeats and the cost in lives and money exposed the gap between imperial rhetoric and reality, sparking a pro-Boer movement.

cards.front: Why was the Representation of the People Act 1918 only a 'partial victory' for women?
cards.answer: The age of 30 and property requirement excluded most young working-class women, precisely those who had contributed most in munitions factories.

cards.front: Why did the Parliament Act 1911 matter for what governments could achieve?
cards.answer: It confirmed the elected Commons was supreme over the hereditary Lords, allowing controversial legislation to pass without a permanent Lords veto.

cards.front: Name the four assessment objectives tested in this unit's exam.
cards.answer: Recall and understanding (knowledge) / Explanation and analysis of second-order concepts / Source analysis (source evaluation) / Interpretation analysis (interpretation evaluation)
items: Explanation and analysis of second-order concepts

cards.front: What are the four paragraphs in the essay planning framework for extended essays?
cards.answer: Paragraph 1: agree with the interpretation, strongest evidence / Paragraph 2: disagree or complicate it / Paragraph 3: second point or developed counter-argument (16-mark only) / Conclusion: substantiated overall judgement
items: Paragraph 1: agree with the interpretation, strongest evidence
Paragraph 3: second point or developed counter-argument (16-mark only)

cards.front: Why must a source utility answer specify the enquiry it is judging usefulness for?
cards.answer: Because usefulness depends on purpose — a source can be highly useful for one enquiry, like Spanish justifications, but poor for another, like Aztec perspectives.

cards.front: Why might Bernal Díaz's eyewitness account still be limited as evidence?
cards.answer: He wrote it about fifty years after the events, so his memory may have been affected by the subsequent history of the conquest.

cards.front: Name the four examples the lesson gives of when lossless compression must be used.
cards.answer: Text files / Medical images / Software executables / Master audio files

cards.front: Name the three examples the lesson gives of when lossy compression is appropriate.
cards.answer: Streaming video / Social media images / Downloaded music

cards.front: Why does a '500 GB' hard drive show only about 465 GB of usable space once formatted?
cards.answer: Manufacturers count storage in base-10 (1000 bytes per KB) but formatting reports it in base-2 (1024), making the same capacity look smaller.

cards.front: Why can MP3 compression remove certain audio frequencies without a noticeable loss in quality?
cards.answer: It removes frequencies below the threshold of human hearing and reduces detail in frequencies masked by louder sounds.

cards.front: Name the three poems in the Relationships collection that explore parental protection between parents and children.
cards.answer: A Child to his Sick Grandfather / Nettles / My Father Would Not Show Us
items: A Child to his Sick Grandfather
My Father Would Not Show Us

cards.front: Give the three different methods of parental protection shown in Baillie's, Scannell's and de Kok's poems.
cards.answer: Child protects grandfather through innocent kindness / Father protects son through physical action against nettles / Father protects children by hiding his vulnerability
items: Child protects grandfather through innocent kindness
Father protects son through physical action against nettles
Father protects children by hiding his vulnerability

cards.front: How does the military semantic field in 'Nettles' reflect Scannell's own experience?
cards.answer: As a WWII veteran, Scannell turns the domestic scene into a battle, showing the nettles as an enemy that always returns despite being fought off.

cards.front: Why does the father's silence in 'My Father Would Not Show Us' create distance instead of protecting his children?
cards.answer: He believes hiding his pain shields them, but this denies them the chance to comfort him, causing emotional absence rather than safety.

cards.front: Name the five stages of Scrooge's arc that a strong essay tracks across the novella.
cards.answer: Hard-hearted capitalist (Stave 1) / Grieving the lost boy (Stave 2) / Awakened to others (Stave 3) / Confronted with death (Stave 4) / Active giver (Stave 5)

cards.front: Name the four briefly sketched women in the novella and the narrow moral slot each occupies.
cards.answer: Fan, the loving sister / Mrs Cratchit, the loyal wife / The laundress at Old Joe's, a cynical thief / The charwoman, a cynical thief
items: The laundress at Old Joe's, a cynical thief

cards.front: Why does Dickens have Tiny Tim's 'God bless us, every one!' line recycled as the novella's final line?
cards.answer: It links Tim directly to the novella's moral message, making him the test of Scrooge's humanity.

cards.front: Why is Fred's role important even though essays often overlook him?
cards.answer: He opens and closes Scrooge's transformation, stating Dickens's thesis on Christmas and modelling forgiveness by inviting Scrooge despite refusal.

title: Eschatology and the Problem of Evil
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What are the three divergences the lesson gives between Christian and Islamic beliefs about life after death?
cards.answer: Purgatory exists in Christianity but not in Islam / Salvation through Christ vs submission to Allah / Christian Trinity vision vs no Trinity in Islam
items: Purgatory exists in Christianity but not in Islam
Salvation through Christ vs submission to Allah
Christian Trinity vision vs no Trinity in Islam

cards.front: What are the three ways Christians interpret the nature of hell?
cards.answer: Eternal conscious punishment / Final annihilation of the unrepentant / Universal salvation of all people

cards.front: Why does the free will defence fail to fully explain natural evil?
cards.answer: It explains only moral evil caused by human choices, not suffering from natural events like earthquakes or disease.

cards.front: Why did Irenaeus believe evil and suffering are necessary for humans?
cards.answer: Humans were created immature, in God's image but not yet his likeness, and need suffering to grow morally and spiritually.

title: Piaget's Theory and the Three Mountains Task
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name Piaget's four stages of cognitive development in order.
cards.answer: Sensorimotor (0-2 years) / Pre-operational (2-7 years) / Concrete operational (7-11 years) / Formal operational (11 years onwards)

cards.front: Why does the cycle of assimilation, accommodation and equilibrium drive cognitive development forward?
cards.answer: When new information doesn't fit an existing schema, the imbalance motivates the child to accommodate their thinking until balance is restored.

cards.front: How did Hughes' research suggest Piaget's Three Mountains Task underestimated young children?
cards.answer: Hughes used a more relatable task, hiding a boy doll from policeman dolls, and found even three- and four-year-olds could show less egocentrism.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says human activities reduce biodiversity.
cards.answer: Deforestation (habitat loss) / Pollution / Over-exploitation of species / Introduction of invasive non-native species

cards.front: Name the three assumptions needed for a valid capture-recapture population estimate.
cards.answer: Marked individuals mix randomly back into the population / Marking doesn't affect survival, behaviour or attractiveness to predators / Population is closed (no births, deaths, immigration or emigration)
items: Marked individuals mix randomly back into the population
Marking doesn't affect survival, behaviour or attractiveness to predators
Population is closed (no births, deaths, immigration or emigration)

cards.front: Why does placing quadrats at random coordinates avoid bias?
cards.answer: The researcher has no influence over where quadrats land, so every area has an equal chance of being sampled.

cards.front: How does an algal bloom cause aquatic plants below the surface to die?
cards.answer: Dense algae covering the water surface block sunlight from reaching the plants below, so they cannot photosynthesise and die.

title: Themes: continuity and change in twentieth-century Britain
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four second-order concepts the lesson identifies as most important for analysing this period.
cards.answer: Change / Continuity / Cause / Consequence

cards.front: Name the five periods the lesson divides the British economy into between 1919 and 1990.
cards.answer: Pre-Depression boom (1919-29) / Depression and uneven recovery (1929-39) / Wartime command economy (1939-45) / Mixed economy and managed capitalism (1945-79) / Free-market restructuring (1979-90)

cards.front: Why was the Means Test introduced in Britain in the 1930s?
cards.answer: It was an emergency response to government bankruptcy caused by the Depression, not a deliberately designed welfare policy.

cards.front: Why do historians debate whether the Falklands War (1982) restored Britain's global standing?
cards.answer: Britain kept a UN Security Council seat and nuclear weapons, but its economy and armed forces were far smaller relative to superpowers than in 1919.

cards.front: Name the nine wasting processes covered in the specification.
cards.answer: Sawing / Shearing (guillotine/tin snips only) / Drilling / Filing / Threading (tap and die only) / Routing / Laser cutting / Turning / Milling

cards.front: Name the four questions to ask when choosing the right joining method.
cards.answer: Are both parts metal? / Must the joint be permanent? / Is only one side accessible? / How heavy is the load?

cards.front: How does brazing join metal parts without melting the metal itself?
cards.answer: A filler metal is melted with a gas torch and flows by capillary action between the closely fitting parts, solidifying without melting the base metals.

cards.front: Why can't a shape with deep vertical walls be vacuum formed?
cards.answer: Without a draft angle the heated sheet would lock onto the mould's vertical walls and could not be released after cooling.

cards.front: Name the four main sources of finance a growing business can use.
cards.answer: Retained profit / Selling unused assets / Loan capital / Share capital

cards.front: Name the three benefits the lesson gives of a business becoming larger.
cards.answer: Spreads fixed costs across more units / Negotiates better prices with suppliers / Gains a stronger foothold in its market
items: Spreads fixed costs across more units
Gains a stronger foothold in its market

cards.front: Why is internal growth generally lower risk than external growth?
cards.answer: It builds on what the business already knows and avoids the problems of integrating a different company's culture, systems and staff.

cards.front: Why can mergers and takeovers create economies of scale?
cards.answer: The combined business can buy supplies in larger quantities, reducing the cost per unit.

cards.front: Name the three techniques the lesson says advertisers use with schema-consistent cues to shape memory
cards.answer: Familiar cues linked to viewer's schema / Repeating key images or messages / Avoiding information overload
items: Familiar cues linked to viewer's schema

cards.front: How can a leading question distort a witness's memory of a car crash?
cards.answer: Asking how fast the car was going when it 'smashed' rather than 'what happened' can make them recall the crash as more severe than it was.

cards.front: Name the five main sampling methods covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Random sampling / Systematic sampling / Stratified sampling / Quota sampling / Snowball sampling

cards.front: Name the three practical issues in sociological research given as a Key Fact.
cards.answer: Time / Cost / Access

cards.front: Why is quota sampling not considered fully representative?
cards.answer: Because researchers select participants non-randomly until set quotas for each group are filled.

cards.front: Why can a gatekeeper's restrictions create sampling bias in a study of school exclusion?
cards.answer: A head teacher who only allows access to 'well-behaved' pupils excludes the most relevant participants for the study.

title: Balance of Payments & the Distribution of Income
subject: economics-aqa

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why a current account deficit can arise.
cards.answer: High consumer spending increases imports / Domestic firms are relatively uncompetitive / A strong exchange rate makes exports dearer and imports cheaper
items: A strong exchange rate makes exports dearer and imports cheaper

cards.front: Name the four causes of income and wealth inequality given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Education and skills / Inheritance / Market power of firms / Structural changes like deindustrialisation

cards.front: Why can a persistent current account deficit weaken the value of the pound?
cards.answer: Because more pounds are sold to buy foreign currency to pay for imports, reducing the pound's value.

cards.front: Why might very high income inequality reduce overall consumer spending in the economy?
cards.answer: Because people at the top of the income scale tend to save most of their income rather than spend it, holding back demand.

cards.front: Name the five common mistakes the lesson warns against in 19th-century novel responses.
cards.answer: Only writing about the extract / Retelling the story instead of analysing / Bolting on context without linking it / Spending time on presentation / Not using literary terminology
items: Retelling the story instead of analysing
Bolting on context without linking it

cards.front: What four steps does the lesson recommend planning for each of your 3–4 key points about an extract?
cards.answer: What technique or language Dickens uses / What it reveals about character/theme / How it connects to the wider novella / Relevant context
items: What technique or language Dickens uses
How it connects to the wider novella

cards.front: Why should context be integrated rather than bolted on in an extract response?
cards.answer: Because bolted-on context just lists facts, while integrated context links context to Dickens's method and purpose, showing deeper analysis.

cards.front: Why does the lesson suggest treating the extract as a 'window' rather than a 'destination'?
cards.answer: Because the extract gives close textual evidence, but the argument should range across the whole novella to make wider connections.

title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the seven renewable energy resources the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Solar / Wind / Hydroelectric / Tidal / Geothermal / Wave power / Biofuels

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson gives to increase a device's efficiency.
cards.answer: Reducing friction (lubrication, streamlining) / Using thermal insulation / Improving design to minimise energy dissipation
items: Improving design to minimise energy dissipation

cards.front: Why does double glazing reduce energy transfer from a house?
cards.answer: A layer of gas between two panes of glass reduces energy transfer by conduction and convection.

cards.front: Why does a house with thicker walls lose thermal energy more slowly?
cards.answer: The thicker the walls of a house, the slower the rate of thermal energy transfer through them.

cards.front: What three reasons does Mr Collins give, in order, for wanting to marry?
cards.answer: A clergyman should set an example / It will add to his happiness / Lady Catherine de Bourgh advised it
items: A clergyman should set an example
It will add to his happiness
Lady Catherine de Bourgh advised it

cards.front: Why did Darcy separate Jane and Bingley, according to his letter?
cards.answer: He genuinely believed Jane did not return Bingley's feelings.

cards.front: Why can Elizabeth afford to refuse Collins while Charlotte cannot?
cards.answer: Elizabeth has youth, beauty, and confidence in her own judgement, advantages Charlotte lacks.

title: Health, Disease and the Immune System
subject: science-ocr

cards.front: Name the five non-specific (first line) defences the body uses to stop pathogens entering.
cards.answer: Skin (physical barrier) / Mucus in nose and airways / Cilia sweeping mucus out / Stomach acid (pH 1-2) / Tears and saliva (lysozyme enzyme)

cards.front: Name the five risk factors the lesson gives for non-communicable diseases.
cards.answer: Smoking / Poor diet / Lack of exercise / Obesity / Excessive alcohol consumption

cards.front: How do viruses destroy the cells they infect?
cards.answer: Viruses invade host cells, take over the cell's machinery to replicate, then burst out (lysis), destroying the cell.

cards.front: How does the inflammatory response help fight infection after pathogens breach the skin?
cards.answer: Damaged cells release chemicals causing blood vessels to dilate and become more permeable, increasing blood flow so white blood cells reach the infection site faster.

cards.front: Name the three natural archives (besides ice cores) the lesson gives for reconstructing past climate.
cards.answer: Tree rings / Pollen records in lake sediments / Historical sources like harvest records and paintings
items: Historical sources like harvest records and paintings

cards.front: Name the three main sources of human greenhouse gas emissions the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Burning fossil fuels / Agriculture (cattle, rice, fertilisers) / Tropical deforestation

cards.front: Why did the 1815 Tambora eruption cause a 'year without a summer' in 1816?
cards.answer: Ash and sulphur particles from the eruption reflected sunlight back into space, cooling the planet.

cards.front: Why does tropical deforestation add to climate change in two ways?
cards.answer: Burning trees releases stored carbon, and fewer trees reduce the planet's ability to absorb future emissions.

title: Jojo Rabbit: Narrative and Comic Distance
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why does the editing of Jojo Rabbit treat the imaginary Hitler scenes the same as real scenes?
cards.answer: It uses the same shot-reverse-shot cutting rhythm, forcing the spectator to inhabit Jojo's credulous view while recognising its absurdity.

cards.front: Why does the public-square hanging sequence use the same warm palette and framing as the comic scenes?
cards.answer: The formal continuity shows fascist violence was embedded in ordinary community life and did not look different to those inside it.

cards.front: Why is the camera in Jojo Rabbit mounted at Jojo's eye level, roughly waist-height on an adult?
cards.answer: This low angle makes the imaginary Adolf slightly over-large and distorted, sustaining a child's-eye view where the adult world seems imposing and absurd.

title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three examples of formulations given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Medicines / Paints / Alloys

cards.front: How can you test whether a substance is pure using its melting point?
cards.answer: Compare its melting point to the known value; a sharp match shows purity, while melting over a range shows a mixture.

cards.front: How can running a known substance alongside an unknown one on the same chromatogram identify it?
cards.answer: If a spot in the unknown lines up exactly with a spot from the known substance, they are the same compound.

title: Part 1: Meshak, Otis & the Coram Men
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three seeds Part 1 plants that echo through the rest of the novel.
cards.answer: Alexander's passion for music (reappears via Aaron's singing) / Meshak's secret act of defiance (has consequences decades later) / Otis's crimes (eventually exposed)
items: Alexander's passion for music (reappears via Aaron's singing)
Meshak's secret act of defiance (has consequences decades later)

cards.front: How does Otis maintain total control over Meshak?
cards.answer: He controls Meshak through fear and intimidation, exploiting his son's disability and dependence on him.

cards.front: Why is Alexander and Melissa's baby given to Otis in the first place?
cards.answer: When Melissa's family discover the pregnancy, they hand the baby to Otis, unwittingly condemning the child to death.

cards.front: Name the five reasons the lesson gives for why Christians go on pilgrimage.
cards.answer: To deepen their faith / To seek healing / To do penance / To experience God in a special way / To feel connection to events in Christian history
items: To experience God in a special way
To feel connection to events in Christian history

cards.front: What three things does the site of Lourdes include, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Grotto of Massabielle / Basilica of the Immaculate Conception / Hospitals and care facilities for the sick
items: Hospitals and care facilities for the sick

cards.front: Why is Easter considered the most important festival in the Christian calendar?
cards.answer: It celebrates the resurrection, the foundation of Christian faith, without which Christians believe there would be no hope of salvation or eternal life.

cards.front: Why are some Christians concerned about how Christmas is celebrated today?
cards.answer: They believe the religious meaning has been overshadowed by commercialism, and focus should be on Jesus's birth, not shopping and materialism.

cards.front: Name the four conditions the lesson says homeostasis controls in the body.
cards.answer: Body temperature / Blood glucose concentration / Water levels / Ion levels

cards.front: Name the six steps in the pathway of a normal nervous response, from stimulus to response.
cards.answer: Stimulus / Receptor / Sensory neurone / Relay neurone (in CNS) / Motor neurone / Effector

cards.front: Which brain region is responsible for consciousness, thought and memory?
cards.answer: The cerebral cortex.

cards.front: In the ruler drop test, what does a shorter drop distance tell you about reaction time?
cards.answer: A shorter distance means the person reacted faster.

title: There's a Certain Slant of Light
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Why does Dickinson's poem never explain what causes the 'Heavenly Hurt'?
cards.answer: She presents despair as something that simply arrives like weather, not the result of any human decision.

cards.front: How does Dickinson's use of dashes affect the poem's language?
cards.answer: The dashes interrupt each line, forcing pauses that mimic hesitation as the speaker struggles for words.

cards.front: Why does the poem isolate the speaker's suffering from others?
cards.answer: It insists the state cannot be shared or taught, and there is no enemy to identify or action to end it.

title: Two world wars and total war 1914-1945
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the five 'giants' the Beveridge Report (1942) said the welfare system should attack.
cards.answer: Want / Disease / Ignorance / Squalor / Idleness

cards.front: Which four items were rationed comprehensively during the Second World War?
cards.answer: Food / Clothing / Petrol / Furniture

cards.front: Why did Britain introduce conscription in 1916 despite the earlier success of voluntary recruitment?
cards.answer: Catastrophic losses like the Somme meant volunteers alone could no longer replace army casualties fast enough.

cards.front: How did total war experience during the Second World War create conditions for post-war welfare reform?
cards.answer: Shared suffering from bombing and rationing built social solidarity, making voters expect the state to provide healthcare, education and housing after the war.

cards.front: Name the first four alkanes in order of increasing chain length.
cards.answer: Methane / Ethane / Propane / Butane

cards.front: Why does boiling point increase as hydrocarbon chain length increases?
cards.answer: Longer chains have stronger intermolecular forces between molecules, so more energy is needed to boil them.

cards.front: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous even though it's colourless and odourless?
cards.answer: It cannot be detected by smell or sight, and it binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport in the blood.

cards.front: Name the ten main aims of retail businesses given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Survival/break-even / Profit maximisation / Increase sales / Increase market share / Customer satisfaction / Diversification / Be ethical / Environmental awareness / Social responsibility / Retail-specific aims

cards.front: Why might a furniture chain run a Bank Holiday sale even if it reduces profit margins?
cards.answer: It deliberately prioritises increasing sales volume, accepting temporarily reduced margins to boost turnover.

cards.front: How can pursuing market share through price matching conflict with the aim of profit maximisation?
cards.answer: Heavily discounting prices to increase market share can reduce profit margins in the short term, so the aims conflict.

cards.front: What is different about the aim of a charity shop compared with a profit-making retailer?
cards.answer: Charity shops aim to raise funds for a cause while covering running costs, rather than maximise profit for owners.

title: Allah in the Qur'an: Al-Fatiha, Tawhid and the 99 Names
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three things al-Fatiha establishes as a summary of the whole Qur'an
cards.answer: Who Allah is (the Lord, the Merciful) / What the human relationship with Allah should be (worship and dependence) / What the goal of human life is (guidance to paradise)
items: Who Allah is (the Lord, the Merciful)
What the human relationship with Allah should be (worship and dependence)
What the goal of human life is (guidance to paradise)

cards.front: Why do Muslims say Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim both come from a root linked to the womb?
cards.answer: Because the root r-h-m suggests mercy as fundamental and enveloping as a mother's care for a child.

cards.front: How does belief in Tawhid shape how Muslims see human authority?
cards.answer: Tawhid means ultimate loyalty belongs to Allah alone, so no human authority can override divine command.

title: Development of sport: medieval to industrial
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three continuities the lesson identifies across medieval and early modern sport.
cards.answer: Sport tied to social rank / Religion shaped the leisure calendar / War shaped sporting culture

cards.front: Name the four upper-class activities the lesson says were exclusive to the elite because they required expensive equipment, land or royal permission.
cards.answer: Jousting / Falconry / Deer hunting / Real tennis

cards.front: Why did the Church repeatedly condemn tournaments?
cards.answer: Knights died and events could become an excuse for settling feuds, making tournaments dangerous and wasteful.

cards.front: Why did real tennis remain confined to royal palaces and great nobles' homes?
cards.answer: Because the courts were expensive to build and maintain.

cards.front: What three inscriptions appear on Portia's three caskets (gold, silver, lead)?
cards.answer: Gold: 'shall gain what many men desire' / Silver: 'shall get as much as he deserves' / Lead: 'must give and hazard all he hath'
items: Gold: 'shall gain what many men desire'
Silver: 'shall get as much as he deserves'
Lead: 'must give and hazard all he hath'

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present Shylock's bond as more than unprovoked villainy?
cards.answer: Antonio has spat on Shylock, called him 'dog', kicked him, and damaged his business by lending without interest, so the bond responds to real persecution.

cards.front: How does Arragon's choice of the silver casket fail the appearance-versus-reality test?
cards.answer: He chooses by outward show rather than looking beyond surfaces, and finds a fool's head inside instead of the prize.

cards.front: Why does Shylock's 'merry bond' harden into a genuine desire for revenge?
cards.answer: It is only after Jessica's betrayal and Antonio's continued abuse that Shylock's wish for revenge becomes determined rather than a joke.

cards.front: Name the four things international standards govern in engineering, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dimensions (interchangeable parts) / Material properties / Test methods / Quality management systems / Environmental management

cards.front: Why did UK manufacturing employment fall sharply in the 1980s and 1990s?
cards.answer: Industries relocated production to countries where wages were a fraction of UK rates, a process called offshoring.

cards.front: Name the three types of documents Arthur uses to piece together Jennet's backstory.
cards.answer: Letters from Jennet begging to see Nathaniel / Legal documents recording the adoption / Jennet's own anguished writings
items: Letters from Jennet begging to see Nathaniel

cards.front: Name the three things a typical Victorian ghost story does that Hill's ending breaks.
cards.answer: The ghost is defeated / The protagonist survives / Normality returns

cards.front: Why do the townspeople of Crythin Gifford stay silent about the woman in black?
cards.answer: They believe acknowledging her presence increases the danger, so silence is a survival strategy rather than mere superstition.

cards.front: Why does Hill use letters and documents to reveal Jennet's backstory?
cards.answer: It gives the revelation authenticity, creates a detective-story structure, and lets us discover the truth alongside Arthur.

title: Population & Urban Change in the UK
subject: geography-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson gives three types of factors behind falling UK birth rates. Name them.
cards.answer: Economic factors / Political factors / Social factors

cards.front: Name the four consequences of an ageing UK population the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Pressure on NHS and social care / Rising pension spending / Workforce shortages / Positive contributions from older people
items: Pressure on NHS and social care

cards.front: Why has the UK's average life expectancy risen to about 81 years?
cards.answer: Better healthcare, falling smoking rates and improved diets have raised average life expectancy.

cards.front: Why do workforce shortages appear in jobs like nursing, teaching and engineering?
cards.answer: The over-65 group is leaving work faster than school leavers can replace them.

cards.front: Name the four industries the TUC called workers out from in support of the miners during the General Strike of 1926.
cards.answer: Transport / Printing / Building / Steel

cards.front: Name the four things the government used to keep supplies moving and win the propaganda battle during the 1926 General Strike.
cards.answer: Deployed the military / Recruited middle-class strikebreakers / BBC broadcast government messages / Produced the British Gazette newspaper

cards.front: Why did the TUC call off the General Strike after only nine days?
cards.answer: It feared the strike was seen as an attack on the constitution and worried prolonging it would provoke harsher legal action, especially as the government kept supplies moving effectively.

cards.front: Why did the Representation of the People Act 1918 only give the vote to women over 30 with property?
cards.answer: The partial reform reflected nervousness that women would immediately form a majority of the electorate if given equal terms with men.

title: Monasticism, Learning and the Investiture Controversy
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What four reasons does the lesson give for why Norman lords founded so many abbeys?
cards.answer: Religious: monks prayed for his soul and family / Political: an abbey stabilised his hold on the area / Economic: the abbey cleared land and improved estate value / Cultural: it showed status as part of the Christian elite
items: Religious: monks prayed for his soul and family
Political: an abbey stabilised his hold on the area
Economic: the abbey cleared land and improved estate value
Cultural: it showed status as part of the Christian elite

cards.front: Name the three languages that made Norman England a trilingual society, and who used each one.
cards.answer: Anglo-Norman, spoken by Norman lords and clerks / Old English, spoken by peasants / Latin, used by the Church, schools and royal documents
items: Anglo-Norman, spoken by Norman lords and clerks
Latin, used by the Church, schools and royal documents

cards.front: How did monasteries become economically powerful under Norman rule?
cards.answer: Wealthy patrons gave monasteries land in exchange for prayers for their souls and their family's souls.

cards.front: Why did William II leave the see of Canterbury vacant for four years after Lanfranc's death?
cards.answer: He needed money to crush the 1088 rebellion, defend Normandy against Robert Curthose and pay mercenaries, so he kept the revenues himself.

title: Transport: Diffusion, Osmosis and Active Transport
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives that affect the rate of diffusion.
cards.answer: Concentration gradient (steeper = faster) / Temperature (higher = faster) / Surface area

cards.front: Name the four features shared by specialised exchange surfaces.
cards.answer: Large surface area / Thin walls / Good blood/fluid supply / Ventilation (in some cases)

cards.front: Why does a higher temperature increase the rate of diffusion?
cards.answer: Higher temperature makes particles move faster, so they collide more often and spread out more quickly.

cards.front: Why do root hair cells contain many mitochondria?
cards.answer: To supply the ATP from respiration needed for active transport of mineral ions into the cell.

title: Loving and Serving: Catholic Social Teaching in Britain
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five principles that Catholic Social Teaching rests on.
cards.answer: Human dignity / The common good / Solidarity / Subsidiarity / Care for creation

cards.front: How do Catholics in Britain support CAFOD, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Parish fundraising / Fast Days (giving up a meal and donating the money) / Advocacy campaigns
items: Fast Days (giving up a meal and donating the money)

cards.front: Why does Laudato Si' say that care for the poor and care for the earth cannot be separated?
cards.answer: It calls for an 'ecological conversion' that sees the planet as a shared home entrusted to all humanity, not a resource to consume.

cards.front: Why does Catholic Social Teaching interpret humanity's 'dominion' over the earth (Genesis 1:28) as stewardship, not ownership?
cards.answer: Because God declared creation 'very good' and entrusted it to human care as a gift, to be respected for the Creator and future generations.

title: The Great Depression and the New Deal
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Why did the Wall Street Crash lead to widespread bank collapses?
cards.answer: Banks had invested depositors' money in shares, so when share prices collapsed banks failed and savings were wiped out.

cards.front: Why did Hoover refuse to give direct federal relief during the Depression?
cards.answer: He believed in rugged individualism, fearing government handouts would make Americans dependent on the state.

cards.front: Why was the National Recovery Administration struck down in 1935?
cards.answer: The Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional.

cards.front: Why did farmers in the Midwest suffer a 'double blow' during the Depression?
cards.answer: Banks repossessed their farms while drought turned the Great Plains into a Dust Bowl, driving many west.

cards.front: Name the four key functions of the cardiovascular system in physical activity.
cards.answer: Transport of oxygen to muscles / Transport of carbon dioxide away from muscles / Transport of nutrients to fuel muscle contractions / Regulation of body temperature
items: Transport of carbon dioxide away from muscles
Transport of nutrients to fuel muscle contractions

cards.front: Name the four components that make up blood.
cards.answer: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) / White blood cells (leucocytes) / Platelets (thrombocytes) / Plasma

cards.front: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?
cards.answer: Having no nucleus maximises their oxygen-carrying capacity.

cards.front: Why do arteries have thick, muscular and elastic walls?
cards.answer: So they can withstand and smooth out the surges of pressure produced by each heartbeat.

cards.front: Name the three categories of network protection described in the lesson's key fact.
cards.answer: Access control / Physical security / Firewalls

cards.front: In the school pen test scenario, name the three vulnerabilities the testers found.
cards.answer: Three devices with outdated software / Wi-Fi accepted default admin password / Tailgating into the server room worked
items: Tailgating into the server room worked

cards.front: How do identifying vulnerabilities and protecting networks work together in a mature security strategy?
cards.answer: Protections reduce the chance of attack, but pen testing and ethical hacking find weaknesses protections have missed or that appeared since they were reviewed.

cards.front: Why might an ethical hacker find vulnerabilities that an organisation's own IT staff overlook?
cards.answer: They approach the system with fresh eyes and use attacker techniques, unlike staff who designed the system and may miss its flaws.

title: Supplying the Cell and Challenges of Size
subject: science-ocr

cards.front: Name the three environmental factors the lesson gives that affect transpiration rate.
cards.answer: Light intensity / Temperature / Air movement/wind

cards.front: Name the three types of blood vessel in the human circulatory system.
cards.answer: Arteries / Veins / Capillaries

cards.front: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle?
cards.answer: It has to pump blood further, all the way around the whole body, so needs more force.

cards.front: Why does water move upwards through the xylem in the transpiration stream?
cards.answer: Water evaporates from the leaves through stomata, creating a pull that draws water up through the xylem.

cards.front: Name the ten school facilities vocabulary words given in the lesson.
cards.answer: una biblioteca - a library / una cantina - a canteen / un gimnasio - a gym / un laboratorio de ciencias - a science lab / una piscina - a swimming pool / un patio - a playground
items: un laboratorio de ciencias - a science lab

cards.front: Name the seven days of the week in Spanish given in the lesson.
cards.answer: lunes / martes / miércoles / jueves / viernes / sábado / domingo

cards.front: Why do you say 'es la una' but 'son las dos' when telling the time in Spanish?
cards.answer: Es la una is singular because it is one o'clock, but son las is used with all other numbers because they are plural.

cards.front: How do adjectives describing teachers change to agree, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: They change for gender and number, e.g. estrictos for masculine plural and estrictas for feminine plural, but -e adjectives like paciente stay the same.

cards.front: The lesson describes how dialogue reveals character for four figures in Pride and Prejudice — name them with their speech style.
