cards.answer: Collins - verbose and obsequious / Lady Catherine - commands and declarations / Elizabeth - quick, witty and direct / Darcy - evolves from stiff to honest and vulnerable
items: Darcy - evolves from stiff to honest and vulnerable

cards.front: Why does Lydia's elopement with Wickham feel more painful to the reader because of dramatic irony?
cards.answer: The reader already knows from Darcy's letter that Wickham is a fortune-hunter, unlike Elizabeth, making the crisis more painful.

cards.front: How does free indirect discourse work when Elizabeth reads Darcy's letter?
cards.answer: The narration turns serious and reflective to match Elizabeth's tone, giving her self-blame the narrator's authority.

cards.front: Name the four factors that increase the rate of diffusion.
cards.answer: Steeper concentration gradient / Larger surface area / Shorter diffusion distance / Higher temperature

cards.front: Name the four structural features of a villus that help nutrient absorption.
cards.answer: Thin epithelium (one cell thick) / Dense network of blood capillaries / A lacteal (lymph vessel) / Microvilli on epithelial cells

cards.front: Why do intestinal epithelial cells need active transport to absorb glucose from the gut lumen?
cards.answer: Active transport uses ATP from respiration to move glucose against its concentration gradient, into the blood.

cards.front: Why does having two circuits in the double circulatory system help deliver blood efficiently?
cards.answer: Having two separate circuits maintains high blood pressure, allowing efficient delivery of blood to the lungs and body tissues.

title: Imperial Policy: Trade Monopoly, Slavery and the Missionaries
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three layers of Spain's trade monopoly with the Indies.
cards.answer: Only Castile could trade with the Indies / Only Seville (later also Cadiz) could send/receive ships / Only licensed Spanish ships and crews could sail
items: Only Castile could trade with the Indies
Only Seville (later also Cadiz) could send/receive ships
Only licensed Spanish ships and crews could sail

cards.front: Name the four pillars of Spanish imperial policy described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Trade monopoly / Encomienda labour system / Licensed African slave trade / Catholic mission

cards.front: Why did the Crown keep such tight control over Atlantic shipping through the Casa de Contratacion?
cards.answer: To capture the royal fifth of all gold and silver returning from the Indies and to keep out Portuguese, French and English ships.

cards.front: Why was Montesinos's 1511 sermon such a shock to the Spanish colonists?
cards.answer: Because he was attacking the moral story Spain told about itself, that encomenderos were performing a Christian service.

cards.front: Name the three flawed models of religion the novel presents through different characters.
cards.answer: Brocklehurst's hypocrisy / Helen's passivity / St John's cold duty

cards.front: Name the four assessment objectives used in GCSE English Literature.
cards.answer: AO1 response with quotations / AO2 language, form and structure / AO3 context / AO4 written accuracy

cards.front: Why does Jane refuse St John's proposal at Moor House?
cards.answer: Because it offers marriage without love, only cold duty, which would corrupt her self-respect.

cards.front: Why does Brontë establish Jane's moral claim to equality before she inherits money?
cards.answer: To prove her worth comes from character, not fortune; the money only removes the practical obstacle.

cards.front: Name the three acts of eavesdropping/noting the lesson gives as structuring the play.
cards.answer: Gulling scenes (benevolent trick into love) / Window scene (malevolent trick into rage) / Watch overhearing Borachio's confession (accidental truth)

cards.front: Name the four performances/disguises the lesson lists as saturating the play with theatricality.
cards.answer: The masked ball / Don Pedro impersonating Claudio to woo Hero / Margaret impersonating Hero at the window / Hero's staged 'death'
items: Don Pedro impersonating Claudio to woo Hero
Margaret impersonating Hero at the window

cards.front: Why does Claudio use verse when he denounces Hero at the altar?
cards.answer: Verse gives his denunciation rhetorical power, lending his cruelty a public, ceremonial quality.

cards.front: How does the play's structure show that observation is never neutral?
cards.answer: The same device of noting produces different outcomes depending on what characters already expect to see.

cards.front: Name the three lines plotted on a break-even chart.
cards.answer: Fixed cost line (flat) / Total cost line (rises with output) / Total revenue line (rises faster)

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says break-even helps a business make decisions.
cards.answer: Informs pricing decisions / Informs marketing choices / Guides planning for expansion / Supports talks with a lender

cards.front: Why does opening a second shop roughly double the break-even point?
cards.answer: Because fixed costs like rent, a manager and insurance roughly double, and break-even rises as fixed costs rise.

cards.front: How does a low margin of safety make it harder for a business to get a loan?
cards.answer: A forecast that only just scrapes above break-even shows little cushion, so lenders see it as a riskier, less credible loan.

title: Types of Reaction: Redox, Acids and Neutralisation
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the fourteen metals in the reactivity series, from most to least reactive.
cards.answer: Potassium / Sodium / Calcium / Magnesium / Aluminium / Zinc / Iron / Tin / Lead / Hydrogen / Copper / Silver / Gold / Platinum

cards.front: Name the three types of acid reaction given, other than with an alkali, and their products.
cards.answer: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen / Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide / Acid + metal oxide → salt + water
items: Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide

cards.front: Why does copper sulfate solution fade from blue to colourless when zinc is added?
cards.answer: Zinc displaces copper, forming colourless zinc sulfate as the copper ions are reduced and deposited as copper metal.

cards.front: Why can zinc displace copper from copper sulfate solution but copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulfate?
cards.answer: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

cards.front: Name the five sources of background radiation the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Radon gas / Cosmic rays / Food / Building materials / Artificial sources

cards.front: Name the three types of radiation emitted by unstable nuclei, from weakest to strongest penetrating power.
cards.answer: Alpha / Beta / Gamma

cards.front: Why is alpha radiation strongly ionising but only weakly penetrating?
cards.answer: Its large charge and mass make it ionise atoms quickly, transferring its energy rapidly so it is stopped after a short distance.

cards.front: Why is radioactive decay described as random but still statistically predictable?
cards.answer: No individual nucleus's decay time can be predicted, but the overall behaviour of large numbers of nuclei is reliable and predictable.

title: Patterns of Criminal and Deviant Behaviour
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four main social factors sociology says shape patterns of criminal behaviour.
cards.answer: Social class / Gender / Ethnicity / Age

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three things do sociologists use to explain ethnic minority overrepresentation in official crime statistics?
cards.answer: Selective policing and stop-and-search practices / Institutional racism in the criminal justice system / Structural factors such as material deprivation
items: Institutional racism in the criminal justice system
Structural factors such as material deprivation

cards.front: Why does offending peak among 15 to 24 year olds?
cards.answer: This age group has the lowest social responsibility, being less likely to own property, hold stable jobs or have family ties.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say official statistics on domestic violence and sexual assault are particularly unreliable?
cards.answer: Women are overrepresented as victims in these categories, but very high levels of non-reporting create a large dark figure of crime.

cards.front: The lesson compares three types of bonding. What type of atoms combine to form each: ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding?
cards.answer: Ionic: metal + non-metal / Covalent: non-metal + non-metal / Metallic: metal atoms

cards.front: Why do both ions become stable after an ionic bond forms, such as in sodium chloride?
cards.answer: Because losing or gaining electrons gives both ions full outer electron shells.

cards.front: Name the four aspects of society the lesson says the novel examines through the eyes of a child.
cards.answer: race / class / gender / community

cards.front: Why does economic decline in the Black Country fuel resentment towards immigrants in the novel?
cards.answer: When people feel their livelihoods are threatened by job losses, they look for someone to blame, and immigrants become that target.

cards.front: How does the novel's dual narrative voice (child and adult Meena) create humour?
cards.answer: Humour comes from the gap between what the child Meena misunderstands or overlooks and what the adult narrator lets the reader see clearly.

title: The Charge of the Light Brigade & Bayonet Charge
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: In 'The Charge of the Light Brigade', what three directions surround the soldiers in the cannon repetition?
cards.answer: Cannon to right of them / Cannon to left of them / Cannon in front of them

cards.front: Why does Tennyson's final quotation 'Honour the charge they made! / Honour the Light Brigade' use the imperative 'Honour'?
cards.answer: It directly instructs the reader to remember and respect the soldiers, turning the poem into a memorial.

cards.front: How does the casualty toll of the real Battle of Balaclava show the scale of the disaster behind Tennyson's poem?
cards.answer: Around 110 of the 600 soldiers were killed, 160 wounded, and 375 horses destroyed due to a miscommunication in orders.

title: The Five Pillars, Ten Obligatory Acts & Shahadah
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the six extra duties in the Ten Obligatory Acts beyond the four shared Pillars.
cards.answer: Khums (20% tax on surplus income) / Jihad (striving in the way of God) / Amr bil ma'ruf (commanding good) / Nahi anil munkar (forbidding evil) / Tawalla (loving the Ahl al-Bayt) / Tabarra (dissociating from their enemies)
items: Jihad (striving in the way of God)

cards.front: Why is Khums considered particularly important in Shi'a Islam?
cards.answer: Because the money is partly given to descendants of Muhammad, supporting the religious scholars who guide the Shi'a community.

cards.front: How does believing in Tawhid shape a Muslim's daily life?
cards.answer: If Allah alone is God, only He deserves worship, so Muslims must not place money, status or people above Him.

cards.front: Name the four ingredients of a top-band thematic change essay given in the lesson.
cards.answer: evidence from all three eras / clear argument about change AND continuity / explanation of why things changed / substantiated overall judgement in conclusion
items: clear argument about change AND continuity

cards.front: Name the four things a strong essay paragraph should do, according to the lesson's pattern.
cards.answer: make a point / support with specific evidence / explain what it shows about change or continuity / link back to the question
items: explain what it shows about change or continuity

cards.front: Why does an essay covering only the modern period cap itself in the middle band?
cards.answer: Because it misses evidence from the medieval and early modern eras, and the essay must cover all three eras to access the top bands.

cards.front: Why does writing 'sport changed because football was codified in 1863' only earn a description mark, not an explanation mark?
cards.answer: Because it states what happened without explaining the causes, such as public schools, railways, the Saturday half-holiday and urban growth.

cards.front: Name the four types of secondary storage the lesson compares.
cards.answer: Magnetic storage (HDD) / Solid-state storage (SSD) / Optical storage / Cloud storage

cards.front: Name the five criteria used to compare secondary storage types.
cards.answer: Capacity / Durability / Portability / Speed / Cost

cards.front: How does the operating system free up RAM when it becomes full?
cards.answer: It moves the least-recently-used sections of RAM to a page file on secondary storage, freeing RAM for the current task.

cards.front: Why must ROM be used to start a computer rather than RAM?
cards.answer: ROM is non-volatile and keeps its start-up instructions without power, so it can run the BIOS before the OS loads.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why beginners should avoid outcome goals.
cards.answer: Winning may be unrealistic against experienced opponents / Repeated failure can demotivate / Shifts focus away from technique development onto the scoreboard
items: Winning may be unrealistic against experienced opponents
Shifts focus away from technique development onto the scoreboard

cards.front: Why can outcome goals still be useful for a highly experienced performer like an elite rower?
cards.answer: An outcome goal like winning a final sharpens focus and intensity, especially when combined with controllable performance goals for daily targets.

title: How Materials, Smart Technologies & Microelectronics Changed Everyday Life
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Name four products the lesson gives as only possible because of miniaturisation.
cards.answer: Implantable pacemakers / In-ear hearing aids / GPS chips in children's shoes / Wrist-worn fitness trackers

cards.front: Why is stainless steel used for kitchen utensils, sinks and medical instruments?
cards.answer: It is an alloy of iron with chromium added to resist corrosion, giving the hygiene and durability those uses need.

cards.front: Why did Wi-Fi let engineers design new products without planning for cable routing?
cards.answer: A single router gives every device internet access wirelessly, so engineers could assume connectivity without running network cables.

cards.front: Name the four poems the lesson compares with 'Lullaby'.
cards.answer: Bright Star by John Keats / Love After Love by Derek Walcott / Morning Song by Sylvia Plath / The Perseverance by Raymond Antrobus
items: Love After Love by Derek Walcott

cards.front: Name the four stages the lesson identifies in the structure of 'Lullaby'.
cards.answer: Opening stanza uses sibilance / Stanzas two and three set up opposites / A later stanza personifies the planet / Final stanzas move backwards in time
items: Stanzas two and three set up opposites
A later stanza personifies the planet
Final stanzas move backwards in time

cards.front: Why does Asghar write 'Lullaby' as an invented story rather than a memory of her parents?
cards.answer: Both her parents died before she turned five, so she built the poem from stories her sister told her instead of memories.

cards.front: Why is the title 'Lullaby' fitting for a poem about two dead parents?
cards.answer: A lullaby usually soothes a child to sleep, and the poem soothes grief by imagining the parents reunited rather than mourning them as lost.

title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church forbid artificial contraception but allow natural family planning?
cards.answer: Artificial contraception deliberately separates the unitive and procreative purposes of sex, while natural family planning works with the body's natural process.

cards.front: Why do Christians who use situation ethics say a strict no-divorce rule can be wrong?
cards.answer: Because remaining in a loveless or harmful marriage cannot be the most loving outcome for the couple or their children.

cards.front: Name the three different approaches to remarriage after divorce found among Christian groups in this lesson.
cards.answer: Catholic annulment instead of divorce / Church of England discretionary remarriage since 2002 / Orthodox penitential remarriage through oikonomia
items: Church of England discretionary remarriage since 2002

title: Policing Whitechapel: H Division and the beat constable
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three pieces of equipment (besides uniform) a Met beat constable carried on patrol.
cards.answer: Wooden truncheon / Whistle for raising the alarm / Bullseye lantern with a sliding shutter
items: Bullseye lantern with a sliding shutter

cards.front: Name the five types of crime that filled Whitechapel beat constables' casebooks.
cards.answer: Drunkenness and street fights / Prostitution / Protection rackets / Domestic violence / Pickpocketing and street theft

cards.front: Why was it structurally difficult for a beat constable to catch criminals while patrolling the rookeries?
cards.answer: He walked at a fixed, predictable pace so locals could time and avoid him, and fog, coal-smoke and unlit alleys often cut visibility to a few yards.

cards.front: Why did Sir Charles Warren order the Goulston Street graffito to be erased before dawn?
cards.answer: He feared that if the public read it at first light it would trigger anti-Jewish riots.

title: Characters: Mickey, Edward, Mrs Johnstone, Mrs Lyons
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three physical qualities the lesson gives for child Mickey's physicality.
cards.answer: Quick direction changes / Low centre of gravity / Hands constantly busy

cards.front: Name the three physical qualities the lesson gives for adult Mickey in the depression scenes of Act Two.
cards.answer: Slow movements / Sunken posture / Voice that has lost its colour and pace
items: Voice that has lost its colour and pace

cards.front: Why must a performer play Edward as genuinely warm rather than just a symbol of privilege?
cards.answer: Otherwise the friendship between the brothers will feel implausible.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Johnstone sing through some of her most painful moments in the play?
cards.answer: Because the songs are not relief from grief but a way of bearing it.

cards.front: Name the three changes the lesson gives for why coastal flood risk is increasing.
cards.answer: Rising sea levels / More powerful and frequent storms / Continued building on the coast

cards.front: Why does a sea wall at Bridlington cause the beach in front of it to erode?
cards.answer: The wall reflects wave energy back, scouring away the beach in front of it.

cards.front: How does dune restoration at Studland Bay protect the coast?
cards.answer: Marram grass is planted to bind and trap sand, and fenced walkways keep walkers off the dunes.

cards.front: How does the Medmerry realignment scheme protect land further inland?
cards.answer: The sea wall was breached to flood farmland, creating salt marsh that absorbs wave energy and defends land behind.

title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four benefits of recycling metals given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Saves energy / Reduces use of limited ore resources / Reduces landfill waste / Reduces environmental damage from mining and emissions
items: Reduces use of limited ore resources
Reduces environmental damage from mining and emissions

cards.front: Name the three metals the lesson says react with cold water.
cards.answer: Potassium / Sodium / Lithium

cards.front: Why does carbon reduction work to extract metals like iron from their oxide ores?
cards.answer: Carbon is more reactive than iron, so it removes the oxygen from the metal oxide, reducing it to the metal.

cards.front: In a displacement reaction, why is the less reactive metal ion reduced?
cards.answer: Because it gains electrons from the more reactive metal, and gaining electrons is reduction.

cards.front: The lesson gives six problems you can mention about your local area. Name them.
cards.answer: too much traffic / not enough for young people / buses don't run often enough / too much noise / problems with rubbish/litter / rents too expensive

cards.front: Name the three short adjectives the lesson gives as examples that add an umlaut in the comparative.
cards.answer: groß → größer / alt → älter / klein → kleiner

cards.front: Why does the lesson say you should give opinions with reasons when describing where you live?
cards.answer: Because giving opinions with reasons helps you access higher marks.

cards.front: How do you form the comparative of a German adjective according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Add -er to the adjective, and short adjectives often also add an umlaut.

title: Wave Behaviour and the EM Spectrum
subject: science-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the three uses of infrared given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Remote controls / Thermal imaging / Optical fibre communication / radiant heaters

cards.front: Name the three properties of a wave that stay unchanged during reflection.
cards.answer: Speed / Frequency / Wavelength

cards.front: Why does sound diffract around a doorway but visible light does not?
cards.answer: Sound wavelengths are similar in size to doorways, while visible light wavelengths are millions of times shorter.

cards.front: Why do higher-frequency EM waves like UV and gamma rays tend to be more hazardous to living tissue?
cards.answer: They carry more energy per photon and are more ionising, which can damage DNA.

cards.front: Why does Dickens have the ghost repeat Scrooge's own words about the death of Tiny Tim?
cards.answer: It forces Scrooge to hear the cruelty of his own Malthusian language applied to a real, innocent child.

cards.front: Why does the Ghost of Christmas Present age and die within one day?
cards.answer: It shows that opportunities for generosity are fleeting, creating urgency because a missed chance may never return.

title: Creation and the Dignity of the Human Person
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four spiritual and moral capacities the lesson says imago Dei refers to.
cards.answer: Reason / Free will / Conscience / Capacity for love and relationship

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says imago Dei leads Catholic teaching to condemn.
cards.answer: Slavery / Abortion / Murder / Euthanasia

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching not treat Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 as competing creation stories?
cards.answer: They are understood as complementary theological accounts revealing different truths about God, the world and humans, not as science.

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching say evolution is compatible with belief in God as Creator?
cards.answer: God is the ultimate cause of existence, so the scientific 'how' doesn't compete with the theological 'why', provided souls are directly created by God.

cards.front: Why were the English ships better suited to fighting the Armada in the Channel than the Spanish ships?
cards.answer: English ships were smaller, faster and more manoeuvrable with longer-range guns, while Spanish ships were large and built for boarding.

cards.front: Why was the Armada unable to return to Calais to rendezvous with Parma's army after Gravelines?
cards.answer: Its formation was broken and the wind had changed, forcing it to sail north around Scotland and Ireland instead.

cards.front: Why did Mary Queen of Scots' execution in 1587 give Philip extra motivation for the Armada, even though it could no longer put her on the throne?
cards.answer: The Armada could instead avenge her death and break England's interference in his empire.

cards.front: Name the three parts that make up a nucleotide, the repeating unit of DNA.
cards.answer: A sugar (deoxyribose) / A phosphate group / One of four organic bases

cards.front: Name the four types of protein described in the lesson, with the job each does.
cards.answer: Enzymes catalyse chemical reactions / Structural proteins like collagen give tissues strength / Hormones like insulin regulate body processes / Antibodies defend against infection
items: Structural proteins like collagen give tissues strength
Hormones like insulin regulate body processes

cards.front: Why does complementary base pairing make it possible to copy DNA accurately before cell division?
cards.answer: The sequence of bases on one strand automatically determines the sequence on the other strand.

cards.front: How does the base sequence in DNA ultimately determine a protein's function?
cards.answer: Triplets of bases code for a sequence of amino acids, which fold into a specific shape that gives the protein its function.

cards.front: Name the five sections a typical business plan contains, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Executive summary / Market section / Operations section / Finance section / People section

cards.front: How does writing a business plan reduce risk before launch?
cards.answer: Writing down sales, costs and cash flow forces the entrepreneur to check research and prices, revealing problems while they are still cheap to fix.

cards.front: Why does a written plan help a founder get finance from a bank?
cards.answer: Banks almost always require a plan with a realistic cash flow forecast, and clear numbers and evidence make the idea more credible than a verbal pitch.

cards.front: Name the eight spokes of Egan's wheel.
cards.answer: Governance / Transport / Services / Environment / Economy / Housing / Social and cultural life / Equity

cards.front: Name the three successes of Cardiff Bay regeneration given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Rising house prices brought in professional residents / Landmark buildings boosted Welsh national identity / Freshwater lake supports water sports and birds
items: Rising house prices brought in professional residents
Landmark buildings boosted Welsh national identity
Freshwater lake supports water sports and birds

cards.front: Why does UK national planning policy presume brownfield development first?
cards.answer: Because reusing existing land cuts emissions from new road and sewer construction, protects the green belt, and revives struggling neighbourhoods.

cards.front: Why did building the Cardiff Bay barrage cause an environmental concern?
cards.answer: It destroyed an internationally important mudflat habitat that wading birds relied on.

cards.front: Name the four components of blood described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets / Plasma

cards.front: Name the four adaptations of alveoli for efficient gas exchange.
cards.answer: Very large total surface area / Walls just one cell thick / Moist inner surface / Rich network of capillaries

cards.front: Why do guard cells open the stomata in light?
cards.answer: In light, guard cells absorb water and become turgid, causing them to swell and open the stoma.

cards.front: How does bile help the digestion of fats?
cards.answer: Bile emulsifies fats, breaking large fat droplets into smaller ones, which increases the surface area for lipase enzymes to act on.

cards.front: Name the five actions employers must take under COSHH to control hazardous substances.
cards.answer: Identify hazardous substances used / Assess the risks / Provide protective equipment / Train staff in safe handling / Store chemicals correctly / Keep records

cards.front: What four things must a completed HACCP document record?
cards.answer: The hazard / The critical control point / The control measure / The corrective action

cards.front: Why do the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 require trolleys and lifting training in kitchens?
cards.answer: To reduce the risk of injury when staff move heavy boxes, hot pans, and catering equipment that cannot be avoided.

cards.front: Why must deaths, specified injuries and dangerous occurrences be reported to the HSE without delay under RIDDOR?
cards.answer: Because these are the most serious reportable incidents, so employers must notify the Health and Safety Executive immediately.

cards.front: Name the four properties used to describe all waves.
cards.answer: Amplitude / Wavelength / Frequency / Wave speed

cards.front: Name the three things that can happen when a wave meets a boundary between materials.
cards.answer: Reflected / Refracted / Absorbed

cards.front: Why does a wave bend away from the normal when it speeds up entering a new medium?
cards.answer: Refraction occurs because the wave changes speed at the boundary, and speeding up bends it away from the normal.

cards.front: Why do longitudinal waves have areas of compression and rarefaction?
cards.answer: Because the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, squashing particles together or spreading them apart.

cards.front: Name the four 'special areas' designated by the Special Areas Act of 1934 for government investment.
cards.answer: South Wales / North-east England / West Cumberland / Central Scotland

cards.front: What four reasons does the lesson give for new consumer industries preferring the Midlands and south-east over the north?
cards.answer: Closer to the largest consumer markets / Land was cheaper / Better road and rail links to the south / No entrenched union culture from staple industries
items: Closer to the largest consumer markets
Better road and rail links to the south
No entrenched union culture from staple industries

cards.front: Why was the National Insurance scheme unable to cope with unemployment in the 1930s?
cards.answer: It had been designed before the First World War, not for long-term mass unemployment, so by 1931 the fund was bankrupt.

cards.front: Why did the Jarrow Crusade organisers deliberately keep the march disciplined and non-violent?
cards.answer: To distance themselves from the communist-led Hunger Marches of the same period and win public sympathy.

cards.front: Name the four solutions the lesson gives for dealing with non-biodegradable polymer waste.
cards.answer: Mechanical recycling / Chemical recycling (cracking) / Incineration for energy recovery / Biodegradable bioplastics

cards.front: Name the three variables the lesson says must be controlled in the enthalpy of combustion practical.
cards.answer: Mass of water / Draught conditions / Distance between flame and calorimeter

cards.front: Why can fermentation not produce ethanol concentrations above about 12–15%?
cards.answer: Higher ethanol concentrations kill the yeast, stopping fermentation.

cards.front: Why is the experimental value from the alcohol combustion practical lower than the true enthalpy of combustion?
cards.answer: Heat loss to surroundings, incomplete combustion, and evaporation of alcohol all reduce the measured energy value.

title: Act 1: The Engagement and the Inspector Arrives
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: How does Mr Birling react when the Inspector reveals he sacked Eva Smith?
cards.answer: He shows no remorse, calling it a 'perfectly straightforward case' and insisting he 'can't accept any responsibility.'

cards.front: Why does Priestley time the Inspector's arrival to interrupt Birling's speech to Gerald and Eric?
cards.answer: It cuts off Birling's capitalist philosophy mid-sentence, positioning the Inspector as its direct answer.

title: Act 3: Eric’s Confession and the Inspector’s Speech
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the three techniques the lesson identifies in the Inspector's final speech.
cards.answer: Repetition / Tricolon / Direct address

cards.front: Why is Eric's treatment of Eva considered the most serious wrongdoing in the play?
cards.answer: He used her sexually, got her pregnant, and tried to buy her off with stolen money.

cards.front: Why does Priestley use Eric's drinking problem as a device in the play?
cards.answer: To show that the Birling family's obsession with appearances blinded them to real problems in their own household.

title: Tropical Storm Effects & Management: Hurricane Ida
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four tools the lesson gives for reducing tropical storm risk.
cards.answer: Monitoring / Prediction / Protection / Planning

cards.front: Why did Hurricane Ida intensify so rapidly from Category 1 to Category 4?
cards.answer: It passed over Caribbean waters around 30°C, well above the 26.5°C threshold needed for hurricanes to strengthen.

cards.front: Why can a slow-moving Category 1 hurricane still be as deadly as a Category 4?
cards.answer: The Saffir-Simpson scale only predicts wind damage, not storm surge or rainfall flooding, which is often the biggest killer.

cards.front: What three tests had Rochester posed before, all now answered by the time Jane returns to him?
cards.answer: Money / Mistress / Manipulation

cards.front: Why does Jane refuse to marry St John even though she considers his offer seriously?
cards.answer: Marrying without love would mean losing her private inner self, described as a kind of enslavement or bondage.

cards.front: Why does Brontë use Morton to show Jane's growing independence?
cards.answer: It proves Jane is now fully self-supporting, living out materially the independence her refusal at Thornfield began.

cards.front: Why does Dickens repeat the word 'his own' four times at the start of Stave 5?
cards.answer: It shows Scrooge reclaiming control of his life after being a passive observer in the previous three staves.

cards.front: Why does Dickens mix comedy and emotion when Scrooge wakes, like the 'Laocoön' stockings image?
cards.answer: The humour signals that genuine transformation has occurred, showing Scrooge is now joyfully, messily human rather than cold and calculating.

cards.front: Name three changes glasnost brought to Soviet media and public life.
cards.answer: Previously banned books published / Newspapers criticised government policies / TV showed reality of Afghanistan / Stalinism's crimes discussed openly

cards.front: Name three economic problems perestroika caused according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Inflation from relaxed price controls / Disrupted supply chains / Wages rose without productivity gains / Economic output fell

cards.front: Why did the Chernobyl disaster become a symbol of Soviet institutional failure?
cards.answer: The government tried to conceal the accident but glasnost meant journalists reported the truth, exposing the gap between official claims and crumbling reality.

cards.front: Why did Gorbachev's reforms spiral out of his control?
cards.answer: Glasnost exposed Soviet failures without improving living conditions, so people demanded political freedom and independence, squeezing Gorbachev between conservatives and reformers.

cards.front: Name the five key themes this lesson covers in A Christmas Carol.
cards.answer: Redemption / Social responsibility / Poverty / Christmas / Isolation

cards.front: What are the three stages of Scrooge's redemption journey?
cards.answer: Confronting the past (regret) / Witnessing the present (empathy) / Facing the future (terror)

cards.front: Why did Dickens choose the novella form for A Christmas Carol rather than a novel or short story?
cards.answer: A full novel would have diluted the emotional intensity while a short story lacked space for Scrooge's gradual transformation, so the novella's compactness creates urgency.

cards.front: How does the simile 'solitary as an oyster' show Scrooge's isolation in Stave 1?
cards.answer: It compares Scrooge to a creature sealed inside a hard shell, suggesting he has deliberately shut himself off from the world.

cards.front: Name the four factors of production an entrepreneur combines.
cards.answer: Land / Labour / Capital / Enterprise

cards.front: What four things do customers want that a business must understand to meet their needs?
cards.answer: Price / Quality / Choice / Convenience

cards.front: Why must an entrepreneur's three core functions all happen at the same time?
cards.answer: Missing any one causes failure: poor decisions ruin good organising and risk-taking, and refusing risk means nothing new is built.

cards.front: How does quality add value to a product?
cards.answer: A product that lasts longer, performs better or feels more premium justifies charging a higher price than a mass-produced alternative.

title: Medieval Warfare: Cavalry, Castles and Crossbows
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four main groups that made up Edward I's armies.
cards.answer: Heavy cavalry of knights and men-at-arms / Mass infantry of foot-soldiers / Longbow archers / Crossbowmen
items: Heavy cavalry of knights and men-at-arms

cards.front: Name the three ways a medieval siege could end.
cards.answer: Defenders ran out of food / Defenders surrendered to spare their lives / A breach was forced
items: Defenders surrendered to spare their lives

cards.front: Why did Edward send his archers forward before the cavalry charged at Falkirk in 1298?
cards.answer: The Scottish schiltrons resisted cavalry, so volleys of arrows were used to break up the static formations before the cavalry charged home.

cards.front: Why did Edward build ring after ring of stone castles in Wales instead of fighting repeated field campaigns?
cards.answer: Long sieges cost heavily in money, men and time, so castles aimed to make Welsh resistance impossible without repeated battles.

cards.front: Name the three Chamberlain-Hitler meetings that made up the Sudeten Crisis.
cards.answer: Berchtesgaden (15 September) / Bad Godesberg (22 September) / Munich Conference (29-30 September)

cards.front: Why did Henlein keep raising his demands even after Beneš offered concessions in 1938?
cards.answer: Hitler had instructed Henlein to make demands the Czech government could never accept, so agitation would continue regardless of concessions.

cards.front: Why did Chamberlain and Daladier decide to leave Czechoslovakia out of the Munich Conference?
cards.answer: They reasoned the alternative was war, and Czechoslovakia's consent was unobtainable but unnecessary since Britain and France would not fight for it.

cards.front: Why did Munich's failure to secure lasting peace only become clear in March 1939?
cards.answer: Hitler's seizure of the rump Czech lands in March 1939, not Munich itself, ended Czech independence and British appeasement.

cards.front: Name the eight key techniques the lesson lists as part of Brecht's approach.
cards.answer: Verfremdungseffekt / gestus / direct address / placards / songs that interrupt the action / visible stage machinery / episodic structure / narrators who comment on the action

cards.front: Why did Brecht want his audience to think rather than feel, unlike Stanislavski?
cards.answer: He believed emotional immersion made audiences passive, lulling them into accepting the world as it was.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception that Brechtian performance means deliberately bad or robotic acting?
cards.answer: Brecht wanted skilled performers; the alienation effect comes from theatrical framing like narrators, songs and placards, not poor acting.

cards.front: Name the five other anthology poems the lesson says 'Prayer' connects well to for comparison.
cards.answer: Baby Song / Holy Thursday / Cold Knap Lake / Equilibrium / Tea With Our Grandmothers

cards.front: What features of form and structure does the lesson say 'Prayer' uses to mimic struggling speech?
cards.answer: short lines / short sentences / frequent caesura / shifts in tense

cards.front: Why does Kunial use short lines and frequent caesura in 'Prayer'?
cards.answer: They mimic a person struggling to get words out under pressure, forcing the reader to pause where the speaker pauses for breath.

cards.front: Why does Kunial place the Arabic phrase 'Allah hu Akbar' inside an English poem?
cards.answer: It places his father's Muslim inheritance directly inside the English poem, holding two languages of faith together like his own dual identity.

title: Inequality in Contemporary UK: Class, Gender, Ethnicity
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson identifies seven domains where inequality is documented in the contemporary UK. Name them.
cards.answer: Income and wealth / Education / Crime / Health / Family / Work / Media representation

cards.front: Which three earlier laws did the Equality Act 2010 consolidate into a single framework?
cards.answer: Equal Pay Act / Sex Discrimination Act / Race Relations Act

cards.front: Why do sociologists say official crime statistics can exaggerate offending by certain ethnic minority groups?
cards.answer: Because the statistics reflect policing and prosecution patterns as much as actual offending, amplified by media labelling and moral panics.

cards.front: Why does the gender pay gap persist in the UK workplace despite formal equality laws?
cards.answer: Women are over-represented in part-time, lower-paid feminised jobs and face the glass ceiling restricting access to senior roles.

cards.front: Name the five comparative structures the lesson gives for comparing types of transport in Spanish.
cards.answer: más … que / menos … que / tan … como / mejor … que / peor … que

cards.front: Name the three connectives the lesson gives for justifying transport choices.
cards.answer: porque es / dado que es / ya que es
items: dado que es (given that it is)

cards.front: How does the lesson say you form 'by [vehicle]' phrases in Spanish, and what are the two exceptions?
cards.answer: You use 'en' plus the vehicle (e.g. en coche, en tren), except a pie (on foot) and a caballo (on horseback), which use 'a'.

cards.front: According to the lesson's example sentences, why might someone prefer to travel by bike?
cards.answer: Because going by bike is better for the environment and better for your health, as shown using 'mejor'.

cards.front: What three phases did Kohl's Ten-Point Plan envisage for reunification?
cards.answer: Expanded cooperation between the two Germanies / A confederal arrangement / Eventually full unification
items: Expanded cooperation between the two Germanies

cards.front: What four things did the Two Plus Four Treaty settle about reunified Germany?
cards.answer: Germany's existing borders were confirmed / Occupation rights of the four powers ended / Germany agreed not to develop weapons of mass destruction / NATO's jurisdiction would not extend to former GDR territory
items: Occupation rights of the four powers ended
Germany agreed not to develop weapons of mass destruction
NATO's jurisdiction would not extend to former GDR territory

cards.front: How did losing Soviet military backing make the SED regime vulnerable in 1989?
cards.answer: Without Soviet tanks as a guarantor, the SED could no longer rely on force to crush popular opposition as it had in 1953.

cards.front: Why did the SED become increasingly isolated in the late 1980s?
cards.answer: Honecker rejected Gorbachev's reforms and blocked reform-minded material, leaving the SED committed to a hard-line course even the USSR was abandoning.

cards.front: Name the three desperate tactics Leah uses to try to get Phil's attention in the field.
cards.answer: Mentions killing her pet / Threatens to harm herself / Talks about death

cards.front: Name the three minor group members who show discomfort but still comply with Phil's instructions.
cards.answer: Danny / Brian / Lou

cards.front: Why is John Tate instantly sidelined once Phil offers a plan?
cards.answer: He offers no resistance because, deep down, he knows he has nothing useful to contribute.

cards.front: Why does Cathy's behaviour support Kelly's idea that group pressure liberates rather than creates cruelty?
cards.answer: Cathy does not become cruel because of the group; it gives her permission to express cruelty she already possessed.

cards.front: Name the four line shapes on a distance-time graph and what each means, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: horizontal line = stationary / straight diagonal line = constant speed / curve getting steeper = accelerating / steeper line = faster object

cards.front: Name the three lines on a velocity-time graph and what each means, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: horizontal line = constant velocity / line sloping upwards = acceleration / line sloping downwards = deceleration

cards.front: In the required practical, why does plotting force against acceleration show F = ma?
cards.answer: Varying force while keeping total mass constant gives a straight line through the origin, showing force and acceleration are proportional.

cards.front: What does a negative value of acceleration mean?
cards.answer: The object is decelerating, meaning it is slowing down.

title: Civil Rights, 1955-1970: King, Malcolm X and legislation
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three US cities where urban rebellions broke out in the 1960s, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Watts, Los Angeles (1965) / Detroit (1967) / Newark (1967)

cards.front: What two things did the Black Panther Party combine, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Armed self-defence patrols / Community programmes like free breakfasts for children
items: Community programmes like free breakfasts for children

cards.front: Why did President Kennedy call for federal civil rights legislation after Birmingham in 1963?
cards.answer: Televised footage of Bull Connor's fire hoses and police dogs used against peaceful protesters, including children, shocked and outraged the nation.

cards.front: Why did President Johnson push for the Voting Rights Act after Bloody Sunday in 1965?
cards.answer: Televised scenes of state troopers beating marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge shocked Johnson into acting on voting rights.

title: Santo Domingo, Smallpox and the Caribbean Settlements
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three reasons does the lesson give for why Santo Domingo was sited on the south coast of Hispaniola instead of La Navidad's location?
cards.answer: Safer harbours / Closer to gold-bearing rivers / Away from alienated caciques' territory

cards.front: What four things does the lesson say happened to Tainos on Hispaniola under Spanish forced labour and violence?
cards.answer: Fields left untended / Villages broken up / Family structures destroyed by sexual violence / Resisters enslaved or killed
items: Family structures destroyed by sexual violence

cards.front: Why did the Taino settlers at La Navidad end up killed within a year?
cards.answer: The garrison quarrelled among themselves, kidnapped Taino women and turned on Guacanagarí's rivals, who then wiped them out.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say smallpox and Spanish conquest cannot be treated as separate disasters?
cards.answer: Forced labour, malnutrition, dispossession and warfare had already weakened Taino communities, making them far more vulnerable when smallpox arrived.

cards.front: According to Jacobean belief, name the three powers witches were thought to have.
cards.answer: Predict the future / Control the weather / Cause disease

cards.front: Name the three unnatural events that occur in nature after Duncan's murder.
cards.answer: Horses eat each other / The sky darkens / An owl kills a falcon

cards.front: Why does nature descend into chaos after Duncan's murder?
cards.answer: The murder ruptures the divinely ordained order of the Great Chain of Being, so the natural world reacts with unnatural chaos.

cards.front: Why is it ambiguous whether the witches cause Macbeth's downfall or simply reveal ambitions he already has?
cards.answer: The witches prophesy he will become king but never tell him to murder anyone; Macbeth and Lady Macbeth choose to act on the prophecies themselves.

title: Case Study: York under the Vikings
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five craft goods produced in the Coppergate workshops that archaeologists have found.
cards.answer: Amber jewellery / Glass beads / Leather shoes / Ironwork / Bone combs

cards.front: Name the four goods York's Viking-age merchants exported in return for imported luxuries.
cards.answer: Wool / Cloth / Leather / Fine craftwork

cards.front: Why did Jorvik become such a strong magnet for migrants in the Viking period?
cards.answer: Because work and wealth were readily available there, pulling in a growing population through economic opportunity.

cards.front: How did the Church in York respond to Viking settlement rather than being destroyed by it?
cards.answer: Religious institutions adapted, blending Norse and Christian styles, and became a route by which Norse migrants were absorbed into English society.

cards.front: What three stages mark Jordan's drift into gang life, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Expelled from school / Steals for the Crew for cigarettes and protection / Carries a knife
items: Steals for the Crew for cigarettes and protection

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say boys like Jordan lack, making the gang their only option?
cards.answer: No jobs / No prospects / No safe spaces

cards.front: How does the Dell Farm Crew fill a void in the estate, according to Kelman?
cards.answer: It provides structure, identity, and belonging where schools, police, and social services fail.

cards.front: Why does Lydia's own situation leave her unable to protect Harri?
cards.answer: She is fighting her own battles against peer pressure, estate life, and expectations on immigrant women, leaving her unavailable.

cards.front: Name the five examples the lesson gives of appearance concealing reality in the play.
cards.answer: Shylock's 'merry sport' hides a deadly trap / Portia's disguise hides her intelligence / Antonio's calm hides sadness / Venice's fair reputation hides prejudice / Bassanio's charm hides recklessness
items: Shylock's 'merry sport' hides a deadly trap

cards.front: Name the two exam tasks the lesson describes for Shakespeare questions and their focus.
cards.answer: Extract task: close reading of language and structure within printed lines / Whole-play task: discuss the theme across the whole play using memorised quotations and context
items: Extract task: close reading of language and structure
Whole-play task: theme across the play with memorised quotations

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare use money and commerce to shape relationships in The Merchant of Venice?
cards.answer: Because money mediates love, justice, mercy and revenge in Venice, shown through Bassanio's courtship, the bond, usury and the casket test.

cards.front: How does the play show that prejudice in Venice is structural rather than just individual?
cards.answer: Prejudice appears across institutions and characters, from the alien statute to insults from Antonio, Solanio, Salerio, Gratiano and Portia.

title: The impact of the Spanish conquest
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three types of Spanish missionary friars who established missions across Mexico.
cards.answer: Franciscan / Dominican / Augustinian

cards.front: What six things does the lesson say passed from Europe to the Americas in the Columbian Exchange?
cards.answer: Wheat / Cattle / Horses / Sugar cane / Diseases / Enslaved Africans

cards.front: Why was working in the silver mines of Potosí especially deadly for indigenous labourers?
cards.answer: Men worked in near-darkness inhaling toxic mercury vapour, with minimal food and no safety equipment, drastically shortening life expectancy.

cards.front: Why did Spain's silver wealth paradoxically weaken its own economy?
cards.answer: Easy silver money reduced incentives for domestic industry, so Spain used it to pay for imports instead of building its own manufacturing base.

cards.front: Why can depression return when antidepressant medication is stopped?
cards.answer: Antidepressants only treat brain chemistry and do not address the underlying thought patterns that maintain depression.

cards.front: How does CBT use behavioural activation to treat depression?
cards.answer: It gradually reintroduces activities the person has withdrawn from, helping build healthier patterns of behaviour.

cards.front: Name the five aims of criminal sentencing given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Retribution / Deterrence / Public protection / Rehabilitation / Reparation

cards.front: Name the five types of civil disputes the lesson gives as examples.
cards.answer: Breach of contract / Negligence / Defamation / Employment disputes / Family law matters

cards.front: Why is the standard of proof set so high (beyond reasonable doubt) in criminal cases?
cards.answer: Because criminal punishment is severe, this high standard protects defendants from being wrongly convicted.

cards.front: Why can the same harmful act sometimes lead to both a criminal prosecution and a civil claim?
cards.answer: Because criminal and civil law are separate systems, an act like an unsafe building can breach safety law and cause harm, triggering both as separate processes.

title: Theatre, stage and screen: medieval to Victorian
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three things Charles II brought back to English theatre after the Restoration.
cards.answer: Painted scenery / Indoor candlelit theatres / Professional women actors

cards.front: Name the five types of performers the lesson says appeared in rotation at Victorian music halls.
cards.answer: Comic singers / Acrobats / Jugglers / Magicians / Sentimental balladeers

cards.front: Why did Elizabethan theatre rely on spoken language, costume and convention rather than scenery?
cards.answer: Because the open-air stage had no ability to change lighting, so scenery could not be used effectively.

cards.front: Why were early commercial theatres built in the suburbs of London rather than inside the city?
cards.answer: Because they were outside the jurisdiction of city authorities, who disapproved of theatre as immoral and disruptive.

cards.front: Name the four measures the Long Parliament used in 1640-41 to limit royal power.
cards.answer: Abolished ship money / Outlawed the Personal Rule's courts / Passed the Triennial Act / Passed the Attainder of Strafford

cards.front: Why did Personal Rule collapse in 1640?
cards.answer: Charles's attempt to impose a Prayer Book on Scotland provoked the Bishops' Wars, forcing him to call Parliament to fund an army.

cards.front: Why did the Parliamentarians ultimately win the Civil War?
cards.answer: They had the superior financial resources of London and the south-east and reorganised their military into the New Model Army.

cards.front: Name the four types of proteins the lesson gives as examples.
cards.answer: Enzymes / Structural proteins (collagen and keratin) / Hormones (insulin) / Antibodies

cards.front: Name the four factors affecting enzyme activity described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Temperature / pH / Substrate concentration / Enzyme concentration

cards.front: Why does increasing substrate concentration eventually stop increasing the rate of an enzyme reaction?
cards.answer: All the active sites become occupied at once (the enzyme is saturated), so adding more substrate has no further effect.

cards.front: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction up to the optimum?
cards.answer: Molecules move faster and collide more frequently with the enzyme, increasing the rate of reaction.

title: The Structure and Process of Memory
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three processes that turn raw input into a usable memory.
cards.answer: Encoding / Storage / Retrieval

cards.front: What four things might someone with retrograde amnesia fail to recall from before their injury?
cards.answer: Family members they knew / Events they experienced / Skills they had learned / Facts they had learned

cards.front: Why can a fact feel like it's 'on the tip of your tongue'?
cards.answer: It has been encoded and stored successfully, but retrieval temporarily fails to bring it back out.

cards.front: How can someone with severe anterograde amnesia still hold a normal conversation?
cards.answer: Information can pass briefly through short-term memory, but fails to transfer into long-term storage.

title: Foods of Rich and Poor Households
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four foods from Juvenal's farmhouse dinner alongside the young kid, as listed in the poem.
cards.answer: wild asparagus / warm eggs in hay / preserved grapes / pears and apples

cards.front: Why did the Licinian law set exact limits on dried meat and pickled fish but not on fruit and vegetables?
cards.answer: Meat and fish had to be bought and showed off wealth, while homegrown produce cost nothing and did not display wealth.

cards.front: Why does Juvenal say the senate's old-fashioned meal now seems contemptible even to a ditch-digger?
cards.answer: Roman standards of luxury had risen so much that what was once a luxurious senate meal is now seen as beneath contempt.

cards.front: How does Petronius use Trimalchio's dinner to mock hosts who show off their wealth?
cards.answer: He exaggerates the luxury, like dormice on soldered bridges and fake century-old wine, to mock using food to advertise wealth rather than honour guests.

cards.front: Name the sections included in a complete business plan (8 given in the lesson).
cards.answer: Business idea / Aims and objectives / Target market / Forecast revenue, costs and profit / Cash-flow forecast / Sources of finance / Planned location / Marketing mix

cards.front: How can a cash-flow forecast help a café owner avoid running out of cash before opening?
cards.answer: It reveals in advance, such as month three, when cash will run short, letting her arrange an overdraft beforehand.

cards.front: Name the four purposes of marriage given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Lifelong companionship / A stable environment for children / Sexual intimacy within a committed relationship / Following God's plan (for religious believers)
items: Sexual intimacy within a committed relationship

cards.front: Name the five common reasons for divorce in Britain given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Adultery / Unreasonable behaviour / Growing apart / Financial problems / Domestic abuse

cards.front: Why is there an ethical tension around divorce according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because marriage is seen as sacred and permanent, yet compassion says it is cruel to force people to stay in harmful or loveless marriages.

cards.front: Why does the Church of England permit divorce while the Catholic Church does not?
cards.answer: Catholics see marriage as an unbreakable sacrament, while the Church of England allows divorce as a last resort out of compassion.

cards.front: Name the three roots of Enid's controlling behaviour, as the lesson identifies them.
cards.answer: Her abusive marriage — won't let daughters experience the same / Her mother's death and their estrangement — can't bear losing daughters that way / Her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant — believes assimilation is protection
items: Her abusive marriage — won't let daughters experience the same
Her mother's death and their estrangement — can't bear losing daughters that way
Her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant — believes assimilation is protection

cards.front: Why did Enid's husband become abusive towards her?
cards.answer: His cruelty was rooted in the racism and humiliation he suffered at work, which he inflicted on Enid.

cards.front: Why does Viv walk out of one of her exams?
cards.answer: It is an act of defiance against a Eurocentric curriculum that she feels has no place for her.

title: Piaget in Education: Conservation and Egocentrism
subject: psychology-aqa

cards.front: Name the three features of primary classrooms that reflect Piaget's insight about concrete operational learning.
cards.answer: Hands-on materials / Practical activities / Discovery learning

cards.front: Why do pre-operational children fail standard conservation tasks like the tall thin glass vs short wide glass?
cards.answer: They focus on the height of the water, what they can see, rather than reasoning about the actual quantity.

cards.front: How did children's responses in Piaget's Three Mountains Task demonstrate egocentrism?
cards.answer: Pre-operational children consistently described what they themselves could see, not what the doll's position would show.

title: Legacy of the Black Death: labour, wages and the Statute of Labourers
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What were the three aims of the Statute of Labourers (1351)?
cards.answer: Fix wages at pre-Black Death levels / Forbid labourers leaving for higher pay elsewhere / Fine employers who paid above the legal rate
items: Fix wages at pre-Black Death levels
Forbid labourers leaving for higher pay elsewhere
Fine employers who paid above the legal rate

cards.front: Name the three long-term effects of the sustained population decrease after the Black Death, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Marginal land converted to sheep pasture / The wool trade benefited / Gradual emergence of a mobile wage-labour economy
items: Marginal land converted to sheep pasture
Gradual emergence of a mobile wage-labour economy

cards.front: Why did some marginal farmland get converted to sheep pasture after the Black Death?
cards.answer: There were fewer workers available, and sheep pasture required much less labour than farming the land.

cards.front: How did some physicians' observations after the Black Death hint at contagion theory, even though miasma theory still dominated?
cards.answer: They noticed people who had close contact with the sick were more likely to fall ill themselves.

title: Act 2: Geof, Helen's Return & the Ending
subject: english-literature-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six practical things Geof does to care for Jo during her pregnancy.
cards.answer: Cooks / Cleans / Buys baby clothes / Prepares for the birth / Asks practical questions about the baby / Encourages her to see a doctor
items: Asks practical questions about the baby
Encourages her to see a doctor

cards.front: What three things happen in the play's final unresolved scene?
cards.answer: Helen discovers the baby's father was Black and reacts with racist horror / Helen goes out for a drink / Jo is left alone on stage as the birth approaches
items: Helen discovers the baby's father was Black and reacts with racist horror
Helen goes out for a drink
Jo is left alone on stage as the birth approaches

cards.front: Why was Geof thrown out of his lodgings before moving in with Jo?
cards.answer: Likely because his landlady discovered his sexuality.

cards.front: How does the relationship between Jo and Geof challenge conventional ideas of family?
cards.answer: Helen, Jo's biological mother, fails at maternal duty, while Geof, with no blood tie, provides real care, showing family is defined by actions not blood.

cards.front: Name the four job roles the lesson says an organisational structure sets out, from top to bottom.
cards.answer: Directors set strategy / Managers plan / Supervisors organise / Operatives carry out the work

cards.front: Name the three types of communication the lesson describes within an organisation.
cards.answer: Vertical (up or down the chain) / Horizontal (between colleagues at the same level) / Diagonal (across departments)
items: Horizontal (between colleagues at the same level)

cards.front: Why do flat structures give a business lower management costs?
cards.answer: Because there are fewer layers of management, meaning fewer managers need to be employed and paid.

cards.front: Why does a wide span of control usually push a business towards horizontal communication?
cards.answer: Because a manager cannot brief every worker in person, so staff communicate directly with colleagues at the same level.

cards.front: Name the three generations through which the pilot's story passes in 'Kamikaze'.
cards.answer: The father who lived it / The daughter recounting it to her children / The readers, who receive it second-hand
items: The daughter recounting it to her children
The readers, who receive it second-hand

cards.front: Why does the pilot turn his plane around in 'Kamikaze'?
cards.answer: The overwhelming beauty and movement of the natural world, like the fish and fishing boats, pulls him back to life over duty.

cards.front: How does shame spread through the pilot's family in 'Kamikaze'?
cards.answer: His children, who first chattered and laughed around him, eventually learn to be silent, spreading rejection to a generation who never witnessed the mission.

cards.front: How does the poem's structure mirror the conflict between the pilot's freedom and the code he is trapped in?
cards.answer: Free, unpunctuated, enjambed sentences flow against a rigidly regular shape of seven six-line stanzas, mirroring the pilot's rigid code.

cards.front: Name the three limited options the lesson says were available to working-class women like Helen in the 1950s.
cards.answer: Marriage / Factory work / Dependence on men

cards.front: Why does the lesson say poverty is more than just background detail in A Taste of Honey?
cards.answer: Poverty is the defining force shaping the characters' lives, trapping Jo and Helen in their cramped, comfortless flat and each other's company.

cards.front: Why can context still help a drama answer even though it earns no marks by itself?
cards.answer: It can help explain a moment in the play if kept short and embedded within analysis, rather than a separate paragraph.

cards.front: Name the five thermosetting polymers given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Epoxy resin / Polyester resin / Melamine / Polyurethane / Vulcanised rubber

cards.front: Name the four factors that the lesson says determine the properties of a composite.
cards.answer: Type of reinforcement / Direction of the fibres / Volume fraction of fibres / Type of matrix

cards.front: How does cross-graining in plywood overcome timber's natural weakness across the grain?
cards.answer: Alternating the grain direction of each glued veneer layer makes the panel strong and stiff in both directions and resistant to splitting.

cards.front: How does prestressing improve concrete's resistance to tensile loads?
cards.answer: Tensioned steel tendons put the concrete into permanent pre-compression, allowing it to resist higher tensile loads before cracking.

cards.front: Name the five towns where anti-Jewish riots broke out in 1190.
cards.answer: King's Lynn / Norwich / Stamford / Lincoln / Bury St Edmunds

cards.front: What three types of institutions did medieval Jewish communities in England maintain?
cards.answer: Synagogues / Schools / Charitable networks

cards.front: Why were Jewish financiers essential to the Crown, Church and nobility in medieval England?
cards.answer: Canon law forbade Christians from lending money at interest, so Jews filled this role and became indispensable to royal and noble finance.

cards.front: How did the 1218 requirement for Jews to wear a badge increase their vulnerability?
cards.answer: It visually marked Jews as different, an early form of state-enforced exclusion that made physical attacks against them easier.

cards.front: What three prevention measures did the government enforce during the Great Plague of 1665?
cards.answer: Quarantine of infected houses for 40 days / Watchmen posted to stop people leaving / Killing of dogs and cats / Bodies collected by dead carts / Large gatherings banned
items: Quarantine of infected houses for 40 days
Watchmen posted to stop people leaving

cards.front: What three continuities does the lesson give between the Black Death (1348) and the Great Plague (1665)?
cards.answer: Blamed on miasma / Blamed on God's punishment / Blamed on the humours / Same ineffective treatments used / No effective cure existed

cards.front: How did Harvey's ligature experiment prove blood flows in one direction through veins?
cards.answer: Veins below the ligature swelled, showing blood couldn't return to the heart, while veins above emptied, showing blood had already passed through.

cards.front: Why did many physicians reject Harvey's theory of blood circulation?
cards.answer: They trusted Galen's ancient authority and thought a doctor disagreeing with Galen must be unreliable, so some lost patients.

cards.front: Name the four groups of people the lesson describes as economically inactive.
cards.answer: Retired people / Full-time students / People caring for family members / People who have stopped looking for work
items: People who have stopped looking for work

cards.front: Name the three criteria the Labour Force Survey uses to count someone as unemployed.
cards.answer: Without a job / Available to start within two weeks / Actively seeking work in the past four weeks
items: Available to start within two weeks
Actively seeking work in the past four weeks

cards.front: How does rising unemployment cause lost output for the economy as a whole?
cards.answer: Idle workers mean the goods and services they could have produced are not made, so output falls below productive potential.

cards.front: Why does a long spell of unemployment make it harder for an individual to find a new job?
cards.answer: Their skills become outdated and gaps appear in their CV, which employers notice.

title: Singin' in the Rain and Grease: The Hollywood Musical
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three named sequences from Singin' in the Rain (1952) used for micro-analysis in this lesson.
cards.answer: The title number on the rain-soaked back lot / The 'Make 'Em Laugh' solo / The 'Good Morning' three-hander
items: The title number on the rain-soaked back lot

cards.front: Why does the title number in Singin' in the Rain use a long, locked-off master shot instead of cutting away?
cards.answer: It insists the body itself is the spectacle, refusing the implication that the performance needs cinematic assistance to be impressive.

cards.front: Why is the 'Greased Lightnin'' garage number in Grease edited with rapid cuts every two to three seconds?
cards.answer: To prioritise the sensation of energy and spectacle over letting the audience see any one performer's full movement clearly.

cards.front: What is the most common error the lesson identifies when comparing Singin' in the Rain and Grease?
cards.answer: Writing all of one film then all of the other, with a transitional sentence, instead of relating the two films within each paragraph.

cards.front: Name the five uses of glucose produced by photosynthesis in a plant.
cards.answer: Respiration to release energy / Converted to starch for storage / Converted to cellulose for cell walls / Combined with nitrates to make amino acids/proteins / Converted to lipids for storage in seeds
items: Converted to cellulose for cell walls
Combined with nitrates to make amino acids/proteins
Converted to lipids for storage in seeds

cards.front: What are the four steps of the iodine test for starch in a leaf?
cards.answer: Boil the leaf in water / Boil the leaf in ethanol to remove chlorophyll / Rinse the leaf in water / Add iodine solution
items: Boil the leaf in ethanol to remove chlorophyll

cards.front: Why does the rate of photosynthesis increase as light intensity increases (before it plateaus)?
cards.answer: More light energy is available for the light-dependent stage, so more water can be split and more glucose produced.

cards.front: Why does the rate of photosynthesis drop below the optimum temperature?
cards.answer: Molecules have less kinetic energy so they collide less frequently with enzyme active sites, slowing the reaction.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says Othello's suicide can be read.
cards.answer: Justice / Repentance / Hubris

cards.front: Name the three interpretations the lesson gives for Desdemona's 'Nobody; I myself' line.
cards.answer: Proof of saintly forgiveness / Ultimate expression of victim's conditioning under patriarchy / Both simultaneously
items: Ultimate expression of victim's conditioning under patriarchy

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Emilia's murder by Iago mirrors Othello's murder of Desdemona?
cards.answer: Both men kill women who threaten their control, showing a repeated pattern of male violence in the play.

cards.front: Why does the lesson describe the play's ending as 'hollow' despite Iago facing punishment?
cards.answer: Desdemona and Emilia are dead, Othello has destroyed himself, and Iago's silence leaves his true motivation unknown.

title: Uses and Dangers of Radiation, Fission and Fusion
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six precautions given for reducing radiation dose when handling sources.
cards.answer: Lead-lined containers / Tongs or remote handling / Minimising time near source / Maximising distance from source / Dosimetry badges / Minimum dose necessary for patients

cards.front: What are the three main engineering challenges to achieving fusion power?
cards.answer: Reaching and sustaining required temperature / Confining the plasma without touching walls / Achieving net energy gain
items: Confining the plasma without touching walls

cards.front: Why is beta radiation used for thickness gauging rather than alpha or gamma?
cards.answer: Alpha would be completely blocked by the material, while gamma would pass through unaffected by small thickness changes; beta partially penetrates, making it sensitive to thickness.

cards.front: Why is alpha contamination especially dangerous even though alpha can't penetrate skin from outside?
cards.answer: If inhaled or ingested, alpha particles are absorbed by internal organs at very short range, causing intense damage close to living cells.

cards.front: Why does Macbeth order Banquo's murder without telling Lady Macbeth?
cards.answer: He fears Banquo's noble nature and the prophecy that Banquo's descendants, not his, will be kings.

cards.front: How does the escape of Fleance affect the play's outcome?
cards.answer: The prophecy that Banquo's descendants will be kings remains intact, so Macbeth's murder achieves nothing.

cards.front: How does Macbeth manipulate the murderers he hires to kill Banquo?
cards.answer: He challenges their masculinity by questioning whether they are too pious to act against Banquo, copying Lady Macbeth's tactic.

cards.front: Name the three acts that show Ralph is capable of guilt and violence despite being the novel's hero.
cards.answer: Betrays Piggy's nickname / Participates in the mock hunt / Present at Simon's murder

cards.front: Name the three stages of Roger's arc across the novel's chapters.
cards.answer: Chapter 4: throws stones but deliberately misses / Chapter 11: murders Piggy with calculated precision / Chapter 12: sharpens a stick for Ralph's head
items: Chapter 4: throws stones but deliberately misses
Chapter 11: murders Piggy with calculated precision
Chapter 12: sharpens a stick for Ralph's head

cards.front: Why does Golding show Ralph committing acts of complicity and violence?
cards.answer: To prove that the darkness of man's heart exists even in the most civilised, most sympathetic character.

cards.front: Why is Roger presented as more dangerous than Jack?
cards.answer: Jack wants power and adulation, whereas Roger simply enjoys causing pain for its own sake.

cards.front: Name the three weaknesses of top-down strategies that the lesson gives for Mumbai.
cards.answer: Communities evicted with little notice or fair compensation / Slum-rehabilitation towers break up tight-knit migrant communities / Mega-projects overrun on cost and time (e.g. bullet train)
items: Communities evicted with little notice or fair compensation
Slum-rehabilitation towers break up tight-knit migrant communities
Mega-projects overrun on cost and time (e.g. bullet train)

cards.front: Name the three strengths of top-down strategies that the lesson gives for Mumbai.
cards.answer: Can shift millions of people quickly / Attract foreign investment and World Bank funding / National prestige projects give visible, politically useful results
items: Can shift millions of people quickly
Attract foreign investment and World Bank funding
National prestige projects give visible, politically useful results

cards.front: Why did Mumbai's first elevated coastal road cut journey times so much?
cards.answer: It bypassed the choked road system, turning a one-hour drive into 20 minutes and easing pressure off roads and rail.

cards.front: How does the Slum Rehabilitation Scheme get funded without costing the city money?
cards.answer: Private developers build rehousing blocks for slum dwellers in return for rights to build profitable luxury towers on the cleared land.

title: The Northern Rebellion, excommunication and the missionary threat
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What three grievances drove the earls to launch the Northern Rebellion, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Resented the 1559 religious settlement / Lost influence to southern Protestants / Plan to marry Mary to Duke of Norfolk
items: Plan to marry Mary to Duke of Norfolk

cards.front: Name the three Catholic plots against Elizabeth that the lesson says the 1570 bull fed into.
cards.answer: Ridolfi Plot (1571) / Throckmorton Plot (1583) / Babington Plot (1586)

cards.front: Why did Regnans in Excelsis turn English Catholics into a national-security problem for the regime?
cards.answer: It released Catholics from their oath of allegiance, so any recusant could now be seen as a potential traitor.

cards.front: Why did the 1585 Act make it treason for foreign-trained priests just to be in England?
cards.answer: After the bull, the regime assumed any secretly entering priest was working towards the queen's deposition.

cards.front: Name the three main types of board used in GCSE D&T.
cards.answer: Corrugated board / Folding boxboard (FBB) / Mounting board

cards.front: Besides laminating, name the three other finishing techniques mentioned for papers and boards.
cards.answer: Spot UV varnish / Embossing / Foil blocking

cards.front: Why does mechanical pulp paper yellow over time?
cards.answer: Because lignin remains in the fibres, unlike chemically produced pulp which has lignin removed.

cards.front: Why does recycled paper lose strength over successive recycling cycles?
cards.answer: Because each recycling cycle shortens the paper fibres slightly, weakening the sheet.

cards.front: Name the three main schemes the lesson gives for reducing unemployment under the Nazis.
cards.answer: RAD labour service / Autobahn road-building programme / Rapid rearmament from 1935

cards.front: Name the four school subjects/areas the lesson says were changed under Nazi education.
cards.answer: History / Biology / Physical education / Girls' education

cards.front: Why was the official unemployment figure of under one million by 1938 misleading?
cards.answer: Because women and Jewish workers were excluded from the count, so the true unemployment figure was higher.

cards.front: Why did Nazi policy towards women become contradictory by the late 1930s?
cards.answer: Rearmament expanded and the economy increasingly needed female labour, so women were quietly encouraged back into work despite the official domestic ideal.

cards.front: Why does Ralph feel a moment of existential dread when looking at the ocean in Chapter 7?
cards.answer: He realises the sea is 'the divider, the barrier', making him grasp for the first time that rescue may never come.

cards.front: How does the storm act symbolically after Simon's murder?
