cards.answer: It breaks the parachutist's body free and blows it out to sea, symbolically removing the 'beast', though the evil is already done.

cards.front: Name the three things the Good Friday Agreement (1998) established.
cards.answer: A power-sharing executive of unionist and nationalist parties / A North-South Ministerial Council / Commitments to human rights and decommissioning of weapons
items: A power-sharing executive of unionist and nationalist parties
Commitments to human rights and decommissioning of weapons

cards.front: Name the four areas of power given to the Scottish Parliament when it opened in 1999.
cards.answer: Health / Education / Justice / Local government

cards.front: Why was the 1979 Scottish devolution referendum result invalidated even though more people voted Yes than No?
cards.answer: A rule required 40% of the total electorate to vote Yes, and this threshold was not reached.

cards.front: Why did the 2010 general election lead to a coalition government?
cards.answer: No party won an overall majority, producing a hung Parliament, so the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats negotiated a coalition agreement.

title: Common Medical Conditions: Epilepsy & Sudden Cardiac Arrest
subject: cambridge-nationals-sport-science

cards.front: Name the three symptom areas of the body affected by an epileptic seizure, as listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Eyes / Mouth / Limbs

cards.front: What immediate steps should you take if a performer has a seizure?
cards.answer: Protect them from injury / Do not restrain them / Place in recovery position once convulsions stop / Stay with them / Call 999 if seizure lasts over 5 minutes or no consciousness
items: Place in recovery position once convulsions stop
Call 999 if seizure lasts over 5 minutes or no consciousness

cards.front: Why can intense physical activity trigger sudden cardiac arrest in some athletes?
cards.answer: It places extreme demand on an already abnormal heart in those with undetected underlying heart conditions.

cards.front: Why must you never put anything in the mouth of a performer having a seizure?
cards.answer: Because swallowing the tongue is not actually possible, so it is unnecessary and could cause harm.

title: Government, the Prime Minister and Cabinet
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the four mechanisms the lesson gives for holding government accountable.
cards.answer: Parliament (questions, debates, select committees) / National Audit Office checking public spending / Courts using judicial review / Elections removing an unpopular government
items: National Audit Office checking public spending

cards.front: Name the three cabinet positions the lesson gives as examples, with their areas of responsibility.
cards.answer: Chancellor of the Exchequer (economic policy and budget) / Home Secretary (policing, immigration, national security) / Foreign Secretary (international relations)
items: Chancellor of the Exchequer (economic policy and budget)

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the Prime Minister's role is hard to define legally?
cards.answer: Because the role has grown by convention rather than statute, with no single law defining it.

cards.front: Why is the separation between ministers and civil servants an important constitutional safeguard?
cards.answer: Ministers set policy while civil servants impartially implement it, keeping government running neutrally regardless of who is in power.

title: Sorting Algorithms: Bubble Sort and Merge Sort
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three advantages of bubble sort given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Simple to understand and implement / Sorts in place (no extra memory) / Can detect an already-sorted list early
items: Can detect an already-sorted list early

cards.front: Name the two advantages of merge sort given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Much faster for large datasets / Consistent performance regardless of initial order
items: Consistent performance regardless of initial order

cards.front: During a merge step in merge sort, how does the algorithm decide which item to place next?
cards.answer: It compares the first elements of the two sub-lists and picks the smaller one.

cards.front: Why is merge sort harder to implement than bubble sort?
cards.answer: It is more complex, using divide-and-conquer with splitting and merging, and needs extra memory for sub-lists.

cards.front: Name the three anthology poems the lesson pairs with 'Sonnet 29' for comparison.
cards.answer: 'Dusting the Phone' by Jackie Kay / 'Origin Story' by Eve L. Ewing / 'Catrin' by Gillian Clarke

cards.front: What three things should you focus on if 'Sonnet 29' is your specified poem?
cards.answer: the vine-and-tree conceit / the early volta / the closing paradox

cards.front: Why does the early volta in 'Sonnet 29' matter for understanding the speaker?
cards.answer: It shows the speaker correcting herself almost as soon as she notices the problem, not waiting for the form to catch up with her feelings.

cards.front: Why does the speaker stop thinking of her lover once he is truly present in 'Sonnet 29'?
cards.answer: Thinking usually arises from absence, but here presence itself satisfies what imagination could only approximate, so thought stops.

cards.front: Name the three poems studied in this lesson on Memory & Loss, with their poets.
cards.answer: 'Where the Picnic was' by Hardy / 'First Flight' by Fanthorpe / 'Absence' by Jennings

cards.front: How does Hardy's stanza structure in 'Where the Picnic was' reflect the speaker's emotion?
cards.answer: The short, clipped lines and shrinking stanzas give a controlled, restrained quality, showing the speaker holding back deeper emotion.

cards.front: How does the final stanza's 'earthquake tremor' work in Jennings's 'Absence'?
cards.answer: It breaks the poem's calm tone, showing the speaker's own thought about the absent person shaking the still scene.

cards.front: Why does Fanthorpe's shift in perspective in 'First Flight' end with 'At this height nothing lives'?
cards.answer: As the plane climbs, the familiar place becomes abstract and impersonal, ending in a distance where nothing recognisable remains.

cards.front: Name the three naturalist strategies the lesson identifies as shaping Rocks's aesthetic.
cards.answer: Available light / Hand-held cinema verite camera / Ensemble group framing

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three things make Rocks atypical of the social-realist tradition?
cards.answer: Black British teenage girl as lead / Multicultural female friendship group as social world / Female-majority crew
items: Black British teenage girl as lead
Multicultural female friendship group as social world

cards.front: Why is holding the whole friendship group in one ensemble shot a departure from conventional drama technique?
cards.answer: Conventional drama cuts to individual close-ups at emotional peaks to guide identification with one character, but Rocks refuses to single anyone out.

cards.front: Why does the score's arrival in the closing reunion scene mark it as emotionally significant?
cards.answer: The score has been minimal throughout, so its gentle non-diegetic rise in this otherwise score-free sequence signals significance without overwriting the moment.

title: The Origin of the Universe and Stewardship
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six things God creates in order in the Genesis 1 creation account.
cards.answer: Light / Sky / Land / Vegetation / Animals / Humanity

cards.front: What are the three stages of the universe's cycle in Hindu teaching?
cards.answer: Srishti (creation) / Sthiti (maintenance) / Pralaya (dissolution)

cards.front: Why do many religious thinkers argue that science and religion do not conflict over the universe's origin?
cards.answer: Because science answers the question 'how' the universe began while religion answers 'why', so both can be held together.

cards.front: Why does the Talmud's story of Honi teach Jewish environmental responsibility?
cards.answer: It shows a man planting a tree that takes seventy years to fruit, teaching that people should provide for future generations as others provided for them.

cards.front: The lesson names three ways Meena's identity crisis changed her behaviour after Sam's speech. What are they?
cards.answer: Becomes more reckless / More willing to follow Anita into danger / Less connected to her family
items: More willing to follow Anita into danger

cards.front: What three qualities did Meena once admire in Anita, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Toughness / Defiance / Freedom

cards.front: Why do immigrant families become scapegoats for Tollington's economic decline?
cards.answer: They are visible and different, so blaming them is easier than confronting the real economic causes of decline.

cards.front: How does Sam Lowbridge work as both a character and a symbol in the novel?
cards.answer: As a character he is shaped by poverty and lack of education, while as a symbol he represents wider racist forces threatening Meena's belonging.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why reported rates of mental health problems have increased over recent decades.
cards.answer: Increased challenges of modern living / Increased recognition of mental health problems / Lessening of social stigma
items: Increased recognition of mental health problems

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says cultural variations affect regarding mental health.
cards.answer: Help-seeking behaviour / Willingness to disclose symptoms / Type of treatment preferred

cards.front: Why can significant mental health problems damage a person's relationships?
cards.answer: Withdrawal, irritability or changes in behaviour make it hard to maintain friendships, romantic partnerships or family bonds.

cards.front: Why might untreated mental health conditions be linked to increased crime rates?
cards.answer: Individuals experiencing a mental health crisis may act in ways they otherwise would not.

cards.front: Name the five key offerings the lesson gives for puja.
cards.answer: Water (purification) / Flowers (beauty) / Incense (sweet fragrance rising to God) / Food/prasad (shared as blessing) / Light (arati lamp)

cards.front: What are the three core religious duties in Hinduism named in the lesson, alongside yajna (sacrifice)?
cards.answer: Yajna (sacrifice) / Dana (giving) / Tapas (austerity)

cards.front: How does the fire in havan purify participants and the space around them?
cards.answer: The fire burns away impurity while the smoke is believed to carry prayers upward to the deities.

cards.front: Why does puja focus on worshipping a murti rather than meditating directly on formless Brahman?
cards.answer: The Bhagavad Gita says meditating on unmanifest Brahman is difficult, so a murti gives an accessible route for devotees who relate to God in personal form.

cards.front: Name the three things Dolly Winthrop teaches Silas as his guide to parenthood.
cards.answer: How to care for a child / How to discipline gently / How to participate in community traditions like christening
items: How to care for a child
How to participate in community traditions like christening

cards.front: Name the three ways Silas learns to engage with village life after raising Eppie.
cards.answer: Attending church / Visiting neighbours / Celebrating festivals

cards.front: Why does Eliot contrast Dolly Winthrop's faith with the Lantern Yard congregation's?
cards.answer: Dolly uses religion to welcome and support, while Lantern Yard used it to judge and exclude, showing genuine faith is kindness not doctrine.

cards.front: Why does Godfrey's secret about Eppie eat at him for sixteen years after marrying Nancy?
cards.answer: His marriage to Nancy is childless, and Godfrey knows this is punishment for hiding that Eppie is his daughter.

cards.front: Name the six life stages in Pearson's model of human lifespan development.
cards.answer: Infancy / Early childhood / Adolescence / Early adulthood / Middle adulthood / Later adulthood

cards.front: Name the seven categories of factors that can affect growth and development given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Physical factors / Lifestyle factors / Emotional factors / Social factors / Cultural factors / Environmental factors / Economic factors

cards.front: Why is Component 3 described as a synoptic exam?
cards.answer: Because it draws on knowledge from Components 1 and 2 as well as the Component 3 content itself.

cards.front: How does social development typically change as someone moves through the life stages?
cards.answer: It moves from dependence on family, towards wider relationships, and in later life sometimes back to a smaller social circle.

cards.front: Name the three categories that props divide into in film analysis.
cards.answer: Functional (serve a practical purpose) / Symbolic (carry meaning beyond their literal use) / Signature (linked to one character's identity)
items: Symbolic (carry meaning beyond their literal use)

cards.front: Name the five elements the lesson says mise-en-scene encompasses.
cards.answer: Setting (sets and locations) / Props / Costume and wardrobe / Make-up / Performance and blocking of actors

cards.front: Why does a protagonist's costume shifting from dull, neutral tones to richer, saturated colours communicate character change?
cards.answer: The spectator absorbs the shift as signalling growing confidence or power even without consciously noticing it.

cards.front: Why might a production designer deliberately break period accuracy, such as putting modern trainers on a historical figure?
cards.answer: To make a statement about the universality or relevance of the story's themes to a modern audience.

cards.front: Name the four jobs the lesson says promotion does.
cards.answer: Inform / Persuade / Remind / Build brand image

cards.front: Besides point of sale and advertising, name the four other promotional methods on the specification.
cards.answer: Price reductions / Loss leaders / Competitions / Free samples

cards.front: Why does point-of-sale promotion work well at boosting sales?
cards.answer: It reaches the customer at the exact moment they are deciding what to buy, lifting impulse purchases.

cards.front: Why is Greggs' distribution almost entirely physical rather than digital?
cards.answer: Because a sausage roll needs to be eaten hot, so it must be sold and eaten in person.

title: The Second World War and American Recovery
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four home-front groups the lesson describes as being drawn into new roles or restrictions during the war (besides African-Americans and women).
cards.answer: Japanese-Americans interned under Executive Order 9066 / Mexican-American workers under the Bracero Programme / Native Americans including Navajo Code Talkers / Households under rationing
items: Mexican-American workers under the Bracero Programme
Native Americans including Navajo Code Talkers

cards.front: Why does the lesson argue that war spending ended the Depression when New Deal spending could not?
cards.answer: War spending reached $98 billion in 1944, about twenty times the New Deal's peak, and conscription removed 12 million men from the unemployment count.

cards.front: Why did A. Philip Randolph's threatened march on Washington in 1941 lead Roosevelt to act?
cards.answer: Randolph threatened the march unless Roosevelt banned discrimination in defence industries, so Roosevelt issued Executive Order 8802 to prevent it.

cards.front: Why were women's wartime job gains described as partial and contested?
cards.answer: Female wages were only around 60% of men's, and about 4 million women were dismissed after 1945 to make way for returning servicemen.

cards.front: Name the three things the Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes illegal.
cards.answer: Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system / Gaining access with intent to commit a further crime / Making unauthorised changes to data
items: Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system
Gaining access with intent to commit a further crime

cards.front: Under the Data Protection Act 2018, name the four things an organisation must do with personal data.
cards.answer: Keep it secure and accurate / Use it only for the reason it was collected / Keep it no longer than needed / Let people see the data held about them
items: Use it only for the reason it was collected
Keep it no longer than needed
Let people see the data held about them

cards.front: Why can being on the wrong side of the digital divide cause problems for someone?
cards.answer: They can miss out on jobs, education and services that are increasingly only available online.

cards.front: Why might a school with little money but skilled staff choose open source software?
cards.answer: To save on licence fees and to customise the software for their lessons.

title: Rock and Pop: The Features That Give the Style Away
subject: music-aqa

cards.front: Name the six individual features the lesson says you should listen for one at a time to identify rock or pop in an unfamiliar extract.
cards.answer: Line-up / Structure / Riff / Backbeat / Feel / Production

cards.front: Name the sections that can appear in a rock/pop verse-chorus form, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Intro / Verse / Chorus / Bridge / Middle eight

cards.front: How does layering build up the sound of a modern pop track?
cards.answer: Producers stack drums, bass, synth chords and vocal harmonies on top of each other, building the sound gradually across the track.

cards.front: Why is a middle eight often placed after the second chorus in a song?
cards.answer: It is a contrasting passage that takes the listener somewhere new, such as a different chord pattern, key change or texture drop, before the final chorus returns.

cards.front: Why does excess demand for a new games console (like the £300 launch) push its price up?
cards.answer: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so shoppers bid up the price until demand contracts and supply extends to restore equilibrium.

cards.front: Why does a rise in house prices lead to more homes being built over time?
cards.answer: High profits give construction firms an incentive to build, so resources flow into housebuilding until increased supply moderates the price rise.

cards.front: Name the six categories of performance-enhancing drugs the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Stimulants / Anabolic steroids / Narcotic analgesics / Peptide hormones (EPO/GH) / Diuretics / Beta blockers

cards.front: Name the four consequences of doping scandals for a sport described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Damaged public trust in results / Sponsors withdraw funding / Governing bodies divert resources to anti-doping / Clean athletes disadvantaged and harmed
items: Governing bodies divert resources to anti-doping

cards.front: Why do narcotic analgesics carry a risk of injuries worsening undetected?
cards.answer: They block pain signals, allowing athletes to keep training or competing on injuries without realising the damage is worsening.

cards.front: Why is the Biological Passport used instead of just testing for specific substances?
cards.answer: It monitors an athlete's blood values over time and flags abnormal fluctuations, catching doping methods that specific substance tests miss.

cards.front: Name the five sources of support the lesson identifies for coping with life events.
cards.answer: Family, friends, neighbours, partners / Professional carers and services / Community, voluntary and faith-based organisations / Multi-agency working / Multidisciplinary working

cards.front: Name the three types of life event the lesson groups events into.
cards.answer: Health and wellbeing events / Relationship changes / Life circumstances

cards.front: In Carol's bereavement case study, why is professional emotional support especially important for her?
cards.answer: Her low self-esteem means she may not believe she can cope alone, so professional emotional support is vital.

cards.front: Why does Carol's negative disposition affect the type of support she needs?
cards.answer: Because she focuses on problems rather than solutions, she needs encouragement to see progress from her daughter and church group.

cards.front: Name the three functions Pinnock's code-switching serves in Leave Taking.
cards.answer: Characterisation (reveals cultural position) / Thematic (mirrors heritage vs assimilation tension) / Dramatic (exposes Enid's contradiction)

cards.front: Name the two theatre productions the lesson cites as key to Leave Taking's critical reception.
cards.answer: 1994 National Theatre production / 2018 Bush Theatre revival

cards.front: Why should analysis of Leave Taking connect specific details to social and historical context?
cards.answer: Because top-band responses must explain not just what Pinnock shows but why she chose to show it, linking to Windrush-era experience.

cards.front: Why is Winsome Pinnock's own background significant to the context of Leave Taking?
cards.answer: She writes from within a community whose stories had been largely absent from mainstream British theatre.

title: Identifying Substances: Flame Tests and Gas Tests
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four gases the lesson gives specific chemical tests for.
cards.answer: Hydrogen / Oxygen / Carbon dioxide / Chlorine

cards.front: In the silver nitrate test for halide ions, what precipitate colour does each halide give?
cards.answer: Chloride - white precipitate / Bromide - cream precipitate / Iodide - yellow precipitate

cards.front: Why must the nichrome wire loop be cleaned in concentrated hydrochloric acid before a flame test?
cards.answer: To remove residues from previous tests, which could contaminate the sample and give a misleading colour result.

cards.front: Why can flame emission spectroscopy identify potassium in a mixture where a simple flame test cannot?
cards.answer: It produces a spectrum with separate lines for each metal, so sodium's intense colour can't mask potassium's lines.

cards.front: Why does a car's environmental impact come mainly from its use rather than its manufacture?
cards.answer: A car emits far more carbon dioxide over its driving lifetime than was released during manufacture.

cards.front: Why do minimum energy performance standards (MEPS) drive engineering innovation?
cards.answer: Governments set limits on appliance power consumption, forcing manufacturers to redesign motors, insulation and control systems to meet them.

cards.front: Give three malapropisms Dogberry uses in the play.
cards.answer: 'dissembly' for assembly / 'everlasting redemption' for damnation / 'aspicious' for suspicious

cards.front: Why does Leonato's belated challenge to Claudio raise uncomfortable questions?
cards.answer: It only comes after he already believes Hero is dead, following his own failure to defend her during the church scene.

cards.front: How does Claudio's reaction to learning the truth about Hero reveal his love is still superficial?
cards.answer: He speaks of Hero's 'image' and 'semblance' rather than expressing personal anguish, showing he still thinks in terms of appearance.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare's title 'Much Ado About Nothing' work as ironic commentary on the ending?
cards.answer: The characters treat the resolution as if nothing happened, but the audience knows the fractures the play exposed were never truly healed.

cards.front: Name the seven main biomes described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Tropical rainforest / Hot desert / Temperate forest / Tundra / Polar regions / Boreal forest (taiga) / Grasslands

cards.front: How does fertiliser runoff cause fish to suffocate in a pond ecosystem?
cards.answer: It causes an algal bloom that blocks sunlight, killing deeper plants, whose decomposition uses up oxygen, suffocating fish.

cards.front: Why does the global pattern of biomes follow latitude, such as rainforest at the equator and desert at 30°?
cards.answer: Because biomes are determined by climate, and climate follows the global atmospheric circulation system.

cards.front: How do nutrients return to the soil after plants and animals die?
cards.answer: Bacteria and fungi decompose the dead bodies chemically, releasing nutrients back into the soil as inorganic compounds.

title: Engineering Calculations: Area, Volume, Density and Pressure
subject: engineering-aqa

cards.front: Name the three area formulas given in the lesson (for rectangle, triangle and circle).
cards.answer: Rectangle: A = length × width / Triangle: A = ½ × base × height / Circle: A = πr²

cards.front: Name the five SI prefixes given in the lesson, with their multipliers.
cards.answer: milli = ×10⁻³ / centi = ×10⁻² / kilo = ×10³ / mega = ×10⁶ / giga = ×10⁹

cards.front: Why does a stiletto heel damage a wooden floor more than a flat shoe, for the same person's weight?
cards.answer: The same force is applied over a much smaller area, which concentrates it into a much higher pressure.

cards.front: Why do students often lose marks on calculation questions even when their arithmetic is correct?
cards.answer: They leave the answer in the wrong unit instead of converting to the required unit as the final step.

cards.front: Name the five components the lesson describes I–V characteristics for.
cards.answer: Fixed resistor / Filament lamp / Diode / Thermistor / LDR

cards.front: Why does a filament lamp not obey Ohm's law as current increases?
cards.answer: As current increases the filament heats up, which increases its resistance, so the I-V graph curves and flattens.

cards.front: Why does a diode's I-V graph show almost no current in reverse bias?
cards.answer: A diode only allows current to flow in one direction, so in reverse bias essentially no current flows.

cards.front: Why is the I-V graph for a fixed resistor a straight line through the origin?
cards.answer: Current is directly proportional to potential difference because the resistor's resistance stays constant, obeying Ohm's law.

title: Popular entertainment and fashion: from teddy boys to punk
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four youth subcultures the lesson lists appearing in Britain from the 1950s to the 1970s.
cards.answer: Teddy boys / Mods and Rockers / Hippies / Punks

cards.front: Name the four fashion features of teddy boys described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Drape jackets / Drainpipe trousers / Brothel creeper (crepe-soled) shoes / Quiff hairstyles

cards.front: Why did a distinct teenage consumer culture emerge in Britain in the 1950s?
cards.answer: Rising wages gave young workers disposable income for the first time, creating a new commercial culture of music, fashion and cinema aimed at them.

cards.front: Why did punk reject the hippie movement and progressive rock?
cards.answer: Punk was a violent reaction against hippie idealism's 'peace and love' message and against the pomposity and commercial success of progressive stadium rock.

cards.front: What three types of response to catastrophe does each main character represent in The War of the Worlds?
cards.answer: Practical endurance (narrator) / Religious collapse (curate) / Empty rhetoric (artilleryman)

cards.front: Why does Wells make the narrator write his account retrospectively?
cards.answer: It combines the immediacy of first-person experience with the authority of hindsight, creating tension between terror and calm analysis.

cards.front: Why is the narrator described as morally ambiguous rather than heroic?
cards.answer: He kills or knocks out the curate and struggles with cowardice, showing an ordinary man surviving rather than a traditional heroic protagonist.

cards.front: Why does the artilleryman's talk of selecting the 'able-bodied, clean-minded' feel disturbing?
cards.answer: It echoes Social Darwinist and eugenic thinking about dividing humanity into strong and weak, shown as seductive but hollow since he never acts.

title: Act 4: The Friar’s Plan and the Sleeping Potion
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the four steps of the Friar's plan to reunite Juliet and Romeo.
cards.answer: Juliet drinks a potion to fake death / Family places her in the Capulet tomb / Friar sends word to Romeo / Romeo rescues her and they flee to Mantua
items: Juliet drinks a potion to fake death
Family places her in the Capulet tomb
Romeo rescues her and they flee to Mantua

cards.front: Name the three adults who fail Juliet before she turns to the Friar.
cards.answer: Lord Capulet / Lady Capulet / The Nurse

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare create suspense around the Friar's plan in Act 4?
cards.answer: The plan is fragile and depends on perfect timing, so the audience, knowing the lovers will die, sees exactly how it can fail.

cards.front: Why does Lady Capulet refuse to help Juliet even though she may sympathise?
cards.answer: As a woman trapped by the same patriarchal system, she cannot oppose her husband publicly even if she privately sympathises.

cards.front: Name the three family relationships described as having failed or collapsed in the lesson's family theme.
cards.answer: Ed's marriage collapsed / Judy left Christopher and moved to London / Ed's relationship with Mrs Shears collapsed
items: Judy left Christopher and moved to London
Ed's relationship with Mrs Shears collapsed

cards.front: Why does discovering Ed's lies harm Christopher more than the truth would have?
cards.answer: Because Christopher values truth absolutely, so learning his father lied leads him to logically conclude his father might harm him.

cards.front: Why does Anne Brontë's own life as a governess matter for understanding 'The Bluebell'?
cards.answer: Her real experience of working away from home explains why the speaker's 'toilsome life' far from loved ones feels so heartfelt.

cards.front: How does the poem's word choice show the contrast between childhood and adult life?
cards.answer: Childhood is described with soft, warm words like 'kindred hearts', while the present uses hard, negative words like 'heartless' and 'thankless'.

cards.front: How does the structure of 'The Bluebell' move from general idea to personal memory?
cards.answer: The first two stanzas make a general statement about flowers, then 'Yet I recall not long ago' pivots into a specific narrated memory.

cards.front: Name the three other poems the lesson compares 'The Bluebell' with in the cluster.
cards.answer: Cold Knap Lake / Theme for English B / Happy Birthday Moon / Tea With Our Grandmothers

title: Development in a Developing or Emerging Country
subject: geography-edexcel-a

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why India's coastal and southern states form the economic core.
cards.answer: Access to ports for trade / Longer history of education investment / Better infrastructure / Stronger state governance

cards.front: Name the three government schemes the lesson gives as responses to the negative impacts of India's rapid development.
cards.answer: National Clean Air Programme / Swachh Bharat sanitation drive / Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana housing scheme
items: Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana housing scheme

cards.front: Why is female labour force participation in India so low, at around 27%?
cards.answer: It is held back by social expectations, safety concerns and limited childcare.

cards.front: How does the lesson say India's government makes megaprojects and welfare schemes work together most effectively?
cards.answer: By using tax revenue from megaprojects to fund welfare schemes, combining the scale of top-down projects with the fairness of bottom-up schemes.

cards.front: Name the four demands the Levellers made, as stated in the lesson.
cards.answer: a widened male franchise / equality before the law / freedom of conscience in religion / an end to arbitrary imprisonment

cards.front: Name the three other radical religious groups the lesson mentions besides the Quakers.
cards.answer: Ranters (denied sin and conventional morality) / Fifth Monarchists (believed Second Coming was imminent) / Muggletonians
items: Fifth Monarchists (believed Second Coming was imminent)

cards.front: Why did the New Model Army become a political as well as military force after 1645?
cards.answer: Its soldiers debated theology and read pamphlets, and religious ferment combined with grievances over pay and disbandment to politicise them.

cards.front: Why did Ireton want the vote restricted to property owners at the Putney Debates?
cards.answer: He feared that if all men could vote, the propertyless majority would use it to abolish property rights.

title: Planet Earth: Shape, Structure and Atmosphere
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five named parallels of latitude given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Equator (0°) / Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N) / Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S) / Arctic Circle (66.5° N) / Antarctic Circle (66.5° S)

cards.front: Why is the magnetosphere important for observers on Earth?
cards.answer: It deflects the solar wind, which would otherwise strip away Earth's atmosphere and expose the surface to harmful charged particles.

cards.front: Why does the magnetosphere have an asymmetrical teardrop shape?
cards.answer: Solar wind compresses it on the dayside facing the Sun and stretches it into a long magnetotail on the night-side.

cards.front: Why does the sky turn red and orange at sunset instead of staying blue?
cards.answer: The low Sun's light passes through a much thicker layer of atmosphere, scattering away nearly all the blue light and leaving reds and oranges.

title: The Civil War: Impact on Civilians
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four pieces of legislation the lesson gives that expanded federal power during the Civil War.
cards.answer: 1861 Revenue Act / 1862 Legal Tender Act / 1863 National Banking Act / Homestead Act and Pacific Railroad Act (1862)
items: Homestead Act and Pacific Railroad Act (1862)

cards.front: Name the three battles/turning points the lesson identifies as mattering most for civilians.
cards.answer: Antietam (September 1862) / Gettysburg (July 1863) / Vicksburg (July 1863)

cards.front: Why did working-class Northerners see conscription as a 'rich man's war and a poor man's fight'?
cards.answer: Because a wealthy man could pay $300 to avoid service or hire a substitute, while poorer men could not.

cards.front: Why did Sherman's March to the Sea target railroads, plantations and livestock rather than just Confederate armies?
cards.answer: His 'total war' strategy aimed to break Confederate civilian morale by destroying the economy and showing the war could reach them directly.

title: Nutritional Needs, Life Stages and Diet Planning
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: Name the four life stages the lesson covers in detail for changing nutritional needs.
cards.answer: Young children (1-5 years) / Teenagers / Adults / The elderly

cards.front: Name the five practical ways the lesson gives to reduce the cost of a balanced diet.
cards.answer: Planning meals in advance / Writing a shopping list / Using seasonal ingredients / Buying own-brand products / Avoiding food waste

cards.front: Why are elderly adults at higher risk of dehydration?
cards.answer: The sense of thirst becomes less reliable with age, so they may not notice they need fluids.

cards.front: Why should young children's meals be nutritionally dense rather than bulky?
cards.answer: Their stomachs are small but they need relatively high energy, protein, calcium and vitamin D for rapid growth.

cards.front: Why do professional programmers split large programs into many small subroutines instead of one long block of code?
cards.answer: Each subroutine can be tested independently (unit testing), so if a bug appears later, only that subroutine needs checking.

cards.front: Why can using too many global variables make a program harder to debug?
cards.answer: Because any part of the program can read or change a global variable unexpectedly, making unwanted changes hard to trace.

cards.front: Name the five main types of data retail businesses collect.
cards.answer: Sales revenue/turnover / Footfall / Stock/inventory data / Customer/loyalty data / Profit data

cards.front: Why might a retail manager use qualitative data alongside quantitative data when sales figures show a problem?
cards.answer: Quantitative data shows what is happening, but qualitative data like reviews or focus groups explains why, allowing a solution to be designed.

cards.front: Why is monitoring profit important, not just sales revenue, for a retail manager?
cards.answer: Profit shows what is left after costs, telling managers whether the business is genuinely succeeding rather than just busy.

title: Stolypin, the Dumas and Reform to 1914
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three structural problems the lesson gives for why the Dumas failed as parliaments.
cards.answer: State Council could veto Duma laws / Tsar controlled the army/navy/court budget / Deputies had no control over ministers
items: State Council could veto Duma laws
Deputies had no control over ministers

cards.front: Why did Nicholas II dissolve the Second Duma in June 1907?
cards.answer: He used a fabricated charge that Social Democrat deputies were plotting against him.

cards.front: How did the new electoral law after 1907 make the Third Duma one Stolypin could work with?
cards.answer: It gave one landlord vote the same weight as 260 peasant votes and 543 workers' votes, favouring the propertied classes.

cards.front: Why did Stolypin's land reform fail to fully solve peasant land hunger?
cards.answer: The poorest peasants often sold their consolidated plots and drifted back to the cities as proletarian recruits.

cards.front: Name the four impacts on sustainability that the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Transportation costs / Demand on natural resources / Pollution / Waste generated

cards.front: Name the four scales of production described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Batch production / Continuous production / One-off production / Mass production

cards.front: Why does crowd funding reduce financial risk for a designer compared with a bank loan?
cards.answer: It tests demand by collecting pledges before manufacturing, so money is only spent once demand is proven.

cards.front: How does just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing cut costs?
cards.answer: It orders stock only when needed for production, cutting the cost of storing large amounts of material.

cards.front: Name the four levels at which duality operates in the novella.
cards.answer: Character (Jekyll/Hyde) / Setting (respectable front/decayed laboratory) / Narrative (multiple perspectives) / Title ('Strange Case')

cards.front: Why did Jekyll's experiment to split good and evil ultimately fail?
cards.answer: Because good and evil are not separable — they are woven into the fabric of every person.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson's novella suggest science should be limited in exploring human nature?
cards.answer: Because although the chemistry works, it is the moral cost of ignoring boundaries that destroys Jekyll.

cards.front: Name the four functions of the family identified by Murdock in his 1949 study.
cards.answer: Sexual / Reproductive / Economic / Educational

cards.front: Name the three sociological perspectives that compete over what functions the family performs.
cards.answer: Functionalists (Murdock, Parsons) / Feminists (Oakley, Delphy and Leonard) / Marxists (Zaretsky, Engels)

cards.front: Why did Murdock conclude that the nuclear family is universal?
cards.answer: His study of 250 societies found the nuclear family present in every one, performing four essential functions.

cards.front: Why do Marxists argue the family acts as a unit of consumption under capitalism?
cards.answer: Because family members purchase goods and services that generate profit for the bourgeoisie.

cards.front: Name the four members of the Birling family analysed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Arthur Birling / Sybil Birling / Sheila Birling / Eric Birling

cards.front: What three things does Arthur Birling's concern in the play focus on throughout?
cards.answer: His potential knighthood / his family's social standing / avoiding a public scandal

cards.front: Why did Eric turn to alcohol and theft instead of asking his parents for help?
cards.answer: The family's obsession with appearances meant Eric felt he couldn't confide in his parents, so he drank and stole money secretly instead.

cards.front: How do Sheila's and Eric's reactions to the Inspector's message differ?
cards.answer: Sheila's awakening is intellectual and moral, understanding the systemic problem, while Eric's is emotional and instinctive, driven by guilt and anger.

cards.front: Name the four forms the 'beast' takes as it evolves through the novel.
cards.answer: Beastie or snake-thing (littluns' nightmare) / Beast from water / Beast from air (the dead parachutist) / The Lord of the Flies itself
items: The Lord of the Flies itself

cards.front: What four locations does Golding map onto his philosophical argument, and what does each represent?
cards.answer: Beach and platform - democratic, open governance / Castle Rock - tyranny / Mountain - truth and knowledge / Jungle - the unknown and darkness within
items: Beach and platform - democratic, open governance
Jungle - the unknown and darkness within

cards.front: Why does Golding make Piggy's death happen at the same moment as the conch's destruction?
cards.answer: He binds the symbol and its champion together, showing that democracy and rational thought rise and fall as one.

cards.front: How does Golding use face paint to invert colonial assumptions about 'savages'?
cards.answer: Victorian literature linked face paint to primitive non-European 'savages', so by having British schoolboys wear it, Golding shows the 'civilised' become the savages.

cards.front: Name the five roles religious houses played in local communities before 1535.
cards.answer: Landlords renting out farms / Employers of servants and labourers / Hosts for travellers / Schools for gentry's sons / Almoners giving food to the poor
items: Almoners giving food to the poor

cards.front: Name the three historians' explanations the lesson gives for the dissolutions.
cards.answer: Bernard: Henry's personal greed and suspicion of independent institutions / MacCulloch: Cromwell's genuine evangelical reforming conviction / National Archives: long fiscal afterlife creating a gentry landowning class
items: Bernard: Henry's personal greed and suspicion of independent institutions
MacCulloch: Cromwell's genuine evangelical reforming conviction
National Archives: long fiscal afterlife creating a gentry landowning class

cards.front: Why did the crown sell off most monastic land instead of keeping it?
cards.answer: Selling raised cash for war and bound gentry, lawyers and merchants to the Reformation, as they'd lose land if Catholicism returned.

cards.front: How did the Pilgrimage of Grace lead to the fall of the larger monasteries?
cards.answer: After it was crushed in 1537 and abbots were implicated, larger houses lost political protection and were pressured into surrendering with pensions.

cards.front: Name the two themes the lesson gives for Ozymandias besides the power of art.
cards.answer: Power of nature over human power / Transience of political power
items: Power of nature over human power

cards.front: Why does the sibilance in 'Half sunk, a shattered visage lies' matter?
cards.answer: It creates a sense of violent destruction, showing time has erased even the most powerful figures.

cards.front: Why is 'the hand that mocked them' ambiguous?
cards.answer: 'Mocked' can mean the sculptor imitated the king's expressions or ridiculed him, enriching the poem's exploration of power.

cards.front: How does Ozymandias compare to London in exploring power?
cards.answer: Both criticise abuse of power, Shelley through the ancient tyrant and Blake through Georgian London's institutions, showing oppressive power is destructive.

cards.front: Name the seven stages Doyle uses to structure the pacing of The Sign of Four.
cards.answer: Slow beginning / Mystery builds / Revelation / Shock / Investigation / Climax / Resolution

cards.front: Why does Doyle use real Victorian fog symbolically in The Sign of Four?
cards.answer: Fog obscures, distorts and confuses, representing the appearance versus reality theme that nothing is what it first seems.

cards.front: Why does the Agra treasure ending up in the Thames suit the novel's themes?
cards.answer: The treasure is swallowed by the same waterway that connects London to the empire it was stolen from.

cards.front: Name the three ways electronic systems can be represented.
cards.answer: System block diagram / Circuit schematic / PCB layout

cards.front: What four steps should you follow to complete a partially drawn block diagram in an exam?
cards.answer: Identify blocks already drawn and their stage / Identify what is missing / Work out each empty block's function / Draw signal arrows between every block
items: Identify blocks already drawn and their stage
Work out each empty block's function
Draw signal arrows between every block

cards.front: Why is the freezer temperature alarm system classed as closed loop?
cards.answer: The microcontroller continuously reads the thermistor's output, checking and re-checking temperature rather than acting once, creating a feedback loop.

cards.front: How do you tell if a missing block in a diagram is an input block?
cards.answer: It is an input block if it converts an environmental signal, like temperature, into an electrical signal.

cards.front: Name the three caskets Portia's suitors must choose between.
cards.answer: Gold / Silver / Lead

cards.front: What two grievances does Shylock have against Antonio, beyond religion and money?
cards.answer: publicly humiliated by Antonio / daughter Jessica betrayed him / cultural identity under constant assault

cards.front: Why does Shylock hate Antonio?
cards.answer: Antonio is a Christian who has humiliated him publicly, and he lends money for free, undercutting Shylock's livelihood.

cards.front: Why do the Prince of Morocco and Prince of Arragon both fail the casket test?
cards.answer: They are guided by surface appearances and self-importance rather than true worth, choosing gold and silver over lead.

cards.front: What three specific charitable actions does Scrooge take at the start of Stave 5?
cards.answer: Buys the prize turkey for the Cratchits / Donates generously to the charity collectors / Goes to Fred's for dinner
items: Buys the prize turkey for the Cratchits
Donates generously to the charity collectors

cards.front: Why does Dickens refuse to show the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come's face or form?
cards.answer: By describing it only in the negative, Dickens denies the reader reassurance, making it the most frightening spirit.

cards.front: Why does seeing his own name on the gravestone affect Scrooge more than the earlier warnings?
cards.answer: It moves the abstract idea of death into sensory, undeniable reality, forcing him to speak the pledge of change himself.

cards.front: How does the novella's cyclical structure support Dickens's argument that people can change?
cards.answer: The ending circles back to the Christmas-story frame, moving Scrooge from mean to generous, arguing change is possible for anyone.

cards.front: Name the five stages of Rostow's model.
cards.answer: Traditional society / Preconditions for take-off / Take-off / Drive to maturity / High mass consumption

cards.front: Name the four organisations that partnered to fund Nigeria's polio vaccination teams.
cards.answer: World Health Organization / UNICEF / Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation / Rotary International

cards.front: Why did falling oil prices in 2014 and 2020 cause Nigeria to fall into recession?
cards.answer: Because oil supplies most government income, so falling prices weakened the naira and pushed the economy into recession.

cards.front: Why do most geographers place Nigeria at stage 3, 'take-off', of Rostow's model?
cards.answer: Because a few sectors like oil, telecoms and fintech are growing fast, infrastructure is improving, and a small middle class has appeared.

cards.front: Why is a trained 5,000 m runner racing at full pace still working aerobically, even though the intensity is high?
cards.answer: Because oxygen delivery keeps pace with demand throughout the multi-minute race, so it can be sustained aerobically.

cards.front: Why is a basketball player's overall fitness classed as predominantly aerobic despite frequent explosive sprints and jumps?
cards.answer: Because most of the match is spent jogging and walking, even though critical moments demand anaerobic bursts.

cards.front: Why does a designer use both sketching and modelling when generating ideas, rather than just one?
cards.answer: Sketching is fast and cheap for exploring many forms, but modelling reveals fit, proportions and interference that sketching cannot show.

cards.front: Why does the iterative cycle restart if a manufactured prototype does not meet the specification?
cards.answer: The designer returns to the design stage to modify the idea and make a revised prototype until it meets all criteria.

cards.front: How does a model differ from a prototype in the iterative design process?
cards.answer: A model tests specific aspects like proportions before full manufacture, while a prototype is a working version evaluated against the whole brief and specification.

title: DNA Structure, Cloning and the History of Genetics
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four steps of genetic engineering used to make a genetically modified organism.
cards.answer: Cut out desired gene with restriction enzymes / Insert gene into a vector / Vector carries gene into target cells / Target organism expresses new gene, makes protein
items: Cut out desired gene with restriction enzymes
Vector carries gene into target cells
Target organism expresses new gene, makes protein

cards.front: Name the four steps of adult cell cloning used to create Dolly the sheep.
cards.answer: Nucleus from adult cell removed / Nucleus inserted into enucleated egg cell / Electric shock stimulates egg to divide / Embryo implanted into surrogate mother
items: Nucleus inserted into enucleated egg cell
Electric shock stimulates egg to divide

cards.front: Why was Mendel's work on inheritance not recognised until the early 1900s?
cards.answer: Because the mechanism of inheritance, chromosomes and DNA, had not yet been discovered when he published his work.

cards.front: Why does plant tissue culture cloning produce genetically identical plants?
cards.answer: Small groups of cells taken from a plant are grown in a sterile medium with nutrients and hormones, so each develops into an identical copy.

cards.front: Name the three things Orwell's use of allegory achieves, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Makes complex politics accessible through familiar characters / Creates emotional engagement with the story / Achieves universality beyond Russia
items: Makes complex politics accessible through familiar characters
Creates emotional engagement with the story

cards.front: Name the three specific luxury items in the farmhouse that symbolise privileges the revolution was meant to abolish.
cards.answer: Beds / China / Whisky

cards.front: Why is the farm itself described as a microcosm in Animal Farm?
cards.answer: Its closed boundaries let Orwell trace the full arc of a society from rebellion to tyranny in one contained world.

cards.front: How does Minimus's replacement anthem show that cultural control serves political power?
cards.answer: It replaces 'Beasts of England' with a bland song about the farm, hiding the gap between promises and reality.

cards.front: Name the four activities included in Hector's general studies lessons.
cards.answer: Reciting poetry / Re-enacting scenes from films / Singing songs / Debating ideas

cards.front: What three things does Hector's 'passing the parcel' metaphor reveal about his teaching?
cards.answer: He is part of a chain from his own teachers / Knowledge is not for anything, just passed on / He hands it on to people he'll never meet
items: He is part of a chain from his own teachers
Knowledge is not for anything, just passed on
He hands it on to people he'll never meet

cards.front: Why is the Headmaster so eager to sack Hector once the abuse is revealed?
cards.answer: He resents that Hector's teaching produces results he cannot measure, so the abuse gives him a convenient excuse to remove him.

cards.front: Why does Irwin tell the boys to argue that the dissolution of the monasteries was a good thing?
cards.answer: To demonstrate contrarian thinking — arguing against the obvious, even the indefensible, to stand out to Oxbridge examiners.

cards.front: Name the four sampling methods the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Random sampling / Stratified sampling / Volunteer sampling / Opportunity sampling

cards.front: Name the three research designs the lesson identifies for organising participants across conditions.
cards.answer: Independent measures / Repeated measures / Matched pairs

cards.front: Why does using different participants in each condition (independent measures) avoid order effects?
cards.answer: Because each participant only takes part once, so there is no practice or fatigue across conditions.

cards.front: Why is stratified sampling likely to produce a highly representative sample?
cards.answer: Because it divides the population into subgroups and selects participants from each in proportion to their size.

cards.front: Name the five steps of the systematic fault-finding approach described in the lesson, in order.
cards.answer: Visually inspect the circuit / Check the power supply with a multimeter / Use a continuity tester on connections / Measure voltage stage by stage / Use an oscilloscope on waveforms
items: Check the power supply with a multimeter
Use a continuity tester on connections

cards.front: How must a multimeter's probes be connected to measure voltage across a component?
cards.answer: The probes are placed across (in parallel with) the component being measured.

cards.front: Why can't a multimeter be used to test rapidly changing or high-frequency AC signals?
cards.answer: A multimeter cannot capture rapidly changing signals, so an oscilloscope is needed instead.

cards.front: How do you find the peak-to-peak voltage of a waveform from an oscilloscope trace?
cards.answer: Count the vertical divisions from the lowest to highest point of the wave and multiply by the volts/div setting.

cards.front: What three themes does the lesson identify in 'Love After Love'?
cards.answer: Self-love as recovery / Neglect and return / Ritual

cards.front: Name the four anthology poems given as comparison partners for 'Love After Love'.
cards.answer: Poem for My Love / The Perseverance / Flirtation / Lullaby

cards.front: Why does Walcott use second-person address ('you') throughout 'Love After Love'?
cards.answer: It makes the poem feel like direct advice or a personal promise, collapsing the 'you' addressed and the welcomed self into one person.

cards.front: How does the poem's free verse form suit its theme of breaking old patterns?
cards.answer: Free verse refuses the tight, repeating shapes that might suggest an unchanging relationship, keeping movement forward before tightening into short commands.

cards.front: Why does alpha decay only happen in large, heavy nuclei?
cards.answer: Because the nucleus is too big to remain stable, so it ejects an alpha particle to become more stable.

cards.front: Why is gamma radiation often emitted after alpha or beta decay?
cards.answer: The daughter nucleus is left in an excited energy state and releases the excess energy as gamma radiation.

cards.front: In nuclear equations, what must balance on both sides?
cards.answer: The total mass number on both sides must match, and the total atomic number on both sides must match.

title: How Citizens Bring About Political Change
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the three levels at which political campaigns can take place, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Local / National / International

cards.front: Name the five methods campaigners use, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Social media / Press releases / Rallies / Door-knocking / Producing written materials

cards.front: Why does digital exclusion concern critics of digital democracy?
cards.answer: Older citizens, disabled people, or those without internet access may find digital channels harder to use, so some voices are heard less.

cards.front: Why is standing for election seen as one of the most direct forms of democratic participation?
cards.answer: It places an individual in a position to make decisions, scrutinise legislation, and represent a constituency.

title: Spitalfields: Irish, Jewish and Bangladeshi communities
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three main types of work Irish migrants did in Spitalfields.
cards.answer: Dock labourers / Street sellers / Casual labouring trades

cards.front: Name the four trades/occupations Jewish migrants worked in around Spitalfields.
cards.answer: Garment trade / Furniture-making / Cabinet-making / Market traders

cards.front: Why did Irish migrants in Spitalfields face hostility from English workers?
cards.answer: Irish workers competed with English labourers for scarce casual work in the East End docks.

cards.front: Why is the repeated conversion of the Brick Lane building (chapel to synagogue to mosque) significant to historians?
cards.answer: It shows the physical layering of different migrant communities succeeding one another in the same building.

cards.front: Name the three types of paper named in the specification.
cards.answer: Copier paper / Cartridge paper / Tracing paper

cards.front: Name the three working properties used to compare papers and boards.
cards.answer: Flexibility / Printability / Biodegradability

cards.front: Why does folding boxboard crease cleanly without cracking?
cards.answer: It is a lightweight multi-layer board with a bulky mechanical-pulp core between two bleached chemical-pulp liners, giving stiffness at low weight.

cards.front: How does plywood become strong in every direction?
cards.answer: It is built from thin veneer layers glued with the grain of each layer running at right angles to the next.

cards.front: Name the six key methods the lesson lists as applied to crime and stratification research.
cards.answer: Official crime statistics / Crime Survey for England and Wales / Self-report studies / Ethnographic observation / Surveys (e.g. Townsend on poverty) / Longitudinal studies
items: Crime Survey for England and Wales

cards.front: Why does the Crime Survey for England and Wales still under-represent some crimes despite capturing more offending than official statistics?
cards.answer: It misses crimes with no individual victim like corporate crime and drug supply, and crimes victims can't or won't disclose, like domestic violence.

cards.front: Why did Townsend's questionnaire findings on poverty raise questions about validity?
cards.answer: Critics questioned whether the absence of certain foods or activities showed real deprivation or just personal choice or cultural difference.

cards.front: Why is Fiona Devine's return to Luton considered a restudy rather than a true longitudinal study?
cards.answer: She interviewed a fresh sample of workers rather than following the same people over time, so it shows change without tracking individuals.

title: Particle Model: Density, States and the Gas Laws
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three steps for measuring the density of a liquid in the core practical.
cards.answer: Measure mass of empty container / Add liquid and measure combined mass / Pour liquid into measuring cylinder to find volume
items: Add liquid and measure combined mass
Pour liquid into measuring cylinder to find volume

cards.front: Why does increasing the temperature of a gas increase its pressure?
cards.answer: Particles move faster and hit the container walls harder and more often.

cards.front: Why does decreasing the volume of a gas increase its pressure, according to the kinetic model?
cards.answer: Particles collide with the walls more frequently because they travel shorter distances between collisions.

cards.front: Name the five other anthology poems the lesson pairs with Boat Stealing for comparison.
cards.answer: Songs for the People / Colonization in Reverse / Papa-T / We Lived Happily during the War / Thirteen
items: We Lived Happily during the War

cards.front: Which three short quotable phrases does the lesson recommend memorising for exam use?
cards.answer: troubled pleasure / like a living thing / unknown modes of being

cards.front: Why does Wordsworth tell Boat Stealing through an adult narrator looking back on a boyhood memory?
cards.answer: The retrospective narration lets him frame a simple childhood incident as the origin of the idea that nature shapes a person's growth of mind and conscience.

cards.front: Why does the calm, graceful imagery at the start of the poem matter for the cliff's appearance?
cards.answer: The calm imagery of the boat moving like a swan makes the sudden, shocking appearance of the huge cliff feel far more dramatic.

cards.front: Name the four tenses the Spanish specification expects you to use when discussing technology.
cards.answer: present / preterite / imperfect / future

cards.front: Give the three disadvantages of technology listed about signal, cost and safety.
cards.answer: A veces la señal puede ser débil / Puede ser cara / Hay sitios peligrosos
items: A veces la señal puede ser débil

cards.front: How do you form the perfect tense in Spanish for regular -ar verbs like comprar?
cards.answer: Use haber plus the past participle, formed by changing -ar to -ado, e.g. he comprado.

cards.front: How can you structure a balanced argument about technology in Spanish?
cards.answer: Use por un lado… por otro lado… (on one hand… on the other hand…) to present both sides.

title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three steps in the practical to make a pure, dry salt from an acid and an insoluble base.
cards.answer: Add excess base or metal oxide to the acid / Filter off the excess solid / Evaporate water from the filtrate to leave crystals
items: Add excess base or metal oxide to the acid
Evaporate water from the filtrate to leave crystals

cards.front: Why is an excess of insoluble base or metal oxide added to the acid when making a salt?
cards.answer: To make sure all the acid reacts, so no acid is left in the final salt solution.

cards.front: Name the five pricing methods covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Price skimming / Penetration pricing / Competitive pricing / Loss leader / Cost-plus

cards.front: Name the four factors that influence a business's pricing decisions.
cards.answer: Costs / Nature of the market / Degree of competition / Product life cycle stage

cards.front: Why does a strong brand image make it easier for a business to launch new products?
cards.answer: Customers already trust the established brand name, so they are willing to try its new products, as with Apple's move into phones and watches.

cards.front: Why do businesses carry out market research before launching a new product?
cards.answer: To reduce the risk of the new product failing before the business commits cash to it.

cards.front: What are the four combinations of reinforcement and punishment in operant conditioning?
cards.answer: Positive reinforcement / Negative reinforcement / Positive punishment / Negative punishment

cards.front: Why might approval from a peer group keep a young offender's criminal behaviour going?
cards.answer: It acts as a powerful secondary reinforcer, giving learned rewards like praise and status that reinforce the behaviour.

cards.front: Why might a younger sibling copy an older sibling's shoplifting without being rewarded themselves?
cards.answer: Vicarious reinforcement means seeing someone else rewarded for a behaviour makes the observer more likely to copy it.

cards.front: Why is it a weakness that the Bobo doll study used a doll rather than a real victim?
cards.answer: The artificial setting means findings may lack validity when generalised to real aggressive or criminal behaviour outside the laboratory.

cards.front: Name the four creative concepts the lesson says shape how sounds are arranged for media.
cards.answer: Texture / Mood / Style / Impact

cards.front: Name the five export formats the lesson explains for finished audio/video.
cards.answer: MP4 / MOV / MP3 / WAV / AIF (AIFF)

cards.front: Why do sound designers create contrast between high-impact and low-impact sounds in a scene?
cards.answer: Contrasting a loud, attention-grabbing sound with a quiet background one creates drama.

cards.front: How is the final audio combined with the video file for delivery?
cards.answer: The DAW or video editor bounces the finished audio mix and embeds it into the video container, such as MP4 or MOV.

title: Consumerism, coffee houses and political activism
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three things London's coffee houses were centres of, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Political debate / Commerce (e.g. Lloyd's marine insurance) / Press culture (newspapers read aloud)

cards.front: Name the six types of workers/industries the lesson says participated indirectly in the slave trade in Britain's slave ports.
cards.answer: Shipbuilders / Rope-makers / Ironmongers / Textile merchants / Insurance brokers / Dock workers

cards.front: Why did ideas of racial hierarchy become more systematised in British thought from the late seventeenth century?
cards.answer: Because the slave trade required ideological justification, so ideas classifying people by skin colour with different capacities and rights developed.

cards.front: How did journals like The Spectator reach a wide readership in the 1710s and 1720s?
cards.answer: Through coffee houses, where copies were passed from reader to reader.

cards.front: Name the four ways given in the lesson to increase the rate of a reaction.
cards.answer: Raising temperature / Increasing concentration (or pressure for gases) / Increasing surface area of solid reactants / Using a catalyst
items: Increasing surface area of solid reactants

cards.front: Name the three common methods the lesson gives for measuring reaction rate.
cards.answer: Gas collection / Mass loss / Colour/turbidity change

cards.front: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of reaction, according to collision theory?
cards.answer: Particles gain more kinetic energy, move faster and collide more often, with a greater proportion exceeding the activation energy.

cards.front: Why does increasing concentration increase the rate of reaction?
cards.answer: More particles in a given volume means collisions between reactant particles happen more frequently.

title: The Trinity and the Nicene Creed
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three persons of the Trinity and the role the lesson gives each.
cards.answer: Father - creator and sustainer of all things / Son - incarnate Word who redeems humanity / Holy Spirit - presence of God active in the world
items: Father - creator and sustainer of all things
Son - incarnate Word who redeems humanity
Holy Spirit - presence of God active in the world

cards.front: Why did the Council of Constantinople (381 CE) refine the Nicene Creed?
cards.answer: To add a fuller statement on the Holy Spirit, reaching the form Catholics recite at Mass today.

cards.front: Why does the play's non-linear structure create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: The audience learns future outcomes, like Irwin's wheelchair and Hector's death, before the characters live through them.

cards.front: How does Posner use the song 'Bewitched, Bothered, and Bewildered' to express himself?
cards.answer: He channels his unrequited love for Dakin through the song's lyrics about helpless infatuation, since he cannot say it directly.

title: Sit-Ins, Freedom Riders and James Meredith, 1960-62
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three types of abuse sit-in students were trained to absorb without responding.
cards.answer: Verbal abuse / lit cigarettes pushed into their hair / food poured over them
items: Lit cigarettes pushed into their hair

cards.front: Name the three campaigns of 1960-62 that forced the federal government to enforce a Supreme Court ruling Southern states were ignoring.
cards.answer: The Greensboro sit-ins / the Freedom Riders / the Meredith/Ole Miss case

cards.front: Why did press photographs of the Greensboro sit-ins help persuade public opinion?
cards.answer: They showed well-dressed students sitting calmly while white teenagers screamed abuse at them.

cards.front: Why was Robert Kennedy forced to send federal marshals to protect the Freedom Riders after Anniston?
cards.answer: Photographs of the firebombed bus and Birmingham beatings were broadcast worldwide, forcing federal action despite his reluctance.

cards.front: Name Macbeth's five character stages across the play, as the lesson traces his arc.
cards.answer: Act 1: celebrated warrior with dangerous ambition / Act 2: reluctant murderer consumed by guilt / Act 3: paranoid king who plans murder alone / Act 4: tyrant who massacres innocents / Act 5: nihilistic, despairing figure who dies fighting
items: Act 1: celebrated warrior with dangerous ambition
Act 2: reluctant murderer consumed by guilt
Act 3: paranoid king who plans murder alone
Act 5: nihilistic, despairing figure who dies fighting

cards.front: Why does Banquo's caution about the witches' prophecies not make him a simple moral paragon?
cards.answer: He suspects Macbeth of foul play after the murder but does nothing to act on his suspicions, and thinks about his own descendants becoming kings.

cards.front: Why does Malcolm test Macduff by pretending to be lustful, greedy and lacking every kingly virtue?
cards.answer: It is political shrewdness to check Macduff's loyalty before trusting him, showing Malcolm's careful judgement.

title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps: The March
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: According to Passage A, what two reasons does Livy give for the Second Punic War being the most memorable war ever fought?
cards.answer: Both sides equally strong in resources and manpower / The two nations fought with unusual hatred
items: Both sides equally strong in resources and manpower
The two nations fought with unusual hatred

cards.front: Why does Livy include the story of Hannibal's childhood oath?
cards.answer: It explains Hannibal's lifelong hostility to Rome as instilled in childhood and foreshadows that he will never turn back.

cards.front: How does the hyperbaton in Passage E, delaying 'montani' to the last word, create suspense?
cards.answer: It stops the reader knowing who threatens the column until the final word, recreating the soldiers' own fear as danger appears above them.

cards.front: Why did veteran soldiers believe 'Hamilcarem iuvenem redditum esse sibi' when they saw Hannibal?
cards.answer: Because Hannibal's face and manner were so like his father's that it felt as if a young Hamilcar had been given back to them.

cards.front: Name the six key themes the lesson identifies in My Name is Leon.
cards.answer: Racism and the care system / Family and separation / Identity and belonging / Childhood, neglect and innocence / Class and poverty / The 1981 riots — resistance and voice

cards.front: Why does De Waal draw a parallel between Leon and the Black community in the riots theme?
cards.answer: Both are silenced — Leon by a system that doesn't listen to children, the community by a state that doesn't listen to citizens.

cards.front: How does De Waal use Leon's identity to make a political point?
cards.answer: Mixed-race children placed with white families who couldn't build a positive racial identity often felt they belonged nowhere.

cards.front: What two joining words does the lesson say you should use to give a reason after an opinion in French?
cards.answer: parce que (because) / car (as/because)

cards.front: Name the two French school stages given in the lesson, with their age ranges.
cards.answer: le collège (ages 11-15) / le lycée (ages 15-18)

cards.front: Why must the adjective change between 'Le prof est strict' and 'La prof est stricte'?
cards.answer: Because adjectives must agree in gender with the noun they describe.

cards.front: Why do French students have a longer lunch break than English students, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because French law requires a lunch break of at least 90 minutes.

title: Cattle's End, the Range Wars and Frontier Law and Order
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four developments the lesson gives that turned the High Plains into a wheat-growing region within a decade.
cards.answer: Mechanical reaper and combine harvester / John Deere's steel plough / Refrigerated railcars / Bonanza farms of the Dakotas

cards.front: Why did British investors pull their money out of Wyoming and Montana ranching within months of spring 1887?
cards.answer: The spring thaw revealed valleys filled with rotting cattle carcasses, showing the Big Die-Up had devastated their herds.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the OK Corral gunfight was not simply a case of law versus lawlessness?
cards.answer: It was a fight inside the law, between Earp's town marshals and the Clantons' rural cattle interests, not an absence of law.

title: The Buddha and the Four Noble Truths
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: What are the three forms of craving (tanha) the Buddha identified?
cards.answer: Craving for sense pleasures / Craving for existence (wanting things to continue) / Craving for non-existence (wanting things to stop)
items: Craving for existence (wanting things to continue)
Craving for non-existence (wanting things to stop)

cards.front: What are the three parts of the Threefold Way that structure the Eightfold Path?
cards.answer: Ethics / Meditation / Wisdom

cards.front: Why is ignorance (moha) considered the deepest of the Three Poisons?
cards.answer: Because it produces the false belief in a fixed, permanent self, from which greed and hatred then arise.

cards.front: Why did Siddhartha abandon the path of extreme asceticism after nearly dying from it?
cards.answer: He recognised that extreme self-mortification, like extreme luxury, would not lead to liberation, so he sought a balanced Middle Way.

cards.front: Name the four levels of Regency society's social hierarchy, from top to bottom.
cards.answer: Aristocracy / Landed gentry / Professionals / Servants and labourers

cards.front: Why is Mrs Bennet's frantic matchmaking not simply comic?
cards.answer: Because entailment means she and her daughters will lose their home and income when Mr Bennet dies, so marriage is a survival strategy.

cards.front: Why does Mr Collins propose to Elizabeth?
cards.answer: Partly to 'make amends' for inheriting the Bennet estate that would otherwise have gone to the daughters.

cards.front: Name the three reasons Mr Collins gives for proposing to Elizabeth (without ever mentioning love).
cards.answer: Lady Catherine's approval / his duty as a clergyman / the entail

cards.front: How does Austen use Wickham as a foil to Darcy?
cards.answer: Wickham is charming but morally bankrupt while Darcy seems proud but is genuinely honourable, reversing first impressions.

cards.front: Why is Darcy's letter the novel's structural turning point?
cards.answer: It reveals Wickham's true character and forces Elizabeth to recognise her own prejudice, splitting the novel into before and after.

title: The Solar System: Planets, Dwarf Planets and Small Bodies
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five recognised dwarf planets in the Solar System.
cards.answer: Pluto / Ceres / Eris / Haumea / Makemake

cards.front: Name the three distance units used in astronomy.
cards.answer: Astronomical unit (AU) / Light year (ly) / Parsec (pc)

cards.front: Why does Venus have the highest surface temperature of any planet, despite not being closest to the Sun?
cards.answer: Venus has an extreme greenhouse effect, which raises its surface temperature to about 460°C regardless of its distance from the Sun.

cards.front: Why did the rocky material in the asteroid belt never accrete into a planet?
cards.answer: Jupiter's strong gravitational influence constantly stirred the region, preventing the remnant planetesimals from accreting into a planet.

cards.front: Name the three forces the lesson says drove twentieth-century medical advances.
cards.answer: New scientific discoveries like radiation and antibiotics / Industrial-scale research and manufacturing from WWII / Expansion of public healthcare
items: New scientific discoveries like radiation and antibiotics
Industrial-scale research and manufacturing from WWII

cards.front: Name the four modern cancer treatment advances the lesson describes beyond radiotherapy and chemotherapy.
cards.answer: Keyhole surgery / Genetic research into cancer genes / Stem cell therapy / Targeted drug therapy

cards.front: Why did Marie Curie's research on radioactivity matter for cancer treatment?
cards.answer: She discovered that radioactive substances could destroy living tissue, laying the foundation for radiotherapy to treat tumours.

cards.front: Why did Albert Alexander die despite improving after his 1941 penicillin treatment?
cards.answer: The limited supply of penicillin ran out before he was fully cured, so he was not treated for long enough.

cards.front: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
cards.answer: Many strong electrostatic forces act in all directions between ions, needing lots of energy to break.

cards.front: Why is graphite soft and slippery?
cards.answer: Its layers are held together by weak forces, so they can slide over each other.

cards.front: What three tones does the lesson give for Hood's, Clare's and Wordsworth's poems about childhood belonging?
cards.answer: Hood: elegiac and mournful / Clare: celebratory and communal / Wordsworth: urgent and optimistic

cards.front: What structural technique does the lesson say each poet uses — Hood, Clare and Wordsworth?
cards.answer: Hood: regular stanzas with a past-to-present turning point / Clare: rhyming couplets running on smoothly / Wordsworth: short punchy stanzas with imperative verbs
items: Hood: regular stanzas with a past-to-present turning point
Clare: rhyming couplets running on smoothly
Wordsworth: short punchy stanzas with imperative verbs

cards.front: Why is Clare's celebration of childhood freedom in nature described as especially poignant?
cards.answer: Because his later life was marked by mental illness and institutional confinement, contrasting with his memories of open countryside freedom.

cards.front: How does Hood's stanza structure reinforce the theme that belonging is easier in childhood than adulthood?
cards.answer: Each stanza contrasts bright, elevated childhood memories with a present-day adult perspective heavy with loss.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives for choosing the right production process.
cards.answer: Volume of output needed / Degree of customisation required by customers / Target cost per unit / Level of flexibility the market demands
