items: Unpaid Iraqi war debts to Kuwait
Kuwaiti oil overproduction pushing down prices
Border dispute over Bubiyan and Warbah islands

cards.front: From inside Baghdad, what four benefits did the invasion of Kuwait seem to offer Iraq?
cards.answer: Cancelled Iraq's debts / doubled Iraq's oil reserves / intimidated the Gulf states / offered a pan-Arab nationalist triumph
items: Doubled Iraq's share of world oil reserves
Intimidated the rest of the Gulf

cards.front: How did Iraq's original invasion plan change before the attack on Kuwait was launched?
cards.answer: It grew from a limited operation to seize Bubiyan, Warbah and Rumaila into a plan for full annexation of Kuwait.

cards.front: Why did outside powers unite against Iraq after the invasion of Kuwait?
cards.answer: Saudi Arabia feared its own oil fields were next, the US saw a state seizing a fifth of world oil reserves, and even the Soviet Union would not defend annexation at the UN.

cards.front: Name the five types of structure the lesson describes for substances.
cards.answer: Giant ionic lattices / Simple molecular structures / Giant covalent structures / Polymers / Metallic structures

cards.front: Name the three limitations of dot-and-cross diagrams given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Don't show 3D shape of molecules / Don't show relative sizes of atoms / Don't show distances between atoms
items: Don't show relative sizes of atoms

cards.front: Why do most atoms bond with other atoms?
cards.answer: Most atoms don't naturally have a full outer shell of electrons, and bonding lets them achieve one, making them more stable.

cards.front: Why don't Group 0 elements readily form bonds?
cards.answer: Group 0 elements already have full outer shells of electrons, so they don't need to lose, gain or share electrons.

title: Synovial Joints and Types of Movement
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the six key structures of a synovial joint.
cards.answer: Synovial membrane / Synovial fluid / Joint capsule / Bursae / Cartilage / Ligaments

cards.front: Name the six movements possible at the shoulder joint (ball-and-socket).
cards.answer: Flexion / Extension / Abduction / Adduction / Rotation / Circumduction

cards.front: Why do cartilage injuries take so long to heal and can end sporting careers?
cards.answer: Cartilage has no blood supply of its own, relying on synovial fluid for nourishment, so damage heals very slowly.

cards.front: Why does warming up reduce the risk of ligament and tendon tears?
cards.answer: Higher body temperature during a warm-up makes ligaments and tendons more pliable, reducing the risk of tears.

cards.front: What three types of documents does Kipps find among Mrs Drablow's papers that reveal the truth?
cards.answer: Letters / Birth certificates / Adoption records

cards.front: The curse's child deaths appear as what three kinds of accidents?
cards.answer: Drownings / Falls / Illnesses

cards.front: Why does Jennet's revenge as the Woman in Black target innocent children rather than those who actually wronged her?
cards.answer: Her grief has become so vast and indiscriminate that she punishes the innocent, inflicting on others the same loss that destroyed her.

cards.front: Why does Hill refuse to give the novel a conventional, comforting ending?
cards.answer: The ghost cannot be defeated because Jennet's grief can never be resolved, since her child is dead and nothing can undo that.

cards.front: Name the four impulsive actions that define Romeo's character in the play.
cards.answer: Falls in love instantly / Marries within a day / Kills Tybalt in a rage / Buys poison without confirming Juliet's death
items: Buys poison without confirming Juliet's death

cards.front: From the balcony scene onwards, name the three ways Juliet drives the relationship.
cards.answer: Proposes marriage / Challenges the power of names / Makes practical plans

cards.front: Why does Mercutio's death change the tone of the play?
cards.answer: Without his irreverent energy the tone becomes unrelentingly tragic, marking the end of comedy in the play.

cards.front: How does Tybalt's aggression directly cause tragedy at the ball?
cards.answer: He insists on duelling Romeo despite Capulet's orders, which directly causes Mercutio's death and his own.

cards.front: Name the six circuit parameters covered in this course.
cards.answer: Potential difference / Current / Resistance / Capacitance / Power / Frequency

cards.front: Name the six unit prefixes used in circuit calculations, from largest to smallest.
cards.answer: Mega (M) / Kilo (k) / Milli (m) / Micro (µ) / Nano (n) / Pico (p)

cards.front: Why is 'potential difference' considered more precise than 'voltage'?
cards.answer: Potential difference always refers to the difference in electrical potential energy per unit charge between two specific points, never a single point.

cards.front: Why is confusing the prefix milli (m) with mega (M) such a serious mistake?
cards.answer: They differ by a factor of one billion, so mistaking 1 mW for 1 MW changes the value hugely and causes a serious error.

cards.front: What two symbolic items does a baby receive during infant baptism?
cards.answer: White garment symbolising purity / Candle symbolising the light of Christ
items: Candle symbolising the light of Christ

cards.front: How does full immersion in believers' baptism symbolise dying and rising to new life?
cards.answer: Being submerged under water mirrors dying to the old sinful life, and being raised up mirrors Jesus's death and resurrection into new life.

cards.front: Why do Baptists see believers' baptism as a more meaningful commitment than infant baptism?
cards.answer: It is a personal choice and public declaration of faith made by someone old enough to understand the commitment, unlike a baby.

title: Active and Passive Audiences and Uses & Gratifications Theory
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four audience needs identified by Blumler and Katz in Uses and Gratifications theory.
cards.answer: Information (surveillance of the world) / Personal identity (reinforcing values and self-image) / Integration and social interaction (maintaining relationships) / Entertainment (diversion and pleasure)

cards.front: Why did the two-step flow model weaken the hypodermic needle model?
cards.answer: It showed audiences were not uniform, as opinion leaders interpreted media first and social relationships filtered messages before reaching the wider group.

cards.front: Why can the same media product satisfy different needs for different audiences, according to Uses and Gratifications theory?
cards.answer: Because audiences use media purposefully, so one viewer might watch for information, another for identity reinforcement, and another for social interaction.

cards.front: Name the four essential interior features every synagogue contains.
cards.answer: The Ark (Aron Kodesh) / The Bimah / The Ner Tamid / The Sefer Torah

cards.front: Name four ways Jews worship or pray at home, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Fixing a mezuzah to the doorpost / Lighting Shabbat candles on Friday evening / Reciting blessings over wine and bread / Teaching children to pray
items: Fixing a mezuzah to the doorpost
Lighting Shabbat candles on Friday evening
Reciting blessings over wine and bread

cards.front: Why is the yad used when reading from the Sefer Torah?
cards.answer: So the sacred text is never touched directly by bare fingers.

cards.front: Why were local synagogues seen as having religious authority even though the Temple was destroyed?
cards.answer: Ezekiel had described G-d as a 'little sanctuary' for the people in exile, giving authority to local prayer places.

cards.front: Why does Aaron have no sense of true identity at the Foundling Hospital?
cards.answer: He was given a new name, has no surname, and possesses no token linking him to his real parents.

cards.front: How does Aaron's musical gift connect him to his father Alexander?
cards.answer: Aaron inherits an extraordinary singing voice from Alexander, an invisible thread linking father and son without either knowing it.

cards.front: Name the four comfortless details of the flat where Jo and Helen live, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Broken heating / Leaking roof / One bed to share / A view of a slaughterhouse

cards.front: Name the three instruments in the live jazz trio used in Theatre Workshop's original production.
cards.answer: Cornet / Guitar / Double bass

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to call A Taste of Honey simply 'naturalistic'?
cards.answer: Its dialogue and content are realist, but its original staging used direct address, songs, dance and a live band, which are stylised devices.

cards.front: Why was sex between men in 1958 a key context for Geof's character throughout the play?
cards.answer: Sex between men was illegal under an 1885 law, making Geof's private life a criminal offence for the entire play.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson describes cities reshaping themselves internally (besides growth).
cards.answer: Suburbanisation / Counter-urbanisation / Re-urbanisation

cards.front: Name the four push factors the lesson gives for rural-urban migration.
cards.answer: Rural poverty / Mechanisation reducing farm labour needs / Drought or land degradation / Limited access to schools or hospitals
items: Limited access to schools or hospitals

cards.front: Why does migration to cities accelerate urban growth even further over time?
cards.answer: Migrants are typically young adults of working age, so once they arrive they have children, boosting natural increase.

cards.front: Why do developed countries now have slow or slightly negative urban growth?
cards.answer: They are already 80% or more urban and people are retiring to the coast or countryside instead.

cards.front: Name the three characteristics that have the biggest effect on CPU performance.
cards.answer: Clock speed / Cache size / Number of cores

cards.front: In what order does a CPU check the three levels of cache before going to RAM?
cards.answer: L1 cache / L2 cache / L3 cache

cards.front: Why does a higher clock speed usually give better CPU performance?
cards.answer: More cycles per second means the CPU can carry out more instructions per second.

cards.front: Why might a CPU with a very high clock speed but a tiny cache still perform poorly?
cards.answer: It keeps stalling waiting for data from RAM because the small cache gives few cache hits.

cards.front: Why does Miller's formal, controlled stage language make John and Elizabeth Proctor's unspoken feelings more powerful in the linen scene?
cards.answer: Because the surface language is so controlled and formal, the subtext beneath it becomes more powerful and noticeable.

cards.front: Why does dramatic irony in the courtroom scenes carry political weight for Miller's 1953 audience?
cards.answer: Audiences were living through McCarthyism, where accusation counted as proof and telling the truth was dangerous, just as in the play.

cards.front: Why does Proctor tear up the signed confession in the final act instead of saving his life?
cards.answer: Because surrendering his name would betray his integrity, and Miller stages this as showing integrity is the only response to a system built on lies.

cards.front: Why is treating The Crucible like a novel (discussing only metaphors and themes) considered a mistake in analysing it?
cards.answer: Drama is a performance art, so Miller's intentions only matter if explained through how staging, vocal and physical choices realise them.

cards.front: Name the three generations held at once in 'Partition'.
cards.answer: The aunt who acts / The mother who listens but stays home / The poet who receives the story decades later
items: The mother who listens but stays home
The poet who receives the story decades later

cards.front: What four short quotations does the lesson suggest learning from 'Partition'?
cards.answer: the cries of the people / she felt afraid / I still feel guilty about that / a man who knew nothing about geography
items: I still feel guilty about that
a man who knew nothing about geography

cards.front: Why does Bhatt never give the young woman in 'Partition' a name?
cards.answer: It is a distancing device that makes her feel like any woman living through Partition, not one unique individual.

cards.front: Why does Bhatt keep the horror of Partition off-page, heard only as distant cries?
cards.answer: It makes the reader share the young woman's own limited, frightened perspective on events she cannot see.

title: Propaganda, the police state and Nazi culture
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five main propaganda tools the lesson lists for the Nazi regime.
cards.answer: Radio / Film / Press / Posters / Rallies

cards.front: What were the four core elements of the Nazi propaganda message, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Hitler as saviour / The Volk as racial community / Versailles 'stab in the back' as a wound to reverse / Communism and Jewry as threats
items: Versailles 'stab in the back' as a wound to reverse

cards.front: Why did the lesson describe radio as the regime's most powerful single propaganda tool?
cards.answer: The Volksempfanger and public loudspeakers reached almost every household, spreading Nazi messages while blocking foreign broadcasts.

cards.front: How did self-policing let the Nazi regime control the population despite having only 32,000 Gestapo officers?
cards.answer: Fearing unknown informers, most Germans policed their own conversations, so terror worked through self-censorship as much as actual surveillance.

cards.front: Name the five stages of Jekyll's tragic arc, from voluntary transformation to his final escape.
cards.answer: Transforms voluntarily and enjoys the freedom / Hyde grows stronger / Transformations become involuntary / The potion stops working / Jekyll is trapped as Hyde and commits suicide
items: Transforms voluntarily and enjoys the freedom
Jekyll is trapped as Hyde and commits suicide

cards.front: Why does trying to separate good and evil make Jekyll's situation worse rather than better?
cards.answer: Separating good from evil makes both sides more extreme, so repressing his evil side only intensifies it.

cards.front: According to Stevenson, why did Jekyll really need the experiment in the first place?
cards.answer: Victorian society's pressure for respectability forced Jekyll to suppress his desires entirely instead of finding a healthy balance.

title: Castles: Instruments of Conquest and Control
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five kinds of buildings the lesson says were found inside a bailey.
cards.answer: Stables / Kitchens / A chapel / A hall / Quarters for the garrison

cards.front: The lesson gives three things Norman castles were sited to control. What are they?
cards.answer: Movement (rivers, roads, town gates) / People (rebellious regions, urban populations) / Patronage networks (centre of a tenant-in-chief's lands)
items: Patronage networks (centre of a tenant-in-chief's lands)

cards.front: Why did William need castles that could be built quickly after 1066?
cards.answer: The Normans were a tiny ruling minority controlling millions of Anglo-Saxons, so fast timber castles let them project control and crush rebellions immediately.

cards.front: Why did William replace timber castles with stone in places like the White Tower?
cards.answer: Wood could rot, burn or be chopped down, so stone gave permanence and made a visible, lasting statement of Norman power in major centres.

title: The Catholic Question: Popish Plot and Rye House Plot
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three existing fears the lesson gives that made the country primed to believe the Popish Plot.
cards.answer: Louis XIV's dominant Catholic France / Charles II's secret Treaty of Dover with French money / James, Duke of York's open conversion to Catholicism
items: Charles II's secret Treaty of Dover with French money
James, Duke of York's open conversion to Catholicism

cards.front: Why did Edward Coleman's letters make Oates's fabricated story seem believable?
cards.answer: The letters were genuinely incriminating about wider Catholic plans, so seizing them seemed to confirm Oates's claims even though Coleman knew nothing of the assassination story.

cards.front: How did the Rye House Plot allow Charles II to weaken Whig power in borough corporations?
cards.answer: The government used quo warranto writs to challenge corporation charters, forcing boroughs to surrender them and accept new charters giving the Crown veto power.

title: The Five Pillars and Ten Obligatory Acts
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam.
cards.answer: Shahadah / Salah / Zakah / Sawm / Hajj

cards.front: What four Hajj rites does the lesson describe?
cards.answer: Tawaf (circling Ka'aba seven times) / Walking between Safa and Marwa / Standing on the plain of Arafat / Stoning the devil
items: Standing on the plain of Arafat

cards.front: How does Hajj create a sense of equality among pilgrims?
cards.answer: Male pilgrims all wear the same plain white ihram and women wear simple modest dress, erasing distinctions of wealth and rank.

cards.front: Why is Shahadah not included among the Ten Obligatory Acts in Shi'a Islam?
cards.answer: Shi'a Islam places belief in the oneness of Allah among the Five Roots instead of the Ten Obligatory Acts.

cards.front: Name the three factors the specification says designers must consider when selecting materials and components.
cards.answer: Functional need / Cost / Availability

cards.front: Name the five marking out methods the specification requires understanding of.
cards.answer: Reference datum points / Coordinates / Templates / Jigs / Patterns

cards.front: Why must designers plan the cutting and shaping of materials to minimise waste?
cards.answer: Wasted material is wasted money (economic), and less waste means a smaller environmental footprint.

cards.front: Why does the grain direction of fabric matter when cutting pattern pieces?
cards.answer: Cutting across the grain can affect the way the garment hangs and stretches.

cards.front: What are the five central themes of Boys Don't Cry, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Masculinity / Prejudice and acceptance / Family / Responsibility / Identity

cards.front: What features of the novel's setting reflect the realities of many British families?
cards.answer: Council estates / Stretched finances / Single-parent households / Pressure to succeed academically

cards.front: Why does dual narration create dramatic irony in Boys Don't Cry?
cards.answer: The reader sees both Dante's and Adam's inner worlds, so notices connections and parallels between their struggles that the brothers themselves miss.

cards.front: Why was Blackman's focus on Dante as a teen father socially significant when she wrote the novel?
cards.answer: Government campaigns focused on young mothers while teen fathers were largely invisible, so centring Dante challenged that assumption.

cards.front: Name three comic details Wells uses to show the crowd's complacency at Horsell Common.
cards.answer: People arrive by carriage and bicycle / Boys throw stones / A man sells apples
items: People arrive by carriage and bicycle

cards.front: Name three ways Wells shows social order dissolving during the evacuation.
cards.answer: People trample one another / People steal food / People abandon the weak

cards.front: How does Wells's simile describing Heat-Ray victims dehumanise them?
cards.answer: Saying each man was 'turned to fire' reduces people to fuel, stripping their dignity, mirroring how colonial powers described conquered peoples.

cards.front: Why does the narrator keep expecting the army and government to restore order?
cards.answer: His mind clings to normality, showing denial and confusion, mirroring how real people respond to disaster by refusing to accept the world has changed.

cards.front: Name the four quarters of the planning method for the anthology comparison question, in order.
cards.answer: Read question and named poem, underline/circle / Choose comparison poem sharing the theme / Jot 2-3 quotations with technique and effect / Write one-sentence thesis and paragraph plan
items: Read question and named poem, underline/circle
Choose comparison poem sharing the theme
Jot 2-3 quotations with technique and effect
Write one-sentence thesis and paragraph plan

cards.front: Name the five common pitfalls listed for the anthology comparison essay.
cards.answer: Feature-spotting without analysis / Retelling the poem / Writing about poems separately / Ignoring form and structure / Vague context

cards.front: Why must every paragraph in the anthology comparison answer discuss both poems together?
cards.answer: Because writing about poems separately is a listed pitfall — the task requires genuine comparison, not description of each poem alone.

cards.front: Why is naming a specific historical event or biographical detail better than saying a poem 'was written a long time ago'?
cards.answer: Because vague context earns nothing, whereas specific movements, events or biographical details show precise contextual understanding.

cards.front: Name the three responses to mortality the three guardians represent in Never Let Me Go.
cards.answer: Miss Emily: justification / Madame: guilt / Miss Lucy: rebellion/truth-telling

cards.front: Why does Kathy's narration count as an act of resistance despite her calm tone?
cards.answer: By telling her story and memorialising Tommy, Ruth and Hailsham, she asserts her humanity even though she was conditioned not to rage.

cards.front: Why does Madame cry when she sees Kathy dancing to 'Never Let Me Go'?
cards.answer: Her tears suggest deep, conflicted emotion — she is repulsed by clones yet secretly compassionate towards them.

cards.front: Name the four institutions the SS controlled by 1939, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Gestapo / Concentration camps / SD (Security Service) / RSHA (Reich Security Main Office)

cards.front: Which four groups were concentration camps initially set up for in 1933?
cards.answer: Communists / Social Democrats / Trade unionists / Clergy who criticised the regime

cards.front: Why were the SD's frank reports on public opinion useful to Hitler?
cards.answer: SD officers reported discontent accurately, giving Hitler information about where public support for the regime was weak.

cards.front: How did the SS's self-image make it capable of committing extreme crimes?
cards.answer: Its combination of an elite self-image (racially pure, ideologically trained) with unconstrained power let it act where ordinary bureaucracies might resist.

cards.front: Name the four sustainable UK transport options the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Electric vehicles / Rail electrification / Active travel infrastructure / Bus franchising

cards.front: Name the three ways the Lake District National Park Authority responds to tourism pressure.
cards.answer: Footpath repair / Sustainable farming grants under Environmental Land Management schemes / Limits on second-home conversions in some parishes

cards.front: Why has footpath erosion become a problem at popular Lake District peaks like Helvellyn?
cards.answer: High visitor numbers, around 18 million a year, wear down footpaths at popular peaks through constant foot traffic.

cards.front: Why was HS2 scaled back in 2023 seen as a setback for sustainable transport?
cards.answer: It was reduced to just a London-Birmingham line, leaving northern England feeling short-changed on rail investment.

cards.front: Name the five categories of customer requirement the lesson identifies for hospitality and catering.
cards.answer: Customer needs / Customer rights and inclusion / Lifestyle and dietary needs / Customer expectations / Customer demographics

cards.front: Name the seven factors the lesson says shape customer expectations.
cards.answer: Service quality / Value for money / Current trends / Awareness of competition / Media influence / Environmental concerns / Seasonality

cards.front: Why does failing to be inclusive harm a hospitality business itself, not just excluded customers?
cards.answer: It breaks equality legislation and also loses the business potential customers, damaging its reputation.

cards.front: How can media influence affect a hospitality business's bookings?
cards.answer: A positive review or TV feature can boost bookings, while a negative social media post can cause lasting damage.

cards.front: Name the three definitions of history given in the play.
cards.answer: Performance and entertainment (Irwin) / Commentary on male failure (Mrs Lintott) / Cultural inheritance between generations (Hector)

cards.front: Why are Posner and Mrs Lintott the only characters who do not perform?
cards.answer: Posner is painfully honest about his identity and Mrs Lintott sees through everyone else's performances, showing Bennett links authenticity to being marginalised.

cards.front: In extract-based exam questions, why is background context not enough on its own?
cards.answer: Background may sharpen a point but only close analysis of quotations, language and structure in the extract is credited.

cards.front: Name the three levels on which dramatic irony operates in An Inspector Calls.
cards.answer: Historical - audience knows Birling's predictions are wrong / Investigative - audience sees implications before characters do / Structural - audience knows the investigation will repeat
items: Historical - audience knows Birling's predictions are wrong
Investigative - audience sees implications before characters do
Structural - audience knows the investigation will repeat

cards.front: What three things does the cyclical ending of An Inspector Calls achieve, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Punishes the older generation for wasting their chance / Validates the younger generation's belief in accountability / Extends the warning to the real audience
items: Punishes the older generation for wasting their chance
Validates the younger generation's belief in accountability
Extends the warning to the real audience

cards.front: How does confining the play to one room in real time affect the audience watching it?
cards.answer: It makes the audience feel the same trapped pressure as the characters, with no time jumps, scene changes or relief from the revelations.

cards.front: Why does the Inspector's power not depend on documents or institutional evidence?
cards.answer: He has only a photograph and no files, so his power comes entirely from moral authority and the characters' guilty consciences.

cards.front: Name the four key erosional landforms produced by glacial plucking and abrasion in upland areas.
cards.answer: Corries / Arêtes / Pyramidal peaks / U-shaped glacial troughs

cards.front: Give the three ways people use UK glaciated uplands today, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Sheep farming / Conifer forestry plantations / Settlement and tourism in valleys / Reservoirs for water supply

cards.front: Why do truncated spurs form when a glacier flows down a valley?
cards.answer: The glacier widens, deepens and straightens the valley, shearing off the interlocking spurs of the original river valley.

cards.front: How does a terminal moraine form at the end of a glacier?
cards.answer: Rock debris piles up at the glacier's snout because ice melts as fast as it advances, forming a curved ridge.

cards.front: Name the seven Spanish phrases the lesson gives for talking about relationships with friends.
cards.answer: Me llevo bien con / No me llevo bien con / Me llevo mal con / Nos llevamos bien / Nos peleamos a veces / Tenemos mucho en común / Somos muy diferentes

cards.front: Name the eight opinion phrases the lesson gives for reaching higher marks in speaking and writing.
cards.answer: Creo que / Pienso que / En mi opinión / A mi modo de ver / Me parece que / Lo mejor es que / Lo peor es que / Me da la impresión de que

cards.front: Why is it important to use a variety of opinion phrases, not just me gusta, in Spanish speaking and writing exams?
cards.answer: Using a range of opinion phrases like a mi modo de ver demonstrates sophisticated language use needed for higher mark bands.

cards.front: How does the form of llevarse bien/mal con change depending on who is speaking?
cards.answer: It is a reflexive verb, so it changes form with the subject, e.g. me llevo bien or se lleva mal.

cards.front: Name the five types of accommodation given in the lesson vocabulary list.
cards.answer: un hotel / un hotel de lujo / un albergue juvenil / un camping / una casa rural

cards.front: Name the four hotel problems given as example complaint phrases.
cards.answer: air conditioning doesn't work / no hot water / the room is dirty / the lift doesn't work

cards.front: Why is quisiera preferred over quiero when booking a hotel room in a role-play?
cards.answer: Quisiera is more formal and polite than quiero, showing you can vary your register.

cards.front: How are the preterite and imperfect tenses used together to describe past accommodation?
cards.answer: The preterite describes the action of staying there, while the imperfect describes what the hotel or room was like.

title: Exchange, Transport and the Circulatory System
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four components of blood.
cards.answer: Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets / Plasma

cards.front: Name the three types of blood vessel.
cards.answer: Arteries / Veins / Capillaries

cards.front: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker wall than the right ventricle?
cards.answer: It must generate higher pressure to pump blood all the way around the entire body, not just to the lungs.

cards.front: Why is extra oxygen needed after intense exercise (oxygen debt)?
cards.answer: It is needed to break down the lactate that has accumulated from anaerobic respiration during exercise.

title: Sources and interpretations: how 1951-79 has been remembered
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four pieces of evidence the Thatcherite narrative emphasises about 1951-1979.
cards.answer: IMF crisis of 1976 / Winter of Discontent 1978-79 / Slow growth vs West Germany and France / High inflation of the mid-1970s
items: Slow growth vs West Germany and France

cards.front: Name the four groups whose experiences oral history has recovered for this period.
cards.answer: Caribbean migrants arriving 1940s-50s / Women in women's liberation campaigns / Miners in the 1972 and 1974 strikes / Catholic families in early Troubles

cards.front: Why did Andy Beckett challenge the dominant memory of the 1970s as a decade of gloom?
cards.answer: He argued the decade also had genuine creativity and change, like punk, feminism, gay liberation and environmentalism, showing the Thatcherite narrative caricatured it.

cards.front: Why can't oral testimony from 2005 about events in 1968 be taken as a simple record of 1968?
cards.answer: Memory is fallible and testimony may be shaped by later experiences, so it can reflect as much about 2005 as 1968.

title: Characters: Sephy, Callum and Their Families
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four things a sophisticated costume design answer should specify, according to the lesson, to avoid the 'black and white' misconception.
cards.answer: The fabric type / The fit / The colour palette / The condition of the clothing

cards.front: What three physical adjustments might a director ask the performer playing Callum to make in Cross spaces?
cards.answer: Keep arms closer to the body / Reduce gesture / Avoid direct eye contact with Cross characters
items: Keep arms closer to the body
Avoid direct eye contact with Cross characters

cards.front: Why does Callum reduce his physical expressiveness in Cross spaces?
cards.answer: He has learned to make himself smaller as self-policing to appear safe, contrasting with his freer physicality around Sephy or in nought spaces.

cards.front: How could lighting design signal Sephy's emotional arc across the play?
cards.answer: Early scenes use a warm overhead wash suggesting unexamined confidence, shifting later to a cooler, isolating lighting state showing her contracted world.

cards.front: The lesson names four site features that explain the Armada's fate through chains of feature and consequence. What are they?
cards.answer: Missing deep-water port / Open roadstead at Calais / Sandbanks off Zeeland / Beacon chains and home ports / North-about route home

cards.front: Why was the English fleet able to react faster to the Armada's movements than Philip's planners could?
cards.answer: Chains of hilltop beacons carried the alarm across southern England in hours, while Philip's planners worked on months-old information.

cards.front: Why did the Armada almost get wrecked on the Zeeland sandbanks off Gravelines?
cards.answer: The wind pushed the battered fleet towards shoaling water with no sea room, and only a last-moment wind shift let it escape.

cards.front: Why did cutting anchor cables to escape the fireships at Calais cause so many wrecks weeks later?
cards.answer: Ships without anchors could not hold themselves off the storm coasts of Scotland and Ireland during the autumn gales.

cards.front: Name the four elements of Hitler's ideology that Mein Kampf outlined.
cards.answer: Extreme nationalism / Anti-Semitism / Lebensraum / The need for a dictatorial leader
items: The need for a dictatorial leader

cards.front: Name the three crises that converged in Germany during 1923.
cards.answer: The Ruhr occupation / Hyperinflation / The Munich Putsch

cards.front: Why did Stresemann call off passive resistance in September 1923?
cards.answer: He recognised the printing presses had to stop, accepting the political cost of appearing to surrender to France.

cards.front: Why did the Munich Putsch fail within 24 hours?
cards.answer: The Bavarian government and the army did not support it, as Hitler had miscalculated loyalty to the republic.

cards.front: Name the three components a mains-powered PSU chain contains to produce stable DC.
cards.answer: Step-down transformer / Bridge rectifier / Smoothing capacitor

cards.front: Name the four factors that decide the choice between a mains and a battery power supply.
cards.answer: Power requirement / Portability / Safety / Cost

cards.front: Why do transformers only work with AC and not DC?
cards.answer: DC creates a static (unchanging) magnetic field in the core, which induces no voltage in the secondary coil.

cards.front: How does a bridge rectifier produce full-wave rectification?
cards.answer: It uses four diodes arranged in a diamond so both the positive and negative half-cycles contribute to the output.

title: Empire, Slavery and the End of the Reign 1685
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three chartered companies that drove English overseas expansion under Charles II.
cards.answer: East India Company / Royal African Company / Hudson's Bay Company

cards.front: What did Catherine of Braganza's 1662 dowry give England, besides £300,000 in cash?
cards.answer: Bombay / Tangier / trading rights in Brazil / trading rights in the Portuguese East Indies
items: trading rights in the Portuguese East Indies

cards.front: Why did planters in Jamaica and Barbados turn to enslaved African labour rather than European workers for sugar production?
cards.answer: A sugar mill needed many workers continuously, but indentured European labour was scarce, expensive and unwilling to do field work in tropical heat.

cards.front: How did the Royal African Company's slave trading differ from earlier English slaving voyages?
cards.answer: It flowed through a royally chartered company with the Crown itself as a shareholder, a major escalation from earlier private voyages.

title: Robert Peel and the birth of the Metropolitan Police
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four recruitment standards required of Peel's new police officers.
cards.answer: Under 35 years old / At least 5 feet 7 inches tall / Literate / Of good character

cards.front: Why did Peel's police wear a blue coat instead of military red and carry only a truncheon?
cards.answer: To make the force look deliberately civilian and reassure a public fearful of a French-style state spying force.

cards.front: Why did Peel's constables patrol fixed beats rather than investigate crimes after they happened?
cards.answer: So the public knew which officer to expect and the officer learned the local people, aiming for prevention through visible presence.

cards.front: Why did Peel reform the Bloody Code before setting up the Metropolitan Police?
cards.answer: Harsh laws were more enforceable when paired with proportionate punishment, preparing the ground for a police force.

cards.front: Name the three social factors the lesson gives that affect conformity.
cards.answer: Group size / Anonymity / Task difficulty

cards.front: Give the three weaknesses of Asch's study mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sample limited to male American students, reducing generalisability / Artificial lab task lacks ecological validity / Deception raised ethical concerns about consent
items: Sample limited to male American students, reducing generalisability
Artificial lab task lacks ecological validity
Deception raised ethical concerns about consent

cards.front: Why does a strong need for social approval increase conformity?
cards.answer: People who need social approval fear rejection, so they are more likely to go along with the group.

cards.front: Why is a controlled lab experiment considered a strength of Asch's study?
cards.answer: The conditions could be carefully controlled and repeated, and confederates gave consistent behaviour across trials.

cards.front: Why does Boxer's loyalty make him especially vulnerable to Napoleon's control?
cards.answer: His genuine trust means he cannot imagine someone he trusts would betray him, so he never questions Napoleon.

cards.front: How does the changed commandment about beds show Orwell's point about education and manipulation?
cards.answer: The animals cannot read well enough to challenge the subtle change, showing uneducated populations are vulnerable to manipulation.

cards.front: Name the three golf etiquette customs the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Repair divots / Rake bunkers / Maintain silence when others are playing
items: Maintain silence when others are playing

cards.front: Name the three gamesmanship examples the lesson gives from different sports.
cards.answer: Excessive ball bouncing before serving in tennis / Lying on wrong side of ruck in rugby / Changing gloves to break bowler's rhythm in cricket
items: Excessive ball bouncing before serving in tennis
Lying on wrong side of ruck in rugby
Changing gloves to break bowler's rhythm in cricket

cards.front: Why does the contract to compete matter for fair play in sport?
cards.answer: Without it, sport would allow any unethical tactic as long as it helped a competitor win.

cards.front: How does a fielding side in cricket traditionally show etiquette towards a batsman?
cards.answer: By applauding a departing batsman who has played well, even though this is not required by the rules.

title: Sea Level Change and Drowned Forests
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name three pieces of evidence used to confirm Doggerland once existed as inhabited dry land.
cards.answer: Worked flint tools dredged up / Animal bones dredged up / Land bridge exposed at low sea level 120m below present
items: Land bridge exposed at low sea level 120m below present

cards.front: Why is southern England slowly sinking relative to sea level while Scotland is rising?
cards.answer: Southern England is further from the centre of ice loading, so it is tilting downward as the crust readjusts, unlike Scotland which is rebounding upward.

cards.front: How does radiocarbon dating of peat beneath British drowned forests support the theory of post-glacial sea level rise?
cards.answer: Dating gives ages of roughly 4,000–8,000 years, showing the land was submerged during early Holocene sea level rise after ice retreat.

title: War Communism, Kronstadt and the NEP
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four measures that made up War Communism (1918-21).
cards.answer: Nationalised all industry above smallest workshops / Banned private trade / Drafted workers into labour battalions paid in rations / Grain requisitioning at fixed low prices
items: Nationalised all industry above smallest workshops
Drafted workers into labour battalions paid in rations
Grain requisitioning at fixed low prices

cards.front: Name the four features of the New Economic Policy introduced in 1921.
cards.answer: Tax in kind replacing requisitioning / Small private workshops and shops legalised / Foreign concessions granted for capital / State kept the commanding heights of the economy
items: Small private workshops and shops legalised
State kept the commanding heights of the economy

cards.front: Why did peasants stop growing surplus grain under War Communism?
cards.answer: Armed detachments seized any surplus at fixed low prices, so peasants had no reason to grow more than they needed.

cards.front: Why did the Kronstadt Rising frighten Lenin more than other revolts like Tambov?
cards.answer: The demands came from Bolshevik-loyal sailors once called the revolution's pride, showing the regime's own base had turned against it.

cards.front: Name the three main causes of the doubling of global water demand since 1975.
cards.answer: Population growth / Rising affluence / Industrialisation in emerging economies

cards.front: What are the two drawbacks of desalination given in the lesson, besides high cost?
cards.answer: Heavy energy use, often fossil-fuel-powered / Salty brine discharged into coastal waters
items: Salty brine discharged into coastal waters

cards.front: Why does agricultural water use take up a much bigger share of total water in developing countries than in developed ones?
cards.answer: Irrigation is essential to feed growing populations and earn foreign currency from food exports, while developed countries often import food instead.

cards.front: Why does waterborne disease kill so many children in poorer countries?
cards.answer: Rivers are polluted by untreated sewage, factory waste and fertiliser run-off, and many lack access to treated drinking water at home.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why celebrities can be good role models.
cards.answer: They work hard and show success is possible / They support charitable causes and donate money / They inspire young people to follow their dreams
items: They work hard and show success is possible
They support charitable causes and donate money
They inspire young people to follow their dreams

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why celebrities can be bad role models.
cards.answer: They show an unrealistic lifestyle / Young people compare themselves and feel low self-esteem / There is too much pressure to look perfect
items: Young people compare themselves and feel low self-esteem
There is too much pressure to look perfect

cards.front: How can comparing yourself to celebrities affect young people, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It can lead to low self-esteem.

cards.front: How does using 'einerseits ... andererseits' improve a German opinion answer?
cards.answer: It lets you present a balanced argument by showing both sides of an issue.

cards.front: Name the three musculo-skeletal long-term adaptations to training given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Muscle hypertrophy / Increased bone density / Stronger ligaments and tendons

cards.front: Why does a trained athlete's heart rate recover faster after exercise than an untrained person's?
cards.answer: Their higher resting stroke volume means the cardiovascular system achieves adequate oxygen delivery even at lower heart rates.

cards.front: Why does hypertrophy require adequate rest to occur?
cards.answer: Muscle fibres are damaged by training, and satellite cells repair and grow them during rest, not during the session itself.

cards.front: Name the four types of synovial joint covered for GCSE PE.
cards.answer: Pivot joint / Hinge joint / Condyloid joint / Ball-and-socket joint

cards.front: Name the three hinge joints relevant to sport.
cards.answer: Elbow / Knee / Ankle

cards.front: Why do ligament sprains heal slowly compared to muscle injuries?
cards.answer: Ligaments have a relatively poor blood supply, so the limited blood flow makes the repair process slow.

cards.front: Why can't the wrist rotate like a screwdriver even though it's a moveable joint?
cards.answer: The wrist is a condyloid joint which only flexes, extends, abducts and adducts; rotation actually comes from the radioulnar pivot joint.

cards.front: How does Harri's immigrant experience create both opportunity and vulnerability in Pigeon English?
cards.answer: His family came to London for a better life, but estate life falls far short of that dream, exposing him to danger.

cards.front: Why does every paragraph of a Modern Text essay need to answer 'what is Kelman doing here, and why?'
cards.answer: So the essay analyses authorial method and purpose rather than just narrating the plot.

cards.front: Name the five main agencies of informal social control listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: The family / The peer group / Education / Religion / The media

cards.front: Name the four stated purposes of prison given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Punishment / Deterrence / Rehabilitation / Incapacitation

cards.front: How does feminist theory say family-based informal control differs for boys and girls?
cards.answer: Daughters are typically given less freedom of movement, face earlier curfews and are held to different standards than sons.

cards.front: How can the peer group encourage deviance rather than conformity, according to subcultural theorists like Cohen?
cards.answer: Peer groups can exert control towards deviance when their shared norms actually celebrate breaking rules.

title: Communist Control: Propaganda, Censorship and the Cult of Mao
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four pillars the lesson says communist control in Mao's China rested on.
cards.answer: Propaganda / Cult of Mao / Censorship / Forced labour (laogai)

cards.front: Name the four types of prisoner the lesson says were held in laogai camps.
cards.answer: Former GMD officials / Denounced 'rightists' / Religious clergy / 'Capitalist roaders'

cards.front: Why did the CCP rely on propaganda rather than just police control to rule China?
cards.answer: Because ruling around 600 million people, mostly illiterate peasants across vast countryside, made direct rule by police alone impossible.

cards.front: How did censorship work alongside propaganda to control what people believed?
cards.answer: By banning and removing alternative narratives, censorship made the regime's own propaganda message the only one in circulation.

title: Act 1: The Ball & Love at First Sight
subject: english-literature-eduqas

cards.front: What three driving forces does the Prologue establish in its opening quatrain?
cards.answer: The feud ('ancient grudge') / The doomed love ('star-cross'd lovers') / The link between love and death ('fatal loins')
items: The link between love and death ('fatal loins')

cards.front: Name the four Petrarchan oxymorons Romeo uses to describe his love for Rosaline.
cards.answer: Feather of lead / Bright smoke / Cold fire / Sick health

cards.front: Why does the Prologue's dramatic irony affect how the audience experiences the play?
cards.answer: It reveals the lovers' deaths before the action starts, so every joyful moment is filled with foreboding.

cards.front: Why is Prince Escalus's decree in Act 1 Scene 1 crucial to the plot?
cards.answer: It threatens death for further street violence, making Romeo's later killing of Tybalt punishable by banishment or death.

title: Igneous Rocks: Texture, Mineralogy and Classification
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four igneous rock types classified in this lesson.
cards.answer: Peridotite / Basalt / Andesite / Granite

cards.front: What three rock names must you avoid writing because they are outside the four spec igneous rocks?
cards.answer: Gabbro / Dolerite / Rhyolite

cards.front: Why do coarse-grained igneous rocks form?
cards.answer: They cool slowly deep underground, giving crystals time to grow larger than 3 mm.

cards.front: How does the colour of an igneous rock relate to its mineral content?
cards.answer: Colour reflects mineral make-up: dark minerals are iron- and magnesium-rich, pale minerals are silica- and aluminium-rich.

title: Quantitative Chemistry: Moles, Mass and Yield
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three steps used to find the mass of a product from a known mass of reactant in a balanced equation.
cards.answer: Calculate moles of the reactant / Use the equation ratio to find moles of product / Convert moles of product to mass
items: Use the equation ratio to find moles of product
Convert moles of product to mass

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why percentage yield is lowered.
cards.answer: Incomplete reactions / Reversible reactions reaching equilibrium before completion / Losses during filtration or evaporation
items: Reversible reactions reaching equilibrium before completion

cards.front: Why is the amount of product in a reaction calculated from the limiting reactant rather than the excess reactant?
cards.answer: The limiting reactant runs out first, so it caps the maximum amount of product that can form.

cards.front: Why do addition reactions have a high atom economy?
cards.answer: All the reactants combine into one single product, so no atoms are wasted in by-products.

cards.front: According to Greek myth, name the three ways the Amazons were said to differ from ordinary women.
cards.answer: Cut off one breast to improve their aim with a bow / Rejected men except for reproduction / Chose to fight rather than to weave
items: Cut off one breast to improve their aim with a bow
Chose to fight rather than to weave

cards.front: What three-part pattern do both the Amazon myths and Camilla's story share, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Excellence is acknowledged / Death restores proper order / A male hero is the agent of that restoration
items: A male hero is the agent of that restoration

cards.front: Why do some scholars think the Amazon myth was inspired by real Scythian or Sarmatian women?
cards.answer: Archaeology found women buried with weapons and horses in Central Asian kurgans, and Herodotus described Sauromatae women riding and hunting.

cards.front: Why does the scene of Achilles killing Penthesilea on the red-figure cup show both violence and recognition?
cards.answer: Because Achilles is said to have fallen in love with Penthesilea at the very moment he killed her, creating a compelling paradox.

cards.front: Why does Piggy's denial that Simon's death was murder matter thematically?
cards.answer: It shows even the most rational character uses self-deception when confronted with moral horror.

cards.front: Why is the fire that leads to Ralph's rescue ironic?
cards.answer: It was lit to kill Ralph, so destruction rather than civilisation is what brings the rescue.

cards.front: The lesson breaks Ralph's final tricolon into three meanings — what are they?
cards.answer: The end of innocence / The darkness of man's heart / The fall through the air of Piggy
items: The fall through the air of Piggy

title: Preventing disease: from alchemy to vaccination
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five methods communities used to try to prevent the Black Death in 1348.
cards.answer: Flagellants whipping themselves / Quarantine of infected houses/streets / Bonfires to burn away miasma / Carrying sweet-smelling herbs / Advice from alchemists and soothsayers

cards.front: What three factors does the lesson say drove change in disease prevention from 1500 to today?
cards.answer: Scientific progress (germ theory, bacteriology) / Government action (compulsory vaccination laws) / Improvements in education and communication

cards.front: Why did Jenner think cowpox might protect people against smallpox?
cards.answer: He noticed milkmaids who caught cowpox rarely contracted smallpox, so hypothesised cowpox infection conferred protection.

cards.front: How did Jenner test whether his vaccination actually protected James Phipps from smallpox?
cards.answer: After vaccinating Phipps with cowpox matter, Jenner exposed him to smallpox matter multiple times and he showed no ill effects.

title: Workers' Rights: General Strike to Thatcher, 1926-1990
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three key Thatcher trade union reforms the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: 1980 Employment Act narrowed picketing / 1982 Act let employers sue unions and restricted closed shop / 1984 Trade Union Act required secret ballots before strikes
items: 1982 Act let employers sue unions and restricted closed shop
1984 Trade Union Act required secret ballots before strikes

cards.front: How did returning to the gold standard in 1925 help trigger the miners' dispute that led to the General Strike?
cards.answer: It over-valued the pound, pricing coal exports out of world markets, so owners demanded wage cuts and longer hours which miners refused.

cards.front: Why did the 1926 General Strike ultimately fail?
cards.answer: The TUC was divided over industrial versus political aims, government preparation via the OMS kept services running, and it lost the propaganda battle with no plan beyond day nine.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why quality matters to a business.
cards.answer: Protect the reputation of the business / Gain and retain customers / Reduce product returns and recalls
items: Protect the reputation of the business

cards.front: Why did the Toyota 2009–2010 recalls damage the company so heavily?
cards.answer: About 9 million cars across many models were recalled, costing an estimated $2 billion.

cards.front: Name the four main advantages of networking given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Shared resources (hardware and internet) / Centralised data storage / Easier communication between users / Security policies applied from one point
items: Security policies applied from one point

cards.front: Name the four network topologies covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Star / Mesh / Ring / Bus

cards.front: Why is performance consistent for devices in a star topology?
cards.answer: Each device has its own dedicated link to the switch, so one device's traffic doesn't slow another's down.

cards.front: Why does adding or removing a device in a ring topology cause downtime?
cards.answer: It requires temporarily breaking the ring, which disrupts the network while the change is made.

title: Dramatic Methods: Verse, Prose and the Sonnet
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: How is the shared sonnet's fourteen lines divided between Romeo and Juliet at the Capulet feast?
cards.answer: Romeo speaks the first quatrain / Juliet answers with the second quatrain / they share the third quatrain between them / the rhyming couplet crowns the exchange
items: Juliet answers with the second quatrain
they share the third quatrain between them
the rhyming couplet crowns the exchange

cards.front: How might a director stage the shared sonnet to show Romeo and Juliet becoming rhythmically coupled?
cards.answer: Have the lovers' proxemics slowly close as the sonnet progresses, so they become close enough to kiss by the couplet.

cards.front: Why must a Drama student translate iambic pentameter into performance decisions rather than just literary analysis?
cards.answer: Because a Drama exam requires the form to become a physical choice, like a pause or dropped gaze, not just a label.

cards.front: How might lighting differ between a direct-address soliloquy and a private, naturalistic one?
cards.answer: Direct address gets a pool of light isolating the character with the rest fading; private delivery gets a warmer, tighter special with a quieter voice.

title: I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name six commercial Valentine's gifts the speaker rejects before the final twist in Lochhead's poem.
cards.answer: Red-padded satin hearts / Interflora red roses / Singing telegrams / Pints of Chanel Five / A solitaire / An orchid

cards.front: How does Lochhead use clashing registers to create the poem's main joke?
cards.answer: She mixes formal romantic vocabulary like 'promises solemn' with slang and Scots phrasing, undercutting grand language with a bored, sarcastic voice.

cards.front: Why is the postcard with three Xs able to succeed where diamonds and orchids failed?
cards.answer: Because it told her how her partner genuinely felt, showing she wants sincerity rather than expensive spectacle.

cards.front: According to the lesson's Key Fact, what three things does the graveyard opening establish?
cards.answer: Pip's isolation as an orphan among tombstones / Introduces the convict Magwitch / Triggers the novel's central irony
items: Pip's isolation as an orphan among tombstones

cards.front: What three details show that time has stopped at Satis House?
cards.answer: Clocks frozen at twenty to nine / Wedding breakfast rotting on the table / Miss Havisham wears her yellowed bridal dress
items: Clocks frozen at twenty to nine
Wedding breakfast rotting on the table
Miss Havisham wears her yellowed bridal dress

cards.front: Why did Magwitch devote his life to making Pip a gentleman?
cards.answer: He was repaying the terrified kindness Pip showed him as a child, when no one else showed him humanity.

cards.front: How did Mrs Joe end up brain-damaged and dependent?
cards.answer: She was attacked by Orlick, who struck her with a convict's leg-iron.

cards.front: According to Gupta, what four things does justice for Indian people require instead of mere charity?
cards.answer: Legal rights / Equal pay / Protection from exploitation / An end to the racial hierarchy
items: An end to the racial hierarchy

cards.front: What three issues does Gupta show are still relevant today by refusing to give the play closure?
cards.answer: Racism / Exploitation / Erased histories

cards.front: Why does Gupta avoid giving The Empress a neat, happy ending?
cards.answer: A neat resolution would suggest the problems of Empire had been solved, which would be historically dishonest.

cards.front: How does the Ayahs' Home raise the question of who gets to define progress?
cards.answer: From a British view the Home seems generous, but from the ayahs' view it is only a bare minimum response to catastrophic injustice.

cards.front: How do you decide whether to use jouer à or faire de for a sport in French?
cards.answer: Use jouer à if it's a ball or team sport, otherwise use faire de for individual sports and activities.

cards.front: How does the past participle change when a subject using être is feminine plural in the passé composé?
cards.answer: Add -es to the past participle to agree with the feminine plural subject.

cards.front: Name the four ways the past participle can change to agree with the subject when using être in the passé composé.
cards.answer: no extra letter (masculine singular) / add -e (feminine) / add -s (masculine plural) / add -es (feminine plural)

title: Wallace, Bruce and the 'Hammer of the Scots', 1297-1307
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four turning points of the First War of Scottish Independence given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Stirling Bridge, September 1297 / Falkirk, July 1298 / Campaign of 1303-04 ending at Strathord / Methven, June 1306

cards.front: Name the three harsh English policies the lesson gives for provoking the 1297 Scottish risings.
cards.answer: Forcing lords to swear loyalty on the Ragman Roll / Taxing Scottish trade for Edward's war chest / Trying to conscript Scots for the French campaign
items: Forcing lords to swear loyalty on the Ragman Roll
Taxing Scottish trade for Edward's war chest
Trying to conscript Scots for the French campaign

cards.front: How did Wallace and Murray win the Battle of Stirling Bridge?
cards.answer: They let the English cross the narrow bridge two abreast, then charged when only half the army had crossed, cutting the vanguard to pieces as the bridge collapsed.

cards.front: How did the English defeat the Scottish schiltrons at Falkirk?
cards.answer: Cavalry charges failed against the schiltrons, so Edward used longbowmen to pour arrows into the static formations until they crumbled, then charged with cavalry.

cards.front: Name the three decisive PLA campaigns that ended the Chinese Civil War in 1948-49.
cards.answer: Liaoshen Campaign (Manchuria) / Huaihai Campaign (central China) / Pingjin Campaign (Beijing-Tianjin)

cards.front: What four problems in the cities caused Chiang to lose the war 'in the urban classroom and marketplace'?
cards.answer: Hyperinflation / Corruption / Brutal conscription / Student protest

cards.front: How did the Outline Land Law of 1947 help bind peasants to the CCP?
cards.answer: Peasants who received redistributed land had a direct stake in communist victory and became a steady source of recruits.

cards.front: Why did c.$3 billion in US aid fail to save Chiang's regime?
cards.answer: The aid did not buy political legitimacy, because the GMD's real problems—corruption and inflation—were internal, not financial.

title: The impact of the First World War on Germany
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five main terms the Treaty of Versailles imposed on Germany.
cards.answer: War guilt (Article 231) / Reparations of £6.6 billion / Loss of 13% of territory / Rhineland demilitarised / Army limited to 100,000 men

cards.front: Why did the use of the Freikorps to crush the Spartacist Rising damage the Weimar Republic?
cards.answer: Ebert used right-wing ex-soldiers to kill left-wing revolutionaries, permanently alienating the German left from his government.

cards.front: Why was the German army seen as a 'state within the state' under Weimar?
cards.answer: It remained largely loyal to the old imperial order and was never fully committed to supporting democratic government.

cards.front: Besides schemas, name the three factors the lesson gives that can distort memory accuracy.
cards.answer: Interference / Context / False memories

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three things make eyewitness testimony less reliable?
cards.answer: Witnesses unconsciously alter memories using schemas / Witnesses are affected by leading questions (post-event information) / Witnesses may form false memories
items: Witnesses unconsciously alter memories using schemas
Witnesses are affected by leading questions (post-event information)

cards.front: How does proactive interference disrupt memory, using the language example from the lesson?
cards.answer: An older memory disrupts recall of a newer one, e.g. previously learned Spanish interfering with learning Italian.

cards.front: How does retroactive interference disrupt memory, using the phone number example from the lesson?
cards.answer: A newer memory disrupts recall of an older one, e.g. learning a new phone number makes you forget the old one.

title: The Cattle Industry and the Cowboy
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five roles that made up a long drive cattle crew.
cards.answer: Trail boss / Cook with chuck wagon / Point riders at the front / Swing and flank riders along the herd / Drag riders at the back
items: Swing and flank riders along the herd

cards.front: Name the cow towns that took over from Abilene as the railroads spread, before Dodge City.
cards.answer: Newton / Wichita / Ellsworth / Caldwell

cards.front: Why did Joseph Glidden's barbed wire (1874) increase conflict between ranchers and homesteaders?
cards.answer: It gave homesteaders a cheap way to fence their land for the first time, blocking the open range ranchers relied on.

cards.front: Why did the romantic 'Wild West' cowboy image develop mostly after the open-range era?
cards.answer: It was manufactured after the open range collapsed in the 1886–87 Big Die-Up, through Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show, dime novels and film.

title: Key ministers: Cecil, Walsingham and the Privy Council
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six types of issues the Elizabethan Privy Council debated.
cards.answer: Foreign policy / Military matters / Religious enforcement / Granting of monopolies / Management of the harvest / Law-and-order issues

cards.front: Name the four methods Walsingham's spy network used to gather intelligence.
cards.answer: Posed as Catholic exiles in Paris and Rome / Infiltrated seminaries training English priests / Watched ports for forbidden books / Opened, copied and resealed letters secretly
items: Posed as Catholic exiles in Paris and Rome
Opened, copied and resealed letters secretly

cards.front: How did Elizabeth use the Privy Council while keeping ultimate power in her own hands?
cards.answer: She let ministers debate and summarise the options, often demanded more information, then made the final decision herself.

cards.front: Why did Robert Cecil's rivalry with Essex matter for later Elizabethan politics?
cards.answer: Essex saw the Cecils as rivals blocking his ambition, and this clash helped set up the rebellion of 1601.

cards.front: Name the three key power equations given in the lesson.
cards.answer: P = E / t / P = I × V / P = I² × R

cards.front: How does a resistor heat up when current flows through it?
cards.answer: Moving electrons collide with metal ions in the lattice, transferring energy and making the ions vibrate more, heating the resistor.

cards.front: How can unwanted heating in wires be reduced?
cards.answer: Use wires that are thicker and shorter, since these have lower resistance and so waste less energy as heat.

cards.front: Name the four vegetation layers found in a tropical rainforest.
cards.answer: Emergent layer (giant trees up to 60m) / Canopy layer (main 30-45m layer) / Under-storey (adapted to filtered light) / Ground layer (sparse, deep shade)

cards.front: Name the four main causes of deforestation threatening the Amazon.
cards.answer: Cattle ranching / Soya farming / Illegal logging / Gold mining

cards.front: How does transpiration help the Amazon rainforest make its own rain?
cards.answer: Trees draw water from soil and release it through leaves, adding to evaporation, which forms clouds that fall as rain on the canopy.

cards.front: Why could crossing the Amazon's tipping point cause rainforest to shift to savannah?
cards.answer: Beyond 20-25% deforestation the forest can no longer recycle enough rainfall to stay wet, causing large areas to dry out and change.

cards.front: Name the four poems studied in this lesson on celebrating place.
cards.answer: To Autumn / Composed upon Westminster Bridge / Adlestrop / Home Thoughts from Abroad

cards.front: What form does each of the four poets use for their poem about place?
cards.answer: Keats: a formal ode / Wordsworth: a Petrarchan sonnet / Thomas: four short quatrains / Browning: irregular stanzas with exclamatory syntax
items: Browning: irregular stanzas with exclamatory syntax

cards.front: Why does 'To Autumn' carry an underlying melancholy despite its imagery of abundance?
cards.answer: Because autumn inevitably gives way to winter, and Keats himself was aware of his failing health.

cards.front: How does 'Home Thoughts from Abroad' create its idealised, patriotic view of England?
cards.answer: It only mentions blossoms, birdsong and dew, leaving out politics, poverty or industry, giving a selective idealised vision.

title: Red Terror, the Cheka and the Kronstadt Mutiny
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What five demands did the Kronstadt sailors' fifteen-point resolution include (name four)?
cards.answer: Fresh elections to soviets by secret ballot / Freedom of speech and press for socialist parties / Release of political prisoners / End to grain requisitioning / Right of peasants to farm freely
items: Fresh elections to soviets by secret ballot
Freedom of speech and press for socialist parties
Right of peasants to farm freely

cards.front: What three groups did the Cheka target during the Red Terror?
cards.answer: Whites / The bourgeoisie and clergy / The Kadets

cards.front: Why did the Kronstadt Mutiny shock the Bolsheviks so much?
cards.answer: Because it came from sailors who had been the 'pride and glory' of the 1917 revolution, showing the Bolsheviks' own base had turned against them.

cards.front: Why did the Tenth Party Congress both ban factions and launch the New Economic Policy in March 1921?
cards.answer: Kronstadt showed peasant discontent was dangerous, so Lenin tightened party control while loosening grain requisitioning to ease peasant anger.

cards.front: Name the six Proppian character roles applied to Trigger Point in the lesson.
cards.answer: Lana Washington - the hero / Danny - the helper / Hassan - the dispatcher / Thom - the princess who is saved / Commander Francis - the false hero / The terrorists - the villains
items: Thom - the princess who is saved

cards.front: Name the four genre conventions the lesson says to look for when analysing media language in the Trigger Point extract.
cards.answer: Urban settings such as the power station / Iconography including protective equipment and explosions / Diegetic sound such as sirens and jargon / Non-diegetic music that builds tension
items: Urban settings such as the power station
Iconography including protective equipment and explosions
Diegetic sound such as sirens and jargon

cards.front: How does the worked example say Trigger Point's extract reverses traditional gender roles?
cards.answer: Close-ups of Lana's calm face and wide shots of Thom's trembling hands, plus contrasting firm and panicked dialogue, position the woman as competent and the man as vulnerable.

cards.front: Why was Man Like Mobeen originally only available online via iPlayer?
cards.answer: Because BBC Three had become an online-only channel, illustrating industry convergence.

cards.front: Name the four types of switch the lesson gives as simple input devices.
cards.answer: Push switches / Toggle switches / Tilt switches / Reed switches

cards.front: Name the three roles a microcontroller can be programmed to perform.
cards.answer: Counters / Timers / Decision makers

cards.front: How does a microcontroller act as a decision maker in an electronic system?
cards.answer: It uses logic to choose between actions based on sensor data, e.g. switching on a fan if temperature is above 25°C.

cards.front: How does a microcontroller's timer function control an output device?
cards.answer: It triggers an action after a set time has passed, such as switching off a light 30 seconds after activation.

cards.front: Why does Hailsham's kindness act as a form of control over the students?
cards.answer: By giving students a good childhood, the guardians make them less likely to question their fate.

cards.front: Why was Miss Lucy dismissed from Hailsham?
cards.answer: She broke the unspoken rule by telling the students their fate directly instead of letting them only sense it.

cards.front: Name the four stages in Roger's arc from restraint to cruelty across the novel.
cards.answer: Throws stones near Henry, deliberately missing / Becomes one of Jack's loyal followers / Levers a boulder onto Piggy, killing him / Sharpens a stick at both ends
items: Throws stones near Henry, deliberately missing
Becomes one of Jack's loyal followers
Levers a boulder onto Piggy, killing him
Sharpens a stick at both ends

cards.front: Why does Jack encourage the boys' fear of the beast even though he claims fear can't hurt them?
cards.answer: He exploits fear as a political tool, offering himself as protector through hunting to consolidate his own power.

cards.front: How does Golding use Castle Rock's geography to represent political systems?
cards.answer: The open, exposed beach fosters debate and democracy, while the defensible, exclusive Castle Rock fosters tyranny.

cards.front: Name the three relationships Act 1 establishes in A Taste of Honey.
cards.answer: Jo and Helen / Jo and the Boy / Helen and Peter

cards.front: Name the three consequences Act 2 shows following on from Act 1's relationships.
cards.answer: Jo's pregnancy / Geof's care for Jo / Helen's return

cards.front: What happens during the interval between Act 1 and Act 2?
cards.answer: It marks a significant time jump, with Jo going from a schoolgirl to a pregnant young woman.

cards.front: Why is jazz music particularly linked to the Boy and Jo's scenes together?
cards.answer: It creates a sensual, dreamlike atmosphere associated with the Boy and Jo's brief period of happiness.

cards.front: Name the five senses covered by sensory imagery in poetry analysis.
cards.answer: Sight (visual) / Sound (auditory) / Touch (tactile) / Smell (olfactory) / Taste (gustatory)

cards.front: How does the connotation of 'swallowed' create sympathy in 'the city swallowed him whole'?
cards.answer: It suggests consumption and destruction, presenting the city as a predator and the person as prey, making the reader sympathise with the vulnerable individual.

cards.front: How does pathetic fallacy work in poetry?
cards.answer: Weather or landscape reflects the character's emotion, such as a storm during anger or sunshine during joy, mirroring the speaker's inner state.

cards.front: Why is a simile described as more distanced than a metaphor?
cards.answer: A simile acknowledges the comparison using 'like' or 'as', whereas a metaphor asserts the two things are identical.

cards.front: Name the five demands the 1381 rebels made, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: End to serfdom / Abolition of the poll tax / Death of 'traitors' like John of Gaunt / Dissolution of corrupt landlordism / New relationship between king and people
items: Death of 'traitors' like John of Gaunt
New relationship between king and people

cards.front: Name the five AQA factors the lesson says converged to cause the 1381 revolt.
cards.answer: Chance (Black Death) / The economy (poll tax) / Communication (preachers like John Ball) / Role of the individual (Tyler and Ball) / Government (weak boy-king regime)
items: Role of the individual (Tyler and Ball)

cards.front: How did the Black Death give peasants real bargaining power over wages?
cards.answer: It killed about 40% of the population, causing a labour shortage, so lords had to compete for workers and pay higher wages.

cards.front: Why was John of Gaunt so unpopular in the years before the revolt?
cards.answer: He held real power as young Richard II's uncle and was loathed for corruption and links to a costly, unsuccessful war with France.

title: Dialogue Within and Between Religious Groups
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the three broad models theologians use to describe how religions relate to each other.
cards.answer: Exclusivism / Inclusivism / Pluralism

cards.front: What five key philosophical concepts does the lesson say describe the conditions for meaningful religious dialogue?
cards.answer: Consensus / Diversity / Uniformity / Freedom of choice / Freedom of expression

cards.front: Why can proselytisation create tension with inter-faith dialogue?
cards.answer: If the goal of engagement is to win converts, dialogue becomes a form of sales rather than genuine mutual understanding.

cards.front: Why has identifying Christianity with British national identity become contested in modern Britain?
cards.answer: As Britain has become more religiously diverse, equating national identity with Christianity can feel excluding to religious minorities, as though belonging requires religious conformity.

cards.front: The lesson gives three sources that shaped most Elizabethans' understanding of Judaism — name them.
cards.answer: Crude stereotypes / Religious teachings blaming Jews for Christ's crucifixion / Sensationalised stories like the Lopez case
items: Religious teachings blaming Jews for Christ's crucifixion
Sensationalised stories like the Lopez case

cards.front: Why was Venice's commercial law system ironic for the trial scene's outcome?
cards.answer: Venice's laws promised impartial justice, yet the law was twisted to strip Shylock of his wealth and force his conversion, serving Christian interests.

cards.front: Why did money-lending become one of the few jobs open to Jewish people in medieval Europe?
cards.answer: The Christian Church banned usury as sinful, but Jewish law allowed charging interest to non-Jews, while Jews were barred from most other trades and guilds.

cards.front: How does the contrast between Venice and Belmont support the play's theme of appearance versus reality?
cards.answer: Venice seems ruled by fair law but is full of prejudice, while Belmont seems harmonious but is funded by exploitative Venetian wealth and Portia's racism.

cards.front: Name the six alkali metals in Group 1.
cards.answer: Lithium / Sodium / Potassium / Rubidium / Caesium / Francium

cards.front: Name the three practical uses of noble gases given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Helium in weather balloons and airships / Neon in display lighting / Argon in tungsten filament bulbs and welding
items: Helium in weather balloons and airships
Argon in tungsten filament bulbs and welding

cards.front: Why does the modern periodic table (ordered by atomic number) not have the anomalies Mendeleev's table had?
cards.answer: Arranging elements by atomic number instead of atomic weight resolved the few anomalies present in Mendeleev's arrangement.

cards.front: Why must the wire loop be cleaned before each flame test?
cards.answer: To avoid contamination from previous samples, which could give a false flame colour.

cards.front: Give the seven adverbios de frecuencia (frequency adverbs) listed in the lesson, from always to never.
cards.answer: siempre (always) / a menudo (often) / normalmente (normally) / a veces (sometimes) / de vez en cuando (from time to time) / raramente (rarely) / nunca (never)
items: de vez en cuando (from time to time)

cards.front: What are the six present tense endings for -AR verbs like jugar (yo to ellos)?
cards.answer: juego (yo) / juegas (tú) / juega (él/ella) / jugamos (nosotros) / jugáis (vosotros) / juegan (ellos)

cards.front: How should you structure a Spanish opinion sentence to make it stronger, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Follow an opinion phrase with porque (because) and a reason, e.g. me gusta nadar porque es relajante.

cards.front: How can you make your writing about hobbies sound more varied instead of always saying 'me gusta'?
cards.answer: Use alternative phrases like 'lo que más me gusta es', 'lo paso bomba cuando', or 'me resulta divertido'.

cards.front: Name the four behaviours the lesson gives that show Anita defying adult rules.
cards.answer: Swears / Steals / Defies adults / Roams the village unsupervised

cards.front: Name the three ways Anita controls the friendship with Meena.
cards.answer: Sets the rules / Decides the games / Controls who is 'in' or 'out'

cards.front: Why does Meena accept the unequal power dynamic in her friendship with Anita?
cards.answer: Because Anita's approval feels like acceptance into Englishness itself.

cards.front: Why does Anita ignore and belittle her sister Tracey?
