cards.answer: Fluttering in a breeze / Unfurling from a pole / Rising over a tent / Flying across a field

cards.front: Why does the friendly, casual tone of the final stanza make its warning more disturbing?
cards.answer: Because Agard offers patriotism as if it's a casual favour, while its real cost is a permanent loss of moral judgement.

cards.front: Why does Agard never name a specific country or flag in the poem?
cards.answer: So the critique applies to any nationalism, inviting readers to examine their own assumptions about patriotism and loyalty.

cards.front: What five areas does pre-conception health cover, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Diet / Weight / Exercise / Substance use / Screening for infections and inherited conditions
items: Screening for infections and inherited conditions

cards.front: Name the four food sources of folic acid mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Leafy green vegetables / Broccoli / Chickpeas / Fortified breakfast cereals

cards.front: Why is obesity linked to reduced fertility?
cards.answer: Obesity is associated with hormonal imbalance, irregular menstrual cycles and a higher risk of miscarriage.

cards.front: Why must a woman wait one month after having the MMR vaccine before trying to conceive?
cards.answer: The MMR vaccine uses a live virus, so conception must be delayed a month after having it.

title: The Five Pillars and Ten Obligatory Acts
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam.
cards.answer: Shahadah / Salah / Zakah / Sawm / Hajj

cards.front: Beyond the four shared pillars, what six extra duties make up the Shi'a Ten Obligatory Acts?
cards.answer: Khums (20% levy) / Jihad / Amr-bil-Maroof (commanding good) / Nahy-anil-Munkar (forbidding evil) / Tawalla (love) / Tabarra (disavowal)

cards.front: Why is Zakah described as 'purification'?
cards.answer: Because giving 2.5% of savings purifies the giver's remaining wealth from greed while supporting the poor.

cards.front: Why is the Shahadah not one of the Shi'a Ten Obligatory Acts?
cards.answer: Because for Shi'a Muslims the declaration of faith belongs with the Five Roots of belief, not the acts of practice.

title: Britain & Europe: From EEC to Brexit
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three answers Britain considered for what kind of country to be after empire.
cards.answer: The United States (special relationship) / The Commonwealth / Europe

cards.front: Name the five sectors that became structurally dependent on East European labour before the 2016 referendum.
cards.answer: Agriculture / Hospitality / Construction / Transport / Food processing

cards.front: Why did Britain choose to stay outside the EEC when it was founded in 1957?
cards.answer: Britain preferred to bet on the Commonwealth and the 'special relationship' with the United States instead.

cards.front: Why did net migration reach record highs after free movement ended in 2020, despite Brexit aiming to cut immigration?
cards.answer: A global recruitment drive for the NHS and care sector, plus visa schemes for Hong Kongers and Ukrainians, drove numbers up.

title: The Origins of the Korean War
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five stacked causes of the Korean War by June 1950 given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Korean nationalist division / two rival regimes under Kim and Rhee / 1949 communist victory in China / Acheson speech excluding Korea from US defence / Stalin's green light after lobbying
items: two rival regimes under Kim and Rhee
Acheson speech excluding Korea from US defence

cards.front: Why did Stalin and Mao eventually agree to let Kim Il Sung invade South Korea?
cards.answer: They believed the Americans would not fight for Korea, especially after Acheson's speech excluding it from the defence perimeter.

title: Blinded by the Light: Aesthetic and Musical Realism
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What are the three aesthetic registers the lesson identifies in Blinded by the Light?
cards.answer: Lyric-text overlay and superimposition in musical set-pieces / Warm autumnal ambers and golds in domestic/high-street scenes / Colder greyer palette in National Front and New Jersey scenes
items: Lyric-text overlay and superimposition in musical set-pieces
Warm autumnal ambers and golds in domestic/high-street scenes
Colder greyer palette in National Front and New Jersey scenes

cards.front: How does the National Front street-confrontation scene avoid glamourising racism?
cards.answer: The threat and imagery appear at the edges of a wider-focus frame rather than centre, making racism ambient rather than a dramatic centrepiece.

cards.front: Why does Chadha keep the camera in the cramped bedroom during Javed's first Springsteen listen?
cards.answer: So the music transforms the ordinary space Javed already occupies rather than transporting him somewhere spectacular.

cards.front: How does close mid-shot framing in the Khan family kitchen link to the film's themes?
cards.answer: It compresses the family together, linking the claustrophobic space to the intergenerational pressure the Springsteen songs represent an escape from.

cards.front: The lesson names three types of support that government schemes provide to new businesses. What are they?
cards.answer: Grants (money that does not need to be repaid) / Information and guidance on starting up / Training or mentoring schemes
items: Grants (money that does not need to be repaid)
Information and guidance on starting up

cards.front: What four kinds of support can charitable organisations offer an early-stage business?
cards.answer: Free or subsidised business mentoring / Access to shared workspace / Help with writing a business plan / Connections to grant funding
items: Help with writing a business plan

cards.front: Why can it be hard for a brand-new business with no trading history to get finance from a bank?
cards.answer: Banks want evidence of a credible plan and a realistic chance of repayment, which a new business without a trading history struggles to prove.

cards.front: Why is local council support often more accessible than national government schemes for a brand-new small business?
cards.answer: Local council support is tailored to businesses in that area, whereas national programmes may be more competitive.

cards.front: Name the five monocular depth cues the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Height in the plane / Relative size / Superimposition / Linear perspective / Texture gradient

cards.front: Name the three types of visual illusion the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Fictions / Ambiguous figures / Distortions

cards.front: Why do monocular depth cues still work in a photograph but binocular cues do not?
cards.answer: Monocular cues are properties of the scene itself, while binocular cues come from the physical set-up of two eyes, not the picture.

cards.front: Why do the arrowheads in the Müller-Lyer illusion make equal lines look different lengths?
cards.answer: The arrowheads mimic the converging and diverging lines used in linear perspective, so the brain misapplies this depth cue.

title: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle: Reviewing the Whole Investigation
subject: statistics-aqa

cards.front: Why can describing what an investigation did lose marks in a Statistical Enquiry Cycle evaluation?
cards.answer: Description alone doesn't explain why it's a weakness or matters for the conclusion, so it only scores Developing at best.

cards.front: Why does a vague hypothesis at the Initial Planning stage cause problems later in the enquiry?
cards.answer: A vague hypothesis leads to ambiguous data, since decisions at this stage affect every other stage of the cycle.

cards.front: Why might a lurking variable weaken the reliability of a statistical finding?
cards.answer: It could offer an alternative explanation for the pattern seen, rather than the one concluded from the data.

cards.front: Name the four increasingly extreme actions Mrs Lyons takes as her paranoia grows.
cards.answer: Fires Mrs Johnstone / Slaps Edward / Spies on him / Attempts to stab Mrs Johnstone with a knife
items: Attempts to stab Mrs Johnstone with a knife

cards.front: Name the three things Eddie's wealthy upbringing gives him according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Boarding school / University / Becomes a councillor

cards.front: Why is Sammy structurally important to the play's plot?
cards.answer: He hides the gun Mickey later takes and draws Mickey into the robbery that leads to prison.

cards.front: Why is Mrs Lyons more miserable than Mrs Johnstone despite her wealth?
cards.answer: Her guilt and paranoia make her more miserable, while Mrs Johnstone at least has genuine love and warmth.

cards.front: Name the three metal ions that all produce a white precipitate when NaOH is added to their solution.
cards.answer: Calcium (Ca²⁺) / Magnesium (Mg²⁺) / Aluminium (Al³⁺)

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for preferring instrumental methods over chemical tests in industry.
cards.answer: More accurate / More sensitive / Faster / Smaller sample sizes needed

cards.front: Why is dilute acid added before silver nitrate or barium chloride in halide and sulfate tests?
cards.answer: It removes any carbonate ions first, which would otherwise interfere by forming their own precipitates.

cards.front: How can you tell calcium and magnesium apart when both give a white precipitate with NaOH?
cards.answer: Do a flame test: calcium burns orange-red, while magnesium produces no visible flame colour.

cards.front: Name the three human behaviours the pigs adopt by living in the farmhouse, besides walking on hind legs and carrying whips.
cards.answer: Sleep in beds / Wear clothes / Move into Mr Jones's farmhouse

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why the animals fail to stop the pigs' tyranny.
cards.answer: They cannot read / They trust blindly / They let pigs monopolise information

cards.front: Why is Boxer's collapse and disposal so devastating to the reader?
cards.answer: He gave everything through genuine dedication, but the regime valued him only for labour and discarded him once he could no longer produce.

cards.front: Why does propaganda still work on the animals even though their lives are clearly worse under Napoleon?
cards.answer: Propaganda does not need to be believed to be effective, it just needs to be the only narrative the animals have access to.

cards.front: What tasks did barefoot doctors carry out in rural communes, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Carried a basic kit of medicines / Taught hygiene / Delivered vaccinations / Ran family-planning clinics
items: Carried a basic kit of medicines

cards.front: What did education include in Chinese primary schools before 1966, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Arithmetic / Passages of Mao's thought / Agricultural work experience / Industrial work experience

cards.front: How did simplified characters and Pinyin together speed up mass literacy in China?
cards.answer: Simplified characters cut the strokes needed to write common words while Pinyin gave a Roman-letter system for teaching pronunciation, cutting time to functional literacy.

cards.front: Why did rural healthcare improve so much under the barefoot doctor system despite uneven results overall?
cards.answer: Around one million trained paramedics were dispatched to communes, delivering vaccinations, hygiene teaching and family planning where clinics had never existed before.

cards.front: Name the four hard engineering strategies the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Sea walls / Rock armour (rip-rap) / Groynes / Gabions

cards.front: Name the four Shoreline Management Plan options for deciding how much coast to defend.
cards.answer: Hold the line / Advance the line / No active intervention / Managed realignment

cards.front: Why does Happisburgh get 'no active intervention' while Cromer holds the line, even though they're on the same coast?
cards.answer: Cost-benefit reasoning: defending low-population Happisburgh costs more than buying out residents, while Cromer's tourism economy is worth defending.

cards.front: How does salt-marsh creation protect the coast from storm surges?
cards.answer: Low-value land is allowed to flood so mud, plants and tidal channels develop, absorbing storm surges before they reach the sea wall behind.

cards.front: What three fragments does De Waal weave through Part 3 to build tension toward the riots?
cards.answer: Conversations Leon overhears between adults / A heightened police presence / Neighbours boarding up windows

cards.front: What three things does Leon do as his search for Jake intensifies in Part 3?
cards.answer: Gathering information / Memorising addresses / Planning how to reach his brother
items: Planning how to reach his brother

cards.front: Why does De Waal keep Leon's restricted, child's-eye viewpoint during the political build-up in Part 3?
cards.answer: To maintain the child's perspective while still conveying historical context, creating tension for readers who grasp the danger Leon doesn't.

cards.front: How does Leon's solo search for Jake highlight the absurdity of his situation?
cards.answer: It shows a nine-year-old child fighting an entire institutional system completely alone.

title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three noble gases mentioned and their practical uses.
cards.answer: Helium in balloons and airships / Neon in advertising signs / Argon in light bulbs and welding
items: Argon in light bulbs and welding

cards.front: Name the three ways transition metals differ from Group 1 metals.
cards.answer: Less reactive / Harder / Denser

cards.front: Why was Mendeleev's periodic table widely accepted after being published?
cards.answer: Because elements later discovered, such as gallium and germanium, matched the properties he had predicted for the gaps.

cards.front: Why are the reactivity trends of Group 1 and Group 7 opposite going down each group?
cards.answer: Because Group 1 metals lose their outer electron while Group 7 non-metals gain one, so distance from the nucleus affects each differently.

cards.front: Name the three mechanisms the lesson gives for how effective goal setting improves performance.
cards.answer: Directs training effort towards specific weaknesses / Sustains motivation through visible progress milestones / Enables systematic evaluation of whether training works
items: Directs training effort towards specific weaknesses
Sustains motivation through visible progress milestones
Enables systematic evaluation of whether training works

cards.front: Why are performance goals generally more powerful motivators than outcome goals?
cards.answer: Because the performer has full control over performance goals, whereas outcome goals depend partly on the quality of the opposition.

cards.front: Why does a goal accepted by the performer generate more intrinsic motivation than one imposed by a coach?
cards.answer: Because the performer feels ownership of the target, which generates greater intrinsic motivation.

cards.front: Name the four criteria a test programme evaluates a prototype against, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Fitness for purpose / Functionality / Marketability / Safety

cards.front: Name the three structured methods used in user testing, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Task-based testing / Think-aloud protocols / Rating scales

cards.front: Why must ergonomic testing be carried out under realistic conditions rather than light use?
cards.answer: A tool comfortable during light use may still cause wrist fatigue after prolonged heavy use, which only realistic testing reveals.

cards.front: How does the EN 71-1 small parts test decide whether a toy component is a choking hazard?
cards.answer: Any component fitting entirely inside a cylinder 57.1mm tall by 31.7mm diameter is classed a choking hazard, banned for under-3s toys.

cards.front: Name the three constructs algorithms are built from.
cards.answer: Sequence / Selection / Repetition

cards.front: Besides variables and constants, name the three data structures described for storing data.
cards.answer: One-dimensional array / Two-dimensional array / Record

cards.front: Why would you choose count-controlled repetition instead of condition-controlled repetition?
cards.answer: Because you know in advance exactly how many times the steps need to repeat.

cards.front: How does a flowchart show a 'while' loop continuing versus ending?
cards.answer: The diamond tests the condition; the Yes exit loops back to an earlier step, and the No exit leaves the loop.

cards.front: Name the four Gothic features the lesson gives for Thornfield when Jane first arrives.
cards.answer: Battlements on the house / Locked third storey / Disembodied laughter in the corridor / Nighttime fires

cards.front: Name the four things Bertha does while hidden on the third storey, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Laughs at night / Sets fire to Rochester's bed / Attacks her brother Mason with a knife / Tears Jane's wedding veil
items: Attacks her brother Mason with a knife

cards.front: Why is Rochester's blaming of Grace Poole for the bedroom fire an example of dramatic irony?
cards.answer: Jane believes him at the time, but the reader later learns, retrospectively, that Rochester is lying.

cards.front: Why does the lesson call Jane's later refusal to be Rochester's mistress an act of moral resistance rather than prudishness?
cards.answer: Because Rochester's past affair is excused while Jane must stay untouched, so her refusal challenges this Victorian gender double-standard.

title: Reflection, Sound Waves and Waves for Detection
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things that can happen when a wave hits a boundary between two materials.
cards.answer: Reflected / Absorbed / Transmitted

cards.front: What are the three key differences between P-waves and S-waves given in the lesson?
cards.answer: P-waves longitudinal, S-waves transverse / P-waves travel through solids and liquids, S-waves only solids / P-waves faster and arrive first
items: P-waves travel through solids and liquids, S-waves only solids

cards.front: Why does specular reflection produce a clear image but diffuse reflection does not?
cards.answer: On smooth surfaces the normal is the same everywhere so reflected rays stay parallel, but on rough surfaces the normal differs at every point so rays scatter.

cards.front: How do scientists use P-wave behaviour as evidence for density changes at the mantle-core boundary?
cards.answer: P-waves are refracted as they pass through different layers, which shows density changes at the mantle-core boundary.

title: Scenes 1–3: Enid, Viv & the Obeah Woman
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Why does Enid distance herself from her Caribbean heritage?
cards.answer: She believes respectability and English education will protect her daughters from the racism she has experienced.

cards.front: Why does Mai take a special interest in Del?
cards.answer: Mai recognises Del's potential as her spiritual successor in Obeah from the start.

cards.front: The lesson gives three things about Brod's life in England. What are they?
cards.answer: Serious drinking problem / Wife and children still in Jamaica / Deeply disenchanted with life in England
items: Wife and children still in Jamaica
Deeply disenchanted with life in England

cards.front: Why does Enid advise sending money to Cynthia even though she suspects exaggeration?
cards.answer: It is Mai who advises Enid to send the money anyway, despite Enid's suspicion Cynthia is exaggerating.

cards.front: Name the four costs of maintaining quality the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Staff training / Inspection costs / Product recalls / Bad publicity hit

cards.front: Name the three benefits of maintaining quality the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Better image and reputation / Additional sales / Higher price customers accept

cards.front: Why does a quality failure cost a business more than just the refund bill?
cards.answer: It also causes fewer repeat purchases, weaker brand image and falling market share, which are much bigger costs.

cards.front: Why does outsourcing make it harder for a business to maintain consistent quality?
cards.answer: A different company makes part of the product using its own standards and culture, which head office cannot fully control.

cards.front: Name the three ways ordinary English people felt the impact of the Hundred Years' War, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Heavy taxation to fund campaigns / Disruption to the wool trade / Losses of families with men sent abroad
items: Losses of families with men sent abroad

cards.front: Why did Henry V position his army between two woods at Agincourt?
cards.answer: To force the French to advance along a narrow muddy field, which negated their numerical advantage.

cards.front: Why was the indenture system better than the feudal levy for long campaigns abroad?
cards.answer: Paid soldiers could serve indefinitely, unlike feudal levies who were only obligated to serve forty days a year.

cards.front: How did chevauchée raids help the English against France?
cards.answer: They destroyed French tax revenues and forced the French to fight battles, though they devastated civilians too.

title: What Is Sociology? The Sociological Approach
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: Name the eight core concepts of sociology given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Society / Socialisation / Norms / Values / Roles / Culture / Power / Authority

cards.front: Name the four perspectives on power described in the lesson and who they say holds it.
cards.answer: Functionalists: legitimate authority benefits society / Marxists: power held by the bourgeoisie / Feminists: patriarchal structures favour men / Interactionists: focus on micro-level labelling
items: Marxists: power held by the bourgeoisie

cards.front: How does authority differ from power?
cards.answer: Authority is power that others accept as legitimate or rightful, whereas power can be exercised through force, persuasion or resources without being accepted.

cards.front: Why did Parsons argue the family is the irreplaceable site of primary socialisation?
cards.answer: Because it transmits the core values of society to each new generation.

cards.front: Name the four practical benefits of reprogrammable microcontroller systems given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Flexibility / Firmware updates / Reduced component count / Faster prototyping

cards.front: Name the four limitations of programmable components (microcontrollers) given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Programming expertise required / Higher unit cost for simple tasks / Power consumption / Software dependency
items: Higher unit cost for simple tasks

cards.front: Why does an analogue sensor connected to a microcontroller need an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC)?
cards.answer: Because it converts the continuously varying voltage from the sensor into a number the processor can use.

cards.front: Why can a single microcontroller-based washing machine PCB run different wash programmes instead of needing separate boards?
cards.answer: Because the same hardware can be reprogrammed with different software settings for each wash programme.

title: Postnatal Care of the Mother & Conditions for Development
subject: cambridge-nationals-child-development

cards.front: What four things does the six-to-eight week postnatal GP check cover?
cards.answer: Physical recovery / Pelvic floor health / Contraception / Emotional wellbeing

cards.front: What treatments may be offered if postnatal depression is identified?
cards.answer: Talking therapies (CBT or counselling) / Antidepressant medication / Peer support groups / Referral to perinatal mental health team
items: Referral to perinatal mental health team

cards.front: Why are newborns especially vulnerable to hypothermia without warmth and appropriate clothing?
cards.answer: Because newborns cannot regulate their own body temperature.

cards.front: Why can untreated postnatal depression harm a child's emotional development?
cards.answer: Because it can disrupt attachment between mother and baby, affecting the child's emotional development.

title: Worship in the Gurdwara, Langar and Sikh Initiation
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four steps that happen to a Sikh during the Amrit Sanskar ceremony.
cards.answer: Drinks amrit five times / Has amrit sprinkled on eyes and hair / Repeats the Mool Mantar five times / Commits to the Rehat Maryada and Five Ks
items: Has amrit sprinkled on eyes and hair
Repeats the Mool Mantar five times
Commits to the Rehat Maryada and Five Ks

cards.front: Why does the langar meal express Sikh belief in equality?
cards.answer: Everyone sits together on the floor in rows sharing the same free food, so people of all backgrounds and social positions are made equal.

cards.front: How is a Sikh baby named in the Naam Karan ceremony?
cards.answer: A passage is chosen at random from the Guru Granth Sahib and the baby is given a name starting with the first letter of its first word.

title: The U2 Crisis and the Paris Summit
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What three items made up the agenda for the Paris Summit?
cards.answer: A possible nuclear test ban / The future of Berlin / Steps toward peaceful coexistence

cards.front: What four steps did the US and Soviet Union take in intelligence after the U2 affair?
cards.answer: US switched to Corona reconnaissance satellites / Soviet planners built heavier integrated air-defence networks / CIA developed the SR-71 Blackbird programme / Lower-altitude U2 versions stayed in service
items: US switched to Corona reconnaissance satellites
Soviet planners built heavier integrated air-defence networks
CIA developed the SR-71 Blackbird programme
Lower-altitude U2 versions stayed in service

cards.front: Why did Eisenhower refuse to apologise for the U2 overflights?
cards.answer: He argued the overflights were a necessary defence against the threat of a surprise Soviet attack.

cards.front: Why did the U2 affair push Khrushchev toward a tougher stance on the West?
cards.answer: Soviet hardliners already saw him as too soft on the West, and the affair increased pressure for a harder line.

cards.front: How does Rochester's blindness reverse the power dynamic between him and Jane?
cards.answer: He can no longer judge Jane by her appearance and must value her entirely for her inner qualities.

cards.front: Why does Brontë set Jane and Rochester's reunion at Ferndean rather than a grand house?
cards.answer: Its natural, secluded setting reflects the Romantic ideal that truth and happiness are found away from the corruption of civilisation.

cards.front: Why does Elizabeth initially refuse to visit Pemberley?
cards.answer: She fears an awkward encounter with Darcy, and only agrees once she learns he is away.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Reynolds's praise of Darcy carry more weight than public opinion of him?
cards.answer: Servants see their masters without social masks, so her daily private observation is more trustworthy than public performance.

title: Climate Models and Earth's Energy Balance
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: Name three sources of methane given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Livestock digestion / Rice paddies / Landfill sites / Leaks from natural gas systems

cards.front: Why is water vapour's concentration not directly controlled by human activity, unlike carbon dioxide?
cards.answer: Water vapour's concentration is controlled mainly by temperature rather than directly by human activity.

cards.front: Why do scientists give a range of warming values instead of one precise figure?
cards.answer: Climate models simplify complex systems like clouds, ocean currents and feedback loops, producing uncertainty in the exact magnitude of change.

cards.front: How does the enhanced greenhouse effect shift Earth's energy balance?
cards.answer: Human activities have increased carbon dioxide concentration, trapping more infrared radiation and driving global warming.

cards.front: Name the three observations from electrolysing copper sulfate solution with inert (carbon) electrodes.
cards.answer: Copper metal deposits at the cathode / Cathode gains mass / Oxygen gas produced at the anode / Solution becomes paler
items: Copper metal deposits at the cathode
Oxygen gas produced at the anode

cards.front: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis instead of reduction with carbon?
cards.answer: Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon.

cards.front: How would you test the gas produced at the anode in copper sulfate electrolysis with inert electrodes to confirm it is oxygen?
cards.answer: A glowing splint would relight if the gas is oxygen.

cards.front: In aqueous electrolysis, why does hydrogen gas form at the cathode instead of a metal like sodium or zinc?
cards.answer: Because these metals are more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen is discharged at the cathode instead of the metal.

cards.front: According to Rousseau-influenced philosophy in the novel, why does the Creature become violent?
cards.answer: It begins innocent but turns violent only after repeated rejection, cruelty, and isolation from society.

cards.front: How does the gap between Victor's expectation and the reality of creation criticise him?
cards.answer: Victor expected a beautiful creation but is horrified by the result, showing he planned the creation but not its aftermath.

cards.front: What four things does Alem describe in his tribunal testimony?
cards.answer: The violence in Ethiopia / The persecution his family faced / His father's decision to bring him to England / Fear of what would happen if sent back
items: His father's decision to bring him to England
Fear of what would happen if sent back

cards.front: What losses has Alem already suffered by the end of the play?
cards.answer: His father is gone / His mother Mrs Kelo is dead / His home country is violent and persecuting / He can never return to his old life
items: His mother Mrs Kelo is dead
His home country is violent and persecuting
He can never return to his old life

cards.front: How does Sissay build suspense before the tribunal's verdict?
cards.answer: Through pacing — the hearing concludes, there is a wait, then the verdict is delivered, heightening emotional weight.

cards.front: Why does testimony work differently on stage than in a novel?
cards.answer: A real person stands before real people, so the audience cannot look away, skip ahead, or close the book.

cards.front: Name the four major international agreements of the 1920s, with their dates.
cards.answer: Dawes Plan (August 1924) / Locarno Treaties (December 1925) / Kellogg-Briand Pact (August 1928) / Young Plan (June 1929)

cards.front: Name the three acts of aggression the lesson gives as breaches of the Kellogg-Briand Pact.
cards.answer: Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) / Italy invaded Abyssinia (1935) / Germany remilitarised the Rhineland (1936)

cards.front: Why did the Ruhr occupation lead to hyperinflation in Germany?
cards.answer: Germany responded with 'passive resistance', ordering workers to strike, which disrupted the economy and caused hyperinflation.

cards.front: Why did the Dawes Plan create a dangerous dependency for Germany?
cards.answer: It worked by bringing American capital into the system through US loans, making Germany reliant on continued US lending.

cards.front: Why does the novella argue that Jekyll's experiment ends in catastrophe?
cards.answer: Because good and evil are not separate entities but inseparable parts of the same person.

cards.front: How does Stevenson's own life connect to the theme of duality in the novella?
cards.answer: He grew up in Edinburgh, split between respectable New Town and vice-ridden Old Town, and knew of Deacon Brodie's double life.

cards.front: Name the three modern materials the lesson identifies as key examples.
cards.answer: Graphene / Metal foams / Titanium

cards.front: Name the five technical textiles or textile treatments the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Conductive fabrics / Fire-resistant fabrics / Kevlar / Microfibres / Micro encapsulation

cards.front: Why do metal foams work well for crash protection in vehicles?
cards.answer: They are lightweight but strong, and absorb energy well, cushioning impact during a crash.

cards.front: Why do photochromic pigments make good reactive sunglasses lenses?
cards.answer: They change colour in response to light, darkening in bright sunlight and returning to clear indoors.

cards.front: Besides ship money, name the three other financial measures Charles I used during the Personal Rule.
cards.answer: Distraint of knighthood / Revived forest laws / Granting of monopolies

cards.front: Why did Charles I dissolve the Short Parliament after only three weeks in 1640?
cards.answer: MPs insisted on discussing their grievances before granting him money, so Charles dissolved it.

cards.front: Why did the mutilation of Prynne, Burton and Bastwick in 1637 backfire on Charles and Laud?
cards.answer: The brutal censorship generated public outrage rather than submission, increasing opposition to Laud's reforms.

title: Audience Interpretation and Hall's Reception Theory
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three reading positions in Hall's encoding-decoding model.
cards.answer: Dominant/preferred reading / Negotiated reading / Oppositional reading

cards.front: Why can the same media text produce very different responses in different audiences, according to Hall's model?
cards.answer: Social variables like class, ethnicity and age mean audiences bring different knowledge and experience, so they decode texts differently.

cards.front: Why does Hall's model depend on texts being polysemic?
cards.answer: If a text had only one possible meaning there would be no room for negotiated or oppositional readings to exist.

cards.front: The lesson gives five factors that affect BMR. Name them.
cards.answer: Age / Gender / Body composition / Hormones / Pregnancy

cards.front: How many kilocalories per gram do carbohydrate, protein, fat and alcohol each supply?
cards.answer: Carbohydrate: 4 kcal/g / Protein: 4 kcal/g / Fat: 9 kcal/g / Alcohol: 7 kcal/g

cards.front: Why does BMR increase during pregnancy?
cards.answer: Because the body is supporting fetal development and preparing for breastfeeding.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception that eating fat, rather than carbohydrate, is what causes weight gain?
cards.answer: Weight gain comes from positive energy balance (eating more total kcal than you use), and high-sugar carbohydrate diets can cause this too.

cards.front: Name the three forms of exploitation Hari faces as a lascar sailor.
cards.answer: Low pay / Dangerous work / Racial abuse from white sailors

cards.front: What three key dynamics has Gupta established by the end of the opening scenes?
cards.answer: Hope versus reality / Exploitation versus resistance / Power imbalance between British employers and Indian workers
items: Power imbalance between British employers and Indian workers

cards.front: Why does Gupta give the ayahs a collective voice rather than focusing only on Rani's story?
cards.answer: So the audience cannot dismiss Rani's experience as an isolated case, showing exploitation is the systemic norm, not an exception.

cards.front: How does Susan Matthews justify owing Rani nothing once the ship docks?
cards.answer: She points out there was no written contract between them, so she owes Rani nothing.

cards.front: Name the seven fractions collected during fractional distillation of crude oil, from top to bottom of the column.
cards.answer: Petroleum gases / Petrol (gasoline) / Naphtha / Kerosene (jet fuel) / Diesel / Fuel oil / Bitumen (residue)

cards.front: What three properties change as hydrocarbon chain length increases in fractional distillation?
cards.answer: Boiling point increases / Viscosity increases / Flammability decreases

cards.front: Why does shorter-chain hydrocarbon collect near the top of the fractionating column?
cards.answer: Shorter-chain hydrocarbons have lower boiling points, so they stay as vapour until they reach the cooler top of the column, where they condense.

cards.front: Why does burning fuel with a sulfur impurity or at high temperature contribute to acid rain?
cards.answer: Sulfur impurities burn to form sulfur dioxide, and high combustion temperatures make nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitrogen oxides, both causing acid rain.

cards.front: Name the four main forms of UK taxation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Income tax / National Insurance / VAT / Corporation tax

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says governments can manage unplanned spending risk.
cards.answer: Hold reserves / Borrow by issuing government bonds (gilts) / Adjust tax rates

cards.front: Why do local councils have less room to manage budget risk than central government?
cards.answer: Because, unlike central government, councils cannot borrow freely or print money, so must cut services when grants are reduced.

cards.front: Why is there significant political debate about social care funding compared to the NHS?
cards.answer: Because social care isn't entirely free at the point of use, so individuals may have to contribute based on their savings, unlike the NHS.

cards.front: Name the three main dimensions of educational achievement studied in GCSE Sociology.
cards.answer: Social class / Gender / Ethnicity

cards.front: Name the two steps for reading and describing patterns in an attainment table or chart.
cards.answer: Identify the overall pattern / Describe a trend over time

cards.front: Why has the class attainment gap remained even though overall GCSE results have risen since 1988?
cards.answer: Despite decades of educational policy, FSM pupils remain substantially behind non-FSM peers, so the gap has not closed significantly.

cards.front: Why do ethnic attainment gaps show a more complex trend than the class or gender gaps?
cards.answer: Some minority ethnic groups like Indian and Chinese pupils have improved rapidly, while others like Black Caribbean and White working-class boys have progressed more slowly.

title: Funeral Rites and Evaluating Life and Death
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three religions the lesson states have burial as the traditional funeral practice.
cards.answer: Christianity / Judaism / Islam

cards.front: Name the three religions the lesson states have cremation as the traditional funeral practice.
cards.answer: Hinduism / Sikhism / Buddhism

cards.front: Why are Muslim graves positioned facing the direction of Makkah (qiblah)?
cards.answer: Because it reflects the belief that at the resurrection the dead will rise facing Makkah.

cards.front: Why do Protestant funerals typically not include prayers for the dead, unlike Catholic funerals?
cards.answer: Because most Protestant traditions reject the doctrine of purgatory, which such prayers are linked to.

cards.front: Name the three uses given for acrylic.
cards.answer: Display cases / Light diffusers / Rear lights of vehicles

cards.front: Name the four uses given for silicone.
cards.answer: Baking moulds / Sealants / Medical-grade implants / Gaskets

cards.front: Why can't thermosetting plastics be re-melted after they have been cured?
cards.answer: Curing forms permanent chemical cross-links between chains, so heating causes charring or decomposition rather than melting.

cards.front: How does woven Kevlar fabric absorb a sudden impact?
cards.answer: The fibres resist stretching, so impact energy is absorbed and spread across the fibres rather than concentrated at one point.

cards.front: What number of covalent bonds does each of these molecules have: H2, O2, H2O, CH4, NH3?
cards.answer: H2 – one single bond / O2 – one double bond / H2O – two single bonds / CH4 – four single bonds / NH3 – three single bonds plus a lone pair
items: NH3 – three single bonds plus a lone pair

cards.front: Why are metals malleable and ductile?
cards.answer: Because the layers of positive metal ions can slide over each other in the metallic lattice.

cards.front: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
cards.answer: Because many strong electrostatic attractions between ions must be overcome simultaneously to melt them.

cards.front: Why do simple covalent molecules like water have low boiling points?
cards.answer: Because it is the weak intermolecular forces, not the strong covalent bonds, that break during boiling.

cards.front: Name the five separate actions each Birling character took against Eva Smith.
cards.answer: Birling sacked her / Sheila had her dismissed from Milwards / Gerald used and discarded her / Eric assaulted her / Mrs Birling denied her charity
items: Sheila had her dismissed from Milwards

cards.front: What three class layers does Priestley present in the play?
cards.answer: Landed aristocracy / Industrial middle class / Working class

cards.front: Why does Priestley argue that society, not just individuals, killed Eva Smith?
cards.answer: Each character's actions formed a chain, and a society letting the powerful exploit the vulnerable without consequence is ultimately to blame.

cards.front: How does class privilege enable each Birling character to exploit Eva?
cards.answer: Each uses their social or economic power over her: profit motive, spending power, wealth, status, or class immunity, leaving her no recourse.

cards.front: Besides Sam, name the three examples of everyday racism in Tollington the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Mr Christmas's 'jokes' about Indians / Neighbours' comments on the smell of Mama's cooking / The Kumars treated as exotic curiosities
items: Neighbours' comments on the smell of Mama's cooking
The Kumars treated as exotic curiosities

cards.front: Name the three effects of the racist attack on the Indian man that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Meena's parents are shaken / The Indian community draws closer together / Meena understands racism is physical danger, not just words
items: The Indian community draws closer together
Meena understands racism is physical danger, not just words

cards.front: How does dramatic irony work in the Spring Fete scene?
cards.answer: The reader can sense the danger in Sam's presence, but Meena, caught up in the excitement, cannot.

cards.front: Why is Papa's controlled, restrained anger after the attack more powerful than an outburst?
cards.answer: His restraint highlights the exhausting emotional labour of being an immigrant in a hostile environment.

cards.front: Name the four key dramatic techniques the lesson gives for Macbeth
cards.answer: Soliloquies / Dramatic irony / Pathetic fallacy / Foreshadowing

cards.front: Name the two structural symmetries the lesson gives between the play's first and second halves
cards.answer: Lady Macbeth dominates then disappears / Macbeth is manipulated then becomes the manipulator
items: Macbeth is manipulated then becomes the manipulator

cards.front: Why does dramatic irony create tension when Duncan praises Macbeth's castle's 'pleasant seat'?
cards.answer: The audience knows Duncan will be murdered there, creating a gap between character and audience knowledge.

cards.front: Why do Macbeth's soliloquies matter to the play's tragic effect?
cards.answer: They create intimacy with the audience, so we share his doubts and guilt and cannot simply condemn him.

cards.front: Name the four key exam question types on the Crusades and their marks.
cards.answer: Source utility (5 marks) / Compare interpretations (10 marks) / Evaluate an interpretation (12 marks) / Period essay (16 marks)

cards.front: Name three things a strong Crusades period essay should draw on, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Power of the papacy and reform ideology / Urban II's specific promises / Individual motivations / Role of the military orders / Strategic failures of the Second Crusade
items: Power of the papacy and reform ideology
Strategic failures of the Second Crusade

cards.front: Why is the Gesta Francorum limited for showing the full range of crusader motivations?
cards.answer: Its purpose was to celebrate the crusade as God's work, so it emphasises religious devotion over material or secular motives.

cards.front: Why does a period essay that tells a detailed story of events without an argument only reach the developing band?
cards.answer: Because it describes events rather than building a line of argument with a substantiated judgement weighing the evidence.

cards.front: Name the four stages of the conch's decline through the novel, with their chapters.
cards.answer: Established in Chapter 1 / Challenged in Chapter 2 / Ignored by Chapter 8 / Destroyed in Chapter 11

cards.front: Name the four dictator tactics Jack mirrors from real-world dictatorships.
cards.answer: Uses fear of the beast to unify the group / Provides meat as reward / Demands absolute obedience / Employs Roger as his enforcer
items: Uses fear of the beast to unify the group

cards.front: Why does Jack's authoritarian leadership defeat Ralph's democratic leadership in the novel?
cards.answer: It appeals to primal emotions like fear and hunger with immediate rewards, while democracy requires patience and deferred gratification.

cards.front: Why does Golding describe civilisation as a 'veneer' in the novel?
cards.answer: Boys arrive with civilised habits like politeness, rules and democracy but quickly become murderers once adult restraints are removed.

cards.front: Name the six pieces of evidence the lesson gives for the theme of power and corruption in Animal Farm.
cards.answer: The milk and apples (early privilege) / Dogs chasing Snowball (violence) / Confessions and executions (terror) / Pigs sleeping in beds (breaking their own rules) / Boxer's sale to the knacker's (exploitation) / Final scene with humans (becoming the oppressor)
items: Pigs sleeping in beds (breaking their own rules)
Final scene with humans (becoming the oppressor)

cards.front: What five-step pattern should each main paragraph of an Animal Farm essay follow?
cards.answer: Point / Evidence / Explanation / Context / Link back to the question

cards.front: Why does Orwell argue that power always corrupts those who hold it in Animal Farm?
cards.answer: Because systems without accountability, such as no free press, judiciary or educated citizens, will always produce corruption.

cards.front: How does controlling language allow the pigs to control what the animals believe is true?
cards.answer: By rewriting the commandments, the rules change and with them the animals' own understanding of what is right and wrong.

title: Ending the Bloody Code: Howard, Fry and Pentonville
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What four recommendations did John Howard make to reform prisons?
cards.answer: Prisoners paid for, not made to pay fees / Classified by crime and by sex / Cells clean, ventilated and inspected / Chaplains and surgeons should attend
items: Prisoners paid for, not made to pay fees
Classified by crime and by sex

cards.front: What three things did 'reform' actually mean to Victorians like Howard and Fry?
cards.answer: Religious instruction / Work / Separation from corrupting company

cards.front: Why did reformers think keeping prisoners separate at Pentonville would reform them?
cards.answer: Separation stopped hardened criminals corrupting first offenders and forced each prisoner to confront his conscience without distraction.

cards.front: Why was public execution abolished in 1868?
cards.answer: After decades of complaint that the spectacle attracted huge drunken crowds and brutalised onlookers rather than deterring crime.

cards.front: What four things should a strong essay plan include, according to the 5-minute plan?
cards.answer: Thesis / 3–4 paragraph topics / Key references / Context links

cards.front: Name the four common mistakes to avoid in the modern text essay.
cards.answer: Retelling the story / Bolting on context / Technique-spotting / Only writing about one part of the play
items: Only writing about one part of the play

cards.front: Why does naming a device (e.g. 'Kelly uses a metaphor') earn no credit on its own?
cards.answer: AO2 rewards analysis of the effect a choice creates, not just spotting that a device is used.

cards.front: Why must you show knowledge of at least three different parts of the play in your essay?
cards.answer: You must show knowledge of the whole text, not just one part, so reference events from at least three different parts.

cards.front: Name the four bases found in DNA nucleotides.
cards.answer: Adenine (A) / Thymine (T) / Cytosine (C) / Guanine (G)

cards.front: Name the three organisms the lesson gives as examples of asexual reproducers.
cards.answer: Bacteria / Strawberry plants (runners) / Hydra

cards.front: How does crossing over during the first division of meiosis lead to genetic variation?
cards.answer: Genetic material is shuffled between homologous chromosomes, making all four resulting cells genetically different from each other and the parent.

cards.front: Why is genetic variation important for a species facing a changing environment?
cards.answer: Individuals with alleles better suited to the new conditions are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those alleles on.

cards.front: Name the six key areas that an operating system manages.
cards.answer: CPU scheduling / Memory management / Backing store (file system) management / Peripheral management / User interface / Security

cards.front: Name the six main utility software programs described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Anti-virus software / Backup software / Disk defragmenter / Disk compression / Data recovery software / File manager

cards.front: Why does excessive paging cause a system to slow down dramatically (thrashing)?
cards.answer: Because accessing the backing store is much slower than accessing RAM, so too much swapping of pages badly slows the system.

cards.front: Why is First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) scheduling considered unfair?
cards.answer: Because a long process that arrives first can block shorter processes from running for a long time.

title: Stalin's Response: Cominform, Comecon and Yugoslavia
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things Cominform did in practice, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Coordinated propaganda against the Marshall Plan / Enforced ideological discipline, denouncing deviation / Told local parties when to obstruct, strike, or stand for office
items: Coordinated propaganda against the Marshall Plan
Told local parties when to obstruct, strike, or stand for office

cards.front: Name the three examples the lesson gives of Comecon deciding national specialisation.
cards.answer: Bulgaria grew tomatoes / Hungary built buses / East Germany made chemicals

cards.front: Why did industrial unrest break out in France in autumn 1947?
cards.answer: Cominform ordered the French Communist Party, forced out of government, to fight the Marshall Plan from opposition.

cards.front: How did Comecon's trade rules disadvantage Eastern European countries?
cards.answer: They were forced to sell goods to Moscow below world prices and buy Soviet goods above world prices.

title: Industrial Britain: Irish, Empire and Refugees, c1700–c1900
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four migrant streams that the lesson says shaped 18th- and 19th-century Britain.
cards.answer: Irish famine migrants from 1845 / Lascars, ayahs and African seafarers from the Empire / Political and economic refugees from Europe / Formerly enslaved Africans who became abolitionists
items: Lascars, ayahs and African seafarers from the Empire
Political and economic refugees from Europe
Formerly enslaved Africans who became abolitionists

cards.front: Why did Manchester and Liverpool pull in such large numbers of migrant workers by the mid-19th century?
cards.answer: The Industrial Revolution turned them into booming factory and port cities, creating huge demand for labour.

cards.front: Why did hostility grow towards Italian street musicians and German or Eastern European workers from the 1880s?
cards.answer: Economic competition pinched and the popular press campaigned against them as a threat to wages and jobs.

cards.front: How did Ayahs sometimes end up needing support once they reached Britain?
cards.answer: They travelled with British colonial families to care for children but were sometimes abandoned in London afterwards.

title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the six changes of state given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Melting / Freezing / Evaporation/boiling / Condensation / Sublimation / Deposition

cards.front: Why does water's solid form (ice) take up more space than its liquid form?
cards.answer: When water freezes, molecules arrange into a hexagonal crystal structure that takes up more space than the liquid arrangement.

cards.front: Why do aircraft need low-density materials?
cards.answer: Low-density materials reduce the weight of the aircraft.

cards.front: How does density usually change when a substance changes state?
cards.answer: Particles become more or less tightly packed, changing the volume while the mass stays the same.

title: Earth Structure and the Development of Plate Theory
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four main lines of physical evidence for plate tectonics given in the summary (excluding fossils, jigsaw fit and geology matches).
cards.answer: Sea-floor spreading (age increases from ridges) / Magnetic stripes on ocean floor / Earthquake and volcano distribution matching boundaries / GPS measurements of plate velocities
items: Earthquake and volcano distribution matching boundaries

cards.front: List the Earth's four layers from outermost to innermost.
cards.answer: Crust / Mantle / Outer core / Inner core

cards.front: Why does subduction happen when an oceanic plate meets a continental plate?
cards.answer: The denser oceanic crust sinks beneath the lighter, less dense continental crust.

cards.front: How do magnetic stripes on the ocean floor form?
cards.answer: As new basalt solidifies at the ridge, iron minerals align with the Earth's current magnetic field, recording each reversal as it happens.

title: The Church, sanctuary and trial by ordeal
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the two choices a fugitive had after forty days in sanctuary.
cards.answer: Surrender and stand trial / Abjure the realm (swear to leave the kingdom)
items: Abjure the realm (swear to leave the kingdom)

cards.front: Why did Church courts matter so much to accused criminals in medieval England?
cards.answer: Because Church courts could not impose the death penalty, so trial there instead of a royal court could save a person's life.

cards.front: In the ordeal of hot iron, how was guilt or innocence decided?
cards.answer: The accused carried a red-hot bar, the wound was bandaged, and three days later a clean wound meant innocence but a festering wound meant guilt.

cards.front: Name the three types of hormonal contraception the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Oral contraceptive pill / Contraceptive injection, implant or skin patch / Intrauterine device (IUD)
items: Contraceptive injection, implant or skin patch

cards.front: Name the four non-hormonal methods of contraception the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Barrier methods (condoms, diaphragms) / Spermicidal agents / Surgical methods (sterilisation) / Abstinence or natural family planning

cards.front: How does oestrogen affect FSH and LH release once it reaches a high level?
cards.answer: At high levels, oestrogen stimulates LH release and inhibits FSH production.

cards.front: Why do contraceptive injections, implants or patches give long-term contraception without daily action?
cards.answer: They slowly release progesterone over weeks or months, so no daily action is needed.

title: Sitcom Option: Man Like Mobeen and Friends
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three recurring locations used as setting and iconography in 'Wifey Riddim'.
cards.answer: The family home / The local shop / The market outside the mosque

cards.front: Name the four characters shown sitting together on a sofa outside in the final scene of 'Wifey Riddim'.
cards.answer: Mobeen / Aqsa / Eight / Nate

cards.front: Why does 'Wifey Riddim' use split screen in the supermarket scene?
cards.answer: To show Aqsa texting Mobeen and his phone receiving the message at the same time, creating comedy through editing.

cards.front: How does 'Wifey Riddim' challenge stereotypes of masculinity through Mobeen's character?
cards.answer: He is shown as a maternal, caring figure, working as a care-worker and called 'highly domesticated' by his uncle.

title: Women, education and the One Child Policy
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three areas of social policy under Deng that the lesson says stand out for the exam.
cards.answer: Education (restoration of merit-based university entrance) / The family (the One Child Policy) / The role of women (the 1980 Marriage Law)
items: The role of women (the 1980 Marriage Law)

cards.front: Name the three broad perspectives on the One Child Policy the lesson says should be understood.
cards.answer: PRC government's demographic and economic rationale / Human rights concerns about state coercion of reproduction / Demographic concerns about sex ratio imbalance and ageing population
items: PRC government's demographic and economic rationale
Human rights concerns about state coercion of reproduction
Demographic concerns about sex ratio imbalance and ageing population

cards.front: Why was restoring the gaokao in 1977 more than just an educational reform?
cards.answer: It was also a political statement, signalling that expertise and academic merit mattered again after political credentials had determined entry under Mao.

cards.front: How did rural areas gain some flexibility under the One Child Policy from 1984?
cards.answer: From 1984 many provinces allowed rural families a second child if the first child was a girl, unlike stricter urban enforcement.

cards.front: Name the four biotic factors the lesson gives.
cards.answer: food availability / predators / pathogens / competition

cards.front: Name the four threats to food security the lesson gives.
cards.answer: growing global population / climate change affecting crop yields / spread of new crop diseases / limited freshwater supplies

cards.front: Why can fish farming be more energy-efficient than catching wild fish?
cards.answer: Farmed fish don't lose energy swimming long distances or maintaining body temperature in cold water, unlike wild fish.

cards.front: Why does high biodiversity make an ecosystem more stable and resilient?
cards.answer: If one species declines, other species can take over some of its roles, keeping the ecosystem functioning.

cards.front: Why does Wells set the Martian invasion in Surrey rather than a distant or fictional place?
cards.answer: Setting it in the comfortable middle-class heart of England makes the horror of invasion personal and immediate for readers.

cards.front: How does the novel force Victorian readers to empathise with colonised peoples?
cards.answer: By making the Martians treat humans as inferior beings to be displaced or destroyed, exactly as Europeans treated colonised peoples.

title: Political developments: Liberals, Lords and Labour
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What four new taxes did Lloyd George propose in the 1909 People's Budget?
cards.answer: Super-tax on high incomes / Increased death duties / 20% tax on land value increases / Increased income tax

cards.front: What three changes did the Parliament Act 1911 make?
cards.answer: Lords couldn't reject or amend money bills / Lords could only delay other laws two years / Elections held every five years, not seven
items: Lords couldn't reject or amend money bills
Lords could only delay other laws two years
Elections held every five years, not seven

cards.front: Why did King George V agree to threaten creating up to 500 new Liberal peers?
cards.answer: To force the Conservative-dominated Lords, who would be outnumbered, to capitulate and pass the Parliament Bill.

cards.front: Why did Lloyd George frame the 1909 budget as a class confrontation, attacking hereditary landowners?
cards.answer: To unite Liberal and Labour support behind the budget, though it angered Conservative and aristocratic opponents.

title: Skill, Ability and the Classification of Skills
subject: physical-education-aqa

cards.front: Name the four classification continuums used to describe skills in PE.
cards.answer: Basic – Complex / Open – Closed / Self-Paced – Externally Paced / Gross – Fine

cards.front: Name the four examples of abilities given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Reaction time / Balance / Limb coordination / Explosive power

cards.front: Why is a basketball lay-up placed between the basic and complex ends of the continuum?
cards.answer: It has a set pattern, making it less random, but needs coordination of running, jumping and release angle, making it more demanding.

cards.front: Why is serving in tennis classed as self-paced?
cards.answer: The server decides exactly when to toss the ball and begin the swing, so no external factor dictates their timing.

cards.front: Name the three values the lesson gives that underpin sporting behaviour.
cards.answer: Fair play / Respect / Tolerance

cards.front: Name the four positive spectator behaviours the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Cheering your team / Applauding great play from either side / Staying within designated areas / Following ground regulations
items: Applauding great play from either side

cards.front: How do all-seater stadia help reduce football-related disorder?
cards.answer: They give every fan an assigned seat, reduce crowd surges, and let stewards more easily monitor and remove troublemakers.

cards.front: Why did the shift to all-seater grounds change the culture of watching football?
cards.answer: Individual ticketing reduced anonymity that could mask troublemakers, made CCTV easier to use, and formalised crowd segregation.

title: Materials, Corrosion, Haber Process and Fertilisers
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three metals mixed together to make stainless steel.
cards.answer: Iron / Chromium / Nickel

cards.front: Name the three raw materials NPK fertiliser production uses to provide N, P and K.
cards.answer: Ammonia and nitric/sulfuric acid for nitrogen / Phosphate rock and acid for phosphorus / Potassium chloride or sulfate for potassium
items: Ammonia and nitric/sulfuric acid for nitrogen
Phosphate rock and acid for phosphorus
Potassium chloride or sulfate for potassium

cards.front: How does electroplating protect a metal from corrosion?
cards.answer: Electrolysis is used to coat the metal with a thin layer of a less reactive or more attractive metal, such as chromium on car parts.

cards.front: Why is 200 atmospheres used in the Haber process instead of a much higher pressure?
cards.answer: Very high pressures would give a higher yield but are too expensive and dangerous, so 200 atm is a compromise.

title: Act 1: The Feud and the Party
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: What pattern does the contrast between Benvolio and Tybalt establish for the rest of the play?
cards.answer: Those who try to make peace are overwhelmed by those who choose violence.

cards.front: Why does light/dark imagery become a significant recurring motif in the play?
cards.answer: It shows their love as a point of light surrounded by the darkness of the feud, violence, and death.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson states about Barzakh.
cards.answer: Intermediate state between death and Day of Judgement / Described as a barrier between living and afterlife / Soul remains conscious but cannot return to the world / A waiting period, not permanent reward or punishment
items: Intermediate state between death and Day of Judgement
Described as a barrier between living and afterlife
Soul remains conscious but cannot return to the world
A waiting period, not permanent reward or punishment

cards.front: Name the four events the lesson describes as happening on the Day of Judgement.
cards.answer: All souls are resurrected and brought before Allah / Each person's book of deeds is opened / The scale of deeds decides paradise or punishment / The angel Israfil blows the trumpet to begin it
items: All souls are resurrected and brought before Allah
Each person's book of deeds is opened
The scale of deeds decides paradise or punishment
The angel Israfil blows the trumpet to begin it

cards.front: Why does Allah's foreknowledge of a person's choice not force them to make it, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because Allah's knowledge simply reflects the choice the person freely makes, rather than causing it.

cards.front: Why do Muslim scholars disagree about whether descriptions of al-Jannah and Jahannam are literal or metaphorical?
cards.answer: Some take the vivid imagery at face value as real, while others see it as pointing to spiritual realities beyond human language.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says survive in each of the three poems.
cards.answer: A skill survives, passed father to son (Parker) / Fear survives, the memory of being cornered at thirteen (Femi) / A sentence survives, carried from grandfather to stranger (Antrobus)
items: A skill survives, passed father to son (Parker)
Fear survives, the memory of being cornered at thirteen (Femi)
A sentence survives, carried from grandfather to stranger (Antrobus)

cards.front: Why does the lesson describe Femi's 'Thirteen' as closer to an elegy than a fond memory?
cards.answer: Because it mourns a lost sense of safety rather than celebrating youth, as the boy learns his own street sees him as a threat.

cards.front: Why does the last line of 'The Jewellery Maker' suggest the jewellery means more to the maker than the buyer?
cards.answer: Because 'warming the metal his hands caress' shows his personal care and connection to the work, beyond its value to whoever buys it.

title: Life Factors — What Shapes Health Across the Lifespan
subject: health-social-care-eduqas

cards.front: Name the seven family types the lesson names as life factors.
cards.answer: Nuclear / Extended / Single-parent / Step / Foster / Adoptive / Same-sex parent

cards.front: Name the five barriers to accessing services given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Geography (rural areas) / Financial cost (transport, prescriptions) / Language barriers / Disability / Lack of knowledge about services

cards.front: How does neglect during infancy affect a child's development across the PIES domains?
cards.answer: It disrupts attachment formation (emotional), impairs brain development (intellectual), delays physical growth, and limits socialisation (social).

cards.front: Why does unemployment damage an adult's emotional wellbeing, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Unemployment causes loss of routine, social contacts, and sense of purpose, alongside financial hardship, which damages emotional wellbeing.

title: Notting Hill: Riots, Racism and Policing
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three national stories the lesson says met at Notting Hill in the 1950s.
cards.answer: Post-war reconstruction and labour demand / The end of Empire (Windrush migration) / Wider cultural change (the 'Swinging Sixties')

cards.front: Name the four weapons the lesson says attackers used during the 1958 Notting Hill riots.
cards.answer: Iron bars / Knives / Milk bottles / Homemade petrol bombs

cards.front: Why did Caribbean migrants become concentrated in Notting Hill after the war?
cards.answer: Post-war labour demand pulled them to London, the 1948 British Nationality Act gave them the right to come, and the housing colour bar concentrated them in Notting Hill.

cards.front: Why shouldn't the 1958 Notting Hill attacks be described as a two-sided race riot?
cards.answer: Crowds of up to 400 white men, including outsiders, attacked Caribbean homes while residents only formed defence committees to protect themselves reactively.

title: The Treaty of Tordesillas and Rivalry with Portugal
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three long-term investments Portugal had made in the African route to Asia before 1493.
cards.answer: The fort at El Mina / Decades of royally funded voyages under Prince Henry / Bartolomeu Dias rounding the Cape of Good Hope (1488)
items: Decades of royally funded voyages under Prince Henry
Bartolomeu Dias rounding the Cape of Good Hope (1488)

cards.front: Give the three ways the lesson says Tordesillas mattered for the whole period.
cards.answer: Gave Spain unchallenged Catholic title west of the line / Embedded a religious framing later used in the Requerimiento / Became the template for later European imperial agreements
items: Gave Spain unchallenged Catholic title west of the line
Embedded a religious framing later used in the Requerimiento
Became the template for later European imperial agreements

cards.front: Why was Pope Alexander VI willing to back Spain in Inter caetera?
cards.answer: He was Spanish-born and depended on Ferdinand and Isabella's backing in Italian politics, so favouring Spain cost him nothing and earned their gratitude.

cards.front: Why did King John II push for the Tordesillas line to be moved further west?
cards.answer: Portugal had gathered reports that land lay much closer to the African coast in the southern Atlantic than Inter caetera's line assumed.

title: West Germany: economic recovery and politics
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four countries the lesson says West Germany recruited Gastarbeiter (guest workers) from.
cards.answer: Italy / Spain / Greece / Turkey

cards.front: What four things did the CDU offer voters, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Western integration / Social market economics / Firm opposition to communism / Conservative Christian social order

cards.front: How did the 'constructive vote of no confidence' make West German governments more stable?
cards.answer: It meant a chancellor could only be removed if parliament simultaneously agreed on a replacement, making governments harder to topple.

cards.front: Why did West Germany's economic growth slow down from the 1970s?
cards.answer: The rapid growth of the 1950s–60s relied on easy gains from post-war reconstruction, which ran out as the economy matured.

cards.front: How does Elizabeth's judgement of Wickham show her prejudice?
cards.answer: She trusts his charm and judges harshly by appearance rather than character, misjudging him.

cards.front: Why does Austen not reject the class system entirely in the novel?
cards.answer: She values taste, education and responsibility, but argues these are not exclusive to any one class.

title: Post-war Prosperity, Consumerism and the American Dream
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says the post-war boom rested on.
cards.answer: Cheap oil / Mass car ownership / Federal housing finance / Spending power of the GI Bill
items: Spending power of the GI Bill

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson says made up the 22% of Americans still in poverty in 1960.
cards.answer: Rural African-Americans / Mexican-Americans / Native Americans on reservations / Elderly Americans without Social Security

cards.front: Why could suburbs like Levittown only work once cars became widely owned?
cards.answer: Suburbs were built away from city centres, so residents needed cars to reach jobs, shops and services.

cards.front: How did federal housing policy stop black families sharing in suburban prosperity?
cards.answer: The FHA redlined mixed-race neighbourhoods and refused to insure mortgages there, denying subsidies that built white suburban wealth.

cards.front: Name the three everyday examples the lesson gives of exothermic reactions.
cards.answer: Combustion (burning fuels) / Neutralisation between acids and alkalis / Oxidation of metals

cards.front: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
cards.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react at a given temperature.

cards.front: Why does a match need to be used to light methane gas, even though burning it is exothermic overall?
cards.answer: Even exothermic reactions need an initial energy input (activation energy) to break the first bonds and start the reaction.

cards.front: Name the five animal and insect fibres the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Wool / Cashmere / Mohair / Angora / Alpaca

cards.front: Name the four plant fibres the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Cotton / Linen (flax) / Hemp / Jute

cards.front: Why does wool shrink and felt when agitated in warm water?
cards.answer: The microscopic scales on each wool fibre interlock when agitated in warm water, causing shrinkage and felting.

cards.front: Why is fibre recovery for recycling difficult with blended yarns?
cards.answer: Blended yarns mix two or more fibre types together so tightly that they are impossible to separate.

cards.front: Name the three things Victor has lost by the end, leaving the pursuit as his only identity.
cards.answer: His family / His friends / His health

cards.front: What three things does the Arctic ice symbolise the loss of for both Victor and the Creature?
cards.answer: Love / Warmth / Human connection

cards.front: Why does the Creature leave food and clues for Victor during the Arctic pursuit instead of killing him quickly?
cards.answer: The Creature wants Victor to suffer prolonged misery rather than die quickly, so it keeps him alive.

cards.front: Why does the Creature choose the frozen Arctic as the setting for the final pursuit?
cards.answer: The Creature picks terrain where its superior physical endurance gives it the advantage over Victor.

cards.front: Name the four meals of the day given in the lesson, in Spanish.
cards.answer: el desayuno / la comida / el almuerzo / la cena / la merienda

cards.front: Which three tenses does the model paragraph on food and mealtimes use?
cards.answer: present / preterite / conditional

cards.front: Why does the model paragraph on food use three different tenses?
cards.answer: Using present, preterite and conditional tenses together is essential for accessing higher mark bands in writing and speaking.

cards.front: How do you use 'me gustaría' to say what you would like to do?
cards.answer: Me gustaría is the conditional form of gustar, followed by an infinitive, to politely say 'I would like to...'.

cards.front: Why does a 100-metre sprinter need very little aerobic endurance?
cards.answer: The race lasts under 11 seconds, so ATP-PC and anaerobic energy systems dominate rather than the aerobic system.

cards.front: Why does a striker in football prioritise speed and agility?
cards.answer: Strikers need to outrun defenders and change direction quickly in tight spaces to create scoring chances.

cards.front: Name the four fitness tests the lesson gives for measuring balance, coordination, reaction time and agility.
cards.answer: Stork stand test (balance) / Alternate hand throw test (coordination) / Ruler drop test (reaction time) / Illinois agility test (agility)

cards.front: Name the four things animals compete for within a community.
cards.answer: Food / Territory / Mates / Water

cards.front: Name the four things plants compete for within a community.
cards.answer: Light / Water / Space / Mineral ions from the soil

cards.front: Why did producing insulin using genetically modified bacteria replace the older method of extracting it from animals?
cards.answer: Because extracting insulin from pig or cow pancreases sometimes caused allergic reactions in patients.

cards.front: How does the predator-prey cycle work as prey numbers rise?
cards.answer: More prey gives predators more food so predator numbers rise, which then reduces prey numbers, causing predators to decline.

cards.front: What were Murdock's (1962) method details, in his serial position curve study?
cards.answer: Participants heard word lists / Typically 20 words / Presented at one word per second / Recalled in any order immediately after
items: Presented at one word per second
Recalled in any order immediately after

cards.front: Why does the primacy effect happen?
cards.answer: Early words face little competition in short-term memory so get rehearsed a lot, transferring them into long-term memory.

cards.front: Why does the recency effect disappear if participants do a distracting task before recall?
cards.answer: The distracting task means the short-term memory trace of the last words fades before recall can happen.

cards.front: How does Murdock's study support the multi-store model of memory?
cards.answer: Primacy items being recalled from LTM and recency items from STM shows these are separate, limited stores, as the model predicts.

cards.front: Name the seven episodes that structure The War of the Worlds, in order.
cards.answer: The landing / The Heat-Ray / The tripods / Flight / Entrapment / Survival / Resolution

cards.front: Why does each episode in the novel's structure matter for the narrator's confidence?
cards.answer: Each episode escalates the threat and strips away another layer of the narrator's confidence.

cards.front: Name the three options Victorian society gave middle-class women for their lives, as described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Marriage / Becoming a governess / Dependence on relatives

cards.front: Name the three Gothic features of Thornfield Hall described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dark corridors / A mysterious third-floor room / Unexplained laughter in the night

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Jane occupies an 'impossible position' in the Victorian class system as a governess?
cards.answer: She is educated enough to teach the family's children but too poor to be considered their social equal.

cards.front: Why does Brontë use Gothic elements in Jane Eyre, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: She uses them not just for atmosphere but to externalise Jane's inner psychological conflicts.

cards.front: Name the three ways every adult fails Juliet by the end of Act 3.
cards.answer: Capulet threatens to disown her / Lady Capulet withdraws support / The Nurse advises her to marry Paris (bigamy)
items: The Nurse advises her to marry Paris (bigamy)

cards.front: Name the five characters the feud goes on to destroy, fulfilling Mercutio's curse.
cards.answer: Romeo / Juliet / Tybalt / Paris / Lady Montague

cards.front: Why does Romeo's cry 'O, I am fortune's fool!' raise the fate vs free will debate?
cards.answer: Romeo blames fortune for Tybalt's death, but the audience has just watched him choose to fight.

cards.front: How does the Queen Mab speech show Mercutio's cynical worldview?
cards.answer: It presents dreams, and by extension love, as dangerous illusions, offering a rational alternative to Romeo's romanticism.

title: The Concerto Through Time: The Baroque Era (1650-1750)
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the five features the lesson gives to check together when identifying an unfamiliar extract as Baroque.
cards.answer: Small string orchestra with audible harpsichord continuo / Ritornello form with returning tutti theme / Terraced rather than gradual dynamics / Decorative, ornamented, sequential solo/concertino writing / Clear diatonic tonality without Romantic chromatic drama
