cards.answer: Protects food from contamination / Extends shelf life / Provides labelling information / Enables safe transport

cards.front: Why can plastic film on a prepared salad be justified environmentally, despite being single-use plastic?
cards.answer: It extends shelf life and prevents food waste, potentially saving more environmental damage than the plastic causes if recycled.

cards.front: Why does wasted food represent more than just wasted food?
cards.answer: It also wastes the energy, water and labour used to produce it, and rotting food releases methane in landfill.

cards.front: Name the four common imperfect tense phrases used for describing sport at Foundation tier.
cards.answer: c'était (it was) / il y avait (there was/were) / j'étais (I was) / il faisait (it was - weather)

cards.front: Name the three jerseys given for the Tour de France.
cards.answer: maillot jaune (yellow, overall leader) / maillot vert (green, best sprinter) / maillot à pois (polka dot, best climber)
items: maillot à pois (polka dot, best climber)

cards.front: How do you form the imperfect tense in French for most verbs?
cards.answer: Take the nous form of the present tense, remove -ons, then add the endings -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.

cards.front: Why combine the perfect and imperfect tenses when describing a past sporting event?
cards.answer: The perfect tense describes completed actions or results, while the imperfect describes the atmosphere and feelings at the time.

cards.front: Name the four development opportunities the lesson gives for hot deserts (besides indigenous land rights).
cards.answer: Mineral extraction / Energy (solar farms) / Farming with irrigation / Tourism

cards.front: Name the three challenges of development in hot deserts given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Extreme temperatures limiting working hours / Water supply constraints / Inaccessibility

cards.front: How does a camel's blood let it survive severe dehydration?
cards.answer: Its oval-shaped red blood cells keep flowing even when the blood thickens with dehydration.

cards.front: How does letting its body temperature vary help a camel survive in the desert?
cards.answer: Its temperature can rise from 34°C to 41°C, avoiding the energy cost of sweating until absolutely necessary.

title: The Potion, the Tomb & the Ending
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three impossible circumstances Juliet faces at the start of Act 4, Scene 3.
cards.answer: Father has arranged marriage to Paris / Already secretly married to Romeo / Nurse betrayed her by advising she marry Paris
items: Father has arranged marriage to Paris
Nurse betrayed her by advising she marry Paris

cards.front: Why is Romeo's act of defiance against fate ultimately futile?
cards.answer: His decision to buy poison and rush to the tomb is exactly what fate needs to fulfil the Prologue's promise of death.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare create dramatic irony in Romeo's final speech at the tomb?
cards.answer: Romeo notices Juliet's lips and cheeks are still crimson but tragically reads this as death failing to mar her beauty, not as a sign of life.

cards.front: Name the four themes Act 1 Scene 1 introduces in miniature, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Poverty (the flat) introduces class / Helen's drinking introduces self-destruction / Peter's arrival introduces women depending on inadequate men / Jo left alone introduces abandonment
items: Peter's arrival introduces women depending on inadequate men

cards.front: What three details does the opening stage direction give about the flat?
cards.answer: a comfortless flat / large, sagging furniture / a view of the gasworks

cards.front: Why does Delaney write Jo and Helen's dialogue as rapid-fire exchanges?
cards.answer: It reflects music hall influence, giving sharp wit that masks pain and showing their bickering is habitual rather than new.

cards.front: Why does Jo react calmly rather than crying when Helen leaves her alone with Peter?
cards.answer: Abandonment has become normalised for Jo because she has been left before many times, showing resilience that is also her tragedy.

cards.front: Name the four muscles/muscle groups the lesson describes at the shoulder joint.
cards.answer: Deltoid / Rotator cuffs / Pectorals / Latissimus dorsi

cards.front: Name the three types of muscle contraction the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Isotonic concentric / Isotonic eccentric / Isometric

cards.front: Why must every joint be controlled by at least two muscles working in opposite directions?
cards.answer: Because muscles can only pull, never push, so one muscle contracts to move a joint while its partner relaxes to allow that movement.

cards.front: How do the gluteals and hip flexors act as an antagonistic pair at the hip?
cards.answer: Gluteals are the agonist during hip extension, while hip flexors are the agonist during hip flexion, each relaxing when the other contracts.

title: The Trinity, Creation and Human Nature
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the roles of the three persons of the Trinity given in the lesson (Father, Son, Holy Spirit).
cards.answer: Father: creator and sustainer of all things / Son: incarnate Word who redeems humanity / Holy Spirit: presence of God active in the world and believers
items: Father: creator and sustainer of all things
Son: incarnate Word who redeems humanity
Holy Spirit: presence of God active in the world and believers

cards.front: Why do Catholics say Genesis 1 and 2 should not be read as science?
cards.answer: The Church understands them as theological accounts revealing truths about God and human beings, not scientific explanations.

cards.front: How does Catholic teaching say humans should exercise dominion over creation?
cards.answer: True dominion is exercised as stewardship, caring for the earth as God's creation rather than exploiting it carelessly.

title: Act 5: The Tomb and the Tragedy
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the three young men killed by the feud in the play, in order.
cards.answer: Mercutio / Tybalt / Paris

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare give the play a circular structure, ending with the Prince as it began?
cards.answer: It reinforces that the tragedy was inevitable, as the Prologue already told us the lovers would die.

cards.front: How does Romeo's hamartia of impulsiveness cause his death in Act 5?
cards.answer: He rushes to buy poison and ride to Verona without pausing or checking Balthasar's report, missing the Friar's letter.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare include Paris's death at the tomb?
cards.answer: To show the feud's destruction spreads beyond the two families, killing an entirely innocent third young man.

cards.front: Name the three domains in which Heidensohn argued women face tighter control than men.
cards.answer: Control in the home / Control in public / Control at work

cards.front: Name the four stated purposes of prison given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Punishment / Deterrence / Rehabilitation / Incapacitation

cards.front: Why do interactionist sociologists say formal social control produces unequal outcomes?
cards.answer: Discretion at every stage (police, prosecutors, judges) is shaped by stereotypes and social power, not just evidence, producing selective enforcement.

cards.front: How does Carlen extend Heidensohn's feminist explanation of female crime?
cards.answer: Carlen argues that when the class deal and gender deal both fail working-class women, crime becomes a rational alternative.

title: Lady Bird: Coming-of-Age and Greta Gerwig's Direction
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four key formal signatures of Gerwig's direction in Lady Bird.
cards.answer: Persistent two-shot for mother-daughter scenes / Hard cut vignette structure / Warm Sacramento palette vs cooler New York / Needle-drop soundtrack as temporal anchor
items: Warm Sacramento palette vs cooler New York

cards.front: Why does the musical-theatre-audition sequence use warmer lighting and hand-held close-ups than the exterior school shots?
cards.answer: It codes the drama room as intimate and emotionally significant, a space where Lady Bird can author herself, unlike the school's hierarchies.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to call Lady Bird simply 'realistic' or 'naturalistic'?
cards.answer: Only the dialogue is naturalistic; the cinematography, colour palette, vignette structure and needle-drop score are deliberate aesthetic choices shaping the spectator's experience.

cards.front: What three conditions must the police tell a person once they have been arrested?
cards.answer: The reason for their arrest / Their right to legal advice

cards.front: Why do critics argue that stop and search can be harmful?
cards.answer: It has been applied disproportionately against certain communities, undermining trust in police without reliably reducing crime.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception that judges decide guilt in a Crown Court trial?
cards.answer: The jury decides guilt after hearing all evidence; the judge only rules on law and sets the sentence.

cards.front: Why can a legal adviser support magistrates in court?
cards.answer: Magistrates are ordinary members of the public, not legally qualified judges, so they need advice on points of law.

cards.front: Why can identical twins end up with different body weight even though they share the same genotype?
cards.answer: Because characteristics depend on genes and the environment interacting, so different environments produce different phenotypes despite identical genotypes.

cards.front: Why can a mutation in a non-coding region of DNA still change an organism's phenotype? (Higher tier)
cards.answer: It can alter gene expression, switching a gene on or off, which changes the phenotype without changing any protein's sequence.

title: Factors Shaping Self-Concept & Strategies for Resilience
subject: health-social-care-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three factors affecting self-concept grouped as social and relational influences.
cards.answer: Relationships with others / Culture / Education

cards.front: Name the four factors affecting self-concept grouped under adversity and discrimination.
cards.answer: Abuse / Stereotyping and discrimination / Unconscious bias / Social media

cards.front: How can ageist assumptions damage an older adult's self-concept?
cards.answer: Being spoken to slowly or left out of decisions makes them feel less capable, damaging their sense of self-worth.

cards.front: How does strong emotional development help protect an individual's self-concept?
cards.answer: Secure early attachments build emotional development that buffers a person against the harmful effects of other negative factors.

title: Wolsey's Domestic Policy and the Justice System
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four areas of domestic policy did Wolsey work on as Lord Chancellor?
cards.answer: Justice (Chancery and Star Chamber) / Enclosure (1517 Commission) / Finance (the subsidy) / The royal household (Eltham Ordinances)

cards.front: Why did Wolsey's Star Chamber and Chancery system eventually run into trouble in the longer term?
cards.answer: Courts became swamped with cases, common-law judges resented the encroachment, and Wolsey's personal style invited accusations of bias.

cards.front: Why did the 1517 enclosure commission fail to produce lasting change on the ground?
cards.answer: Prosecutions dragged on for years and many landowners simply paid fines and carried on enclosing land.

cards.front: Why did Wolsey have to abandon enforcement of the enclosure commission by 1523?
cards.answer: He compromised to win Parliament's support for granting war taxation.

title: Edward's Death and the Succession Crisis of 1066
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four men who pursued the English throne in 1066.
cards.answer: Harold Godwinson / William of Normandy / Harald Hardrada of Norway / Edgar Atheling

cards.front: Which earldoms did the Godwin family (Harold and his brothers) hold?
cards.answer: Wessex (Harold) / East Anglia (Gyrth) / Kent (Leofwine) / Northumbria (Tostig, until 1065)

cards.front: Why was Harold Godwinson's claim to the throne legitimate by Anglo-Saxon standards?
cards.answer: He was chosen by the Witan, named by Edward's deathbed gesture, and crowned before the leading nobles.

cards.front: How did William use Harold's alleged oath to justify his invasion?
cards.answer: He claimed Harold had sworn a sacred oath over holy relics to support him, so breaking it was a serious sin, winning papal backing.

cards.front: Name the four techniques the lesson gives for reducing wasted energy in machines and buildings.
cards.answer: Lubrication / Insulation / Streamlining / Better materials

cards.front: Name the three disadvantages the lesson gives for tidal power.
cards.answer: Expensive infrastructure / Limited suitable estuaries / Risk to marine ecosystems

cards.front: Why does the National Grid use step-up transformers at power stations?
cards.answer: To raise voltage to hundreds of thousands of volts, keeping current low for efficient long-distance transmission.

cards.front: Why is nuclear power's radioactive waste a serious problem even though it produces no CO2?
cards.answer: The waste remains hazardous for very long periods and requires secure storage.

cards.front: Name the six industries nationalised by the Attlee government between 1946 and 1951.
cards.answer: Bank of England (1946) / Coal industry (1947) / Railways (1948) / Electricity (1948) / Gas (1949) / Iron and steel (1951)

cards.front: What three concerns did doctors have about the NHS before it launched?
cards.answer: Loss of professional independence / Becoming civil servants on fixed salary / Capitation system disadvantaging poorer areas
items: Becoming civil servants on fixed salary

cards.front: Why did the government introduce prescription and dental charges to the NHS in 1951?
cards.answer: Because huge pent-up demand made the NHS cost far more than expected, forcing the government to bring in charges.

cards.front: How did wartime experience build support for a welfare state after 1945?
cards.answer: Rationing, communal shelters and national mobilisation showed people that the state could organise society efficiently through collective solutions.

cards.front: Name the three Italian associations Elizabethan audiences held that the play maps onto specific features.
cards.answer: Blood feuds (the Capulet-Montague feud) / Catholic ritual (Friar Lawrence's cell) / Female sensuality (Juliet's frank language)

cards.front: Name the four facts the lesson gives about how the play was originally performed.
cards.answer: Written for open-air theatres like the Globe / All actors were men or boys / Performed in the afternoon / No artificial lighting was used
items: Written for open-air theatres like the Globe
All actors were men or boys

cards.front: How does Shakespeare present two competing models of motherhood for Juliet?
cards.answer: The Nurse is the warm hired carer who loves her, while Lady Capulet is the cold biological mother protecting the family's reputation.

cards.front: Why is Romeo's killing of Tybalt a turning point in the play?
cards.answer: Driven by grief for Mercutio, it is the structural pivot after which fate begins to tighten around the lovers.

title: Consequences: Slavery, Indigenous Peoples and Loyalists
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three groups for whom the war's outcome was 'a defeat dressed as victory'.
cards.answer: Enslaved African Americans / Indigenous peoples / Loyalists

cards.front: Name the four Indigenous nations or peoples the lesson says fought on the British side.
cards.answer: Mohawk (under Joseph Brant) / Cherokee / Creek / Shawnee

cards.front: Why did the Peace of Paris of 1783 harm Indigenous nations even though they weren't defeated in battle?
cards.answer: Britain ceded their land east of the Mississippi to the US without consulting them, and the US treated them as defeated and dispossessed.

cards.front: Why did slavery expand in the South after independence while it was being abolished in the North?
cards.answer: The cotton boom of the 1790s entrenched the plantation system in the South, unlike the North where liberty rhetoric drove gradual abolition.

cards.front: Why is the windmill's real purpose in Chapter 10 a betrayal of Snowball's original promise?
cards.answer: It is used to mill corn for profit rather than to ease the animals' workload as promised.

cards.front: Why does Orwell end the novella with the pigs looking indistinguishable from the humans?
cards.answer: To show the revolution has failed and one oppressor has simply been replaced by another.

cards.front: How does Orwell suggest power corrupts regardless of ideology in the final chapters?
cards.answer: Both capitalist Jones and communist Napoleon end up exploiting the working class the same way.

cards.front: Name the two organs that together carry out the digestive functions of churning food, producing enzymes and making bile.
cards.answer: Stomach churns food and adds acid / Pancreas produces enzymes / Liver makes bile
items: Stomach churns food and adds acid

cards.front: How does extreme temperature or pH stop an enzyme working?
cards.answer: It causes denaturation, permanently changing the active site's shape so the substrate no longer fits.

cards.front: What colour change shows a positive result in the Sudan III test for lipids?
cards.answer: A red layer forms if lipids are present.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says memory stores differ from each other.
cards.answer: How they code information / How much they can hold (capacity) / How long they retain information (duration)

cards.front: How does attention decide what moves from the sensory register into short-term memory?
cards.answer: Only information you selectively attend to is transferred into STM; everything else fades within fractions of a second.

cards.front: How did Peterson and Peterson test how long short-term memory lasts without rehearsal?
cards.answer: They gave participants a consonant trigram then made them count backwards to stop rehearsal, testing recall after increasing time intervals.

cards.front: Name the four things tested in the urine sample at the booking appointment.
cards.answer: Protein / Glucose / Bacteria

cards.front: Name the four groups of women offered amniocentesis or CVS testing, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: High-risk screening result / Over 35 / Known family history of a chromosomal or genetic condition / Offered, not required, to any of these women
items: Family history of a genetic condition

cards.front: Why is a high-risk result from the dating scan's screening test not enough to confirm a chromosomal condition like Down's syndrome?
cards.answer: Because it is a screening test giving a statistical risk level, not a diagnostic test analysing the baby's own cells.

cards.front: Why does an obstetrician take over or share care in some pregnancies instead of the midwife?
cards.answer: Because the pregnancy is classified as high-risk, for example due to diabetes, high blood pressure, multiple pregnancy or a history of complications.

cards.front: Name the three quotations the lesson recommends learning as exact short quotes from 'Love and Friendship'.
cards.answer: wild rose-briar / holly-tree / which will bloom most constantly? / deck thee with the holly's sheen
items: deck thee with the holly's sheen

cards.front: Why does Bronte use seasonal imagery across the poem's three stanzas?
cards.answer: It gives the argument natural inevitability, showing love fades because everything that blooms in spring must face winter.

cards.front: How does the poem's structure mirror its growing certainty?
cards.answer: The rhyme tightens from a loose sound in stanza one to a fully alternating, firm rhyme in the final stanza, matching the argument's growing confidence.

cards.front: Why is friendship valued over love according to the poem's argument?
cards.answer: Friendship lacks glamour and does not compete with love's early appeal, but it survives winter when love's beauty cannot.

title: Widescreen, Steadicam and the Push for Spectacle: 1948-1990s
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why did Hollywood studios push for spectacle like widescreen after 1948?
cards.answer: Losing cinema chains under the Paramount decree and losing audiences to television meant studios used bigger, wider, more immersive technology to draw people back.

cards.front: Why did a widescreen frame change how directors composed shots compared to the old near-square frame?
cards.answer: The sides of the frame became active, letting directors place characters in spatial tension or dwarf them with environment, not just center subjects.

cards.front: Why did Kubrick's use of the Steadicam in The Shining feel different from handheld or dolly shots?
cards.answer: It glided smoothly at the child's height, feeling inhuman, patient and predatory, unlike a mechanical dolly or an urgent handheld camera.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to credit the Steadicam's invention to a studio like Panavision or ILM?
cards.answer: It was developed and patented by independent inventor Garrett Brown, then licensed to the industry, not created inside a studio's R&D department.

cards.front: Name the four main pricing strategies the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Competitive pricing / Price skimming / Penetration pricing / Psychological pricing

cards.front: Name the five promotion strategies the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Advertising / Sponsorship / Product trials / Special offers / Branding

cards.front: How has technology made competitive pricing more important?
cards.answer: Online price-comparison websites let customers instantly see if a business is overcharging compared to rivals.

cards.front: Why is viral advertising an unpredictable promotional method?
cards.answer: Success cannot be guaranteed, as many planned viral campaigns fail to spread beyond a small audience.

title: Cyber Security Threats and Social Engineering
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three types of malware specified for this course.
cards.answer: Computer viruses / Trojans / Spyware

cards.front: Name the four other conditions the lesson gives that create cyber security vulnerabilities.
cards.answer: Weak and default passwords / Misconfigured access rights / Removable media / Unpatched or outdated software

cards.front: Why does unpatched or outdated software create a security risk?
cards.answer: It contains known vulnerabilities that developers have since fixed, so old systems remain exposed to attacks exploiting those known weaknesses.

cards.front: Why can misconfigured access rights be dangerous?
cards.answer: Users end up with more permissions than their role needs, so they could accidentally or deliberately delete critical records.

cards.front: Name the five practical constraints the lesson says real investigations must identify and discuss.
cards.answer: Time constraints / Cost constraints / Ethical issues / Confidentiality / Convenience

cards.front: Name the three problems careful investigators plan for before they happen.
cards.answer: Difficulty identifying the population / Non-response / Unexpected outcomes in the data

cards.front: Why can convenience limit a real statistical investigation?
cards.answer: The theoretically ideal population is often not reachable, so researchers must work with who they can actually access.

cards.front: Why should an investigator build in a review stage when an unusually large value appears in the data?
cards.answer: It could be a genuine finding, a recording error, or a sign the hypothesis needs revising, so review catches problems early.

cards.front: Name the eight energy stores given in the lesson.
cards.answer: kinetic / thermal / chemical / elastic potential / gravitational potential / electrostatic / magnetic / nuclear

cards.front: Name the four ways energy can be transferred between stores.
cards.answer: mechanically (by forces) / electrically (by currents) / by heating / by radiation

cards.front: Why does a ball thrown upwards momentarily have zero speed at the top of its path?
cards.answer: All of its kinetic energy has been transferred to the gravitational potential energy store.

cards.front: How is the equation P = Fv derived from P = W/t and W = Fs?
cards.answer: Since work done W = Fs, dividing by time gives P = Fs/t, and s/t equals speed, so P = Fv.

cards.front: Name the three distribution channels the specification names for getting a product to the customer.
cards.answer: Retailers / Wholesalers / Telesales

cards.front: Name the five drawbacks of e-commerce the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Cannot see or try before buying, leading to high returns / Cyber-security and data protection costs / Delivery problems damage the brand / Competition is intense as rivals are one click away / Traditional strengths like staff expertise are lost
items: Cannot see or try before buying, leading to high returns
Competition is intense as rivals are one click away
Traditional strengths like staff expertise are lost

cards.front: Why did Marks & Spencer's marketing mix fail to attract younger customers?
cards.answer: Its product and price were premium but promotion and store fit-out felt old-fashioned compared to rivals like Zara and Next.

cards.front: Why can a new coffee shop with a great product and promotion still struggle?
cards.answer: If its place (location) is hidden down a side street, footfall is too low to support the business.

cards.front: Name the three flaws Russell gives Mrs Johnstone to stop her being idealised.
cards.answer: Gives away her child / Superstitious and easily manipulated / Keeps the secret for decades

cards.front: Name the three fears that drive Mrs Lyons' paranoia.
cards.answer: Eddie will discover the truth / Mrs Johnstone will tell / The superstition will come true

cards.front: Why does Russell present Mrs Johnstone as flawed rather than idealised?
cards.answer: Because her flaws, like giving away her child and being manipulated, are shown as products of her circumstances, not her nature.

cards.front: Why does Russell leave the Narrator's identity deliberately ambiguous?
cards.answer: So he could represent fate, society, guilt, or Russell himself, rather than one fixed meaning.

cards.front: Why must a value from input() be converted with int() or float() before doing arithmetic on it?
cards.answer: Because input() always returns a string, and arithmetic cannot be performed on strings.

cards.front: Why must a program call close() after finishing reading or writing a file?
cards.answer: The lesson states you must close the file once you have finished reading or writing to it.

cards.front: Name the six steps in the worked example for reading a CSV file line by line.
cards.answer: Open file in read mode / readline() to skip header / for line in f to loop rows / strip() to remove newline / split(',') into fields / close() the file
items: for line in f to loop rows

title: Women, the Sheppard-Towner Act and the 19th Amendment
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: The lesson lists four things that did NOT change for women in the 1920s despite the vote and Sheppard-Towner Act. Name them.
cards.answer: Still excluded from professional careers like law and medicine / Legal inequalities remained because the ERA failed to pass / Black women in the South still denied the vote by Jim Crow / Flapper culture's freedoms limited to a minority
items: Still excluded from professional careers like law and medicine
Legal inequalities remained because the ERA failed to pass
Black women in the South still denied the vote by Jim Crow
Flapper culture's freedoms limited to a minority

cards.front: The lesson names three low-paid sectors where women workers remained concentrated in the 1920s. What are they?
cards.answer: Domestic service / Garment manufacture / Clerical work

cards.front: Why did many congressmen support the Sheppard-Towner Act despite opposition from the AMA?
cards.answer: They feared the political consequences of opposing women's welfare issues so soon after the 19th Amendment.

cards.front: Why do historians caution against overstating the significance of flapper culture?
cards.answer: It was largely confined to urban, white, middle-class women, while most women saw little change to their economic position or domestic expectations.

title: The need for social reform: Booth, Rowntree and Liberal reforms
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three key Liberal reforms and the group each targeted.
cards.answer: School Meals Act 1906 (children) / Old Age Pensions Act 1908 (elderly) / National Insurance Act 1911 (sick and unemployed workers)
items: National Insurance Act 1911 (sick and unemployed workers)

cards.front: Name three limitations of the Liberal reforms mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pension age of 70 excluded most workers / National Insurance Part 1 didn't cover dependants / School meals and treatment weren't universal or free
items: Pension age of 70 excluded most workers
National Insurance Part 1 didn't cover dependants
School meals and treatment weren't universal or free

cards.front: Why did Rowntree's idea of 'primary poverty' undermine the Victorian view that poverty was a personal failing?
cards.answer: It proved some families were poor even if they spent perfectly, because they simply did not earn enough money.

cards.front: Why did the Boer War add urgency to calls for social reform?
cards.answer: Recruiters found many urban volunteers too unhealthy to serve, alarming politicians worried about defending the empire.

cards.front: According to the lesson, human language can discuss which five kinds of things that go beyond the immediate here-and-now?
cards.answer: Things distant in time (past and future) / abstract concepts / hypothetical situations / fiction / ideas with no physical referent
items: Things distant in time (past and future)

cards.front: What three limitations does the lesson give for Von Frisch's bee study, even though it is sophisticated?
cards.answer: Limited to one function (food) / limited to one context (the hive) / limited to one species

cards.front: How does human language differ from animal communication in the way it is acquired?
cards.answer: Human language is learnt from the social environment, so different communities use different languages, while animal communication is species-specific and largely instinctive.

cards.front: Why might it be unfair to judge animal communication as inferior to human language?
cards.answer: Animal and human communication are fundamentally different systems serving different purposes, so animal communication perfectly serves its own adaptive purpose.

title: The Prophets: Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail and Yusuf
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What virtue does each of the four prophets (Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail, Yusuf) mainly teach Muslims to imitate?
cards.answer: Nuh: perseverance and gratitude despite rejection / Ibrahim: courage, rational faith and total submission / Ismail: patient obedience across generations / Yusuf: moral integrity, patience and forgiveness
items: Nuh: perseverance and gratitude despite rejection
Ibrahim: courage, rational faith and total submission
Yusuf: moral integrity, patience and forgiveness

cards.front: Why did Ibrahim destroy the idols of his people but leave the largest one standing (Surah 21:57-58)?
cards.answer: So people would have to ask who did it, forcing them to think critically about what they were worshipping.

cards.front: Why do Muslims honour the prophets but not worship them?
cards.answer: Prophets were human, not divine, and only Allah is worthy of worship; worshipping a prophet would be shirk.

title: The Thatcher Years: economy and society
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four major industries privatised between 1979 and 1990 mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: British Telecom (1984) / British Gas (1986) / British Airways (1987) / British Steel (1988)

cards.front: What three criticisms does the lesson give of privatising utilities like water and gas?
cards.answer: Natural monopolies shouldn't be run for profit / Services worsened in poorer areas / Sale prices were often too low
items: Natural monopolies shouldn't be run for profit
Sale prices were often too low

cards.front: Why did Thatcher's monetarist policies of 1979-81 cause a deep recession?
cards.answer: Sharp interest rate rises and public spending cuts to control inflation caused manufacturing output to fall and unemployment to soar.

cards.front: Why did regulators like Ofwat and Ofgem need to be created after utility privatisation?
cards.answer: Privatised utilities had no real competition, so regulation was needed to substitute for the market pressure that didn't exist naturally.

title: Sources of Wisdom and Forms of Expression in Catholic Christianity
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three sacred vessels used in the Mass, mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Chalice (cup for the wine) / Paten (plate for the bread) / Ciborium (vessel for communion hosts)

cards.front: Name the four Vatican II documents named in the lesson, in order of year.
cards.answer: Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963) / Lumen Gentium (1964) / Dei Verbum (1965) / Gaudium et Spes (1965)

cards.front: Why do Catholics use a crucifix rather than a bare cross in their churches?
cards.answer: Because the crucifix shows Christ's body on the cross, emphasising his sacrifice, unlike the bare cross used in many Protestant churches.

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching say scripture cannot be interpreted alone, without the Church?
cards.answer: Because the Bible must be interpreted through the magisterium and the living Tradition of the Church to be properly understood.

title: Diplomacy Outside the League: Locarno and Kellogg-Briand
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three concrete objectives Stresemann pursued through reconciliation diplomacy.
cards.answer: End the Ruhr occupation / Lift the burden of reparations / Bring Germany into the League of Nations
items: Bring Germany into the League of Nations

cards.front: Name the three immediate consequences that flowed from Locarno.
cards.answer: Germany joined the League as Council member / French troops left the Rhineland early / Locarno spirit led to Young Plan and Kellogg-Briand
items: Germany joined the League as Council member
French troops left the Rhineland early
Locarno spirit led to Young Plan and Kellogg-Briand

cards.front: Why did Germany's eastern border ambiguity at Locarno matter later, in 1938-39?
cards.answer: By leaving eastern frontiers open, Locarno let Hitler later use the Sudetenland and Polish Corridor as flashpoints for revision.

cards.front: How did Stresemann pursue rearmament while publicly following reconciliation diplomacy?
cards.answer: He quietly continued secret rearmament cooperation with the Soviet Union under the 1922 Treaty of Rapallo alongside his public policy.

cards.front: Name the four government strategies the lesson gives for narrowing the UK regional economic gap.
cards.answer: Northern Powerhouse / Levelling Up Fund / Freeports / HS2 (transport investment)

cards.front: Name three drawbacks of building on brownfield sites given in the lesson.
cards.answer: high cost of cleaning contaminated soil / complex demolition / gentrification pricing out long-time residents
items: high cost of cleaning contaminated soil

cards.front: Why did net migration to the UK peak at around 944,000 in the year to March 2023?
cards.answer: It was driven by Ukrainian and Hong Kong resettlement schemes, international students, and NHS and care worker visas.

cards.front: Why are UK migration statistics from 2020–22 considered particularly unreliable?
cards.answer: The small International Passenger Survey was suspended in 2020 due to COVID, making estimates for that period uncertain.

cards.front: In DNA Act 4, what three coping methods does the lesson give for how group members handled events?
cards.answer: Denial (John Tate turning to religion) / Chemical numbness (Brian on medication) / New allegiance (following Cathy)

cards.front: Why does Leah disappear from the group by Act 4?
cards.answer: Because her pleas for connection were constantly ignored by Phil, so her conscience eventually fell silent.

title: The Covenant at Sinai, Pikuach Nefesh, the Mitzvot and Life After Death
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Talmud Yoma 83-84 gives three examples of breaking Shabbat to save a child. What are they?
cards.answer: Pulling a child from the sea with a net / Digging free a child trapped in a pit / Breaking open a locked door to reach a frightened child
items: Pulling a child from the sea with a net
Digging free a child trapped in a pit
Breaking open a locked door to reach a frightened child

cards.front: Why do Orthodox and Reform Jews apply Pikuach Nefesh differently?
cards.answer: Orthodox Jews apply it case by case only for genuine immediate threats to life, while Reform Jews extend it more broadly to mental health and long-term wellbeing.

cards.front: Why does Judaism teach that human life has infinite worth?
cards.answer: Because every human life is created by the Almighty, so saving one life is treated as equivalent to saving an entire world.

cards.front: How does Orthodox Jewish belief about resurrection differ from Christian belief about resurrection?
cards.answer: Orthodox resurrection is tied to a future Messianic age for the Jewish people as a whole, while Christian resurrection is linked to individual faith in Jesus's own resurrection.

title: The Night Sky: Constellations, Asterisms and Pointers
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four key naked-eye asterisms the lesson lists as 'signposts' to the sky.
cards.answer: The Plough (Ursa Major) / The Summer Triangle (Cygnus, Lyra, Aquila) / The Square of Pegasus (Pegasus/Andromeda) / The Southern Cross (Crux)

cards.front: Name the five constellations the lesson gives as essential starting points for UK observers.
cards.answer: Orion / Ursa Major / Cassiopeia / Cygnus / Scorpius

cards.front: Why do amateur astronomers use red-light torches when observing?
cards.answer: Red light preserves an observer's dark adaptation, unlike white light.

cards.front: How can Cassiopeia be used to find Polaris when the Plough is below the horizon?
cards.answer: Cassiopeia lies on the opposite side of Polaris from the Plough, so when the Plough is hidden Cassiopeia is high and can serve the same navigation role.

cards.front: Name four things the Cottages students lack despite having a version of freedom.
cards.answer: Money / Family / Career prospects / Any future beyond donations

cards.front: Why does Ruth react defensively when Kathy confronts her about the copied arm-tap gesture?
cards.answer: Her constructed identity is fragile and cannot survive scrutiny because it is borrowed, not authentic.

cards.front: Why does the failed search for Ruth's possible strip away her hope?
cards.answer: It was really a search for human worth, and its failure denies her the chance that her original was 'somebody'.

title: The Nature of God and the Shekhinah
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the five ways Jewish teaching describes God, according to the lesson's key fact.
cards.answer: One (echad) / Creator (borei) / Law-Giver and Judge / Loving and Merciful / Present (Shekhinah)

cards.front: What are the first five of Maimonides' Thirteen Principles of Faith concerning the nature of God?
cards.answer: God exists / God is one / God has no body / God is eternal / God alone is worthy of worship
items: God alone is worthy of worship

cards.front: Why are human descriptions of God, like 'God's hand' or 'God's voice', not taken literally in Jewish teaching?
cards.answer: Because God has no body or physical form, so human terms describing God are understood as metaphor, not literal fact.

cards.front: Why is God described as intimately involved in creation rather than distant, in Jewish teaching?
cards.answer: Because God brought the world into existence through divine speech, making creation an active act, not a distant mechanical event.

cards.front: Name the five common mistakes the lesson warns against in An Inspector Calls essays.
cards.answer: Retelling the story instead of analysing / Bolting on context in a separate paragraph / Ignoring the stimulus quotation / Feature-spotting without explaining the effect / Treating characters as real people
items: Retelling the story instead of analysing
Bolting on context in a separate paragraph

cards.front: What six contextual elements does the lesson say AO3 requires for An Inspector Calls?
cards.answer: The 1912 setting / The 1945 writing context / Priestley's socialism / The class system / The Welfare State / Dramatic irony from the time gap
items: Dramatic irony from the time gap

cards.front: Why does the lesson say a short, well-analysed quotation beats a long, unanalysed one?
cards.answer: It is the analysis that scores marks, not quotation length, and shorter quotes leave more time to analyse.

cards.front: How does the audience's knowledge that the Titanic sank affect their view of Birling's authority?
cards.answer: Knowing his 'unsinkable' prediction failed turns him from a figure of authority into one of ridicule, discrediting his individualist philosophy.

title: Religious worship under Henry and Edward
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the six doctrines reaffirmed by the Act of Six Articles (1539).
cards.answer: Transubstantiation / Withholding the communion cup from laity / Celibacy of priests / Private masses / Auricular confession / Vows of chastity
items: Withholding the communion cup from laity

cards.front: What three sacraments did the Ten Articles (1536) keep as binding, out of the original seven?
cards.answer: Baptism / Eucharist / Penance

cards.front: Why did Henry VIII have ideological reasons, not just religious ones, for destroying Thomas Becket's shrine?
cards.answer: Becket had resisted royal authority in the twelfth century, so destroying his cult helped erase a symbol of defiance against the Crown.

cards.front: How did the role of the clergyman change between Henry's reign and Edward's reign?
cards.answer: Clergy went from being required to be celibate under Henry to being permitted to marry under Edward, as services shifted from Latin to English.

title: Reception, Active Audiences and Aberrant Readings
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three specialised active audience reading practices the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Fan reading / Queer reading / Feminist reading

cards.front: Why can a 1970s sitcom that seemed mainstream at the time produce oppositional readings today?
cards.answer: Because social values around gender, race and class have shifted, so contemporary viewers re-read it through a changed cultural context.

cards.front: Why is aberrant decoding said to be the norm rather than the exception in mass communication?
cards.answer: Because senders and receivers often do not share the same cultural codes, so unintended readings happen regularly.

cards.front: How does a queer reading of a media text work?
cards.answer: It looks for gender and sexuality subtext not necessarily intended by the producer but visible to audiences outside heteronormative norms.

cards.front: Name the six Rs in the 6 Rs sustainability framework.
cards.answer: Rethink / Refuse / Reduce / Reuse / Recycle / Repair

cards.front: Name the four stages a Life Cycle Analysis is usually grouped into.
cards.answer: Raw material extraction / Manufacturing / Use phase / End of life

cards.front: How does reducing the wall thickness of an injection-moulded polymer component help sustainability?
cards.answer: It saves material and speeds up cooling time in the mould, cutting both cost and energy use.

cards.front: Why can a product that takes longer to assemble but can be fully disassembled represent better sustainable design?
cards.answer: It can be taken apart for repair or recycling, rather than being sent to landfill when it fails.

title: Nature of crimes: medieval and early modern
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three new categories of crime that emerged from the Reformation era, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Heresy / Treason / Witchcraft

cards.front: What punishments could repeat vagrancy offenders face under Tudor law?
cards.answer: Branded / Mutilated / Executed

cards.front: Why was secret murder treated more seriously than open homicide in medieval law?
cards.answer: Because secret killing deprived the community of the ability to respond to it collectively, unlike a killing done openly.

cards.front: Why did witch trial accusations often target elderly, poor women?
cards.answer: They had become social liabilities, and accusations often arose from local disputes, illness or misfortune blamed on them.

cards.front: What are the three roles the Odyssey tests Odysseus's heroism in?
cards.answer: Leader / Husband / Father

cards.front: What four things does Athena do to help Odysseus and his family in the poem?
cards.answer: Inspires Telemachus to seek news of his father / Engineers his release from Calypso's island / Gives him his beggar's disguise / Tips the battle in Book 22
items: Inspires Telemachus to seek news of his father
Engineers his release from Calypso's island

cards.front: Why is physical strength (bie) useless against Polyphemus in the Cyclops episode?
cards.answer: Polyphemus is far stronger than Odysseus and his men, so only cunning (metis) — the Nobody trick and the stake — can save them.

cards.front: Why does Odysseus refuse Calypso's offer of immortality?
cards.answer: He would rather be a mortal man with a wife and home than an immortal without them, showing what he truly values.

cards.front: Name the four demonstrative adjective forms given in the lesson, with when each is used.
cards.answer: ce - masculine singular before a consonant / cet - masculine singular before a vowel or silent h / cette - feminine singular / ces - plural, both genders
items: ce - masculine singular before a consonant
cet - masculine singular before a vowel or silent h

cards.front: Name the three 'against' points the lesson gives for whether celebrities are good role models.
cards.answer: Some celebrities give a bad example / They show an unrealistic lifestyle / Young people should not imitate celebrities
items: Some celebrities give a bad example
Young people should not imitate celebrities

cards.front: Why is 'cet' used instead of 'ce' before words like 'acteur' or 'homme'?
cards.answer: Cet replaces ce before masculine nouns starting with a vowel or a silent 'h'.

cards.front: How do you form the 'tu' imperative for -er verbs like écouter or regarder?
cards.answer: Drop the final -s from the normal tu form, e.g. Écoute! or Regarde!

cards.front: What three aspects of Victorian society does Wells critique in The War of the Worlds?
cards.answer: Imperial arrogance / Scientific overconfidence / Social Darwinism turned against humanity

cards.front: What four technologies gave Victorians confidence that human progress was unstoppable?
cards.answer: Railways / Telegraphs / Electric lighting / New weapons

cards.front: Why did Wells make the Martians an evolved species rather than supernatural beings?
cards.answer: His scientific education under Huxley led him to apply Darwin's logic of survival, showing humans as one vulnerable species among many.

cards.front: How does the destruction of Britain's best weapons by the Heat-Ray undermine Victorian confidence in technology?
cards.answer: It shows technology, which Victorians worshipped as proof of superiority, is utterly inadequate against a genuinely superior civilisation.

cards.front: Name the three types of neurone the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Sensory neurone / Relay neurone / Motor neurone

cards.front: Name the three examples of reflex actions given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pulling hand away from a hot surface / Pupil constricting in bright light / Blinking when something approaches the eye
items: Pulling hand away from a hot surface
Blinking when something approaches the eye

cards.front: Why can impulses only travel in one direction across a synapse?
cards.answer: Neurotransmitters are only released from the pre-synaptic side and receptors are only on the post-synaptic side.

cards.front: How does the myelin sheath physically speed up impulse transmission along the axon?
cards.answer: It insulates the axon and causes the electrical impulse to jump between gaps in the sheath.

cards.front: Name the four criteria the lesson says designers balance when selecting a fabric for a product.
cards.answer: Function / Aesthetics / Cost / Environmental considerations

cards.front: What two methods does the lesson give for making bonded/needle-punched non-woven fabrics?
cards.answer: Needle punching (mechanical entangling) / Thermal bonding (heat fuses fibres)

cards.front: Why does more twist make a yarn stronger but less soft?
cards.answer: The twist locks the fibres together tightly, increasing strength, but this reduces the yarn's softness.

cards.front: Why is thread count alone not a reliable way to judge bed linen quality?
cards.answer: Fibre type, yarn quality and finishing treatments also affect quality, and multi-ply yarns can artificially inflate the count.

cards.front: Why has the UK's ageing population created growing markets in areas like retirement living and mobility products?
cards.answer: As more of the population is older, demand grows for products and services suited to older adults' needs.

cards.front: Why might two people of the same age and income sit in different lifestyle segments?
cards.answer: They can have different values and ways of living, such as prioritising sustainability versus prioritising status and luxury.

cards.front: Why does Portia's disguise as Balthazar create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: The audience knows Portia is a woman in disguise, but the characters in the courtroom do not.

cards.front: Why is Portia's mercy speech considered ironic given her later actions in court?
cards.answer: She argues mercy should temper justice, yet she and the other Christians show Shylock no mercy once he is defeated.

cards.front: Why does Shylock refuse to accept three times the loan amount and insist on his bond?
cards.answer: He believes the law is the only protection he has in a society that despises him, so it must be upheld strictly.

cards.front: What three things does Shylock lose as a result of his forced conversion, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: His faith / His community / His wealth (kept only half)

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why historians' interpretations of the Crusades differ.
cards.answer: Historian's purpose / Evidence used / Time at which they write / Historian's perspective and background

cards.front: How does Ibn al-Athir's al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh frame the Crusades differently from Western chronicles?
cards.answer: It presents the Crusades as a catastrophic Christian invasion of Muslim lands, not a holy liberation, celebrating Muslim resistance.

cards.front: Why did Ibn al-Athir's account glorify Muslim resistance and downplay rulers who cooperated with crusaders?
cards.answer: He wrote when Muslim reconquest under Saladin was the dominant political reality, shaping his account to celebrate resistance.

cards.front: How did Carole Hillenbrand's approach shift the question historians asked about the Crusades?
cards.answer: She asked what the Crusades meant to those experiencing them, rather than whether they were justified or crusaders sincere.

cards.front: Name the five things typically placed around a Buddha rupa on a Buddhist shrine.
cards.answer: Candles / Incense / Flowers / Water or food / Bells

cards.front: Name the three mudras (hand positions) mentioned for Buddha rupa images.
cards.answer: Earth-touching gesture (bhumisparshamudra) / Meditation posture (dhyana mudra) / Protection mudra

cards.front: Why do Theravada monks chant passages from the Pali Canon?
cards.answer: It is a devotional practice, a way of memorising and transmitting the Dhamma, and its sound is thought to bring blessings and focus the mind.

cards.front: How does a home shrine connect Buddhist practice to daily life?
cards.answer: Morning puja at the home shrine grounds the day in the Three Jewels, extending Buddhist practice beyond the temple into ordinary domestic life.

cards.front: Name the four distinct manufacturing process families the lesson describes, each shaping material without removing waste chips.
cards.answer: Press forming / Injection moulding / Sand casting / Pressure die casting

cards.front: Name the four related sheet-metal operations described alongside press forming.
cards.answer: Bending and folding / Punching and blanking / Stamping / Composite lay-up

cards.front: Why is pressure die casting only economical at high production volumes?
cards.answer: The steel die costs tens of thousands of pounds to make, so the cost only pays off over many parts.

cards.front: Why does pressure die casting produce a finer grain structure than sand casting?
cards.answer: The steel die conducts heat quickly, giving a much faster cooling rate than a sand mould.

cards.front: Name the three snap judgements made at or after the Meryton assembly that shape the novel's relationships.
cards.answer: Darcy judges Elizabeth as 'tolerable, not handsome enough' / Elizabeth judges Darcy as proud and disagreeable / Mrs Bennet judges Bingley as perfect son-in-law for his money
items: Darcy judges Elizabeth as 'tolerable, not handsome enough'
Elizabeth judges Darcy as proud and disagreeable
Mrs Bennet judges Bingley as perfect son-in-law for his money

cards.front: Why was refusing to dance at a Regency assembly seen as such a big insult?
cards.answer: Dancing publicly signalled interest, so refusing to dance was a public insult, and Darcy's refusal marked him as antisocial.

cards.front: How does the novel's ending overturn the first impressions formed at the assembly?
cards.answer: Darcy, first judged proud and disagreeable, proves honourable and generous, while charming Wickham later proves dishonest and predatory.

cards.front: Why does Austen use the Jane and Bingley subplot alongside the Elizabeth and Darcy story?
cards.answer: It mirrors their relationship, showing passive trusting Jane against active sceptical Elizabeth, arguing marriage needs both feeling and judgement.

cards.front: Name the first four of Heracles's twelve labours in order.
cards.answer: The Nemean Lion / The Lernaean Hydra / The Ceryneian Hind / The Erymanthian Boar

cards.front: Why did Hera's persecution of Heracles ultimately make him great?
cards.answer: By driving him to madness so he killed his family, Hera caused the twelve labours imposed as penance, which became his most famous achievement.

cards.front: Why did placing the twelve labours on the Temple of Zeus at Olympia matter?
cards.answer: It put Heracles's deeds on the holiest temple at the most important sanctuary, showing they were divinely sanctioned and linking him to his father Zeus.

title: River Management & a Distinctive UK River
subject: geography-edexcel-a

cards.front: Name the four natural causes of flooding given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Heavy or prolonged rainfall / Snowmelt on saturated ground / Low-permeability rocks like clay / Steep upland slopes speeding runoff

cards.front: Name the three human causes of flooding given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Urbanisation / Deforestation / Agriculture

cards.front: Why does the River Tees still flood despite having defences like Cow Green Reservoir and channelisation?
cards.answer: Its catchment is small relative to possible rainfall, saturated ground cuts infiltration, and tidal locking at the estuary blocks outflow, amplifying peaks.

cards.front: Why does deforestation in a river catchment increase flood risk?
cards.answer: Without tree roots to soak up rainwater, more water reaches the river faster after a storm.

title: The Kidney, Water Balance and Plant Hormones
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three stages of urine formation in the kidney.
cards.answer: Filtration / Selective reabsorption / Excretion of waste

cards.front: Name the three commercial effects of gibberellins on plants.
cards.answer: End seed dormancy / Promote flowering / Increase fruit size

cards.front: Why does a root bend downwards in response to gravity (gravitropism)?
cards.answer: More auxin builds up on the lower side of the root, inhibiting elongation there, so the upper side grows more and the root bends down.

cards.front: Why do kidney transplant patients take immunosuppressant drugs for life?
cards.answer: To stop the recipient's immune system from rejecting the donor kidney.

cards.front: Name the three anthology poems the lesson compares with Baby Song, alongside the parent-child pairing point each makes.
cards.answer: You're by Sylvia Plath (playful tone vs baby's resentment) / My First Weeks by Sharon Olds (heaven vs regret) / Love by Kate Clanchy (frightened parent's view vs baby's own voice)
items: You're by Sylvia Plath (playful tone vs baby's resentment)
My First Weeks by Sharon Olds (heaven vs regret)
Love by Kate Clanchy (frightened parent's view vs baby's own voice)

cards.front: How does the steady rhyming couplet form of Baby Song create an odd effect against the baby's words?
cards.answer: The couplets sound like a soothing nursery rhyme or lullaby, which sits oddly against the baby's own angry complaints.

cards.front: Why is the gap between the baby's tone and its situation important in Baby Song?
cards.answer: Gunn gives a normally silent, powerless baby a confident, opinionated voice, so its helplessness clashes with its assured complaining.

cards.front: Name the six things a well-written client brief typically specifies.
cards.answer: Purpose (inform, persuade, entertain, promote) / Target audience / Content requirements / Format and technical specifications / Budget / Deadline

cards.front: Why is a creative decision considered a risk if it cannot be justified by the brief?
cards.answer: All creative decisions must be traceable back to the brief's requirements, so an unjustified decision has no basis and may fail to meet the client's needs.

cards.front: Why might a single brand produce several visually and tonally distinct media products?
cards.answer: Because audience segmentation divides a large audience into sub-groups, so the brand tailors different versions to suit each group, such as family-friendly versus adult-rated content.

cards.front: Name the three conflict locations Duffy names directly in the poem's sixth line.
cards.answer: Belfast / Beirut / Phnom Penh

cards.front: Name the three anthology poems the lesson pairs with 'War Photographer' for comparison.
cards.answer: Decomposition by Zulfikar Ghose / Remains by Simon Armitage / Disabled by Wilfred Owen

cards.front: Why does Duffy structure the darkroom as though it were a church?
cards.answer: It suggests the photographer performs a solemn duty, hinting photography has replaced faith as the only order he can impose on a violent world.

cards.front: How does Duffy's use of the word 'solutions' in 'Solutions slop in trays' create a dark pun?
cards.answer: It literally means developing chemicals but also ironically gestures toward political or military solutions that never actually stop the suffering.

cards.front: Name the six central figures introduced together in Act One, Scene One aboard the ship.
cards.answer: Rani / Hari / The Serang / Abdul Karim / Dadabhai Naoroji / The young Gandhi

cards.front: Name the four major characters who only appear once the action reaches London.
cards.answer: Lascar Sally / Firoza / Georgina / Lord Oakham

cards.front: Why is Susan Matthews able to dismiss Rani at Tilbury docks without any legal consequence?
cards.answer: There was no written contract between them, so Susan tells Rani their agreement was not legally binding.

cards.front: How does Abdul rise from an unnamed gift to the Queen's named favourite within a single scene?
cards.answer: Within minutes Victoria discovers he speaks several languages, appoints him to serve her breakfast, and overrules Lady Sarah's objections.

title: Jobs, Work Experience and Future Plans
subject: french-aqa

cards.front: Name the three choices French students can make after le collège (age 15), given in the lesson.
cards.answer: le lycée général (academic sixth form) / le lycée professionnel (vocational school) / un apprentissage (apprenticeship)

cards.front: Name the three future tense structures the lesson says you should combine to show range when discussing future plans.
cards.answer: near future (je vais + infinitive) / conditional (je voudrais) / simple future (je serai, je travaillerai)

cards.front: How is the conditional tense formed in French?
cards.answer: By adding imperfect endings to the infinitive, or to an irregular stem if the verb has one.

cards.front: What happens to French workers on 1st May, la Fête du Travail?
cards.answer: They do not work but still receive their salary, and many join street demonstrations for workers' rights.

title: Inequality: Age, Disability, Sexuality and Religion
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four disadvantages the lesson gives that young people face in the UK.
cards.answer: Over-represented in unemployment statistics / Less likely to own homes than previous generations / Cannot vote below age 18 / Subject to negative media stereotypes
items: Less likely to own homes than previous generations

cards.front: Name the three legal changes the lesson gives for LGBTQ+ equality in the UK.
cards.answer: Decriminalisation of same-sex activity in 1967 / Civil partnerships introduced in 2004 / Same-sex marriage legalised in 2013

cards.front: Why does the conflict perspective say ageism against older workers exists?
cards.answer: Because pushing older workers out of the labour market at reduced cost serves the interests of employers and the state.

cards.front: Why does the disability employment gap persist despite the Equality Act 2010?
cards.answer: Because although employers must make reasonable adjustments, enforcement is weak and attitudinal barriers remain significant.

cards.front: Name the six countries the lesson says had communist governments collapse in 1989.
cards.answer: Poland / Hungary / East Germany (Berlin Wall) / Czechoslovakia / Bulgaria / Romania

cards.front: Name the four types of senior Soviet officials who staged the August 1991 coup.
cards.answer: Vice President / Defence Minister / KGB chief / Prime Minister

cards.front: Why did Yeltsin's election as Russian President in June 1991 undermine Gorbachev's authority?
cards.answer: Yeltsin had a democratic mandate from a direct election that Gorbachev never had, creating a rival power centre.

cards.front: How did the failed August 1991 coup speed up the collapse of the USSR?
cards.answer: It fatally discredited the Communist Party, so Gorbachev suspended it and Soviet republics rushed to declare independence.

cards.front: Name the four sporting skills the lesson gives as examples of sagittal plane movement.
cards.answer: Running / Cycling / Swimming freestyle / Performing a squat

cards.front: Name the three movements the lesson gives as examples of frontal plane movement.
cards.answer: Lateral jumping / Sidesteps / Star jumps

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say the sagittal plane rotates around the sagittal axis?
cards.answer: Each axis is perpendicular to its plane, so every plane pairs with the axis of the opposite name, not the same name.

cards.front: Why does holding the discus at the edge of a longer turning radius increase release speed?
cards.answer: The longer the athlete's arms and the more effectively the discus is held at the turning radius, the greater the release speed achieved.

title: Manifest Destiny and the Pull of the West
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name three of the Indigenous nations the lesson names as already living in the West before Manifest Destiny.
cards.answer: Lakota / Comanche / Nez Perce / Cheyenne

cards.front: The lesson lists several consequences that followed the Gold Rush. Name three of them.
cards.answer: California became a state in 1850 / accelerated the Pacific Railroad debate / Chinese migration to California began / made overland routes across Plains territory a federal priority
items: made overland routes across Plains territory a federal priority

cards.front: Why does the lesson say it is wrong to describe Manifest Destiny as being about 'filling empty land'?
cards.answer: The Plains and Far West were already home to dozens of Indigenous nations, so the doctrine's real work was legitimising their dispossession.

cards.front: Why did most forty-niners not get rich from the Gold Rush?
cards.answer: The gold overwhelmingly enriched San Francisco's merchants and bankers rather than the diggers, leaving many forty-niners poorer than before.

cards.front: What are the three pillars of the UK's sustainable energy strategy?
cards.answer: Scaling renewables / Upgrading the grid / Reducing demand

cards.front: Name the three tensions that shape UK energy debates.
cards.answer: Cost vs climate / Local vs national interest / Energy security vs imports

cards.front: How did the UK manage to phase out coal within about 15 years?
cards.answer: A clear carbon price signal, falling renewable costs and gas-fired replacement, plus climate law targets and public opposition to pollution, drove the switch.

cards.front: How is the UK planning to reduce energy demand as part of its strategy?
cards.answer: By improving building insulation, replacing gas boilers with heat pumps, and increasing electric vehicle uptake.

cards.front: Name the two movements (parts) that structure 'Origin Story'.
cards.answer: The narrative of the parents' meeting / An extended reflection on what the story means for love
items: The narrative of the parents' meeting
An extended reflection on what the story means for love

cards.front: How does enjambment in 'Origin Story' mirror the poem's storytelling?
cards.answer: It lets sentences spill across lines, mirroring how a story keeps unfolding rather than stopping neatly.

cards.front: Why does Ewing include specific, unglamorous details about her parents before the comic-book imagery begins?
cards.answer: These details root the myth in real working lives, resisting the glossy simplicity of an actual comic-book hero's backstory.

cards.front: The lesson gives four steps for a reacting mass calculation. What are they?
cards.answer: Write the balanced equation / Calculate Mr of the known substance and find its moles / Use the molar ratio from the equation to find moles of the unknown substance / Convert moles of the unknown substance to mass
items: Calculate Mr of the known substance and find its moles
Use the molar ratio from the equation to find moles of the unknown substance
Convert moles of the unknown substance to mass

cards.front: Why must you never change the subscripts inside a formula when balancing a symbol equation?
cards.answer: Because changing the subscripts would change the substance itself, rather than just balancing the equation.

cards.front: Why does relative formula mass (Mr) have no units?
cards.answer: Because it is a ratio comparing mass relative to carbon-12, not an actual measured mass.

title: Mechanical Devices and Types of Motion
subject: design-technology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three cam shapes described in the lesson, based on the follower motion they produce.
cards.answer: Snail (drop) cam – slow rise then sudden drop / Eccentric (circular offset) cam – smooth regular rise and fall / Pear-shaped cam – holds a dwell then lifts and lowers smoothly
items: Snail (drop) cam – slow rise then sudden drop
Eccentric (circular offset) cam – smooth regular rise and fall
Pear-shaped cam – holds a dwell then lifts and lowers smoothly

cards.front: Name the three types of linkage described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Reverse motion linkage / Bell crank / Parallel motion linkage

cards.front: Why does a third-order lever sacrifice force?
cards.answer: Because the effort is between the fulcrum and the load, force is traded away to gain speed or a greater range of movement.

cards.front: How does a pear-shaped cam control engine valve timing?
cards.answer: It holds the follower still (dwell) for about half a turn, then lifts and lowers it smoothly to open and close the valve.

title: Chapters 4–6: The Carew Murder and Dr Lanyon
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: How does Stevenson's description of Soho's fog and darkness link to the novella's themes?
cards.answer: The fog mirrors the moral confusion surrounding Jekyll's double life, symbolising London's hidden, immoral side.

cards.front: Why is the broken walking stick significant as a clue in the Carew murder?
cards.answer: It was Utterson's gift to Jekyll, physically connecting Jekyll to the murder and foreshadowing that he and Hyde are one person.

cards.front: What signs in Hyde's Soho rooms suggest he left in a hurry?
cards.answer: Luxury furnishings / Ashes in the fireplace / A burnt cheque book

cards.front: Name the four groups of workers who walked out during the Winter of Discontent (1978-79).
cards.answer: Lorry drivers / Refuse collectors / Gravediggers / Public sector workers

cards.front: What three types of argument did opponents of EEC membership raise in the 1970s?
cards.answer: Sovereignty concerns / Economic/socialist objections / Fears over migration

cards.front: Why did Bloody Sunday intensify the Troubles?
cards.answer: The killing of unarmed civilians by British paratroopers caused outrage that surged Provisional IRA membership and support, escalating violence.

cards.front: Why did the SNP vote against Callaghan's government in the March 1979 no confidence vote?
cards.answer: The SNP's 11 MPs voted against the government in protest at the failure of the Scottish devolution referendum.

cards.front: Name the three exemptions from fighting listed under Deuteronomy 20 for a Milchemet reshut.
cards.answer: A man with a new house / A man with a new vineyard / A man with a new marriage
items: A man with a new house
A man with a new vineyard
A man with a new marriage

cards.front: Name the four practical ways the lesson says Jews work for peace today.
cards.answer: Taking part in interfaith dialogue / Mediating between divided communities / Supporting refugees displaced by conflict / Campaigning for reconciliation

cards.front: Why do some Jews argue that peace cannot be an absolute value in Judaism?
cards.answer: Because the Torah permits war under strict conditions, so peace cannot override everything else.

cards.front: Why do weapons of mass destruction conflict with the Jewish concept of Purity of Arms?
cards.answer: WMD cause indiscriminate destruction harming civilians, while Purity of Arms requires force to be limited to what is necessary.

title: International isolation and the Anti-Apartheid Movement
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three major forms of international pressure that combined to isolate apartheid South Africa.
cards.answer: Sports isolation / Economic sanctions / Diplomatic isolation

cards.front: Why did Barclays Bank sell its South African subsidiary in 1986?
cards.answer: Sustained protests by student union disinvestment campaigns in British universities pressured Barclays into selling its South African subsidiary.

cards.front: Why did the Commonwealth Eminent Persons Group recommend comprehensive sanctions in 1986?
cards.answer: Because South Africa launched military raids into Zambia, Zimbabwe and Botswana during the very week the group was visiting.

cards.front: Name the four causes the lesson gives for counter-urbanisation since the 1980s.
cards.answer: Rising city house prices / Expansion of motorways / Full-fibre broadband enabling rural home-working / Perception that village life is safer and healthier for families
items: Perception that village life is safer and healthier for families

cards.front: Name the four other rural challenges the lesson describes besides housing pressure.
cards.answer: Decline in primary employment (farming) / Reduced healthcare access as surgeries close / Struggling village schools closing since 2010 / Leisure and recreation visits pressuring local services
items: Reduced healthcare access as surgeries close
Leisure and recreation visits pressuring local services

cards.front: Why does the lesson say some rural areas count as deprived even without low headline income?
cards.answer: They are deprived because of poor access to services and isolation, not because of low income.

cards.front: Why couldn't sheep farming alone sustain Lake District villages like Ambleside or Keswick?
cards.answer: Farming couldn't generate enough income, so tourism revenue is needed to keep shops, pubs and cafes open.

cards.front: Name the four addition polymers the lesson gives, with one use each.
cards.answer: Poly(ethene) — carrier bags / Poly(propene) — crates and car parts / PVC — pipes and cable insulation / PTFE — non-stick cookware coatings

cards.front: What two ways does condensation polymerisation differ from addition polymerisation? (HT)
cards.answer: Monomers need two reactive groups / A small molecule (water) is released at each bond
items: A small molecule (water) is released at each bond

cards.front: Why is PET chosen over glass for drinks bottles, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: PET is lighter, reducing transport energy, cheaper to produce, shatterproof, and recyclable compared to glass.

cards.front: Why is life-cycle assessment used to compare materials like PET and glass bottles?
cards.answer: It compares total environmental impact across the whole life cycle — raw material extraction, manufacturing, use and disposal — not just end-of-life.

title: Film Industry: No Time to Die
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four countries where No Time to Die was filmed on location, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Italy / Jamaica / Norway / Faroe Islands

cards.front: Name the three types of rights held by United Artists Releasing for No Time to Die.
cards.answer: North American distribution rights / Worldwide digital rights / Worldwide television rights

cards.front: Why does Amazon's ownership of MGM show vertical integration in the Bond franchise?
cards.answer: Amazon owns both the franchise rights (via MGM) and the streaming platform, Prime, that delivers them to audiences.

cards.front: How does the Billie Eilish theme song for No Time to Die demonstrate synergy?
cards.answer: It was released on Interscope, owned by Universal, the same company distributing the film, promoting the product across music and film.

cards.front: Name the three layers of a UK deciduous woodland, with an example tree/plant group for each.
cards.answer: Canopy of oak, ash and beech / Understorey of holly, hazel and field maple / Ground layer of bluebells, ferns and brambles
items: Canopy of oak, ash and beech
Understorey of holly, hazel and field maple
Ground layer of bluebells, ferns and brambles

cards.front: Name the four drivers of Amazon deforestation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Conversion to agriculture / Resource extraction / Population pressure / Climate change

cards.front: Why do UK deciduous trees shed their broad, flat leaves in autumn?
cards.answer: Broad flat leaves maximise photosynthesis in summer but would be damaged by frost, so trees shed them before winter cold sets in.

cards.front: How does Costa Rica's ecotourism industry help stop deforestation?
cards.answer: Over 3 million visitors a year generate $4 billion of revenue, giving landowners better incomes than cattle ranching so they keep forest standing.

cards.front: Name the six classical conditions that must be met before lesser jihad is permissible.
cards.answer: Legitimate cause (self-defence/defending the oppressed) / All peaceful alternatives exhausted first / Declared by a legitimate authority / Non-combatants protected / Crops and buildings not destroyed / Must cease when enemy stops fighting
items: Must cease when enemy stops fighting

cards.front: Name the four Islamic festivals covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Id-ul-Fitr / Id-ul-Adha / Ashura / Id-ul-Ghadeer

cards.front: Why does the lesson say reducing jihad to 'holy war' misrepresents Islamic teaching?
cards.answer: It ignores greater jihad and strips lesser jihad of its strict conditions, wrongly implying unlimited violence, which the Qur'an prohibits.

cards.front: Why is every act of worship, like Salah, Sawm and Zakah, considered a form of greater jihad?
cards.answer: Because each requires the believer to overcome laziness, selfishness or distraction in order to submit to Allah.

cards.front: Why did Cromwell's cavalry give Parliament an advantage at Marston Moor?
cards.answer: Cromwell's disciplined cavalry returned after charging rather than pursuing off the field, unlike most cavalry of the period.

cards.front: Why did Parliament struggle to win the war quickly despite victory at Marston Moor in 1644?
cards.answer: Commanders Essex and Manchester proved reluctant to press their military advantages, slowing Parliament's progress.

cards.front: Why did Charles refuse to negotiate seriously over the Propositions of Newcastle in 1646?
cards.answer: He was playing for time, hoping to split Parliament from its Scottish and army allies rather than accept permanent subjugation.

cards.front: The lesson says efficiency gains from e-commerce, banking, payroll and mail handling share three things. Name them.
cards.answer: Automate repetitive tasks / Remove geography as a barrier / Enable 24/7 access

cards.front: Before cloud computing, name the four things a small business needed to buy or arrange for reliable IT infrastructure.
cards.answer: Buy servers / Pay for maintenance contracts / Hire IT staff / Find physical space for equipment

cards.front: How do bionic limbs restore function to amputees?
cards.answer: They use sensors and microprocessors that respond to the wearer's nerve signals.

cards.front: How do AI chatbots reduce customer waiting times?
cards.answer: They handle thousands of customer service enquiries at the same time, instead of one at a time.

title: Homeostasis: Thermoregulation, Blood Glucose and Diabetes
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three components that all homeostatic control systems share.
cards.answer: Receptors (detect change) / Coordination centre (processes information) / Effectors (produce the response)

cards.front: Name the four responses the hypothalamus coordinates when the body is too hot.
cards.answer: Vasodilation of skin blood vessels / Increased sweating / Hair follicle muscles relax (hairs lie flat) / Shivering reduces
items: Hair follicle muscles relax (hairs lie flat)

cards.front: Why does shivering warm the body up when it's cold?
cards.answer: Rapid, involuntary contractions of skeletal muscles generate heat through respiration.

cards.front: Why does hair standing up (hair erector muscles contracting) help keep the body warm?
cards.answer: It pulls hairs upright, trapping a thicker layer of insulating air near the skin.
