cards.front: Name the four factors historians give for why Restoration became possible in 1660.
cards.answer: Richard Cromwell's failure removed the only republican successor / Army factionalism discredited military rule / Monck's march provided order without demanding a particular settlement / Charles II's moderation in the Declaration of Breda reassured people
items: Richard Cromwell's failure removed the only republican successor
Monck's march provided order without demanding a particular settlement
Charles II's moderation in the Declaration of Breda reassured people

cards.front: Why was the Restoration not a simple reversal of the revolution?
cards.answer: Charles II returned with his father's pre-1642 powers, but prerogative courts stayed abolished and the Triennial Act remained, preserving Parliament's gains.

cards.front: Why did Monck's march south help stabilise the chaos of 1659-60 even though he didn't openly back the King?
cards.answer: His disciplined army, uninvolved in prior political intrigue, restored order without committing to any particular settlement, reassuring rival factions.

cards.front: Name the four marriage models the novel presents.
cards.answer: Elizabeth and Darcy / Jane and Bingley / Charlotte and Collins / Lydia and Wickham

cards.front: Name the three assessment objectives this extract question is marked on.
cards.answer: AO1 informed personal response with textual references / AO2 analysis of language, form and structure / AO3 understanding of contexts
items: AO2 analysis of language, form and structure

cards.front: How does Elizabeth's prejudice against Darcy connect to her own pride?
cards.answer: Her prejudice against Darcy is rooted in her wounded pride after his insult at the assembly.

cards.front: How does the appearance versus reality theme link to Austen's narrative technique?
cards.answer: Free indirect discourse shows the story through Elizabeth's flawed perspective, so the reader shares her mistaken first impressions until the revelation.

cards.front: Name the three stages the stolen boat episode divides into in The Prelude.
cards.answer: Boy rows out onto the lake confidently / Mountain appears to rise up and chase him / Boy returns the boat and is haunted by huge forms
items: Boy rows out onto the lake confidently
Mountain appears to rise up and chase him
Boy returns the boat and is haunted by huge forms

cards.front: Name the three poems the lesson compares with The Prelude.
cards.answer: Ozymandias / Exposure / Storm on the Island

cards.front: Why does the mountain's appearance humble the boy in The Prelude?
cards.answer: He thought he was in control of nature by rowing the boat, but nature showed him he is insignificant.

cards.front: How does Wordsworth's view of nature's power differ from Owen's in Exposure?
cards.answer: Wordsworth sees the boy's encounter as ultimately positive, a learning experience, while Owen sees only destruction.

cards.front: Name the four broad groups of solutions the lesson gives for reducing desertification risk in the Sahel.
cards.answer: Water and soil management / Tree planting / Appropriate technology / Rotation and reduced livestock

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why the Great Green Wall has been slowed down.
cards.answer: Scale / Funding / Conflict

cards.front: Why does over-cultivation contribute to desertification?
cards.answer: Farming the same field continuously without rest exhausts the soil's nutrients.

cards.front: How does a drought trigger the vicious cycle of desertification in the Sahel?
cards.answer: Drought makes farmers move cattle to new land, which gets overgrazed, thinning vegetation so soil loses grip and washes away, forcing further moves.

cards.front: Name four Greek gods and their Roman equivalents given in the lesson (other than Athena/Minerva or Poseidon/Neptune).
cards.answer: Zeus → Jupiter / Hera → Juno / Ares → Mars / Aphrodite → Venus / Hades → Pluto / Demeter → Ceres

cards.front: Why did the Romans originally focus less on myths about the gods' personal lives than the Greeks did?
cards.answer: Early Roman religion was ritual-focused, believing correct performance of rites maintained the pax deorum and secured Rome's safety and prosperity.

cards.front: How does the breastplate on the Augustus of Prima Porta statue make a political statement?
cards.answer: It shows the sky god Caelus above and earth goddess Terra below, framing Augustus's military victory within a cosmic order under Roman rule.

cards.front: Name the four ways a river transports its load.
cards.answer: Traction (large rocks roll) / Saltation (pebbles bounce) / Suspension (fine silt carried in water) / Solution (dissolved minerals travel invisibly)

cards.front: What four features would you look for on an OS map to identify river landforms?
cards.answer: Tightly packed contours with thin wiggly line / Sweeping line with floodplain label / Curved lines disconnected from main river / Broad estuary mouths with mudflats
items: Tightly packed contours with thin wiggly line
Curved lines disconnected from main river

cards.front: How does a waterfall form where hard rock sits above soft rock?
cards.answer: Water drops over the resistant lip, eroding a plunge pool, while soft rock underneath is undercut until the lip collapses.

cards.front: Why does a delta form where a river meets the sea?
cards.answer: The river loses energy at the sea and drops the rest of its sediment load, building a fan of channels.

title: The Trinity, Creation and Human Nature
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four characteristics of God's nature that the Creation account reveals, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Creator / benevolent / omnipotent / eternal

cards.front: Name the three chapters of Genesis 1-3 and what each covers, as the lesson describes them.
cards.answer: Genesis 1: six days of creation / Genesis 2: forming of first humans / Genesis 3: the Fall

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church read Genesis 1-3 mainly metaphorically rather than literally?
cards.answer: Because the six days are seen as a literary structure conveying theological truths about God and humanity, not a scientific timetable.

cards.front: Why does being made in the imago Dei underpin Catholic teaching on the sanctity of life?
cards.answer: Because every person bears God's image, giving them inherent worth, so every human life deserves respect regardless of ability, age or usefulness.

title: Rock Anthems of the 1970s and 1980s: Stadium Sound and Guitar Power
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the four dramatic devices the lesson says rock anthems use to decorate their otherwise simple verse-chorus-solo structures.
cards.answer: Key changes / Extended guitar solos / A cappella or stripped-back sections / Audience-participation hooks

cards.front: Name the five guitar techniques the lesson lists as being used in rock anthem guitar solos.
cards.answer: String bending / Vibrato / Sliding / Legato (hammer-ons and pull-offs) / Whammy bar

cards.front: How does distortion create the thick, crunchy timbre of rock guitar?
cards.answer: Overdriving the signal clips the clean waveform into a jagged shape, adding extra overtones that create a thick, aggressive timbre.

cards.front: How is a gated reverb drum sound produced?
cards.answer: A natural reverb on the drum is recorded, then a noise gate abruptly cuts it off, leaving a short, punchy, artificially large-sounding hit.

cards.front: Name the three types of intrusive igneous bodies specified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sill / Dyke / Pluton

cards.front: Name the three field features used to recognise a pluton.
cards.answer: Lack of internal layering / Irregular contact with country rock / Metamorphic aureole

cards.front: Why do the rocks on both sides of a sill show baking (contact metamorphism)?
cards.answer: The hot magma of the sill heats the surrounding rock layers it intrudes into, altering them with heat.

cards.front: Why do larger plutons have wider metamorphic aureoles?
cards.answer: Larger plutons have more heat available and cool over a longer period, so they thermally alter a wider zone of surrounding rock.

title: Dramatic Methods: Multi-roling, Mime and Storytelling
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the five core dramatic methods this production uses to tell its story.
cards.answer: Multi-roling / Mime / Direct address narration / Object transformation / Ensemble physical theatre

cards.front: Name the four accessories layered onto the base costume to signal a quick character change.
cards.answer: A hat / A badge / An accent / A way of walking

cards.front: Why did Eason choose the small multi-roling ensemble form instead of a naturalistic large-cast staging?
cards.answer: Watching actors transform live creates theatrical energy a naturalistic staging cannot, mirroring the dizzying speed of Fogg's journey.

cards.front: Why must performers commit fully to the physical logic of an object transformation, like a chair becoming a train carriage?
cards.answer: A chair only convinces as a carriage if the performer behaves exactly as in a moving train; breaking that logic collapses the fiction.

cards.front: Name the four steps in the model comparative paragraph structure.
cards.answer: Opening statement comparing themes / Named poem analysis (AO2) / Comparison connective / Chosen poem analysis then context (AO3)

cards.front: Name the four common mistakes to avoid in the comparison essay.
cards.answer: Writing about poems separately / Feature-spotting without analysis / Treating context as a separate section / Retelling the poem
items: Treating context as a separate section

cards.front: Why should context be woven into analysis rather than bolted on as a separate section?
cards.answer: Because AO2 (analysis of language, form, structure) is the main focus and worth more marks than AO3 context.

cards.front: Why is writing three paragraphs on the named poem then three on the chosen poem a mistake?
cards.answer: It produces two separate essays rather than sustained comparison, since each paragraph must discuss both poems.

cards.front: Name the four carbon allotropes described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Diamond / Graphite / Graphene / Fullerenes

cards.front: Name the three properties of metals the lesson says come from delocalised electrons.
cards.answer: High melting points / Malleable / Good conductors of electricity and heat
items: Good conductors of electricity and heat

cards.front: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water but not as solids?
cards.answer: The ions become free to move and carry charge once molten or dissolved, unlike in the fixed solid lattice.

cards.front: Why does graphite feel soft and work as a lubricant?
cards.answer: Its layers are held together by weak intermolecular forces, so they can slide over each other easily.

title: Physical Theatre: Frantic Assembly and Beyond
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four physical theatre companies/practitioners the lesson identifies as key examples.
cards.answer: Frantic Assembly / Complicite / DV8 / Steven Berkoff

cards.front: What three things signal a shift between roles in multi-roling, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: a postural shift / a change in vocal pitch and pace / a change in levels in the space
items: a change in vocal pitch and pace
a change in levels in the space

cards.front: How can the same physical technique of a lift communicate different meanings in different scenes?
cards.answer: A lift in reconciliation shows trust, while one in another scene shows control or coercion, but both are immediate and viscerally felt by the audience.

cards.front: Why is multi-roling common in physical theatre?
cards.answer: Because physical theatre treats the performer's body as a malleable instrument, making transformation between roles legible and immediate.

title: The Scramble for Africa & the Boer War
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three British presences in Africa that expanded together in the earlier 19th century, giving Britain its 'civilising mission' self-image.
cards.answer: Trade (palm oil) / Missionaries (e.g. David Livingstone) / Royal Navy West Africa Squadron

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says empire was sold to the British public through propaganda.
cards.answer: Cigarette cards / Music hall songs / Boys' Own and Girls' Own Paper / 1924 Empire Exhibition at Wembley
items: Boys' Own and Girls' Own Paper

cards.front: Why did the Berlin Conference's 'effective occupation' rule cause a rush of European activity in Africa?
cards.answer: Powers had to prove control by planting flags and signing treaties with African chiefs to keep claimed territory.

cards.front: Why did the guerrilla phase of the Boer War lead to British concentration camps?
cards.answer: Boer commandos kept fighting after Pretoria fell, so Britain burned farms and corralled civilians into camps to stop them.

title: Falkirk 1298 and Agincourt 1415: medieval battles and their leaders
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: According to the lesson, what three types of troops did Edward I bring to Falkirk?
cards.answer: Heavy cavalry / Men-at-arms / Around 2,000 Welsh and English longbowmen

cards.front: Besides the longbow, what four factors do modern historians say decided Agincourt?
cards.answer: The muddy ground / The funnel terrain / French command failures / Henry V's decisions on dismounting and stake-driving
items: Henry V's decisions on dismounting and stake-driving

cards.front: Why did Edward I change tactics after his first cavalry charge failed at Falkirk?
cards.answer: His knights charged the schiltrons directly and were repulsed, so he pulled the cavalry back and sent longbowmen forward to break the formation with arrows first.

cards.front: Why did morale favour the English over the Scots at the start of Falkirk?
cards.answer: Wallace's army began the battle demoralised after a year of evading fighting, while Edward I had personally led his men since dawn.

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives that shape which energy resources a country can access.
cards.answer: Physical resources (what's naturally there) / Geology and accessibility (how easy to extract) / Technology and capital (wealth to develop it)
items: Geology and accessibility (how easy to extract)
Technology and capital (wealth to develop it)

cards.front: Name the three causes the lesson gives for gaps in energy use per capita between countries.
cards.answer: Economic development / Reliance on traditional fuels / Sectoral mix (industry vs services)

cards.front: Why do Norway and Iceland have unusually high energy use per capita figures?
cards.answer: They have energy-intensive aluminium smelters powered by hydroelectric power.

cards.front: Why did US oil prices briefly fall below zero in 2020?
cards.answer: COVID-19 lockdowns collapsed demand for oil so sharply that prices went negative.

cards.front: Why does a poet use personification, such as 'the wind whispered secrets'?
cards.answer: To make the object seem alive, usually to make it appear more powerful, threatening, or sympathetic.

cards.front: Why should you explain the effect of a sound device rather than just naming it?
cards.answer: Because simply noting a device is feature-spotting, while explaining its effect on the reader is genuine analysis.

title: Malcolm X and the Black Muslims, 1952-65
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six-part community programme the Nation of Islam ran, funded entirely from Black donations.
cards.answer: Drug rehabilitation / Family discipline / Black-owned businesses / Mosques / Schools / Newspapers

cards.front: Name the three ways Malcolm X's public message in his Nation years rejected King's approach.
cards.answer: Separatism instead of integration / Self-defence instead of nonviolent direct action / Dismissed white conscience instead of appealing to it
items: Self-defence instead of nonviolent direct action
Dismissed white conscience instead of appealing to it

cards.front: Beneath the public suspension, what deeper discovery drove Malcolm X's break with the Nation of Islam?
cards.answer: He found that Elijah Muhammad, who preached strict sexual discipline, had fathered children with several Nation secretaries.

cards.front: How did performing the Hajj in April 1964 change Malcolm X's views on race?
cards.answer: Seeing Sunni pilgrims of all colours praying together contradicted the Nation's race theology, leading him to drop sweeping racial indictments.

title: Humanistic Theory, Identity and Free Will
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name Maslow's five levels of needs, from the bottom of the pyramid to the top.
cards.answer: Physiological needs / Safety needs / Love and belonging / Esteem needs / Self-actualisation

cards.front: Name Erikson's eight stages of identity development, in order from infancy to old age.
cards.answer: Trust vs mistrust / Autonomy vs shame / Initiative vs guilt / Industry vs inferiority / Identity vs role confusion / Intimacy vs isolation / Generativity vs stagnation / Integrity vs despair

cards.front: Why does conditional positive regard lead to incongruence?
cards.answer: Children start valuing only the parts of themselves that win approval, creating a gap between real self and ideal self.

cards.front: Why does Maslow argue that people find it hard to pursue self-actualisation when facing poverty or unsafe housing?
cards.answer: Lower, more basic needs like safety must be satisfied before a person can focus on higher needs like self-actualisation.

title: Sharpeville and the turn to armed struggle
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three causes the lesson gives for the Pondoland Revolt of 1960–1961.
cards.answer: Hut tax increases / Bantustan control measures / Forced cattle culling

cards.front: What three types of infrastructure did MK's early sabotage strategy target?
cards.answer: Power lines / Government buildings / Transport links

cards.front: Why did MK's founding strategy target property rather than people?
cards.answer: Mandela and the ANC leadership deliberately decided to avoid killing civilians, so sabotage focused on property, not people.

cards.front: Why is Oliver Tambo's leadership in exile seen as significant for the ANC's survival?
cards.answer: Without Tambo's work in exile, the ANC might have collapsed as an organisation during the long silence of the 1960s and 1970s.

title: Developing Recipes & Meals for Specific Needs
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three time-saving techniques the lesson gives for developing recipes for working parents.
cards.answer: Batch cooking and freezing in portions / Preparing ingredients in advance (e.g. mirepoix) / Choosing methods with shorter active cooking time
items: Batch cooking and freezing in portions
Choosing methods with shorter active cooking time

cards.front: Why does replacing dairy milk with oat milk change the sensory outcome of a lactose-free recipe?
cards.answer: Oat milk has a sweeter flavour than cows' milk, so it can alter the taste of the finished dish.

cards.front: Why can steaming and adjusting flavour with salt improve a dish that tastes flat during recipe testing?
cards.answer: Salt enhances and balances other flavours, so a flat-tasting dish often needs salt rather than more of another ingredient.

cards.front: Why does replacing chicken breast with chicken thighs help adapt a recipe for a low budget?
cards.answer: Chicken thighs cost less per kg than chicken breast, though they contain more fat and give more flavour.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives for why America won the War of Independence.
cards.answer: Washington's leadership / British mistakes / French involvement / Spanish involvement

cards.front: Name the three problems the lesson gives for why Britain lost despite its advantages.
cards.answer: Strategic geography made supply hard / British commanders failed to coordinate / Continental Army only had to stay in the field
items: Continental Army only had to stay in the field

cards.front: Why was the Battle of Saratoga a turning point in the War of Independence?
cards.answer: It persuaded France to sign an open alliance with America, turning a colonial rebellion into a global war Britain could not win.

cards.front: How did Washington stop the Continental Army from disintegrating at Valley Forge?
cards.answer: He held the army together through argument and personal example, and accepted Von Steuben's help drilling it into a professional force.

cards.front: Name the four themes Act 1 Scene 1 establishes in miniature for the whole play.
cards.answer: Poverty (the flat) introduces class / Helen's drinking introduces the cycle of self-destruction / Peter's arrival introduces women depending on inadequate men / Jo left alone introduces abandonment
items: Helen's drinking introduces the cycle of self-destruction
Peter's arrival introduces women depending on inadequate men

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says Helen prioritises herself over Jo's welfare.
cards.answer: Drinks heavily / Dismisses Jo's complaints about the flat / More interested in her own appearance than Jo's schoolwork
items: Dismisses Jo's complaints about the flat
More interested in her own appearance than Jo's schoolwork

cards.front: How does the flat physically represent Jo and Helen's relationship?
cards.answer: It is cramped, uncomfortable and impossible to escape, with no privacy, which intensifies their conflict.

cards.front: Why does Delaney make Jo and Helen entertaining rather than just pitiable?
cards.answer: Their witty, comic dialogue masks genuine pain, making them complicated and deeply human rather than simple objects of pity.

title: The Taliban and Afghanistan as a Rogue State
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name six things the Taliban banned in Afghanistan (other than restrictions on women).
cards.answer: Music / Television / Kite-flying / Photographs of living things / Chess / Football

cards.front: What four reasons does the lesson give for the Taliban's international isolation by 2001?
cards.answer: Exclusion of women from work and school / Persecution of Hazaras and other minorities / Destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas / Sheltering Osama bin Laden
items: Exclusion of women from work and school
Persecution of Hazaras and other minorities

cards.front: Why did the Taliban refuse to hand Osama bin Laden over to the United States?
cards.answer: They insisted on proof of his guilt that the regime would never have accepted anyway.

cards.front: Why did Iran come close to invading Afghanistan in 1998?
cards.answer: Because Iranian diplomats in Mazar-i-Sharif were killed during the Taliban's massacre of Hazara civilians there.

cards.front: Why do a crate and floor warm up slightly when the crate is dragged across the floor?
cards.answer: Friction transfers energy from the kinetic energy store to the thermal energy store of the object and surface.

cards.front: In the falling cyclist example, why does the speed at the bottom of the hill not depend on the cyclist's mass?
cards.answer: Mass appears on both sides of mgh = ½mv², so it cancels out, leaving speed independent of mass.

cards.front: Name the three regions of the brain described in the lesson, along with the cerebellum and brain stem.
cards.answer: Cerebral cortex / Cerebellum / Brain stem

cards.front: Name the three structures found in every neurone.
cards.answer: Cell body (containing nucleus) / Dendrites / Axon

cards.front: How does the pupil light reflex protect the retina in bright light?
cards.answer: Light receptors in the retina send signals via the brain stem to the iris's circular muscles, which contract, narrowing the pupil.

cards.front: Why do doctors use the pupil reflex to check for brain damage after a head injury?
cards.answer: Because an absence of the pupil reflex after a head injury may indicate serious brain damage.

cards.front: Name the four potential effects of climate change given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Rising sea levels / More extreme weather events / Changes in habitats and biodiversity / Disruption to agriculture and food supplies
items: Disruption to agriculture and food supplies

cards.front: Name the four mitigation measures for climate change given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Reducing fossil fuel use / Increasing renewable energy / Improving energy efficiency / Carbon capture and storage

cards.front: Why did carbon dioxide levels in Earth's early atmosphere fall over billions of years?
cards.answer: CO2 dissolved into forming oceans, was locked in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels, and was absorbed by photosynthesising plants and algae.

cards.front: Why does the build-up of oxygen matter for life on Earth?
cards.answer: Rising oxygen allowed complex oxygen-dependent organisms to evolve and led to the ozone layer forming, which blocks harmful ultraviolet radiation.

cards.front: What four things does the novella end with, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Jekyll gone / Hyde dead / Lanyon dead / the truth contained in documents only the reader has seen
items: the truth contained in documents only the reader has seen

cards.front: Why does witnessing Jekyll's transformation destroy Lanyon's mind?
cards.answer: It shatters everything he believed about science and the separation of mind and body, a truth too terrible for his mind to survive.

cards.front: Why does Hyde grow stronger over time while Jekyll weakens?
cards.answer: Each transformation lets Jekyll indulge repressed desires, which strengthens rather than satisfies them, so the evil side grows unchecked.

title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four common compounds given in the lesson, along with their chemical formulas.
cards.answer: Water (H2O) / Carbon dioxide (CO2) / Sodium chloride (NaCl) / Methane (CH4)

cards.front: Name the four stages in the development of the atomic model, in order.
cards.answer: Dalton's solid sphere theory (1803) / Thomson's plum pudding model (1897) / Rutherford's nuclear model (1909) / Bohr's shell model (1913)

cards.front: Why do elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar properties?
cards.answer: Because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which affects how they react.

cards.front: Why don't neutrons affect an atom's chemical properties?
cards.answer: Because neutrons have no charge and only add mass, so they don't take part in bonding.

cards.front: How does shaping differ from forming in the way each process works?
cards.answer: Shaping fills a mould with molten or softened material using fluidity, while forming plastically deforms a solid workpiece using force or heat.

cards.front: Why is injection moulding classed as shaping rather than forming?
cards.answer: Injection moulding uses liquid polymer filling a mould, whereas forming requires a solid workpiece being plastically deformed.

cards.front: Name the five applications of electromagnets given in the lesson that changed everyday life.
cards.answer: Electric telegraph / Electric bell / Relay switch / MRI scanners / Scrapyard cranes

cards.front: How does winding a wire into a solenoid strengthen its magnetic field?
cards.answer: The magnetic fields produced by each turn of wire add together inside the coil.

cards.front: Why does increasing the current in a transformer's secondary coil reduce transmission heat losses?
cards.answer: Stepping up voltage reduces current, and since power loss equals I squared times R, lower current cuts heat losses.

cards.front: How does a current-carrying coil create sound in a loudspeaker? (Higher tier)
cards.answer: The coil's field interacts with the permanent magnet's field, so varying current makes the coil vibrate, pushing a cone to create sound waves.

title: Norman Government, Justice and the Anglo-Saxon Inheritance
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four elements of the Anglo-Saxon system of government that the lesson says the Normans kept largely intact.
cards.answer: Shires and hundreds / Sheriffs as royal officers / The writ / The geld land tax

cards.front: How did Norman tenants-in-chief differ from Anglo-Saxon earls and thegns in how they held power?
cards.answer: Tenants-in-chief held land formally from the king and owed forty days' knight service, making them the king's sworn men first, unlike semi-independent Anglo-Saxon earls.

cards.front: Why did William introduce the murdrum fine?
cards.answer: Because Norman lives were seen as under permanent threat from a hostile Anglo-Saxon population, so it made English communities responsible for protecting Norman incomers.

cards.front: Why did William's use of primogeniture cause political tension after his death in 1087?
cards.answer: Robert Curthose got Normandy while William II got England, leaving younger sons with less and fuelling the 1088 rebellion.

cards.front: Name the four phases of the genre cycle described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Establishment of conventions / Refinement and intensification / Self-parody / Decline or transformation

cards.front: Name the three forms of intertextuality the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Explicit / Implicit / Structural

cards.front: How does a low-angle shot affect how a subject appears?
cards.answer: It makes the subject appear powerful.

cards.front: Why are hybrid genres commercially appealing?
cards.answer: Because they can target audiences from two genre communities simultaneously.

cards.front: Name the four things a Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC) does.
cards.answer: Sets the local police and crime plan / Determines the police budget / Appoints or dismisses the chief constable / Is accountable to the public through elections
items: Sets the local police and crime plan
Appoints or dismisses the chief constable
Is accountable to the public through elections

cards.front: Name the four qualities assessed when someone applies to become a magistrate.
cards.answer: Good character / Social awareness / Sound judgement / Ability to see another's perspective

cards.front: Why do supporters of the jury system argue it reduces biased decisions?
cards.answer: Because twelve citizens deliberate independently, which reduces the risk of arbitrary or biased decisions by a single judge.

cards.front: Why do witness support services offer methods like video link or a screen?
cards.answer: To help vulnerable witnesses, including children and victims of serious offences, give evidence in less intimidating ways.

cards.front: According to the lesson's Key Fact, name the five character-to-theme pairings in Anita and Me.
cards.answer: Meena = dual identity / Anita = the danger of assimilation / Mama/Papa = the cost of integration / Nanima = cultural roots / Sam = racism as a product of decline
items: Sam = racism as a product of decline

cards.front: Name the three groups of minor/background characters (besides Tracey) discussed in the lesson, with what each represents.
cards.answer: The Aunties - a Greek chorus of comic relief and collective wisdom / Mrs Worrall - Tollington's most sympathetic white character / Mr Ormerod and Mr Christmas - casual, unexamined racism
items: The Aunties - a Greek chorus of comic relief and collective wisdom
Mrs Worrall - Tollington's most sympathetic white character
Mr Ormerod and Mr Christmas - casual, unexamined racism

cards.front: How does Papa's controlled anger after the racist attack reveal something deeper about his character?
cards.answer: It reveals the exhaustion hidden beneath his calm, patient exterior of trying to integrate.

cards.front: Why does Syal present Sam Lowbridge as a product of post-industrial decline?
cards.answer: To offer an explanation, not an excuse, showing his racism stems from economic frustration in a declining town.

cards.front: Name the four main macroeconomic objectives fiscal policy can help achieve, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Economic growth / Low unemployment / Price stability (low inflation) / Healthy balance of payments

cards.front: Name the four limitations of fiscal policy given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Time lags before effects are felt / Rising national debt and interest payments / Political distortion from electoral cycles / Expansionary policy may boost imports not UK output
items: Time lags before effects are felt
Rising national debt and interest payments
Expansionary policy may boost imports not UK output

cards.front: How can increased government spending on infrastructure reduce unemployment?
cards.answer: It creates construction jobs directly, and the multiplier effect then boosts wider employment as spending ripples through the economy.

cards.front: Why do rising debt interest payments limit the government's ability to spend on public services?
cards.answer: Large deficits build up national debt, and the interest owed on this debt crowds out spending on schools and hospitals.

cards.front: Name the four roles the lesson says Prospero simultaneously embodies.
cards.answer: Victim / Father / Master / Artist

cards.front: Name the three points on Shakespeare's moral spectrum of characters, with their status.
cards.answer: Gonzalo - consistently virtuous / Alonso - sinful but repentant / Antonio - sinful and unrepentant

cards.front: How can Ariel and Caliban be read as two aspects of Prospero's own personality?
cards.answer: Ariel represents his creative, artistic side (the power to enchant), while Caliban represents his darker impulses to control and dominate.

cards.front: Why is Miranda described as the play's moral heart?
cards.answer: She represents natural empathy, suffering with those she sees suffer, and her innocence offers hope the next generation can be better.

title: Early modern warfare and the New Model Army c1500–c1700
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four types of soldier that made up the early modern English army.
cards.answer: Musketeers / Pikemen / Dragoons / Cavalry

cards.front: What three methods of recruitment were used to raise soldiers in this period?
cards.answer: County trained bands / Volunteers attracted by bounties / Impressment of the unwilling

cards.front: Why were fortifications rebuilt as low, angled bastions instead of tall stone walls in this period?
cards.answer: Reliable cannon could now be brought onto the battlefield, so low angled bastions were needed to deflect shot rather than repel ladders.

cards.front: Why did England move towards keeping a permanent standing army in this period?
cards.answer: Pike-and-shot troops needed long drilled training to work together, and only a permanent administration could afford fortifications and warships.

cards.front: Name the four types of stone tools showing increasing sophistication over time.
cards.answer: Pebble tools / Hand axes / Blades / Finely crafted arrowheads

cards.front: Why can classifying organisms by physical features alone be misleading?
cards.answer: Organisms may look similar due to convergent evolution but actually be distantly related.

cards.front: Why must patients complete the full course of antibiotics?
cards.answer: So all bacteria are killed, preventing resistant bacteria from surviving, reproducing and spreading their resistance allele.

title: Plot and Structure: A Four-Act Tragedy
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three consecutive reversals Miller uses to structure Act 3 of The Crucible.
cards.answer: Proctor confesses his adultery / Elizabeth lies to protect him / Mary Warren turns on Proctor

cards.front: Name the four stages of the classical tragic sequence that map onto the four acts of The Crucible.
cards.answer: Exposition and catalyst / Rising action and complication / Climax and reversal / Falling action and catastrophe

cards.front: Why does Elizabeth's lie in Act 3 destroy Proctor's defence rather than save him?
cards.answer: By lying to protect Proctor's honour, she unknowingly destroys the one piece of evidence that could have discredited Abigail and saved them both.

cards.front: Why did Miller change historical facts, like making Abigail an adult, when writing The Crucible?
cards.answer: He deliberately altered and compressed history so the pattern of accusation and confession would resonate with 1953 McCarthyite America as allegory.

cards.front: Name the eight energy stores the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Kinetic / Gravitational potential / Elastic potential / Chemical / Thermal / Magnetic / Electrostatic / Nuclear

cards.front: Name the four ways engineers reduce wasted energy given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Lubrication / Streamlining / Thermal insulation / LED lighting

cards.front: Why does braking distance increase dramatically at higher speeds?
cards.answer: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples the kinetic energy that must be removed to stop.

cards.front: Why does a 2000 W kettle boil water faster than a 1000 W kettle?
cards.answer: The higher power means it transfers energy at twice the rate, so the same energy is delivered in less time.

title: Placing a Track in Time: Rock, Pop, Broadway and Screen by Era
subject: music-aqa

cards.front: Name the two things Broadway songs did in the 1950s to carry the plot, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: An opening number that sets the scene / A song where the main character states what they want
items: An opening number that sets the scene
A song where the main character states what they want

cards.front: Why can grid-exact drumming not be used alone to date a track?
cards.answer: Drum machines appear from the early 1970s, and many tracks from the 1980s onwards still use a live drummer, so it must be weighed with other clues.

cards.front: What marks out modern film and gaming music from earlier orchestral scoring?
cards.answer: It blends full orchestra with synthesisers, electronic percussion, sound design and driving ostinato patterns under action scenes.

title: The Norman Conquest and William's Forest Laws
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four Anglo-Saxon institutions the lesson says William kept after the Conquest.
cards.answer: the king's peace / tithings / the hue and cry / the shire reeve and local courts
items: the shire reeve and local courts

cards.front: Name four activities the lesson says became crimes under Forest Law inside royal forest land.
cards.answer: hunting deer or wild boar / felling trees / gathering firewood / grazing pigs / owning an unclawed dog capable of catching game
items: owning an unclawed dog capable of catching game

cards.front: Why did William I introduce the Forest Laws and the Murdrum fine?
cards.answer: To protect the small Norman ruling minority and to enrich and project the king's power over land, hunting and movement.

cards.front: Why did the Murdrum fine give English communities an incentive to identify a killer?
cards.answer: Because if the killer of a Norman was not produced, the whole local community had to pay a ruinous collective fine.

cards.front: Why is Don John resentful and driven to villainy in Messina?
cards.answer: As an illegitimate brother he has no status, inheritance or prospects, so his villainy comes from resentment of legitimate social structures excluding him.

cards.front: Why does Leonato call Beatrice and Benedick's relationship a 'merry war'?
cards.answer: They never meet without a skirmish of wit, fighting each other with words the way soldiers fight with swords.

cards.front: Why does Don John's plot succeed despite him not being especially clever?
cards.answer: It succeeds because Claudio is gullible and the honour system makes men quick to believe the worst about women.

title: Kenilworth Castle: location and physical fabric
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four building phases of Kenilworth Castle given in the lesson, in order.
cards.answer: c.1125 Geoffrey de Clinton's motte-and-bailey / 12th century Norman stone keep (Caesar's Tower) / 1361-99 John of Gaunt's great hall / 1560s-70s Robert Dudley's Leicester's Building

cards.front: Why did King John's Great Mere make Kenilworth Castle so easy to defend?
cards.answer: It flooded the surrounding valley so the only land approach was from the north and east, cutting off other routes to attackers.

cards.front: Why can we now only understand the Great Mere through maps and archaeology rather than seeing it?
cards.answer: Because it was drained by Parliamentarians during the 1649-1650 slighting, removing the feature itself.

cards.front: How do the thick walls of Caesar's Tower and the huge windows of Leicester's Building each act as evidence of their purpose?
cards.answer: Thick Norman walls show a priority on military defence, while Leicester's large glazed windows show a priority on display over defence.

cards.front: Name the six characteristics used to compare types of secondary storage.
cards.answer: Capacity / Speed / Portability / Durability / Reliability / Cost

cards.front: Name the three main families of secondary storage.
cards.answer: Magnetic storage / Optical storage / Solid-state storage

cards.front: Why is magnetic tape too slow for everyday use even though it's cheap and holds huge amounts of data?
cards.answer: Tape access is sequential, so the drive must wind through it in order to reach a file rather than jumping straight to it.

cards.front: Why can solid-state storage still become unreliable even though it has no moving parts?
cards.answer: Each flash memory cell can only be rewritten a limited number of times before it wears out.

cards.front: Name the two things the star watches over 'for ever' in the octave of 'Bright Star'.
cards.answer: The tides performing their ritual washing / Fresh snow on the mountains and moors
items: The tides performing their ritual washing
Fresh snow on the mountains and moors

cards.front: Why does the speaker reject the star as a model for his own steadfastness, despite admiring it?
cards.answer: Because the star's constancy is solitary and cold, while he wants constancy combined with physical closeness to his beloved.

cards.front: How does Keats make the sestet's language perform the closeness it describes in 'Bright Star'?
cards.answer: The alliteration of 'tender-taken breath' and rhythm of 'soft fall and swell' mimic the rise and fall of breathing.

cards.front: Name the three end-of-life routes for waste materials given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Recycling / Incineration / Landfill

cards.front: Why might a nanoparticle drug-delivery treatment cause fewer side effects than a conventional drug?
cards.answer: The drug is attached to a nanoparticle designed to travel to a specific tissue, like a tumour, and release it there.

cards.front: Why does landfill waste the resource value of materials and also create extra pollution?
cards.answer: It buries materials instead of reusing them, and decomposing organic material in landfill produces methane.

cards.front: Why are platinum nanoparticles more effective as catalysts in catalytic converters than bulk platinum?
cards.answer: Nanoparticles have a far greater surface area than bulk platinum, making the catalyst more effective.

cards.front: Name the five types of bins German households sort rubbish into for Mülltrennung.
cards.answer: Papier (paper) / Plastik (plastic) / Glas (glass) / Biomüll (organic waste) / Restmüll (general waste)

cards.front: Name the four future predictions the lesson gives for if we do nothing about climate change.
cards.answer: Climate change will get worse / There will be more floods / Many animals will become extinct / The temperature will rise

cards.front: How can you work out the meaning of the German compound noun 'Umweltverschmutzung'?
cards.answer: Break it into its two parts: Umwelt (environment) and Verschmutzung (pollution/contamination).

cards.front: Why do many bottles in Germany have a Pfand?
cards.answer: A Pfand is a deposit that you get back when you return the bottle, encouraging recycling.

title: The 1559 religious settlement and the Church of England
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five levels of Church of England hierarchy set up by the 1559 settlement, from top to bottom.
cards.answer: Archbishops of Canterbury and York / 27 bishops / Archdeacons / Parish priests / Curates

cards.front: What three later challenges of Elizabeth's reign came from people who could not accept the 1559 settlement?
cards.answer: The Northern Rebellion / The papal bull of 1570 / The plots around Mary

cards.front: How did the wording of the communion service in the 1559 Act of Uniformity deliberately blur Catholic and Protestant belief?
cards.answer: It combined the 1549 wording (suggesting Christ was truly present) with the 1552 wording (a memorial in the heart), letting worshippers choose their reading.

cards.front: Why were ornate clerical vestments kept under the 1559 Act of Uniformity?
cards.answer: To make the Church look traditional and Catholic in appearance, keeping moderate Catholics inside the new Protestant Church.

title: Reconstructive Memory: Bartlett and the Reductionism–Holism Debate
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Why is a reductionist approach like the multi-store model useful for memory research?
cards.answer: It produces testable, controlled predictions about capacity and duration that can be measured precisely in a lab.

cards.front: Why is a holistic explanation like Bartlett's theory harder to test scientifically than a reductionist one?
cards.answer: Holistic explanations resist being broken into precisely measurable variables, making cause and effect hard to establish.

title: Catholic Social Teaching: Loving Our Neighbour
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four core principles of Catholic Social Teaching given as the Key Fact in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dignity of the human person / The common good / Preferential option for the poor / Solidarity

cards.front: Name the three global Catholic agencies named in the lesson that put Catholic Social Teaching into action.
cards.answer: CAFOD / Trocaire / Missio

cards.front: Why did the parable of the Good Samaritan matter for how Jesus defined 'neighbour'?
cards.answer: It made clear that 'neighbour' crosses ethnic, religious and social boundaries, not just people close to you.

cards.front: How did Gaudium et Spes change the Church's understanding of its role in the world?
cards.answer: It rejected the idea the Church was only sacramental and otherworldly, teaching it is within the world, sharing humanity's struggles and joys.

cards.front: Name the five zones, in order from street to back, that a visitor passed through in a wealthy Roman domus.
cards.answer: Fauces (entrance passage) / Atrium (public reception hall) / Tablinum (owner's office) / Triclinium (dining room) / Peristyle (private garden)

cards.front: What three types of wealth display did visitors see while waiting in the atrium?
cards.answer: Bronze furniture / Fine floor mosaics / Family portraits (imagines)

cards.front: Why was the tablinum positioned between the atrium and the peristyle?
cards.answer: So the owner could be seen by visitors in the atrium while remaining in a position of authority.

cards.front: How did Second Style Pompeian wall paintings make rooms seem bigger?
cards.answer: They used painted architectural illusions, or trompe l'oeil, to make walls appear to open onto colonnades and landscapes.

cards.front: Name the four tactics the lesson gives for how Chinese forces neutralised US firepower in Korea.
cards.answer: Night-time attacks to negate air power / Mass infantry infiltration to find UN flanks / Bugles and horns instead of radios / Operating without long supply lines
items: Night-time attacks to negate air power
Mass infantry infiltration to find UN flanks
Bugles and horns instead of radios

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says MacArthur wanted to do that went beyond limited war.
cards.answer: Bomb China / Blockade China's coast / Deploy the Nationalist Chinese army from Taiwan
items: Deploy the Nationalist Chinese army from Taiwan

cards.front: Why did Mao decide to intervene in the Korean War despite Politburo opposition?
cards.answer: Hostile forces on the Yalu threatened Chinese industry and the revolution, and letting a fellow communist state fall would damage Beijing's prestige and Sino-Soviet relations.

cards.front: Why did Truman's sacking of MacArthur matter for civil-military relations?
cards.answer: It upheld the principle that elected civilian government controls the military, even at the cost of Truman's approval rating falling to 22 percent.

cards.front: Name the three people Claudio's marriage negotiation for Hero passes through, in order.
cards.answer: Claudio / Don Pedro / Leonato

cards.front: Name the three dark elements the lesson says push against the comedy genre's boundaries in Much Ado.
cards.answer: Hero's public shaming / Leonato's death wish for his daughter / Beatrice's cry of 'Kill Claudio'
items: Leonato's death wish for his daughter

cards.front: Why does Claudio shame Hero publicly at the altar instead of confronting her privately?
cards.answer: Because his love was shallow and public, based on appearance, and chastity determined family honour, so he humiliates her before the community to protect reputation.

cards.front: How does using boy actors for female roles add irony to Much Ado's treatment of gender?
cards.answer: A boy actor performs femininity while characters debate what makes a 'true' woman, blurring masculine and feminine boundaries and questioning enforced gender roles.

title: Puja, Pilgrimage and Hindu Rites of Passage
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four things a worshipper does during daily puja at the home shrine.
cards.answer: Wake the deity / Bathe and dress the image / Offer food, flowers, incense and light / Recite prayers or mantras
items: Offer food, flowers, incense and light

cards.front: Name the four forms bhakti practice can take, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Singing devotional hymns (bhajan) / Chanting God's name (kirtan) / Performing puja with heartfelt emotion / Reading or hearing sacred stories (katha)

cards.front: Why is the fire considered important during a Hindu wedding ceremony?
cards.answer: The couple walk round it seven times making seven vows, and the fire acts as the divine witness to the marriage.

cards.front: How does the mundan ceremony prepare a Hindu child for life ahead?
cards.answer: Shaving the child's first hair removes impurities carried from the previous life, purifying the child.

cards.front: Name the three stages a genre cycle moves through, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: First wave establishes the conventions / Second wave refines or exaggerates them / Third wave subverts or satirises them
items: Second wave refines or exaggerates them
Third wave subverts or satirises them

cards.front: Name the five dominant forms the lesson says the horror genre has cycled between.
cards.answer: Gothic monster film / Supernatural thriller / Slasher film / Psychological horror / Social-commentary horror

cards.front: How does camera angle shape a spectator's sense of a character's power?
cards.answer: A low-angle shot looking up grants a character power, while a high-angle shot looking down diminishes them.

cards.front: Why can a horror film and a western feel completely different even with the same narrative structure?
cards.answer: Because their genre iconography, conventions and spectator contracts differ, even though narrative structure can be identical.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare put Shylock's 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech in prose rather than verse?
cards.answer: Prose strips away poetic formality, showing Shylock speaking from raw, unfiltered emotion rather than calculated rhetoric.

cards.front: Why did Jessica's elopement intensify Shylock's desire for revenge against Antonio?
cards.answer: The Christians took his dignity, his daughter and his wife's ring, leaving the bond as his only remaining source of power.

cards.front: How does the sequencing of Solanio's mockery before Shylock's own speech affect the audience?
cards.answer: It lets the audience absorb the Christian stereotype first, then Shylock's speech demolishes it, forcing them to confront their assumptions.

cards.front: Name the three things Shylock is stripped of by the end of the trial scene, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: His wealth / His forced conversion to Christianity / His identity and community

cards.front: The lesson gives four ways Napoleon appears surrounded by ceremony when he rarely appears in public — what are they?
cards.answer: Surrounded by dogs / Announced with a ceremonial cockerel crow / Eats from Jones's Crown Derby china / Takes meals alone with dogs waiting on him
items: Announced with a ceremonial cockerel crow
Eats from Jones's Crown Derby china
Takes meals alone with dogs waiting on him

cards.front: How does Squealer use Napoleon's cult of personality to explain good events on the farm?
cards.answer: Squealer credits every success, like harvests or eggs laid, personally to 'the leadership of Comrade Napoleon'.

cards.front: Why does Squealer deny that Animalism ever forbade trading with humans?
cards.answer: He insists no such rule existed and claims it was a lie spread by Snowball, so Napoleon's betrayal seems justified.

cards.front: Name the three characters who each witness part of Hyde's story before the truth is revealed.
cards.answer: Utterson investigates / Enfield witnesses Hyde's violence / Lanyon sees the transformation and dies from shock
items: Lanyon sees the transformation and dies from shock

cards.front: What four features does Gothic fiction combine, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: doubles / secrets / transgression / return of the repressed

cards.front: Why does the repressed self erupt so violently in Jekyll and Hyde?
cards.answer: The more rigidly society enforces moral perfection, the more violently the repressed self erupts.

cards.front: Why does Jekyll's potion fail to make him a better person?
cards.answer: The potion does not purify Jekyll; instead it unleashes his worst impulses without restraint.

title: The Nature of God and Human Life in Sikhism
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three key contrasts the lesson gives between Sikh mukti and Christian afterlife belief.
cards.answer: Sikh soul merges with God, losing identity / Christian salvation keeps personal identity with God / Christianity teaches bodily resurrection through faith in Jesus
items: Sikh soul merges with God, losing identity
Christian salvation keeps personal identity with God
Christianity teaches bodily resurrection through faith in Jesus

cards.front: Why does the belief that God's light (Jot) is in every being lead Sikhs to reject caste discrimination?
cards.answer: If every person carries the divine light, all humans have inherent worth and dignity, so discrimination contradicts equality before the one Creator.

cards.front: Why is human birth considered a precious opportunity in Sikhism?
cards.answer: Only humans have the unique capacity to reflect on the divine and choose the path of liberation, ending the cycle of rebirth.

title: Changing attitudes to authority: the permissive society
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five legal reforms passed under Roy Jenkins between 1965 and 1967 during the 'permissive moment'.
cards.answer: Decriminalised homosexuality / Abolished the death penalty / Relaxed divorce law / Legalised abortion / Ended theatre censorship

cards.front: Why was the case of Derek Bentley (hanged 1953) controversial and used in the death penalty debate?
cards.answer: He was hanged despite doubts about his responsibility, raising fears about executing people unjustly.

cards.front: How did the 1968 student protests differ from what the Profumo Affair had exposed about the establishment?
cards.answer: The Profumo Affair showed the ruling class was not morally superior, while 1968 protests challenged whether it was politically legitimate.

cards.front: Why does the lesson describe the 'permissive society' as contradictory when it comes to drugs?
cards.answer: Laws liberalised private behaviour like sex and divorce, but drug law became more restrictive on public safety grounds.

title: Act 3: The Raid, Death & the Ending
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: Why does Stanhope become tender towards Raleigh in the play's final scene, after being furious with him?
cards.answer: His anger was grief and self-protection, not indifference, and Raleigh's death lets his buried love and grief for Osborne surface.

cards.front: How does the play's ending refuse to give the audience catharsis?
cards.answer: It ends with no final speech or reflection, just the dugout being destroyed, leaving the audience with loss and no meaning.

title: Exam technique and synthesis: sources, interpretations and judgements
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three things credited in a 12-mark 'evaluate an interpretation' answer.
cards.answer: Developed points supporting the interpretation with specific evidence / Developed points that challenge or qualify it with specific evidence / A clear overall judgement on which view is more convincing and why
items: Developed points supporting the interpretation with specific evidence
Developed points that challenge or qualify it with specific evidence
A clear overall judgement on which view is more convincing and why

cards.front: What are the three parts of the structure for a 16-mark period essay?
cards.answer: Brief introduction signalling the overall argument / Main paragraphs each organised around one factor with embedded evidence / Conclusion that directly answers the question with a justified judgement
items: Brief introduction signalling the overall argument
Main paragraphs each organised around one factor with embedded evidence
Conclusion that directly answers the question with a justified judgement

cards.front: Why does the worked example say Source A is limited in usefulness for understanding the rebels' own motivations?
cards.answer: It was written by a monk from the Church establishment, which suffered during the revolt, giving the author strong reason to portray rebels negatively.

cards.front: Why does covering two or three factors adequately fail to reach the top band in a period essay?
cards.answer: The top band requires arguing why one factor was more significant than the others, not simply covering everything equally.

cards.front: What are the steps to measure the density of a regular solid like a metal block?
cards.answer: Measure mass using a balance / Measure length, width and height with a ruler or calipers / Calculate volume using V = l × w × h / Calculate density using ρ = m/V
items: Measure length, width and height with a ruler or calipers
Calculate volume using V = l × w × h

cards.front: What are the steps to measure the density of a liquid?
cards.answer: Place empty measuring cylinder on balance and zero it / Pour in a known volume of liquid / Record the mass of the liquid / Calculate density using ρ = m/V
items: Place empty measuring cylinder on balance and zero it
Pour in a known volume of liquid
Record the mass of the liquid

cards.front: Why does ice float on liquid water?
cards.answer: When water freezes its particles form a crystalline structure with gaps, making ice about 9% less dense than liquid water.

cards.front: Why should each dimension of a regular solid be measured in at least two places and averaged?
cards.answer: Taking an average of multiple measurements reduces the effect of irregularities in the solid's shape.

cards.front: Name the four stages of Alem's character arc in Refugee Boy.
cards.answer: Innocence (the hotel with his father) / Confusion and grief (the abandonment) / Gradual adaptation (school, the Fitzgeralds) / Quiet resilience (the tribunal)

cards.front: Name what each of the six characters or systems represents in Refugee Boy.
cards.answer: Mr Kelo represents impossible choices forced on parents by conflict / The Fitzgeralds represent compassion / Mustapha represents solidarity / Sweeney represents prejudice / Ruth represents the family that opens its door / The tribunal represents systemic power
items: Mr Kelo represents impossible choices forced on parents by conflict
Ruth represents the family that opens its door

cards.front: Why is Mr Kelo described as torn between two roles throughout the play?
cards.answer: He is torn between his role as a father wanting to be with Alem and his duty as protector knowing Alem is safer alone in England.

cards.front: Why does Ruth worry about her mother growing too attached to Alem?
cards.answer: Because the Fitzgeralds previously fostered a boy called Themba who died, showing fostering is a risk the whole family carries.

cards.front: Name the four functional properties of proteins identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Denaturation / Coagulation / Gluten formation / Foam formation

cards.front: Name the three functional properties of carbohydrates identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Gelatinisation / Dextrinisation / Caramelisation

cards.front: Why does kneading bread dough for longer make the gluten network stronger?
cards.answer: Kneading works the glutenin and gliadin proteins together, developing a stronger, more elastic gluten network as you knead more.

cards.front: Why does over-whisking egg whites cause the foam to collapse?
cards.answer: Continued whisking eventually breaks the protein film around the air bubbles, so the foam collapses and turns grainy and watery.

title: The Amicable Grant and the Limits of Wolsey's Power
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three consequences the lesson gives for the collapse of the Amicable Grant.
cards.answer: Planned invasion of France abandoned / Wolsey's reputation permanently dented / Principle of parliamentary consent to taxation reasserted
items: Principle of parliamentary consent to taxation reasserted

cards.front: Who did the leadership of the East Anglian revolt against the Amicable Grant come from, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Yeomen / Clothiers / Small employers / Supporting clergy

cards.front: Why did the Dukes of Norfolk and Suffolk negotiate with the East Anglian rebels instead of fighting them?
cards.answer: They recognised it was a tax strike, not a feudal rebellion against the king, so negotiation was more appropriate than battle.

cards.front: Why did taxpayers in Kent refuse to pay the Amicable Grant when commissioners arrived?
cards.answer: They cited Magna Carta and refused to pay without parliamentary consent.

cards.front: Name the cultural features that made Berlin one of Europe's most vibrant cities in the mid-1920s.
cards.answer: Expressionist cinema / Bauhaus design movement / Cabaret / Experimental theatre / Daring visual art

cards.front: Why did rural Germany become fertile ground for radical parties by the late 1920s?
cards.answer: Farmers suffered falling agricultural prices, squeezed between rising costs and falling incomes, so they turned away from mainstream parties.

cards.front: Why is Stresemann's foreign policy described as pragmatic rather than ideological?
cards.answer: He signed the Treaty of Berlin with the Soviet Union in 1926 alongside Locarno, balancing eastern and western relations to suit German interests.

title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three ways to increase the speed of an electric motor.
cards.answer: Increase the current / Use a stronger magnet / Add more turns to the coil
items: Add more turns to the coil

cards.front: Name the four magnetic materials given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Iron / Steel / Cobalt / Nickel

cards.front: Why is steel used to make permanent magnets rather than soft iron?
cards.answer: Soft iron loses its magnetism as soon as it leaves a magnetic field, but steel keeps it.

cards.front: Why does a d.c. motor coil keep spinning continuously instead of stopping after half a turn?
cards.answer: The split-ring commutator reverses the current direction every half turn, keeping the force acting the right way.

cards.front: Why can identical twins, who share the same genotype, have different phenotypes?
cards.answer: Because phenotype is influenced by the environment, such as diet or health conditions, not just genotype.

cards.front: Why can polydactyly appear in every generation, unlike cystic fibrosis?
cards.answer: Because polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele, so only one copy is needed to show the condition, so it cannot be hidden by carriers.

cards.front: In a cross between an affected heterozygous parent (Dd) and an unaffected parent (dd) for polydactyly, what are the offspring outcomes?
cards.answer: Dd genotype / dd genotype / 1:1 ratio / 50% chance per child

cards.front: Why is the fog symbolic when Dunsey steals Silas's gold?
cards.answer: It symbolises Dunsey's moral blindness, as he cannot see beyond his own immediate needs.

cards.front: How does the theft of the gold help Silas rejoin the community?
cards.answer: His desperate visit to the Rainbow Inn shows vulnerability, so villagers start visiting and bringing him gifts of food.

cards.front: Why are the villagers at the Rainbow Inn briefly terrified when Silas bursts in?
cards.answer: They have been telling ghost stories and mistake wild-eyed, distressed Silas for an apparition.

cards.front: The lesson gives four points contrasting the gold with Eppie — what are they?
cards.answer: Gold is inert, Eppie is alive / Gold is private, Eppie is public / Gold is circular, Eppie constantly grows / Gold kept Silas isolated, Eppie draws him into community
items: Gold is inert, Eppie is alive
Gold is private, Eppie is public
Gold is circular, Eppie constantly grows
Gold kept Silas isolated, Eppie draws him into community

cards.front: Name the four main areas the Treaty of Versailles' terms are grouped into.
cards.answer: Territorial / Military / Financial / League of Nations

cards.front: Name the four other Paris peace treaties (besides Versailles) mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Treaty of Saint-Germain / Treaty of Trianon / Treaty of Sèvres / Treaty of Lausanne

cards.front: Why did Italian nationalists call the Paris settlement a 'mutilated victory'?
cards.answer: Italy was denied Fiume and colonial territories in Africa promised by the 1915 Treaty of London, despite receiving South Tyrol and Trieste.

cards.front: Why did General Ferdinand Foch call the Versailles settlement 'an armistice for twenty years'?
cards.answer: He believed the peace was too lenient to stop Germany seeking revenge, so war would return within twenty years.

title: Scripture, Sacred Art and Catholic Symbolism
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three different Christian views on how to interpret the 'days' of Genesis 1.
cards.answer: Literalists (young-earth creationists) — six literal 24-hour days / Day-age theorists — days as long epochs of time / Theistic evolution — God set natural processes in motion
items: Day-age theorists — days as long epochs of time
Theistic evolution — God set natural processes in motion

cards.front: What three truths do Catholic scholars say the Genesis creation accounts communicate, regardless of how the universe actually came into being?
cards.answer: Who God is (Creator, good, personal) / Who humanity is (made in God's image) / What went wrong (the Fall, Original Sin)
items: Who humanity is (made in God's image)
What went wrong (the Fall, Original Sin)

cards.front: Why is the gap between God's and Adam's fingertips in Michelangelo's Creation of Adam theologically significant?
cards.answer: It represents the space between the divine and the human, which is bridged by God's own initiative to give life.

cards.front: How does natural revelation allow humans to gain knowledge of God, according to Catholic teaching?
cards.answer: Through reason and observing creation, since the world itself points to its Creator.

cards.front: Name the three types of organism the lesson gives as examples of asexual reproduction.
cards.answer: Plants / Bacteria / Some animals (e.g. starfish)

cards.front: Name the three benefits the lesson gives of understanding the human genome.
cards.answer: Identify genes linked to diseases / Develop personalised medicines / Trace human migration patterns and evolutionary relationships
items: Trace human migration patterns and evolutionary relationships

cards.front: Why does meiosis produce gametes that are genetically different from each other?
cards.answer: Meiosis involves two divisions that shuffle genetic material, creating four haploid cells each with a different mix of chromosomes.

cards.front: Why does asexual reproduction produce offspring that are clones of the parent?
cards.answer: It involves only one parent with no fusion of gametes, and occurs through mitosis, which copies DNA exactly.

title: The Celestial Sphere and Coordinate Systems
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Why is an object below the horizon at altitude −5° not visible?
cards.answer: Altitude below 0° means the object is below the observer's horizon, so it cannot be seen.

cards.front: Why is a star best placed for observation when it transits the meridian?
cards.answer: At transit the star is at its highest altitude, so light passes through the least amount of atmosphere.

cards.front: Why do constellations have a 'season' when they are best placed at night?
cards.answer: Sidereal time gains four minutes per day on solar time, so objects transit earlier each night and the whole RA range cycles through transit over a year.

cards.front: Name the four things the 1945 Labour government created as the welfare state.
cards.answer: NHS / National insurance / Council housing / Free secondary education

cards.front: What three conventions of a 'well-made play' does An Inspector Calls follow?
cards.answer: Takes place in a single room / Happens on a single evening / Builds towards a climactic revelation
items: Takes place in a single room

cards.front: Why did Priestley choose to set the play two years before the First World War?
cards.answer: So the 1945 audience, who had lived through WWII, would recognise the dramatic irony in characters' confident predictions about the future.

cards.front: How does the Inspector seem to exist outside normal time in the play?
cards.answer: He knows about events before they happen and arrives before Eva Smith has actually died.

title: Case Study: Jewish East End and the Aliens Act, c1880–1914
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three things did the East End offer Jewish migrants that made them settle there?
cards.answer: Cheap lodging in Whitechapel, Spitalfields and Stepney / A garment trade needing cheap labour / An existing Anglo-Jewish community with synagogues and welfare societies
items: Cheap lodging in Whitechapel, Spitalfields and Stepney
A garment trade needing cheap labour
An existing Anglo-Jewish community with synagogues and welfare societies

cards.front: Name the three grounds on which the 1905 Aliens Act let officers refuse entry to migrants.
cards.answer: Could not support themselves / Judged to be of bad character / Had a criminal record
items: Judged to be of bad character

cards.front: Why does the lesson argue the 1905 Aliens Act was not a general immigration control?
cards.answer: It exempted wealthy migrants and, in principle, political refugees, showing it specifically targeted poor Eastern European Jewish migrants.

cards.front: Why did Jewish migrants form trade unions like the Hebrew Cabinet Makers' Association?
cards.answer: To organise against the sweated trades' 12-hour days and low piece-rate wages, demanding limits on hours and minimum rates.

cards.front: What are the four class groupings sociologists commonly identify in the UK?
cards.answer: Upper class / Middle class / Working class / Underclass

cards.front: Why did Marx argue the proletariat are exploited by the bourgeoisie?
cards.answer: Because the value workers create through their labour is greater than the wages they receive, and the bourgeoisie keep this surplus value as profit.

cards.front: Why do functionalists like Davis and Moore see class differences as necessary rather than a problem?
cards.answer: Because they reflect differential rewards attached to roles of varying functional importance, which helps society operate efficiently.

title: Schmitt Inverters and Interfacing Analogue to Digital
subject: electronics-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three circuit methods described for converting an analogue signal into a digital logic signal.
cards.answer: Transistor switch / Op-amp comparator / Schmitt inverter

cards.front: What are the three common errors to avoid when reading Schmitt trigger threshold graphs?
cards.answer: Confusing which threshold triggers which transition / Missing the ruler and estimating by eye / Swapping the hysteresis direction
items: Confusing which threshold triggers which transition
Missing the ruler and estimating by eye

cards.front: Why does a standard logic inverter's output flicker rapidly when noise is present near its switching voltage?
cards.answer: It has only one fixed threshold, so any noise crossing that single level repeatedly flips the output HIGH and LOW.

cards.front: Why do transistor switch and comparator interfaces need extra components to match the Schmitt inverter's noise immunity?
cards.answer: They only have a single threshold, so filtering must be added separately, whereas hysteresis gives the Schmitt inverter noise immunity with no extra parts.

title: Sources, Style and the Whole-Theme Answer
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six prescribed pictures set for this theme.
cards.answer: Fresco of meal preparation with carcass and silver vessel / Decorated bronze food warmer / Garum jar from Scaurus's workshop / Fresco of a fruit bowl from Julia Felix's estate / Banquet scene from the House of the Triclinium / Fresco of a politician distributing bread
items: Fresco of meal preparation with carcass and silver vessel
Fresco of a fruit bowl from Julia Felix's estate
Banquet scene from the House of the Triclinium
Fresco of a politician distributing bread

cards.front: Name the three big ideas an extended evaluative response on this theme should connect back to.
cards.answer: Food eaten in wealthy and poorer households / The importance of hospitality / Food as a display of wealth and power
items: Food eaten in wealthy and poorer households
Food as a display of wealth and power

cards.front: How does Petronius's chiasmus describing Trimalchio's gaming pieces reinforce his wealth?
cards.answer: The crossed word order pairs each colour with its precious replacement, showing Trimalchio turns an ordinary game into a display of wealth.

cards.front: How does Martial's line placing mushrooms and pig-fungus together create its effect?
cards.answer: Placing the two foods side by side in the same line makes the gap in status felt in the grammar itself, not just the meaning.

cards.front: Name the four key endocrine glands (or gland pairs) the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Pituitary gland / Thyroid gland / Adrenal glands / Pancreas / Ovaries and testes

cards.front: How does an electrical impulse cross the gap at a synapse?
cards.answer: Neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synaptic cleft, diffuse across, and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new impulse.

cards.front: Why does the fight or flight response involve both the nervous and endocrine systems?
cards.answer: It involves nerve impulses for fast signalling and adrenaline released from the adrenal glands for a widespread, sustained response.

cards.front: Why must you keep things like the ruler, catcher and hand position constant in the reaction time test?
cards.answer: So the only thing affecting reaction time is the variable being tested, reducing random error and making results reliable.

cards.front: What three types of work make up the 'triple shift' that feminist sociologists say women carry out?
cards.answer: Paid work / Domestic labour / Emotional management of family relationships

cards.front: According to Marxist feminists, what four unpaid tasks does women's domestic labour typically involve?
cards.answer: Cooking / Cleaning / Child rearing / Caring for sick and elderly family members
items: Caring for sick and elderly family members

cards.front: Why did Parsons see segregated conjugal roles as functionally efficient for modern industrial society?
cards.answer: Paid employment was geographically mobile, so one adult needed to be free to move while the other maintained the home.

cards.front: How does the principle of stratified diffusion explain the spread of the symmetrical family, according to Willmott and Young?
cards.answer: Lifestyle changes begin among middle-class families and gradually spread down to working-class families.

title: The Social Construction of Crime and Deviance
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three dimensions of the relativity of deviance given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Across time (historical variation) / Across place (cultural variation) / Across situation (situational variation)

cards.front: How does the interactionist perspective explain why an act becomes labelled as deviant?
cards.answer: No act is inherently deviant; it becomes so only when a label is successfully applied by someone with the power to make it stick.

cards.front: Why did Durkheim argue that some level of crime is normal and functional in society?
cards.answer: Punishing crime clarifies the boundaries of acceptable behaviour and reaffirms shared values, so a moderate amount is beneficial.

cards.front: Why can killing another person be treated as murder in one context but heroic or legal in another?
cards.answer: Situational variation means context, such as warfare or self-defence, shapes whether the same act is considered deviant or criminal.

cards.front: What three predictions does Birling confidently make in Act 1 that history proves wrong?
cards.answer: The Titanic is unsinkable / There will be no war / The future holds nothing but prosperity
items: The future holds nothing but prosperity

cards.front: Name the three things Britain lacked in 1912 that left workers unprotected if they lost their job.
cards.answer: No welfare state / No NHS / No unemployment benefit

cards.front: How does the lighting change in the opening stage directions support Priestley's message?
cards.answer: The lighting shifts from pink and intimate to brighter and harder as the Inspector arrives, symbolising the exposure of the family's hidden secrets.

cards.front: How does the stage direction describing the Birlings' dining room reveal Priestley's criticism of the upper classes?
cards.answer: Details like good solid furniture, champagne and dessert plates show the family living in a comfortable bubble that deliberately shuts out others' suffering.

title: Stalin's terror: purges, show trials and gulag
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What four methods did the NKVD use to extract confessions during the Great Terror?
cards.answer: Prolonged interrogation / Physical abuse / Sleep deprivation / Threats against family members

cards.front: Name four groups of people targeted by the mass operations of the Terror, beyond party elites.
